Chapter 1: What Is Networking? — The Big Picture

Before diving into packets, protocols, and port numbers, let's understand why networking matters for anyone who runs production systems. We'll anchor every concept to your real work — building platforms, debugging incidents, and keeping services running — using our anihpj/jobpost Django application as the concrete example throughout.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2 hours 📖 Concepts 🎯 Foundation

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why networking is non-negotiable for infrastructure professionals — every outage has a network dimension
  • ✅ The OSI Model — networking's periodic table, all 7 layers explained with anihpj examples
  • ✅ Encapsulation — how data travels through the network stack, layer by layer
  • ✅ The TCP/IP Model — what we actually use in the real world (and why OSI is just for teaching)
  • ✅ Your networking toolchain — the essential tools mapped to each layer, with exact commands
🌐 Networking Relevance
OSI / TCP/IP Foundation CORE Infrastructure Fundamentals ESSENTIAL
💡 Understanding "Why" Before "How"

This chapter isn't about configuring routers or writing iptables rules — it's about understanding how data moves. Every networking problem you'll encounter in production (timeouts, connection refused, DNS failures, TLS errors) can be traced to a specific layer. Key concepts to internalize:

  • Encapsulation — Data gets wrapped in headers at each layer. When debugging with tcpdump, you're looking at these layers simultaneously. Knowing which header belongs to which layer is your superpower.
  • The OSI Model — It's a teaching tool, but EVERY network engineer thinks in layers. "Is it a Layer 3 problem or a Layer 4 problem?" is a question you'll ask a hundred times.
  • Layered Debugging — Start at the bottom and work up. Layer 1 (is the cable plugged in?) → Layer 7 (is the app returning 200?). This systematic approach catches issues that intuition misses.

1.1 Why Networking Matters for Infrastructure Professionals

Every production outage has a network dimension. The database is slow — is it the network? The deploy failed — did the container registry become unreachable? Users can't log in — is the load balancer healthy? As someone who runs production systems, networking is not optional — it's the foundation everything else runs on.

What "The Network" Actually Means

When someone says "it's a network issue," they're usually wrong — but the phrase itself reveals a fundamental truth: everything relies on the network. Your Django application doesn't exist in isolation. It talks to PostgreSQL. Users talk to it through load balancers. Monitoring scrapes metrics from it. CI/CD deploys new versions to it. ALL of these interactions happen over the network. When ANY of them breaks, the symptom is the same: "the site is down."

Here's a concrete example from our anihpj/jobpost application. When a user in Lagos searches for "DevOps jobs on Victoria Island," here's the complete network path the request travels:

A Single User Request — The Full Network Journey
  👤 USER in Lagos, Nigeria
    │  Types: https://jobpost.anihpj.com/api/jobs/?location=Victoria+Island
    │
    ▼  (1) DNS Resolution
  🌐 Cloudflare DNS (1.1.1.1) → jobpost.anihpj.com → CNAME → k8s-alb-123.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com → A → 34.120.45.67
    │
    ▼  (2) TCP + TLS to Load Balancer
  🔒 TCP handshake (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK) + TLS 1.3 handshake → encrypted tunnel established to 34.120.45.67:443
    │
    ▼  (3) AWS ALB → K8s NodePort
  ☁️ ALB forwards to a healthy K8s worker node on port 30080 (NodePort)
    │
    ▼  (4) iptables DNAT on K8s Node
  🔀 iptables rule: 192.168.1.10:30080 → ClusterIP 10.96.100.50:8000
    │
    ▼  (5) kube-proxy → Backend Pod
  🔀 Random backend selection → Pod 10.244.1.5:8000 (gunicorn)
    │
    ▼  (6) Django Processes Request
  🐍 jobpost/views.py → JobPost.objects.filter(location="Victoria Island") → PostgreSQL query
    │
    ▼  (7) Django → PostgreSQL (over TCP)
  🗄️ TCP connection from 10.244.1.5:54321 → postgres-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:5432
    │  SELECT * FROM jobpost_jobpost WHERE location LIKE '%Victoria Island%';
    ▼
  📤 Response flows back: PostgreSQL → Django → gunicorn → kube-proxy → NodePort → ALB → TLS → User
    │
  ⏱️ Total time budget: ~200ms (DNS 5ms + TCP 10ms + TLS 50ms + network 30ms + app 100ms + DB 5ms)

  THAT is "the network." 7 distinct hops. 4 protocols. 3 layers of NAT. 2 encryption handshakes.
  When ANY one of these breaks, the user sees "the site is down."

This is why you need to understand networking. The user doesn't care which hop failed. They just know the jobs page isn't loading. Your job is to figure out WHICH of these 7 hops broke, WHY it broke, and HOW to fix it — all while the incident clock is ticking and your manager is asking for an ETA.

📖 The Infrastructure Networking Mindset

Observe → Hypothesize → Verify. Don't guess. Don't assume. Use tools to observe what's happening at each layer, form a hypothesis about the root cause, then verify with concrete evidence. This scientific method separates junior engineers who restart things randomly from senior engineers who fix problems permanently.

Real Incident: "Users Can't Reach jobpost.anihpj.com"

It's 2 AM. You get paged: "The job posting site is down. Users see a blank page." Where do you even start? Here's what you'll actually observe depending on the root cause:

😰 Symptoms You'll See — and What They Actually Mean
  • 🔴 ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED → The server IS reachable but nothing is listening on that port. The gunicorn process crashed.
  • 🔴 ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT → Packets are being dropped somewhere. Firewall? Security Group? Network partition?
  • 🔴 502 Bad Gateway → The load balancer / ingress can't reach the backend pod. Pod crashed? Wrong port?
  • 🔴 ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED → DNS can't resolve. CoreDNS down? Route53 record deleted? TTL expired to old IP?
  • 🔴 ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR → TLS certificate expired at midnight. cert-manager didn't renew in time.
⚠️ GOTCHA: "ping works but curl doesn't" does NOT mean the network is fine!

ICMP (ping) is often allowed by firewalls while TCP ports are blocked. A successful ping only proves Layer 3 reachability — it tells you NOTHING about whether port 8000 is open or whether the application is healthy. Always test at Layer 4 (nc -zv) and Layer 7 (curl) before concluding "the network is fine."

The Layered Observability Mindset — Your Debugging Compass
  🔍 NETWORKING = LAYERED OBSERVABILITY

  Layer 7: "Is the app responding?" — curl, HTTP status codes
  Layer 4: "Is the port open?"      — nc -zv, ss -tlnp, telnet
  Layer 3: "Can I reach it?"        — ping, traceroute, ip route
  Layer 2: "Is ARP resolving?"      — ip neigh show, arping
  Layer 1: "Is the link up?"        — ip link show, ethtool

  ⚡ GOLDEN RULE: START AT THE BOTTOM AND WORK UP
  ⚡ SECOND RULE: THE PACKETS DON'T LIE. Trust tcpdump.
Why Networking Is Non-Negotiable for SRE & Platform Engineers

As an SRE/Platform Engineer, you OWN the infrastructure layer. When the database is slow, the app team blames the network. When the deploy fails, CI/CD blames the network. When customers can't log in, support blames the network. Your job: prove it's NOT the network (or fix it if it is).

This guide teaches you to:

  • Diagnose ANY network issue in under 5 minutes using a systematic layered approach
  • Read tcpdump output as naturally as application logs
  • Design platform networks that survive AZ/region failures
  • Build observability that alerts you BEFORE users complain
  • Automate network configuration so you never SSH to fix things

Remember: In an incident war room, the person who can read packets and trace the full request path is the most valuable person in the room. Be that person.

1.2 The OSI Model — Networking's Periodic Table

The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Model is a 7-layer framework that standardizes how data moves through a network. Think of it as networking's periodic table — it organizes everything into layers, each with a specific job. But unlike the periodic table (which describes physical reality), the OSI model is a teaching framework — the actual internet uses a simpler 4-layer model called TCP/IP.

Why Should You Care About Layers?

Because every networking problem lives at a specific layer — and the fix is different for each one. When you can say "This is a Layer 4 problem" instead of "the network is broken," you've already eliminated 80% of possible causes. Here's what each layer actually does, what can go wrong, and what you'd do about it:

📖 Mnemonic: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away"

Physical → Data Link → Network → Transport → Session → Presentation → Application. Every network engineer knows this. It's corny, but it sticks — and in an interview, knowing it instantly shows you've studied networking properly.

⚠️ GOTCHA: OSI Is a Teaching Tool — The INTERNET Runs on TCP/IP

The TCP/IP model has 4 layers. OSI has 7. The internet was built on TCP/IP, not OSI. OSI was designed by an ISO committee in the 1970s before anyone had built a working global network. TCP/IP was built by engineers at DARPA who needed something that actually worked. By the time OSI was finalized in 1984, TCP/IP was already running ARPANET (the precursor to the internet).

The practical takeaway: Use OSI for teaching and thinking. Use TCP/IP for building and debugging. When troubleshooting, "Is it a Layer 3 or Layer 4 problem?" is the single most useful question you can ask.

LYRNAMEFUNCTIONPROTOCOLSANIH PJ EXAMPLEFAILURE SYMPTOMDEBUG TOOL
7ApplicationUser-facing services & APIsHTTP, DNS, SSHjobpost API returns JSON at /api/jobs/404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Errorcurl, DevTools
6PresentationEncryption & data formattingTLS, SSL, JPEGHTTPS cert on nginx IngressERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR, certificate expiredopenssl s_client
5SessionConnection managementNetBIOS, RPCDjango session cookiesSession timeout, users logged out unexpectedlyBrowser cookie inspector
4TransportReliable delivery, portsTCP, UDPgunicorn on port 8000 (TCP)Connection refused, connection timeoutss -tlnp, nc -zv

What Each Layer Sees: Protocol Data Units (PDUs)

Data has a different name at each layer. Using the right term shows you understand networking at a fundamental level — interviewers notice this.

LAYERDATA UNIT NAMEWHAT IT CONTAINSHEADER SIZEWHO ADDS IT
L7Data / MessageRaw app data: HTTP request, JSON, SQLVariesYour code (Django, gunicorn)
L4Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP)L7 data + TCP/UDP header (ports, seq#, flags)20-60 bytesOS kernel (TCP/IP stack)
L3PacketSegment + IP header (src/dst IP, TTL, protocol)20-60 bytesOS kernel (IP layer)
L2FramePacket + Ethernet header (MACs, EtherType) + FCS18 bytesNIC driver
L1Bits / SymbolsFrame converted to electrical/optical/radio signalsN/AHardware (NIC, transceiver)
🌍 L7 — Application: What your code creates HTTP GET /api/jobs/, DNS queries, SSH. Defines the FORMAT and MEANING of data. When you write requests.get(), you're creating L7 data. Everything below is handled by libraries and the OS.
🔗 L4 — Transport: Where reliability happens (TCP) or doesn't (UDP) TCP guarantees delivery through sequence numbers and ACKs. Breaks messages into segments, numbers them, retransmits lost ones. UDP skips all of this for speed. Port numbers live here. Port 8000 = gunicorn, port 5432 = PostgreSQL.
📍 L3 — Network: Where routing happens (hop by hop) IP addresses identify hosts. Routers move packets hop-by-hop using destination IP. IP is "best-effort" — it does NOT guarantee delivery. Packets can be lost, duplicated, or reordered. TCP (L4) handles that. ICMP (ping) also lives here.
🔌 L2 — Data Link: Hop-to-hop on the local wire MAC addresses identify NICs on the same physical network. ARP translates IP→MAC. MAC addresses NEVER cross a router. Every router hop strips the old L2 header and adds a new one. Ethernet frames carry IP packets between directly-connected devices.

How Encapsulation Works

When you send data, each layer adds its own header (encapsulation). When you receive data, each layer strips its header (decapsulation). Each layer only looks at its own header — Layer 3 (IP) doesn't care about Layer 4's TCP flags.

L7
Application

Creates: GET /api/jobs/

L4
Transport

Adds TCP header + port

L3
Network

Adds IP header + route

L2
Data Link

Adds MAC + frame

L1
Physical

Bits on the wire

1.3 Encapsulation — The Russian Doll of Networking

Encapsulation is the process of wrapping data with headers at each layer as it travels DOWN the stack. Each layer takes the data from the layer above, adds its own header in front, and passes the result down. On the receiving end, the process reverses — each layer strips its header (decapsulation) and passes the remaining data UP.

Why Encapsulation Is the Key to Understanding Networking

If you understand encapsulation, you understand networking. Every single thing that happens on a network follows this pattern. When you look at tcpdump output, you're seeing the result of encapsulation — the outermost headers first, then the inner ones. When you debug, you're essentially "unwrapping" the layers one by one to find where the problem is.

Here's the critical insight: each layer is independent. Layer 3 (IP) doesn't know or care whether Layer 4 is using TCP or UDP. It just sees "protocol number 6" (TCP) or "protocol number 17" (UDP) in its header and forwards accordingly. This independence is what makes the internet work — you can swap Ethernet for Wi-Fi at Layer 2, and Layer 3 doesn't care. You can switch from IPv4 to IPv6 at Layer 3, and Layer 4 doesn't notice.

⚠️ GOTCHA: Same Bytes, Different Names

When you see "TCP payload" in a packet capture, it's actually the HTTP request. When you see "IP payload", it's actually the TCP segment (which contains the HTTP request). Same bytes, different name depending on which layer you're looking from. This is why reading tcpdump output is confusing at first — you're seeing all layers at once, and you need to mentally separate them.

Encapsulation — The Complete anihpj GET /api/jobs/ Request
  📤 SENDER (building the packet — headers added from L7 down to L2)

  L7 Application:  GET /api/jobs/?location=Lagos HTTP/1.1
                   Host: jobpost.anihpj.com
                        │
                        ▼  [TCP wraps HTTP in a TCP segment]
  L4 Transport:    ┌──────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
                   │ TCP HEADER       │ GET /api/jobs/?location=...    │
                   │ SrcPort: 54321   │ Host: jobpost.anihpj.com ...  │
                   │ DstPort: 8000    │                                │
                   │ Seq: 1001, ACK   │                                │
                   └──────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
                        │
                        ▼  [IP wraps TCP segment in an IP packet]
  L3 Network:      ┌─────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐
                   │ IP HEADER   │ TCP HEADER + HTTP DATA              │
                   │ Src:10.244.1.5│ (the entire segment above)         │
                   │ Dst:10.0.1.50│                                    │
                   │ TTL:64       │                                    │
                   │ Proto:TCP(6) │                                    │
                   └─────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘
                        │
                        ▼  [Ethernet wraps IP packet in a frame]
  L2 Data Link:    ┌──────────┬──────────────────────────────────┬──────┐
                   │ETH HEADER│ IP HEADER + TCP HEADER + HTTP    │ FCS  │
                   │Src MAC   │ (the entire IP packet above)     │CRC32 │
                   │Dst MAC   │                                  │      │
                   │Type:0800 │                                  │      │
                   └──────────┴──────────────────────────────────┴──────┘

  📥 RECEIVER (unwrapping — headers stripped from L2 up to L7)
  L2 strips ETH header → L3 strips IP header → L4 strips TCP header
  → L7 receives: GET /api/jobs/?location=Lagos HTTP/1.1
The Russian Doll Analogy
  🪆 OUTERMOST (L2)       🪆 MIDDLE (L3)         🪆 INNER (L4+)
  ┌──────────────────┐   ┌─────────────────┐   ┌─────────────────┐
  │  Ethernet Frame  │   │   IP Packet     │   │  TCP Segment    │
  │  ┌────────────┐  │   │ ┌─────────────┐ │   │ ┌─────────────┐ │
  │  │ IP Packet  │  │   │ │ TCP Segment │ │   │ │ HTTP Req    │ │
  │  │ ┌────────┐ │  │   │ │ ┌─────────┐ │ │   │ │ GET /api/   │ │
  │  │ │TCP Seg │ │  │   │ │ │HTTP Req │ │ │   │ │ jobs/       │ │
  │  │ │┌──────┐│ │  │   │ │ │GET/api/ │ │ │   │ │ Host: ...   │ │
  │  │ ││HTTP  ││ │  │   │ │ │jobs/    │ │ │   │ └─────────────┘ │
  │  │ ││Req   ││ │  │   │ │ │Host:... │ │ │   └─────────────────┘
  │  │ │└──────┘│ │  │   │ │ └─────────┘ │ │
  │  │ └────────┘ │  │   │ └─────────────┘ │
  │  └────────────┘  │   └─────────────────┘
  └──────────────────┘

  Each layer adds its OWN header. Only that layer reads it.
  L2 sees everything as "Ethernet payload" (just bytes).
  L3 sees everything as "IP payload" (just bytes).
  L4 sees everything as "TCP payload" (just bytes).
  L7 sees only the HTTP request text.

1.4 The TCP/IP Model — What We Actually Use

The TCP/IP model has 4 layers (not 7). It's what the actual internet runs on. Why did TCP/IP win over OSI? It was free, working, and already deployed across ARPANET while OSI was still being debated in committee rooms. TCP/IP was built by engineers solving real problems; OSI was designed by a committee imagining ideal ones.

📖 A Quick History: How TCP/IP Conquered the World

In the 1970s, the US Department of Defense funded ARPANET — the precursor to the internet. They needed a networking protocol that could survive nuclear war (routing around damage). Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed TCP/IP in 1974. By January 1, 1983 ("Flag Day"), ARPANET mandated that ALL connected computers switch to TCP/IP. Meanwhile, the ISO committee was still debating the OSI model's 7 layers. By the time OSI was finalized in 1984, TCP/IP was already running the world's largest network. The market had spoken.

OSI (7 Layers) vs TCP/IP (4 Layers) — Side by Side
  🏛️ OSI MODEL (7 Layers)              🌐 TCP/IP MODEL (4 Layers)
  ┌────────────────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │ 7. Application   ─┐   │          │                         │
  │    (HTTP, DNS)     │   │          │  APPLICATION            │
  │ 6. Presentation ─┤   │─────────▶ │  (HTTP, DNS, TLS, SSH,  │
  │    (TLS, SSL)      │───┘          │   SMTP, FTP)            │
  │ 5. Session    ────┘   │          │                         │
  │    (NetBIOS, RPC)     │          ├─────────────────────────┤
  ├───────────────────────┤          │  TRANSPORT              │
  │ 4. Transport          │─────────▶│  (TCP — reliable)       │
  │    (TCP, UDP)         │          │  (UDP — fast)            │
  ├───────────────────────┤          ├─────────────────────────┤
  │ 3. Network            │─────────▶│  INTERNET               │
  │    (IP, ICMP)         │          │  (IPv4/IPv6, ICMP)      │
  ├───────────────────────┤          ├─────────────────────────┤
  │ 2. Data Link          │─────────▶│  LINK / NETWORK ACCESS  │
  │ 1. Physical           │          │  (Ethernet, ARP, Wi-Fi) │
  └───────────────────────┘          └─────────────────────────┘

  💡 Layers 5-6-7 (Session, Presentation, Application) all collapse
     into "APPLICATION" in TCP/IP. In practice, they're all handled
     by the application and TLS library, not the OS network stack.
🏛️
OSI Model — "Designed First"

Created by ISO committee (1977-1984). Designed before implementation. Seven clean layers. Beautiful in theory, but never fully implemented. Still used as the universal TEACHING framework — every networking course starts with OSI.

🌐
TCP/IP — "Built First"

Created by Cerf & Kahn (1974). Implemented first, documented later. Four practical layers. Won because it was FREE, WORKING, and the US government mandated it on ARPANET in 1983. What the actual internet runs on.

How the anihpj Stack Maps to TCP/IP

🌍 APPLICATION Django (jobpost app), gunicorn WSGI server, nginx reverse proxy, PostgreSQL wire protocol, DNS queries via CoreDNS HTTP/1.1TLS 1.3DNS
🔗 TRANSPORT TCP connections: gunicorn:8000, PostgreSQL:5432, Redis:6379. UDP for DNS queries on port 53. TCPUDP
📍 INTERNET Pod IP 10.244.1.5 routes to database at 10.0.1.50 via Calico VXLAN overlay. ICMP for health checks and path MTU discovery. IPv4ICMPVXLAN
🔌 LINK / NETWORK ACCESS Ethernet frames between K8s nodes on the same subnet. ARP resolves next-hop IP to MAC. VLANs isolate dev/staging/prod traffic. EthernetARPVLAN

1.5 Networking in the Infrastructure Toolchain

These are the tools you'll use every day to observe, debug, and verify network behavior. Each tool maps to specific OSI layers. Master these 12 tools, and you'll diagnose issues in seconds that others spend hours Googling.

🔍 Layered Observability Start at L1, work up. Each layer has its own tools and tells its own story.
🏛️ OSI Model (7 Layers) Teaching framework. Physical → Data Link → Network → Transport → Session → Presentation → Application.
🌐 TCP/IP Model (4 Layers) What the internet actually runs on. Link → Internet → Transport → Application.

🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work

When you get paged at 2 AM for "site is down," you now have a framework. Don't panic — start at Layer 1 and work up. Is the link up? Is ARP resolving? Can you ping? Is the port open? Is the app responding? This systematic approach catches issues that guessing misses.

In every incident war room, the person who can read packets and trace the full request path is the most valuable. You're becoming that person. In the next chapters, we'll go deep into each layer — starting with the physical wires in Chapter 2.

📖 Key Terms You've Learned

📦Encapsulation
The process of wrapping data with protocol headers at each OSI layer as it travels DOWN the stack. Each layer adds its own header. On the receiving end, headers are stripped (decapsulation) as the data travels UP.
🏗️Protocol Data Unit (PDU)
The name for data at each layer: Bits (L1) → Frame (L2) → Packet (L3) → Segment (L4) → Data (L5-7). Using the right term shows you know your stuff in an interview.
🔗Protocol Stack
The layered set of protocols that work together. The TCP/IP stack (Link → Internet → Transport → Application) is the actual stack used on the internet. The OSI model is the teaching version.
📏MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit)
The largest packet size (in bytes) that can be sent over a network link without fragmentation. Ethernet default: 1500 bytes. Jumbo frames: 9000 bytes. Wrong MTU = silently dropped packets = nightmare to debug.
🫧Payload
The actual data being transported, excluding all headers and metadata. From L4's perspective, the TCP payload is the HTTP request. From L3's perspective, the IP payload is the TCP segment. Same bytes, different name depending on which layer you're asking.
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 1.1 — Identify the Failing OSI Layer

For each symptom below, identify which OSI layer has failed and what device or protocol is the likely culprit. No terminal needed — think through the architecture.

  1. Your browser shows "ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED" when hitting http://anihpj.local:8000, but ping to the server succeeds and the NIC link light is solid green.
  2. A switch port shows amber LED. ip link on the connected host shows NO-CARRIER. You swap the cable — same result.
  3. curl to https://anihpj.com hangs for 30 seconds then fails with "could not resolve host". Ping to 8.8.8.8 works fine.
  4. SSH to a remote server works, but typing feels laggy with 2-second delays between keystrokes. File transfers via SCP are extremely slow despite a 1 Gbps link.
  5. Your Django app logs show "OperationalError: could not connect to server: Connection refused" when trying to reach PostgreSQL. Both containers are running on the same Docker bridge network.
💡 Hint: Work bottom-up. L1 = physical connectivity (cable, port, signal). L2 = frame delivery (MAC, switch). L3 = packet routing (IP, DNS). L4 = reliable delivery (TCP ports, handshake). L7 = application logic.
📝 View Solution 
# Symptom 1: CONNECTION_REFUSED + ping works + link is up
# Layers 1-3 are fine (link up, ping works = IP reachable).
# CONNECTION_REFUSED = TCP RST received = L4 failure.
# Likely culprit: Django (port 8000) is NOT running, or firewall is
# actively rejecting (not dropping) the connection.
# Check: netstat -tlnp | grep 8000 on the server.

# Symptom 2: Amber LED + NO-CARRIER + cable swap didn't help
# This is a Layer 1 failure. Cable swap ruled out the cable,
# so the NIC port or switch port is faulty.
# Check: ethtool eth0, dmesg | grep -i link, try another switch port.

# Symptom 3: DNS resolution failure + ping to IP works
# Layer 3 (IP routing) works, but name resolution fails.
# This is Layer 7 (DNS is an application-layer protocol).
# Check: cat /etc/resolv.conf, nslookup anihpj.com, systemd-resolve --status

# Symptom 4: SSH works but laggy + slow SCP on 1 Gbps link
# TCP connection is established (L4 is up), but throughput is terrible.
# Could be L1 (high packet loss, CRC errors) or L3 (packet reordering).
# Check: ping -c 100 (look for loss%), ethtool -S eth0 (CRC/drop counters),
# iperf3 between hosts to measure actual throughput.

# Symptom 5: Django can't reach Postgres on same Docker bridge network
# Both containers are on the same L2 segment (docker bridge).
# CONNECTION_REFUSED on L4 = Postgres is not listening, or wrong port.
# Check: docker exec anihpj-db-1 netstat -tlnp | grep 5432,
# docker inspect anihpj-db-1 | jq '.[0].NetworkSettings.Networks'
⏱️ Target: 7 minutes
Drill 1.2 — Trace Encapsulation for an anihpj Request

Trace the full encapsulation path for a user request to the anihpj Django app, then capture it live.

  1. Draw (on paper) the encapsulation stack for: Browser → HTTP GET /api/health → anihpj-web container. Label every header added at each layer.
  2. On your lab machine, run: docker compose -f ~/anihpj/docker-compose.yml up -d
  3. Capture the traffic: sudo tcpdump -i docker0 -nn -A port 8000
  4. From another terminal: curl -v http://localhost:8000/api/health
  5. In the tcpdump output, identify the HTTP request line (GET), the TCP flags (SYN, ACK, PSH), the IP addresses, and the Ethernet MAC addresses.
  6. Count how many layers of encapsulation you can see in the raw hex dump.
💡 Hint: tcpdump captures at L2 by default. You'll see Ethernet frames → IP packets → TCP segments → HTTP data. The -A flag prints the payload as ASCII so you can read the HTTP text. Use -XX instead to see full hex+ASCII.
📝 View Solution 
# Terminal 1: Start capture on the Docker bridge
# docker0 is the default bridge; your compose network may differ
sudo tcpdump -i docker0 -nn -A port 8000

# Terminal 2: Send the request
curl -v http://localhost:8000/api/health

# Expected tcpdump output (annotated):

# [L2 - Ethernet Frame]
# Src MAC: 02:42:ac:11:00:02  Dst MAC: 02:42:ac:11:00:03  EtherType: 0x0800 (IPv4)
# [L3 - IP Packet]
# Src IP: 172.17.0.1 (host) > Dst IP: 172.17.0.2 (container)
# Protocol: TCP (6), TTL: 64
# [L4 - TCP Segment]
# Src Port: 54321 > Dst Port: 8000
# Flags: [S] (SYN) → [S.] (SYN-ACK) → [.] (ACK) → [P.] (PSH+ACK)
# [L7 - HTTP]
# GET /api/health HTTP/1.1
# Host: localhost:8000
# User-Agent: curl/8.x.x
# Accept: */*

# Response (container → host):
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# Content-Type: application/json
# {"status":"healthy","version":"1.0.0"}

# KEY INSIGHT: Each line you see in tcpdump -A is L7 payload.
# But below that ASCII, each packet also has:
#  - 14 bytes Ethernet header (SrcMAC + DstMAC + EtherType)
#  - 20 bytes IP header (version, SrcIP, DstIP, TTL, protocol)
#  - 20 bytes TCP header (SrcPort, DstPort, flags, seq, ack, window)
# That's 54 bytes of overhead per packet BEFORE the HTTP payload!
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 1.3 — Protocol-to-Layer Mapping

Without looking at notes, assign each protocol/technology to its OSI layer(s) and TCP/IP layer. This is a common interview warm-up question.

  1. Map these to OSI layers: HTTP, TLS, TCP, IP, ARP, Ethernet, DNS, BGP, SSH, ICMP, DHCP, Wi-Fi (802.11)
  2. Which of these span multiple layers? Why?
  3. Which protocols are not in the TCP/IP model but are in the OSI model?
  4. If a switch uses ARP to populate its MAC table, what layers are involved?
💡 Hint: Some protocols blur the lines. TLS sits between L4 and L7 (sometimes called "Layer 5.5"). ARP bridges L2 and L3. BGP runs on top of TCP (L4), making it an L7 application that controls L3 routing.
📝 View Solution 
# Protocol → OSI Layer    | TCP/IP Layer | Notes
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
HTTP    → L7 (Application)  | Application  |
TLS     → L5-L6 (Session/Pres)| Application  | Encrypts L7, lives above TCP
TCP     → L4 (Transport)    | Transport    |
IP      → L3 (Network)      | Internet     |
ARP     → L2-L3 (bridge)    | Link/Internet| Resolves IP→MAC, L2 frames
Ethernet→ L1-L2 (Physical/Link)| Link        | Frame format + signaling
DNS     → L7 (Application)  | Application  | Uses UDP/TCP port 53
BGP     → L7 (Application)  | Application  | Uses TCP port 179, controls L3
SSH     → L7 (Application)  | Application  | Uses TCP port 22
ICMP    → L3 (Network)      | Internet     | Control protocol, inside IP
DHCP    → L7 (Application)  | Application  | Uses UDP ports 67/68
Wi-Fi   → L1-L2 (Physical/Link)| Link        | 802.11 = L1 radio + L2 MAC

# Multi-layer protocols:
# - TLS: Session layer (L5) handshake + Presentation layer (L6) encryption
# - ARP: L3 addresses resolved to L2 addresses, carried in L2 frames
# - Wi-Fi/Ethernet: L1 (physical signaling) + L2 (MAC addressing/framing)
# - BGP: L7 application that populates L3 routing tables

# Protocols ONLY in OSI (not TCP/IP):
# - None, really — but the SESSION and PRESENTATION layers don't
#   have distinct protocols in TCP/IP. Their functions are absorbed
#   into the Application layer (e.g., TLS, NetBIOS, RPC).

# ARP in switches:
# Switches operate at L2 (forward by MAC). But ARP packets contain
# L3 (IP) information. The switch doesn't look at the IP — it only
# reads the Ethernet header (L2) to forward the frame. The ARP
# payload is opaque to the switch. Layer 2 only.

📝 Chapter 1 — Practice Questions

Q1
A user reports that the anihpj Django application is unreachable. You SSH into the server and run ping localhost — it works. netstat -tlnp | grep 8000 shows nothing. docker ps shows the anihpj-web-1 container is running. At which OSI layer has the failure occurred, and what is the most likely root cause?
Show Answer
Answer

The failure is at Layer 4 (Transport). ping works (L1-L3 are functional), but nothing is listening on port 8000. The container is running but the Django process inside it may have crashed, or it may be binding to the wrong interface (e.g., 127.0.0.1 inside the container instead of 0.0.0.0). The TCP three-way handshake cannot complete because there's no process to accept the connection — the kernel responds with TCP RST, producing "Connection Refused."

# Verify inside the container
docker exec anihpj-web-1 netstat -tlnp
# If nothing on :8000, check the process:
docker exec anihpj-web-1 ps aux | grep gunicorn
# Check gunicorn bind address:
docker exec anihpj-web-1 cat /app/gunicorn.conf.py
# bind = "0.0.0.0:8000" ← correct
# bind = "127.0.0.1:8000" ← WRONG — not reachable from outside container
Explanation

This scenario tests your ability to isolate the failing layer. Working bottom-up: L1 is up (cable/interface), L2 is up (local communication), L3 is working (ping = ICMP at L3), so the problem is at L4 or above. The absence of a listener on port 8000 confirms L4 failure. In Docker, this is commonly caused by the process binding to 127.0.0.1 (loopback inside the container), which is unreachable from the Docker bridge network. Always bind to 0.0.0.0 in containerized apps.

Q2
Walk through the complete encapsulation process when a browser sends GET / HTTP/1.1 to an NGINX reverse proxy at 192.168.1.10:443. Name every header added at each layer from L7 down to L1, including the approximate header sizes. Where does TLS fit in this stack?
Show Answer
Answer
Layer Added Header Size
L7 — HTTP GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: ...\r\n\r\n ~50-500 bytes
L6 — TLS TLS Record header (encrypts HTTP payload) ~5 bytes + padding
L4 — TCP SrcPort:44384, DstPort:443, Seq, Ack, Flags, Window 20-60 bytes
L3 — IP SrcIP:10.0.0.5, DstIP:192.168.1.10, Proto:TCP(6), TTL:64 20-60 bytes
L2 — Ethernet SrcMAC, DstMAC (gateway), EtherType:0x0800, FCS trailer 18 bytes (14 header + 4 FCS)

TLS sits between L4 (TCP) and L7 (HTTP). It encrypts the entire HTTP payload, so what L4 sees as "TCP payload" is actually a TLS Record containing encrypted HTTP. This is why tcpdump on port 443 shows gibberish — the HTTP is encrypted before it reaches TCP.

Explanation

Encapsulation is the foundational concept of networking. Every layer wraps the data from the layer above. The key insight for HTTPS: TLS is an intermediate layer — it receives HTTP from L7, encrypts it, then hands the ciphertext to TCP at L4. From TCP's perspective, TLS Records are just payload. From the network's perspective (L3/L2), everything above the IP header is opaque payload. This is why middleboxes can route by IP but can't inspect HTTPS traffic.

Q3
Compare the OSI model and the TCP/IP model. Why does TCP/IP have only 4 layers while OSI has 7? Which model do real-world engineers use day-to-day, and why?
Show Answer
Answer

The OSI model (7 layers) was designed by committee (ISO) as a reference model before protocols existed. It separates Session (L5) and Presentation (L6) as distinct layers because, in theory, session management and data formatting are separate concerns. The TCP/IP model (4 layers) was designed by engineers building the actual internet — they folded L5-L7 into a single "Application" layer because, in practice, applications handle their own sessions and encoding.

In practice: Engineers use OSI layer numbers (L1-L7) as a common vocabulary ("It's a Layer 2 problem") because the granularity is useful for troubleshooting. But the actual protocol stack in every machine is TCP/IP. Nobody says "There's a Link layer issue" — they say "Layer 2" or "the switch." The OSI numbering has become the lingua franca of networking even though the OSI protocols themselves (CLNP, etc.) lost to TCP/IP decades ago.

Explanation

This is a classic interview question. The correct answer highlights that OSI is a teaching tool and common vocabulary, while TCP/IP is the real protocol stack. Key differentiators: OSI's L5/L6 functions (session management, encryption, encoding) are handled by TLS, SSL, and application code in TCP/IP. OSI was protocol-agnostic; TCP/IP named its layers after the protocols that run in them.

Q4
In the anihpj Docker Compose setup, the web container (172.20.0.2) needs to reach the database container (172.20.0.3:5432). The web container can ping the database container successfully. However, psql -h 172.20.0.3 -p 5432 hangs for 60 seconds then times out. List every possible cause across all relevant OSI layers, ordered from most likely to least likely.
Show Answer
Answer

Since ping works, L1-L3 are functional. The problem is at L4 or above. Here are the possible causes, ordered by probability:

  1. L4 — PostgreSQL not listening: The postgres process isn't running or is bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0. Verify: docker exec anihpj-db-1 netstat -tlnp | grep 5432
  2. L4 — Docker network misconfiguration: Containers are on different Docker networks. Verify: docker inspect anihpj-web-1 | jq '.[0].NetworkSettings.Networks'
  3. L4 — iptables/nftables DROP rule: The host firewall is dropping port 5432 on the Docker bridge. Check: sudo iptables -L DOCKER-USER -nv
  4. L7 — pg_hba.conf rejection: PostgreSQL's host-based authentication rejects the connection from 172.20.0.2. Check: docker exec anihpj-db-1 cat /var/lib/postgresql/data/pg_hba.conf
  5. L7 — PostgreSQL connection limit reached: max_connections exhausted. Check logs: docker logs anihpj-db-1 | grep "remaining connection slots"
  6. L4 — Wrong port: PostgreSQL is listening on a non-default port (e.g., 5433). Verify: docker exec anihpj-db-1 grep port /var/lib/postgresql/data/postgresql.conf
Explanation

The key diagnostic clue is "hangs then times out" vs "connection refused." A timeout means the SYN packet is being dropped silently (firewall DROP rule, wrong network) — the sender never receives a SYN-ACK or RST. "Connection refused" means a RST was received (port is closed, no listener). This distinction is critical for real-world troubleshooting and is a common exam question pattern. Always distinguish between DROP (timeout) and REJECT/RST (immediate failure).

Q5
Name the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) at each of the 7 OSI layers. Which layer is responsible for the first point of error detection (not correction), and what mechanism does it use?
Show Answer
Answer
Layer PDU Name Error Detection?
L7 — ApplicationData / MessageApp-level (HTTP 5xx)
L6 — PresentationData (encoded/encrypted)TLS record MAC
L5 — SessionData (session state)Session timeout
L4 — TransportSegment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP)TCP checksum
L3 — NetworkPacketIP header checksum (IPv4 only)
L2 — Data LinkFrame✅ FCS (Frame Check Sequence)
L1 — PhysicalBits / SymbolsLine coding violations

The first point of error detection is Layer 2, via the Frame Check Sequence (FCS) — a 4-byte CRC32 checksum appended to every Ethernet frame. The receiving NIC recomputes the CRC and compares it to the FCS. If they don't match, the frame is silently dropped. This catches corrupted bits at the first layer that processes complete frames.

Explanation

PDU names are the bedrock of networking vocabulary. Every engineer should be able to recite: Bits → Frames → Packets → Segments → Data. The FCS at L2 is the first error detection because L1 doesn't process data — it just transmits bits. L2 is the first layer that groups bits into a meaningful unit (the frame) and can verify its integrity. If the FCS check fails, the frame never reaches L3. This is why CRC errors in ethtool -S output indicate L1 problems (noisy cables, bad connectors) even though the detection happens at L2.

Q6
Using the OSI model, explain what happens between typing https://anihpj.com into a browser and seeing the page render. For each of the 7 layers, describe exactly one protocol or function that layer performs during this process. Which layers are involved on the first packet sent by the browser?
Show Answer
Answer
Layer Function in This Request
L7 — ApplicationBrowser constructs GET / HTTP/1.1 with headers (Host, User-Agent, etc.)
L6 — PresentationTLS performs handshake (certificate exchange, cipher negotiation) then encrypts HTTP
L5 — SessionTLS session established; TCP tracks the connection state (ESTABLISHED)
L4 — TransportTCP: 3-way handshake (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK), port 443, reliable delivery with retransmission
L3 — NetworkDNS resolves anihpj.com → IP; IP routes packets hop-by-hop to the server
L2 — Data LinkARP resolves next-hop IP → MAC; Ethernet frames carry IP packets on the local segment
L1 — PhysicalNIC encodes bits as electrical/optical signals onto the cable (1000BASE-T, fiber, or Wi-Fi radio)

The first packet involves: L7 (DNS query to resolve the hostname), L4 (UDP on port 53), L3 (IP routing to DNS server), L2 (Ethernet frame to gateway), L1 (physical signaling). Only after DNS resolution does the browser open a TCP connection (SYN) to the resolved IP on port 443.

Explanation

This question tests end-to-end understanding. The key insight: DNS is the hidden first step most people forget. Before any HTTP/TCP happens, the browser must resolve the hostname. DNS uses UDP (L4), making it an L7 protocol that triggers before the main connection. Also note that TLS spans L5 (session handshake) and L6 (payload encryption), which is why it doesn't fit neatly into one OSI layer — a common interview discussion point.

Q7
You run tcpdump -nn -i eth0 on a server and see:
10.0.1.5.54321 > 10.0.1.10.8000: Flags [S], seq 123456789, win 65535
followed 2 seconds later by another identical SYN with seq 123456789. You never see a SYN-ACK. What layers could be failing? List the diagnostic commands you'd run at each layer to isolate the problem.
Show Answer
Answer

The repeated SYN with the same sequence number (123456789) means TCP retransmission is happening. The client sends SYN, waits ~1 second (initial RTO), then retransmits. No SYN-ACK means the SYN is either not reaching the server or the server's reply is not reaching the client.

Layer Possible Cause Diagnostic Command
L1Cable unplugged, bad port, interface downip link show eth0, ethtool eth0
L2Wrong VLAN, switch port disabled, ARP failureip neigh show, arp -n
L3Routing issue, wrong gateway, IP conflictip route get 10.0.1.10, ping 10.0.1.10
L4Firewall DROP, no listener on :8000ss -tlnp | grep 8000, iptables -L -nv
L7App bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0ss -tlnp (check Local Address column)

Quick check: If ping 10.0.1.10 works, L1-L3 are fine — focus on L4 (firewall, no listener). If ping fails, start at L1 and work up.

Explanation

TCP retransmission is a powerful diagnostic signal. The same sequence number on retransmitted SYNs means the original SYN was never acknowledged — the TCP stack is re-sending the exact same segment. This rules out application crashes (different seq numbers would indicate new connections). The "1 second → 2 seconds → 4 seconds" retransmission pattern (exponential backoff) is a dead giveaway of a silent DROP somewhere. This is a classic interview scenario for SRE/DevOps roles.

Q8
For each of the following anihpj application scenarios, state whether TCP or UDP is the appropriate transport protocol and why:
(a) Django serving an HTML page to a browser
(b) Prometheus scraping metrics from the Django /metrics endpoint every 15s
(c) Streaming application logs from containers to Loki
(d) A WebSocket connection for live dashboard updates
(e) DNS queries from the web container to CoreDNS
Show Answer
Answer
Scenario Protocol Reasoning
(a) Django HTML pageTCPHTML must arrive complete and in order. Missing bytes = broken page. TCP guarantees reliable, ordered delivery.
(b) Prometheus scrapingTCPPrometheus uses HTTP to scrape — HTTP rides on TCP. The metrics payload must be complete and uncorrupted for accurate monitoring.
(c) Loki log streamingTCPLogs must not be lost — missing entries break auditing and debugging. Loki uses HTTP/gRPC, both over TCP. Order matters for log correlation.
(d) WebSocket dashboardTCPWebSockets start as HTTP (TCP) then upgrade. They need reliability — a dropped frame could show stale data on a monitoring dashboard.
(e) DNS queriesUDP (default)DNS uses UDP for speed — queries are small (usually <512 bytes), and if a response is lost, the resolver retries. TCP is used only for large responses (zone transfers, DNSSEC).

The rule of thumb: TCP when you need reliability and ordering (web, email, file transfer, databases). UDP when you need speed and can tolerate loss (streaming, gaming, VoIP, DNS). Most infrastructure workloads (HTTP APIs, databases, message queues) use TCP.

Explanation

This question tests whether you understand why protocol choices matter, not just what they are. Notice that all 5 scenarios in a typical web application use TCP — this is the reality of modern infrastructure. UDP is relegated to DNS (small queries), NTP (time sync), and media streaming. The key insight: TCP's overhead (3-way handshake, retransmission, flow control) is worth it for anything where data integrity matters. UDP's lack of overhead is only valuable when speed trumps reliability.

Q9
Calculate the total encapsulation overhead (in bytes) for an HTTP GET request to https://anihpj.com/api/health over Ethernet. Assume: the HTTP request line + headers = 200 bytes, TLS record overhead = 29 bytes, TCP header = 20 bytes (no options), IPv4 header = 20 bytes (no options), Ethernet = 14 bytes header + 4 bytes FCS. What percentage of the total frame is actual application data (the HTTP GET)?
Show Answer
Answer
Component Size (bytes)
HTTP GET request200
TLS Record overhead29
TCP header20
IPv4 header20
Ethernet header14
Ethernet FCS (trailer)4
Overhead subtotal87 bytes
Total frame size287 bytes
Application data efficiency200/287 = 69.7%

Only ~70% of the frame is actual application data. The other 30% is protocol overhead: 87 bytes of headers wrapped around 200 bytes of HTTP. For small requests (like a health check), overhead dominates. For a full HTML page (say 50KB), overhead is negligible (<1%).

# Overhead percentages for different payload sizes:
# 200 B  HTTP request:  200/(200+87) = 69.7% efficient (30.3% overhead)
# 1.5 KB HTTP response: 1500/(1500+87) = 94.5% efficient (5.5% overhead)
# 50 KB HTML page:      50000/(50000+87) = 99.8% efficient (0.2% overhead)

# This is why small packets (SYN, ACK, health checks) are "expensive" — 
# they carry more header than data. Jumbo frames (9000 MTU) reduce overhead
# for large transfers: 9000/(9000+87) = 99.0% efficient.
Explanation

Overhead calculation is a practical skill for capacity planning. When sizing network links, remember that a 1 Gbps link doesn't carry 1 Gbps of application data — it carries frames. At 70% efficiency for small requests, that's only 700 Mbps of actual HTTP. This is why monitoring tools report "interface utilization" (includes overhead) vs "application throughput" (excludes overhead). It's also why connection pooling (reusing TCP connections) reduces overhead — you skip the 3-way handshake for subsequent requests.

Q10
You're the SRE on-call. The anihpj Kubernetes cluster dashboard shows the anihpj-web pod as Running but Ready: 0/1. The readiness probe is httpGet: path: /healthz, port: 8000 with a 5-second timeout. You exec into the pod and run curl localhost:8000/healthz — it returns 200 OK instantly. However, from another pod on the same node, curl 10.244.2.15:8000/healthz times out. Walk through your diagnostic process by OSI layer. What is the most likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer

Diagnostic by layer:

  1. L7 — App: curl localhost:8000/healthz works → app is healthy and listening ✅
  2. L4 — Port binding: Check ss -tlnp | grep 8000 inside pod → shows 127.0.0.1:8000 (loopback only!) instead of 0.0.0.0:8000 or *:8000. The server is bound to localhost, so it only accepts connections from within the pod. ❌
  3. L3 — Network: Check if pod IP is reachable → ping 10.244.2.15 works from other pod (CNI routes are fine) ✅
  4. L2/L1: Pod-to-pod networking through CNI (Calico/Flannel/Cilium) is operational — other pods can reach each other ✅

Root cause: The application (gunicorn/Django) is binding to 127.0.0.1 (the pod's loopback interface) instead of 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces). This is a Layer 4 issue — the TCP port is open but only on the loopback interface. The readiness probe runs inside the pod (via kubelet exec), so it succeeds. But traffic from other pods arrives on eth0, where nothing is listening.

# Fix: Change the bind address in gunicorn config
# Wrong:
bind = "127.0.0.1:8000"

# Correct:
bind = "0.0.0.0:8000"

# Verify after restart:
kubectl exec anihpj-web-xxx -- ss -tlnp | grep 8000
# Should show: 0.0.0.0:8000 or *:8000
# NOT: 127.0.0.1:8000
Explanation

This is one of the most common container/Kubernetes networking pitfalls. The diagnostic clue: curl localhost works but curl POD_IP doesn't. This always means the process is bound to loopback only. In traditional VMs, binding to 127.0.0.1 is a security best practice — but in containers, it makes the service unreachable. Kubernetes readiness probes run inside the container (via the kubelet's CRI), so they use localhost and succeed — giving a false sense that everything is fine. This is why Ready: 0/1 despite the probe passing internally (the kubelet also tries the pod IP from the node, which would fail here — hence the 0/1 status).

Chapter 2: Layer 1 & 2 — Bits, Frames & The Local Network

Before IP addresses, before TCP ports, before HTTP requests — there are electrons and photons pushing 1s and 0s through copper, fiber, and air. Chapter 2 covers the two layers that make everything else possible: Layer 1 (the physical medium — cables, signals, link state) and Layer 2 (the data link — frames, MAC addresses, switches, ARP). When a server falls off the network, 70% of the time the problem is L1 or L2 — a bad cable, a switch port silently dropping frames, a stale ARP entry. Master these layers and you'll fix problems that others spend hours chasing at the application level.

🟢 BEGINNER ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🔬 3 LABs 🐞 ~70% of outages

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:

  • Read ethtool and ip link output to diagnose physical layer issues (speed mismatch, duplex, CRC errors)
  • Dissect an Ethernet frame byte-by-byte and explain every field
  • Decode MAC addresses — OUI lookup, unicast vs multicast vs broadcast
  • Explain how a switch learns MAC addresses and why VLANs matter in container environments
  • Capture and interpret ARP traffic with tcpdump
  • Trace the full L1→L2 path of a packet leaving a Docker container
🔗 Applies To:
DevOps
SRE
Platform Eng
Cloud Eng
SysAdmin
Weight: 15% of real-world incidents
🎯 SRE Interview Tip

In any infrastructure interview, you will be asked: "A server is unreachable — walk me through your troubleshooting." The correct answer always starts at Layer 1: "First I check if the link is up with ip link show. Then I check link quality with ethtool looking for speed, duplex, and error counters." Starting at L7 ("I check if the application is running") marks you as a junior. Starting at L1 marks you as an SRE.

  • L1 check: ip link show eth0 → is it UP? ethtool eth0 → speed? duplex? errors?
  • L2 check: ip neigh show → can we resolve MACs? tcpdump -i eth0 arp → is ARP working?

2.1 Bits on the Wire — What Actually Travels Through a Cable?

At its core, Layer 1 is about signaling: converting digital 1s and 0s into physical phenomena that can travel through a medium. Your network cable doesn't carry "packets" — it carries voltage transitions, light pulses, or radio waves. Everything above L1 is an abstraction.

📡 Three Physical Media, One Job
MediumSignal TypeExampleMax DistanceSRE Relevance
Copper (Twisted Pair)Voltage changesCat6a Ethernet100mData center rack cabling
Fiber OpticLight pulses (laser/LED)Single-mode (SMF)40km+DC spine-leaf interconnects
Wireless (Radio)Electromagnetic wavesWi-Fi 6E (802.11ax)~50m indoorOffice/laptop connectivity
🔌 Copper Cable Categories — Which Cable for Which Speed?
CategoryMax SpeedMax FrequencyMax DistanceShieldingTypical Use
Cat5100 Mbps100 MHz100mUTPObsolete — do not use
Cat5e1 Gbps100 MHz100mUTPHome/office minimum
Cat61 Gbps (10G @ 37m)250 MHz100m (55m for 10G)UTP/STPOffice/DC rack
Cat6a10 Gbps500 MHz100mSTPDC ToR to server
Cat710 Gbps600 MHz100mS/FTPHigh-interference DC
Cat825/40 Gbps2000 MHz30mS/FTPDC top-of-rack only

SRE note: If you're seeing CRC errors and the link negotiates at 1 Gbps on a Cat5 cable, the cable is the problem — Cat5 isn't rated for Gigabit. Always use Cat5e or better for 1 Gbps+. And never use CCA (Copper-Clad Aluminum) cables — they're cheaper but brittle and cause intermittent failures that are nearly impossible to diagnose.

Encoding is how 1s and 0s become physical signals. Different Ethernet speeds use different encoding schemes:

  • Manchester Encoding (10 Mbps Ethernet): Each bit is a mid-clock transition — high→low = 0, low→high = 1. Simple but wastes 50% bandwidth.
  • NRZ (Non-Return to Zero): 1 = high voltage, 0 = low voltage. Efficient but loses sync on long runs of same bit.
  • PAM4 (Pulse Amplitude Modulation, 4-level): Used by 400GBASE. Encodes 2 bits per symbol (00, 01, 10, 11 → 4 voltage levels). Doubles throughput at the cost of signal-to-noise ratio.

   (frames, packets, segments) is an abstraction built on these signals.
⚠️ GOTCHA: UP ≠ Healthy

A link can show state UP in ip link show but have 90% packet loss from a frayed cable, loose connector, or electromagnetic interference. Always check ethtool -S eth0 for error counters before assuming L1 is clean:

# Link is UP — but is it HEALTHY?
$ ip link show eth0
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc fq_codel state UP
    link/ether aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff

$ ethtool eth0
Settings for eth0:
    Speed: 1000Mb/s          ← should match switch port
    Duplex: Full             ← MUST be Full. Half = collision domain! 🚩
    Link detected: yes       ← physical link present
    Auto-negotiation: on     ← negotiates speed/duplex with switch

$ ethtool -S eth0 | grep -E 'err|drop|crc|collision'
    rx_crc_errors: 14527     ← 🚩🚩🚩 Bad cable! FCS check failing
    rx_missed_errors: 0
    tx_aborted_errors: 0
    collisions: 0            ← Should ALWAYS be 0 in full-duplex

If rx_crc_errors is non-zero and increasing, the cable is physically damaged — replace it immediately. CRC errors mean the Frame Check Sequence at L2 doesn't match the computed checksum, which means bits are being corrupted in transit. The NIC drops these frames silently at L2 before they ever reach the kernel.

📡 Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) & Bit Error Rate (BER) — Why "Good Enough" Isn't

Every signal traveling through a cable fights against noise — electromagnetic interference from nearby cables, fluorescent lights, motors, and even cosmic rays. The Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) measures how much stronger your signal is than the background noise, expressed in decibels (dB).

  • SNR > 30 dB: Excellent — clean signal, near-zero bit errors.
  • SNR 20-30 dB: Good — occasional correctable errors. Marginally acceptable.
  • SNR 10-20 dB: Poor — frequent CRC errors. TCP retransmissions become noticeable.
  • SNR < 10 dB: Unusable — the noise floor is approaching the signal level. Massive packet loss.

Bit Error Rate (BER) is the fraction of bits that arrive corrupted: BER = errored bits ÷ total bits transmitted. Ethernet targets BER ≤ 10⁻¹² (1 error per trillion bits). At 1 Gbps, that's roughly 1 error every 17 minutes — acceptable. If your CRC counters show thousands of errors per second, your BER is orders of magnitude worse — a cable problem, not a protocol problem.

SRE application: When reading optical transceiver DOM (Digital Optical Monitoring) data on fiber links, you'll see values like Tx Power: -2.1 dBm, Rx Power: -15.8 dBm. The difference between them is your link budget. If Rx Power drops below the receiver sensitivity (typically -18 to -22 dBm for 10G SR optics), the link goes down even though the fiber looks fine. This is why you clean fiber connectors with alcohol wipes — a single dust particle can drop Rx power by 3-5 dB.

🔌 How Auto-Negotiation Actually Works — FLP Bursts

When you plug in an Ethernet cable, the two NICs don't just "figure out" speed and duplex magically. They exchange FLP (Fast Link Pulse) bursts — a sequence of 33 pulses (17 odd-numbered clock pulses + 16 data pulses) that encode each device's capabilities as a 16-bit "link code word."

The bits in the code word advertise supported technologies: 10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX, 1000BASE-T, 10GBASE-T, full-duplex, half-duplex, and pause (flow control). Both sides compare their capabilities and select the highest common denominator — the fastest speed both support with full-duplex preferred over half.

Why auto-negotiation fails: If one side has auto-negotiation OFF (hard-coded to 1000/Full) and the other side has it ON, the ON side detects the signal but gets no FLP bursts. It falls back to parallel detection — guessing the speed from the signal timing. It may get the speed right but always defaults to half-duplex when parallel detection is used. Result: 1000/Half on one side, 1000/Full on the other = massive collisions on the half-duplex side, zero collisions on the full-duplex side. The mismatch manifests as "slow network" with no obvious error messages.

🔦 Fiber Optics Deep-Dive — Single-Mode vs Multi-Mode
PropertyMulti-Mode Fiber (MMF)Single-Mode Fiber (SMF)
Core diameter50 or 62.5 microns8-9 microns
Light sourceLED or VCSEL (850nm)Laser (1310nm or 1550nm)
Distance @ 10G~300m (OM3), ~400m (OM4)10-40km
Distance @ 100G~100m (OM4)40-80km
TransceiverSFP-10G-SR (Short Reach)SFP-10G-LR (Long Reach)
CostCheaper optics, thicker fiberMore expensive optics, thinner fiber
Use caseWithin DC rack/row (same room)Between buildings, DC interconnects
Color codingAqua (OM3/OM4), Orange (OM1/OM2)Yellow

Critical rule: Never plug an SMF transceiver into MMF cable (or vice versa). The core size mismatch causes massive signal loss. At best it won't link up; at worst you'll burn out the receiver. Also, never look directly into a fiber transceiver or cable end — the laser is invisible infrared but can permanently damage your retina. Treat every fiber port as if it's live.

⚡ Power over Ethernet (PoE) — When the Cable Delivers Electricity Too

PoE sends DC power over the same twisted-pair copper that carries Ethernet data — up to 90W per port with the latest standard. This powers Wi-Fi access points, IP cameras, VoIP phones, and IoT sensors without needing separate power cables.

StandardMax Power at PDPairs UsedYearDevices Powered
802.3af (PoE)12.95W2 pairs2003VoIP phones, basic APs
802.3at (PoE+)25.5W2 pairs2009Dual-band APs, PTZ cameras
802.3bt Type 351W4 pairs2018High-end APs, small switches
802.3bt Type 471.3-90W4 pairs2018Laptops, monitors, PoE lighting

SRE note: In a data center, you probably won't use PoE for servers. But in office networks, smart buildings, and edge computing (retail stores, warehouses), PoE is everywhere. A PoE switch port can be disabled remotely (power cycle a hung AP), and PoE budget exhaustion (too many high-power devices on one switch) is a real problem — the switch will stop delivering power to new devices silently.

🐞 Real Scenario: The "Slow Website" That Was a Bad Cable

A team spent 3 hours debugging application performance — the Django app was serving pages in 8 seconds instead of 200ms. Database queries looked fine. CPU was idle. Memory was 40%. Finally, someone checked ethtool -S eth0 and found rx_crc_errors: 892,341. Every 5th frame was being dropped at L2, causing TCP retransmissions that added 200ms of delay per retransmit. A $3 Cat6 cable was the culprit. Lesson: Always start at L1.

2.2 Ethernet — The Universal LAN Protocol

Ethernet is the dominant Layer 2 protocol. It defines both L1 (physical signaling) and L2 (frame format, MAC addressing). It won the protocol wars because of three qualities: simplicity (the frame format hasn't fundamentally changed since 1980), cost (cheap NICs, cheap switches), and backward compatibility (a 1990 10BASE-T NIC still plugs into a 2025 switch and works).

ETHERNET FRAME — Complete Byte-by-Byte Anatomy
┌──────────┬────────────────┬───────────────┬──────────┬──────────────────────┬──────┐
│ PREAMBLE │ DEST MAC       │ SOURCE MAC    │ETHERTYPE │       PAYLOAD        │ FCS  │
│  8 bytes │   6 bytes      │   6 bytes     │ 2 bytes  │   46 — 1500 bytes    │4 bytes│
├──────────┼────────────────┼───────────────┼──────────┼──────────────────────┼──────┤
│7×10101010│ aa:bb:cc:      │ 11:22:33:    │ 0x0800   │ ← IP PACKET INSIDE → │CRC32 │
│+1×10101011│ dd:ee:ff       │ 44:55:66     │ = IPv4   │ (headers + data)     │check │
│(sync+start)│               │              │ 0x0806   │                      │      │
│           │               │              │ = ARP    │                      │      │
│           │               │              │ 0x86DD   │                      │      │
│           │               │              │ = IPv6   │                      │      │
└──────────┴────────────────┴───────────────┴──────────┴──────────────────────┴──────┘
Total frame: 8 + 6 + 6 + 2 + (46-1500) + 4 = 72 to 1526 bytes (standard MTU 1500)
Minimum payload: 46 bytes (padded if smaller). Jumbo frames: up to 9026 bytes.
📏 Frame Field Breakdown
FieldSizePurposeSRE Note
Preamble8 bytesClock synchronization. 7 bytes of 10101010, then 1 byte 10101011 (SFD — Start Frame Delimiter) signaling "real data starts now."Stripped by NIC — you'll never see this in tcpdump
Dest MAC6 bytesWho this frame is for. ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff = broadcast (everyone on the segment).The switch reads ONLY this field to decide where to forward
Source MAC6 bytesWho sent this frame. The switch learns from this field.This is how the CAM table gets populated
EtherType2 bytesWhat's inside the payload. 0x0800 = IPv4, 0x0806 = ARP, 0x86DD = IPv6, 0x8100 = VLAN-tagged.If > 1500 (0x05DC), it's EtherType. If ≤ 1500, it's a length field (IEEE 802.3)
Payload46-1500 BThe encapsulated data (IP packet, ARP message, etc.).Padding bytes added if payload < 46 bytes
FCS4 bytesCRC32 checksum of the entire frame (except preamble/FCS).Check ethtool -S \| grep crc — any non-zero = bad cable
