🔑 KEY FLOWCHART TAKEAWAYS:
  • L1 → L2 → L3 → L4 → L7: Always bottom-up. Never start at L7.
  • DNS is the #1 red herring: "site down vs DNS broken" is the first fork.
  • nc -zv (netcat zero-I/O) is faster than telnet for port checks.
  • If ping works but nc fails, the port is blocked (firewall) or not listening.
  • If ping fails, start with ip link show + ethtool. Don't jump to IP routing.
⚠️ GOTCHA: Docker Overlay MTU Black Hole

Docker overlay networks (Swarm/K8s with VXLAN) add 50 bytes of overhead (VXLAN header + UDP + IP + Ethernet). If your physical NIC has MTU 1500:

# Physical NIC: MTU 1500
# VXLAN overhead: 50 bytes (8 VXLAN + 8 UDP + 20 IP + 14 Eth)
# Container MTU MUST be: 1500 - 50 = 1450 (or less)

# If container MTU is still 1500:
# Container sends 1500-byte packet → gets wrapped in VXLAN → becomes 1550 bytes
# Physical NIC drops it (exceeds MTU 1500, DF bit set) → NO ICMP error (PMTU black hole)
# Result: Large packets silently disappear. TCP connections hang. Madness ensues.

# Fix: Set container MTU explicitly
docker network create --opt com.docker.network.driver.mtu=1450 anihpj-net

Debugging PMTU black holes: ping -M do -s 1472 <target> (1472 + 28 ICMP/IP headers = 1500). If it fails but ping -M do -s 1422 works, your path MTU is 1450 — Docker VXLAN overhead confirmed.

💡 Jumbo Frames — When 9000 > 1500

Jumbo frames are Ethernet frames with an MTU larger than the standard 1500 bytes — typically 9000 bytes. They reduce CPU overhead and increase throughput for bulk data transfer by reducing the number of frames (and thus interrupts) needed for large payloads.

ScenarioStandard MTU (1500)Jumbo Frames (9000)Winner
1 GB file transfer~728,000 frames → ~728K interrupts~116,000 frames → ~116K interruptsJumbo (6.3× fewer frames)
iSCSI storage trafficHigh CPU from frequent interruptsLower CPU, higher throughputJumbo — always use for storage
VoIP (64 byte packets)Fits in standard framesWastes 8936 bytes of padding per frameStandard MTU
Internet trafficWorks everywhereBlack holes — most ISPs drop jumbo framesStandard MTU
DC east-west (internal)Works fineBetter for replication/backup trafficJumbo if entire path supports it

The golden rule of jumbo frames: Every device on the L2 segment must support the same MTU. One switch with MTU 1500 on a path where everything else is 9000 = PMTU black hole. This is why jumbo frames are typically only enabled on isolated storage/replication networks, not on general-purpose LANs.

📜 CSMA/CD — The Protocol That Ethernet Outgrew

CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) was the original Ethernet media access method. It's how multiple devices shared a single coaxial cable or hub without a switch to mediate. The algorithm:

  1. Carrier Sense: Listen to the wire. If it's quiet, start transmitting. If it's busy, wait.
  2. Multiple Access: Anyone can transmit when the wire is quiet — there's no central arbitrator.
  3. Collision Detection: While transmitting, listen to your own signal. If what you hear doesn't match what you're sending, a collision occurred (two stations started at the same time).
  4. Jam Signal: On detecting collision, transmit a 32-bit "jam" to ensure all stations notice the collision.
  5. Binary Exponential Backoff: Wait a random time (from 0 to 2ⁿ-1 slot times, where n = attempt number) then retry. After 16 collisions, give up and report error to upper layers.

Why CSMA/CD is dead: It only works in half-duplex mode. Modern switched Ethernet with full-duplex (separate transmit and receive pairs) has zero collisions because each device has a dedicated wire pair to the switch. The switch's buffer handles contention. CSMA/CD hasn't been used in production networks since ~2005, but understanding it explains why the minimum Ethernet frame size (64 bytes) exists — the frame must be long enough for a collision to be detected before transmission completes on the maximum-length cable segment (2500m of coax, 512 bit times at 10 Mbps = 64 bytes).

🛑 Ethernet Flow Control — When the Switch Says "SLOW DOWN"

IEEE 802.3x PAUSE frames allow a switch (or any Ethernet device) to tell its neighbor "I'm overwhelmed — stop sending for X microseconds." When a switch's buffer fills up (traffic arriving faster than it can forward), it sends a PAUSE frame with a quanta value (1 quanta = 512 bit times). The sender stops transmitting for that duration.

The problem with PAUSE frames: They're link-level, not per-flow. A PAUSE frame stops ALL traffic on that link, not just the congested flow. One noisy multicast stream can cause the switch to pause the link, blocking legitimate unicast traffic (head-of-line blocking). This is why flow control is usually disabled in data centers — TCP's own congestion control (which works end-to-end, not just link-local) is smarter and more granular.

SRE check: ethtool -a eth0 shows PAUSE frame settings. If you see Rx PAUSE: on, Tx PAUSE: on and you're experiencing mysterious throughput drops, try disabling flow control: ethtool -A eth0 rx off tx off. Modern DC best practice: flow control OFF, rely on ECN + TCP congestion control instead.

🧠 How a NIC Actually Processes a Frame — DMA, Ring Buffers, Interrupts

When an Ethernet frame arrives at your server's NIC, it doesn't magically appear in your application. Here's the actual path, which matters for performance debugging:

  1. PHY → MAC: The physical layer chip converts voltage/light to bits. The MAC layer verifies the FCS. If FCS fails, the frame is dropped and rx_crc_errors increments. No interrupt is generated.
  2. DMA (Direct Memory Access): The NIC writes the frame directly into a pre-allocated ring buffer in system RAM using DMA — bypassing the CPU. This is why modern NICs achieve line rate: the CPU isn't involved in copying every byte.
  3. Interrupt: After DMA completes, the NIC raises a hardware interrupt (IRQ) to tell the kernel "there's data in the ring buffer." The kernel's NAPI (New API) driver then enters polling mode — processing multiple frames per interrupt instead of one interrupt per frame. This is the difference between "interrupt-driven" (one IRQ per packet, high CPU at high packet rates) and "polling" (process batches, lower CPU).
  4. Kernel processing: The frame (now an sk_buff in Linux) moves through the kernel network stack: netfilter hooks (iptables), routing decision, then up to L4 (TCP/UDP) or forward out another interface.
  5. Userspace delivery: TCP data is copied from kernel space to userspace via recv() or read(). This is the final copy — and the most expensive one for large transfers (context switch overhead).

Performance tuning: ethtool -g eth0 shows ring buffer sizes (RX/TX Ring). If ethtool -S eth0 | grep rx_missed is non-zero, frames are being dropped because the ring buffer is too small — the NIC DMA'd data but the kernel didn't process it fast enough. Increase the ring buffer: ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096. IRQ affinity (/proc/irq/*/smp_affinity) pins NIC interrupts to specific CPU cores to prevent cache bouncing. This is standard SRE work for high-throughput servers (load balancers, database replicas, log shippers).

🎯 Why Ethernet Knowledge Matters for SREs

In modern infrastructure, you rarely configure Ethernet directly — Docker, Kubernetes, and cloud providers abstract it away. But when containers can't communicate, understanding Ethernet is your diagnostic foundation. You need to know: what's the MTU of the underlying interface? Is the switch tagging VLANs? Is ARP resolving correctly? These are L2 questions that CNI plugins, Docker networks, and cloud SDNs all sit on top of.

2.3 MAC Addresses — The Hardware Identity

A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a 48-bit hardware identifier burned into every network interface at the factory. It's the L2 equivalent of a postal address — it identifies which physical device on the local network segment should receive a frame. Unlike IP addresses (which can change), MAC addresses are (mostly) permanent.

MAC ADDRESS ANATOMY — 48 bits, 6 bytes, 12 hex digits
┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│  aa : bb : cc           │  dd : ee : ff            │
│  ─────────────────      │  ─────────────────       │
│  OUI (Organizationally  │  NIC-Specific            │
│  Unique Identifier)     │  (Device ID)             │
│  24 bits — assigned     │  24 bits — assigned      │
│  by IEEE to vendor      │  by vendor to each NIC   │
│                         │                          │
│  Example:               │                          │
│  bc:24:11 = Apple       │  bc:24:11:XX:XX:XX      │
│  00:50:56 = VMware      │  00:50:56:XX:XX:XX      │
│  02:42:ac = Docker      │  02:42:ac:XX:XX:XX      │
│  f0:1f:af = Dell        │  f0:1f:af:XX:XX:XX      │
└─────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
🔍 How to Find MAC Addresses on Linux
$ ip link show | grep ether
    link/ether bc:24:11:4e:0f:2a brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    link/ether 02:42:ac:11:00:02 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff  ← Docker bridge!

$ # Show MAC of all interfaces with vendor lookup
$ ip link show | grep -E '^[0-9]+: ' -A1 | grep ether
📡 Three Types of MAC Destinations
TypeFirst Byte (bit 0)ExampleBehavior
Unicast0 (even)bc:24:11:...Delivered to ONE specific NIC. The switch forwards to a single port.
Multicast1 (odd)01:00:5E:...Delivered to ALL NICs subscribed to that group. Used by OSPF, VRRP, streaming.
BroadcastAll ffff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ffDelivered to EVERY NIC on the L2 segment. ARP requests use this.
📱 MAC Address Randomization — Privacy vs Enterprise

Modern devices (iOS 14+, Android 10+, Windows 11) randomize their MAC addresses for Wi-Fi privacy — the device presents a different random MAC each time it connects to a network or periodically. While great for privacy in coffee shops, this breaks enterprise networks that rely on MAC-based authentication (802.1X with MAC bypass), DHCP static leases, or MAC-based firewall rules. A user's laptop gets a different IP every day because the DHCP server sees a new MAC each time. Solution: Disable private MAC addressing on trusted/corporate networks, or use certificate-based authentication (EAP-TLS) instead of MAC-based.

⚠️ GOTCHA: MAC Addresses Never Cross a Router

MAC addresses are L2-only identifiers. When a frame reaches a router, the router strips the L2 header, makes a routing decision at L3, and encapsulates the packet in a NEW frame with new source/destination MACs for the next hop. If you see the same MAC address on two different subnets, you are not routing — you're on the same L2 broadcast domain. This is a common misconfiguration in "flat" networks.

💡 Docker MAC Addresses

Docker containers get MAC addresses starting with 02:42:ac (a locally-administered prefix). The 02 in the first byte means "locally administered" (bit 1 = 1) — this tells switches "this MAC was manually assigned, not burned in at the factory." Kubernetes pod MACs behave similarly, assigned by the CNI plugin (Calico, Flannel, Cilium).

# Find MAC of your Docker bridge and all containers
$ docker network inspect anihpj_default | jq '.[0].Containers[] | {name: .Name, mac: .MacAddress}'
{
  "name": "anihpj-web-1",
  "mac": "02:42:ac:14:00:02"
}
{
  "name": "anihpj-db-1",
  "mac": "02:42:ac:14:00:03"
}
⚠️ MAC Address Table Overflow Attack — The Switch Becomes a Hub

A switch's CAM table has limited space — typically 8,000 to 128,000 entries depending on the model. In a MAC flooding attack, an attacker sends frames with thousands of random, spoofed source MAC addresses from a single port. The switch dutifully learns each one, filling the CAM table until it overflows.

When the CAM table is full and a frame arrives with an unknown destination MAC, the switch falls back to flooding — sending the frame out ALL ports (like a hub). The attacker can now sniff traffic destined for other hosts, bypassing the switch's normal isolation. This is why managed switches support port security: limiting the number of MAC addresses allowed per port and taking action (shutdown, restrict, or protect) when the limit is exceeded.

# Cisco-style port security configuration (conceptual):
switchport port-security
switchport port-security maximum 5       # Max 5 MACs on this port
switchport port-security violation shutdown # Shut port if exceeded
switchport port-security mac-address sticky # Learn and lock MACs

SRE relevance: In Kubernetes bare-metal deployments, a misbehaving pod (or compromised container) could flood the ToR switch's CAM table with random MACs, degrading performance for every pod on that node. This is why CNI plugins should validate MAC addresses and cloud providers isolate tenant traffic at L3 (not relying on L2 MAC learning).

📐 EUI-64 — When MAC Addresses Had to Grow

Traditional MAC addresses are EUI-48 (48 bits). But IPv6's stateless autoconfiguration (SLAAC) needed a way to generate a 64-bit interface ID from a 48-bit MAC. The solution: EUI-64, which stretches a 48-bit MAC into a 64-bit identifier by inserting FF:FE in the middle and flipping the 7th bit (the universal/local bit).

# EUI-48 MAC:  bc:24:11:4e:0f:2a
# Step 1: Split into two 24-bit halves
#   bc:24:11  |  4e:0f:2a
# Step 2: Insert FF:FE in the middle
#   bc:24:11:FF:FE:4e:0f:2a
# Step 3: Flip the universal/local bit (7th bit of 1st byte)
#   bc = 10111100 → flip bit 7 → 10111110 = be
# EUI-64:  be:24:11:FF:FE:4e:0f:2a

# IPv6 uses this as the interface ID:
# fe80::be24:11ff:fe4e:0f2a/64 (link-local, auto-generated from MAC)

This matters for privacy — because your IPv6 address is derived from your MAC (which is globally unique and permanent), anyone can track your device across networks. Modern OSes use privacy extensions (RFC 4941) that generate random, temporary IPv6 interface IDs instead of using EUI-64.

2.4 Switches — The Silent Workhorses

A switch is a Layer 2 device that forwards Ethernet frames based on destination MAC addresses. Unlike a hub (which repeats every frame to every port), a switch maintains a MAC address table (CAM table) and forwards frames only to the port where the destination MAC lives. This is called microsegmentation — each switch port is its own collision domain.

⚡ Cut-Through vs Store-and-Forward — Latency vs Integrity

Switches have two fundamental forwarding modes. The choice affects latency, error handling, and whether corrupted frames propagate:

PropertyStore-and-ForwardCut-Through
How it worksReceives ENTIRE frame, checks FCS, then forwardsReads only first 14 bytes (dest MAC), immediately starts forwarding
LatencyHigher — stores whole frame first (e.g., 12μs @ 10G for a 1500B frame)Lower — begins forwarding after ~1.2μs (14 bytes @ 10G)
Error handling✅ Drops corrupted frames (FCS mismatch)⚠️ Forwards corrupted frames — FCS not yet received when forwarding starts
Frame size check✅ Drops runts (< 64B) and giants (> MTU)⚠️ May forward illegal-sized frames
Use caseEnterprise/DC access switchesHigh-frequency trading, HPC (where 10μs matters)
VariantStandard on all managed switchesFragment-free: reads first 64 bytes (covers collision window), then forwards

Modern reality: Most data center switches use store-and-forward (or fragment-free) because the latency difference is negligible at 25G+ speeds (~1μs extra) and error propagation through cut-through can cause hard-to-diagnose corruption at upper layers. Cut-through is niche — financial trading firms where every microsecond translates to dollars.

📊 Microbursts — The Hidden Cause of "Mystery Packet Loss"

A microburst is a sub-second spike in traffic that saturates a switch port's buffer, causing tail-drop packet loss — but it's invisible on your 1-minute-average monitoring graphs. Imagine 10 servers all send 1MB to the same destination within 100 microseconds. The switch receives 10MB in 100μs but can only forward at line rate (say 10 Gbps = ~1.25 GB/s). The switch buffer absorbs some, then drops the rest.

Why microbursts are hard to catch: Your monitoring shows 15% utilization (1-minute average). But within that minute, there were 750 microbursts at 100% line rate lasting 50μs each. ethtool -S eth0 | grep tx_dropped shows non-zero — the switch is dropping packets but your graphs look fine. TCP sees random packet loss and slows down (congestion control kicks in), but you don't know why.

Detection: You need sub-second monitoring (hardware counters polled every 100ms, or sFlow/NetFlow with sub-second sampling) to see microbursts. Tools like perfSONAR and switch hardware buffer monitoring (e.g., Cisco's "microburst detection") can help. Mitigation: Increase switch buffer size, implement QoS/priority queuing, or use Data Center TCP (DCTCP) with ECN marking instead of tail-drop.

SWITCH MAC LEARNING — 4-Step Process
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SWITCH MAC ADDRESS TABLE (CAM) — initially empty                   │
│  ┌──────────────────┬─────────┐                                     │
│  │ MAC Address      │ Port    │                                     │
│  ├──────────────────┼─────────┤                                     │
│  │ (empty)          │         │                                     │
│  └──────────────────┴─────────┘                                     │
│                                                                      │
│  Step 1: Host A (MAC aa:bb:cc:11:22:33) on Port 1 sends to Host B  │
│           Switch reads SOURCE MAC → learns A = Port 1               │
│           Switch looks up DEST MAC → NOT FOUND → FLOOD to all ports │
│                                                                      │
│  Step 2: Host B (MAC aa:bb:cc:44:55:66) on Port 2 receives frame   │
│           Host B responds → Switch reads SOURCE MAC → B = Port 2   │
│           Switch looks up DEST MAC (A) → FOUND on Port 1 → FORWARD  │
│                                                                      │
│  ┌──────────────────┬─────────┐                                     │
│  │ aa:bb:cc:11:22:33│ Port 1  │  ← Learned from Step 1              │
│  │ aa:bb:cc:44:55:66│ Port 2  │  ← Learned from Step 2              │
│  └──────────────────┴─────────┘                                     │
│                                                                      │
│  Now all traffic between A and B is FORWARDED only Ports 1↔2       │
│  Other ports never see these frames — that's microsegmentation.     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔄 The Three F's of Switching
ActionWhenWhat Happens
FORWARDDest MAC is in CAM tableFrame goes out ONLY the port where the MAC lives. Efficient.
FLOODDest MAC is NOT in CAM tableFrame goes out ALL ports except the one it came in on. Inefficient but necessary for learning.
FILTERDest MAC is on the SAME port as sourceFrame is dropped — no need to forward back to the sender's port.
🌉 Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) — Why Loops Kill Networks

If you connect two switches together with TWO cables (for redundancy), you've created a bridge loop. A broadcast frame enters one switch, gets flooded out all ports (including both links to the other switch), the other switch floods it back, and the frame circulates forever, multiplying with each loop. Within seconds, the network is saturated with duplicate broadcast traffic — this is a broadcast storm that brings down the entire L2 domain.

STP (IEEE 802.1D) prevents this by disabling redundant links until they're needed. It elects a Root Bridge, then blocks certain ports to ensure there's exactly ONE active path between any two switches. If the active link fails, STP unblocks the backup link within 30-50 seconds (RSTP, 802.1w, does it in < 1 second).

SRE relevance: If you see a port in BLOCKING or DISCARDING state on a managed switch, STP is doing its job — it blocked a redundant path to prevent a loop. Don't disable STP unless you're absolutely sure there's no physical loop. Modern data centers often replace STP with Layer 3 fabrics (BGP/EVPN) that don't need loop prevention because L3 has TTL to kill looping packets.

🏷️ VLANs — Splitting One Physical Switch into Many Logical Networks

A VLAN (Virtual LAN, IEEE 802.1Q) lets you partition a single physical switch into multiple isolated broadcast domains. Frames are tagged with a 4-byte 802.1Q header containing a 12-bit VLAN ID (0-4095). A broadcast on VLAN 10 never reaches VLAN 20 — they behave like separate physical switches. Without VLANs, one physical switch = one broadcast domain = every host sees every broadcast.

Port TypeVLAN BehaviorUse Case
Access PortCarries traffic for ONE VLAN only. Frames are untagged (no 802.1Q header).Connecting a server/container host to VLAN 100.
Trunk PortCarries traffic for MULTIPLE VLANs. All frames are 802.1Q-tagged (except native VLAN).Switch-to-switch links, switch-to-hypervisor (VMware/KVM).
🏭 Managed vs Unmanaged Switches — What's the Difference?
FeatureUnmanaged SwitchManaged Switch
VLAN support❌ None — single broadcast domain✅ 802.1Q VLAN tagging, trunking
SNMP / Monitoring❌ No statistics or alerts✅ SNMP, port counters, RMON, sFlow/NetFlow
Port Mirroring (SPAN)❌ Cannot mirror traffic✅ Mirror any port to analyzer (tcpdump/Wireshark)
Link Aggregation (LACP)❌ No bonding✅ 802.3ad LAG for bandwidth/ redundancy
STP (Spanning Tree)❌ Loop prevention absent✅ STP/RSTP/MSTP prevents broadcast storms
CoS/QoS❌ No prioritization✅ Traffic shaping, 802.1p priority tagging
Security❌ No access controls✅ 802.1X, port security, MAC filtering, ACLs
Cost$15-50 (8-port)$200-5000+ depending on features

SRE relevance: If you're debugging a network issue in an office or small DC, the first question is: "Is this a managed or unmanaged switch?" Unmanaged = you have zero visibility beyond what the server's NIC tells you. Managed = you can check port counters, mirror traffic, and see VLAN assignments. Never deploy production infrastructure behind an unmanaged switch.

⚠️ GOTCHA: The Silent VLAN Drop

If a switch port is configured for VLAN 100 but receives an untagged frame (or a frame tagged with VLAN 200), the switch silently drops it. No ICMP error. No log entry (on unmanaged switches). The packet simply vanishes. This makes VLAN misconfigurations one of the hardest networking problems to debug — the symptoms look exactly like a broken cable, but ethtool shows the link is fine. Always check VLAN assignments when a new server can't communicate.

2.5 ARP — How IP Addresses Become MAC Addresses

Here's the fundamental problem at L2/L3 boundary: IP knows the destination address (192.168.1.5), but Ethernet needs the destination MAC address to actually deliver the frame. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) bridges this gap. It's a simple question-and-answer protocol: "Who has IP X? Tell me your MAC."

ARP EXCHANGE — Request (Broadcast) → Reply (Unicast)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Host A (10.0.1.1, MAC aa:bb:cc:11:22:33)                       │
│  wants to send to Host B (10.0.1.5) but doesn't know B's MAC    │
│                                                                   │
│  STEP 1: ARP REQUEST (Broadcast to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff)            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ Src MAC: aa:bb:cc:11:22:33  Dst MAC: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff    │ │
│  │ EtherType: 0x0806 (ARP)                                     │ │
│  │                                                              │ │
│  │ ARP Message:                                                │ │
│  │   Hardware: Ethernet (1)   Protocol: IPv4 (0x0800)         │ │
│  │   Sender MAC: aa:bb:cc:11:22:33  Sender IP: 10.0.1.1      │ │
│  │   Target MAC: 00:00:00:00:00:00  Target IP: 10.0.1.5      │ │
│  │   Operation: 1 (Request)                                    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                    │                                               │
│                    ▼ (every host on the segment receives this)     │
│                                                                   │
│  STEP 2: ARP REPLY (Unicast — only to Host A)                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ Src MAC: aa:bb:cc:44:55:66  Dst MAC: aa:bb:cc:11:22:33    │ │
│  │ EtherType: 0x0806 (ARP)                                     │ │
│  │                                                              │ │
│  │ ARP Message:                                                │ │
│  │   Sender MAC: aa:bb:cc:44:55:66  Sender IP: 10.0.1.5      │ │
│  │   Target MAC: aa:bb:cc:11:22:33  Target IP: 10.0.1.1      │ │
│  │   Operation: 2 (Reply)                                      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                   │
│  Host A now caches 10.0.1.5 → aa:bb:cc:44:55:66 in its ARP table │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
ARP PACKET WALK-THROUGH — tcpdump Annotated with Hex Dump
$ tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -e -xx arp

# ─── ARP REQUEST (Broadcast) ───
10:23:45.123456 aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42:
  Request who-has 10.0.1.5 tell 10.0.1.1, length 28

  Hex dump (byte-by-byte of the Ethernet frame):
  0x0000:  ffff ffff ffff  ← Destination MAC = Broadcast (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff)
  0x0006:  aabb ccdd ee01  ← Source MAC = 10.0.1.1's NIC (aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01)
  0x000c:  0806            ← EtherType = 0x0806 = ARP
  ─── ARP Payload starts here (bytes 14+) ───
  0x000e:  0001            ← Hardware Type = Ethernet (1)
  0x0010:  0800            ← Protocol Type = IPv4 (0x0800)
  0x0012:  06              ← Hardware Address Length = 6 (MAC)
  0x0013:  04              ← Protocol Address Length = 4 (IPv4)
  0x0014:  0001            ← Operation = 1 (REQUEST)
  0x0016:  aabb ccdd ee01  ← Sender MAC = aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01
  0x001c:  0a00 0101       ← Sender IP = 10.0.1.1 (0x0a000101)
  0x0020:  0000 0000 0000  ← Target MAC = 00:00:00:00:00:00 (unknown!)
  0x0026:  0a00 0105       ← Target IP = 10.0.1.5 (0x0a000105)

# ─── ARP REPLY (Unicast — 2μs later) ───
10:23:45.123458 aa:bb:cc:44:55:66 > aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42:
  Reply 10.0.1.5 is-at aa:bb:cc:44:55:66, length 28

  Hex dump:
  0x0000:  aabb ccdd ee01  ← Destination MAC = Requestor's MAC (unicast!)
  0x0006:  aabb cc44 5566  ← Source MAC = 10.0.1.5's NIC
  0x000c:  0806            ← EtherType = 0x0806 = ARP
  0x000e:  0001            ← Hardware Type = Ethernet
  0x0010:  0800            ← Protocol Type = IPv4
  0x0012:  06              ← HW Addr Len = 6
  0x0013:  04              ← Proto Addr Len = 4
  0x0014:  0002            ← Operation = 2 (REPLY) ← THIS IS THE KEY DIFFERENCE!
  0x0016:  aabb cc44 5566  ← Sender MAC = aa:bb:cc:44:55:66 (target's MAC)
  0x001c:  0a00 0105       ← Sender IP = 10.0.1.5
  0x0020:  aabb ccdd ee01  ← Target MAC = aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01 (requestor)
  0x0026:  0a00 0101       ← Target IP = 10.0.1.1

🔑 KEY DIFFERENCES REQUEST vs REPLY:
  • Request: Dst MAC = ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff (broadcast), Operation = 1
  • Reply:   Dst MAC = requester's MAC (unicast), Operation = 2
  • Request: Target MAC = 00:00:00:00:00:00 (unknown)
  • Reply:   Target MAC = requester's MAC (known, filled in)
📋 ARP Cache States — What ip neigh show Tells You
StateMeaningAction
REACHABLENeighbor confirmed reachable (recently communicated)✅ Good — no action needed
STALEEntry still usable but hasn't been confirmed recently✅ Good — will be re-verified on next use
DELAYWaiting for confirmation after using a STALE entry⏳ Transient — wait for REACHABLE or PROBE
PROBESending unicast ARP probes to confirm reachability⏳ Transient — 3 probes sent, 1s apart
FAILEDAll probes failed — neighbor is unreachable🚩 Problem — check cable, switch, or host state
 
$ ip neigh show
10.0.1.1 dev eth0 lladdr aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01 REACHABLE   ← Default gateway, alive
10.0.1.5 dev eth0 lladdr aa:bb:cc:44:55:66 STALE       ← Hasn't talked recently (OK)
10.0.1.99 dev eth0 lladdr aa:bb:cc:88:99:00 FAILED      ← 🚩 Unreachable neighbor!
10.0.1.200 dev eth0 INCOMPLETE                           ← ARP request sent, no reply yet
⚠️ GOTCHA: STALE ≠ Broken

Many engineers panic when they see STALE entries. STALE is normal. It means "I haven't talked to this host in a while, but the cached MAC might still be good." Linux will use the STALE entry and send a unicast ARP probe in the background to confirm it. Only FAILED or INCOMPLETE (with no subsequent REACHABLE) indicate a real problem.

💡 Gratuitous ARP — "I Am 10.0.1.5!" (Unsolicited)

A Gratuitous ARP (GARP) is an ARP reply sent without a corresponding request. It announces "My IP is X at MAC Y" to the entire broadcast domain. Used by:

  • IP failover (keepalived, VRRP): When the backup takes over the VIP, it sends a GARP so switches and hosts update their ARP caches instantly.
  • Duplicate IP detection: A host sends GARP when bringing up an interface — if someone else responds, there's an IP conflict.
  • Cluster failover: Kubernetes LoadBalancer services, HAProxy, NGINX failover pairs.
🔄 Proxy ARP — When a Router Answers for Another Subnet

Normally, ARP only works within a broadcast domain (same subnet). If Host A (10.0.1.5/24) sends an ARP request for 10.0.2.10 (different subnet), no one on 10.0.1.0/24 will answer — it's a different L2 domain. But with Proxy ARP enabled, the router pretends to be the target host: it answers the ARP request with its OWN MAC address, saying "Send the frame to me, I'll route it to 10.0.2.10."

Proxy ARP was useful when hosts didn't understand subnetting (1980s) and assumed every IP was on the same LAN. Today it's mostly disabled because it breaks network segmentation and creates security risks (an attacker can use Proxy ARP to intercept traffic meant for other subnets).

# Check if Proxy ARP is enabled (should be 0 on modern systems)
$ cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/eth0/proxy_arp
1   ← 🚩 Enabled! Router will answer ARP for other subnets

$ # Disable:
$ sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.eth0.proxy_arp=0
⚠️ ARP Flux — When Multiple Interfaces Have the Same Subnet

ARP flux occurs when a Linux host has two interfaces (e.g., eth0 and eth1) on the same IP subnet. When the host receives an ARP request on eth0 for its IP, it might respond from eth1's MAC address (or vice versa). The requesting host caches the "wrong" MAC, and future unicast traffic goes to an interface that isn't expecting it — or worse, to a completely different physical path.

This is why Linux has ARP filtering (arp_filter) and ARP announce/ignore sysctls:

# ARP filtering: only answer ARP if the requesting IP would route out this interface
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_filter=1

# ARP announce modes (which source IP to use in ARP replies):
# 0 — Use any local address (default, can cause flux)
# 1 — Use address on the same subnet as the target
# 2 — Always use the best local address for the target
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_announce=2

# ARP ignore modes (which ARP requests to respond to):
# 0 — Respond to any local address on any interface
# 1 — Respond only if target IP is on the incoming interface
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_ignore=1

Kubernetes relevance: Nodes with multiple network interfaces (management + pod network) must configure ARP filtering to prevent ARP flux. CNI plugins often set these sysctls automatically. If you ever see a pod reachable by IP but connections flap between interfaces, suspect ARP flux.

🔧 Kernel ARP Tuning for SREs

The Linux kernel exposes extensive ARP tuning parameters under /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh/*/. Here are the ones that matter for infrastructure:

ParameterDefaultPurposeSRE Note
gc_stale_time60sHow often the garbage collector checks for stale ARP entriesReduce to 30s on highly dynamic networks (containers)
gc_thresh1128Minimum ARP table entries before GC activatesIncrease for nodes with many containers (K8s nodes may need 1024+)
gc_thresh2512Soft maximum — GC becomes more aggressive above thisK8s nodes with 100+ pods need 2048-4096
gc_thresh31024Hard maximum — refuses new ARP entries above this🚩 If hit, new neighbors unreachable! Increase for large clusters
base_reachable_time_ms30000How long (ms) a REACHABLE entry stays before becoming STALEIncrease for stable DC (reduces ARP probes)
delay_first_probe_time5sWait before first probe after STALE entry is usedReduce to 1-2s for faster failover detection
mcast_solicit3Number of ARP probes sent before marking FAILEDIncrease to 5 on unreliable networks
 
# Check current ARP cache limits
$ cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh/default/gc_thresh1
$ cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh/default/gc_thresh2
$ cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh/default/gc_thresh3

# For a Kubernetes node with 250 pods (each pod has its own veth pair = ARP entry):
sysctl -w net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh1=2048
sysctl -w net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh2=4096
sysctl -w net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh3=8192

# Verify in dmesg if ARP table overflowed:
$ dmesg | grep -i "neighbour table overflow"
# neighbour: arp_cache: neighbor table overflow!
# ↑ This means gc_thresh3 was hit — increase immediately!
⚠️ ARP Spoofing/Poisoning — The Classic MITM Attack

An attacker sends forged ARP replies claiming "I am the default gateway (10.0.1.1) at MY MAC address." Hosts update their ARP caches and start sending traffic to the attacker instead of the real gateway. The attacker can then inspect, modify, or drop traffic before forwarding it to the real gateway. Mitigation: Static ARP entries for critical infrastructure, DHCP snooping + Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches.

Watch ARP in Real Time with tcpdump 
# Watch all ARP traffic on eth0
$ tcpdump -i eth0 -nn arp
10:23:45.123456 ARP, Request who-has 10.0.1.5 tell 10.0.1.1, length 28
10:23:45.123458 ARP, Reply 10.0.1.5 is-at aa:bb:cc:44:55:66, length 28

# Watch with verbose output (see MAC addresses)
$ tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -e arp
10:23:45.123456 aa:bb:cc:11:22:33 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ARP, length 28: \
  Request who-has 10.0.1.5 tell 10.0.1.1

# Watch for gratuitous ARP (unsolicited replies)
$ tcpdump -i eth0 -nn arp and arp[6:2] == 2
# arp[6:2] = operation field (offset 6, 2 bytes). 2 = Reply.

2.6 🛠️ LAB — Layer 2 Hands-On with anihpj

Put everything together. You'll inspect your interfaces, examine ARP behavior, and debug a simulated L2 connectivity failure in the anihpj Docker Compose environment.

1
Inspect Your Interfaces

Check link state, speed, duplex — the L1 baseline.

$ ip link show
$ ethtool eth0        # Speed? Duplex? Link detected?
$ ethtool -S eth0     # Any error counters?
2
Find Your MAC Addresses

Identify the hardware addresses of host interfaces and Docker containers.

$ ip link show | grep ether    # Host interfaces
$ docker network inspect anihpj_default | jq '.[0].Containers[] | {name: .Name, mac: .MacAddress, ip: .IPv4Address}'
3
Examine the ARP Cache

Inspect neighbor entries — the L2 address resolution table.

$ ip neigh show                          # All neighbors
$ ip neigh show dev docker0               # Only Docker bridge neighbors
$ ping -c 1 172.17.0.2 && ip neigh show  # Trigger ARP, then check state
4
Watch ARP Live

Capture ARP traffic in real time using tcpdump on the Docker bridge.

# Terminal 1: Watch ARP traffic
$ sudo tcpdump -i docker0 -nn -e arp

# Terminal 2: Generate ARP traffic
$ docker exec anihpj-web-1 ping -c 1 anihpj-db-1
5
Debug Scenario: "Pod Can't Reach Gateway"

Symptom: An anihpj container can't reach the internet. ping 8.8.8.8 fails. ping localhost works.

# Step 1: Check L1 — is the interface up?
$ docker exec anihpj-web-1 ip link show eth0
# Look for: state UP

# Step 2: Check L2 — can we resolve the gateway's MAC?
$ docker exec anihpj-web-1 ip neigh show
# Look for: 172.17.0.1 ... REACHABLE (the Docker bridge = gateway)
# If FAILED or INCOMPLETE → ARP is broken

# Step 3: Check ARP manually
$ docker exec anihpj-web-1 arping -c 3 172.17.0.1
# ARPING 172.17.0.1 from 172.17.0.2 eth0
# Unicast reply from 172.17.0.1 [02:42:ac:11:00:01] 0.050ms ← Gateway responds!

# Step 4: If ARP works but ping 8.8.8.8 still fails → L3+ issue (routing/NAT)
$ docker exec anihpj-web-1 ip route show
# default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0 ← Is the default route present?
6
MTU Discovery — Find Your Path MTU

Binary-search for the largest packet that traverses the path without fragmentation.

# Test if 1500-byte packets traverse the path (1472 data + 28 ICMP/IP = 1500)
$ ping -M do -s 1472 -c 3 8.8.8.8
# If it fails, binary search for the MTU:
$ ping -M do -s 1400 -c 3 8.8.8.8    # Works?
$ ping -M do -s 1450 -c 3 8.8.8.8    # Works?
$ ping -M do -s 1470 -c 3 8.8.8.8    # Fails? MTU is 1470 → PMTU = 1470+28 = 1498

# Check your interface MTU
$ ip link show eth0 | grep mtu
# Check the Docker bridge MTU
$ ip link show docker0 | grep mtu

# If container MTU (1500) > path MTU (1450 with VXLAN), large packets die silently
7
Watch ARP Cache State Transitions Live

Observe the complete ARP lifecycle: INCOMPLETE → REACHABLE → STALE → DELAY → PROBE.

# Watch ARP cache in real-time (run in a loop, Ctrl+C to stop)
$ watch -n 0.5 'ip neigh show dev eth0'

# In another terminal, ping a neighbor and watch states change:
# 1. INCOMPLETE → ARP request sent, waiting for reply
# 2. REACHABLE → Reply received, all good
# 3. STALE → Timer expired, but entry is still usable
# 4. DELAY → Was STALE, now used, waiting before probing
# 5. PROBE → Sending unicast ARP to verify
# 6. REACHABLE → Confirmed! (or FAILED if no response)

# Force-delete an ARP entry and watch it rebuild:
$ sudo ip neigh del 10.0.1.5 dev eth0
$ ping -c 1 10.0.1.5  # Triggers new ARP request
$ ip neigh show dev eth0  # Should be back to REACHABLE
8
Check NIC Performance — Ring Buffers & IRQ Affinity

Tune the kernel-to-NIC data pipeline for high-throughput workloads.

# Check ring buffer sizes (RX = receive, TX = transmit)
$ ethtool -g eth0
Ring parameters for eth0:
Pre-set maximums:
RX:             4096        # Max the hardware supports
TX:             4096
Current hardware settings:
RX:             256         # ← Currently only 256 descriptors! Increase if rx_missed > 0
TX:             256

# Increase ring buffer (if rx_missed counter in ethtool -S is non-zero)
$ sudo ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096 tx 4096

# Check which CPU handles NIC interrupts (IRQ affinity)
$ cat /proc/interrupts | grep eth0
 123:   45678901   PCI-MSI  eth0-tx-0
 124:   23456789   PCI-MSI  eth0-rx-0

# See which CPU core each IRQ is bound to:
$ cat /proc/irq/123/smp_affinity
00000001  # CPU 0 only (bitmask)

# For multi-queue NICs, spread IRQs across cores:
$ sudo ethtool -L eth0 combined 4  # Enable 4 RX/TX queues
$ cat /proc/interrupts | grep eth0  # Now shows eth0-tx-0 through tx-3, rx-0 through rx-3

🔭 Chapter 2 — Visual Summary

🔌 Layer 1 = Physical

Cables, signals, link state, speed, duplex. Check with ethtool and ip link show. UP ≠ healthy — always check error counters.

📦 Layer 2 = Frames

Ethernet frames carry IP packets. 72-1526 bytes each. Every frame has a source MAC, destination MAC, and FCS checksum.

🏷️ MAC = Hardware ID

48-bit burned-in address. First 24 bits = vendor (OUI). Docker: 02:42:ac. Never crosses a router.

🔀 Switches Learn

MAC table built from source addresses. Forward (known MAC), Flood (unknown MAC), Filter (same port). VLANs = isolated broadcast domains.

📡 ARP = IP→MAC

Broadcast request: "Who has IP X?" → Unicast reply: "IP X is at MAC Y." Cache states: REACHABLE, STALE, FAILED.

🐞 Start at L1

70% of "server down" issues are L1/L2. Bad cable, CRC errors, VLAN mismatch, stale ARP. Work bottom-up to save hours.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 2

⚡Auto-Negotiation
The process where two Ethernet devices negotiate the highest mutually-supported speed and duplex mode. Failures cause speed/duplex mismatches — one side thinks it's 1000/Full, the other 100/Half = massive collisions and packet loss.
📏MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit)
The largest L3 packet (in bytes) that can be sent without fragmentation. Standard Ethernet: 1500. Jumbo frames: 9000. Docker VXLAN overhead reduces effective MTU by 50 bytes — set container MTU to 1450.
🔍CAM Table (Content Addressable Memory)
The switch's MAC address lookup table. Maps MAC address → switch port. Built automatically by reading source MACs from incoming frames. Limited size (typically 8K-128K entries). When full, switch falls back to flooding.
🏷️802.1Q (VLAN Tagging)
The IEEE standard that inserts a 4-byte tag into Ethernet frames, carrying a 12-bit VLAN ID (0-4095) and a 3-bit priority field (CoS). Tagged frames can carry multiple VLANs on a single trunk link.
🪞FCS (Frame Check Sequence)
A 4-byte CRC32 checksum appended to every Ethernet frame. The receiving NIC recomputes and compares. Mismatch = corrupted frame = silently dropped. Check ethtool -S | grep crc — any non-zero means a physical layer problem.
🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work

You probably won't crimp Ethernet cables or configure switch VLANs daily as an SRE. But every time you debug a connectivity issue, you'll use L1/L2 knowledge: reading ethtool output to spot CRC errors, checking ARP caches to see if a neighbor is reachable, verifying MTU settings when Docker overlay networks drop large packets, and understanding why a Kubernetes node can't reach pods on another node (wrong VLAN, ARP failure, or a bad cable).

What L1/L2 skills look like in practice:

  • On-call: "Server unreachable" alert fires. You SSH in. ip link show → UP. ethtool -S eth0 → 50,000 CRC errors. Cable replaced. Issue resolved in 3 minutes instead of 3 hours of application debugging.
  • Docker networking: Container can't reach external API. You check ip route → default route missing because Docker daemon restarted and didn't re-add it. L3 fix, but you found it by tracing L1→L2→L3.
  • Kubernetes CNI: Pods on node-1 can't reach pods on node-2. You tcpdump on the node interface and see VXLAN packets leaving but none arriving. Switch between nodes has port security blocking unknown MACs. L2 problem at the physical switch level.
  • Interview: "Walk me through troubleshooting an unreachable server." Starting at L1 (ip link, ethtool) marks you as an SRE. Starting at L7 ("I'd check the application logs") marks you as a developer.

🔑 Chapter 2 Key Takeaways

Layer 1 and Layer 2 are the foundation of ALL networking. Every packet, every connection, every HTTP request ultimately travels as voltage changes (L1) inside Ethernet frames (L2). Here's what you must remember:

  1. Always start at L1. ip link show → is the interface UP? ethtool eth0 → speed, duplex, link detected? ethtool -S eth0 → any error counters? Fixing a bad cable takes 2 minutes and solves problems that would otherwise consume hours of application debugging.
  2. UP ≠ Healthy. A link can show UP and still have 90% packet loss from CRC errors. Always check error counters. CRC errors are ALWAYS a physical problem — cable, connector, or port.
  3. MAC addresses are L2-only. They never cross a router. If you see the same MAC on two subnets, you're bridged, not routed. Docker containers use 02:42:ac prefix (locally administered).
  4. Switches learn from source MACs, forward by destination MACs. Empty CAM table = flooding (inefficient). Populated CAM table = forwarding (efficient). VLANs split one switch into many isolated broadcast domains.
  5. ARP bridges L3 (IP) to L2 (MAC). Broadcast request, unicast reply. Cache states: REACHABLE → good, STALE → still usable, FAILED → problem. Gratuitous ARP enables sub-second IP failover.
  6. MTU matters. Docker VXLAN adds 50 bytes overhead. If physical MTU is 1500, container MTU must be ≤ 1450. PMTU black holes cause silent packet drops — the hardest networking problem to debug.
  7. Bottom-up debugging is faster. L1 → L2 → L3 → L4 → L7. The flowchart from Section 2.2 should be your mental model for every connectivity incident.
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 2.1 — Diagnose L1/L2 from ethtool Output

You're handed the following ethtool output from a server experiencing "intermittent connectivity." Identify every problem.

Settings for eth0:
    Speed: 100Mb/s          ← Should be 1000Mb/s
    Duplex: Half             ← 🚩 Should be Full!
    Link detected: yes       ← Physical link present
    Auto-negotiation: off   ← 🚩 Should be ON

$ ethtool -S eth0
    rx_crc_errors: 89721   ← 🚩 Bad cable!
    collisions: 4502
    rx_missed_errors: 1238
  1. What's wrong with the speed and duplex?
  2. Why are there collisions in a "switched" network?
  3. What do CRC errors indicate?
  4. What's the FIRST thing you should do?
💡 Hint: Half-duplex means the NIC is operating like it's on a hub — it waits for silence before transmitting and detects collisions. In a switched full-duplex network, collisions should always be ZERO.
📝 View Solution 
# Problem 1: Speed 100Mb/s + Half Duplex
# Auto-negotiation is OFF — one side (or both) is hard-coded wrong.
# 100/Half in a modern DC = something is very broken.
# Expected: 1000Mb/s, Full duplex.

# Problem 2: 4502 collisions in a switched network
# Collisions only happen in half-duplex mode.
# This NIC is operating in CSMA/CD mode (carrier sense, collision detect).
# Every collision = retransmission = added latency.

# Problem 3: 89,721 CRC errors
# The cable is physically damaged. Frames are arriving corrupted.
# The NIC detects bad FCS and drops the frame silently.
# TCP retransmits, adding 200ms+ per lost frame.

# FIRST THING TO DO:
# 1. Replace the cable immediately (CRC errors = physical damage)
# 2. Enable auto-negotiation on both sides: ethtool -s eth0 autoneg on
# 3. Verify: ethtool eth0 → Speed: 1000Mb/s, Duplex: Full
# 4. Check ethtool -S eth0 | grep -E 'err|drop' → should all be 0 or not increasing
⏱️ Target: 7 minutes
Drill 2.2 — ARP Debugging in anihpj Docker Network

The anihpj-web-1 container (172.18.0.2) needs to reach anihpj-db-1 (172.18.0.3). Run through the full ARP debugging flow.

  1. Check the ARP cache on the web container: docker exec anihpj-web-1 ip neigh show
  2. If 172.18.0.3 shows FAILED or INCOMPLETE, manually trigger ARP: docker exec anihpj-web-1 arping -c 3 172.18.0.3
  3. While arping runs, capture ARP traffic: sudo tcpdump -i br-anihpj -nn -e arp
  4. Identify the ARP request and reply in the tcpdump output. Note the MAC addresses.
  5. If no ARP reply comes, what L1/L2 checks would you make?
💡 Hint: If arping gets no reply, the target host isn't on the same L2 segment, or its interface is down. Check docker exec anihpj-db-1 ip link show eth0 — is it UP?
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Check ARP cache

Drill 2.3 — Ethernet Frame Dissection

Given this raw Ethernet frame (hex), decode every field:

Raw Ethernet Frame (hex) — decode each field:
ff ff ff ff ff ff  bc 24 11 4e 0f 2a  08 06  00 01
08 00  06  04  00 01  bc 24 11 4e 0f 2a  c0 a8 01 01
00 00 00 00 00 00  c0 a8 01 05  00 00 00 00 00 00
00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
  1. What is the destination MAC?
  2. What is the source MAC? Which vendor (OUI)?
  3. What is the EtherType? What protocol does it indicate?
  4. What type of message is this? (Hint: look at the operation field at offset 20-21)
  5. What are the sender and target IP addresses?
💡 Hint: Bytes 0-5 = Dest MAC, 6-11 = Src MAC, 12-13 = EtherType. For ARP (EtherType 0x0806), bytes 14-15 = Hardware type, 16-17 = Protocol type, 20-21 = Operation (1=Request, 2=Reply).
📝 View Solution 
# Byte-by-byte dissection:

# Bytes 0-5: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
# → Destination MAC = BROADCAST (all hosts on the segment)

# Bytes 6-11: bc:24:11:4e:0f:2a
# → Source MAC. OUI bc:24:11 = Apple, Inc.
# → This frame came from an Apple device.

# Bytes 12-13: 0x0806
# → EtherType = ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)

# Bytes 14-15: 0x0001 = Hardware type: Ethernet (1)
# Bytes 16-17: 0x0800 = Protocol type: IPv4
# Byte 18: 0x06 = Hardware address length: 6 (MAC = 6 bytes)
# Byte 19: 0x04 = Protocol address length: 4 (IPv4 = 4 bytes)

# Bytes 20-21: 0x0001 = Operation: 1 (ARP REQUEST)

# Bytes 22-27: bc:24:11:4e:0f:2a = Sender MAC
# Bytes 28-31: c0:a8:01:01 = Sender IP = 192.168.1.1

# Bytes 32-37: 00:00:00:00:00:00 = Target MAC (unknown — this is what we're asking!)
# Bytes 38-41: c0:a8:01:05 = Target IP = 192.168.1.5

# Bytes 42+: Padding (zeros to reach minimum 46-byte payload)

# SUMMARY: This is an ARP REQUEST from an Apple device (192.168.1.1)
# asking "Who has 192.168.1.5? Tell me your MAC address!"

📝 Chapter 2 — Practice Questions

Q1
A server's ip link show eth0 shows state UP and ethtool eth0 shows Link detected: yes, Speed: 1000Mb/s, Duplex: Full. However, ethtool -S eth0 shows rx_crc_errors: 245,891 and the count is increasing by ~100/second. Packets are being dropped — applications report timeouts. What is the most likely cause, and what is the FIRST action you should take?
Show Answer
Answer

The most likely cause is a physically damaged Ethernet cable or a faulty connector/port. CRC errors mean the Frame Check Sequence at L2 doesn't match — bits are being corrupted in transit. The link appears UP and negotiated at correct speed/duplex, but the signal quality is terrible.

First action: Replace the cable immediately. If CRC errors persist after cable replacement, try a different switch port. If they still persist, replace the NIC. CRC errors are ALWAYS a physical layer problem — never an application or protocol issue.

Explanation

This scenario tests the critical distinction between "link is UP" and "link is healthy." Auto-negotiation only negotiates speed and duplex — it doesn't test signal quality. A cable with a broken conductor may still pass enough signal to keep the link UP while corrupting every Nth frame. CRC errors are the definitive L1 health indicator because they're checked at L2 before the frame enters the kernel — if the FCS doesn't match, the NIC drops the frame and increments the counter. The kernel never sees it.

Q2
Draw and label the complete Ethernet frame structure. What is the minimum and maximum frame size (in bytes)? Why is the minimum payload 46 bytes? What happens if an IP packet is smaller than 46 bytes?
Show Answer
Answer

The Ethernet frame: Preamble(8) + DestMAC(6) + SrcMAC(6) + EtherType(2) + Payload(46-1500) + FCS(4) = 72-1526 bytes.

The minimum payload of 46 bytes exists because Ethernet's collision detection (CSMA/CD) requires a minimum frame size of 64 bytes (excluding preamble) for the signal to propagate across the maximum cable length and back before transmission ends. 64 - 6(DestMAC) - 6(SrcMAC) - 2(EtherType) - 4(FCS) = 46 bytes minimum payload.

If an IP packet is smaller than 46 bytes (e.g., a 32-byte ARP message), the Ethernet layer pads the payload with zeros to reach 46 bytes. The EtherType or IP header's length field tells the receiver where the real data ends and padding begins. This padding is invisible to L3 and above.

Explanation

The 46-byte minimum is a historical artifact of CSMA/CD collision detection, which is irrelevant in modern full-duplex switched networks. But the minimum remains for backward compatibility. This is a classic interview question that tests whether you understand the why behind protocol design, not just the what.

Q3
A switch receives a frame destined for MAC aa:bb:cc:11:22:33. Its CAM table is empty. What does the switch do? Walk through the learning process that follows.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Unknown Unicast Flooding: The switch floods the frame out ALL ports except the one it arrived on. This is an "unknown unicast" — the switch knows it's not a broadcast (MAC isn't ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff) but doesn't know which port the destination is on.

2. Source Learning: Simultaneously, the switch reads the source MAC from the incoming frame and records it in the CAM table: "MAC aa:bb:cc:XX:XX:XX lives on Port N."

3. Response Learning: When the destination host responds, the switch reads THAT frame's source MAC and learns the destination MAC → port mapping. Now the CAM table has both entries, and subsequent frames are forwarded only between the two ports.

Explanation

This is the fundamental switch learning algorithm. The key insight: switches learn from source MACs but forward based on destination MACs. An empty CAM table causes flooding (inefficient but functional), and as traffic flows, the table populates and the switch becomes efficient. This is why new devices on a network cause a brief burst of flooding before the switch learns their location.

Q4
Explain the difference between an Access Port and a Trunk Port on a managed switch. If you connect a server to a Trunk Port without configuring the server's NIC for VLAN tagging, what happens? Why?
Show Answer
Answer

Access Port: Carries traffic for ONE VLAN only. Frames are untagged (no 802.1Q header). The switch internally associates all frames from this port with the configured VLAN. This is what you use for end devices (servers, workstations).

Trunk Port: Carries traffic for MULTIPLE VLANs. All frames (except the native VLAN) carry an 802.1Q tag. Used for switch-to-switch links and switch-to-hypervisor links.

If you connect an untagged server to a trunk port: The server sends untagged frames. The switch receives them on a trunk port and associates them with the native VLAN (usually VLAN 1). If the server should be on VLAN 100, the frames go to the wrong VLAN. Conversely, frames FROM the switch TO the server will be tagged (e.g., VLAN 100), and the server's NIC (untagged) will not understand the 802.1Q header — it will either drop the frame or misinterpret the 4-byte tag as part of the payload. Result: broken connectivity with no clear error.

Explanation

This is one of the most common datacenter misconfigurations. The native VLAN concept on trunk ports is a footgun: it allows untagged traffic on a trunk, which creates ambiguity. Best practice: set the native VLAN to an unused VLAN ID and tag ALL traffic on trunks. This prevents accidental VLAN leakage when someone plugs an access device into a trunk port.

Q5
In the anihpj Docker Compose environment, containers on the default bridge network (172.18.0.0/16) can ping each other by IP but NOT by container name (ping anihpj-db-1 fails). Containers on a user-defined bridge network CAN ping by name. Explain why, referencing L2 and L7 where relevant.
Show Answer
Answer

The default Docker bridge (docker0) does NOT provide built-in DNS resolution. Containers on the default bridge can only communicate by IP address. Container name resolution requires an embedded DNS server, which Docker only provides on user-defined bridge networks.

On user-defined networks, Docker runs an embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 inside each container. When a container resolves anihpj-db-1, the DNS query goes to 127.0.0.11:53 (UDP, L4), which resolves it to the container's IP. DNS is an L7 protocol that uses L4 UDP, and name resolution is an application-layer function — it has nothing to do with L2 switching or ARP.

Explanation

This question tests your understanding of where DNS fits in the stack. Many engineers confuse "can't ping by name" with an L2/L3 problem when it's actually an L7 (DNS) problem. The containers are on the same L2 segment and can ARP each other's IPs, but name resolution is a separate service. Always isolate: does ping <IP> work? If yes, the network is fine — the problem is DNS.

Q6
What is "gratuitous ARP" and why is it critical for high-availability infrastructure? Give a concrete example using keepalived VIP failover.
Show Answer
Answer

A Gratuitous ARP (GARP) is an unsolicited ARP reply — a host announces "IP X is at MAC Y" without being asked. It's sent as a broadcast so every host on the L2 segment updates its ARP cache.

Keepalived VIP failover example: Two NGINX servers share a Virtual IP (VIP) 10.0.1.100. Server A (MAC aa:bb:cc:11:22:33) is the active master. Server B (MAC aa:bb:cc:44:55:66) is the backup. When Server A fails, Server B takes over the VIP and immediately sends a GARP: "10.0.1.100 is now at aa:bb:cc:44:55:66." Every switch and host on the subnet updates their ARP cache instantly. Without GARP, traffic would continue flowing to Server A's MAC until the ARP cache entries expire (typically 30-60 seconds) — causing a 30+ second outage.

Explanation

GARP is what makes sub-second IP failover possible. Without it, ARP cache timers (30s-4h depending on OS) would cause extended outages during failover. GARP is also used by Kubernetes LoadBalancer services (when a new node takes over), VMware vMotion (when a VM moves to a new host), and any cluster using a floating IP.

Q7
You run ip neigh show and see 10.0.1.5 dev eth0 INCOMPLETE. What does INCOMPLETE mean? What's happening in the background, and how long until it either resolves or fails?
Show Answer
Answer

INCOMPLETE means the kernel has sent an ARP request for 10.0.1.5 but has not yet received a reply. The ARP request is in flight.

Background process: The kernel sends a broadcast ARP request. If no reply is received within ~1 second, it retransmits (typically 3 attempts at 1-second intervals). If all attempts fail, the state transitions to FAILED and the kernel returns "No route to host" or "Host unreachable" to the application. Total time: approximately 3-4 seconds from INCOMPLETE to FAILED.

Explanation

INCOMPLETE is the transient state between "I need to reach this IP" and "I have (or have failed to get) its MAC." It's normal to see briefly and then disappear. If you see INCOMPLETE persistently (not transitioning to REACHABLE or FAILED), the ARP reply is being lost — check for a bad cable (CRC errors dropping the reply frame), a switch port issue, or the target host being down.

Q8
A Docker container on network anihpj_default with MTU 1500 can curl small API responses but hangs on large responses (>1400 bytes). There are no firewall rules. ping -M do -s 1472 8.8.8.8 works from the host but fails from the container. What is the problem, and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

This is a classic PMTU (Path MTU) black hole caused by VXLAN/tunnel overhead. The container thinks its MTU is 1500, but the underlying network path (through Docker overlay/VXLAN) has a smaller effective MTU (typically 1450 after 50 bytes of VXLAN overhead).

When the container sends a 1500-byte packet, it fits in the container's MTU. But when Docker wraps it in VXLAN headers, it becomes 1550 bytes. The physical NIC drops it because 1550 > 1500. With the DF (Don't Fragment) bit set, the router should send an ICMP "Fragmentation Needed" message — but this ICMP message is often filtered by firewalls or doesn't reach the container (PMTU black hole).

Fix: Lower the container network MTU:

# Fix: Create Docker network with correct MTU (1500 - 50 VXLAN overhead)
docker network create --opt com.docker.network.driver.mtu=1450 anihpj_network

# Or for an existing docker-compose network:
# networks:
#   anihpj_net:
#     driver_opts:
#       com.docker.network.driver.mtu: 1450
Explanation

PMTU black holes are one of the nastiest networking problems because they're intermittent (only large packets trigger them) and silent (no error — the connection just hangs). The diagnostic test: ping -M do -s 1472 <target> works = MTU is 1500 end-to-end. ping -M do -s 1422 <target> works but -s 1472 fails = PMTU is 1450. This is a must-know diagnostic for any infrastructure engineer working with tunnels (VXLAN, GRE, IPsec, WireGuard).

Q9
List ALL possible reasons why an ARP request might receive NO reply, categorized by OSI layer. For each, state the diagnostic command you would run.
Show Answer
Answer
LayerCauseCommand
L1Cable unplugged, NIC down, port disabledip link show, ethtool eth0
L2Wrong VLAN, switch filtering ARP, MAC table overflowtcpdump -i eth0 arp (check if ARP leaves the host)
L3Target on different subnet (ARP only works within broadcast domain)ip addr show, ip route show
L3/L4Firewall blocking ARP (iptables arptables)arptables -L, iptables -L
L7Target host is down/offline, IP not assigned to any hostssh target, console access, IPAM check
Explanation

ARP is the most fundamental L2/L3 bridging protocol. If ARP fails, no IP communication can happen on that segment. This question tests systematic troubleshooting: working bottom-up ensures you don't waste time checking L3 routes when the cable is unplugged.

Q10
You're debugging a production issue where a Kubernetes node's kubelet reports network plugin is not ready: CNI config uninitialized. The CNI plugin (Calico) cannot assign IPs to new pods. At which OSI layers could the failure exist? Walk through your diagnostic steps from L1 upward.
Show Answer
Answer

L1: ip link show — is the primary interface UP? ethtool eth0 — link detected? Any CRC errors?

L2: ip neigh show — can the node ARP its default gateway? Is the switch port configured correctly (right VLAN, not disabled)?

L3: ip route show — is the default route present? Can the node reach the Kubernetes API server? ping kube-apiserver-ip

L4/L7: Is the CNI daemon (calico-node) running? kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep calico. Is it able to reach the Kubernetes API? Check kubectl logs calico-node-xxx. Is the CNI config file present at /etc/cni/net.d/? Is the CNI binary present at /opt/cni/bin/?

Most often, this is an L7 issue: the CNI daemon can't reach the API server (wrong kubeconfig, expired cert) or the CNI config file was deleted. But starting at L1 ensures you don't miss a physical connectivity issue masquerading as a CNI problem.

Explanation

CNI failures are common in Kubernetes environments, but the error message doesn't tell you WHERE the failure is. A systematic L1→L7 approach prevents tunnel vision. Many SREs jump to "check the CNI logs" when the actual problem is a bad cable causing the CNI daemon's etcd connection to flap. Bottom-up is always faster than top-down for infrastructure problems.

Chapter 3: Wireshark & Packet Analysis — The SRE's Microscope

Logs tell you what happened. Metrics tell you how much. But packets tell you the truth. When the logs say "connection timeout" and the metrics show "latency spike," only packet analysis reveals why — was it a TCP retransmission storm? A TLS handshake failure? A DNS server returning NXDOMAIN? A firewall silently dropping SYNs? Packet analysis is the highest-resolution debugging tool in your arsenal. This chapter teaches you to read packets like a language — to look at a tcpdump trace and immediately know what's happening on your network.

🎯 SRE Interview Tip

In any SRE interview, you'll face a scenario like "Users report timeouts on the API." The correct answer involves tcpdump. Your response: "First, I'd capture traffic on the server with tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -s 0 port 8000 -w /tmp/capture.pcap. Then I'd analyze it — looking for TCP retransmissions (duplicate sequence numbers), RST packets (connection resets), or slow TLS handshakes. I can share the capture with the team via scp or open it in Wireshark for deep analysis." Mentioning specific BPF filters (-s 0 for full capture, -w for file output, port 8000 for app-specific) immediately distinguishes you from candidates who just say "I'd check the logs."

3.1 Why Packet Analysis Is a Superpower

Applications lie. Logs are incomplete. Metrics are averages. Packets don't lie. Every network problem — from a misconfigured firewall to a failing TLS certificate to a DNS outage — leaves its fingerprint in the packets. Learning to read those fingerprints is what separates SREs who debug in minutes from those who debug in hours.

🔬 Three Tools, Three Use Cases
ToolTypeBest ForLimitation
tcpdumpCLI packet snifferRemote servers, containers, quick captures, scripting, production-safe ring-buffer modeText-only output, harder to analyze complex conversations
TSharkCLI (Wireshark engine)Scriptable analysis, JSON/XML output, programmatic packet dissection. tshark -r capture.pcap -T jsonSlightly slower than tcpdump for raw capture
WiresharkGUI analyzerDeep analysis, following TCP streams, visual protocol hierarchy, I/O graphs, file extractionRequires GUI — can't run headless (use TShark instead)
🤖 TShark — The Scriptable Packet Analyzer

TShark is Wireshark's command-line sibling. It uses the same protocol dissectors (2,000+ protocols) but outputs to text, JSON, or XML instead of a GUI. This makes it perfect for CI/CD pipelines, automated analysis, and servers without a display.

# Read a capture and output as JSON (machine-parseable)
$ tshark -r capture.pcap -T json > packets.json

# Extract only HTTP request URIs
$ tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'http.request' -T fields -e http.request.uri
/api/health
/api/users
/admin/login

# Count packets by protocol
$ tshark -r capture.pcap -q -z io,phs
Protocol Hierarchy Statistics:
  Ethernet: 100%
    IP: 100%
      TCP: 85%
        HTTP: 60%
        TLS: 25%
      UDP: 15%
        DNS: 15%

# Find the top talkers (most active IPs)
$ tshark -r capture.pcap -q -z conv,ip
IPv4 Conversations:
  10.0.1.5  ↔ 10.0.1.10   TCP 8000  4,521 packets  6.2 MB
  10.0.1.5  ↔ 8.8.8.8     UDP 53      12 packets  1.2 KB

# Realtime capture + display filter (like tcpdump but with protocol dissection)
$ tshark -i eth0 -Y 'http.request.method == "GET"' -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri
📥 Capturing Packets in Production Environments
EnvironmentCommandNotes
Bare-metal serversudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -s 0 -w /tmp/cap.pcapDirect interface access
Docker containersudo nsenter -t $(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' anihpj-web-1) -n tcpdump -i eth0 -nnEnters the container's network namespace
Kubernetes podkubectl debug -it anihpj-web-xxx --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- tcpdump -i eth0 -nnEphemeral debug container with netshoot image
All containers on nodesudo tcpdump -i cni0 -nn or -i docker0 -nnCaptures all pod traffic on that bridge
Rotating capture (production)sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -W 5 -C 100 -w /tmp/dump5 files × 100MB each, auto-rotates, never fills disk
⚠️ GOTCHA: tcpdump Can Overwhelm Your CPU

BPF filters run inside the kernel (in the BPF virtual machine) — they're fast and efficient. But outputting every matching packet to stdout is expensive. On a server handling 50,000 packets/second, running tcpdump -i eth0 -nn (no filter) will consume 100% of a CPU core and may drop packets. Always use a filter: at minimum host, port, or net. And in production, write to a file (-w) instead of stdout — it's 10-50× faster because the kernel can batch writes.

🔄 The Packet Capture Workflow
1. Capture → 2. Filter → 3. Analyze → 4. Fix → 5. Verify

Capture: Run tcpdump with a targeted filter. Filter: In Wireshark/TShark, narrow down to relevant conversations. Analyze: Follow TCP streams, check retransmissions, inspect payloads. Fix: Apply the fix (restart service, adjust MTU, update firewall rule). Verify: Capture again — confirm the problem is gone. Never skip step 5.

🔬 Reading Raw Hex — Manual Packet Dissection

When Wireshark isn't available, you can decode packets directly from tcpdump -xx hex output. Here's the dissection of a single HTTP packet:

# Raw hex dump of one Ethernet frame (tcpdump -xx):
0x0000:  aabb ccdd ee01 1122 3344 5566 0800 4500
0x0010:  00a8 0000 4000 4006 0000 0a00 0105 0a00
0x0020:  010a d431 1f40 0000 0001 0000 0001 5018
0x0030:  ffff 0000 0000 4745 5420 2f61 7069 2f68
0x0040:  6561 6c74 6820 4854 5450 2f31 2e31 0d0a

# ─── BYTE-BY-BYTE DISSECTION ───
# [L2 — Ethernet Header: 14 bytes]
0x0000: aabb ccdd ee01 = Destination MAC (aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01)
0x0006: 1122 3344 5566 = Source MAC (11:22:33:44:55:66)
0x000c: 0800           = EtherType 0x0800 = IPv4

# [L3 — IPv4 Header: 20 bytes standard]
0x000e: 45             = Version 4, IHL 5 (5×4=20 bytes)
0x000f: 00             = DSCP/ECN (best-effort)
0x0010: 00a8           = Total Length 0x00A8 = 168 bytes
0x0012: 0000           = Identification
0x0014: 4000           = Flags/Fragment Offset: DF bit set (don't fragment)
0x0016: 40             = TTL 64 (0x40)
0x0017: 06             = Protocol 6 = TCP
0x0018: 0000           = Header Checksum (set by NIC, not shown by tcpdump)
0x001a: 0a00 0105      = Source IP = 10.0.1.5 (0x0A000105)
0x001e: 0a00 010a      = Destination IP = 10.0.1.10 (0x0A00010A)

# [L4 — TCP Header: starts at byte 34 (14 Ethernet + 20 IP)]
0x0022: d431           = Source Port 0xD431 = 54321
0x0024: 1f40           = Dest Port 0x1F40 = 8000
0x0026: 0000 0001      = Sequence Number = 1
0x002a: 0000 0001      = Acknowledgment Number = 1
0x002e: 5              = Data Offset = 5 (5×4=20 bytes)
0x002f: 018            = Flags 0x018 = PSH + ACK
0x0030: ffff           = Window Size = 65535
0x0032: 0000           = TCP Checksum
0x0034: 0000           = Urgent Pointer

# [L7 — HTTP: starts at byte 54 (14 Eth + 20 IP + 20 TCP)]
0x0036: 4745 5420 ...  = "GET /api/health HTTP/1.1"
# 0x47='G', 0x45='E', 0x54='T', 0x20=' ', etc.

Why learn manual dissection? When you're SSH'd into a server at 3 AM with no Wireshark, being able to read hex output and identify "that SYN packet arrived at port 8000 with TTL 64" confirms connectivity at every layer without needing a GUI. This skill separates SREs from developers.

🎯 Protocol Signatures — Identify Traffic at a Glance

Every protocol leaves a unique fingerprint in the packet bytes. Here's how to identify common protocols without Wireshark:

ProtocolHex SignatureWhere to LookASCII Clue (tcpdump -A)
HTTP4745 54 (GET) or 504F 53 (POST)Bytes after TCP headerPlain text: GET / HTTP/1.1
TLS Client Hello16 03 01 (TLS 1.0) or 16 03 03 (TLS 1.2)First 3 bytes after TCP headerGibberish (encrypted) — ..<...&...& ...
DNSxxxx 0100 (transaction ID + flags)UDP payload, bytes 0-3Mixed binary + domain name fragments
ARP0806 at EtherType (byte 12-13)Ethernet frame headerBinary — not human-readable in ASCII
ICMP Echo0800 (Echo Request) or 0000 (Echo Reply)ICMP type field (byte 34)Not ASCII — use tcpdump -nn icmp
SSH5353 482d ("SSH-")First bytes after TCP handshakeSSH-2.0-OpenSSH_8.9
VXLAN0800 at UDP port 4789 with VXLAN headerUDP payload, byte 0-7Inner packet follows VXLAN flags (0x08)

Quick check pattern: If you see ASCII "GET" or "POST" right after the TCP header → HTTP. If you see gibberish starting with 0x16 0x03 → TLS. If you see port 53 with binary data → DNS. This instant identification saves seconds per packet when scanning through thousands in a capture.

🧮 Advanced BPF — Bit-Level Packet Filtering

BPF can inspect individual bits and bytes at arbitrary offsets inside packets. This enables filters that would be impossible with simple host/port expressions:

# Filter: TCP packets with SYN flag set (bit 1 of byte 13 in TCP header)
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn) != 0'

# Filter: TCP packets with ONLY SYN (not SYN-ACK)
# SYN = 0x02, SYN-ACK = 0x12. We want flags == 0x02 exactly.
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn'

# Filter: Only the first 5 packets of each TCP connection (handshake + first data)
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn) != 0 or tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-fin) != 0 or tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-rst) != 0'

# Filter: Packets where the TCP data offset > 5 (TCP options present, e.g., SACK, timestamp)
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[12] >> 4 > 5'

# Filter: HTTP GET requests (magic bytes 0x47455420 = "GET " at TCP payload start)
tcpdump -A -i eth0 'tcp port 80 and tcp[((tcp[12:1] & 0xf0) >> 2):4] = 0x47455420'

# Filter: ICMP Destination Unreachable (type 3) or Time Exceeded (type 11)
tcpdump -i eth0 'icmp[0] == 3 or icmp[0] == 11'

# Filter: All traffic from 10.0.1.0/24 EXCEPT 10.0.1.5
tcpdump -i eth0 'net 10.0.1.0/24 and not host 10.0.1.5'

# Complex: TLS Client Hello on non-standard port (8443 instead of 443)
# Check if TCP payload starts with 0x16 (handshake) and 0x0301/0x0303 (TLS version)
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp port 8443 and tcp[((tcp[12:1] & 0xf0) >> 2):1] = 0x16'

The BPF offset trick: tcp[((tcp[12:1] & 0xf0) >> 2):4] reads the TCP data offset (upper nibble of byte 12), multiplies by 4 to get the TCP header length in bytes, and uses that as the starting offset to read 4 bytes — the first 4 bytes of the TCP payload. This is how you filter on application-layer content with BPF.

3.2 tcpdump — The Command-Line Packet Sniffer

tcpdump is the universal packet capture tool. It runs on every Linux server, every container, every CI runner. If you can SSH into a machine, you can capture its traffic. Mastering tcpdump is non-negotiable for infrastructure work.

tcpdump: Basic Syntax 
tcpdump -i <interface> [options] [BPF filter expression]

# Essential options:
# -i eth0       Interface to capture on (any = all interfaces)
# -n            Don't resolve hostnames (faster)
# -nn           Don't resolve hostnames OR port names (fastest)
# -s 0          Capture full packet (default = only first 96 bytes!)
# -w file.pcap  Write to file (10-50× faster than stdout)
# -r file.pcap  Read from file
# -c 100        Capture only 100 packets then exit
# -v / -vv / -vvv  Verbose (more detail at each level)
# -e            Print link-level headers (MAC addresses)
# -A            Print packet payload in ASCII
# -X            Print packet payload in hex AND ASCII
# -xx           Print full Ethernet frame hex (including MAC headers)
📖 Reading tcpdump Output — Line by Line
TIMESTAMP            SRC               DST           FLAGS  SEQ     ACK     WIN   LEN
10:23:45.123456 10.0.1.5.54321 > 10.0.1.10.8000: Flags [S], seq 123456789, win 65535, length 0
│                │         │          │       │         │            │          │
│                │         │          │       │         │            │          └─ TCP payload length (0 = just headers)
│                │         │          │       │         │            └─ TCP window size (receiver's buffer)
│                │         │          │       │         └─ Acknowledgment number
│                │         │          │       └─ Sequence number
│                │         │          └─ TCP flags: S=SYN, .=ACK, P=PSH, F=FIN, R=RST
│                │         └─ Destination IP.port
│                └─ Source IP.port (ephemeral port > 1024)
└─ Microsecond-precision timestamp
🎯 Essential BPF Filter Expressions
FilterMatchesExample
host 10.0.1.5Any traffic to/from 10.0.1.5tcpdump -i eth0 -nn host 10.0.1.5
port 8000Any traffic on port 8000 (TCP or UDP)tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 8000
tcp port 8000TCP traffic on port 8000 onlytcpdump -i eth0 -nn tcp port 8000
net 10.0.1.0/24Any traffic to/from the 10.0.1.0/24 subnettcpdump -i eth0 -nn net 10.0.1.0/24
src 10.0.1.5Only traffic FROM 10.0.1.5tcpdump -i eth0 -nn src 10.0.1.5
dst port 53Only traffic TO port 53tcpdump -i eth0 -nn dst port 53
arpOnly ARP packetstcpdump -i eth0 -nn arp
icmpOnly ICMP (ping, traceroute)tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp
not port 22Exclude SSH (don't capture your own session)tcpdump -i eth0 -nn not port 22
greater 1400Only packets > 1400 bytes (MTU debugging)tcpdump -i eth0 -nn greater 1400
⚠️ GOTCHA: tcpdump Only Captures 96 Bytes by Default

The default snaplen (snapshot length) is only 96 bytes — enough for the Ethernet + IP + TCP headers, but not enough for the HTTP body or application payload. If you capture traffic with tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap (without -s 0) and try to view the HTTP response body in Wireshark, it will be truncated. Always use -s 0 for full packet capture. The 96-byte default is a legacy performance optimization from the 1990s that no longer makes sense on modern hardware.
