4.5 Bridges — Virtual Switches in Linux

A Linux bridge is a software L2 switch. It learns MAC addresses from incoming frames, maintains a forwarding database (FDB), and forwards frames only to the correct port. docker0 and cni0 (Kubernetes) are just Linux bridges.

🔍 Inspecting a Linux Bridge
# See all bridges and their member ports
$ bridge link show
3: veth12345 state UP @eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> master docker0
4: veth67890 state UP @eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> master docker0

# See the MAC forwarding table (like a switch's CAM table)
$ bridge fdb show dev docker0
aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01 dev veth12345 master docker0
aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:02 dev veth67890 master docker0
# ↑ Container with MAC aa:bb:01 is reachable via veth12345

# Create a bridge manually
$ ip link add br0 type bridge
$ ip link set br0 up
$ ip link set eth1 master br0  # Add eth1 as a bridge port
🏗️ Bridge + veth + Netns = The Complete Container Pattern

Here's the exact sequence Docker (or any container runtime) follows to connect a container to the network:

  1. Create netns: ip netns add container1 — new isolated network stack.
  2. Create veth pair: ip link add veth-host type veth peer name veth-cont.
  3. Move one end to netns: ip link set veth-cont netns container1.
  4. Rename inside netns to eth0: ip netns exec container1 ip link set veth-cont name eth0.
  5. Connect host end to bridge: ip link set veth-host master docker0.
  6. Assign IP inside netns: ip netns exec container1 ip addr add 172.17.0.2/16 dev eth0.
  7. Bring interfaces up: ip link set veth-host up, ip netns exec container1 ip link set eth0 up, ip netns exec container1 ip link set lo up.
  8. Add default route: ip netns exec container1 ip route add default via 172.17.0.1.

After these 8 steps, the container has its own eth0 with IP 172.17.0.2, can reach other containers on the same bridge, and can reach the internet via the host's MASQUERADE rule.

🗺️ Tracing Container-to-Container and Container-to-Internet Paths

Container-1 → Container-2 (same host, same bridge):

# Pure L2 forwarding — never leaves the bridge
container-1 eth0 (172.17.0.2)
  → veth-host-1 (host side of veth pair)
  → docker0 bridge (MAC lookup: aa:bb:02 → veth-host-2)
  → veth-host-2 (host side of veth pair)
  → container-2 eth0 (172.17.0.3)

# No iptables. No routing. No ARP after first lookup.
# The bridge's FDB table handles everything at L2.

Container-1 → Internet:

# L2 → L3 → NAT → L2
container-1 eth0 (172.17.0.2)
  → veth-host-1
  → docker0 bridge (container's default gateway = 172.17.0.1)
  → iptables POSTROUTING MASQUERADE (src IP: 172.17.0.2 → 192.168.1.100)
  → host routing table (which interface to reach internet?)
  → host eth0 (192.168.1.100) → physical switch → router → Internet

# Reply (Internet → Container-1):
# Internet → router → physical switch → host eth0 (dst IP: 192.168.1.100)
# conntrack looks up original connection → DNAT (dst IP: 192.168.1.100 → 172.17.0.2)
# docker0 bridge forwards to veth-host-1 → container-1 eth0
🔄 nftables — The Modern Successor to iptables

iptables has been the Linux firewall since 1999, but it has fundamental limitations: each table (filter, nat, mangle) is a separate API, rules are processed linearly (O(n) lookup), and IPv4/IPv6 require separate tools. nftables (available since kernel 4.0) replaces iptables, ip6tables, arptables, and ebtables with a single unified framework:

Featureiptablesnftables
Rule lookupLinear (O(n)) — slow with many rulesSet-based (O(1) with maps) — fast at any scale
IPv4/IPv6Separate tools: iptables + ip6tablesSingle nft tool handles both
Rule updatesAtomic per-rule (flush then rebuild)Atomic rule set replacement (no gap in filtering)
Multi-action rulesOne action per ruleMultiple actions per rule (e.g., log + drop)
Kernel memory~400KB for 25K rules~20KB for 25K rules (20× more efficient)
 
# iptables: Block port 80 from 10.0.1.5
iptables -A INPUT -s 10.0.1.5 -p tcp --dport 80 -j DROP

# nftables equivalent (single family, unified syntax):
nft add table inet myfilter
nft add chain inet myfilter input { type filter hook input priority 0; }
nft add rule inet myfilter input ip saddr 10.0.1.5 tcp dport 80 drop

# nftables: Set-based lookup (O(1) instead of O(n))
nft add set inet myfilter blocked_ips { type ipv4_addr\; }
nft add element inet myfilter blocked_ips { 10.0.1.5, 10.0.1.10, 10.0.1.20 }
nft add rule inet myfilter input ip saddr @blocked_ips drop
# ↑ Adding 1000 IPs to the set = same performance as 1 IP. iptables would be 1000× slower.

Kubernetes relevance: kube-proxy in iptables mode adds ~25 rules per service. At 5000 services, that's 125,000 iptables rules — taking seconds to update and consuming 2+ MB of kernel memory. kube-proxy in nftables mode (in development) or IPVS mode solves this. Cilium uses eBPF to bypass both iptables and nftables entirely.

🚀 XDP & eBPF — When the Kernel Stack Is Too Slow

XDP (eXpress Data Path) and eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) allow you to run custom programs directly in the NIC driver — before the packet enters the kernel network stack. This enables packet processing at line rate (40M+ packets/sec per core) for use cases like DDoS mitigation, load balancing, and observability.

TechnologyWhere It RunsPerformanceUse Case
iptables/nftablesKernel netfilter hooks~1-2M pps/coreTraditional firewalling, NAT
XDPNIC driver (before sk_buff allocation)~40M pps/coreDDoS mitigation, L4 load balancing (Facebook Katran, Cloudflare)
eBPF (tc hook)Traffic control ingress/egress~5-10M pps/coreCilium CNI, observability (Falco, Pixie)
DPDKUserspace (bypasses kernel entirely)~80M pps/coreTelco NFV, high-frequency trading

SRE context: You probably won't write XDP programs daily, but you'll use tools built on them. Cilium (the leading K8s CNI) uses eBPF to replace kube-proxy, enforce NetworkPolicies, and provide observability — all without iptables. Falco uses eBPF for runtime security monitoring. Katran (Facebook's L4 load balancer) uses XDP to handle 100+ Gbps per server. Understanding the technology stack (XDP → eBPF → kernel → userspace) helps you choose the right tool for performance-critical workloads.

4.6 The /proc/net/ Filesystem — The Kernel's Network State

The /proc/net/ directory exposes the kernel's network state as human-readable files. You can inspect ARP tables, TCP connections, routing tables, and interface statistics without any tools — just cat. This is invaluable when debugging minimal containers that don't have ip, ss, or tcpdump installed.

📂 Essential /proc/net/ Files for SREs
FileWhat It ShowsEquivalent CommandWhen to Use
/proc/net/arpARP cache — IP → MAC mappingsip neigh showMinimal container, no iproute2
/proc/net/tcpAll TCP sockets (hex-encoded)ss -tCheck open ports without ss/netstat
/proc/net/udpAll UDP socketsss -uDNS/DHCP debugging in containers
/proc/net/routeRouting table (hex-encoded)ip route showVerify default gateway exists
/proc/net/devPer-interface packet/byte/error countersip -s link showCheck for dropped packets, errors
/proc/net/if_inet6IPv6 addresses per interfaceip -6 addr showVerify IPv6 is configured
/proc/net/netstatExtensive TCP/UDP statisticsnetstat -sRetransmission counts, listen drops
/proc/net/snmpSNMP-like IP/TCP/UDP/ICMP countersnetstat -sForwarding stats, fragment reassembly
📖 Reading /proc/net/tcp — Decode Hex Sockets
# Raw /proc/net/tcp output (one line per socket):
$ cat /proc/net/tcp
  sl  local_address rem_address   st tx_queue rx_queue tr tm->when retrnsmt   uid  timeout inode
   0: 00000000:1F40 00000000:0000 0A 00000000:00000000 00:00000000 00000000     0        0 12345 1 ...

# Decode:
# local_address: 00000000:1F40
#   00000000 = 0.0.0.0 (listening on all interfaces)
#   1F40 = 8000 (hex → decimal port)
# rem_address: 00000000:0000
#   0.0.0.0:0 (no remote — this is a LISTENING socket)
# st: 0A = LISTEN state (01=ESTABLISHED, 06=TIME_WAIT, 0A=LISTEN)

# TCP state hex codes:
# 01 = ESTABLISHED   06 = TIME_WAIT     0A = LISTEN
# 02 = SYN_SENT      07 = CLOSE         0B = CLOSING
# 03 = SYN_RECV      08 = CLOSE_WAIT
# 04 = FIN_WAIT1     09 = LAST_ACK
# 05 = FIN_WAIT2
📊 /proc/net/netstat — Deep TCP Statistics

/proc/net/netstat exposes detailed TCP metrics that are invaluable for performance debugging. The file has two lines per metric group: the first line has header names, the second line has values (hex).

# Key /proc/net/netstat metrics for SREs:
$ cat /proc/net/netstat | grep -E '^TcpExt:' | head -1
TcpExt: SyncookiesSent SyncookiesRecv SyncookiesFailed ...

# Critical counters to watch:
# ListenOverflows    → SYN backlog full. Increase net.core.somaxconn.
# ListenDrops        → Socket refused connection. App not accept()ing fast enough.
# TCPFastRetrans     → Fast retransmits triggered. Packet loss detected.
# TCPTimeouts        → Retransmission timeout. Severe packet loss.
# TCPLossProbes      → Lost probe packets.
# TCPSpuriousRTOs    → False retransmission timeouts (usually buffer bloat).
# PruneCalled        → Socket memory pressure — kernel pruning buffers.
# TCPAbortOnTimeout  → Connections killed due to timeout.
# TCPBacklogDrop     → Packets dropped because SYN backlog full.

# Check /proc/net/snmp for IP-level stats:
$ cat /proc/net/snmp | grep -E '^Ip:|^Tcp:|^Udp:'
# Ip: Forwarding DefaultTTL InReceives InHdrErrors ForwDatagrams ...
# Tcp: RtoAlgorithm RtoMin RtoMax MaxConn ActiveOpens PassiveOpens ...
# Udp: InDatagrams NoPorts InErrors OutDatagrams ...
⚙️ /proc/sys/net/ — Kernel Tunables Reference

/proc/sys/net/ is where ALL kernel network parameters live. You can read them with cat and write with sysctl -w or echo >. These are the parameters that matter for infrastructure:

PathWhat It ControlsDefaultSRE Note
net.ipv4.ip_forwardEnable IP forwarding (must be 1 for routers/containers)0🚩 Must be 1 for Docker/K8s nodes and VPN gateways
net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuseReuse TIME_WAIT sockets for outgoing connections0Enable on high-connection-rate servers (API gateways)
net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeoutSeconds before forced close in FIN-WAIT-2 state60Reduce to 30 on busy web servers to free sockets faster
net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_timeSeconds idle before first keepalive probe7200Reduce to 300-600 for cloud environments (detect dead peers sooner)
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_controlCongestion control algorithmcubicConsider BBR for high-throughput WAN links
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookiesSYN flood protection10=off, 1=enabled when needed, 2=always on (CPU cost)
net.ipv4.ip_local_port_rangeEphemeral port range for outbound connections32768-60999~28K ports. High-connection servers may need wider range
net.core.somaxconnMax SYN backlog for listen()4096Increase from default 128 to 4096+ for production servers
net.core.netdev_max_backlogMax packets queued when interface is busy1000Increase for high-throughput NICs (drop indicator)
net.core.rmem_maxMax socket receive buffer size (bytes)212992Increase to 16MB+ for 10G+ links (BDP calculation)
net.core.wmem_maxMax socket send buffer size (bytes)212992Match rmem_max for symmetric throughput
 
# Check current congestion control algorithm
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control = cubic

# Available algorithms (BBR requires kernel 4.9+):
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_available_congestion_control
net.ipv4.tcp_available_congestion_control = cubic reno bbr

# Switch to BBR for better throughput on lossy/high-latency links:
$ sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr
⚠️ GOTCHA: /proc/net/tcp IPs Are Little-Endian Hex

IP addresses in /proc/net/tcp are stored in little-endian hexadecimal — the bytes are reversed from what you'd expect. 10.0.1.5 becomes 0501000A (not 0A000105). To decode manually: split into bytes (05 01 00 0A), reverse them (0A 00 01 05), convert each to decimal (10.0.1.5). Port numbers, however, are big-endian — 1F40 = 8000 directly. This inconsistency (IPs little-endian, ports big-endian) is a historical artifact from the kernel's internal struct sockaddr_in memory layout. Use ss instead — it decodes everything correctly.

🔄 Socket Buffer Tuning — When the App Can't Keep Up

When ss -tlnp shows non-zero Recv-Q on a listening socket, the kernel has data that the application hasn't read yet. This is backpressure — the app is the bottleneck, not the network.

ParameterDefaultWhat It ControlsWhen to Increase
net.core.rmem_max212992Max receive buffer size (bytes)High-throughput receivers (load balancers, log shippers)
net.core.wmem_max212992Max send buffer size (bytes)High-throughput senders (file servers, CDN origins)
net.core.somaxconn4096Max SYN backlog (pending connections)High-connection-rate servers (web servers, API gateways)
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem4096 131072 6291456TCP receive buffer (min default max)Long-fat networks (high BDP). Middle value is default.
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem4096 16384 4194304TCP send buffer (min default max)Same as rmem — tune for bandwidth×delay product.

BDP (Bandwidth-Delay Product) rule: For a 1 Gbps link with 50ms RTT: BDP = 1 Gbps × 0.05s = 6.25 MB. Your TCP buffer must be at least 6.25 MB to fully utilize the link. Default buffers (128KB-6MB) may not fill a high-latency 1 Gbps pipe.

4.7 🛠️ LAB — Linux Network Stack Exploration

Build container networking from scratch — create namespaces, veth pairs, and a bridge. This is exactly what Docker does under the hood.

1
Create Two Network Namespaces

Each namespace starts with only loopback — completely isolated.

$ sudo ip netns add ns1
$ sudo ip netns add ns2
$ sudo ip netns list
ns2
ns1
2
Create a Bridge and veth Pairs

Build the virtual switch and virtual cables.

# Create the bridge (virtual switch)
$ sudo ip link add br0 type bridge
$ sudo ip link set br0 up
$ sudo ip addr add 10.0.1.1/24 dev br0

# Create veth pairs (one for each namespace)
$ sudo ip link add veth-ns1 type veth peer name veth-ns1-br
$ sudo ip link add veth-ns2 type veth peer name veth-ns2-br

# Connect host-side ends to the bridge
$ sudo ip link set veth-ns1-br master br0
$ sudo ip link set veth-ns2-br master br0
$ sudo ip link set veth-ns1-br up
$ sudo ip link set veth-ns2-br up
3
Move veth Ends into Namespaces & Configure

Give each namespace its own interface with an IP address.

# Move veth ends into namespaces
$ sudo ip link set veth-ns1 netns ns1
$ sudo ip link set veth-ns2 netns ns2

# Configure ns1
$ sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip link set lo up
$ sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip link set veth-ns1 name eth0
$ sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip addr add 10.0.1.10/24 dev eth0
$ sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip link set eth0 up
$ sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip route add default via 10.0.1.1

# Configure ns2
$ sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip link set lo up
$ sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip link set veth-ns2 name eth0
$ sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip addr add 10.0.1.20/24 dev eth0
$ sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip link set eth0 up
$ sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip route add default via 10.0.1.1
4
Test Connectivity & Inspect the Bridge

Verify the two namespaces can communicate through the bridge.

# Test ping between namespaces
$ sudo ip netns exec ns1 ping -c 3 10.0.1.20
PING 10.0.1.20 (10.0.1.20) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 10.0.1.20: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.045 ms ✅
64 bytes from 10.0.1.20: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.038 ms ✅

# Inspect the bridge's MAC learning table
$ bridge fdb show dev br0
# Shows MACs for both namespaces' eth0 interfaces

# Check ARP inside ns1
$ sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip neigh show
10.0.1.20 dev eth0 lladdr ... REACHABLE ← ARP resolved across the bridge!
5
Inspect /proc/net/ Inside a Namespace

See the kernel's view of the namespace's network state.

# View ARP cache from /proc
$ sudo ip netns exec ns1 cat /proc/net/arp
IP address       HW type     Flags       HW address            Mask     Device
10.0.1.20        0x1         0x2         aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:02     *        eth0

# View TCP sockets (after establishing a connection)
$ sudo ip netns exec ns1 cat /proc/net/tcp
# Shows listening and established sockets in hex

# Clean up when done
$ sudo ip netns del ns1
$ sudo ip netns del ns2
$ sudo ip link del br0
6
Trace a Packet Through Netfilter

Use iptables TRACE to watch every hook a packet hits.

# Enable TRACE on PREROUTING (logs every packet entering the stack)
$ sudo iptables -t raw -I PREROUTING -j TRACE

# Watch the kernel log for netfilter hook traces
$ sudo tail -f /var/log/kern.log | grep TRACE
# Or on systems with journald:
$ sudo journalctl -k -f | grep TRACE

# Each packet will show every hook it passes through:
# TRACE: raw:PREROUTING:policy:2 ... (entering raw PREROUTING)
# TRACE: mangle:PREROUTING:policy:3 ... (entering mangle PREROUTING)
# TRACE: nat:PREROUTING:rule:1 ... (hitting a DNAT rule)
# TRACE: filter:INPUT:policy:4 ... (entering filter INPUT)

# Remove trace when done (it's VERY verbose!)
$ sudo iptables -t raw -D PREROUTING -j TRACE
7
Inspect Connection Tracking

See every active connection the kernel is tracking and the conntrack table size.

# Show all tracked connections
$ sudo conntrack -L
tcp 6 431999 ESTABLISHED src=172.17.0.2 dst=93.184.216.34 sport=54321 dport=443 \
    src=93.184.216.34 dst=172.17.0.2 sport=443 dport=54321 [ASSURED] mark=0 use=1

# Show connection count vs maximum
$ sudo conntrack -C
1247
$ sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 262144

# Show top talkers by connection count
$ sudo conntrack -L | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
    523 src=10.0.1.5
    312 src=10.0.1.10
    201 src=172.17.0.2
8
Debug "Address Already in Use" with ss

Scenario: anihpj gunicorn fails to start: OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use.

# Check what's already listening on port 8000
$ ss -tlnp | grep 8000
LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:8000 0.0.0.0:* users:((\"python3\",pid=1234,fd=5))
# ↑ PID 1234 (old gunicorn process) still has port 8000

# Kill the old process
$ sudo kill 1234

# If it won't die (stuck in D state — uninterruptible sleep):
$ ps aux | grep 1234
$ cat /proc/1234/status | grep State
State: D (disk sleep)  ← 🚩 Can't be killed! Reboot or fix the I/O issue.

# Also check: are there TIME_WAIT sockets holding the port?
$ ss -tan state time-wait sport = :8000
# TIME_WAIT lasts 60s. Set SO_REUSEADDR in your app to reuse immediately.
🎯 PLATFORM ENGINEERING — You Build the Platform, You Own the Stack

As a Platform Engineer, you're not just using Linux networking — you're building the platform that other engineers use. Network namespaces are the foundation of every container on your platform. Understanding them means you can debug any pod. veth pairs are the virtual cables connecting those containers. Bridges are the virtual switches forwarding their traffic. iptables rules are the firewalls and NAT gateways between them. /proc/net/ is the kernel's API — always available, never requiring installation. When a developer says "my pod can't reach the database," you trace: container netns → veth → bridge → iptables → host interface → physical network. You fix it at whatever layer is broken, not by restarting the pod and hoping.

🔭 Chapter 4 — Visual Summary

🧱 Kernel Stack Pipeline

NIC → DMA → netfilter hooks → routing → TCP/UDP → socket → app. Every packet follows this exact path. Know where to look at each stage.

🔌 Interfaces Are Everything

Physical (eth0), virtual (veth, bridge, VLAN, VXLAN), loopback (lo). Linux treats ALL as interfaces. The ip command manages them all.

🛠️ ip Replaces Legacy Tools

Forget ifconfig/route/arp. ip link, ip addr, ip route, ip neigh, ip netns — the modern toolkit.

📦 Netns = Container Isolation

Each netns has its own interfaces, routes, iptables, ARP cache. Docker/K8s pods = one netns per container. veth pairs connect them.

🌉 Bridges = Virtual Switches

docker0 and cni0 are Linux bridges. They learn MACs, forward frames. bridge fdb show reveals the MAC table.

📂 /proc/net/ = Kernel Truth

No tools needed. cat /proc/net/tcp for sockets, /proc/net/arp for neighbors, /proc/net/dev for counters.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 4

📦Network Namespace (netns)
A Linux kernel feature that provides complete isolation of the network stack — interfaces, routes, iptables, and sockets. Each container/pod gets its own netns. Created with ip netns add, entered with ip netns exec or nsenter.
🔗veth Pair
A pair of virtual Ethernet interfaces connected like a virtual cable. Whatever enters one end exits the other. Used to connect a container's netns to a bridge. Created: ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1.
🌉Linux Bridge
A software L2 switch implemented in the kernel. Learns MAC addresses, maintains a forwarding database (FDB), forwards frames between ports. docker0 and cni0 are bridges. Inspect with bridge fdb show.
🪝netfilter Hooks
Five hook points in the kernel where packet processing can be intercepted: PREROUTING, INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT, POSTROUTING. iptables/nftables rules attach to these hooks. NAT happens at PREROUTING (DNAT) and POSTROUTING (SNAT/MASQUERADE).
📊conntrack (Connection Tracking)
Kernel subsystem that tracks the state of all connections. Required for stateful firewalling (RELATED,ESTABLISHED) and NAT. Has a size limit (nf_conntrack_max). Overflow = new connections silently dropped.
🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work
  • Debugging container connectivity: Two containers can't communicate? nsenter -t PID -n ip addr to see their interfaces. bridge fdb show dev docker0 to check the MAC table. iptables -L DOCKER-USER -nv to check firewall rules. You're tracing the exact kernel pipeline from Section 4.1.
  • Conntrack table overflow: "New connections are timing out but existing ones work." dmesg | grep conntrack shows "table full." Increase nf_conntrack_max or reduce nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established. This is a daily issue on high-traffic NAT gateways and Kubernetes nodes.
  • Building test environments: Need to simulate a network without Docker? ip netns add test; ip link add veth0 type veth peer veth1 — you've built an isolated network in 2 commands. This is how CI/CD pipelines test network configurations.
  • Minimal container debugging: Container doesn't have ip or ss? cat /proc/net/tcp shows listening ports. cat /proc/net/route shows the routing table. cat /proc/net/arp shows neighbors. /proc is always available — it's the kernel's API.

🔑 Chapter 4 Key Takeaways

  1. Every packet follows the same path: NIC → DMA → netfilter → routing → TCP/UDP → socket → app. Know where to look at each stage for debugging.
  2. netfilter is the packet filter framework. PREROUTING (DNAT), INPUT (local), FORWARD (routing), OUTPUT (local), POSTROUTING (SNAT/MASQUERADE). iptables rules attach to these hooks.
  3. The ip command replaces ifconfig/route/arp. ip link for interfaces, ip addr for IPs, ip route for routing, ip neigh for ARP, ip netns for namespaces.
  4. Network namespaces are the foundation of containers. Each container gets its own netns. veth pairs connect netns to bridges. This is exactly how Docker and Kubernetes isolate networking.
  5. Bridges are virtual switches. docker0 and cni0 are Linux bridges. They learn MACs (bridge fdb show), forward frames (bridge link show), and support VLAN filtering.
  6. /proc/net/ is always available. Even in minimal containers without any tools, the kernel exposes its network state via /proc. cat /proc/net/tcp = your last resort socket inspector.
  7. conntrack overflow kills new connections. When the connection tracking table fills up, the kernel silently drops packets for new connections. Existing connections continue to work — making this a confusing failure mode.
⏱️ Target: 8 minutes
Drill 4.1 — Build Container Networking from Scratch

Without Docker, create two isolated network namespaces connected by a bridge — exactly as Docker does.

  1. Create two netns: ip netns add alpha; ip netns add beta
  2. Create bridge: ip link add mybr0 type bridge; ip link set mybr0 up; ip addr add 192.168.100.1/24 dev mybr0
  3. Create veth pairs and connect to bridge
  4. Move veth ends into namespaces, rename to eth0, assign IPs
  5. Ping from alpha (192.168.100.10) to beta (192.168.100.20)
  6. Verify: bridge fdb show dev mybr0 shows both MACs
  7. Clean up: delete namespaces and bridge
💡 Hint: After moving veth into netns, you must bring up BOTH ends (the host end first, then the namespace end). Loopback must be explicitly brought up inside each namespace.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1-2: Create netns and bridge
ip netns add alpha
ip netns add beta
ip link add mybr0 type bridge
ip link set mybr0 up
ip addr add 192.168.100.1/24 dev mybr0

# Step 3: Create veth pairs
ip link add veth-a type veth peer name veth-a-br
ip link add veth-b type veth peer name veth-b-br
ip link set veth-a-br master mybr0
ip link set veth-b-br master mybr0
ip link set veth-a-br up
ip link set veth-b-br up

# Step 4: Move into namespaces and configure
ip link set veth-a netns alpha
ip netns exec alpha ip link set veth-a name eth0
ip netns exec alpha ip addr add 192.168.100.10/24 dev eth0
ip netns exec alpha ip link set eth0 up
ip netns exec alpha ip link set lo up

ip link set veth-b netns beta
ip netns exec beta ip link set veth-b name eth0
ip netns exec beta ip addr add 192.168.100.20/24 dev eth0
ip netns exec beta ip link set eth0 up
ip netns exec beta ip link set lo up

# Step 5-6: Test and verify
ip netns exec alpha ping -c 3 192.168.100.20
bridge fdb show dev mybr0

# Step 7: Clean up
ip netns del alpha
ip netns del beta
ip link del mybr0
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 4.2 — Enter a Container's Network Namespace

Find a running Docker container's PID, enter its network namespace, and inspect its network state from the inside.

  1. Find container PID: docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' container-name
  2. Enter its netns: nsenter -t PID -n ip addr show
  3. Check its routing table, ARP cache, and listening sockets
  4. Run tcpdump inside the container's netns from the host: nsenter -t PID -n tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 8000
💡 Hint: nsenter -t PID -n enters only the network namespace (-n). Combined with -m (mount) and -u (UTS), you can fully enter a container's environment from the host.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. Find the container's PID
$ PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' anihpj-web-1)
$ echo $PID
12345

# 2. Enter the netns and inspect
$ nsenter -t $PID -n ip addr show
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536
2: eth0@if47: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500
    inet 172.18.0.2/16 brd 172.18.255.255 scope global eth0

# 3. Check routing and ARP from inside the container's perspective

default via 172.18.0.1 dev eth0

Drill 4.3 — Decode /proc/net/tcp

On any Linux machine, read /proc/net/tcp and decode at least 3 sockets by hand — IP addresses, ports, and TCP states — without using ss or netstat.

  1. cat /proc/net/tcp | head -5
  2. Identify which lines are LISTEN (0A) vs ESTABLISHED (01)
  3. Convert the hex local_address to IP:port (remember: hex is little-endian for IP, big-endian for port)
  4. Verify your decoding with ss -tlnp
💡 Hint: IP addresses in /proc/net/tcp are stored in little-endian hex. 0100007F = 127.0.0.1 (bytes reversed). Ports are big-endian hex. 1F40 = 8000. State 0A = LISTEN.
📝 View Solution 
# Sample /proc/net/tcp line (simplified):
# 0: 00000000:1F40 00000000:0000 0A ...
#
# local_address: 00000000:1F40
#   IP: 00000000 → 0.0.0.0 (listening on all interfaces)
#   Port: 1F40 → 8000 (1×16³ + 15×16² + 4×16 + 0 = 8000)
#
# rem_address: 00000000:0000
#   0.0.0.0:0 → no remote (listening socket)
#
# State: 0A = LISTEN

# Another example:
# 0: 0100007F:0050 00000000:0000 0A ...
#   IP: 0100007F (little-endian) → 7F.00.00.01 → 127.0.0.1
#   Port: 0050 → 80
#   State: 0A → LISTEN
#   → A web server listening on 127.0.0.1:80 (localhost only!)

# Verify with ss:
$ ss -tlnp | grep -E ':8000|:80'

📝 Chapter 4 — Practice Questions

Q1
Trace the complete path of an inbound packet arriving at a Linux server's NIC destined for a local application on port 8000. Name every kernel subsystem it passes through, in order, and what each does.
Show Answer
Answer

NIC → DMA → netfilter PREROUTING → routing decision (local) → netfilter INPUT → TCP stack → socket → application.

  1. NIC: Receives electrical/optical signal, verifies FCS (drops if CRC error), strips preamble.
  2. DMA: NIC writes frame directly to pre-allocated RX ring buffer in RAM — zero CPU.
  3. Hardware IRQ: NIC fires interrupt. Kernel's NAPI driver begins polling the ring buffer.
  4. netfilter PREROUTING: Raw table, connection tracking, mangle table, DNAT (if port forwarding).
  5. Routing decision: Kernel checks destination IP — is it local (on one of our interfaces)? Yes.
  6. netfilter INPUT: Filter table — iptables rules decide ACCEPT/DROP/REJECT.
  7. TCP stack: Verify checksum, find socket by port, check sequence numbers, update congestion window, queue data in receive buffer.
  8. Socket layer: Application's recv() unblocks, data copied from kernel to userspace.
Explanation

This is the most fundamental networking question for Linux SREs. The key distinction: PREROUTING is for ALL incoming packets (routed AND local), while INPUT is only for packets destined for this host. If you're debugging why a packet isn't reaching your application, check: is it being dropped at PREROUTING (DNAT issue?), INPUT (firewall?), or is it reaching the TCP stack but the socket buffer is full (application not reading)?

Q2
A Docker container on the default bridge network can ping other containers by IP but cannot reach the internet. ping 8.8.8.8 fails. What kernel mechanisms enable outbound internet access, and what's the most likely missing piece?
Show Answer
Answer

iptables MASQUERADE (SNAT) in the POSTROUTING chain of the nat table. Docker adds: iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 172.17.0.0/16 ! -o docker0 -j MASQUERADE. This rewrites the source IP of outbound container traffic from the container's IP (172.17.0.x) to the host's IP — so reply packets from the internet come back to the host, which then DNATs them back to the container.

Most likely missing piece: IP forwarding is disabled: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=0. The host kernel refuses to route packets between interfaces. Or the MASQUERADE rule was deleted. Or the container has no default route pointing to the bridge gateway.

Explanation

Container internet access requires 3 kernel settings: (1) net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 — enable IP forwarding, (2) iptables MASQUERADE rule for the container subnet, (3) the container's default route pointing to the bridge IP. If any of these is missing, outbound internet fails. Docker sets these automatically, but manually-created netns won't have them.

Q3
What does bridge fdb show dev docker0 display? How does a Linux bridge learn these entries, and what happens when it receives a frame with a destination MAC not in this table?
Show Answer
Answer

It displays the Forwarding Database (FDB) — the bridge's MAC address table, mapping MAC addresses to bridge ports (veth interfaces). Each entry shows which MAC is reachable via which port.

Learning: The bridge reads the source MAC of every incoming frame and records: "MAC X arrived on port Y." This is identical to how a physical switch learns.

Unknown destination: When a frame arrives with a destination MAC not in the FDB, the bridge floods the frame to all ports except the one it arrived on (unknown unicast flooding). The destination, if present, will respond, and the bridge learns its location from the response's source MAC.

Explanation

Linux bridges behave exactly like physical switches. The FDB is the CAM table equivalent. bridge fdb show is the Linux equivalent of show mac address-table on Cisco. This is fundamental to understanding how Docker containers on the same bridge communicate directly (L2) without going through the host's IP stack.

Q4
You run cat /proc/net/tcp and see a line with local_address 00000000:1F40 in state 0A. What does this mean? Translate the hex to human-readable IP:port and state. Why might this socket be unreachable from another host?
Show Answer
Answer

Translation: 00000000 = 0.0.0.0 (listening on ALL interfaces). 1F40 = 8000 (port). State 0A = LISTEN. The process has bound to 0.0.0.0:8000, meaning it accepts connections on any interface — eth0, lo, docker0, anything.

Why unreachable: If the socket shows 00000000:1F40 (0.0.0.0) it SHOULD be reachable from any interface. If it's unreachable from another host, the issue is likely: (1) iptables INPUT chain DROP, (2) a network-level firewall (security group), (3) the process bound to 0.0.0.0 but the interface isn't in the same namespace, or (4) net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 for routed traffic.

Explanation

The distinction between 00000000:PORT (0.0.0.0, all interfaces) and 0100007F:PORT (127.0.0.1, loopback only) is critical. A process bound to 127.0.0.1 is invisible to external hosts even if the port is open. This is a common Docker issue — Django bound to 127.0.0.1 inside the container means the port is unreachable from the Docker bridge.

Q5
Explain the difference between PREROUTING, INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT, and POSTROUTING in netfilter. At which hook does Docker's MASQUERADE (container → internet NAT) happen? At which hook would you block incoming traffic to a specific port?
Show Answer
Answer
HookWhenUsed For
PREROUTINGAs soon as packet enters the network stackDNAT (port forwarding), connection tracking
INPUTPackets destined for LOCAL processesFirewall (block port 22 from outside)
FORWARDPackets ROUTED through this hostRouter/firewall between networks
OUTPUTLocally-GENERATED packetsRestrict outbound connections from host
POSTROUTINGJust before packet leaves the network stackSNAT/MASQUERADE (Docker internet access)

MASQUERADE happens at POSTROUTING. Docker's rule: iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 172.17.0.0/16 ! -o docker0 -j MASQUERADE. Block incoming: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j DROP at the INPUT hook.

Explanation

The netfilter hook order is the single most important concept for Linux firewall debugging. When a packet disappears, you need to know which hook to check. Container → internet: check POSTROUTING for MASQUERADE. Internet → container: check PREROUTING for DNAT. Local process unreachable: check INPUT. Host can't reach external: check OUTPUT.

Q6
You run nsenter -t PID -n ip addr to enter a container's network namespace. You see eth0@if47. What does the @if47 mean? What is interface index 47 on the host?
Show Answer
Answer

eth0@if47 means this interface (eth0, inside the container's netns) is one end of a veth pair. The peer interface has index 47 on the other side (the host). The @if47 notation is a convenience — it tells you "the other end of this veth pair is interface index 47 in the peer namespace."

On the host, ip link show | grep "^47:" would show the veth interface connected to this container's eth0. This is how you trace a container's network path: container eth0 → veth47 on host → bridge → ...

Explanation

The @ifN notation is unique to veth pairs. Regular interfaces don't show it. It's an invaluable debugging clue — when you see eth0@if47 inside a container, you immediately know to run ip link show dev type veth | grep "^47:" on the host to find the peer. This is how you map container interfaces to host interfaces without Docker's help.

Q7
Your Kubernetes node has 200 pods. You notice dmesg shows nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet. Existing connections work fine, but new connections time out. Explain what happened, why existing connections still work, and list three fixes.
Show Answer
Answer

The conntrack table (connection tracking table) has a maximum size (nf_conntrack_max, typically 262144). Every tracked connection — TCP, UDP, ICMP — occupies one entry. With 200 pods each making outbound connections, plus service-to-pod NAT entries, the table filled up.

Why existing connections work: They already have entries in the conntrack table. The table is full for NEW entries — packets for established connections match existing entries and are processed normally.

Three fixes:

  1. Increase the limit: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=1048576 (4× default).
  2. Reduce timeouts: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established=600 (10 min instead of 5 days default).
  3. Disable tracking for specific traffic: Add NOTRACK iptables rule for traffic that doesn't need NAT (e.g., pod-to-pod on same node).
Explanation

Conntrack overflow is a top-5 Kubernetes networking issue. It's insidious because monitoring shows "everything is fine" — existing connections work, CPU is low — but new connections silently fail. The default nf_conntrack_max of 262144 is easily exhausted on a busy K8s node. Check conntrack -C for current count vs sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max for the limit.

Q8
What is the difference between ip netns list and lsns -t net? Why might ip netns list show empty output while Docker containers are running? How do you enter a Docker container's network namespace if ip netns doesn't show it?
Show Answer
Answer

ip netns list only shows named network namespaces — those created with ip netns add NAME and mounted at /var/run/netns/NAME. Docker creates unnamed namespaces that aren't registered with iproute2.

lsns -t net lists all network namespaces on the system by scanning /proc/*/ns/net — it sees every namespace regardless of how it was created.

Entering a Docker container's netns: Find the container's PID via docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' container-name, then nsenter -t PID -n bash. This works for ANY namespace, named or unnamed.

Explanation

This is a practical gotcha that confuses many engineers. They run ip netns list, see nothing, and assume namespaces aren't working. Docker's namespaces are perfectly functional — they're just invisible to iproute2. Always use lsns for a complete view, and nsenter to enter any namespace by PID.

Q9
Write the complete sequence of ip commands to create a network namespace, give it a veth pair connected to a bridge, assign an IP, and enable outbound internet access via MASQUERADE. This is exactly what Docker does.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Create and configure namespace
ip netns add mycontainer
ip netns exec mycontainer ip link set lo up

# 2. Create bridge (if not exists)
ip link add docker0 type bridge
ip addr add 172.17.0.1/16 dev docker0
ip link set docker0 up

# 3. Create veth pair and connect
ip link add veth-host type veth peer name veth-cont
ip link set veth-cont netns mycontainer
ip link set veth-host master docker0
ip link set veth-host up

# 4. Configure inside namespace
ip netns exec mycontainer ip link set veth-cont name eth0
ip netns exec mycontainer ip addr add 172.17.0.2/16 dev eth0
ip netns exec mycontainer ip link set eth0 up
ip netns exec mycontainer ip route add default via 172.17.0.1

# 5. Enable internet access (MASQUERADE NAT + IP forwarding)
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 172.17.0.0/16 ! -o docker0 -j MASQUERADE

# Test:
ip netns exec mycontainer ping 8.8.8.8
Explanation

These 12 commands are the essence of container networking. Every container runtime (Docker, containerd, Podman, LXC) follows this exact pattern. Understanding this sequence means you can debug any container networking issue by manually tracing the veth → bridge → iptables path, even if the container runtime is completely broken.

Q10
You suspect a memory leak in a network-intensive application. Using only /proc/net/, how would you check: (a) how many TCP sockets are in TIME_WAIT state, (b) whether socket buffers are filling up, and (c) whether the application is actually reading data or if it's backing up in kernel buffers?
Show Answer
Answer

(a) TIME_WAIT count: cat /proc/net/tcp | awk '$4=="06"' | wc -l — state 06 = TIME_WAIT. High counts (>1000) indicate many short-lived connections being opened and closed rapidly.

(b) Socket buffer fullness: cat /proc/net/tcp shows tx_queue:rx_queue in hex. Non-zero rx_queue means data is sitting in the kernel's receive buffer waiting for the application to read(). Non-zero tx_queue means data queued for sending but not yet acknowledged.

(c) Application reading vs kernel buffering: Compare rx_queue from /proc/net/tcp with the application's reported processing rate. If rx_queue is growing, the app isn't reading fast enough. Also check cat /proc/net/netstat | grep TcpExt for TCPBacklogDrop and TCPOFODrop — these indicate kernel-level drops due to full buffers.

# Quick TIME_WAIT count
$ cat /proc/net/tcp | awk '$4=="06"' | wc -l
247

# Check receive queue for a specific socket (field 5 = rx_queue in hex)
$ cat /proc/net/tcp | awk '{print $2, $5, $4}'
local_address rx_queue state
00000000:1F40 00000000 0A  ← LISTEN, no queue
0A000105:1F40 7B000000 01  ← ESTABLISHED, rx_queue = 0x7B = 123 bytes waiting!
Explanation

/proc/net/ is the ultimate fallback when tools aren't available. It's always there — it's the kernel's API. TIME_WAIT sockets consume memory but don't affect functionality unless they exhaust the ephemeral port range. Growing rx_queue indicates the application is the bottleneck — the kernel has the data but the app won't read it. This is the classic "app is slow, not the network" indicator.

🟢 Part 2: Layer 3 — IPChapters 5-7

Chapter 5: IPv4 — Addressing, Subnetting & the Routing Table

Layer 3 is where networks become internetworks. At L2 (Ethernet), you can only reach devices on the same physical segment. At L3 (IP), you can reach any device on any network anywhere in the world — because IP provides global addressing and hop-by-hop routing. This chapter covers the IP address (what those 4 numbers actually mean), subnetting (how to divide a network into smaller pieces), the IP header (what's inside every IP packet), and routing (how packets find their way across the internet). If L1/L2 is the highway, L3 is the GPS.

🟢 BEGINNER ⏱️ ~3 hours 🧮 Subnetting Math 🌐 BGP + ECMP

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:

  • Decode any IPv4 address into its network and host portions using CIDR notation
  • Calculate subnet ranges in your head — network address, broadcast address, usable hosts
  • Dissect the IPv4 header byte-by-byte and explain every field
  • Understand how routing tables work — longest prefix match, default routes, static vs dynamic
  • Explain how BGP routes traffic across the internet and inside modern data centers
  • Understand ECMP and how it enables spine-leaf Clos fabrics
🔗 Applies To:
DevOps
SRE
Cloud Eng
Network Eng
SysAdmin
Weight: 25% of network incidents involve IP misconfiguration
🎯 SRE Interview Tip

In any infrastructure interview, you'll be asked to subnet. The question might be disguised: "You need to allocate IP space for 3 environments (dev, staging, prod) each needing 50 hosts. What CIDR blocks do you use?" The correct answer: /26 per environment (64 addresses, 62 usable — enough for 50 hosts with room for growth). Break the parent /24 into four /26 subnets: .0/26, .64/26, .128/26, .192/26. Practice mental subnetting math — being able to calculate CIDR ranges without a subnet calculator marks you as infrastructure-savvy in any interview.

5.1 What Is an IP Address Really?

An IPv4 address is exactly 32 bits — 32 ones and zeros. We write it as four decimal numbers separated by dots (each called an octet because it represents 8 bits) purely for human readability. The IP address 192.168.1.1 is actually 11000000.10101000.00000001.00000001 in binary. The subnet mask tells us which part is the network (which subnet this host belongs to) and which part is the host (which specific device on that subnet).

IP ADDRESS AS 32 BITS — Network (Green) vs Host (Blue)
IP:  192.168.1.100 /24  (CIDR notation — 24 network bits)
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │ 11000000  10101000  00000001  01100100                          │
     │   192   .   168   .    1    .   100                             │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Mask: /24 = 255.255.255.0
     ┌────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  NETWORK (24 bits)          │  HOST (8 bits)                     │
     │  11000000.10101000.00000001 │  01100100                          │
     │  192     .168     .1       │  .100                              │
     └────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘
     Network address: 192.168.1.0    (host bits = all zeros)
     Broadcast addr:  192.168.1.255  (host bits = all ones)
     Usable range:    192.168.1.1 — 192.168.1.254 (254 hosts)
🗺️ Public vs Private IP Addresses (RFC 1918)
RangeCIDRTotal AddressesTypical Use
10.0.0.0 — 10.255.255.25510.0.0.0/816,777,216Large enterprise networks, cloud VPCs
172.16.0.0 — 172.31.255.255172.16.0.0/121,048,576Mid-size networks, Docker default bridge
192.168.0.0 — 192.168.255.255192.168.0.0/1665,536Home/office networks, VM host-only

Private IPs are NOT routable on the public internet. When a packet with a private source IP reaches an internet router, it's dropped. This is why NAT exists — to translate private IPs to public ones at the network edge.

Historical note — why CIDR replaced classful addressing: Before 1993, IP addresses were divided into rigid classes: Class A (/8, 16M hosts — only 126 networks), Class B (/16, 65K hosts), Class C (/24, 254 hosts). A company needing 300 hosts had to take a Class B (wasting 65,234 addresses). This was rapidly exhausting the IPv4 space. CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) replaced this in 1993 — it allows any prefix length (/23, /25, /26, etc.), dramatically reducing waste. This is why you see /24, /26, /28 today instead of just /8, /16, /24.

⭐ Special IP Addresses Every SRE Should Know
AddressNameMeaningSRE Context
0.0.0.0Unspecified / "Any"Can mean "all interfaces" when listening, or "default route" in routing0.0.0.0:8000 = app listens on all interfaces. 0.0.0.0/0 = default route.
127.0.0.1Loopback / localhostAlways refers to the local machine. Traffic never leaves the host.Binding to 127.0.0.1 = only accessible from within this host (container isolation!)
255.255.255.255Limited BroadcastDelivered to ALL hosts on the local L2 segment. Never forwarded by routers.DHCP DISCOVER uses this. ARP requests use L2 broadcast, not this.
169.254.x.xLink-Local (APIPA)Auto-assigned when DHCP fails. Only works within the local L2 segment.If you see 169.254.x.x on eth0, DHCP failed. Check DHCP server.
🔄 NAT — How Private IPs Reach the Internet

NAT (Network Address Translation) rewrites the source or destination IP address of packets as they pass through a router. It's the reason your laptop (with private IP 192.168.1.100) can browse the internet (which only routes public IPs).

TypeWhat It ChangesWhere (netfilter hook)Use Case
SNAT (Source NAT)Rewrites SOURCE IPPOSTROUTINGOutbound internet access — many private IPs share one public IP
DNAT (Destination NAT)Rewrites DESTINATION IPPREROUTINGPort forwarding — external IP:80 → internal server:8000
MASQUERADEDynamic SNAT (auto-detects outgoing IP)POSTROUTINGDocker containers → internet. DHCP clients with changing IPs.
 
# Docker MASQUERADE rule (how containers reach the internet):
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 172.17.0.0/16 ! -o docker0 -j MASQUERADE
# Packet from container (src=172.17.0.2) → MASQUERADE rewrites src=host-IP
# Reply (dst=host-IP) → conntrack reverses: dst=172.17.0.2

# Manual SNAT (static public IP):
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.0.1.0/24 -o eth0 -j SNAT --to-source 203.0.113.5

# DNAT port forwarding (external 80 → internal 8000):
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i eth0 -p tcp --dport 80 -j DNAT --to-destination 10.0.1.50:8000

Why NAT exists: IPv4 has ~3.7 billion usable public addresses but there are ~15 billion internet-connected devices. NAT lets millions of devices share a single public IP. IPv6 eliminates the need for NAT (every device gets a globally unique address), but NAT will persist in IPv4 networks indefinitely.

DHCP — How Devices Get Their IP Addresses (DISCOVER→OFFER→REQUEST→ACK)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NEW DEVICE BOOTS UP — No IP address yet (0.0.0.0)                             │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌──────────────┐                                    ┌──────────────────┐    │
│  │ CLIENT       │                                    │ DHCP SERVER      │    │
│  │ MAC: aa:bb:cc│                                    │ 10.0.1.1         │    │
│  │ IP: 0.0.0.0  │                                    │ (gateway/router) │    │
│  └──────┬───────┘                                    └────────┬─────────┘    │

│         │    src=0.0.0.0:68 → dst=255.255.255.255:67          │              │
│         │    "Is there a DHCP server out there?"              │              │

│         │                                                     │              │

│         │    src=10.0.1.1:67 → dst=255.255.255.255:68         │              │

🔑 conntrack is the magic — it remembers every NAT mapping so replies

│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │ 1. conntrack looks up: (src=142.250.80.46:443, dst=203.0.113.5:54321)│     │
│  │ 2. Finds entry #1: REPLY column matches!                             │     │
│  │ 3. Un-NATs: dst=203.0.113.5:54321 → dst=10.0.1.10:54321             │     │
│  │ 4. Delivers to 10.0.1.10:54321 (the original laptop)                │     │
│  │ 5. Refreshes timer → 432000 (5 days for ESTABLISHED TCP)             │     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                               │
│  ⚠️ WHAT HAPPENS WHEN TABLE IS FULL (nf_conntrack_max reached):               │
│     New SYNs arrive → kernel tries to create new conntrack entry → FAILS      │
│     → Packet DROPPED silently. No RST. No ICMP. Just timeout.                 │
│     → dmesg: "nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet"                    │
│     EXISTING connections continue to work (their entries are still there).     │
│     This is why "some connections work, new ones don't" = conntrack full.    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

5.2 Subnetting — The Art of Dividing Networks

Subnetting splits a large IP network into smaller, isolated subnetworks. Why? To control broadcast domains (fewer hosts = fewer broadcasts), improve security (finance can't reach HR at L3), and organize infrastructure (web servers on one subnet, databases on another).

SUBNETTING — Visual Breakdown of a /24 Divided into Four /26 Subnets
10.0.1.0/24  (256 total addresses, 254 usable hosts)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ██████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

DIVIDED INTO 4 × /26 SUBNETS (64 addresses each, 62 usable hosts)

┌────────────────────┬────────────────────┬────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
│ ██████████████████ │ ██████████████████ │ ██████████████████ │ ██████████████████ │
└────────────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────────┘

10.0.1.0/26          10.0.1.64/26        10.0.1.128/26       10.0.1.192/26
  .0   = network       .64  = network      .128 = network       .192 = network
  .1   = first host    .65  = first host   .129 = first host    .193 = first host
  .62  = last host     .126 = last host    .190 = last host     .254 = last host
  .63  = broadcast     .127 = broadcast    .191 = broadcast     .255 = broadcast

USE CASE:
  /26 Subnet A (10.0.1.0/26)   → Web servers (62 hosts max)
  /26 Subnet B (10.0.1.64/26)  → Application servers
  /26 Subnet C (10.0.1.128/26) → Database servers
  /26 Subnet D (10.0.1.192/26) → Management/Bastion hosts

CIDRSubnet MaskTotal AddrsUsable HostsExample (10.0.1.0)
/16255.255.0.065,53665,53410.0.0.0 — 10.0.255.255
/24255.255.255.025625410.0.1.0 — 10.0.1.255
/25255.255.255.12812812610.0.1.0 — 10.0.1.127
/26255.255.255.192646210.0.1.0 — 10.0.1.63
/27255.255.255.224323010.0.1.0 — 10.0.1.31
/28255.255.255.240161410.0.1.0 — 10.0.1.15

Mental math trick: Subtract the CIDR from 32, then 2^result = total addresses. /26 = 32-26 = 6 → 2^6 = 64 addresses. Subtract 2 (network + broadcast) = usable hosts. /28 = 32-28 = 4 → 2^4 = 16 total, 14 usable.

Supernetting (route aggregation): The reverse of subnetting — combining multiple smaller networks into one larger route advertisement. If you have 10.0.0.0/24, 10.0.1.0/24, 10.0.2.0/24, and 10.0.3.0/24, you can advertise them as a single 10.0.0.0/22 (4 × 256 = 1024 addresses). This reduces routing table size — BGP prefers aggregated routes. Kubernetes pod CIDRs use this: each node gets a /24, but the entire cluster advertises a single /16 aggregate via BGP.

SUPERNETTING / ROUTE AGGREGATION — 4× /24 → 1× /22
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BEFORE AGGREGATION (4 separate /24 routes):                         │
│                                                                       │
│  10.0.0.0/24  ┌────────────────┐                                     │
│  10.0.1.0/24  │ .0────.255     │  ← 4 routes × 256 IPs each         │
│  10.0.2.0/24  │ .0────.255     │    BGP sends 4 announcements        │
│  10.0.3.0/24  │ .0────.255     │    Routing table: 4 entries         │
│               └────────────────┘                                     │
│                                                                       │
│  AFTER AGGREGATION (1 aggregated /22 route):                          │
│                                                                       │
│               ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐           │
│  10.0.0.0/22  │ .0──────────────────────────.3.255      │           │
│               │ 1024 addresses (4 × 256)                  │           │
│               │ BGP sends 1 announcement                  │           │
│               │ Routing table: 1 entry                     │           │
│               └──────────────────────────────────────────┘           │
│                                                                       │
│  BINARY EXPLANATION:                                                  │
│  10.0.0.0  = 00001010.00000000.000000|00.00000000                   │
│  10.0.3.0  = 00001010.00000000.000000|11.00000000                   │
│             └── first 22 bits identical ──┘                          │
│  These 4 networks share the same first 22 bits → aggregate to /22!   │
│                                                                       │
│  KUBERNETES EXAMPLE:                                                  │
│  Node-1: 10.244.1.0/24 ┐                                             │
│  Node-2: 10.244.2.0/24 ├─ All nodes advertise single 10.244.0.0/16  │
│  Node-3: 10.244.3.0/24 │  via BGP to ToR switch (1 route, not 250!)  │
│  ... up to 255 nodes   ┘                                             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
