│  ├───┴───┼─────┴───┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┼───┴──────────┤│
│  │  TTL  │ Protocol│  Hdr Checksum    │     Source IP (32 bits)         ││
│  ├───────┴─────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ Dest IP (32)    │   OPTIONS (0-40 bytes, if IHL > 5)                 ││
│  └─────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│  13 fields. Variable length. Checksum recalculated at every hop.          │
│  Routers may fragment. Options inline (every router processes them).      │
│                                                                           │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  IPv6 HEADER (40 bytes, FIXED — ALWAYS)                                   │
│  ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐│
│  │Ver│ Traffic Class  │         Flow Label (20 bits)                     ││
│  ├───┼────────────────┼───────────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┤│
│  │ Payload Length     │ Next Header       │ Hop Limit     │               ││
│  ├────────────────────┴───────────────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┤│
│  │                                                                        ││
│  │                    SOURCE ADDRESS (128 bits — 4 rows of 32)             ││
│  │                                                                        ││
│  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │                                                                        ││
│  │                 DESTINATION ADDRESS (128 bits — 4 rows of 32)           ││
│  │                                                                        ││
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│  8 fields. Fixed length. No checksum (L2+L4 handle it).                    │
│  Routers NEVER fragment. Extension headers are chained, not inline.        │
│                                                                           │
│  FIELD-BY-FIELD COMPARISON:                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ Purpose             │ IPv4                 │ IPv6                    │ │
│  ├─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤ │
│  │ Header Length       │ IHL × 4 (20-60 bytes)│ FIXED 40 bytes          │ │
│  │ Fragmentation       │ In IP header          │ Extension header only   │ │
│  │ Error Detection     │ Header Checksum       │ NONE (removed!)         │ │
│  │ QoS                 │ ToS/DSCP (8 bits)     │ Traffic Class (8 bits)  │ │
│  │ Flow Identification │ NONE (L4 ports used)  │ Flow Label (20 bits!)   │ │
│  │ Loop Prevention     │ TTL (8 bits)          │ Hop Limit (8 bits)      │ │
│  │ Next Protocol       │ Protocol (8 bits)     │ Next Header (8 bits)    │ │
│  │ Options             │ Inline (ALL routers)  │ Chained (destination)   │ │
│  └─────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
IPv6 EXTENSION HEADERS — Chained After the Fixed Header
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  IPv6 FIXED HEADER (40 bytes)                                     │
│  Next Header = 0 (Hop-by-Hop Options)                             │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  HOP-BY-HOP OPTIONS HEADER                                        │
│  Next Header = 44 (Fragment Header)                               │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  FRAGMENT HEADER                                                  │
│  Next Header = 6 (TCP)                                            │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  TCP HEADER + PAYLOAD                                             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

COMMON NEXT HEADER VALUES (same as IPv4 Protocol field):
  0  = Hop-by-Hop Options    6  = TCP
  17 = UDP                   58 = ICMPv6
  43 = Routing Header        44 = Fragment Header
  50 = ESP (IPsec)           51 = AH (IPsec)
  59 = No Next Header (end of chain)

KEY DIFFERENCE FROM IPv4 OPTIONS:
  IPv4 options are INLINE in the IP header (every router processes them).
  IPv6 extension headers are CHAINED after the fixed header.
  Only the Hop-by-Hop header is processed by every router.
  Other extension headers are only processed by the destination.
🧬 IPv6 Address Structure — The 128 Bits Are Organized, Not Random

Every global unicast IPv6 address follows a precise, hierarchical structure. Understanding this structure is the key to IPv6 network design, subnetting, and troubleshooting. The 128 bits are divided into three logical parts:

IPv6 ADDRESS STRUCTURE — Routing Prefix, Subnet ID, Interface ID
128-BIT IPv6 ADDRESS:  2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334
                        └──────────────────────────────┘└──────────────────┘
                                 ROUTING PREFIX              INTERFACE ID
                            (usually /48 to /64)             (64 bits)

MORE PRECISE BREAKDOWN (typical ISP delegation):

  2001:0db8:85a3:   0000:   0000:8a2e:0370:7334
  └──────────────┘  └────┘  └────────────────────┘
   ISP /48 prefix    Subnet   Interface ID (EUI-64 or random)
                     ID       (64 bits — identifies the HOST)
                     (16 bits
                     = 65,536
                     subnets!)

HOW A /48 GETS TO YOU (the delegation chain):

  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐
  │  IANA    │────▶│   RIR    │────▶│   ISP    │────▶│   YOU    │
  │(top pool)│     │(ARIN/RIPE│     │(Comcast, │     │(business)│
  │          │     │ APNIC..) │     │ AWS,etc) │     │          │
  └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘
       │                │                │                │
  /12 or larger    /23 to /32       /48 to you!    You allocate
  to each RIR      to each ISP      (65K /64s)     /64 per VLAN

WHY /64 IS SPECIAL:
  • SLAAC requires exactly 64 bits for the interface ID (EUI-64 or random).
  • Any prefix longer than /64 breaks SLAAC (not enough bits for interface ID).
  • Any prefix shorter than /64 wastes space without benefit.
  • /64 per subnet is the gold standard — every LAN gets one /64.

THE MATH AT EACH LEVEL:
  • ISP gives you /48  → 2^(64-48) = 2^16 = 65,536 /64 subnets
  • ISP gives you /56  → 2^(64-56) = 2^8  = 256 /64 subnets (residential)
  • ISP gives you /60  → 2^(64-60) = 2^4  = 16 /64 subnets (small office)

WHY YOU CAN'T JUST USE SMALLER SUBNETS:
  • /96 = only 32 bits for interface ID. SLAAC breaks.
  • /80 = 48 bits for interface ID. Non-standard, no SLAAC.
  • The /64 boundary is baked into EVERYTHING: SLAAC, NDP, multicast,
    privacy extensions, secure neighbor discovery — they all assume /64.

Practical takeaway: When your ISP says "here's your IPv6 block," they're giving you a routing prefix. You subdivide it into /64 subnets for each VLAN, floor, or purpose. The interface ID (last 64 bits) is auto-generated by each host — you never manually assign it (unless you're configuring a server with a static address). This is fundamentally different from IPv4 where you manually assign every octet.

6.2 IPv6 Addressing — Demystified

An IPv6 address is 128 bits — four times longer than IPv4. It's written as 8 groups of 4 hexadecimal digits separated by colons. The notation looks intimidating at first, but once you learn the shortening rules (two simple rules), reading IPv6 becomes second nature.

🎯 SRE Interview Tip

In any infrastructure interview, you should be able to look at an IPv6 address and instantly classify it. fe80: = link-local (never routed). 2xxx: or 3xxx: = global unicast (internet-routable). fdxx: = unique local (private). ffxx: = multicast. ::1 = loopback. Also know: IPv6 uses /64 for all LAN subnets (period — no exceptions in standard practice). An ISP typically delegates /48 to businesses and /56 to residential. You will be asked why IPv6 doesn't need NAT — the answer is 340 undecillion addresses and restored end-to-end connectivity. You will be asked the #1 IPv6 security mistake — it's forgetting to configure ip6tables, leaving IPv6 completely unfirewalled.

IPv6 ADDRESS — 128 Bits Visualized (Color-Coded Fields)
FULL ADDRESS:  2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334  (128 bits, 8 groups)
               ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
               │2001 │0db8 │85a3 │0000 │0000 │8a2e │0370 │7334 │  ← 8 hextets
               └─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘
                16b   16b   16b   16b   16b   16b   16b   16b   ← 16 bits each

SHORTENING RULE #1 — Drop leading zeros in each group:
   0db8 → db8    0000 → 0    0370 → 370
   → 2001:db8:85a3:0:0:8a2e:370:7334

SHORTENING RULE #2 — Replace ONE consecutive run of zero groups with ::
   → 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334
      (the :: replaces the two consecutive zero groups :0:0:)

⚠️ CRITICAL RULE: :: can only be used ONCE in an address.
   If you have two runs of zeros, only compress one — otherwise
   the address becomes ambiguous (you can't tell how many zeros
   each :: represents).

EXAMPLES OF LEGAL SHORTENING:
   Full:                   2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
   Shortened:              2001:db8::1  (7 zero groups compressed to ::)

   Full:                   fe80:0000:0000:0000:0a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f
   Shortened:              fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f

   Full:                   0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
   Shortened:              ::1  (IPv6 loopback — 127 zeros, then 1)
🏷️ IPv6 Address Types — Know Them at a Glance

Unlike IPv4 where all addresses look similar, IPv6 address types are immediately recognizable by their first bits (the prefix). You can look at the first few hex digits and instantly know what type of address you're dealing with.

TypePrefixFirst DigitsScopeRoutable?IPv4 Equivalent
Loopback::1/128::1Host only❌127.0.0.1
Link-Localfe80::/10fe80: — febf:Single L2 segment❌ (never forwarded)169.254.x.x (APIPA)
Unique Local (ULA)fc00::/7fcxx: or fdxx:Organization (site)❌ (private only)10.0.0.0/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16
Global Unicast2000::/32xxx: or 3xxx:Entire Internet✅ YESPublic IPv4 (e.g., 8.8.8.8)
Multicastff00::/8ffxx:Varies (see scope)N/A (multicast)224.0.0.0/4
IPv6 ADDRESS TYPE VISUAL IDENTIFICATION
IF FIRST DIGITS ARE...         THEN IT'S...

fe80:  ──────────────────►  LINK-LOCAL (never leaves the L2 segment)
                            Every IPv6 interface has one. Auto-generated.
                            Example: fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f

fdxx:  ──────────────────►  UNIQUE LOCAL (private, like RFC 1918)
                            Use for internal networks. Not internet-routable.
                            Example: fd12:3456:789a:1::10

2xxx:  ──────────────────►  GLOBAL UNICAST (public internet)
or 3xxx:                    Your routable internet address. ISP assigns
                            a /48 or /56 prefix. You assign /64 subnets.
                            Example: 2001:4860:4860::8888 (Google DNS)

ffxx:  ──────────────────►  MULTICAST (one-to-many)
                            Replaces IPv4 broadcast. NDP uses multicast.
                            Example: ff02::1 = all nodes on link
                                     ff02::2 = all routers on link

::1    ──────────────────►  LOOPBACK (same host only)
                            Format: exactly ::1. Used exactly like 127.0.0.1.

::     ──────────────────►  UNSPECIFIED (no address yet)
                            All zeros. Used when interface has no address.
                            Like 0.0.0.0 in IPv4.
🔗 Link-Local Addresses — Why Every IPv6 Interface Has fe80::

Every IPv6-enabled interface automatically generates a link-local address (fe80::/10) — even if no router is present and no global address is configured. This is fundamentally different from IPv4, where an interface without DHCP or static config has NO address at all (except maybe 169.254.x.x APIPA).

Why it matters: Link-local addresses enable IPv6 devices to communicate on the same L2 segment WITHOUT any configuration — no DHCP, no SLAAC, no manual config needed. This is how NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) works: routers and hosts discover each other using link-local addresses. In Kubernetes, pod IPv6 addresses are typically link-local or global depending on the CNI configuration.

IPv6 INTERFACE — Multiple Addresses Are Normal
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  $ ip -6 addr show eth0                                         │
│                                                                  │
│  eth0:                        │
│      inet6 fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f/64 scope link         │
│         └── LINK-LOCAL: Always present. Auto-generated from MAC  │
│             Used for NDP (router discovery, neighbor discovery) │
│                                                                  │
│      inet6 2001:db8:1234:5678:a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f/64 scope global│
│         └── GLOBAL UNICAST: Routable internet address            │
│             Derived via SLAAC (Router Advertisement + EUI-64)    │
│                                                                  │
│      inet6 fd12:3456:789a:1::10/64 scope global                  │
│         └── UNIQUE LOCAL: Private (internal) address             │
│             Manually configured for internal services            │
│                                                                  │
│  THREE ADDRESSES on ONE interface — completely normal in IPv6!   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🤖 SLAAC — How IPv6 Hosts Auto-Configure Without DHCP

SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) is IPv6's killer feature: hosts configure their own global addresses without any DHCP server. The process is elegant:

  1. Host generates a link-local address (fe80::/10) from its MAC address via EUI-64.
  2. Host sends a Router Solicitation (RS) to ff02::2 (all routers multicast).
  3. Router replies with a Router Advertisement (RA) containing the /64 prefix (e.g., 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64).
  4. Host combines the prefix with its interface ID (from EUI-64 or privacy extensions) → full 128-bit global address.
  5. Host performs DAD (Duplicate Address Detection) to ensure no other device is using this address.
SLAAC — Stateless Address Autoconfiguration Flow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NEW HOST BOOTS — interfaces comes up, no IPv6 config yet             │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────┐                          ┌──────────────────┐      │
│  │ HOST         │                          │ ROUTER           │      │
│  │ (no address) │                          │ 2001:db8:5678::1 │      │
│  └──────┬───────┘                          └────────┬─────────┘      │
│         │                                           │                │
│         │ 1. Generate Link-Local (fe80::/10)         │                │
│         │    from MAC via EUI-64                     │                │
│         │    → fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f             │                │
│         │                                           │                │
│         │ 2. Router Solicitation (RS)                │                │
│         │    src=fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f           │                │
│         │    dst=ff02::2 (all routers)               │                │
│         │    "Is there a router on this link?"       │                │
│         │──────────────────────────────────────────▶│                │
│         │                                           │                │
│         │              3. Router Advertisement (RA)  │                │
│         │    src=fe80::1 (router's link-local)       │                │
│         │    dst=ff02::1 (all nodes)                 │                │
│         │    "Prefix is 2001:db8:5678::/64"          │                │
│         │    "I can be your default gateway"         │                │
│         │◀──────────────────────────────────────────│                │
│         │                                           │                │
│         │ 4. Combine prefix + EUI-64 interface ID    │                │
│         │    Prefix:   2001:db8:5678:0000::/64       │                │
│         │    Intf ID:  a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f           │                │
│         │    = 2001:db8:5678:0000:a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f│                │
│         │                                           │                │
│         │ 5. DAD (Duplicate Address Detection)       │                │
│         │    Sends NS to solicited-node multicast    │                │
│         │    "Does anyone else have this address?"   │                │
│         │    (no response = address is unique)        │                │
│         │                                           │                │
│  ┌──────┴───────┐                                    │                │
│  │ HOST NOW HAS │                                    │                │
│  │ 3 ADDRESSES: │                                    │                │
│  │ fe80::...    │ ← Link-local (always)              │                │
│  │ 2001:db8:... │ ← SLAAC global                     │                │
│  └──────────────┘                                    │                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔐 EUI-64 and Privacy Extensions — How Interface IDs Are Generated

EUI-64 stretches a 48-bit MAC address into a 64-bit interface ID by inserting FF:FE in the middle and flipping the 7th bit (universal/local bit). This means your IPv6 address is derived from your MAC — which is globally unique and permanent — making your device trackable across networks.

EUI-64 — From 48-bit MAC to 64-bit IPv6 Interface ID
MAC ADDRESS:  08:00:27:8c:5e:9f  (48 bits)
                              │
                              ▼
INSERT FFFE in the middle:
              08:00:27:FF:FE:8c:5e:9f  (64 bits)
              │        │
              │        └── Inserted FFFE (IEEE-defined marker)
              │
FLIP 7th bit (universal/local):
   08 → 0000 1000 → flip bit 7 → 0000 1010 → 0a
              0a:00:27:FF:FE:8c:5e:9f

IPv6 INTERFACE ID:  0a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f  (64 bits)
IPv6 FULL ADDRESS:  2001:db8:5678:0000:0a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f/64

🔒 PRIVACY EXTENSIONS (RFC 4941 / RFC 8981):
   Modern OSes (Windows 10+, macOS 14+, Linux NetworkManager)
   use RANDOM temporary interface IDs instead of EUI-64:
   → 2001:db8:5678:0000:3f7a:c2e1:9b4d:1a5f  (random, temporary)
   → Changes daily → prevents tracking across networks
   → Stable privacy addresses (RFC 7217) keep the same address
     per network (different per SSID, but consistent over time)
🚫 No Broadcast in IPv6! — NDP Replaces ARP

IPv6 has no broadcast addresses. The concept of "send to everyone on this subnet" simply doesn't exist. Instead, IPv6 uses multicast for everything: neighbor discovery, router discovery, duplicate address detection. The protocol that handles all of this is NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) — it replaces IPv4's ARP, ICMP Router Discovery, and ICMP Redirect, all rolled into one.

This means: no ARP spoofing (ARP doesn't exist in IPv6), no broadcast storms (no broadcast), and more efficient neighbor discovery (only interested nodes join the relevant multicast groups).

FunctionIPv4 ProtocolIPv6 ProtocolIPv6 Multicast Address
Find MAC for IPARPNDP Neighbor SolicitationSolicited-node multicast (ff02::1:ffxx:xxxx)
Find routersICMP Router DiscoveryNDP Router Solicitationff02::2 (all routers)
Announce prefix— (DHCP only)NDP Router Advertisementff02::1 (all nodes)
Duplicate detectionGratuitous ARPNDP DAD (Neighbor Solicitation)Solicited-node multicast
Better gatewayICMP RedirectNDP RedirectUnicast to source
SIDE-BY-SIDE: ARP (IPv4) vs NDP (IPv6) — Same Goal, Different Mechanism
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  IPv4 ARP — "Who has 10.0.1.50? Tell 10.0.1.5"                            │
│                                                                            │
│  Host-A (10.0.1.5)                   Host-B (10.0.1.50)                   │
│  ┌──────────────┐                    ┌──────────────┐                      │
│  │ Wants to send │                    │ Quietly       │                      │
│  │ to 10.0.1.50 │                    │ listening     │                      │
│  └──────┬───────┘                    └──────┬───────┘                      │
│         │                                   │                              │
│         │ 1. ARP Request (BROADCAST)         │                              │
│         │    "Who has 10.0.1.50?"           │                              │
│         │    dst MAC = ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff    │                              │
│         │──────────────────────────────────▶│ ← EVERY host receives this!  │
│         │                                   │   ALL 254 hosts interrupted  │
│         │                                   │   Only B replies             │
│         │              2. ARP Reply         │                              │
│         │    "10.0.1.50 is at aa:bb:cc:dd"  │                              │
│         │◀──────────────────────────────────│                              │
│         │                                   │                              │
│  ISSUE: Broadcast wakes up EVERY host on the subnet.                        │
│  In a /16 with 65K hosts, that's 65K interrupts per ARP request.            │
│                                                                            │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  IPv6 NDP — "Who has 2001:db8::50? Respond to fe80::5"                     │
│                                                                            │
│  Host-A (fe80::5)                     Host-B (2001:db8::50)               │
│  ┌──────────────┐                    ┌──────────────┐                      │
│  │ Wants to send │                    │ Joined its    │                      │
│  │ to 2001:db8::50│                   │ own multicast │                      │
│  └──────┬───────┘                    │ group         │                      │
│         │                            └──────┬───────┘                      │
│         │ 1. Neighbor Solicitation (MULTICAST)                             │
│         │    "Who has 2001:db8::50?"                                       │
│         │    dst = ff02::1:ff00:50 (solicited-node mcast)                  │
│         │──────────────────────────────────▶│ ← ONLY Host-B (and maybe 1-2 │
│         │   How? Host-A computes:            │   others sharing last 24    │
│         │   ff02::1:ff00:50 =                │   bits of .50) receive this │
│         │   ff02::1:ff + last 24 bits        │                              │
│         │   of target IP (00:0050)           │                              │
│         │                                    │ 2. Neighbor Advertisement   │
│         │    "2001:db8::50 is at aa:bb:cc:dd"│                              │
│         │◀──────────────────────────────────│                              │
│                                                                            │
│  ADVANTAGE: Only the target host is interrupted.                            │
│  OS NIC filters multicast in hardware — CPU never sees irrelevant packets.  │
│  No broadcast storms. No ARP cache poisoning (harder attack surface).       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📡 IPv6 Multicast Scopes — Where the Packet Travels

IPv6 multicast addresses encode the scope (how far the packet travels) in the 4th hex digit (bits 12-15). This is far more granular than IPv4 multicast (which only has TTL-based scoping).

Scope IDPrefix ExampleMeaningTravels As Far As
1ff01::Interface-LocalNever leaves the interface (loopback only)
2ff02::Link-LocalSame L2 segment (most NDP traffic uses this)
3ff03::Realm-LocalDefined by network admin (rarely used)
4ff04::Admin-LocalSmallest administratively configured region
5ff05::Site-LocalSingle site/organization
8ff08::Organization-LocalMultiple sites in one org
e (14)ff0e::GlobalEntire internet (routable multicast)
 
# MULTICAST ADDRESS STRUCTURE:
# ff0s:xxxx:xxxx:xxxx:xxxx:xxxx:xxxx:xxxx
#  ││ │└─── Flags (4 bits, usually 0)
#  ││ └──── Scope (4 bits — see table above)
#  └└────── Always ff (marks it as multicast)

# CRITICAL MULTICAST ADDRESSES EVERY SRE SHOULD KNOW:
# ff02::1        — All nodes on this link (like broadcast, but multicast)
# ff02::2        — All routers on this link
# ff02::1:2      — All DHCPv6 servers/relays on this link
# ff02::1:ffXX:XXXX — Solicited-node multicast (for NDP)
#                     XX:XXXX = last 24 bits of target IPv6 address
#                     Only the target host(s) join this group → efficient!
🏪 DHCPv6 — Stateful Addressing When SLAAC Isn't Enough

SLAAC gives hosts an address and a default gateway, but it doesn't provide DNS servers, NTP servers, or other configuration parameters. For that, you need DHCPv6 — the IPv6 equivalent of DHCP (but with key differences from IPv4 DHCP).

FeatureIPv4 DHCPSLAAC (Stateless)DHCPv6 (Stateful)
Address assignmentServer assigns IPHost auto-generatesServer assigns IP
Default gatewayDHCP option 3Via RA from routerVia RA from router (NOT DHCPv6!)
DNS serversDHCP option 6RDNSS in RA (or DHCPv6)DHCPv6 option 23
NTP, domain, etc.DHCP optionsNot availableDHCPv6 options
Client identifierMAC addressN/A (stateless)DUID (Device Unique ID)
Lease trackingServer tracks all leasesNo tracking (stateless!)Server tracks all leases
DHCPv6 — The 4-Message Exchange (Solicit→Advertise→Request→Reply)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HOST BOOTS — needs DNS, NTP, possibly an address                     │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────┐                          ┌──────────────────┐      │
│  │ HOST         │                          │ DHCPv6 SERVER    │      │
│  │ (may already  │                          │                  │      │
│  │  have SLAAC   │                          │                  │      │
│  │  address)     │                          │                  │      │
│  └──────┬───────┘                          └────────┬─────────┘      │
│         │                                           │                │
│         │ 1. SOLICIT (multicast to ff02::1:2)        │                │
│         │    "Any DHCPv6 servers out there?"         │                │
│         │──────────────────────────────────────────▶│                │
│         │                                           │                │
│         │              2. ADVERTISE (unicast)        │                │
│         │    "I can give you DNS=2001:4860::8888"   │                │
│         │    "and an address if you need one"        │                │
│         │◀──────────────────────────────────────────│                │
│         │                                           │                │
│         │ 3. REQUEST (unicast)                       │                │
│         │    "I want that configuration!"            │                │
│         │──────────────────────────────────────────▶│                │
│         │                                           │                │
│         │              4. REPLY (unicast)            │                │
│         │    "Confirmed. DNS=2001:4860::8888"        │                │
│         │    "Lease valid for 86400 seconds"         │                │
│         │◀──────────────────────────────────────────│                │
│                                                                       │
│  KEY DIFFERENCES FROM IPv4 DHCP:                                      │
│  • DHCPv6 does NOT provide default gateway (that's from RA/SLAAC)    │
│  • DHCPv6 uses DUID, not MAC, for client identification               │
│  • DHCPv6 can be COMBINED with SLAAC: get address via SLAAC,          │
│    get DNS/NTP via DHCPv6 (this is called "stateless DHCPv6")         │
│  • The 'M' flag in Router Advertisements tells hosts:                 │
│    M=1 → Use DHCPv6 for address AND config (stateful)                 │
│    M=0, O=1 → Use SLAAC for address, DHCPv6 for other config          │
│    M=0, O=0 → Use SLAAC only (no DHCPv6)                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

When to use which: Most home/office networks use SLAAC (address) + stateless DHCPv6 (DNS). Enterprise networks often use stateful DHCPv6 for address assignment (for audit/logging — you know exactly which device had which IP at which time). Mobile networks (4G/5G) use SLAAC exclusively (no DHCPv6 at all — everything is in the RA).

🗺️ IPv6 Routing — How It's Different from IPv4 Routing

IPv6 routing works on the same principle as IPv4 (longest prefix match), but with key differences in how routes are distributed and how the routing table is structured:

IPv6 ROUTING TABLE — How a Host Decides Where to Send Packets
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  $ ip -6 route show                                                  │
│                                                                       │
│  ::1 dev lo proto kernel metric 256 pref medium                       │
│     └── Loopback: all ::1 traffic stays local                         │
│                                                                       │
│  2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev eth0 proto ra metric 100 pref medium    │
│     └── LOCAL SUBNET: directly connected, no gateway needed           │
│         Learned via Router Advertisement (SLAAC)                      │
│                                                                       │
│  fe80::/64 dev eth0 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium               │
│     └── LINK-LOCAL: traffic within fe80::/64 stays on eth0           │
│                                                                       │
│  default via fe80::1 dev eth0 proto ra metric 100 pref medium         │
│     └── DEFAULT ROUTE: everything else goes to the router             │
│         Notice: gateway is LINK-LOCAL (fe80::1), not global!          │
│         This is the BIGGEST IPv4→IPv6 routing mental shift.           │
│                                                                       │
│  ff00::/8 dev eth0 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium                │
│     └── MULTICAST: all multicast traffic (NDP, etc.)                  │
│                                                                       │
│  KEY DIFFERENCES FROM IPv4 ROUTING:                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Aspect              │ IPv4                 │ IPv6               │  │
│  ├─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────────────────┤  │
│  │ Default gateway addr│ Public or private IP  │ LINK-LOCAL fe80::1 │  │
│  │ How routes learned  │ DHCP option 3 or     │ RA from router     │  │
│  │                     │ static config        │ (SLAAC)            │  │
│  │ On-link detection   │ Subnet mask + ARP    │ Prefix in RA + NDP │  │
│  │ Route preference    │ Metric only          │ Metric + pref      │  │
│  │                     │                      │ (high/medium/low)  │  │
│  └─────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                       │
│  WHY DEFAULT GATEWAY IS LINK-LOCAL:                                   │
│  This is a brilliant design choice. Since every IPv6 interface        │
│  always has a link-local address, the gateway is always reachable     │
│  on fe80::1 — no matter what global prefix your ISP assigns.          │
│  Your global prefix can change, but fe80::1 never changes.            │
│  This eliminates the "I changed ISPs and now my default gateway       │
│  is wrong" problem that plagues IPv4 networks.                        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📐 IPv4 vs IPv6 Subnetting — Different Philosophy, Different Math

IPv4 subnetting is about conservation — how many hosts do you need, and what's the smallest subnet that fits? IPv6 subnetting is about hierarchy — you always use /64 for LANs, and the math is about how many /64s your allocation provides.

ConceptIPv4IPv6
Standard subnet size/24 (256 hosts) — but varies widely/64 (ALWAYS) — 18 quintillion hosts per subnet
Why this size?Good balance of hosts vs broadcast domain sizeSLAAC requires 64-bit interface IDs. /64 enables stateless autoconfiguration.
ISP allocationUsually a single IP or small block (/29)/48 for businesses, /56 for residential (RFC 6177)
How many subnets from ISP allocation?/29 = 8 IPs, maybe 6 usable/48 = 65,536 /64 subnets. /56 = 256 /64 subnets.
Point-to-point links/30 or /31 (2-4 IPs)/127 (RFC 6164) or /64 (yeah, seriously — 18 quintillion IPs for a P2P!)
Planning approach"What's the smallest subnet that fits + 20% growth?""How should I organize my /48 hierarchically? DC→Floor→VLAN→Purpose"
Formula to remember2^(32-CIDR) - 2 = usable hosts2^(64-CIDR) = /64 subnets available (e.g., /48 → 2^16 = 65,536 /64s)

6.3 IPv6 in Kubernetes & Cloud

Cloud providers have been slow to adopt IPv6, but the landscape is changing rapidly. As of 2024-2025, all major cloud providers support IPv6 — but with caveats. Kubernetes dual-stack is GA since 1.23 (December 2021), and many production clusters now run dual-stack.

☁️ Cloud Provider IPv6 Support — Current State (2025)
ProviderIPv6 VPC/VNetIPv6-only SubnetsIPv6 K8s (Managed)IPv6 Load BalancerNotes
AWS✅ Dual-stack VPC✅ (2024+)✅ EKS dual-stack✅ NLB (dual-stack), ALB (dual-stack)Egress-only Internet Gateway for IPv6. No NAT for IPv6!
GCP✅ Dual-stack VPC✅✅ GKE dual-stack✅ External L4/L7 LBStrong IPv6 support. Cloud NAT supports IPv6.
Azure✅ Dual-stack VNet⚠️ Limited✅ AKS dual-stack (preview)✅ Azure LB (dual-stack)IPv6 support improving but still lagging behind AWS/GCP.
☸️ Kubernetes Dual-Stack — How It Works

Kubernetes dual-stack (GA since v1.23) allows Pods and Services to have both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. The key components:

  • kube-apiserver: --service-cluster-ip-range=10.96.0.0/16,fd00:10:96::/112 (IPv4 + IPv6 ranges)
  • kube-controller-manager: --node-cidr-mask-size-ipv4=24 --node-cidr-mask-size-ipv6=64
  • kubelet: --node-ip=10.0.1.10,2001:db8::10
  • kube-proxy: Manages both IPv4 and IPv6 iptables/IPVS rules simultaneously
DUAL-STACK KUBERNETES — Pod and Service Addressing
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DUAL-STACK KUBERNETES CLUSTER                                        │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────────────┐│
│  │ Pod: anihpj-web-7d4f5b-abc   │  │ Pod: anihpj-db-0              ││
│  │ IPv4: 10.244.1.5              │  │ IPv4: 10.244.2.10             ││
│  │ IPv6: 2001:db8:10:244:1::5    │  │ IPv6: 2001:db8:10:244:2::10   ││
│  └───────────────┬───────────────┘  └───────────────┬───────────────┘│
│                  │                                   │                │
│  ┌───────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┴───────────────┐│
│  │ Service: anihpj-web (ClusterIP)                                  ││
│  │ IPv4: 10.96.100.50       IPv6: fd00:10:96::50                   ││
│  │                                                                  ││
│  │ DNS: anihpj-web.default.svc.cluster.local                        ││
│  │   → A record:    10.96.100.50  (IPv4 clients)                    ││
│  │   → AAAA record: fd00:10:96::50 (IPv6 clients)                   ││
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│                                                                       │
│  CONNECTIVITY:                                                        │
│  • IPv4-only pod → IPv4 Service IP → IPv4 backend pod                 │
│  • IPv6-only pod → IPv6 Service IP → IPv6 backend pod                 │
│  • Dual-stack pod chooses IPv4 or IPv6 per connection (Happy Eyeballs)│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
☁️ AWS IPv6 in Practice — VPC, Subnets, and Egress-Only Internet Gateway

AWS has the most mature IPv6 support among cloud providers. Here's what you actually need to configure for a production IPv6-enabled VPC hosting the anihpj/jobpost application:

AWS IPv6 VPC — Dual-Stack Architecture for anihpj
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AWS VPC: 10.0.0.0/16 (IPv4) + 2001:db8:abcd::/56 (IPv6 from AWS)   │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ PUBLIC SUBNET (AZ-a): 10.0.1.0/24 + 2001:db8:abcd:1::/64       │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────────┐                                 │ │
│  │  │ ALB/NLB  │  │ NAT Gateway  │  ← IPv4 only!                    │ │
│  │  │ dual-stk│  │ (IPv4 out)   │    No NAT needed for IPv6        │ │
│  │  └──────────┘  └──────────────┘    (use Egress-Only IGW)        │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  Route Table:                                                     │ │
│  │    0.0.0.0/0 → Internet Gateway (IPv4 out)                       │ │
│  │    ::/0      → Egress-Only Internet Gateway (IPv6 out!)          │ │
│  │    2001:db8:abcd::/56 → local (VPC internal)                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ PRIVATE SUBNET (AZ-a): 10.0.16.0/20 + 2001:db8:abcd:10::/64    │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐          │ │
│  │  │ anihpj-web   │  │ anihpj-app   │  │ anihpj-db    │          │ │
│  │  │ EC2 instance │  │ EC2 instance │  │ RDS instance │          │ │
│  │  │ IPv4:10.0.16.5│  │ IPv4:10.0.16.6│  │ IPv4:10.0.16.7│         │ │
│  │  │ IPv6:        │  │ IPv6:        │  │ IPv6:        │          │ │
│  │  │ 2001:db8:abcd│  │ 2001:db8:abcd│  │ 2001:db8:abcd│          │ │
│  │  │ :10::5       │  │ :10::6       │  │ :10::7       │          │ │
│  │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘          │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  Route Table:                                                     │ │
│  │    0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway (IPv4 out to internet)                │ │
│  │    ::/0      → Egress-Only Internet Gateway (IPv6 out!)          │ │
│  │    2001:db8:abcd::/56 → local                                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  KEY AWS IPv6 CONCEPTS:                                               │
│  • Egress-Only Internet Gateway: IPv6 outbound only (no inbound!)    │
│    Like a NAT Gateway, but for IPv6. No stateful inbound allowed.    │
│  • No NAT for IPv6: Instances with public IPv6 are DIRECTLY          │
│    reachable from the internet. Use Security Groups for protection.  │
│  • IPv6 CIDR from AWS: AWS assigns a /56 to your VPC automatically   │
│    from Amazon's pool. You subdivide into /64 per subnet.            │
│  • Bring Your Own IP (BYOIP): You can bring your own /48 IPv6 block  │
│    and advertise it via AWS. Used by enterprises with their own IPs. │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🐳 Docker + IPv6 — What You Need to Know for the anihpj Stack

Docker's IPv6 support is opt-in — it's disabled by default even if your host has working IPv6. For the anihpj/jobpost Django application running in containers, you need explicit configuration:

# /etc/docker/daemon.json — Enable IPv6 for all containers
{
  "ipv6": true,
  "fixed-cidr-v6": "fd00:dead:beef::/48",
  "ip6tables": true,
  "experimental": true
}

# After editing, restart Docker:
$ systemctl restart docker

# Verify container has IPv6:
$ docker run --rm alpine ip -6 addr show
# Should show an fd00:dead:beef:: address

# docker-compose.yml for anihpj with IPv6:
version: '3.8'
services:
  anihpj-web:
    image: anihpj/jobpost:latest
    ports:
      - "80:8000"
    networks:
      - anihpj-net
    sysctls:
      - net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=0  # Ensure IPv6 is ON in container

networks:
  anihpj-net:
    enable_ipv6: true
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.20.0.0/16
        - subnet: fd00:dead:beef:1::/64

Why this matters for anihpj: If you deploy anihpj/jobpost on a dual-stack K8s cluster or Docker host, clients with IPv6 will try to reach the app via IPv6 first (Happy Eyeballs). If the container/pod doesn't have IPv6 configured, those clients experience a 300ms timeout before falling back to IPv4 — making your app feel slow. Always enable dual-stack for production-facing services.

🛠️ LAB: Enable IPv6 Dual-Stack in a kind Cluster
1
Create dual-stack kind config 
# kind-dualstack.yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
networking:
  ipFamily: dual
  podSubnet: "10.244.0.0/16,fd00:10:244::/56"
  serviceSubnet: "10.96.0.0/16,fd00:10:96::/112"
2
Create the cluster 
kind create cluster --config kind-dualstack.yaml
3
Verify dual-stack is active 
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses}'
# Should show both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses

kubectl get svc -o wide
# CLUSTER-IP column should show IPv4 or IPv6
4
Deploy a dual-stack pod and service 
kubectl run dual-pod --image=nginx --overrides='
{"spec":{"hostNetwork":false}}'

kubectl expose pod dual-pod --port=80
kubectl get svc dual-pod
# Note: Service gets IPv4 ClusterIP by default
# Use ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack for both

6.4 IPv6 — What You Actually Need Daily

This section covers the practical IPv6 skills you'll use every day: reading IPv6 in tcpdump, checking AAAA DNS records, writing firewall rules for IPv6, and avoiding the common gotchas that trip up even experienced engineers.

📡 Reading IPv6 in tcpdump — Recognizing the Patterns
# ICMPv6 — Neighbor Discovery (NDP)
$ tcpdump -i eth0 -nn ip6
# NDP Neighbor Solicitation (like ARP request):
IP6 fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f > ff02::1:ff00:1: ICMP6, neighbor solicitation,
    who has 2001:db8::1, length 32

# NDP Neighbor Advertisement (like ARP reply):
IP6 2001:db8::1 > fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f: ICMP6, neighbor advertisement,
    tgt is 2001:db8::1, length 32

# TCPv6 — Normal application traffic:
IP6 2001:db8::5.54321 > 2001:db8::10.443: Flags [S], seq 123456789,
    win 65535, options [mss 1440,sackOK,TS val 123456 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7],
    length 0

# Recognizing ICMPv6 (protocol 58, NOT ICMPv4 protocol 1):
$ tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp6
# Shows all ICMPv6: NDP, Router Solicitations, Router Advertisements,
# Echo Request/Reply (ping6), etc.
🌐 IPv6 in DNS — AAAA Records

IPv6 addresses are stored in AAAA records (pronounced "quad-A"). The name comes from the fact that an IPv6 address is 128 bits — four times the 32 bits of an IPv4 A record. AAAA = four As.

# Query A records (IPv4):
$ dig example.com A +short
93.184.216.34

# Query AAAA records (IPv6):
$ dig example.com AAAA +short
2606:2800:220:1:248:1893:25c8:1946

# Query both in one shot:
$ dig example.com ANY +short | grep -E '^[0-9]|^[2-3a-f]'
93.184.216.34
2606:2800:220:1:248:1893:25c8:1946

# Reverse DNS for IPv6 (PTR — much longer!):
$ dig -x 2606:2800:220:1:248:1893:25c8:1946 +short
# The PTR name uses nibble format (each hex digit separated by dots):
# 6.4.9.1.8.c.5.2.3.9.8.1.8.4.2.0.1.0.0.0.0.2.2.0.0.8.2.6.0.6.0.2.ip6.arpa
🔥 ip6tables — IPv6 Firewall Rules (Separate from iptables!)

Critical gotcha: iptables rules ONLY apply to IPv4 traffic. IPv6 traffic is governed by ip6tables — an entirely separate firewall with its own rules, chains, and tables. If you only configure iptables, your IPv6 traffic is completely unfirewalled.

# List current IPv6 firewall rules:
$ ip6tables -L -v -n

# Block all incoming IPv6 except SSH:
$ ip6tables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
$ ip6tables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
$ ip6tables -A INPUT -j DROP

# Allow ICMPv6 (CRITICAL! Without ICMPv6, NDP breaks):
$ ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 -j ACCEPT
$ ip6tables -A OUTPUT -p icmpv6 -j ACCEPT

# Blocking ICMPv6 = broken IPv6. NDP uses ICMPv6.
# You MUST allow ICMPv6 Type 133-137 for NDP to work.
# 133 = Router Solicitation, 134 = Router Advertisement
# 135 = Neighbor Solicitation, 136 = Neighbor Advertisement
# 137 = Redirect

# Docker IPv6 example — enable IPv6 for containers:
$ cat /etc/docker/daemon.json
{
  "ipv6": true,
  "fixed-cidr-v6": "fd00:dead:beef::/48",
  "ip6tables": true
}

The #1 IPv6 security mistake: Organizations roll out IPv6 on their networks but forget to configure ip6tables. Result: every device has a globally routable IPv6 address with NO firewall. Attackers scan IPv6 ranges and find exposed services. Always configure ip6tables alongside iptables.

🔍 Real-World IPv6 Troubleshooting — A Step-by-Step Debugging Scenario

Scenario: You've deployed the anihpj/jobpost Django application on a dual-stack Kubernetes cluster. Users report that the site is "slow" — pages take 3-5 seconds to load instead of the usual 200ms. Let's debug this methodically, checking every layer of the IPv6 stack.

IPv6 TROUBLESHOOTING WORKFLOW — Systematic Debugging from L1 to L7
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TROUBLESHOOTING SCENARIO: anihpj-web is slow for IPv6 clients      │
│                                                                       │
│  STEP 1: CONFIRM IPv6 ENABLED ON THE HOST                            │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ $ cat /proc/sys/net/ipv6/conf/all/disable_ipv6                  │  │
│  │ 0   ← Good! IPv6 is enabled.                                    │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │ $ ip -6 addr show eth0                                          │  │
│  │ inet6 2001:db8:abcd:10::5/64 scope global                       │  │
│  │ inet6 fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f/64 scope link                    │  │
│  │   ← Both global and link-local present. Good.                    │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                       │
│  STEP 2: CHECK IPv6 ROUTING                                          │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ $ ip -6 route show                                              │  │
│  │ 2001:db8:abcd:10::/64 dev eth0 proto ra metric 100              │  │
│  │ fe80::/64 dev eth0 proto kernel metric 256                       │  │
│  │ default via fe80::1 dev eth0 proto ra metric 100                 │  │
│  │   ← Default route via link-local gateway. Looks correct.         │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │ $ ip -6 route get 2001:4860:4860::8888                          │  │
│  │ 2001:4860:4860::8888 from :: via fe80::1 dev eth0               │  │
│  │   ← Routing works! Packet would go out eth0.                     │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                       │
│  STEP 3: TEST IPv6 CONNECTIVITY                                      │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ $ ping6 -c 3 2001:4860:4860::8888                               │  │
│  │ 3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss                │  │
│  │ rtt min/avg/max = 1.2/1.5/1.8 ms                                 │  │
│  │   ← IPv6 ping works! L3 connectivity is fine.                    │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                       │
│  STEP 4: CHECK DNS (AAAA records)                                    │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ $ dig AAAA anihpj-web.default.svc.cluster.local +short          │  │
│  │ fd00:10:96::50                                                   │  │
│  │   ← Service has AAAA record. DNS is fine.                        │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                       │
│  STEP 5: CHECK THE SERVICE ITSELF                                    │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ $ curl -6 -w "\nTotal time: %{time_total}s\n" \                 │  │
│  │        http://[fd00:10:96::50]:8000/health                      │  │
│  │ {"status":"ok"}                                                  │  │
│  │ Total time: 3.421s  ← PROBLEM! 3.4 seconds for a health check!  │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │ $ curl -4 -w "\nTotal time: %{time_total}s\n" \                 │  │
│  │        http://10.96.100.50:8000/health                          │  │
│  │ {"status":"ok"}                                                  │  │
│  │ Total time: 0.023s  ← IPv4 is blazing fast!                     │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                       │
│  DIAGNOSIS: IPv6 is SLOW (3.4s) while IPv4 is FAST (0.023s).         │
│  This is the Happy Eyeballs problem in reverse! Clients prefer        │
│  IPv6, but the IPv6 path has a performance issue.                     │
│                                                                       │
│  STEP 6: DEEP DIVE — TRACE THE IPv6 PATH                             │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ $ traceroute6 fd00:10:96::50                                    │  │
│  │ 1  fe80::1 (node gateway)  0.2ms  0.1ms  0.2ms                  │  │
│  │ 2  * * *                                                         │  │
│  │ 3  fd00:10:96::50  3001ms  2998ms  3002ms  ← 3 SECOND latency!  │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │ $ ip6tables -L -v -n | head -20                                  │  │
│  │ Chain INPUT (policy ACCEPT 0 packets, 0 bytes)                   │  │
│  │ Chain FORWARD (policy DROP 45K packets, 34M bytes)               │  │
│  │   ← FORWARD chain is DROPPING packets!                           │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │ $ ip6tables -L FORWARD -v -n --line-numbers                      │  │
│  │ 1   ACCEPT  all  *  *  ::/0  ::/0  state RELATED,ESTABLISHED    │  │
│  │ 2   DROP    all  *  *  ::/0  ::/0  ← Rule 2 drops everything!   │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │ ROOT CAUSE: ip6tables FORWARD chain drops IPv6 traffic between   │  │
│  │ pods on different nodes. kube-proxy's rules are on the INPUT     │  │
│  │ chain, but pod-to-pod traffic goes through FORWARD.              │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │ FIX:                                                              │  │
│  │ $ ip6tables -I FORWARD 2 -s fd00:10:244::/56 -d fd00:10:244::/56│  │
│  │   -j ACCEPT                                                      │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │ RETEST:                                                           │  │
│  │ $ curl -6 http://[fd00:10:96::50]:8000/health                    │  │
│  │ Total time: 0.031s  ← FIXED! Same speed as IPv4.                │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Lessons from this scenario: (1) Always test IPv4 and IPv6 independently — curl -4 and curl -6 are your best friends. (2) The FORWARD chain in ip6tables is often forgotten — kube-proxy configures INPUT and OUTPUT, but pod-to-pod traffic goes through FORWARD. (3) A 3-second delay instead of instant failure suggests a timeout being hit repeatedly — in this case, connection tracking timeouts because the forward rule was dropping packets but the SYN was getting through on a different path (asymmetric routing). (4) The "* * *" in traceroute6 is a critical diagnostic signal — it means a hop is silently dropping packets.

⚠️ Common IPv6 Gotchas — What WILL Go Wrong in Production
GotchaSymptomRoot CauseFix
No ARP in IPv6!Can't resolve MAC addressesYou're looking for ARP cache (arp -a) but IPv6 uses NDPUse ip -6 neigh show (shows NDP neighbors, not ARP)
ICMPv6 blockedIPv6 works for a minute, then stops. NDP fails.Firewall blocks ICMPv6. NDP requires ICMPv6 types 133-137.ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 -j ACCEPT
No link-local = no IPv6Interface has global IPv6 but nothing worksfe80::/10 link-local MUST be present for NDP to functionEnsure link-local is auto-generated (it always is, unless manually deleted)
MTU issues (no fragmentation)Some connections hang, large packets droppedIPv6 routers NEVER fragment. Minimum MTU = 1280. PMTUD is mandatory.Ensure ICMPv6 Packet Too Big (Type 2) messages reach the source
DNS returns AAAA but IPv6 brokenWebsites load slowly (300ms+ delay)Happy Eyeballs: browser tries broken IPv6, waits 300ms, falls back to IPv4Fix your IPv6 connectivity, or filter AAAA records at your DNS resolver
ip6tables not configuredIPv6 hosts have NO firewalliptables != ip6tables. Separate firewall, separate rules.Mirror your iptables rules in ip6tables. Audit: ip6tables -L -v -n
::1 vs 127.0.0.1Binding to 127.0.0.1 doesn't accept IPv6127.0.0.1 is IPv4 only. ::1 is IPv6 loopback.Bind to both: 0.0.0.0 and :: (or use dual-stack socket)
💡 IPv6 Quick Reference — Commands You'll Use Daily
# SHOW IPv6 ADDRESSES:
ip -6 addr show                          # All IPv6 addresses on all interfaces
ip -6 addr show eth0                     # IPv6 addresses on eth0

# SHOW IPv6 ROUTES:
ip -6 route show                         # IPv6 routing table
ip -6 route show default                 # Default IPv6 gateway
route -6 -n                              # Legacy way (works on some systems)

# SHOW NDP NEIGHBORS (like ARP cache for IPv6):
ip -6 neigh show                         # NDP neighbor cache (MAC↔IPv6 mappings)

# PING IPv6:
ping6 google.com                         # Linux
ping -6 google.com                       # macOS / newer Linux
ping 2001:4860:4860::8888                # Direct IPv6 address

# TRACEROUTE IPv6:
traceroute6 google.com                   # Linux
traceroute -6 google.com                 # macOS

# CHECK IF IPv6 IS ENABLED:
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv6/conf/all/disable_ipv6  # 0 = enabled, 1 = disabled
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6         # Enabled/disabled status

# DNS LOOKUP:
dig AAAA google.com +short               # Quad-A record (IPv6)
dig -x 2001:4860:4860::8888 +short       # Reverse DNS for IPv6

🔭 Chapter 6 — Visual Summary

📊 340 Undecillion Addresses

IPv6 = 128 bits = 340 trillion trillion trillion addresses. IPv4 ran out in 2011. NAT was the stopgap. IPv6 is the permanent fix.

🔤 8 Hextets, 2 Rules

Write as 8 groups of 4 hex digits. Shorten: drop leading zeros + compress ONE run of zeros with :: . Loopback = ::1.

🏷️ 5 Address Types

Loopback (::1), Link-Local (fe80::), Unique Local (fdxx:), Global Unicast (2xxx:), Multicast (ffxx:). Instantly recognizable by first digits.

🤖 SLAAC = No DHCP Needed

Router sends prefix in RA. Host combines with EUI-64 interface ID. DAD checks uniqueness. Fully automatic global addressing.

☸️ K8s Dual-Stack (GA 1.23)

Pods and Services get both IPv4 and IPv6. Separate ClusterIP ranges. DNS returns A + AAAA. Cloud providers increasingly support IPv6-only.

🛡️ ip6tables ≠ iptables

IPv6 has its OWN firewall. If you only configure iptables, IPv6 is unfirewalled. Always mirror rules. Allow ICMPv6 or NDP breaks.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 6

🔜IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6)
The successor to IPv4, using 128-bit addresses (written as 8 hextets of 4 hex digits). Provides 340 undecillion addresses, eliminates the need for NAT, and restores end-to-end connectivity.
🔄Dual-Stack
Running IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously on the same interface. Devices have both an IPv4 address and an IPv6 address. Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305) selects the fastest protocol per connection.
🤖SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration)
IPv6 hosts auto-configure global addresses without DHCP. Router sends prefix in RA. Host combines with EUI-64 or random interface ID. DAD ensures uniqueness.
🔍NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol)
Replaces ARP, ICMP Router Discovery, and ICMP Redirect in IPv6. Uses ICMPv6 and multicast. Handles MAC resolution (NS/NA), router discovery (RS/RA), and duplicate detection (DAD).
🛡️ip6tables
The IPv6 firewall — completely separate from iptables (IPv4). Must be configured independently. Blocking ICMPv6 breaks NDP. Always mirror your iptables rules in ip6tables.
🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work
  • VPC/VNet design: When creating cloud networks, enable dual-stack from day one. Retrofitting IPv6 into existing VPCs is painful. AWS now supports IPv6-only subnets — consider them for new greenfield deployments.
  • Kubernetes clusters: If you're deploying a new K8s cluster, consider dual-stack from the start. Changing to dual-stack later requires cluster rebuild. The CNI (Calico/Cilium/Flannel) must support dual-stack — check before deploying.
  • Security auditing: Always run both iptables -L -n AND ip6tables -L -n in your security audits. Many penetration testers specifically scan IPv6 because they know it's often unfirewalled.
  • DNS troubleshooting: When a service is "slow," check if DNS returns AAAA records pointing to a broken IPv6 path. curl -4 and curl -6 let you test both protocols independently.
  • Container networking: Docker requires explicit IPv6 config (--ipv6 and --fixed-cidr-v6). Without it, containers are IPv4-only even if the host has IPv6. Kubernetes pod IPv6 requires dual-stack CNI configuration.

🔑 Chapter 6 Key Takeaways

  1. IPv4 is exhausted. IPv6 is the future. 340 undecillion addresses eliminate NAT, restore end-to-end connectivity, and simplify network design. Every infrastructure engineer must be IPv6-fluent by 2025+.
  2. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as 8 hextets. Two shortening rules: drop leading zeros, compress ONE run of zeros with ::. Address types are instantly identifiable by the first digits: fe80:: (link-local), 2xxx:: (global), fdxx:: (private), ffxx:: (multicast).
  3. SLAAC enables automatic addressing without DHCP. Router sends prefix in RA. Host combines with EUI-64 interface ID. DAD ensures uniqueness. Privacy extensions use random IDs to prevent tracking.
  4. NDP replaces ARP, uses multicast (not broadcast). No broadcast storms in IPv6. More efficient neighbor discovery via solicited-node multicast. ICMPv6 must be allowed through firewalls or NDP breaks.
  5. ip6tables is SEPARATE from iptables. The #1 IPv6 security mistake is forgetting to configure ip6tables, leaving IPv6 completely unfirewalled. Always mirror your rulesets and allow ICMPv6 types 133-137.
  6. Dual-stack is the standard transition strategy. Run both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously. Happy Eyeballs selects the fastest protocol per connection. Kubernetes dual-stack is GA since v1.23.
🛡️ SRE Reality Check — IPv6 Security Scanning

Attackers and penetration testers routinely scan IPv6 ranges because they know many organizations deploy IPv6 without configuring ip6tables. The pattern is predictable: companies lock down IPv4 meticulously (iptables rules, security groups, NACLs), but their IPv6 stack runs with default-ACCEPT policy. Since every IPv6 device has a globally routable address (no NAT hiding), exposed services are directly reachable from anywhere on the internet. Action item: Add ip6tables-save to your configuration management (Ansible/Puppet/Chef). Include IPv6 rules in your security group definitions. Run regular scans against BOTH your IPv4 AND IPv6 addresses. The IPv4-only scan that shows everything locked down gives a false sense of security if your IPv6 is wide open.

⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.1 — Shorten IPv6 Addresses

Apply both shortening rules to each full IPv6 address:

  1. 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
  2. fe80:0000:0000:0000:0a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f
  3. 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334
  4. 0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
💡 Hint: Rule 1 — drop leading zeros in each hextet. Rule 2 — compress exactly ONE run of consecutive zero hextets with ::. If there are multiple runs, only compress the longest (or the leftmost if equal).
📝 View Solution 
# 1. 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
#    Drop leading zeros: 2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1
#    Compress zeros: 2001:db8::1  (7 zero groups compressed)

# 2. fe80:0000:0000:0000:0a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f
#    Drop leading zeros: fe80:0:0:0:a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f
#    Compress zeros: fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f  (3 zero groups compressed)

# 3. 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334
#    Drop leading zeros: 2001:db8:85a3:0:0:8a2e:370:7334
#    Compress zeros: 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334  (2 zero groups compressed)

# 4. 0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
#    Drop leading zeros: 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1
#    Compress zeros: ::1  (IPv6 loopback address)
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 6.2 — Identify IPv6 Address Types

For each address, identify the type (Loopback, Link-Local, Unique Local, Global Unicast, or Multicast) and explain how you knew instantly:

  1. ::1
  2. fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f
  3. 2001:4860:4860::8888
  4. fd12:3456:789a:1::10
  5. ff02::1
💡 Hint: Look at the FIRST hextet. ::1 = loopback. fe80 = link-local. 2xxx = global unicast. fdxx = unique local. ffxx = multicast. You can identify any IPv6 address type in under a second.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. ::1
#    Type: LOOPBACK. IPv6 equivalent of 127.0.0.1.
#    Only valid address for loopback. Traffic never leaves the host.

# 2. fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f
#    Type: LINK-LOCAL (fe80::/10).
#    NOT routable. Only works on the local L2 segment.
#    Auto-generated from MAC address (EUI-64 visible: ff:fe in middle).
#    Every IPv6 interface has at least one fe80 address.

# 3. 2001:4860:4860::8888
#    Type: GLOBAL UNICAST (2000::/3).
#    This is Google's public IPv6 DNS server.
#    Routable across the entire internet.

# 4. fd12:3456:789a:1::10
#    Type: UNIQUE LOCAL (fc00::/7, fd prefix = randomly generated).
#    Private IPv6 — like 10.0.0.0/8 in IPv4.
#    Not internet-routable. Use for internal networks.

# 5. ff02::1
#    Type: MULTICAST (ff00::/8).
#    ff02 = link-local scope multicast.
#    ff02::1 = "all nodes on this link" (replaces IPv4 broadcast).
#    Used by NDP for Router Advertisements (sent to all nodes).
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 6.3 — IPv6 Firewall Audit

You've configured iptables to allow SSH (22), HTTP (80), and HTTPS (443), dropping all other inbound traffic. A security scan reveals that ports 22, 80, and 443 are accessible via IPv6 with NO restrictions.

Tasks:

  1. Why are the IPv6 ports wide open?
  2. Write the ip6tables commands to mirror the IPv4 ruleset.
  3. What additional IPv6-specific rule must you add that doesn't exist in IPv4?
💡 Hint: iptables and ip6tables are completely separate. IPv6 uses ICMPv6 (protocol 58) instead of ICMP (protocol 1). NDP requires specific ICMPv6 types (133-137). Blocking ICMPv6 = broken IPv6.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. WHY IPv6 IS WIDE OPEN:
#    iptables ONLY filters IPv4 traffic (protocol 2/raw socket).
#    ip6tables filters IPv6 traffic. If you never configured ip6tables,
#    the default policy (ACCEPT) applies to all IPv6 traffic.
#
#    Result: IPv4 = locked down, IPv6 = completely open.
#    This is THE most common IPv6 security vulnerability.

# 2. MIRROR IPv4 RULES IN ip6tables:
#    Allow loopback:
ip6tables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT
#    Allow established/related connections:
ip6tables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
#    Allow SSH (22):
ip6tables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
#    Allow HTTP (80):
ip6tables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
#    Allow HTTPS (443):
ip6tables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
#    Drop everything else:
ip6tables -A INPUT -j DROP
#    Save rules (persist across reboots):
ip6tables-save > /etc/ip6tables/rules.v6  # Debian/Ubuntu
ip6tables-save > /etc/sysconfig/ip6tables  # RHEL/CentOS

# 3. IPv6-SPECIFIC RULE — MUST ALLOW ICMPv6:
#    IPv6 requires ICMPv6 (protocol 58) for NDP to function.
#    Without this, neighbor discovery breaks → IPv6 stops working.
ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 -j ACCEPT
ip6tables -A OUTPUT -p icmpv6 -j ACCEPT

#    For stricter control, allow only essential ICMPv6 types:
ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 133 -j ACCEPT  # Router Solicitation
ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 134 -j ACCEPT  # Router Advertisement
ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 135 -j ACCEPT  # Neighbor Solicitation
ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 136 -j ACCEPT  # Neighbor Advertisement
ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 137 -j ACCEPT  # Redirect
#    Also allow Packet Too Big (type 2) for PMTUD:
ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 2 -j ACCEPT   # Packet Too Big

📝 Chapter 6 — Practice Questions

Q1
Why was IPv6 created? What is the fundamental problem with IPv4 that IPv6 solves, and why wasn't NAT a permanent solution?
Show Answer
Answer

IPv6 was created because IPv4's 32-bit address space (4.3 billion addresses) is exhausted. IANA ran out in 2011. NAT extended IPv4's life but broke end-to-end connectivity: devices behind NAT can't receive incoming connections, breaking peer-to-peer protocols (VoIP, gaming, WebRTC), complicating IPsec, and requiring ALGs (Application Layer Gateways) that rewrite application-layer data. IPv6 provides 340 undecillion addresses with true end-to-end connectivity — no NAT needed.

IPv4 32-bit:  4.3B addrs → RAN OUT 2011
IPv6 128-bit: 340 undecillion → essentially infinite
NAT = life support (breaks end-to-end). IPv6 = cure.
Explanation

The key insight: NAT was never designed as a security mechanism — it was an address conservation hack. IPv6 restores the original internet architecture where every device is uniquely addressable. This enables true peer-to-peer applications without the complexity of STUN/TURN/ICE NAT traversal.

Q2
Shorten this IPv6 address using both rules: 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001. Why can't you use :: twice in an address like 2001::85a3::7334?
Show Answer
Answer

Shortened: 2001:db8::1 (drop leading zeros: 2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1; compress 7 zero groups to ::).

Why no double :: : :: represents an unknown number of zero groups. If you write 2001::85a3::7334, there's no way to know how many zero groups each :: represents. It could be 2001:0:85a3:0:0:0:0:7334 or 2001:0:0:0:85a3:0:0:7334 or any other combination — the address becomes ambiguous.

Explanation

The :: notation is a compression rule, not a separator. Think of it as "fill in the missing zeros to make 8 groups." If you have two :: markers, the missing zeros can't be uniquely determined. This is why RFC 4291 explicitly forbids multiple :: in an address.

Q3
You see fe80::a00:27ff:fe8c:5e9f on an interface. What type of address is this? Can packets with this source address be routed to the internet? Why does every IPv6 interface have one?
Show Answer
Answer

This is a Link-Local address (fe80::/10 prefix). It CANNOT be routed — not even to another subnet, let alone the internet. Routers never forward packets with link-local source or destination addresses. Every IPv6 interface auto-generates one because NDP (router discovery, neighbor discovery, DAD) requires link-local communication. Without it, you can't even discover your default gateway.

Explanation

Link-local addresses are IPv6's equivalent of 169.254.x.x (APIPA) in IPv4 — but mandatory, not fallback. They're always present, always fe80::/10, and always tied to the interface's MAC address. This is why ip -6 addr show always shows at least one fe80 address per interface.

Q4
How does SLAAC work? Walk through the steps from a host booting up with no IPv6 configuration to having a fully routable global IPv6 address — without any DHCP server.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Host generates a link-local address (fe80::/10) from its MAC via EUI-64. 2. Host sends a Router Solicitation (RS) to multicast address ff02::2 (all routers). 3. Router responds with a Router Advertisement (RA) containing the /64 prefix and its own link-local as the gateway. 4. Host combines the /64 prefix with its EUI-64 interface ID to form a 128-bit global address. 5. Host performs DAD (Duplicate Address Detection) by sending a Neighbor Solicitation to its own solicited-node multicast — if no response, the address is unique and ready to use. Total time: <1 second.

Explanation

SLAAC is IPv6's killer feature — fully automatic global addressing with zero infrastructure beyond a router sending RAs. Privacy extensions (RFC 8981) replace the predictable EUI-64 with random interface IDs that change over time, preventing device tracking.

Q5
What is the key difference between iptables and ip6tables? If you only configure iptables rules and enable IPv6 on your server, what security risk do you create?
Show Answer
Answer

iptables filters IPv4 traffic only. ip6tables filters IPv6 traffic only. They are completely separate — different kernel hooks, different rules, different tables. If you only configure iptables (locking down IPv4), your IPv6 stack is completely unfirewalled with default ACCEPT policy. Since IPv6 addresses are globally routable, every service on your server is exposed to the entire internet via IPv6 — even if iptables correctly blocks them via IPv4.

Explanation

This is the #1 IPv6 security mistake. Many organizations deploy IPv6, test that it works, but never configure ip6tables. Attackers scan IPv6 ranges specifically looking for servers with IPv4 locked down but IPv6 wide open. Always mirror your iptables rules in ip6tables, and add ICMPv6 allow rules or NDP breaks.

Q6
What is Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305)? How does it affect user experience when a website has both A and AAAA DNS records but the IPv6 path is broken?
Show Answer
Answer

Happy Eyeballs is the algorithm browsers use to pick between IPv4 and IPv6: 1. DNS returns both A and AAAA records. 2. Browser immediately tries IPv6 (preferred). 3. If IPv6 SYN doesn't get SYN-ACK within ~300ms, browser initiates an IPv4 connection in parallel. 4. Whichever succeeds first is used. Broken IPv6 impact: Users experience a 300ms delay on EVERY new connection while the browser waits for the IPv6 timeout before falling back to IPv4. For a page loading dozens of resources, this adds seconds to page load time.

Explanation

Happy Eyeballs prevents broken IPv6 from making sites completely inaccessible — it gracefully degrades. But partially broken IPv6 (packets route but are silently dropped) is worse than no IPv6 at all because every connection incurs the 300ms timeout penalty. This is why you should monitor IPv6 connectivity as carefully as IPv4.

Q7
Compare IPv4 ARP with IPv6 NDP. What are the key protocol differences? Why does NDP use multicast instead of broadcast?
Show Answer
Answer

ARP (IPv4): Uses L2 broadcast (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff) — every host on the segment receives and processes every ARP request. Single protocol that only resolves MAC addresses. NDP (IPv6): Uses solicited-node multicast (ff02::1:ffxx:xxxx) — only the target host (and any others sharing the last 24 bits of their address) receives the Neighbor Solicitation. NDP handles multiple functions: MAC resolution (NS/NA), router discovery (RS/RA), prefix advertisement, DAD, and redirect. No broadcast — more efficient, and no broadcast storms possible in IPv6.

Explanation

NDP's use of solicited-node multicast is a significant improvement over ARP's broadcast. In a /64 subnet with thousands of hosts, ARP broadcasts interrupt every host. NDP multicasts only target the relevant host(s). This is one reason IPv6 scales better in large L2 domains. Bonus: no ARP spoofing in IPv6 (though NDP has its own security considerations addressed by SEND/SAVI).

Q8
You're debugging an issue where IPv6 works for about 60 seconds after boot, then stops — new connections fail and existing connections time out. What's the most likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer

Most likely: ICMPv6 is being blocked by a firewall that was configured after boot (or the default rules load with a delay). NDP uses ICMPv6 types 133-137 for neighbor discovery, router discovery, and DAD. If ICMPv6 is blocked: existing neighbor cache entries expire (~30-60s), new Neighbor Solicitations can't reach their targets, MAC resolution fails, and IPv6 connectivity dies. Check with ip6tables -L -v -n — look for DROP rules on ICMPv6.

Explanation

The 60-second symptom is the smoking gun — it's the neighbor cache expiration time. During those 60 seconds, the host uses cached NDP entries. Once they expire and new ones can't be created (ICMPv6 blocked), IPv6 dies. Always allow ICMPv6 types 133-137 inbound and outbound, plus type 2 (Packet Too Big) for PMTUD.

Q9
How does Kubernetes dual-stack work? What happens when an IPv4-only pod tries to reach a Service that has both IPv4 and IPv6 ClusterIPs?
Show Answer
Answer

In dual-stack Kubernetes (GA since 1.23), Pods can have IPv4-only, IPv6-only, or dual-stack IPs. Services get separate ClusterIPs for each family. When an IPv4-only pod resolves a dual-stack Service via CoreDNS, it receives only the A record (IPv4 ClusterIP) because the pod's DNS resolver filters out the AAAA record — the pod has no IPv6 stack to use it. The pod then connects to the IPv4 ClusterIP, kube-proxy load-balances to an IPv4-capable backend. IPv6-only pods similarly use only the AAAA record. Dual-stack pods use Happy Eyeballs to pick the fastest protocol.

Explanation

The key architectural insight: CoreDNS is dual-stack aware and only returns address families the requesting pod can actually use. This prevents pods from receiving addresses of a protocol they can't route. Kube-proxy maintains separate iptables/IPVS rule sets for IPv4 and IPv6, and the CNI plugin must support dual-stack (Calico, Cilium, and Flannel all support it).

Q10
You're designing an IPv6 addressing plan for your organization. Your ISP has assigned you 2001:db8:abcd::/48. How many /64 subnets can you create? How would you allocate them across 3 data centers, 5 floors per DC, and 4 VLANs per floor?
Show Answer
Answer

A /48 provides 65,536 /64 subnets (2^16 = 65,536). This is more than enough for even the largest enterprise.

Allocation plan: Use the next 16 bits (bits 49-64) for subnet ID. Allocate by hierarchy: bits 49-52 = DC (16 values, using 3), bits 53-56 = floor (16 per DC, using 5), bits 57-64 = VLAN (256 per floor, using 4).

/48 FROM ISP:  2001:db8:abcd:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000
               └─── ISP /48 ──┘└────── 16-bit subnet ID ──────┘

ALLOCATION:
  DC-1, Floor-1, VLAN-10:  2001:db8:abcd:110a::/64
  DC-1, Floor-2, VLAN-20:  2001:db8:abcd:1214::/64
  DC-2, Floor-1, VLAN-10:  2001:db8:abcd:210a::/64
  ...
  USED: 3 DCs × 5 floors × 4 VLANs = 60 /64 subnets
  REMAINING: 65,536 − 60 = 65,476 subnets (99.9% free)
Explanation

IPv6 addressing abundance changes how you plan. With IPv4 you carefully conserve every /24. With IPv6 you can allocate a /64 per VLAN — the standard subnet size in IPv6 — without ever worrying about exhaustion. A single /48 from your ISP gives you more subnets than you'll ever use. This is why IPv6 network design focuses on hierarchy and readability, not conservation.

Chapter 7: ICMP — The Diagnostic Protocol

ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is the network's messenger, not a data transport. It doesn't carry your application data — it carries control messages between routers and hosts: "destination unreachable," "time exceeded," "packet too big," "echo reply." Every network diagnostic tool you use daily — ping, traceroute, Path MTU Discovery — is built on ICMP. If TCP/UDP are the cargo trucks of the internet, ICMP is the traffic control system — the warning lights, detour signs, and road condition reports that keep traffic flowing. Understanding ICMP deeply means understanding WHY your network is failing, not just THAT it's failing.

🟢 BEGINNER ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🔍 Diagnostics 📡 ping + traceroute

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:
