🎯 SRE Interview Tip

Every infrastructure interview includes a networking diagnostic question. The most common trap: "ping failed — is the host down?" The correct answer: Not necessarily. ICMP may be blocked by a firewall, rate-limited by the cloud provider, or deprioritized by intermediate routers. Always verify with a TCP-based test (tcping, curl, nc -zv). Also know: ICMP Type 3 Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed) MUST be allowed through firewalls for PMTUD to work. Blocking it creates PMTU black holes — large transfers hang but small ones work. You WILL be asked this in cloud/SRE interviews.

7.1 What Is ICMP and Why Every Infrastructure Engineer Uses It Daily

ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is the network's built-in error reporting and diagnostic mechanism. It operates directly on top of IP (protocol number 1 — not TCP, not UDP) and has no concept of ports. ICMP messages are generated by routers and hosts to communicate network-layer information: "the destination you're trying to reach doesn't exist," "the path you're taking is too slow," "your packet was too big for this link," or "I received your echo request and here's my reply."

WHERE ICMP LIVES — Not L4, But Inside L3
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PROTOCOL STACK — ICMP Sits at Layer 3, Alongside IP                  │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ L7  │ HTTP, DNS, SSH, SMTP                                      │ │
│  ├─────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │ L4  │ TCP (6), UDP (17)                                         │ │
│  ├─────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │ L3  │ IP (routing & addressing)                                  │ │
│  │     │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │ │
│  │     │ │ ICMP (protocol 1) — Control Messages                 │   │ │
│  │     │ │ • Error reporting: "Destination Unreachable"          │   │ │
│  │     │ │ • Diagnostics: "Echo Request/Reply" (ping)            │   │ │
│  │     │ │ • Path info: "Time Exceeded" (traceroute)             │   │ │
│  │     │ │ • MTU info: "Fragmentation Needed" (PMTUD)            │   │ │
│  │     │ │ • Router info: "Redirect" (better gateway exists)     │   │ │
│  │     │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │ │
│  ├─────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │ L2  │ Ethernet, Wi-Fi                                           │ │
│  └─────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  IMPORTANT DISTINCTION:                                                │
│  • ICMP is NOT carried inside TCP or UDP — it has its OWN protocol    │
│    number (1) in the IP header's Protocol field.                      │
│  • ICMP messages are the PAYLOAD of an IP packet, just like TCP       │
│    segments — but they serve control, not data transport.             │
│  • No ports. ICMP uses Type + Code fields instead of ports.           │
│  • ICMP is NOT just ping! Ping is ONE of 40+ ICMP message types.      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 ICMP Message Structure — Type, Code, Checksum, and Payload
# ICMP HEADER (8 bytes) — Followed by variable payload
# ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
# │ Type (8) │ Code (8) │ Checksum(16) │ Message Body (variable)     │
# └──────────┴──────────┴──────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

# TYPE: What kind of ICMP message (0=Echo Reply, 8=Echo Request, etc.)
# CODE: Sub-type within the message type (e.g., Type 3, Code 4 = Frag Needed)
# CHECKSUM: 16-bit one's complement checksum of the entire ICMP message
# BODY: Depends on type. For Echo, contains identifier + sequence + data.
#       For Destination Unreachable, contains the original IP header +
#       8 bytes of the original datagram (so the sender knows which
#       packet caused the error).
📊 ICMP Types & Codes — Every Infrastructure Engineer's Quick Reference

ICMP has 40+ message types. Here are the ones you'll encounter daily in production:

TypeCodeNameWhat It Tells YouWhen You'll See It
00Echo Reply"I'm alive and I received your ping"Every successful ping response
30Network UnreachableNo route to the destination network existsRouting table missing a route. Wrong gateway.
31Host UnreachableNetwork reachable, but the specific host is notHost is down, disconnected, or ARP/NDP failed
33Port UnreachableNo application listening on that UDP porttraceroute uses UDP; this signals "destination reached!"
34Fragmentation Needed (DF set)Packet too big for this link, and DF=1 prevents fragmentationPMTUD! Router tells sender to reduce packet size
313Administratively ProhibitedFirewall or ACL actively blocking this trafficSecurity group, iptables DROP, or cloud firewall
40Source Quench"Slow down! I'm overloaded" (deprecated)Rarely seen. Replaced by TCP congestion control.
50Redirect (Network)"There's a better gateway for this destination"Multiple routers on same subnet. One is closer.
80Echo Request"Are you there? Please reply"Every ping command sends this
90Router Advertisement"I'm a router; here's my address"Router discovery (mostly replaced by DHCP)
110TTL Exceeded in Transit"Your packet's TTL reached 0 — it died here"traceroute hop! Also routing loops.
111Fragment Reassembly Time Exceeded"I waited for all fragments, they didn't arrive"Fragment loss or extreme network asymmetry
120Parameter Problem"Your IP header has a bad value"Malformed packet or IP option not supported
130Timestamp Request"What's your current time?"Network time measurement (rare)
140Timestamp Reply"Here's my current time"Response to Timestamp Request
↪️ ICMP Redirect — When Routers Tell Hosts About Better Paths

ICMP Type 5 (Redirect) is one of the most misunderstood ICMP types. It's a router telling a host: "You sent a packet to me for network X, but there's a better gateway on this same subnet. Use that gateway instead." The redirect includes the IP of the better gateway, and the host adds a temporary route.

ICMP REDIRECT — Router Tells Host "Use That Gateway Instead"
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HOST-A (10.0.1.5) sends to 10.0.5.50 via default gateway R1          │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌──────────┐         ┌──────────┐         ┌──────────┐             │
│  │ HOST-A   │────────▶│ ROUTER R1│         │ ROUTER R2│             │
│  │10.0.1.5  │   pkt   │10.0.1.1  │         │10.0.1.254│             │
│  │          │   to    │          │         │(direct   │             │
│  │          │ 10.0.5  │          │         │ path to  │             │
│  │          │         │          │         │ 10.0.5!) │             │
│  └──────────┘         └────┬─────┘         └────┬─────┘             │
│                            │                    │                    │
│  1. R1 looks at routing table: "I can forward this, but R2 is on    │
│     the same subnet and has a direct path..."                       │
│                                                                       │
│  2. R1 FORWARDS the packet to R2 anyway (not dropped!) ──────▶       │
│                            │                                           │
│  3. R1 SENDS ICMP REDIRECT to HOST-A:                                │
│     Type=5, Code=1 (Host Redirect)                                    │
│     "For 10.0.5.0/24, use gateway 10.0.1.254 (R2) instead of me"     │
│     ◄──────────────────────│                                           │
│                                                                       │
│  4. HOST-A adds route: 10.0.5.0/24 via 10.0.1.254 dev eth0           │
│     → Future packets to 10.0.5.x go DIRECTLY to R2!                  │
│                                                                       │
│  REDIRECT CODES:                                                      │
│  Type 5, Code 0 = Redirect for Network (entire destination network)  │
│  Type 5, Code 1 = Redirect for Host (specific destination host)      │
│                                                                       │
│  WHY OFTEN DISABLED:                                                  │
│  • Security: Fake redirects can hijack traffic                        │
│  • Cloud: AWS/GCP use hypervisor routing, not ICMP redirects         │
│  • Simplicity: Well-designed networks have single default gateway     │
│                                                                       │
│  DISABLE (common security hardening):                                 │
│  $ sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0                    │
│  $ sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects=0                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ GOTCHA — Cloud Providers Rate-Limit or Block ICMP

A failed ping does NOT mean the host is down. Cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure) and many ISPs rate-limit or completely block ICMP at various points in their networks. AWS Security Groups block ICMP by default (you must explicitly allow it). Azure blocks ICMP from the internet to VMs by default. Some transit networks deprioritize ICMP responses under load.

Always verify with TCP-based tests: tcping (TCP SYN to a specific port), curl -v (HTTP), nc -zv HOST PORT (netcat TCP check). An ICMP failure plus a TCP success means ICMP is blocked — not that the host is down. An ICMP failure plus a TCP failure means the host is actually unreachable.

# ICMP ping fails — but is the host down?
$ ping -c 3 10.0.1.50
3 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss  ← ICMP blocked? Host down?

# VERIFY WITH TCP:
$ nc -zv 10.0.1.50 22
Connection to 10.0.1.50 22 port [tcp/ssh] succeeded!  ← Host is UP, ICMP blocked!

# VERIFY WITH HTTPS:
$ curl -v --connect-timeout 3 https://10.0.1.50/health
< HTTP/2 200 OK  ← Application is UP, ICMP just blocked
🔀 ICMP vs ICMPv6 — Two Different Protocols, Same Job

ICMP for IPv4 (protocol number 1) and ICMPv6 for IPv6 (protocol number 58) are closely related but NOT the same protocol. ICMPv6 has additional responsibilities because ARP doesn't exist in IPv6 — NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) uses ICMPv6 for everything. This means ICMPv6 is NOT optional in IPv6 networks — blocking it breaks IPv6 completely.

FeatureICMP (IPv4)ICMPv6 (IPv6)
Protocol Number158
Echo Request/ReplyType 8 / Type 0Type 128 / Type 129
Destination UnreachableType 3 (Codes 0-15)Type 1 (Codes 0-7)
Packet Too Big (MTU)Type 3, Code 4 (Frag Needed)Type 2 (Packet Too Big) — dedicated type!
Time ExceededType 11Type 3
Neighbor DiscoveryARP (separate protocol!)ICMPv6 Types 133-137 (NDP)
Router DiscoveryICMP Types 9/10 (optional)ICMPv6 Types 133/134 (mandatory via NDP)
Blocking consequenceping/traceroute breakALL IPv6 breaks (NDP requires ICMPv6!)
 
# Capturing ICMPv6 (separate filter from ICMPv4):
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp6           # ICMPv6 only (protocol 58)
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp            # ICMPv4 only (protocol 1)

# ICMPv6 ping (note: different type numbers):
IP6 2001:db8::5 > 2001:db8::10: ICMP6, echo request, id 1, seq 1, length 64
  └── Type 128 (IPv6 Echo Request — NOT Type 8 like IPv4)

IP6 2001:db8::10 > 2001:db8::5: ICMP6, echo reply, id 1, seq 1, length 64
  └── Type 129 (IPv6 Echo Reply — NOT Type 0 like IPv4)

# ICMPv6 Packet Too Big (replaces IPv4 Type 3 Code 4):
IP6 fe80::1 > 2001:db8::5: ICMP6, packet too big, mtu 1450, length 1240
  └── Type 2 (IPv6 dedicated PMTUD type — cleaner than IPv4!)
☁️ How Cloud Providers Handle ICMP — AWS vs GCP vs Azure

Cloud providers don't all treat ICMP the same way. Knowing these differences is critical when debugging connectivity across clouds:

ICMP BehaviorAWSGCPAzure
Inbound from internet❌ Blocked by default (Security Group must allow)❌ Blocked by default (Firewall rule required)❌ Blocked by default
Within VPC/VNet✅ Allowed (same SG rules apply)✅ Allowed (firewall rules apply)✅ Allowed (NSG rules apply)
Between VPCs (peered)✅ Allowed if SG allows✅ Allowed if firewall allows✅ Allowed if NSG allows
Load Balancer health checksTCP/HTTP/HTTPS only (NO ICMP)TCP/HTTP/HTTPS only (NO ICMP)TCP/HTTP/HTTPS only (NO ICMP)
PMTUD support✅ ICMP Type 3 Code 4 forwarded✅ ICMP Type 3 Code 4 forwarded✅ ICMP Type 3 Code 4 forwarded
traceroute works?⚠️ Partial (intermediate hops may show ***)⚠️ Partial⚠️ Partial
Path MTU1500 (standard) or 9000 (jumbo)1460 (some regions)1500 (standard)

Practical implication for anihpj/jobpost: If you're deploying on AWS, your security groups must explicitly allow ICMP from your monitoring/management CIDR for ping and traceroute to work. If you're multi-cloud (AWS+GCP), GCP's default MTU of 1460 means you need to set your container MTU accordingly, or PMTUD issues will appear when communicating with GCP services. Always test ping -M do -s from your application hosts to all external dependencies.

⚙️ How the Kernel Generates ICMP Messages — The Internals

When you run ping, you're not just sending packets — you're triggering a cascade of kernel operations. Understanding this internal flow is what separates infrastructure engineers who can debug weird ICMP issues from those who can't:

ICMP MESSAGE LIFECYCLE — From Application to Wire

│  HOW ping GENERATES AND RECEIVES ICMP (Full Kernel Path)             │
│                                                                       │
│  USER SPACE                    KERNEL SPACE                  NETWORK  │
│  ┌────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────┐  │
│  │ ping       │    │                              │    │          │  │

│  │            │───▶│   socket(AF_INET, SOCK_RAW,  │    │          │  │
│  │            │    │          IPPROTO_ICMP)       │    │          │  │
│  │            │    │   → Raw socket: bypasses L4  │    │          │  │
│  │            │    │     (no TCP/UDP)              │    │          │  │
│  └────────────┘    └────────────┬─────────────────┘    │          │  │
│                                 │                       │          │  │

│  │ ping waits │    │   ICMP MODULE                 │    │          │  │
│  │ for reply  │    │   • Builds ICMP header        │    │          │  │
│  │            │    │     Type=8, Code=0            │    │          │  │
│  │            │    │     id=pid, seq=counter        │    │          │  │

│  │            │    │   • Calculates checksum        │    │          │  │
│  └────────────┘    └────────────┬─────────────────┘    │          │  │
│                                 │                       │          │  │
│                    ┌────────────▼─────────────────┐    │          │  │
│                    │   IP LAYER                    │    │          │  │
│                    │   • Wraps in IP header        │    │          │  │
│                    │     Protocol=1 (ICMP)         │    │          │  │
│                    │     DF=1, TTL=64              │    │          │  │

│                    └────────────┬─────────────────┘    │          │  │
│                                 │                       │          │  │
│                    ┌────────────▼─────────────────┐    │          │  │
│                    │   ETHERNET LAYER              │    │          │  │
│                    │   • ARP/NDP for next-hop MAC │    │          │  │

│                    └──────────────────────────────┘    └──────────┘  │
│                                                                       │
│  REPLY PATH (mirror image):                                           │
│  NIC → Ethernet → IP (Protocol=1→ICMP module) → ICMP(Type=0,Code=0)  │
│  → Match id=ping_pid, seq=expected → Calculate RTT → Return to user  │

│  KEY INSIGHT: ping uses SOCK_RAW — a raw socket that gives the       │
│  application direct access to IP packets. This is why ping requires   │
│  ROOT (or CAP_NET_RAW capability) — raw sockets bypass the normal    │
│  TCP/UDP stack and could be used to craft arbitrary packets.          │
│                                                                       │

│  When a router sends ICMP Destination Unreachable or Time Exceeded,   │
│  it includes the original IP header + first 8 bytes of the original   │
│  payload. This lets the SOURCE identify WHICH of its packets caused   │
│  the error. traceroute relies on this: it matches the returned ICMP   │
│  Time Exceeded to its probe packets using the UDP source port.        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

7.2 ping — The Universal Reachability Test

ping is the single most-used network diagnostic tool on the planet. It sends an ICMP Echo Request (Type 8, Code 0) and waits for an ICMP Echo Reply (Type 0, Code 0). The round-trip time tells you the latency; packet loss tells you about congestion or failures; TTL tells you how many router hops are between you and the target. Simple, elegant, and universally available.

PING — Full Echo Request/Reply Exchange (tcpdump View)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  $ ping -c 1 8.8.8.8                                                  │
│                                                                       │
│  YOUR HOST (10.0.1.5)                  GOOGLE DNS (8.8.8.8)          │
│  ┌──────────────────┐                  ┌──────────────────┐          │
│  │ ping sends:      │                  │                  │          │
│  │ ICMP Echo Req    │                  │                  │          │
│  │ Type=8, Code=0   │                  │                  │          │
│  │ id=0x1234        │                  │                  │          │
│  │ seq=1            │                  │                  │          │
│  │ data: 56 bytes   │                  │                  │          │
│  └────────┬─────────┘                  └────────┬─────────┘          │
│           │                                     │                    │
│           │ 1. ICMP Echo Request                │                    │
│           │    src=10.0.1.5, dst=8.8.8.8        │                    │
│           │    Type=8 (Echo), Code=0             │                    │
│           │    TTL=64                            │                    │
│           │────────────────────────────────────▶│                    │
│           │                                     │                    │
│           │        2. ICMP Echo Reply            │                    │
│           │    src=8.8.8.8, dst=10.0.1.5        │                    │
│           │    Type=0 (Echo Reply), Code=0       │                    │
│           │    TTL=117 (128 - 11 hops)           │                    │
│           │◀────────────────────────────────────│                    │
│           │                                     │                    │
│  PING OUTPUT:                                                    │
│  64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=1 ttl=117 time=12.3 ms          │
│  │        │              │          │         │                   │
│  │        │              │          │         └── RTT (latency)   │
│  │        │              │          └── TTL (hops remaining)     │
│  │        │              └── Which request this reply is for    │
│  │        └── Who responded                                     │
│  └── Payload size received (64 bytes = 56 data + 8 ICMP header) │

🔍 ping vs tcping — ICMP vs TCP-Based Reachability
ToolProtocolWhat It TestsWhen to UseLimitation
pingICMP (Type 8/0)L3 reachability + latencyQuick "is the host alive?" checkICMP may be blocked even if host is up
tcpingTCP SYN to portL4 reachability — is the port open?Testing if a specific service is listeningOnly tests one port at a time
hping3TCP/UDP/ICMPCustom packet craftingFirewall testing, advanced diagnosticsRequires root; more complex

# ping: ICMP — host-level reachability
$ ping -c 3 10.0.1.50
3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss  ← Host is reachable

# tcping: TCP — is port 8000 open?
$ tcping 10.0.1.50 8000
10.0.1.50 port 8000 open  ← Application is listening

# curl: HTTP — is the health endpoint responding?
$ curl http://10.0.1.50:8000/health
{"status": "ok"}  ← Full application health check passed

# nc: TCP — quick port scan
$ nc -zv 10.0.1.50 8000
Connection to 10.0.1.50 8000 port [tcp/*] succeeded!
🔧 How ping Actually Works — Raw Sockets and the ICMP Socket

ping doesn't use normal TCP or UDP sockets — it uses a raw socket (SOCK_RAW) with protocol IPPROTO_ICMP. This gives the application direct access to ICMP packets at the IP layer, bypassing the transport layer entirely. Understanding this explains why ping requires special privileges and why it can measure things TCP tools cannot:

Socket TypeWhat It AccessesExample ToolsRequires Root?
SOCK_STREAM (TCP)TCP stream — reliable, orderedcurl, nc, ssh, browsers❌ No
SOCK_DGRAM (UDP)UDP datagrams — unreliable, unordereddig, ntpdate, DNS clients❌ No
SOCK_RAW (ICMP)Raw ICMP packets — direct L3 accessping, traceroute -I, nping✅ Yes (CAP_NET_RAW)
SOCK_RAW (IP)Raw IP packets — any protocolhping3, nmap, scapy✅ Yes (CAP_NET_RAW)
 
# ping's system calls (strace reveals the magic):
$ strace -e socket,setsockopt,sendto,recvfrom ping -c 1 8.8.8.8

socket(AF_INET, SOCK_RAW, IPPROTO_ICMP) = 3  # Raw ICMP socket!
setsockopt(3, SOL_SOCKET, SO_TIMESTAMP, [1])  # Enable kernel timestamps for RTT
# (ping builds ICMP header: Type=8, Code=0, id=pid, seq=1, checksum)
sendto(3, "ICMP_ECHO_REQUEST...", 64, 0, {8.8.8.8}, 16)  # Send!
recvfrom(3, "ICMP_ECHO_REPLY...", 1024, 0, ...)          # Wait for reply
# (ping computes RTT from SO_TIMESTAMP vs current time)

# Why raw sockets need CAP_NET_RAW (or root):
# Without this capability, ping fails:
$ ping 8.8.8.8
ping: socket: Operation not permitted  # Can't create raw socket!

# Modern fix: give ping the capability, not full root:
$ sudo setcap cap_net_raw+ep /usr/bin/ping
# Now ping works without sudo. Same for traceroute.

# How ping identifies ITS replies (among all ICMP traffic):
# Every ICMP Echo has an 'identifier' field (usually the PID) and
# a 'sequence number'. The kernel delivers ICMP Echo Replies to the
# socket that matches the identifier. Multiple ping processes don't
# interfere because each has a different PID → different identifier.

Why this matters for SREs: If ping works but your application can't connect, the problem is at L4 or L7 — your network and IP stack are fine. If ping works from host A but not host B to the same destination, the problem is in the routing or firewall rules for host B specifically. Raw sockets let you test L3 independently of the application stack.

☁️ ICMP in Cloud Load Balancers — Health Checks and anihpj

Cloud load balancers (AWS ALB/NLB, GCP Cloud LB, Azure LB) use TCP, HTTP, or HTTPS health checks — not ICMP. This is by design: ICMP only tells you if the host's IP stack is alive, not if your application is serving traffic. For the anihpj/jobpost deployment:

Check TypeWhat It TestsFailure Meansanihpj Example
ICMP (ping)Host network stack aliveHost down or ICMP blockedRarely used by cloud LBs
TCP (port check)Port is open and accepting connectionsApplication not listeningNLB health check on port 8000
HTTP (path check)Application responds with 200 OKApp is running but brokenALB checks /health endpoint
HTTPS (TLS + path)TLS cert valid + app healthyCert expired or app downProduction ALB on /health
 
# AWS ALB health check for anihpj (HTTP-based, NOT ICMP):
# alb.amazonaws.com → GET /health → expects 200 OK
# If /health returns non-200 → instance marked UNHEALTHY
# If /health times out → instance marked UNHEALTHY after 3 failures

# Simulate a health check manually:
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://10.0.1.50:8000/health
200  ← Healthy! ALB would keep this instance in rotation.

# IMPORTANT: ICMP ping is NOT sufficient for production health checks.
# The app can be hung (threads blocked, deadlocked) while ICMP still
# responds (kernel handles ICMP, not the application).
# Always health-check at L7 (HTTP/health endpoint) for production.
⚡ ICMP Rate-Limiting — The Right Way to Protect Against Floods

Some organizations block ALL ICMP as a knee-jerk reaction to ICMP-based attacks (Smurf, ping flood). This is like removing your car's dashboard because you don't like warning lights. The correct approach is rate-limiting, not blocking:

# WRONG: Block all ICMP (breaks PMTUD, traceroute, diagnostics)
$ iptables -A INPUT -p icmp -j DROP  ← DO NOT DO THIS

# RIGHT: Rate-limit ICMP Echo (prevents floods, preserves diagnostics)
$ iptables -A INPUT -p icmp --icmp-type echo-request \
    -m limit --limit 1/second --limit-burst 5 -j ACCEPT
$ iptables -A INPUT -p icmp --icmp-type echo-request -j DROP
# Allows 1 ping/second with burst of 5. Floods are dropped.
# All OTHER ICMP types (PMTUD, Time Exceeded) pass through normally!

# RIGHT: Allow essential ICMP types for IPv4
$ iptables -A INPUT -p icmp --icmp-type 0 -j ACCEPT   # Echo Reply
$ iptables -A INPUT -p icmp --icmp-type 3 -j ACCEPT   # Dest Unreachable (PMTUD!)
$ iptables -A INPUT -p icmp --icmp-type 11 -j ACCEPT  # Time Exceeded (traceroute!)
$ iptables -A INPUT -p icmp --icmp-type 8 -m limit \
    --limit 1/s -j ACCEPT  # Echo Request (rate-limited)

# RIGHT: Allow essential ICMPv6 types for IPv6
$ ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 1 -j ACCEPT   # Dest Unreachable
$ ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 2 -j ACCEPT   # Packet Too Big (PMTUD!)
$ ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 3 -j ACCEPT   # Time Exceeded
$ ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 128 -m limit \
    --limit 1/s -j ACCEPT  # Echo Request (rate-limited)
$ ip6tables -A INPUT -p icmpv6 --icmpv6-type 133:137 -j ACCEPT  # NDP (mandatory!)

7.3 traceroute — Mapping the Path

traceroute reveals every router between you and a destination by exploiting the TTL (Time To Live) field in the IP header. It's one of the most elegant diagnostic tools ever designed — no special protocol, no magic, just clever manipulation of a standard IP field.

TRACEROUTE MECHANISM — How TTL Reveals Every Hop
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HOW TRACEROUTE WORKS — Sending probes with TTL=1,2,3...N             │
│                                                                       │
│  SOURCE (10.0.1.5) → R1 (10.0.1.1) → R2 (192.168.1.1) → TARGET      │
│                                                                       │
│  PROBE 1: TTL=1, UDP port 33434                                       │
│  ┌──────┐     ┌──────┐     ┌──────┐     ┌────────┐                  │
│  │SOURCE│────▶│  R1  │     │  R2  │     │ TARGET │                  │
│  └──────┘     └──┬───┘     └──────┘     └────────┘                  │
│                  │ TTL→0! R1 drops packet                            │
│                  │ R1 sends ICMP Time Exceeded (Type 11, Code 0)     │
│                  │ SOURCE learns: Hop 1 = 10.0.1.1, 0.5ms            │
│                                                                       │
│  PROBE 2: TTL=2, UDP port 33435                                       │
│  ┌──────┐     ┌──────┐     ┌──────┐     ┌────────┐                  │
│  │SOURCE│────▶│  R1  │────▶│  R2  │     │ TARGET │                  │
│  └──────┘     └──────┘     └──┬───┘     └────────┘                  │
│                              │ TTL→0! R2 drops                      │
│                              │ Sends ICMP Time Exceeded              │
│                              │ SOURCE learns: Hop 2 = 192.168.1.1    │
│                                                                       │
│  PROBE 3: TTL=3, UDP port 33436                                       │
│  ┌──────┐     ┌──────┐     ┌──────┐     ┌────────┐                  │
│  │SOURCE│────▶│  R1  │────▶│  R2  │────▶│ TARGET │                  │
│  └──────┘     └──────┘     └──────┘     └───┬────┘                  │
│                                            │ TARGET receives!        │
│                                            │ Port 33436 has no       │
│                                            │ listener → ICMP Port    │
│                                            │ Unreachable (Type 3,    │
│                                            │ Code 3)                 │
│                                            │ SOURCE knows: DEST!     │
│                                                                       │
│  KEY INSIGHT: traceroute on Linux sends UDP probes to high ports     │
│  (33434+). The target sends ICMP Port Unreachable because nothing    │
│  is listening on those ports — that's how traceroute knows it        │
│  reached the destination! On Windows, tracert uses ICMP Echo.        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
TRACEROUTE ANNOTATION — Packet Journey from Laptop to anihpj
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  $ traceroute -n jobpost.anihpj.com                                   │
│                                                                       │
│  1  192.168.1.1       1.2 ms   0.8 ms   0.9 ms  ← HOME ROUTER       │
│     └── Your home router. Sub-1ms = you're on the same LAN.          │
│                                                                       │
│  2  10.20.30.1       12.5 ms  11.3 ms  13.1 ms  ← ISP GATEWAY       │
│     └── First ISP hop. 10.x.x.x = private (ISP internal).            │
│         ~12ms RTT suggests ~3-5 km to ISP's local office.            │
│                                                                       │
│  3  72.14.215.1      25.0 ms  24.1 ms  25.8 ms  ← ISP BACKBONE     │
│     └── ISP's regional backbone router. Public IP.                   │
│         ~25ms RTT suggests ~100-200 km from you.                     │
│                                                                       │
│  4  108.170.245.1    30.2 ms   *       31.0 ms  ← TRANSIT          │
│     └── * means one probe got no response (ICMP rate-limited).      │
│         This is NORMAL. Transit routers deprioritize ICMP.            │
│                                                                       │
│  5  142.250.215.1    35.0 ms  34.5 ms  35.1 ms  ← GOOGLE PEERING   │
│     └── Google's edge router at a peering point.                     │
│         142.250.x.x = Google's network.                               │
│                                                                       │
│  6  34.120.45.67     40.1 ms  39.8 ms  40.5 ms  ← CLOUD LB         │
│     └── Cloud load balancer fronting the application.                │
│         34.120.x.x = likely GCP/AWS public IP.                        │
│                                                                       │
│  7  10.0.1.100       41.2 ms  40.9 ms  41.5 ms  ← anihpj K8s LB    │
│     └── Internal K8s LoadBalancer IP (10.x = private).               │
│         This is where anihpj/jobpost lives!                           │
│                                                                       │
│  PATTERN RECOGNITION:                                                 │
│  • Private IPs (10.x, 192.168.x) → internal network hops             │
│  • Public IPs → internet/transit hops                                 │
│  • Latency increases with distance → each hop adds 1-15ms            │
│  • * * * → ICMP blocked or rate-limited (normal for transit)         │
│  • Sudden latency spike → congested link or long-distance hop        │
│  • Last hop private IP → application is behind internal LB           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔄 traceroute vs mtr — Snapshot vs Continuous Monitoring
Featuretraceroutemtr (My Traceroute)
How it works3 probes per hop, one-timeContinuous probes, updates in real-time
OutputStatic list of hopsLive-updating table with loss% per hop
Best forQuick path discoveryIdentifying intermittent packet loss
Loss detectionOnly shows if ALL 3 probes lostShows loss% at each hop over time
Typical commandtraceroute HOSTmtr -n -r HOST (report) or mtr HOST (interactive)
 
# mtr — continuous path monitoring (identifies intermittent issues!)
$ mtr -n -r -c 100 8.8.8.8
HOST: anihpj-web            Loss%   Snt   Last   Avg  Best  Wrst StDev
  1.|-- 10.0.1.1             0.0%   100    0.3   0.3   0.2   0.5   0.1
  2.|-- 192.168.1.1          0.0%   100    1.2   1.1   0.9   2.1   0.2
  3.|-- 72.14.215.1          2.0%   100   12.5  12.3  11.8  15.2   0.8
     └── 2% packet loss at hop 3! Intermittent problem.              
  4.|-- 142.250.215.1        0.0%   100   35.0  34.8  34.2  36.1   0.4
     └── Loss disappears — hop 3's ICMP generation is rate-limited,  
         not actually dropping traffic. This is normal for transit.
🔀 Traceroute Modes — UDP, ICMP, TCP, and Paris Traceroute

Not all traceroutes are created equal. Different implementations use different probe types, and the choice affects what you can discover and which firewalls will block you:

ModeProbe TypeCommandAdvantageLimitation
UDP (default Linux)UDP to ports 33434+traceroute HOSTStandard, works through most networksFirewalls may block high UDP ports
ICMP EchoICMP Echo Request (like ping)traceroute -I HOSTBypasses UDP filteringICMP may be rate-limited in transit
TCP SYNTCP SYN to specified porttraceroute -T -p 80 HOSTPasses through most firewalls!Only reveals path to that specific port
Paris TracerouteMultiple probes with controlled headersparis-traceroute HOSTCorrectly maps ECMP paths!Requires separate tool installation
PARIS TRACEROUTE — Why Standard Traceroute Fails with ECMP
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THE ECMP PROBLEM WITH STANDARD TRACEROUTE:                           │
│                                                                       │
│  When routers use ECMP (multiple equal-cost paths), standard          │
│  traceroute can produce misleading results:                           │
│                                                                       │
│                    ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐                        │
│                    │ SPINE 1  │  │ SPINE 2  │   ← ECMP paths          │
│                    └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘                        │
│                         │  ╲    ╱    │                                │
│                         │   ╲  ╱     │                                │
│                    ┌────┴─────┐  ┌───┴──────┐                        │
│                    │ LEAF 1   │  │ LEAF 2   │                        │
│                    └──────────┘  └──────────┘                        │
│                                                                       │
│  STANDARD traceroute (UDP):                                           │
│    Hop 1: TTL=1 → goes to Spine 1 (hash of 5-tuple)                  │
│    Hop 2: TTL=2 → goes to Spine 2! (different 5-tuple, different     │
│             hash!) → appears as DIFFERENT path than TTL=1 probe!      │
│                                                                       │
│    Result: traceroute shows a NON-EXISTENT path like:                 │
│    Leaf1 → Spine1 → ???  (because TTL=1 and TTL=2 probes took        │
│    different ECMP paths, creating an impossible topology!)            │
│                                                                       │
│  PARIS TRACEROUTE fix:                                                │
│    • Keeps the 5-tuple CONSTANT across all probes                     │
│    • Only varies TTL — same hash = same path every time               │
│    • Result: accurately maps the ACTUAL path through ECMP networks    │
│    • Install: apt install paris-traceroute                            │
│                                                                       │
│  PRACTICAL TIP for DATA CENTER SREs:                                  │
│    If you're debugging a spine-leaf fabric (common in K8s DCs),       │
│    switch to TCP traceroute on a FIXED port to keep the 5-tuple       │
│    consistent across probes:                                          │
│    $ sudo traceroute -T -p 80 --sport=55555 DEST                     │
│    This forces all probes through the same ECMP path.                 │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

7.4 ICMP Beyond ping — Path MTU Discovery

Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) determines the largest packet that can travel from source to destination without fragmentation. It relies entirely on ICMP Type 3, Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed) messages. When PMTUD breaks, the symptoms are maddening: small requests work fine, large requests hang indefinitely.

PMTUD IN ACTION — How TCP Discovers the Path MTU
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SENDER                        ROUTER                    RECEIVER     │
│  MTU=1500                      MTU=1400                              │
│  ┌──────────┐                  ┌──────────┐              ┌──────────┐ │
│  │ TCP SYN  │                  │          │              │          │ │
│  │ MSS=1460 │                  │          │              │          │ │
│  │ DF=1     │                  │          │              │          │ │
│  └────┬─────┘                  └────┬─────┘              └────┬─────┘ │
│       │                             │                         │       │
│       │ 1500B pkt, DF=1             │                         │       │
│       │────────────────────────────▶│                         │       │
│       │                             │ MTU=1400 < 1500!       │       │
│       │                             │ DROP packet            │       │
│       │      ◄── ICMP Frag Needed ──│                         │       │
│       │      Type=3, Code=4,        │                         │       │
│       │      Next-Hop MTU=1400      │                         │       │
│       │                             │                         │       │
│       │ TCP learns: reduce MSS to   │                         │       │
│       │ 1400 - 40 (TCP/IP hdr) =    │                         │       │
│       │ 1360 bytes                   │                         │       │
│       │                             │                         │       │
│       │ 1400B pkt, DF=1             │                         │       │
│       │────────────────────────────▶│─────────────────────────▶       │
│       │                             │  ✓ Fits! Forwarded      │       │
│                                                                       │
│  MANUAL MTU DETECTION:                                                │
│  $ ping -M do -s 1472 8.8.8.8     ← 1472+28 = 1500. Works?          │
│  $ ping -M do -s 1473 8.8.8.8     ← 1473+28 = 1501. Fails?          │
│  → Path MTU = 1500 (1472 data + 28 ICMP/IP headers)                  │
│                                                                       │
│  $ ping -M do -s 1422 10.0.2.10   ← 1422+28 = 1450 (VXLAN path)     │
│  $ ping -M do -s 1423 10.0.2.10   ← Fails at 1423+28 = 1451          │
│  → Path MTU = 1450 (VXLAN reduces usable MTU by 50 bytes!)           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ PMTU Black Hole — When ICMP Type 3 Code 4 Is Blocked

A PMTU black hole occurs when a router drops an oversized packet (because MTU is too small) but the ICMP "Fragmentation Needed" message never reaches the sender — typically because a firewall blocks it. The sender keeps retransmitting the same oversized packet, which keeps getting silently dropped. The connection appears to hang. Small packets (SYN, ACK, small data) work fine because they fit within the MTU. Large packets (file transfers, API responses) hang forever.

PMTU BLACK HOLE — Silent Failure Pattern
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SYMPTOMS OF A PMTU BLACK HOLE:                                       │
│                                                                       │
│  ✓ ping works                   ← Small ICMP packets (84B) fit MTU   │
│  ✓ SSH connection works         ← Interactive traffic is small       │
│  ✓ curl small-page works       ← MTU, silently dropped    │
│  ✗ scp large-file hangs        ← Data segments >MTU get dropped     │
│  ✗ git clone hangs             ← Pack objects exceed MTU            │
│                                                                       │
│  THE BLACK HOLE MECHANISM:                                            │
│                                                                       │
│  Sender ──1500B DF=1──▶ [MTU=1450 Router] ──DROP──▶ [FIREWALL]      │
│                                                    │                  │
│                                                    │ Blocks ICMP      │
│                                                    │ Type 3 Code 4!   │
│                                                    ▼                  │
│  Sender ←──────── (ICMP never arrives) ─────────────────────         │
│  Sender: retransmits... times out... retransmits... HANG              │
│                                                                       │
│  THE FIX:                                                             │
│  1. ALLOW ICMP Type 3 Code 4 through ALL firewalls (absolutely       │
│     critical for PMTUD).                                              │
│  2. Clamp MSS at the edge:                                            │
│     $ iptables -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN \           │
│                -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu                          │
│  3. Reduce MTU on containers/VMs to match the overlay network.       │
│  4. Enable TCP MTU Probing:                                           │
│     $ sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1                            │
│     (Kernel auto-discovers PMTU even if ICMP is blocked!)             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧠 How PMTUD Works at the Kernel Level — TCP's Secret Weapon

Path MTU Discovery isn't just an ICMP trick — it's deeply integrated into the Linux kernel's TCP stack. Understanding this integration explains why some fixes work and others don't:

MechanismHow It WorksICMP Required?When to Use
Standard PMTUDTCP sets DF=1. Router sends ICMP Type 3 Code 4. Kernel reduces route MTU. TCP adjusts MSS.✅ YES — ICMP must reach senderDefault. Works when ICMP is allowed.
TCP MTU ProbingKernel periodically sends larger packets to test if PMTU has increased. If they succeed, MTU is raised.❌ NO — uses TCP retransmissionWhen ICMP is blocked. Slower to discover MTU.
MSS Clampingiptables rewrites the MSS option in TCP SYN packets to match the path MTU. Prevents oversized packets from ever being created.❌ NO — operates at L4At network edges (routers, firewalls). Most reliable fix.
PLPMTUD (RFC 4821)Packetization Layer PMTUD. TCP probes the path by sending progressively larger packets and watching for successful ACKs. No ICMP dependency.❌ NO — uses TCP ACKsModern Linux (kernel 4.1+). Enabled via tcp_mtu_probing=2.
 
# Check current PMTUD-related kernel settings:
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing
net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing = 0  # 0=off, 1=enabled (RFC 4821), 2=enabled on black hole detection

$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_no_pmtu_disc
net.ipv4.ip_no_pmtu_disc = 0  # 0=PMTUD enabled (default), 1=PMTUD disabled (DANGEROUS!)

# Check learned PMTU for a specific route:
$ ip route get 8.8.8.8
8.8.8.8 via 10.0.1.1 dev eth0 src 10.0.1.5
    cache expires 596sec mtu 1500  ← Kernel remembers the PMTU!

# Force PMTU rediscovery (clear cached MTU):
$ ip route flush cache

# Enable TCP MTU Probing (survives ICMP blocking!):
$ sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1
# Mode 1: Probe when ICMP black hole detected
# Mode 2: Always probe (more aggressive, RFC 4821)

# THE KERNEL'S PMTUD STATE MACHINE (simplified):
# 1. New connection → use interface MTU (e.g., 1500) as initial PMTU
# 2. Send packet with DF=1
# 3. If ICMP Type 3 Code 4 arrives → reduce PMTU to reported next-hop MTU
# 4. Periodically (every 10 min) → try larger PMTU (probe)
# 5. If probe succeeds → raise PMTU. If probe fails → keep current PMTU.
# 6. If no ICMP arrives but packets are lost → tcp_mtu_probing=1 kicks in
#    and the kernel tries PLPMTUD (RFC 4821) to discover MTU without ICMP.
eth0: mtu 1500 ← Physical NIC # Check pod MTU (inside container): $ kubectl exec -it anihpj-web-xxx -- ip link show eth0 eth0: mtu 1450 ← VXLAN already reduced it (if CNI configured correctly) # Discover path MTU to a destination: $ traceroute --mtu jobpost.anihpj.com # Shows MTU at each hop. Look for the SMALLEST value. # Manual MTU detection with ping: $ ping -M do -s 1422 10.0.2.10 ← 1422 + 28 = 1450. Works? $ ping -M do -s 1423 10.0.2.10 ← 1423 + 28 = 1451. Fails? # → Path MTU = 1450 # Fix: Configure CNI to set correct MTU: # Calico: CALICO_MTU=1450 (in calico-config ConfigMap) # Flannel: --iface-mtu=1450 (in flannel daemonset args) # Cilium: mtu: 1450 (in cilium-config ConfigMap)

🐞 DEBUGGING: anihpj Container Can't Reach External API for Large Responses

Real-world scenario from networking.txt: The anihpj/jobpost Django app runs in Docker. Health checks and small API responses (<1KB) work perfectly. But when the app tries to fetch a large JSON response from an external payment API (150KB), the connection hangs, then times out after 30 seconds. Here's the systematic tcpdump-based debugging walkthrough:

# STEP 1: Confirm the symptom pattern
$ curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/small/  # ✓ Works (200B response)
$ curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/large/  # ✗ Hangs for 30s, then timeout

# STEP 2: Check MTU inside the container
$ docker exec anihpj-web ip link show eth0 | grep mtu
eth0:  mtu 1500  ← Container thinks MTU is 1500!

# STEP 3: Check host's Docker bridge MTU
$ ip link show docker0 | grep mtu
docker0:  mtu 1500  ← Same! So far looks OK...

# STEP 4: Is there a VXLAN or overlay between host and external API?
$ ip link show | grep vxlan
vxlan0:  mtu 1450 ← THERE IT IS! VXLAN MTU=1450!

# STEP 5: Capture what happens when the large request is sent
$ sudo tcpdump -i any -nn -s 0 -w /tmp/anihpj-mtu.pcap \
    'host 172.17.0.2 and (port 80 or port 443 or icmp)'

# In another terminal, trigger the large request:
$ curl -m 10 http://localhost:8000/api/large/

# STEP 6: Analyze the capture
$ sudo tcpdump -r /tmp/anihpj-mtu.pcap -nn -v | head -30
# You'll see:
# 1. TCP handshake completes ✓ (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — all small packets)
# 2. HTTP GET sent ✓ (small packet)
# 3. Server starts sending response segments
# 4. One large segment (len 1500) is sent...
# 5. NO ICMP Fragmentation Needed comes back! (firewall blocked it)
# 6. TCP retransmits the same large segment 5, 6, 7 times
# 7. After 30 seconds, TCP gives up → RST

# STEP 7: The fix — reduce container path MTU
# Option A: Set MTU in docker-compose.yml
networks:
  anihpj-net:
    driver_opts:
      com.docker.network.driver.mtu: "1450"

# Option B: Clamp MSS in iptables (works even if MTU can't be changed)
$ sudo iptables -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN \
    -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu

# Option C: Enable TCP MTU probing (kernel auto-detects PMTU)
$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1
# This makes the kernel discover PMTU itself if ICMP is blocked.

# STEP 8: Verify the fix
$ curl -s -w "\nTime: %{time_total}s\nSize: %{size_download}B\n" \
    http://localhost:8000/api/large/
Time: 0.234s
Size: 153600B  ← FIXED! Large response in 234ms.

Key debugging pattern to remember: When you see "small works, large hangs," immediately suspect MTU. The three-line verification: (1) check MTU on all interfaces along the path (ip link | grep mtu), (2) binary-search the path MTU with ping -M do -s SIZE, (3) capture ICMP with tcpdump to see if Fragmentation Needed messages are being sent/received/blocked.

⚠️ PMTUD Edge Cases — ECMP, Asymmetric Routing, and Tunnels

PMTUD is simple in theory but has treacherous edge cases in real networks. These are the scenarios that cause the hardest-to-debug PMTU issues:

Edge CaseWhat HappensSymptomFix
ECMP + PMTUDICMP Frag Needed takes a DIFFERENT ECMP path back than the data path forward. The ICMP may never reach the sender (wrong hash on return path).Intermittent black holes — some flows work, others don'tUse MSS clamping at edge. Don't rely on ICMP in ECMP networks.
Asymmetric RoutingForward path has MTU 1500, return path has MTU 1400. The ICMP for the return path goes to the wrong host.One direction works, the other hangsCheck both directions independently. Use traceroute --mtu in both directions.
IPsec/VPN TunnelsTunnel adds 50-100 bytes overhead. Inner packet MTU must be reduced by tunnel overhead, or packets get dropped after encryption.Unencrypted traffic works, encrypted traffic hangsSet tunnel interface MTU correctly. Use MSS clamping for TCP.
GRE TunnelsGRE adds 24 bytes. Path MTU 1500 → GRE tunnel MTU must be 1476. If set to 1500, 1500-byte packets become 1524 after encapsulation.Large packets across GRE tunnel silently droppedip tunnel add gre0 ... ttl 255 (inherit TTL). Set MTU 1476.
Nested TunnelsVXLAN inside GRE = 50 + 24 = 74 bytes overhead. Path MTU 1500 → usable MTU = 1426. Triple-nested tunnels quickly exhaust MTU.Deeply nested overlay networks break PMTUD entirelyAvoid nesting tunnels. Use native routing (Calico BGP) instead of overlays.
 
# CHECKING ECMP PMTUD ISSUES:
# If you suspect ECMP is breaking PMTUD, test with a fixed 5-tuple:
$ ping -M do -s 1472 -p 1234 8.8.8.8  # -p sets the pattern (affects hash)

# For TCP, force a specific source port:
$ curl --local-port 55555 http://example.com/large-file
# (only works if your curl supports --local-port)

# TUNNEL OVERHEAD QUICK REFERENCE:
# VXLAN:    50 bytes (8 VXLAN + 8 UDP + 20 outer IP + 14 outer Eth)
# GRE:      24 bytes (4 GRE + 20 outer IP)
# IP-in-IP: 20 bytes (outer IP only)
# IPsec ESP: 50-70 bytes (ESP header + trailer + outer IP)
# WireGuard: 32 bytes (very efficient!)
#
# FORMULA: usable_MTU = path_MTU - tunnel_overhead
# VXLAN on 1500 path: 1500 - 50 = 1450 usable for containers
# GRE on 1500 path:   1500 - 24 = 1476 usable
# VXLAN+GRE nested:   1500 - 50 - 24 = 1426 usable! (very tight!)

7.5 LAB: ICMP Diagnostic Lab

Hands-on exercises to build muscle memory with ICMP diagnostics. Complete these in order — each builds on the previous.

🛠️ ICMP Diagnostic Lab — 4 Hands-On Exercises
1
Ping Across Your Network & Measure Latency 
# Ping your local gateway:
$ ping -c 10 192.168.1.1
# Observe: RTT should be < 1ms (same LAN). TTL likely 64.

# Ping Google DNS:
$ ping -c 10 8.8.8.8
# Observe: Higher RTT (10-50ms typical). TTL will be lower.

# Ping with specific packet size:
$ ping -c 5 -s 1000 8.8.8.8
# 1000 bytes of data + 28 bytes header = 1028B on wire

# Flood ping (stress test — USE WITH CAUTION):
$ sudo ping -f -c 1000 10.0.1.50
# Sends 1000 pings as fast as possible. Shows packet loss under load.
2
traceroute to 8.8.8.8 — Read Every Line 
# Standard traceroute:
$ traceroute -n 8.8.8.8

# ICMP-based (bypasses UDP filtering):
$ sudo traceroute -I -n 8.8.8.8

# TCP-based (port 80 — passes through most firewalls):
$ sudo traceroute -T -p 80 -n 8.8.8.8

# For each hop, identify:
# 1. Is the IP private (10.x, 192.168.x) or public?
# 2. Is the latency consistent across 3 probes?
# 3. Any * * * (blocked/rate-limited)?
# 4. Sudden latency jumps (crossing an ocean or congested link)?
3
Find Your Path MTU 
# Start with a working size:
$ ping -M do -s 1472 -c 3 8.8.8.8
# 1472 + 28 = 1500. If this works, MTU is at least 1500.

# Test if MTU is exactly 1500:
$ ping -M do -s 1473 -c 3 8.8.8.8
# If this FAILS with "message too long" → MTU = 1500

# If it succeeds, try larger sizes to find the actual MTU.
# Jumbo frames: try -s 8972 (8972+28=9000, common jumbo MTU)

# For containers/VXLAN paths, test smaller sizes:
$ ping -M do -s 1422 -c 3 10.0.2.10
# 1422 + 28 = 1450 (typical VXLAN MTU)
4
Capture ICMP with tcpdump — Identify Each Message Type 
# Terminal 1: Start capture
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp -v
# (or 'icmp6' for IPv6 ICMP)

# Terminal 2: Generate traffic
$ ping -c 1 8.8.8.8
$ traceroute -n 8.8.8.8

# Identify in tcpdump output:
# • ICMP echo request (type 8, code 0)
# • ICMP echo reply (type 0, code 0)
# • ICMP time exceeded (type 11, code 0) ← from traceroute
# • ICMP port unreachable (type 3, code 3) ← traceroute destination

# BONUS: Capture only specific ICMP types:
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'icmp[0] = 3'   # Dest Unreachable only
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'icmp[0] = 11'  # Time Exceeded only
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'icmp[0] = 8 or icmp[0] = 0'  # Echo only

🔭 Chapter 7 — Visual Summary

📨 ICMP = Network Messenger

Protocol 1, no ports. Type+Code identify messages. 40+ types. NOT just ping. Carries control info between routers and hosts.

🏓 ping = Echo Request/Reply

Type 8→0. Measures RTT and packet loss. TTL reveals hop count. ICMP failure ≠ host down (firewall may block ICMP).

🗺️ traceroute = TTL Exploitation

Sends probes with TTL=1,2,3... Each router sends ICMP Time Exceeded. Destination sends Port Unreachable. Maps every hop.

📏 PMTUD = MTU Discovery

DF=1 + ICMP Frag Needed (Type 3 Code 4). Discover the smallest MTU on the path. Broken PMTUD = large transfers hang.

🕳️ PMTU Black Hole

Firewall blocks ICMP Type 3 Code 4. Router drops oversized packets silently. Small packets work, large ones hang.

🐳 VXLAN MTU = 1450

Overlay adds 50 bytes. Physical 1500 → usable 1450. Containers must use 1450 or PMTUD breaks. Configure CNI MTU.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 7

📨ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol)
Protocol 1 in IP. Carries error reports and diagnostic messages between routers and hosts. Uses Type+Code fields (no ports). 40+ message types including Echo (ping), Destination Unreachable, Time Exceeded (traceroute), and Fragmentation Needed (PMTUD).
🏓ping (ICMP Echo Request/Reply)
Sends ICMP Type 8 (Echo Request), expects Type 0 (Echo Reply). Measures RTT and packet loss. TTL in reply reveals network path length. A ping failure does NOT mean the host is down — ICMP may be firewalled.
🗺️traceroute
Sends probes with incrementing TTL values. Each router decrements TTL; when TTL=0, router sends ICMP Time Exceeded (Type 11). The source records each router's IP, building a hop-by-hop map of the path.
📏PMTUD (Path MTU Discovery)
Uses ICMP Type 3 Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed) to discover the smallest MTU along a path. TCP sets DF=1 on all packets. Critical for VXLAN/overlay networks where MTU is smaller than physical.
🕳️PMTU Black Hole
A condition where ICMP Fragmentation Needed messages are blocked by a firewall, preventing PMTUD from working. Oversized packets are silently dropped. Small connections work, large transfers hang indefinitely.
🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work
  • First response to "the site is down": Run ping (L3), then nc -zv HOST 443 (L4), then curl -v https://HOST/health (L7). In 10 seconds you know exactly which layer is failing. Write this sequence into your on-call runbook.
  • Slow connections debugging: Run mtr for 100 probes. Look for loss% that persists to all subsequent hops (real loss) vs loss that disappears (ICMP rate-limiting). Sudden latency spikes at a specific hop = congested link or peering issue.
  • Container/K8s networking issues: Always check MTU when "small works, large hangs." Run ping -M do -s from inside containers to discover the actual path MTU. Configure your CNI to set the correct MTU.
  • Firewall rule auditing: Ensure ICMP Type 3 Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed) and Type 11 Code 0 (Time Exceeded) are allowed through all firewalls. Blocking them doesn't improve security, it breaks your network diagnostics.
  • Cloud migration testing: When migrating to cloud, always test ICMP reachability first. Many cloud providers block ICMP by default. Configure security groups to allow it for diagnostic purposes.

🔑 Chapter 7 Key Takeaways

  1. ICMP is the network's control plane, not just ping. Protocol 1, no ports, 40+ message types. It carries error reports, diagnostics, and path information between routers and hosts. Understanding ICMP types and codes is a core infrastructure diagnostic skill.
  2. A ping failure does NOT mean the host is down. ICMP filtering is ubiquitous in cloud environments. Always verify with TCP-based tests (nc, curl, tcping) before concluding a host is unreachable.
  3. traceroute exploits TTL to map networks. Probes with TTL=1,2,3... cause routers to send ICMP Time Exceeded, revealing each hop. mtr provides continuous monitoring for intermittent issues.
  4. PMTUD is critical and fragile. It depends entirely on ICMP Type 3 Code 4 reaching the sender. Block this message and you create PMTU black holes — large transfers fail silently while small ones work fine.
  5. VXLAN reduces MTU by 50 bytes. Physical NIC 1500 → usable 1450 in pods/containers. Configure CNI MTU correctly. This is the #1 container networking issue.
  6. Test at every layer: L3 (ping) → L4 (nc/tcping) → L7 (curl). Systematic layer-by-layer testing isolates the failure point in seconds. Build this into your on-call response.
🛡️ SRE Reality Check — The ICMP Blocking Epidemic

Many organizations block ALL ICMP traffic as a "security measure," not realizing they're breaking critical network functions. You MUST allow these ICMP types: Type 0/8 (Echo — ping), Type 3 Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed — PMTUD), Type 11 (Time Exceeded — traceroute). Blocking Type 3 Code 4 creates PMTU black holes that cause mysterious, intermittent application failures that are extremely difficult to diagnose. Blocking Type 11 makes traceroute useless during outages. The security benefit of blocking diagnostic ICMP is negligible compared to the operational damage it causes. Use rate-limiting for flood protection, not blanket blocking.

⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 7.1 — Identify ICMP Types from Scenarios

For each scenario, identify the ICMP Type and Code:

  1. A router receives a packet for 10.0.5.50 but has no route to that network.
  2. You run ping 8.8.8.8 and get a response.
  3. A traceroute probe reaches its 5th hop; the router drops it.
  4. A packet with DF=1 arrives at a router with a smaller MTU interface.
  5. A firewall explicitly rejects traffic to port 22.
💡 Hint: Type 3 = Destination Unreachable (various codes). Type 0/8 = Echo. Type 11 = Time Exceeded. Codes specify the reason: 0=Network, 1=Host, 3=Port, 4=Frag Needed, 13=Admin Prohibited.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. No route to 10.0.5.50
#    → Type 3 (Destination Unreachable), Code 0 (Network Unreachable)
#    Router cannot reach the network at all.

# 2. ping 8.8.8.8 response
#    → Type 0 (Echo Reply), Code 0
#    Sent in response to Type 8 (Echo Request).

# 3. Traceroute's 5th hop drops packet
#    → Type 11 (Time Exceeded), Code 0 (TTL Exceeded in Transit)
#    This is how traceroute discovers each hop!

# 4. DF=1 packet exceeds MTU
#    → Type 3 (Destination Unreachable), Code 4 (Frag Needed, DF Set)
#    Critical for PMTUD. The message includes the next-hop MTU.

# 5. Firewall blocks port 22
#    → Type 3 (Destination Unreachable), Code 13 (Administratively Prohibited)
#    "I could forward this, but my admin said no."
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.2 — Decode ping and traceroute Output

Given this output, answer the questions below:

PING 10.0.1.50 (10.0.1.50) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 10.0.1.50: icmp_seq=1 ttl=62 time=0.5 ms
64 bytes from 10.0.1.50: icmp_seq=2 ttl=62 time=0.4 ms
64 bytes from 10.0.1.50: icmp_seq=3 ttl=62 time=15.8 ms
64 bytes from 10.0.1.50: icmp_seq=4 ttl=62 time=0.3 ms
64 bytes from 10.0.1.50: icmp_seq=5 ttl=62 time=0.5 ms
--- 10.0.1.50 ping statistics ---
5 packets transmitted, 5 received, 0% packet loss, time 4005ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.3/3.5/15.8/6.1 ms

Questions:

  1. What was the original TTL set by 10.0.1.50? What OS is it likely running?
  2. What does the spike in seq=3 (15.8ms) indicate when others are 0.3-0.5ms?
  3. Why is mdev (6.1ms) so high relative to the typical RTT?
💡 Hint: Linux default TTL=64, Windows=128. Replied TTL=62 means 2 hops were subtracted (64-62). seq=3 spike = temporary congestion or CPU contention. mdev = standard deviation of RTT.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. ORIGINAL TTL & OS:
#    Reply TTL = 62. Likely initial TTL = 64 (Linux).
#    64 - 62 = 2 router hops between you and 10.0.1.50.
#    If Windows (TTL=128), it would be 128-62 = 66 hops — unlikely
#    on a local network. So: Linux, 2 hops away.

# 2. THE 15.8ms SPIKE:
#    seq=3's RTT is ~40× higher than others (15.8ms vs 0.3-0.5ms).
#    Possible causes:
#    • Transient network congestion (burst of traffic on the link)
#    • CPU contention on either host (busy processing something)
#    • Interrupt coalescing or NIC driver buffering
#    • Wireless interference (if on Wi-Fi)
#    Single spike is not concerning. Repeated spikes = problem.

# 3. HIGH mdev (6.1ms):
#    mdev = standard deviation of RTT values = 6.1ms.
#    This is HIGH because of the single 15.8ms spike pulling
#    the average up. Without seq=3:
#    Values: 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.5 → avg=0.425ms, mdev≈0.08ms
#    → Jitter is actually very low. The spike was an outlier.
#    → Run mtr to see if spikes are frequent or rare.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.3 — PMTU Black Hole Diagnosis

You're running anihpj/jobpost in Docker with the default bridge network. Small API requests (health check, <200B responses) work perfectly. But when a client requests a large JSON report (150KB response), the connection hangs for 30 seconds then times out. SSH to the container works fine. ping to the container works fine.

Tasks:

  1. What is the most likely cause?
  2. What diagnostic commands would you run to confirm?
  3. What are two possible fixes?
💡 Hint: Small works, large hangs = classic PMTUD failure. Docker bridge + overlay/VXLAN = MTU mismatch. Use ping -M do -s to binary-search the MTU. Check if ICMP Type 3 Code 4 is allowed through your firewall.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. MOST LIKELY CAUSE: PMTU Black Hole
#    Small packets (< MTU) pass through. Large packets (> MTU)
#    are silently dropped because:
#    • Docker bridge MTU = 1500
#    • But there may be VXLAN/GRE overlay reducing effective MTU
#    • ICMP Frag Needed (Type 3, Code 4) is blocked by firewall
#    • TCP keeps retransmitting the large segment → never succeeds

# 2. DIAGNOSTIC COMMANDS:
#    Check MTU on host:
$ ip link show docker0 | grep mtu
#    docker0: mtu 1500

#    Check MTU inside container:
$ docker exec anihpj-web ip link show eth0 | grep mtu
#    eth0: mtu 1500 ← Container thinks MTU is 1500!

#    Binary-search path MTU with ping:
$ ping -M do -s 1472 -c 3 172.17.0.2    # 1472+28=1500. Works?
$ ping -M do -s 1422 -c 3 172.17.0.2    # 1422+28=1450. Works?
#    If 1472 fails but 1422 works → MTU is between 1450-1500

#    Check if ICMP Frag Needed reaches the source:
$ sudo tcpdump -i any icmp[0]==3 and icmp[1]==4
#    Send a large ping with DF=1 and see if ICMP comes back.

# 3. TWO FIXES:
#    Fix A — Reduce container MTU:
#    In docker-compose.yml:
networks:
  default:
    driver_opts:
      com.docker.network.driver.mtu: "1450"

#    Or on container start:
$ docker run --sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1 ...

#    Fix B — Clamp MSS at firewall (iptables):
$ iptables -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN \
           -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu
#    This rewrites the MSS option in TCP SYN packets to match
#    the path MTU, preventing the sender from ever creating
#    packets larger than the path can handle.

📝 Chapter 7 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is ICMP and why is it NOT accurate to call it "the ping protocol"? What protocol number does ICMP use, and how does it differ from TCP and UDP?
Show Answer
Answer

ICMP is the Internet Control Message Protocol — the network's error reporting and diagnostic mechanism. It uses protocol number 1 in the IP header (TCP=6, UDP=17). Unlike TCP and UDP, ICMP has no ports — it uses Type+Code fields. ICMP is NOT just ping: ping is ONE of 40+ ICMP message types (Type 8/0). Other critical types include Destination Unreachable (Type 3), Time Exceeded (Type 11, used by traceroute), Fragmentation Needed (Type 3 Code 4, used by PMTUD), and Redirect (Type 5). ICMP messages are generated by routers and hosts, not applications.

Explanation

The key misconception: ICMP = ping. In reality, ICMP is the control plane of the internet. It reports errors, discovers paths, and enables diagnostics. Without ICMP, you lose PMTUD (large transfers break), traceroute (can't map paths), and network error reporting. Blocking all ICMP is a common but harmful security practice — you must selectively allow critical types.

Q2
You ping a server and get 100% packet loss. Does this mean the server is down? What additional tests would you run to determine the actual state?
Show Answer
Answer

No. 100% ping packet loss means ICMP is not reaching the target or replies aren't coming back. This could mean: (1) ICMP blocked by a firewall (most common in cloud environments), (2) ICMP rate-limited by an intermediate router, (3) the host is actually down. To determine actual state: nc -zv HOST 22 (TCP SYN to SSH port), curl http://HOST:8000/health (HTTP health check), tcping HOST 443 (TCP-based ping). If TCP succeeds but ICMP fails → firewall blocking ICMP. If both fail → host is down or unreachable.

Explanation

This is the #1 networking diagnostic trap. AWS security groups block ICMP by default. Azure blocks internet ICMP to VMs. Always triangulate with TCP-based tests. The pattern "ping fails, SSH works" is so common it's practically diagnostic of ICMP filtering.

Q3
Explain exactly how traceroute works at the IP layer. What field does it exploit? Why does the destination send an ICMP Port Unreachable rather than an Echo Reply?
Show Answer
Answer

traceroute exploits the TTL field in the IP header. It sends UDP packets to high-numbered ports (33434+) with TTL=1, TTL=2, TTL=3, etc. At each hop, a router decrements TTL; when TTL reaches 0, the router drops the packet and sends an ICMP Time Exceeded (Type 11, Code 0) back to the source — revealing the router's IP. When the packet finally reaches the destination (TTL high enough), the destination receives a UDP packet on a port with no listener. It responds with ICMP Port Unreachable (Type 3, Code 3) — this tells traceroute "destination reached!"

Explanation

traceroute's brilliance: it uses standard protocol behavior — TTL expiry and port unreachable — in a creative way. No special protocol needed. Linux traceroute uses UDP; Windows tracert uses ICMP Echo with incrementing TTL. The destination sends Port Unreachable (not Echo Reply) because traceroute deliberately targets a port nothing is listening on.

Q4
What does * * * mean in traceroute output? Is it always a problem? What are three possible causes?
Show Answer
Answer

* * * means all three probes to that hop received no response. Three causes: (1) ICMP rate-limiting: The router deprioritizes ICMP generation (very common on internet backbone routers). This is NORMAL and not a problem. (2) Firewall blocking ICMP: A firewall silently drops ICMP Time Exceeded responses. (3) Asymmetric routing + filtering: The probe takes one path but the ICMP reply takes a different path where it's filtered. If subsequent hops respond normally, the * * * is rate-limiting — not a problem.

Explanation

The key diagnostic insight: if you see * * * at hop 5 but hop 6 responds, hop 5 is just not generating ICMP (or it's being filtered on the return path). The traffic IS passing through hop 5 — it just doesn't tell you about it. Only worry if ALL subsequent hops after a * * * are also * * * — that suggests a real failure at that hop.

Q5
What is Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) and which ICMP message type makes it work? What happens if that ICMP message is blocked by a firewall?
Show Answer
Answer

PMTUD uses ICMP Type 3, Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed, DF Set) to discover the smallest MTU along a network path. TCP sets the DF (Don't Fragment) flag on all packets. When a router with a smaller MTU receives a DF=1 packet that's too large, it drops the packet and sends ICMP Type 3 Code 4 back to the source, including the next-hop MTU. The source reduces its packet size accordingly. If this ICMP message is blocked: the source never learns to reduce packet size, keeps retransmitting oversized packets that are silently dropped → PMTU Black Hole. Small packets work, large transfers hang.

Explanation

PMTU black holes are one of the most frustrating network problems because they're inconsistent — SSH works, small API calls work, but file transfers and large responses fail. The fix: allow ICMP Type 3 Code 4 through all firewalls, or use MSS clamping at the network edge to prevent oversized packets from ever being created.

Q6
You're running Kubernetes with Flannel VXLAN. Your physical NIC has MTU 1500. What is the usable MTU inside pods, and why? What happens if a pod tries to send a 1500-byte packet?
Show Answer
Answer

VXLAN adds 50 bytes of overhead (8 VXLAN header + 8 UDP header + 20 outer IP header + 14 outer Ethernet = 50 bytes). Usable pod MTU = 1500 − 50 = 1450 bytes. If a pod sends a 1500-byte packet with DF=1: the packet is encapsulated in VXLAN (becoming 1550 bytes), which exceeds the physical NIC MTU. The physical NIC drops it. If PMTUD is working, the pod receives ICMP Frag Needed and reduces its MSS. If PMTUD is broken (ICMP blocked), the 1500-byte packets are silently dropped → PMTU Black Hole: small requests work, large ones hang.

Explanation

This is the #1 Kubernetes networking issue with overlay CNIs. The fix: configure the CNI to set pod MTU=1450 (Calico: CALICO_MTU, Flannel: --iface-mtu, Cilium: mtu in ConfigMap). Or use a CNI in native routing mode (Calico BGP) where no encapsulation overhead exists. AWS VPC CNI also avoids this by using the VPC's native networking.

Q7
Compare ping, tcping, curl, and nc -zv. What layer does each test? When would you use each one?
Show Answer
Answer

ping = ICMP (L3). Tests if the host's IP stack is reachable. Use for: quick "is the machine alive?" check. Limitation: ICMP may be blocked. tcping = TCP SYN (L4). Tests if a specific port is open. Use for: verifying a service is listening. curl = HTTP over TCP (L7). Tests the full application stack. Use for: health checks, API testing. nc -zv = TCP SYN scan (L4). Quick port open/closed check. Use for: verifying firewall rules allow a port. Best practice: use all four layers. ping failure + tcping success = ICMP blocked. tcping failure + curl success = something wrong with your tcping (rare). All fail = host is down.

Explanation

The diagnostic hierarchy: L3 (ping) → L4 (tcping/nc) → L7 (curl). Each layer tells you something different. A host can be pingable but have no services running (L3 up, L4/L7 down). A host can have SSH working but HTTP failing (L3/L4 up for port 22, L7 down for port 80). Systematic layer-by-layer testing is the key to fast network diagnosis.

Q8
You're troubleshooting an anihpj/jobpost deployment where users report intermittent "connection reset" errors during large file uploads. Small uploads (<1MB) work fine. traceroute shows normal latency with no loss. ping shows 0% packet loss. What's the most likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer

Most likely: PMTU Black Hole caused by VXLAN/overlay MTU mismatch combined with blocked ICMP Type 3 Code 4. Small uploads (<1MB) fit within the MTU and work fine. Large uploads create packets exceeding the overlay MTU (1450 for VXLAN). These packets are silently dropped because the ICMP Fragmentation Needed message is blocked somewhere on the path. After repeated retransmissions, TCP gives up and resets the connection. ping and traceroute work because their packets are small (<100 bytes). The symptom pattern — "small works, large fails" — is the classic PMTUD failure signature.

Explanation

The diagnostic signature: (1) small transfers always succeed, (2) large transfers always fail, (3) ping and traceroute are clean, (4) connection eventually resets rather than hanging (TCP gives up after repeated retransmission failures). This is virtually always MTU-related. Fix: reduce pod MTU to 1450 or clamp MSS at the network edge.

Q9
What's the difference between traceroute and mtr? In what scenario would mtr reveal a problem that traceroute would miss?
Show Answer
Answer

traceroute: Sends 3 probes per hop, one-time snapshot. Shows the path and latency at that moment. mtr: Sends continuous probes and shows running statistics (loss%, avg/best/worst latency per hop). mtr catches: intermittent packet loss that occurs only occasionally. traceroute sends only 3 probes per hop — if loss happens 5% of the time, all 3 probes might succeed and you'd see 0% loss. mtr running for 100 probes would show 5% loss clearly. Also catches: latency spikes that happen every 30 seconds (traceroute's 3 probes might miss the window).

Explanation

traceroute is a photograph. mtr is a video. For intermittent problems (the most difficult kind), mtr is essential. Run mtr -r -c 100 HOST for a 100-probe report. Look for: (1) loss% that starts at one hop and persists to all subsequent hops = real loss at that hop, (2) loss% at one hop that disappears at subsequent hops = ICMP rate-limiting (not real loss).

Q10
How would you manually determine the Path MTU to a destination using only ping? Walk through the commands and explain the binary search approach.
Show Answer
Answer

Binary search with ping:

# Step 1: Start with a known working size (e.g., 1400)
$ ping -M do -s 1400 -c 2 8.8.8.8   ← 1400+28=1428. Should work.

# Step 2: Try a larger size (midpoint between 1400 and 1500)
$ ping -M do -s 1450 -c 2 8.8.8.8   ← 1450+28=1478. Works?

# Step 3: Binary search up or down
$ ping -M do -s 1472 -c 2 8.8.8.8   ← 1472+28=1500 (Ethernet max)

# If 1472 works, MTU ≥ 1500. Try jumbo:
$ ping -M do -s 8972 -c 2 8.8.8.8   ← 8972+28=9000 (jumbo frame)

# If 1472 fails but 1450 works:
# Try 1460, then 1465, 1468, 1470... binary search the boundary.
# The largest value that succeeds + 28 = Path MTU.

-M do = "Don't fragment" (sets DF=1, mandatory for PMTUD testing). -s = payload size in bytes (excluding ICMP header + IP header = 28 bytes). Path MTU = largest working -s value + 28.

Explanation

Manual PMTU discovery with ping is one of the most important diagnostic skills. The binary search approach finds the exact MTU in ~5-7 probes instead of dozens. Remember: ping -s specifies the ICMP payload size, not the total packet size. Total = -s value + 28 (8 ICMP header + 20 IP header). For IPv6, use ping6 -s and add 48 (8 ICMPv6 + 40 IPv6 header).

🟡 Part 3: Layer 4 — TCP & UDPChapters 8-10

Chapter 8: TCP — The Reliable Workhorse (Deep Dive)

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is the protocol that makes the internet reliable. IP is "best effort" — packets can be lost, duplicated, reordered, or corrupted in transit. TCP takes this unreliable foundation and builds a reliable, ordered, error-checked byte stream on top of it. Every web request, every SSH session, every database query — virtually every application you depend on — runs over TCP. Understanding TCP at a deep level is understanding the foundation of modern distributed systems. This is the longest chapter for a reason: TCP is the most important protocol you'll ever learn.

🟡 INTERMEDIATE ⏱️ ~5 hours 📦 Reliability ⚡ Performance

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:

  • Explain exactly how TCP transforms IP's unreliable datagram service into a reliable byte stream
  • Trace the 3-way handshake byte-by-byte and explain why 3 exchanges (not 2, not 4)
  • Dissect the TCP header — every field, every flag, every mechanism
  • Navigate the 11-state TCP state machine and diagnose connections stuck in any state
  • Understand sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmission, and Selective Acknowledgment (SACK)
  • Explain flow control (sliding window) and congestion control (Slow Start, CUBIC, BBR)
  • Diagnose TIME_WAIT accumulation, tune kernel TCP parameters, and apply production best practices
🔗 Applies To:
DevOps
SRE
Cloud Eng
Backend Dev
SysAdmin
Weight: Critical. TCP knowledge directly impacts reliability, performance, and debugging.
🎯 SRE Interview Tip

TCP is the most common deep-dive topic in infrastructure interviews. You WILL be asked to trace the 3-way handshake, explain TIME_WAIT, describe congestion control, and diagnose "too many connections in TIME_WAIT." Know the difference between flow control (receiver-driven, window field) and congestion control (network-driven, cwnd). Know why tcp_tw_recycle was REMOVED from Linux (it broke NAT'd clients). Know that BBR can 10× throughput on lossy links. TCP mastery is the #1 signal of infrastructure depth.

8.1 What Problem Does TCP Solve?

IP (Internet Protocol) is best-effort delivery. It makes exactly zero guarantees: packets can be lost, duplicated, delivered out of order, or corrupted. This is by design — IP's simplicity is what made the internet scale globally. But applications need more. They need to reliably transfer files, stream video, execute database transactions. TCP bridges the gap between "send and pray" (IP) and "send and know" (applications).

BEFORE/AFTER — Why Applications Can't Use Raw IP
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WITHOUT TCP — Raw IP (best effort, no guarantees)                    │
│                                                                       │
│  SENDER                          RECEIVER                             │
│  ┌──────────┐                    ┌──────────┐                        │
│  │ App sends│                    │ App recv │                         │
│  │ 3 chunks │                    │ ???      │                         │
│  └────┬─────┘                    └────┬─────┘                        │
│       │                               │                               │
│  IP:  send(A) ──────────────▶  arrives? (maybe lost)                 │
│  IP:  send(B) ──────────────▶  arrives OUT OF ORDER (B before A!)    │
│  IP:  send(C) ──────────────▶  arrives DUPLICATED (C twice!)         │
│                                                                       │
│  APP received: B, C, C, (A lost forever)                              │
│  APP: "What order? Are any missing? Did duplicates happen?"           │
│  → Application must handle ALL of this itself. Nightmare.             │
│                                                                       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WITH TCP — Reliable, ordered byte stream                              │
│                                                                       │
│  SENDER                          RECEIVER                             │
│  ┌──────────┐                    ┌──────────┐                        │
│  │ App sends│                    │ App recv │                         │
│  │ "ABC"    │                    │ "ABC"    │                         │
│  └────┬─────┘                    └────┬─────┘                        │
│       │                               │                               │
│  TCP: send(A) seq=1 ──────────▶  TCP buffers, waits for B            │
│  TCP: send(B) seq=2 ──────────▶  TCP has A,B → delivers A,B to app  │
│  TCP: send(C) seq=3 (LOST!)      TCP: "I'm missing seq=3! SACK=3!"   │
│  TCP: RESEND(C) seq=3 ────────▶  TCP has A,B,C → delivers C to app  │
│                                                                       │
│  APP received: A, B, C (in order, exactly once, no gaps!)            │
│  → Application doesn't even know there was a problem!                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 The TCP Abstraction — A Reliable Byte Stream
