10.2 What Is a Socket?

A socket is an endpoint for communication — the combination of an IP address, a port, and a protocol. The kernel represents every active connection as a socket pair linked by a 5-tuple: (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol). This 5-tuple MUST be unique for every connection on the system.

THE 5-TUPLE — What Uniquely Identifies Every TCP Connection
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CLIENT SOCKET                    SERVER SOCKET                       │
│  192.168.1.100:54321         ↔    10.0.1.50:8000                     │
│                                                                       │
│  The 5-tuple for this connection:                                     │
│  {192.168.1.100, 54321, 10.0.1.50, 8000, TCP}                       │
│                                                                       │
│  HOW MULTIPLE CLIENTS CONNECT TO THE SAME SERVER:                     │
│  Server is bound to 10.0.1.50:8000 (one socket, LISTEN state).       │
│  When clients connect, the kernel creates NEW sockets:               │
│                                                                       │
│  Client A: {192.168.1.100, 54321, 10.0.1.50, 8000, TCP} ← unique!   │
│  Client B: {192.168.1.101, 54321, 10.0.1.50, 8000, TCP} ← unique!   │
│  Client C: {192.168.1.100, 54322, 10.0.1.50, 8000, TCP} ← unique!   │
│                                                                       │
│  All different because either source IP OR source port differs!       │
│  Server 10.0.1.50:8000 can accept (2^32 src IPs × 2^16 src ports)   │
│  = 2^48 ≈ 281 TRILLION unique connections (theoretically).           │
│                                                                       │
│  HOW MANY CAN A SERVER ACTUALLY HANDLE?                               │
│  Theoretical: 2^48 connections (impossibly large).                    │
│  Practical limit: file descriptors (ulimit -n, default 1024!).        │
│  Production limit: kernel memory (each socket ~4KB), CPU, NIC queues. │
│  A well-tuned server can handle 1M+ concurrent connections:           │
│    ulimit -n 1048576                                                  │
│    net.core.somaxconn=65536                                           │
│    Enough RAM (1M sockets × ~4KB = ~4GB)                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
TCP SOCKET STATES — Every State You'll See in `ss` Output (and What Each Means)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TCP STATE MACHINE — the life of a single TCP socket (one direction) │
│                                                                       │
│  CLIENT (active open)                    SERVER (passive open)        │
│  ─────                                   ──────                       │
│  [CLOSED]                                [CLOSED]                     │
│     │                                       │                         │
│     │ socket()                              │ socket()                │
│     │ bind(ephemeral port)                  │ bind(service port)      │
│     │ connect(server) ──SYN──▶              │ listen()                │
│     ▼                                       ▼                         │
│  [SYN_SENT]                             [LISTEN]                      │
│     │                                       │                         │
│     │         ◀──SYN+ACK──                  │                         │
│     │         ──ACK──────▶                 │  new socket created     │
│     ▼                                       ▼                         │
│  [ESTABLISHED] ◀═══════════════════▶  [SYN_RCVD] → [ESTABLISHED]     │
│     │                                       │                         │
│     │ close() ──FIN──▶                     │                         │
│     ▼                                       ▼                         │
│  [FIN_WAIT_1]                           [CLOSE_WAIT]  ←──FIN──        │
│     │                                       │                         │
│     │         ◀──ACK──                      │ close() → ──FIN──▶     │
│     ▼                                       ▼                         │
│  [FIN_WAIT_2]                           [LAST_ACK]                    │
│     │                                       │                         │
│     │         ◀──FIN──                      │ ◀──ACK──               │
│     │         ──ACK──▶                      ▼                         │
│     ▼                                    [CLOSED]                     │
│  [TIME_WAIT] — 2*MSL (120s) ─────────────────────────────────────    │
│     │                                                                 │
│     ▼  (after 120s)                                                   │
│  [CLOSED]                                                             │
│                                                                       │
│  KEY INSIGHTS FROM ss OUTPUT:                                         │
│  ┌──────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│
│  │ STATE        │ WHAT IT TELLS YOU                                  ││
│  ├──────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ LISTEN       │ Server ready, waiting for SYNs. Recv-Q = backlog  ││
│  │ SYN_SENT     │ Client sent SYN, waiting for SYN+ACK (connecting) ││
│  │ SYN_RCVD     │ Server received SYN, sent SYN+ACK (rarely seen)   ││
│  │ ESTABLISHED  │ Normal data transfer (both directions)            ││
│  │ FIN_WAIT_1   │ Active closer sent FIN, waiting for ACK           ││
│  │ FIN_WAIT_2   │ Active closer received ACK, waiting for remote FIN││
│  │ CLOSE_WAIT   │ Passive closer received FIN, waiting for app close││
│  │ LAST_ACK     │ Passive closer sent FIN, waiting for final ACK    ││
│  │ TIME_WAIT    │ Active closer: waiting 120s to ensure remote ACK  ││
│  │ CLOSING      │ Both sides close simultaneously (rare)            ││
│  │ CLOSED       │ Socket doesn't exist (not shown in ss)            ││
│  └──────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│                                                                       │
│  CRITICAL DIAGNOSTICS:                                                │
│  ‣ 1000s of TIME_WAIT? → Normal for active-closer (proxy). Tune      │
│    tcp_tw_reuse if needed. NOT a problem unless exhausting ports.     │
│  ‣ CLOSE_WAIT sockets accumulating? → Application BUG! The app       │
│    received FIN but NEVER called close(). Socket leak. Fix the code. │
│  ‣ SYN_SENT hanging? → Firewall/routing issue. Remote not reachable. │
│  ‣ Recv-Q > 0 on LISTEN? → Accept queue backing up. App too slow.    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔄 The listen() Backlog — SYN Queue + Accept Queue Explained

When a server calls listen(sockfd, backlog), it creates TWO queues in the kernel:

From SYN to accept() — The Two-Queue Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CLIENT SENDS SYN                                                    │
│       │                                                               │
│       ▼                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────┐     SYN+ACK sent, enters SYN_RCVD                   │
│  │  SYN QUEUE  │ ←── pending connections (incomplete 3-way handshake)│
│  │ (syns queue)│     Size: min(backlog, net.core.somaxconn,           │
│  └──────┬──────┘           net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog)             │
│         │ 3-way handshake completes                                   │
│         ▼                                                             │
│  ┌────────────────┐  Connection established, waiting for accept()    │
│  │  ACCEPT QUEUE  │  Size: min(backlog, net.core.somaxconn)          │
│  │ (backlog queue)│  ss shows Recv-Q on LISTEN socket = this queue!  │
│  └───────┬────────┘                                                  │
│          │ accept() called by application                             │
│          ▼                                                            │
│  ┌────────────────┐  Application gets fd, can read/write             │
│  │  APPLICATION   │  ESTABLISHED state                                │
│  └────────────────┘                                                  │
│                                                                       │
│  IF ACCEPT QUEUE IS FULL → new SYNs are DROPPED (silently!)          │
│  This is "SYN flooding" — but can happen under normal load if        │
│  your app calls accept() too slowly.                                  │
│                                                                       │
│  WATCH FOR IT:                                                        │
│  $ ss -tlnp 'sport = :8000'  # Look at Recv-Q column!           │
│  State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port                              │
│  LISTEN 2048   0      0.0.0.0:8000                                   │
│  # ↑ Recv-Q = 2048 means ~2048 connections waiting for accept()!  │
│  #   The app is TOO SLOW accepting connections.                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# TUNE THESE FOR HIGH-CONNECTION SERVERS:
# Maximum SYN backlog (incomplete handshakes):
$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=8192

# Maximum accept queue (complete, waiting for accept()):
$ sudo sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=65536

# In your application code, the listen() backlog parameter:
# Python:  server.socket.listen(128)  → actual = min(128, somaxconn)
# Go:      net.Listen("tcp", ":8000") → uses somaxconn directly
# Nginx:   listen 80 backlog=4096;    → sets explicitly

# INSTANT DIAGNOSIS — are you dropping connections?
$ ss -tlnp | awk 'NR>1 && $2>0 {print "WARNING: "$1" port "$4" Recv-Q="$2" (connections queued!)"}'
# If you see Recv-Q > 0 on LISTEN sockets: your app is too slow at accept()
📦 Socket Buffer Sizes — SO_RCVBUF, SO_SNDBUF & The Bandwidth-Delay Product

Every socket has two kernel buffers: receive buffer (data from network waiting for read()) and send buffer (data from write() waiting for network). The size of these buffers determines throughput — if they're too small, you're limited by buffer space, not by network speed.

How Socket Buffers Affect Throughput (BDP)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THE BANDWIDTH-DELAY PRODUCT (BDP)                                    │
│  BDP = Bandwidth (bits/s) × RTT (seconds)                            │
│                                                                       │
│  Example: 1 Gbps link, 30ms RTT between us-east-1 and eu-west-1      │
│  BDP = 1,000,000,000 × 0.030 = 30,000,000 bits = 3.75 MB            │
│                                                                       │
│  YOUR SOCKET BUFFER MUST BE ≥ BDP FOR FULL THROUGHPUT!               │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  64KB buffer (default) on 1Gbps/30ms link:                   │    │
│  │  Max throughput = 64KB / 30ms = 17 Mbps  ← ONLY 1.7% of 1Gbps│   │
│  │                                                              │    │
│  │  4MB buffer (tuned) on 1Gbps/30ms link:                      │    │
│  │  Max throughput = 4MB / 30ms = ~1 Gbps  ← FULL LINE RATE!    │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                       │
│  KERNEL AUTO-TUNING (Linux 2.6.17+, enabled by default):             │
│  ‣ tcp_rmem: min, default, max (receive buffer auto-tuning)          │
│  ‣ tcp_wmem: min, default, max (send buffer auto-tuning)             │
│  ‣ The kernel starts at "default" and grows toward "max" as needed   │
│  ‣ net.core.rmem_max, net.core.wmem_max: absolute caps               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# CHECK CURRENT BUFFER SETTINGS:
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_rmem
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem = 4096    131072    6291456
#                    ↑min    ↑default   ↑max (6MB)

$ sysctl net.core.rmem_max
net.core.rmem_max = 212992  # System-wide cap: ~208KB
# ↑ THIS IS THE BOTTLENECK! Even though tcp_rmem max is 6MB,
#   net.core.rmem_max caps it at 208KB!

# FIX — raise the system-wide cap:
$ sudo sysctl -w net.core.rmem_max=16777216  # 16MB
$ sudo sysctl -w net.core.wmem_max=16777216
$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem="4096 131072 16777216"
$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_wmem="4096 65536 16777216"

# VERIFY BUFFER USAGE ON ACTIVE SOCKETS:
$ ss -tm
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local:Port     Peer:Port
ESTAB  0      0      10.0.1.5:54321 10.0.2.100:5432
  skmem:(r0,rb131072,t0,tb65536,f0,w0,o0,bl0,d0)
#        │  │          │  │
#        │  rcv buf=    │  snd buf=
#        │  128KB       │  64KB
#        rcv low-water  snd low-water (0 = default)

# For DB connections across regions (high BDP):
# - US-East → EU-West PostgreSQL: ~30ms RTT, 1Gbps → need ~4MB buffers
# - Same-AZ: ~0.5ms RTT → 64KB is plenty
🚨 Socket Error Codes — What They Mean & How to Fix

These are the errors you'll encounter daily. Memorize them — each tells a specific story about what went wrong.

ErrorOperationWhat It MeansFix
EADDRINUSEbind()Port is already bound by another process (or the same port is in TIME_WAIT from a previous instance without SO_REUSEADDR)ss -tlnp 'sport = :PORT' → find the PID → kill or change port
EADDRNOTAVAILconnect()No ephemeral ports available (all are in TIME_WAIT or the range is exhausted)Increase ip_local_port_range, tcp_tw_reuse=1, connection pooling
ECONNREFUSEDconnect()Port is NOT being listened on (no process bound). The remote kernel sent RSTCheck if the service is running: ss -tlnp | grep PORT
ECONNRESETread()/write()The remote side sent RST (crashed, firewall, or application closed socket without proper FIN)Check remote app logs, firewall rules, or tcpdump for RST packets
ETIMEDOUTconnect()SYN packets were sent but no SYN+ACK came back. Firewall dropping? Route missing?nc -zv HOST PORT → if also times out, check firewall/route
EPIPEwrite()Writing to a socket that the remote side already closed. SIGPIPE signal is also sentHandle SIGPIPE in your app. Check why remote side closed early
EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCKconnect()/read()Non-blocking socket — operation would block. Normal for async I/O (epoll, select)Retry when the socket becomes ready. This is expected, not an error
EMFILEsocket()/accept()Process has hit its file descriptor limit (ulimit -n). Cannot create more socketsIncrease ulimit -n, or fix fd leaks (close unused sockets)
ENFILEsocket()System-wide file descriptor limit reached (cat /proc/sys/fs/file-max)Increase fs.file-max sysctl, reduce fd usage system-wide
 
# QUICK DEBUG: What error does my connect() get?
$ strace -e trace=connect nc -zv 10.0.1.50 9999 2>&1 | tail -5
connect(3, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(9999), sin_addr=inet_addr("10.0.1.50")}, 16) = -1 ECONNREFUSED
# ↑ ECONNREFUSED = nothing listening on 10.0.1.50:9999

# CHECK FILE DESCRIPTOR USAGE:
$ cat /proc/$(pidof gunicorn)/limits | grep "open files"
Max open files  1024  4096  # Soft limit 1024, hard 4096
$ ls /proc/$(pidof gunicorn)/fd | wc -l  # Current fd count
1022  # Almost at limit! About to get EMFILE
⚙️ Essential Socket Options — What Every SRE Should Set (or At Least Understand)

Socket options control fundamental behavior — timeout, keep-alive, Nagle's algorithm, and graceful shutdown. The defaults are often wrong for modern workloads.

OptionLevelWhat It DoesWhen to Use
SO_KEEPALIVESOL_SOCKETSends probe packets after idle period. Detects dead peers (crashed, network partitioned) that never sent FIN. Default: 2hr idle, 9 probes at 75s intervals.Long-lived connections (DB pools, WebSocket, gRPC). Without it, dead connections hang forever until you try to write.
TCP_NODELAYIPPROTO_TCPDisables Nagle's algorithm. Data is sent IMMEDIATELY, not buffered waiting for ACKs. Nagle delays small sends to combine them — great for telnet, terrible for latency.ALWAYS for request-response (HTTP, gRPC, Redis). Without it, 40ms extra latency per request due to delayed ACK + Nagle deadlock.
SO_LINGERSOL_SOCKETControls close() behavior. l_onoff=0: default (close returns immediately, kernel sends remaining data). l_onoff=1, l_linger=0: send RST immediately (abortive close). l_onoff=1, l_linger>0: block close() up to N seconds.RST close: when you want to kill stale connections fast (load balancer health checks). Blocking close: when you MUST ensure data is sent.
TCP_KEEPIDLEIPPROTO_TCPSeconds of idleness before first keepalive probe (overrides system default). Linux-specific.Reduce from 7200s default to 60-300s for cloud workloads. Detects dead connections faster in K8s environments.
TCP_KEEPINTVLIPPROTO_TCPSeconds between keepalive probes.Default 75s is fine for most. Reduce to 10-30s for faster dead-peer detection.
TCP_KEEPCNTIPPROTO_TCPNumber of unacknowledged probes before declaring connection dead.Default 9 probes × 75s = 11+ minutes! Reduce to 3-5 for ~1 minute detection.
 
# CHECK SYSTEM-WIDE TCP KEEPALIVE DEFAULTS:
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time
net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time = 7200  # 2 HOURS! Way too long for cloud.
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_intvl
net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_intvl = 75   # 75 seconds between probes
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_probes
net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_probes = 9   # 9 failed probes → dead
# TOTAL: 7200 + (75×9) = ~132 minutes before dead peer detected!

# TUNE FOR CLOUD/K8s (detect dead peers in ~2 minutes):
$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time=120
$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_intvl=20
$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_probes=3
# Now: 120 + (20×3) = 180 seconds (~3 minutes)

# CHECK IF A SOCKET HAS KEEPALIVE ENABLED:
$ ss -tno | head -3
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local:Port  Peer:Port
ESTAB  0      0      10.0.1.5:54321  10.0.2.100:5432  timer:(keepalive, 1.952ms, 0)
#                                                      ↑ keepalive timer running!

# CHECK IF NAGLE IS DISABLED (TCP_NODELAY):
$ ss -tno | grep ESTAB
# Look for "nodelay" in timer output (not always visible in ss)
# Better: check the application code or strace
🔌 Unix Domain Sockets vs Network Sockets
FeatureNetwork Socket (AF_INET/AF_INET6)Unix Domain Socket (AF_UNIX)
AddressingIP:Port (e.g., 127.0.0.1:5432)Filesystem path (e.g., /var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432)
ReachabilityAny host on the networkSame host only (local IPC)
PerformanceFull TCP/IP stack overhead2-3× faster (no TCP/IP stack, no checksums)
SecurityFirewall rules, TLS neededFilesystem permissions (chmod, chown)
anihpj exampleApp → PostgreSQL via TCP/5432Nginx → gunicorn via /tmp/gunicorn.sock
 
# List Unix domain sockets:
$ ss -xlpn
Netid State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
u_str LISTEN 0      128    /var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432 0
u_str LISTEN 0      128    /tmp/gunicorn.sock 0
# Much faster than TCP for same-host communication!

10.3 Essential Socket Tools — ss, lsof, nc, /proc/net

📊 netstat vs ss — Why We Switched (and You Should Too)
Featurenetstat (Old)ss (Modern)
Data sourceReads /proc/net/tcp (slow, parses text)Reads from Netlink socket (kernel API, binary, fast)
Performance (10K sockets)~2-3 seconds (parses /proc line by line)~0.05 seconds (direct kernel query)
TCP internalsNot availableShow RTT, CWND, retransmits, pacing rate (ss -ti)
Socket memoryNot availableShow mem, rmem, wmem per socket (ss -tm)
Filteringgrep/awk manuallyBuilt-in: ss state established dst 10.0.1.50
StatusDeprecated (removed from some distros)Default, actively maintained (iproute2 package)
How to remembernetstat -tlnp (8 chars)ss -tlnp (7 chars, same flags!)

The flags are 100% compatible: Every netstat -tlnp becomes ss -tlnp. No retraining needed — just type ss instead of netstat. ss is part of the iproute2 package (same package as the ip command that replaced ifconfig).

# OLD HABIT (still works because of muscle memory):
$ netstat -tlnp | grep 8000
# SAME OUTPUT, 40× FASTER:
$ ss -tlnp 'sport = :8000'

# On a busy server with 50K connections, the difference is dramatic:
$ time netstat -tan > /dev/null   # ~3.2 seconds
$ time ss -tan > /dev/null        # ~0.08 seconds
� epoll & Non-Blocking I/O — How One Thread Handles 10,000 Connections

The classic C10K problem: how do you handle 10,000 concurrent connections without creating 10,000 threads? The answer is I/O multiplexing — letting the kernel tell you which sockets are ready, instead of you checking each one. Linux's solution is epoll (since 2.5.44, 2002).

select() vs poll() vs epoll() — The Evolution of I/O Multiplexing
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THE PROBLEM: You have 10,000 connected sockets. Which ones have     │
│  data ready to read? How do you efficiently find them?               │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ METHOD       │ HOW IT WORKS               │ SCALES TO           │ │
│  ├──────────────┼────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤ │
│  │ BLOCKING     │ One thread per connection  │ ~100 before threads │ │
│  │ (pre-2000)   │ read() blocks until data   │ become bottleneck   │ │
│  ├──────────────┼────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤ │
│  │ select()     │ Pass fd_set bitmap to      │ ~1024 (FD_SETSIZE   │ │
│  │ (1983, BSD)  │ kernel, kernel checks ALL  │ hard limit). O(n)   │ │
│  │              │ fds on every call. O(n).   │ scan every call.    │ │
│  ├──────────────┼────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤ │
│  │ poll()       │ Pass array of pollfd       │ No hard limit,      │ │
│  │ (1997, SVR4) │ structs. Still O(n) scan.  │ but still O(n) per  │ │
│  │              │ Better than select but     │ call. ~10K max in   │ │
│  │              │ still not scalable.        │ practice.           │ │
│  ├──────────────┼────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤ │
│  │ epoll()      │ REGISTER fds once. Kernel  │ MILLIONS. O(1) per  │ │
│  │ (2002, Linux)│ queues events to ready     │ ready fd. Only      │ │
│  │              │ list. Only returns READY   │ returns fds with    │ │
│  │              │ fds. O(1) per ready fd.    │ data. C10M solved!  │ │
│  └──────────────┴────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  HOW epoll WORKS (simplified):                                        │
│                                                                       │
│  ① epoll_create() → creates epoll instance (returns epfd)            │
│  ② epoll_ctl(epfd, ADD, sockfd, events) → register a socket          │
│     "Wake me up when sockfd has data to read"                        │
│  ③ epoll_wait(epfd, events, maxevents, timeout)                      │
│     Blocks until ANY registered socket has data.                     │
│     Returns ONLY the ready sockets (not all 10,000!).                │
│  ④ Process ready sockets, loop back to ③                             │
│                                                                       │
│  MENTAL MODEL: epoll is like a restaurant buzzer. Instead of          │
│  checking every table to see if food is ready (poll), you get a       │
│  buzzer that ONLY goes off when YOUR food is ready (epoll).           │
│                                                                       │
│  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│  WHY THIS MATTERS FOR PORTS & SOCKETS:                                │
│  ‣ Each epoll instance can watch thousands of sockets                 │
│  ‣ One thread + epoll can handle 10K+ connections (Node.js, nginx)   │
│  ‣ ss shows the socket, but epoll manages the waiting                │
│  ‣ When ss shows Recv-Q > 0, the app's epoll_wait() ISN'T returning │
│    fast enough — the app is the bottleneck, not the kernel           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# CHECK if a process is using epoll:
$ ls -la /proc/$(pidof nginx)/fd | grep eventpoll
lrwx------ 1 root root 64 Jun 21 10:00 12 -> anon_inode:[eventpoll]
#                                                  ↑ epoll instance!

# HOW MANY epoll instances does a process have?
$ ls /proc/$(pidof nginx)/fd -l | grep -c eventpoll
8  # 8 worker processes, each with its own epoll instance

# WHAT SOCKETS IS EPOLL WATCHING? (root required)
$ sudo ls -la /proc/$(pidof nginx)/fd | grep socket
lrwx------ 1 root root 64 Jun 21 10:00 6 -> socket:[876543]
lrwx------ 1 root root 64 Jun 21 10:00 7 -> socket:[876544]
# Each socket inode is registered with epoll

# THE KEY LANGUAGES/FRAMEWORKS USING EPOLL:
# Node.js:    libuv → epoll on Linux (the event loop)
# nginx:      Direct epoll (worker_connections = epoll events)
# Python:     asyncio → epoll (EventLoop uses selector)
# Go:         netpoller → epoll (goroutine scheduler uses it!)
# Rust:       tokio → epoll (async runtime)

🔧 nc (netcat) — The TCP/UDP Swiss Army Knife
# TEST IF A PORT IS OPEN (like a TCP ping):
$ nc -zv 10.0.1.50 22
Connection to 10.0.1.50 22 port [tcp/ssh] succeeded!
# -z = scan only (no data), -v = verbose

# TEST AN HTTP ENDPOINT MANUALLY:
$ echo -e "GET /health HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: anihpj\r\n\r\n" | nc 10.0.1.50 8000
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"status": "ok"}

# CREATE A QUICK LISTENER (useful for debugging!):
$ nc -l 9999  # Terminal 1: listens on port 9999
$ echo "hello" | nc localhost 9999  # Terminal 2: send data
# "hello" appears in Terminal 1!

# TRANSFER A FILE (quick and dirty):
# Receiver:  nc -l 9999 > received_file.tar.gz
# Sender:    nc 10.0.1.50 9999 < file.tar.gz

# UDP MODE:
$ nc -u -l 9999  # Listen on UDP/9999
$ echo "test" | nc -u localhost 9999  # Send UDP datagram
