📖 Reading dig Output — Every Section Explained
$ dig jobpost.anihpj.com

; <<>> DiG 9.18.18 <<>> jobpost.anihpj.com
;; HEADER SECTION — flags tell you if query succeeded
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 12345
;; flags: qr rd ra;  qr=query response, rd=recursion desired, ra=recursion available
;; status: NOERROR = success, NXDOMAIN = name doesn't exist, SERVFAIL = resolver error

;; QUESTION SECTION — what you asked
;jobpost.anihpj.com.          IN      A

;; ANSWER SECTION — the answer!
jobpost.anihpj.com.    300    IN      CNAME   k8s-alb-abc123.elb.amazonaws.com.
k8s-alb-abc123.elb.amazonaws.com. 60 IN A     34.120.45.67
;;                       ↑TTL    ↑class  ↑type  ↑value

;; Query time: 12 msec — HOW LONG it took (watch this in production!)
;; SERVER: 10.96.0.10#53 — WHICH resolver answered
;; WHEN: Mon Jun 21 10:30:00 UTC 2026
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 112
� 🔧 nslookup vs dig vs host — Which DNS Tool When?
Featuredignslookuphost
Best forDetailed debugging, production troubleshootingQuick interactive lookups, teachingUltra-simple one-liners
Output detailComplete: HEADER, QUESTION, ANSWER, AUTHORITY, ADDITIONAL, statsDefault: Server + Address + Name. Interactive mode for more.Minimal: "name has address IP"
ScriptingExcellent: +short, +noall +answer, predictable outputPoor: inconsistent output format across versionsDecent: host -t A anihpj.com
Record typesAll: A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS, SOA, CNAME, PTR, SRV, CAA, ANYCommon: A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS, SOA, CNAME, PTRCommon: -t flag for any type
+trace support✅ dig +trace (shows every delegation)❌ Not supported❌ Not supported
Query specific serverdig @8.8.8.8 anihpj.comnslookup anihpj.com 8.8.8.8host anihpj.com 8.8.8.8
Status✅ Actively maintained (ISC BIND)⚠️ "Deprecated" per man page, but still ubiquitous✅ ISC BIND toolkit (same as dig)
SRE recommendation✅ USE THIS. It's the standard.❌ Avoid for scripts. Use dig.⚠️ Quick checks only.
 
# SAME QUERY, THREE TOOLS:
$ dig +short anihpj.com A           # 34.120.45.67 (clean, reliable)
$ host -t A anihpj.com              # anihpj.com has address 34.120.45.67
$ nslookup anihpj.com               # Server: 10.96.0.10\nAddress:...\nName: anihpj.com\nAddress: 34.120.45.67

# SRE RULE: Always use dig in scripts. nslookup output varies by version.
# dig +short gives you exactly the IP — nothing else. Parseable.
�🔐 Modern Encrypted DNS — DoH, DoT & Why You Should Care

Traditional DNS (UDP/53) is completely unencrypted — anyone on the network can see every domain you resolve. Two modern standards fix this:

FeatureDNS over TLS (DoT)DNS over HTTPS (DoH)
Port853 (dedicated)443 (same as HTTPS)
ProtocolDNS over TLS (RFC 7858)DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484)
Detectable?Yes — port 853 traffic is identifiableNo — looks identical to regular HTTPS. Cannot be blocked without blocking all HTTPS.
Use caseSystem-level resolver (stubby, systemd-resolved)Browser-level (Firefox, Chrome), apps
Providers1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare), 8.8.8.8 (Google), 9.9.9.9 (Quad9)Same providers, different endpoint URLs
dig supportdig +tls @1.1.1.1 anihpj.comdig +https @1.1.1.1 anihpj.com (dig 9.18+)
CoreDNS supporttls plugin (forward to DoT upstream)Not natively supported (use forward to DoH proxy)
 
# CONFIGURE systemd-resolved FOR DoT (modern Linux):
$ cat /etc/systemd/resolved.conf
[Resolve]
DNS=1.1.1.1#cloudflare-dns.com
DNSOverTLS=yes
# Now all DNS queries from this host are encrypted!

# VERIFY DoT works:
$ dig +tls @1.1.1.1 anihpj.com
# Look for ";; Connection to 1.1.1.1#853(1.1.1.1) via TLS"
📏 The UDP 512-Byte Limit & EDNS0 — Why DNS Sometimes Uses TCP

Traditional DNS over UDP has a 512-byte payload limit. If a response exceeds 512 bytes, the server sets the TC (Truncated) flag, and the client MUST retry over TCP. EDNS0 (RFC 6891) extends this to 4096+ bytes, eliminating most TCP fallbacks.

# SEE IF A RESPONSE WAS TRUNCATED (TC flag):
$ dig +noall +comments anihpj.com TXT
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 4, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1
# If "tc" appears in flags → response was TRUNCATED → retry with +tcp

# FORCE TCP (bypass UDP 512-byte limit):
$ dig +tcp anihpj.com ANY

# CHECK EDNS0 SUPPORT (UDP buffer size advertised):
$ dig +noall +comments anihpj.com
;; OPT PSEUDOSECTION:
; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 1232
# ↑ "udp: 1232" = this resolver supports up to 1232-byte UDP responses
# Modern EDNS0 default: 1232 bytes (fits in most MTUs without fragmentation)

# WHEN TCP FALLBACK MATTERS IN PRODUCTION:
# • DNSSEC responses are LARGE (signatures add 100s of bytes)
# • ANY queries almost always exceed 512 bytes
# • TXT records with SPF + DKIM + DMARC can be huge
# • Firewall rules MUST allow TCP/53 for full DNS functionality
🔢 DNS Response Codes (RCODEs) — What Every dig Status Means
RCODEdig StatusMeaningWhat to Do
0NOERRORQuery succeeded. Answer may be empty (name exists but no records of requested type).Check ANSWER section. Empty answer with NOERROR means the name exists but has no matching records.
1FORMERRDNS query was malformed — the server couldn't parse it.Rare. Usually a bug in the DNS client library.
2SERVFAILServer failed to process query. Authoritative NS unreachable, DNSSEC validation failed, or upstream timeout.In K8s: CoreDNS forward plugin upstream unreachable. Check CoreDNS logs.
3NXDOMAINName definitively does NOT exist. The authoritative server confirmed it.Check for typos. Verify the domain/zone actually exists. dig +trace to see where it fails.
4NOTIMPServer doesn't support the requested operation.Rare. Usually when querying a server that doesn't support certain record types.
5REFUSEDServer refuses to answer. Often: recursion not allowed, or ACL blocks the client IP.Check if the server allows recursive queries. Check ACLs/firewall at the resolver.
6YXDOMAINName exists when it shouldn't (used in dynamic DNS updates).Very rare. Only seen in DDNS update scenarios.
7YXRRSETRecord set exists when it shouldn't (DDNS).Very rare. DDNS-related.
8NXRRSETRecord set doesn't exist (DDNS).Very rare. DDNS-related.
9NOTAUTHServer is not authoritative for the zone.You queried a server that doesn't host this zone.
10NOTZONEName not in zone (DDNS).Very rare. DDNS-related.

11.7 DNS Resolution Under the Microscope — resolv.conf & ndots

/etc/resolv.conf is the file that controls ALL DNS resolution on a Linux system. Understanding every field — especially ndots — is critical for debugging why DNS behaves the way it does.

DNS RESOLUTION WITH NDOTS — The Hidden Performance Killer
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Default Kubernetes /etc/resolv.conf in a pod:                        │
│                                                                       │
│  nameserver 10.96.0.10                                                │
│  search anihpj.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local      │
│  options ndots:5                                                      │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  THE NDOTS RULE:                                                │ │
│  │  If a name has FEWER dots than ndots → APPEND search domains    │ │
│  │  If a name has ndots OR MORE dots → try the name AS-IS first    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  SCENARIO 1: Pod resolves "jobpost-service" (0 dots)                  │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                        │
│  0 dots < ndots:5 → append search domains:                            │
│  Query 1: jobpost-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local → ✅ SUCCESS!      │
│  But glibc also tries (if first fails):                               │
│  Query 2: jobpost-service.svc.cluster.local                           │
│  Query 3: jobpost-service.cluster.local                               │
│  RESULT: 3 queries when only 1 was needed                             │
│                                                                       │
│  SCENARIO 2: Pod resolves "github.com" (1 dot)                        │
│  ───────────────────────────────────────────                          │
│  1 dot < ndots:5 → append search domains FIRST:                       │
│  Query 1: github.com.anihpj.svc.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN 😤          │
│  Query 2: github.com.svc.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN 😤                 │
│  Query 3: github.com.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN 😤                     │
│  Query 4: github.com → ✅ SUCCESS! (finally!)                         │
│  RESULT: 4 DNS queries when 1 should have worked!                     │
│                                                                       │
│  FIX:                                                                 │
│  • ndots:1 → only append search for 0-dot names (like "redis")       │
│  • ndots:2 → treat "github.com" as-is, append for "redis" only       │
│  • Use FQDN: "github.com." (trailing dot = absolute, no search)      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ The ndots:5 Problem — It Amplifies DNS Query Volume 5×

Kubernetes defaults to ndots:5. This means any name with fewer than 5 dots gets ALL search domains appended. For an app that mostly calls external APIs (stripe.com, sendgrid.com, s3.amazonaws.com), every single external DNS lookup generates 3-4 wasted queries before resolving. On a busy pod making 100 DNS queries/second, that's 400 queries/second hitting CoreDNS — 75% of which are NXDOMAIN. Fix: set ndots:1 in pod spec dnsConfig for external-heavy workloads, or use FQDNs (trailing dot).

# FIX IN POD SPEC:
spec:
  dnsConfig:
    options:
    - name: ndots
      value: "1"  # Only try search domains for 0-dot names

# OR use FQDN in your application code:
# Instead of:  http.Post("https://api.stripe.com/...")
# Use:         http.Post("https://api.stripe.com./...")  ← trailing dot!
⚙️ resolv.conf Options Deep Dive — timeout, attempts, rotate

The options line in /etc/resolv.conf controls HOW the resolver behaves — not just ndots. These options directly affect DNS reliability and performance:

OptionDefaultWhat It DoesProduction Tuning
timeout:N5 (seconds)How long to wait for a response from a nameserver before trying the next one. 5 seconds is an ETERNITY for a modern app.timeout:1 or timeout:2. Fail fast, retry faster.
attempts:N2 (per nameserver)How many times to retry each nameserver before giving up. Total queries = nameservers × attempts.attempts:2 is fine for most. Increase to 3 for unreliable networks.
rotateOff (always try nameserver 1 first)Round-robin through nameservers instead of always trying the first one. Prevents "hot" nameserver.Enable if you have multiple resolvers. Distributes load evenly.
ndots:N1 (Linux), 5 (K8s pods)Dots threshold for search domain appending. See full explanation above.ndots:1 for external-heavy, ndots:2 for mixed
single-requestOff (send A + AAAA in parallel)Send A and AAAA queries separately instead of in parallel. Avoids issues with broken DNS servers.Enable if you see "unexpected RCODE" errors in DNS logs.
single-request-reopenOffUse a new socket for each query (not recommended for performance)Only for debugging. Don't use in production.
 
# PRODUCTION resolv.conf FOR A BUSY API POD:
nameserver 10.96.0.10  # CoreDNS (internal cluster DNS)
nameserver 1.1.1.1     # Cloudflare (backup external)
search anihpj.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local
options ndots:1 timeout:2 attempts:2 rotate

# TOTAL WORST-CASE: 2 nameservers × 2 attempts × 2s timeout = 8 seconds
# Default worst-case: 1 nameserver × 2 attempts × 5s timeout = 10 seconds
# With rotate: balances queries between CoreDNS and Cloudflare

11.8 Split-Horizon DNS & DNS Views

Split-horizon DNS (also called split-view or split-brain DNS) returns different answers for the same query depending on WHO is asking. Internal clients get private IPs; external clients get public IPs. This is how jobpost.anihpj.com resolves to an internal ALB for pods but a public ALB for internet users.

Internal DNS vs External DNS — Same Query, Different Answers
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  INTERNAL QUERY (from inside VPC / K8s cluster):                      │
│                                                                       │
│  dig jobpost.anihpj.com → 10.0.1.50 (internal ALB, private subnet)   │
│                                                                       │
│  EXTERNAL QUERY (from the internet):                                  │
│                                                                       │
│  dig jobpost.anihpj.com → 34.120.45.67 (public ALB, internet-facing) │
│                                                                       │
│  HOW AWS ROUTE53 PRIVATE HOSTED ZONES DO THIS:                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Route53 Private Hosted Zone: anihpj.internal                 │    │
│  │  jobpost.anihpj.internal.  300  IN  A  10.0.1.50            │    │
│  │  (Only resolvable from within the VPC)                       │    │
│  │                                                              │    │
│  │  Route53 Public Hosted Zone: anihpj.com                      │    │
│  │  jobpost.anihpj.com.  300  IN  A  34.120.45.67              │    │
│  │  (Resolvable from anywhere on the internet)                  │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                       │
│  K8s SPLIT-HORIZON with CoreDNS:                                      │
│  ‣ CoreDNS kubernetes plugin handles cluster.local internally         │
│  ‣ All other queries forwarded to upstream (VPC resolver or public)   │
│  ‣ VPC resolver (.2 in each AWS subnet) handles Route53 private zones│
│  ‣ Result: pod resolves jobpost.anihpj.com → VPC resolver → internal  │
│    ALB IP if jobpost is in a Route53 private hosted zone              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

11.9 Common DNS Issues Everyone Faces

"It's always DNS" is a meme for a reason. DNS failures are silent — your app doesn't crash, it just can't reach anything. Here are the most common DNS issues, how to recognize them, and how to fix them.

🐞 The Classic DNS Issues — Recognition & Fix
SymptomRoot CauseFix
App works for some users but not othersDNS propagation delay — different resolvers have different cached answers. Old TTL not yet expired.Reduce TTL to 60s BEFORE migration. Wait 2× old TTL after change. Check with dig @multiple-resolvers.
Migration complete but old IP still being hitNegative caching or stale positive cache. Some resolvers cache NXDOMAIN. Java caches DNS forever by default.Check Java security properties (networkaddress.cache.ttl). Flush resolver caches. Reduce TTL before migration.
NXDOMAIN for a name that existsWrong nameserver, typo in domain, or the domain's NS records point to deleted Route53 zone.dig +trace to see WHERE it fails. Check NS records at parent zone. Verify zone exists.
SERVFAIL from resolverResolver can't reach authoritative NS, or DNSSEC validation failed (bad signatures).Check authoritative NS are reachable. Check DNSSEC chain with dig +dnssec +trace.
Pod resolves internal services but not externalCoreDNS forward plugin pointing to broken upstream. kubernetes plugin works, forward fails.Check CoreDNS logs. Test: dig @10.96.0.10 github.com. Fix forward plugin upstream servers.
DNS works but VERY slow (2-5 second delays)ndots:5 causing cascade of NXDOMAIN queries. Or upstream resolver is slow.Set ndots:1. Check dig query time. Change upstream to faster resolver (1.1.1.1).
🔐 DNSSEC Basics — When DNS Answers Are Cryptographically Signed

DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records, proving they haven't been tampered with. It prevents DNS cache poisoning attacks (where an attacker injects fake DNS answers). Without DNSSEC, there's no way to verify that the A record you received is genuine. With DNSSEC, every record is signed by the zone's private key, and resolvers verify the signature chain from root → TLD → domain. The chain of trust: root's DS record → TLD's DS record → your domain's DNSKEY → RRSIG on each record. Check with: dig +dnssec +multi jobpost.anihpj.com — look for the "ad" (authenticated data) flag.

11.10 LAB: DNS Hands-On

🛠️ DNS Lab — 6 Hands-On Exercises
1
Read dig Output Line by Line 
$ dig anihpj.com A
# Read every section: HEADER, QUESTION, ANSWER, Stats
# What's the TTL? Which resolver answered? How fast?
$ dig +noall +answer anihpj.com A  # Just the answer
$ dig +short anihpj.com A          # Just the IP
2
Trace Full Resolution Path 
$ dig +trace anihpj.com
# Watch: root → .com TLD → Route53 NS → A record
# Count the queries. Which took longest?
# Bonus: dig +trace jobpost.anihpj.com vs www.google.com
3
Reverse DNS Lookup 
$ dig -x 8.8.8.8
# What hostname does 8.8.8.8 resolve to?
$ dig -x 1.1.1.1
# Why do reverse lookups use in-addr.arpa?
4
Inside a K8s Pod — Test Service Discovery 
$ kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- sh
/ # nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
/ # cat /etc/resolv.conf
/ # nslookup github.com  # External resolution works?
5
Observe ndots Search Domain Behavior 
$ kubectl run netshoot --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
bash-5.1# dig +search kubernetes
# See how "kubernetes" gets search domains appended!
bash-5.1# dig +search github.com
# See how github.com.anihpj.svc.cluster.local is tried first!
6
Break DNS and Fix It 
# 1. Edit CoreDNS ConfigMap to add a broken forward:
$ kubectl edit configmap coredns -n kube-system
# Change forward . /etc/resolv.conf to forward . 10.255.255.255
# 2. Wait for CoreDNS to reload (or delete pods to force restart)
# 3. Test: external DNS now FAILS (SERVFAIL)
# 4. Fix it back: restore original forward config
# 5. Verify: DNS works again
# LESSON: DNS is fragile. Change carefully. Always have rollback.
🎯 SRE Incident Pattern — "It's Always DNS" Is a Meme for a Reason

DNS is the #1 cause of obscure production outages. As an SRE:

  • DNS failures are SILENT. Your app doesn't crash — it just can't reach anything. Symptoms: timeouts, partial outages, "works for me but not for users." DNS is always suspect #1.
  • DNS caching hides problems. A bad record with TTL 300 means the problem persists for 5 minutes AFTER you fix it. Reduce TTL BEFORE any DNS change.
  • CoreDNS is a SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE for your entire cluster. Run ≥2 replicas with podAntiAffinity. Monitor query latency and error rate.
  • The ndots:5 problem silently amplifies DNS query volume 5×. Tune it per workload — ndots:1 for external-heavy apps.
  • SRE rule: In ANY incident, check DNS first. It takes 5 seconds with dig and eliminates the #1 cause of obscure failures.

🔭 Chapter 11 — Visual Summary

🌳Hierarchical Tree

Root (13 clusters) → TLD (.com, .org) → Domain (anihpj.com) → Subdomain (jobpost). Each level delegates to the next.

🔄Recursive Query

Your resolver walks the entire tree for you. You get one answer. Caching at every level speeds up subsequent queries.

📋10 Record Types

A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SOA, PTR, SRV, CAA. CNAME cannot exist at zone apex. SRV includes port numbers.

☸️CoreDNS

K8s DNS server. Service format: name.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Corefile ConfigMap controls all behavior.

🔍dig = DNS Debugger

dig +trace (full path), dig +short (quick answer), dig -x (reverse), dig @server (specific resolver).

⚠️ndots:5 Problem

K8s default silently causes 3-4 wasted queries per external lookup. Fix: ndots:1 or use FQDNs with trailing dot.

🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work
  • Every incident starts with DNS. Before checking logs, before checking metrics, before restarting anything: dig +short the-service-thats-down.internal. 30% of outages are DNS-related.
  • DNS changes require planning. Reduce TTL to 60s at least 1× old TTL before any migration. Never change DNS and IP at the same time — you can't tell which broke.
  • CoreDNS is your cluster's spinal cord. Monitor it. Run ≥2 replicas. Know how to read its Corefile. When CoreDNS is down, nothing works.
  • ndots tuning is free performance. Check your app's DNS patterns. If >80% of queries are external, set ndots:1 and save 4× DNS query volume.

🔑 Chapter 11 Key Takeaways

  1. DNS is a hierarchical, distributed, cached database. Root → TLD → Authoritative. Each level delegates. Caching at every layer means changes take TTL seconds to propagate.
  2. dig +trace shows you the entire resolution path. This is your #1 DNS debugging tool. If something is wrong, trace it — you'll see exactly which query fails.
  3. Kubernetes DNS: service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. CoreDNS handles internal resolution via the kubernetes plugin and forwards external queries via the forward plugin.
  4. ndots:5 is the hidden DNS performance killer in K8s. Every external name with <5 dots triggers wasted search domain queries. Tune to ndots:1 for external-heavy apps.
  5. "Check DNS first" is the #1 SRE incident response rule. It takes 5 seconds and eliminates the most common cause of obscure failures.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 11

🏛️Recursive Resolver
The DNS server that does all the work for you. Walks the tree from root → TLD → authoritative. Caches answers. Examples: 8.8.8.8 (Google), 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare), 10.96.0.10 (CoreDNS in K8s).
📜Authoritative Nameserver
The single source of truth for a domain's DNS records. Only this server can answer with authority (AA flag). Managed by the domain owner. For anihpj.com: Route53 hosted zone NS records.
⏱️TTL (Time To Live)
How long a DNS answer can be cached (in seconds). Low TTL (60s) = fast propagation but more queries. High TTL (86400) = fewer queries but slow changes. Reduce TTL BEFORE any DNS migration.
#️⃣ndots
Controls when search domains are appended to DNS queries. ndots:5 (K8s default) causes 4 wasted queries per external lookup. ndots:1 fixes this for external-heavy workloads.
🔀Split-Horizon DNS
Returns different DNS answers based on who's asking. Internal clients get private IPs; external get public IPs. AWS Route53 Private Hosted Zones + VPC resolver implement this automatically.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 11.1 — Trace the Resolution Path

Run dig +trace github.com. How many queries were made? What is the TLD for .com? What are github.com's authoritative nameservers? What's the final A record TTL?

💡 Hint: Count the sections in dig +trace output. Each section with NS records is a delegation point.
📝 View Solution
# 3 query steps:
# 1. Root (.) → returns .com TLD NS (a.gtld-servers.net, etc.)
# 2. .com TLD → returns github.com NS (ns1.p16.dynect.net, etc.)
# 3. github.com authoritative → returns A record with TTL
# TTL is typically 60 seconds (GitHub uses low TTL for flexibility)
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 11.2 — Debug a DNS Failure

A pod in namespace "anihpj" can't resolve "redis-service". You run kubectl exec pod -- nslookup redis-service and get "server can't find redis-service: NXDOMAIN". What are the 3 most likely causes? How do you check each?

💡 Hint: Check: (1) Does the service exist? (2) Is the pod in the right namespace? (3) Are CoreDNS pods running?
📝 View Solution
# 1. Does the service exist in the anihpj namespace?
$ kubectl get svc redis-service -n anihpj
# If "not found" → service doesn't exist or wrong namespace

# 2. Try FQDN to rule out namespace mismatch:
$ kubectl exec pod -n anihpj -- nslookup redis-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local

# 3. Check CoreDNS:
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
# If not Running → DNS is broken cluster-wide
⏱️ Target: 2 minutes
Drill 11.3 — ndots in Action

Your pod has ndots:5. It resolves "api.stripe.com". Using the search domains [anihpj.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local], list EVERY DNS query the pod will make, in order. How many are wasted?

💡 Hint: "api.stripe.com" has 2 dots. Since 2 < ndots:5, search domains are tried FIRST.
📝 View Solution
# 2 dots < ndots:5 → append search domains first:
# Query 1: api.stripe.com.anihpj.svc.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN (wasted)
# Query 2: api.stripe.com.svc.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN (wasted)
# Query 3: api.stripe.com.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN (wasted)
# Query 4: api.stripe.com → SUCCESS!
# 3 out of 4 queries are WASTED (75% waste rate!)
# Fix: ndots:2 → 2 dots >= 2, so try api.stripe.com FIRST → 1 query.

📝 Chapter 11 — Practice Questions

Q1
Walk through the complete DNS resolution for jobpost.anihpj.com starting from a cold cache. What queries are made and in what order?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Query root servers (.) → "Who handles .com?" → returns .com TLD nameservers (a.gtld-servers.net, etc.) 2. Query .com TLD → "Who handles anihpj.com?" → returns Route53 nameservers (ns-1234.awsdns-56.org, etc.) 3. Query anihpj.com authoritative NS → "What's jobpost.anihpj.com?" → returns CNAME to ALB + ALB's A record (34.120.45.67). Total: 3 queries from cold cache.

Explanation

The resolver walks the DNS tree from root → TLD → authoritative. Each level only knows about the level below — this delegation is what makes DNS scale to billions of domains. With caching, subsequent queries for api.anihpj.com skip steps 1 and 2.

Q2
What's the difference between a recursive and an iterative DNS query? Which does your laptop make to 8.8.8.8?
Show Answer
Answer

Recursive query: "Give me the final answer. Do whatever you need to do." Your laptop → 8.8.8.8 is recursive. Iterative query: "Here's what I know, go ask someone else." 8.8.8.8 → root/TLD/authoritative are iterative. The resolver does the hard work; you just get the answer.

Explanation

The "RD" (Recursion Desired) flag in the DNS header indicates you want the resolver to do recursive resolution. Most public resolvers support it. CoreDNS in K8s also does recursive resolution for cluster.local via the kubernetes plugin.

Q3
Why can't you create a CNAME record at the zone apex (anihpj.com)? What's the workaround?
Show Answer
Answer

A CNAME at the apex would conflict with mandatory SOA and NS records. RFC 1034 prohibits it. Workarounds: Route53 ALIAS record (AWS-specific, resolves at apex, free), Cloudflare CNAME flattening/ANAME, or simply use an A record with a script to update it when the target IP changes.

Explanation

The zone apex (root domain) MUST have SOA and NS records. A CNAME cannot coexist with other record types for the same name. ALIAS/ANAME records are proprietary solutions that behave like CNAMEs but are implemented as the DNS provider dynamically resolving the target and returning A/AAAA records.

Q4
A pod in namespace "anihpj" can resolve "redis.anihpj.svc.cluster.local" but not "redis" (short name). What's the likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer

The pod's /etc/resolv.conf is missing the search domain "anihpj.svc.cluster.local". Without it, short names like "redis" don't get the namespace suffix appended. Check with kubectl exec pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf — the "search" line should list the namespace's search domains. Could be caused by custom dnsPolicy or dnsConfig in the pod spec.

Explanation

Short name resolution relies on search domains. "redis" → resolver appends ".anihpj.svc.cluster.local" → "redis.anihpj.svc.cluster.local" → CoreDNS resolves it. Without search domains, "redis" is treated as a top-level name and fails.

Q5
Explain the ndots:5 problem. How many DNS queries does a pod make to resolve "api.github.com" with default K8s DNS config?
Show Answer
Answer

"api.github.com" has 2 dots. Since 2 < ndots:5, search domains are appended FIRST: (1) api.github.com.anihpj.svc.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN, (2) api.github.com.svc.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN, (3) api.github.com.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN, (4) api.github.com → SUCCESS. 4 queries total, 3 wasted (75% waste). Fix: ndots:1 or ndots:2.

Explanation

ndots:5 was designed for environments where most lookups are internal (many dots in service FQDNs). In cloud-native apps where most calls are external, it's counterproductive. Modern recommendation: ndots:1 for external-heavy apps, ndots:2 for mixed workloads.

Q6
CoreDNS pods are CrashLoopBackOff. What's the impact on the cluster, and how do you debug?
Show Answer
Answer

Impact: NO pod in the cluster can resolve anything — internal services OR external domains. This is a total cluster outage for any app that uses DNS (which is all of them). Debug: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50. Common causes: Corefile syntax error (check ConfigMap), node out of resources, or anti-affinity violation (all CoreDNS pods on same failed node).

Explanation

CoreDNS is the single DNS entry point for all pods. The kubelet configures every pod's /etc/resolv.conf to point to the kube-dns Service (10.96.0.10). If no CoreDNS pods are running, that Service has no endpoints, and all DNS queries timeout.

Q7
How would you use dig to check if a specific DNS resolver (8.8.8.8) returns a different answer than your default resolver for anihpj.com?
Show Answer
Answer

dig @8.8.8.8 anihpj.com A queries 8.8.8.8 specifically. dig anihpj.com A uses the default resolver from /etc/resolv.conf. Compare the ANSWER SECTION from both queries. If they differ, you have a split-horizon or caching issue. Also: dig @8.8.8.8 anihpj.com A +short for quick IP comparison.

Explanation

The @ symbol in dig specifies which DNS server to query, overriding /etc/resolv.conf. This is essential for testing split-horizon setups, checking propagation, and verifying that different resolvers see the same records.

Q8
You migrated anihpj.com to a new IP. Some users still hit the old IP 10 minutes later. Why? How do you prevent this?
Show Answer
Answer

DNS caching. If the old A record had TTL=3600 (1 hour), resolvers that queried just before the change cache the old IP for 1 hour. Some resolvers ignore TTL. Java applications cache DNS forever by default. Prevention: reduce TTL to 60-300 seconds at least 1× old TTL before migration. Verify with dig @multiple-resolvers after change.

Explanation

DNS propagation is NOT instant. The TTL is a suggestion — some resolvers enforce minimum TTLs, some ignore them entirely. Corporate networks often have internal caching resolvers with their own policies. Always reduce TTL well in advance of any DNS change.

Q9
What's the difference between NXDOMAIN and SERVFAIL in dig output? What does each tell you about the DNS failure?
Show Answer
Answer

NXDOMAIN: The name definitively does NOT exist. The authoritative nameserver said "I am authoritative for this zone, and this name is not in it." SERVFAIL: The resolver tried to resolve but encountered an error — it could not reach the authoritative NS, or DNSSEC validation failed, or the query timed out. SERVFAIL means "something is broken," NXDOMAIN means "this name doesn't exist."

Explanation

NXDOMAIN is a legitimate answer — the domain doesn't exist. SERVFAIL is an error condition — the DNS infrastructure couldn't complete the query. In K8s, SERVFAIL from CoreDNS often means the forward plugin's upstream is unreachable.

Q10
How do you add a custom stub domain so that queries for "consul.internal" go to a specific DNS server (10.0.5.10) while all other queries use the default forward path?
Show Answer
Answer

Edit the CoreDNS ConfigMap and add a stub domain block: consul.internal:53 { forward . 10.0.5.10 { max_concurrent 100 } cache 30 errors }. This must go BEFORE the default "." block (or CoreDNS matches the specific block first). CoreDNS auto-reloads the ConfigMap. Verify: kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup service.consul.internal.

Explanation

CoreDNS matches queries against the most specific zone first. A block for "consul.internal:53" takes priority over ".:53" for queries ending in consul.internal. This is how you integrate external DNS systems (Consul, Active Directory, custom resolvers) with Kubernetes DNS.

Chapter 12: HTTP — The Language of the Web

HTTP is the most successful application protocol in history. Every web page, every API call, every mobile app backend request speaks HTTP. It's deceptively simple — a text-based request/response protocol — yet its evolution from HTTP/0.9 through HTTP/3 represents decades of engineering to squeeze every millisecond of performance from the internet. Understanding HTTP means understanding how modern applications actually communicate. This chapter teaches you HTTP from the wire up.

🟡 INTERMEDIATE ⏱️ ~2 hours 🌐 HTTP 🔧 curl

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:

  • Understand HTTP's evolution from 0.9 through HTTP/3 and why each version exists
  • Read and write HTTP requests and responses at the wire level (methods, headers, status codes)
  • Explain HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, pipelining, and Head-of-Line blocking
  • Master HTTP/2 binary framing, multiplexing, and HPACK compression
  • Understand HTTP/3's QUIC foundation and why it eliminates TCP HOL blocking
  • Use curl as your HTTP Swiss Army knife for debugging and testing
🔗 Applies To:
DevOps
SRE
Backend Dev
Cloud Eng
SysAdmin
Weight: Every API, every web app, every microservice call is HTTP. Debugging starts with curl -v.
🎯 SRE Interview Tip

You WILL be asked to explain the difference between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3. Key points: HTTP/1.1 uses 6 parallel TCP connections with text headers (HOL blocking per connection). HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over ONE TCP connection with binary framing (still has TCP-level HOL blocking). HTTP/3 runs over QUIC/UDP, eliminating HOL blocking entirely with per-stream independence and 0-RTT handshakes. Also know: HTTP/2 Server Push (deprecated in Chrome), HPACK vs QPACK compression, and that most K8s ingress controllers default to HTTP/2 with TLS.

12.1 HTTP From First Principles

HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a request/response protocol at Layer 7. A client sends a text request; a server sends a text response. That's it. The elegance of HTTP is that it's stateless — each request is independent — and extensible via headers. Over 30+ years, it evolved from a one-line protocol to a binary multiplexed powerhouse.

📜 HTTP Version Evolution — What Changed and Why
VersionYearKey Innovation
HTTP/0.91991One-line: GET /page → HTML back. No headers, no status codes, no version.
HTTP/1.01996Headers! Content-Type, status codes, version number. One request per connection.
HTTP/1.11997Keep-alive (reuse connections), Host header (virtual hosting), chunked encoding, pipelining
HTTP/22015Binary framing, multiplexing (multiple streams per connection), HPACK header compression, server push
HTTP/32022Runs over QUIC (UDP), 0-RTT handshake, per-stream flow control, no TCP HOL blocking, connection migration
📖 The 3 Pillars of HTTP — What Makes It Universal

1. Stateless: Each request is independent. The server doesn't remember previous requests. This makes HTTP simple to scale — any server can handle any request. State is maintained via cookies, tokens, and session IDs in headers.
2. Text-based (HTTP/1.x): Requests and responses are human-readable text. You can telnet to port 80 and type an HTTP request by hand.
3. Extensible via Headers: New capabilities are added through headers — caching (Cache-Control), authentication (Authorization), compression (Accept-Encoding), CORS, security policies. The core protocol hasn't changed since 1997; headers evolve it.

🛡️ SRE Reality Check — HTTP Status Codes Are Your First Clue

When an incident strikes, the HTTP status code distribution tells you where to look before you read a single log line:

  • Spike in 502: The proxy (nginx/ALB) can't reach the backend. Backend crashes, pod restarts, or network partition.
  • Spike in 504: The backend is too slow. Check database query times, upstream timeouts, thread pool exhaustion.
  • Spike in 503: Service intentionally unavailable — circuit breaker open, rate limiter triggered, or maintenance mode.
  • Spike in 499: Clients are disconnecting before the server responds. Your backend is so slow users are giving up.
  • Spike in 429: Rate limiting is working. Either an attacker, a buggy client in a retry loop, or legitimate traffic exceeding your limits.

Pro tip: Set up a Grafana dashboard showing status code distribution (2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx) over time. A sudden shift from mostly-2xx to mostly-5xx is your first signal that something is wrong — often before users report it.

12.2 The HTTP Request — Anatomy of a GET

Every HTTP request has three parts: the request line (method + path + version), headers (metadata), and an optional body (POST/PUT data).

ANNOTATED HTTP REQUEST — Every Line Explained
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  REQUEST LINE                                                         │
│  GET /api/jobs/?location=Lagos HTTP/1.1                               │
│  │   │          │              │                                       │
│  │   │          │              └── HTTP version                        │
│  │   │          └── Path + query string                               │
│  │   └── Method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, HEAD, OPTIONS)        │
│                                                                       │
│  REQUEST HEADERS (metadata about the request)                         │
│  Host: jobpost.anihpj.com           ← WHICH website (virtual hosting) │
│  User-Agent: curl/8.4.0             ← WHAT client is making the call  │
│  Accept: application/json           ← WHAT format the client wants     │
│  Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...  ← WHO is making the call (JWT)    │
│  Content-Type: application/json     ← WHAT format the body is in      │
│  Cookie: session_id=abc123          ← Session identifier              │
│  Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate     ← Client supports compression     │
│  Connection: keep-alive             ← Keep TCP connection open        │
│                                                                       │
│  EMPTY LINE (CRLF) — separates headers from body                      │
│                                                                       │
│  REQUEST BODY (for POST/PUT/PATCH only — empty for GET)               │
│  {"title": "DevOps Engineer", "location": "Lagos"}                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔤 HTTP Methods — The Verbs of the Web
MethodPurposeHas Body?Idempotent?anihpj Example
GETRetrieve a resource❌ No✅ YesGET /api/jobs/?location=Lagos
POSTCreate a new resource✅ Yes❌ NoPOST /api/jobs/ with JSON body
PUTReplace a resource entirely✅ Yes✅ YesPUT /api/jobs/42/ full replacement
PATCHPartially update a resource✅ Yes❌ NoPATCH /api/jobs/42/ update title only
DELETERemove a resource❌ No✅ YesDELETE /api/jobs/42/
HEADGet headers only (no body)❌ No✅ YesHEAD /api/health/ — check if alive
OPTIONSWhat methods does the server support?❌ No✅ YesCORS preflight: OPTIONS /api/jobs/

12.3 The HTTP Response — Anatomy of a 200 OK

ANNOTATED HTTP RESPONSE — Every Line Explained
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STATUS LINE                                                          │
│  HTTP/1.1 200 OK                                                      │
│  │        │   │                                                        │
│  │        │   └── Reason phrase (human-readable)                       │
│  │        └── Status code (200 = success)                              │
│  └── HTTP version                                                      │
│                                                                       │
│  RESPONSE HEADERS                                                      │
│  Content-Type: application/json     ← WHAT format the response body is │
│  Content-Length: 2347              ← HOW big the response body is     │
│  Set-Cookie: session=xyz; HttpOnly ← SET a cookie in the browser      │
│  Cache-Control: max-age=3600       ← HOW LONG to cache (1 hour)       │
│  Server: nginx/1.25                ← WHAT server software responded   │
│  Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *    ← WHO can call this API (CORS)     │
│                                                                       │
│  EMPTY LINE (CRLF)                                                      │
│                                                                       │
│  RESPONSE BODY (the actual content)                                    │
│  {"jobs": [{"id": 42, "title": "DevOps Engineer", ...}], "count": 237}│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
HTTP STATUS CODES — Categorized Visualization
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1xx INFORMATIONAL         2xx SUCCESS         3xx REDIRECTION        │
│  ┌──────┐                   ┌──────┐            ┌──────┐              │
│  │ 100  │ Continue          │ 200  │ OK         │ 301  │ Moved Perm   │
│  │ 101  │ Switching Proto   │ 201  │ Created    │ 302  │ Found        │

⚠️ GOTCHA — CORS Is Enforced by the BROWSER, Not the Server

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) errors happen when a browser blocks a cross-origin request. The server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers, but the BROWSER enforces them. curl, Postman, and backend-to-backend calls completely bypass CORS. If you get a CORS error in curl, the problem is something else (usually TLS, authentication, or the server returning a different error masked as CORS).

🛡️ Security Headers — What Every Production API Should Have
HeaderPurposeExample Value
Strict-Transport-SecurityHSTS: force browsers to use HTTPS only, never HTTPmax-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
X-Content-Type-OptionsPrevent MIME-type sniffing (browser guessing content type)nosniff
X-Frame-OptionsPrevent clickjacking (your page embedded in an iframe)DENY or SAMEORIGIN
Content-Security-PolicyCSP: limit which resources can be loaded (scripts, images, fonts)default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'
Access-Control-Allow-OriginCORS: which domains can call this API from a browserhttps://jobpost.anihpj.com (not * in production!)
 
# CHECK SECURITY HEADERS ON ANY SITE:
$ curl -I https://anihpj.com 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'strict-transport|content-security|x-frame|x-content|access-control'
strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
x-content-type-options: nosniff
x-frame-options: DENY
# These headers protect your users from common web attacks

12.5 HTTP/1.1 — The Workhorse

HTTP/1.1 (1997) introduced keep-alive (reuse TCP connections), the Host header (enabling virtual hosting), and chunked transfer encoding. It's still the most widely deployed version — nearly every API, every web server, every curl command defaults to HTTP/1.1. But it has fundamental performance limits that HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 were designed to solve.

Before HTTP/1.1, every single HTTP request required a brand new TCP connection. Request index.html → TCP handshake → request → response → TCP close. Request style.css → TCP handshake → request → response → TCP close. A page with 50 resources required 50 TCP connections — 50 handshakes, 50 slow starts, 50 TLS negotiations (if HTTPS). Keep-alive changed everything: one TCP connection could handle multiple requests sequentially, amortizing the handshake cost across an entire page load. This single optimization made the modern web possible — without keep-alive, HTTPS would be unbearably slow for any page with more than a handful of resources.

The Host header was equally revolutionary. Before it, one IP address could only serve one website — because the server had no way to know which site the client wanted. The Host header (Host: jobpost.anihpj.com) tells the server which website to serve, enabling virtual hosting — thousands of websites sharing a single IP address. Every shared hosting provider, every cloud load balancer, and every Kubernetes Ingress relies on the Host header to route requests to the correct backend. It's such a fundamental part of HTTP that HTTP/2 made it a pseudo-header (:authority) because every request needs it.

But HTTP/1.1's design has a fundamental flaw that became apparent as web pages grew more complex: requests on a single connection are serial. You send request 1, wait for response 1, then send request 2. If request 1 is for a slow API endpoint or a large database query, every resource behind it waits — images, CSS, JavaScript, fonts — all blocked by one slow request. Browsers worked around this by opening 6 parallel TCP connections per origin, but this is a hack: 6× TCP handshakes, 6× TLS negotiations, 6× congestion control windows, 6× kernel buffers. Each connection discovers bandwidth independently — they don't share congestion information. On a 2% packet loss connection, all 6 connections compete, causing unnecessary retransmissions and underutilizing available bandwidth.

HTTP/1.1 — Six Parallel Connections, Serial Per Connection
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     HTTP/1.1 CONNECTION MODEL                              │
│                                                                           │
│  BROWSER ──────── 6 TCP CONNECTIONS ────────► WEB SERVER                  │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ CONN 1: [GET index.html ════════════▶] [◀═══════════ response]      │ │
│  │ CONN 2: [GET style.css  ═══▶]          [◀══════ response]           │ │
│  │ CONN 3: [GET app.js     ═══════════▶]  [◀══════════════ response]   │ │
│  │ CONN 4: [GET logo.png   ══▶]           [◀══ response]               │ │
│  │ CONN 5: [GET font.woff  ═══════▶]      [◀═══════ response]          │ │
│  │ CONN 6: [GET api/data   ═══════════════════════▶]  [◀══ response]   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  WITHIN EACH CONNECTION — requests are SERIAL (HOL blocking!):           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ CONN 1: [Req1 ═══════▶][◀══ R1][Req2 ═══▶][◀══ R2][Req3══▶][◀═ R3]│ │
│  │          Req2 MUST wait for Req1 to finish. Req3 waits for Req2.    │ │
│  │          A slow resource on Conn 1 blocks ALL resources on Conn 1.  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  WASTE PER CONNECTION:                                                    │
│  ‣ TCP 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) × 6 = 18 packets              │
│  ‣ TLS handshake (if HTTPS) × 6 = expensive!                             │
│  ‣ TCP buffers × 6 = memory overhead                                     │
│  ‣ Slow start × 6 = bandwidth discovery repeated 6 times                 │
│                                                                           │
│  HTTP/2 FIX: One TCP connection, all resources multiplexed.              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔌 HTTP/1.1 Key Features & Limitations

The table below captures HTTP/1.1's design tradeoffs. Each feature solved a critical problem in 1997 but created limitations that became apparent as the web scaled. Keep-alive reduced connection overhead but serialized requests. The 6-connection limit added parallelism but multiplied resource waste. Chunked encoding enabled streaming but added parsing complexity. Understanding these tradeoffs is the key to understanding why HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 exist — each "limitation" column below is the problem the next HTTP version was designed to solve.

FeatureHow It WorksLimitation
Keep-AliveTCP connection stays open for multiple requests (Connection: keep-alive). Huge improvement over HTTP/1.0.Requests are still serial — one at a time per connection.
6-Connection LimitBrowsers open up to 6 parallel TCP connections per origin to load resources in parallel.Wastes resources. 6 TCP connections × TLS handshakes × buffer memory.
Head-of-Line BlockingRequest 1 must complete before Request 2 can start on the same connection. A slow resource blocks everything behind it.This is HTTP/1.1's fatal flaw. Fixed by multiplexing in HTTP/2.
Header OverheadHeaders are plain text, repeated on every request (Cookie, User-Agent, Accept — same bytes every time).Can be 500-800 bytes of headers per request. HPACK in HTTP/2 fixes this.
Chunked EncodingSend data without knowing Content-Length in advance. Each chunk has its own size prefix.Useful for streaming. Still serial per connection.
📦 Chunked Transfer Encoding — How Streaming Works in HTTP/1.1

When a server doesn't know the response size ahead of time (live data, large file generation, streaming), it uses Transfer-Encoding: chunked instead of Content-Length. The response body is sent in sized chunks — each chunk prefixed with its hex size, terminated by a zero-size chunk.

# ANATOMY OF A CHUNKED RESPONSE:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Transfer-Encoding: chunked       # ← Instead of Content-Length

1A\r\n                           # Chunk 1: 0x1A = 26 bytes
{"status": "processing"...}\r\n   # The 26 bytes of data
14\r\n                           # Chunk 2: 0x14 = 20 bytes
{"progress": "50%"...}\r\n       # The 20 bytes of data
0\r\n                            # Final chunk: size 0 = END OF BODY
\r\n                             # Trailer (optional headers after body)

# SEE CHUNKED ENCODING IN ACTION:
$ curl -v http://example.com/stream --raw
# Look for "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" in response headers
🗄️ HTTP Caching Deep Dive — Cache-Control Directives You Must Know

HTTP caching is controlled by headers, not by the protocol itself. The Cache-Control header has powerful directives that control every aspect of caching behavior:

DirectiveMeaningWhen to Use
max-age=3600Cache this response for 3600 seconds (1 hour)Static assets (CSS, JS, images)
no-cacheMUST revalidate with server before using cached copy (but CAN cache!)API responses that change (but can use ETag)
no-storeMUST NOT store ANY copy (not even in memory)Banking data, PII, sensitive information
publicCan be cached by any cache (CDN, browser, proxy)Public API responses, static assets
privateOnly browser can cache (not CDN/proxy)User-specific data, authenticated responses
must-revalidateMUST check with origin before using stale cached copyData that becomes dangerous if stale
immutableContent will NEVER change (no revalidation needed)Versioned assets (style.v2.css)
 
# ETag + If-None-Match = Smart Caching:
# Server sends: ETag: "abc123" with response
# Client sends: If-None-Match: "abc123" on next request
# If unchanged → server returns 304 Not Modified (no body, saves bandwidth!)
# If changed → server returns 200 OK with new ETag and full body
🔄 HTTP Pipelining vs Multiplexing — Why Pipelining Failed

HTTP/1.1 introduced pipelining — sending multiple requests on one connection without waiting for responses. In theory, this eliminates the serial request problem. In practice, it was a disaster:

FeatureHTTP/1.1 PipeliningHTTP/2 Multiplexing
How it worksSend requests 1,2,3 on same connection. Responses MUST come back in order (1,2,3).Send streams 1,3,5 on same connection. Responses can come in ANY order (interleaved frames).
HOL Blocking❌ SEVERE: Response 1 delays responses 2,3. One slow response blocks ALL behind it.✅ Streams are independent — stream 5 can complete before stream 1.
Adoption❌ Basically abandoned. Browsers disabled it. Too many broken proxy implementations.✅ Widely deployed. 50%+ of web traffic.
Why it failedMiddleboxes (proxies, load balancers) assumed one-request-per-connection. They broke pipelining. No way to detect broken intermediaries.Binary framing + TLS means middleboxes can't interfere with stream multiplexing.

12.6 HTTP/2 — Binary Framing & Multiplexing

HTTP/2 (2015, standardized as RFC 7540) is not an evolution of HTTP/1.1 — it's a complete redesign of the wire protocol while preserving HTTP's semantics. The methods (GET, POST), status codes (200, 404), and headers are the same — but how they're encoded on the wire is completely different. HTTP/1.1 is a text protocol: you can read it with your eyes. HTTP/2 is a binary protocol: the same information is encoded in compact binary frames. This fundamental shift enables everything that makes HTTP/2 fast.

Why binary? Because parsing text is slow and ambiguous. HTTP/1.1 headers have no fixed length — the parser must scan for \r\n\r\n to find the end. Header names are case-insensitive (Content-Type vs content-type), values can be folded across multiple lines, and there are dozens of edge cases that parsers must handle. A binary frame has a fixed 9-byte header with explicit length, type, and flags — the parser knows exactly how many bytes to read. This makes HTTP/2 faster to parse, harder to implement incorrectly, and more compact on the wire.

The killer feature of HTTP/2 is multiplexing: multiple concurrent streams over a single TCP connection. Each stream has a unique identifier (1, 3, 5, 7... — odd numbers for client-initiated streams). The client sends HEADERS and DATA frames for multiple streams, interleaved on the wire. The server processes them concurrently and sends responses interleaved as well. A browser loading a page with 50 resources opens one TCP connection (not six) and requests all 50 resources simultaneously. The server pushes frames for all 50 streams over that single connection. This eliminates the 6-connection hack, amortizes TCP slow start across all resources, and dramatically reduces connection overhead.

But there's a catch — and it's the reason HTTP/3 exists. HTTP/2 still runs over TCP, and TCP guarantees in-order delivery. If a TCP packet carrying data for stream 3 is lost, TCP must retransmit it before delivering any subsequent packets — even if those packets carry data for streams 1, 5, and 7, which are completely independent. This is TCP-level head-of-line blocking, and it's worse than HTTP/1.1's HOL blocking because it affects ALL streams, not just one connection's request queue. On a connection with 0.1% packet loss, HTTP/2 can be slower than HTTP/1.1 because one lost packet blocks everything, while HTTP/1.1's 6 connections isolate the damage to one connection. This counterintuitive result is why Google developed QUIC and why HTTP/3 exists.

HTTP/2 MULTIPLEXING — How Streams Share One Connection
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     SINGLE TCP CONNECTION                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │ STREAM 1: GET /index.html  [HEADERS] [DATA]                  │    │
│  │ STREAM 3: GET /style.css   [HEADERS]        [DATA]           │    │
│  │ STREAM 5: GET /app.js      [HEADERS]              [DATA]     │    │
│  │ STREAM 7: POST /api/login  [HEADERS] [DATA]                  │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                       │
│  All streams multiplexed over ONE TCP connection — no 6-conn limit!  │
│  Frame order: H1 H3 D1 H5 H7 D5 D3 D7 (interleaved!)                  │
│                                                                       │
│  HTTP/2 KEY FEATURES:                                                 │
│  ‣ Binary framing (not text!) — frames instead of lines               │
│  ‣ Streams: multiple concurrent requests over ONE TCP connection      │
│  ‣ HPACK compression: headers compressed with static+dynamic tables   │
│  ‣ Server Push: server sends resources before client asks (deprecated)│
│  ‣ Stream prioritization: client tells server what's important first  │
│  ‣ STILL HAS TCP HOL BLOCKING: one lost packet blocks ALL streams!    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📦 HTTP/2 Frame Types — The Binary Building Blocks

HTTP/2 communication happens through binary frames — each frame has a 9-byte header (length, type, flags, stream ID). There are 10 frame types:

Frame TypeCodePurpose
DATA0x0Request/response body data. Can be split across multiple frames.
HEADERS0x1HTTP headers (compressed with HPACK). Opens a new stream.
PRIORITY0x2Stream priority and dependency (which stream depends on which).
RST_STREAM0x3Abruptly terminate a stream (e.g., client cancels request).
SETTINGS0x4Connection-level parameters (max concurrent streams, window size).
PUSH_PROMISE0x5Server Push: "I'm about to send you style.css before you ask." (Deprecated)
PING0x6Keep-alive and RTT measurement. Must be responded to with highest priority.
GOAWAY0x7Graceful shutdown: "Stop creating new streams, finish existing ones."
WINDOW_UPDATE0x8Flow control: "I have more buffer space, send more data."
CONTINUATION0x9Continuation of a HEADERS/PUSH_PROMISE that didn't fit in one frame.
🗜️ HPACK Compression — How HTTP/2 Shrinks Headers

HTTP/1.1 headers are plain text repeated on every request (Cookie, User-Agent, Accept — same 500+ bytes every time). HPACK compresses headers using two tables:

# STATIC TABLE (61 predefined header fields — never changes):
# Index 1:  :authority       Index 2:  :method GET
# Index 3:  :method POST     Index 8:  :status 200
# Index 32: cookie           Index 51: content-type

# DYNAMIC TABLE (grows during connection — caches actual values):
# After first request:  :authority: jobpost.anihpj.com → index 62
# After first request:  cookie: session=abc123 → index 63
# Next request just sends: index 62, index 63 (just 2 bytes each!)

# REAL COMPRESSION RATIO (typical API):
# First request:  ~500 bytes of headers
# Second request: ~50 bytes of headers (90% compression!)
# Third+ request: ~20 bytes of headers (96% compression!)

12.7 HTTP/3 — QUIC & the Future

HTTP/3 is the only version that truly fixes Head-of-Line blocking. By running over QUIC (UDP) instead of TCP, each stream is fully independent — a lost packet on stream 3 only delays stream 3, not streams 1, 2, and 4. This is the culmination of 30 years of HTTP evolution, and it's being adopted rapidly by every major platform.

HTTP/3 QUIC — Per-Stream Independence, No More HOL Blocking
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     HTTP/3 — QUIC OVER UDP                                 │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │                    SINGLE QUIC CONNECTION (UDP)                       │ │
│  │                                                                       │ │
│  │  STREAM 1: [HDR][DATA══════════════▶]  ◀══ LOST PACKET ON STREAM 3  │ │
│  │  STREAM 2: [HDR][DATA══════▶][DATA══▶]  ← Stream 2 UNAFFECTED!      │ │
│  │  STREAM 3: [HDR][DATA══▶][█ LOST █]     ← Only Stream 3 waits       │ │
│  │  STREAM 4: [HDR][DATA══════════▶][DATA▶] ← Stream 4 UNAFFECTED!      │ │
│  │                                                                       │ │
│  │  Each stream: OWN flow control, OWN ordering, OWN retransmission.    │ │
│  │  Lost packet on Stream 3 → retransmitted → others flow freely.       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  TCP (HTTP/2) vs QUIC (HTTP/3):                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  TCP:  Packet 5 lost → stalls ALL data after packet 5.              │ │
│  │         Packets 6,7,8 (for streams 2,3,4) are HELD HOSTAGE.         │ │
│  │         Must wait for packet 5 retransmission before ANY delivery.   │ │
│  │                                                                       │ │
│  │  QUIC: Packet 5 (stream 3) lost → only stream 3 data is delayed.    │ │
│  │         Packets 6 (stream 2), 7 (stream 4), 8 (stream 1) delivered. │ │
│  │         Stream 3 retransmits independently. Others flow freely.      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  ADDITIONAL HTTP/3 BENEFITS:                                              │
│  ‣ 0-RTT Handshake: Reconnect without handshake (cached keys)            │
│  ‣ Connection Migration: Switch Wi-Fi→cellular without dropping          │
│  ‣ Built-in TLS 1.3: Everything encrypted, always                        │
│  ‣ QPACK: Header compression without HOL blocking (unlike HPACK)         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚡ HTTP Version Performance Comparison
FeatureHTTP/1.1HTTP/2HTTP/3anihpj use
TransportTCP (6 conns)TCP (1 conn)QUIC (UDP)K8s Ingress
Multiplex6 conn limitStreams (1)Streams (1)TLS+HTTP/2
HOL BlockPer-connPer-TCP-connPer-streamdefault
HandshakeTCP+TLS (2-3RTT)TCP+TLS(1.5)QUIC (0-1RTT)
Header CompNoneHPACKQPACKReduces
AdoptionUniversal~50% web~30% growingbandwidth
🚀 HTTP/3 Key Innovations

0-RTT Handshake: Skip the entire handshake on reconnect — send data immediately using cached keys. Connection Migration: Switch from Wi-Fi to cellular without dropping connections (QUIC connection IDs, not IP:port tuples). No TCP HOL: Each stream is independent — lost packet on stream 3 doesn't block streams 1, 2, 4. Built-in TLS 1.3: QUIC encrypts everything by default — no cleartext mode. Where it's used: Google, Facebook, Cloudflare, YouTube. In K8s: Ingress controllers are adding QUIC support.
