12.9 LAB: HTTP in Slow Motion

🛠️ HTTP Lab — 5 Hands-On Exercises
1
Examine Every Line of a Real HTTP Request
$ curl -v http://jobpost.anihpj.com/api/jobs/
# Read every > (request) and < (response) line
# Find: request line, Host header, status line, Content-Type
2
Measure Timing Breakdown
$ curl -w "DNS:%{time_namelookup}s TCP:%{time_connect}s TLS:%{time_appconnect}s TTFB:%{time_starttransfer}s Total:%{time_total}s\n" -o /dev/null -s https://anihpj.com
# Which phase takes longest? DNS? TCP? TLS? TTFB?
3
Capture HTTP with tcpdump
$ sudo tcpdump -i any -A port 80 -s 0
# In another terminal: curl http://example.com
# See the raw HTTP request and response in ASCII!
4
Test Different Status Codes
$ curl -v http://jobpost.anihpj.com/api/jobs/       # 200 OK
$ curl -v http://jobpost.anihpj.com/api/jobs/99999  # 404 Not Found
$ curl -v -X POST http://jobpost.anihpj.com/api/jobs/ # 400 or 401
5
Compare HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2
$ curl --http1.1 -v https://jobpost.anihpj.com -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep "ALPN"
$ curl --http2 -v https://jobpost.anihpj.com -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep "ALPN"
# ALPN: h2 = HTTP/2, http/1.1 = HTTP/1.1

🔭 Chapter 12 — Visual Summary

📜HTTP/0.9→HTTP/3

30 years of evolution. From one-line GET to binary multiplexed QUIC. Each version fixes the previous one's bottleneck.

📤Request = Method+Path+Headers+Body

GET/POST/PUT/DELETE. Headers carry auth, format, cookies. Body carries JSON.

📥Response = Status+Headers+Body

2xx=success, 3xx=redirect, 4xx=your fault, 5xx=server's fault. Status codes tell the story.

🔌HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive

Reuse connections. 6-connection limit. HOL blocking per connection. Headers are repeated text.

🚀HTTP/2 Multiplexing

Binary frames. Multiple streams over ONE TCP connection. HPACK compression. Still TCP HOL blocking.

⚡HTTP/3 QUIC

Runs over UDP. Per-stream independence. 0-RTT handshake. Connection migration. No HOL blocking.

🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work
  • Every API debug starts with curl -v. See the full request/response. Check status codes. Read headers. This is your first debugging tool for any HTTP issue.
  • HTTP/2 is the default for modern infrastructure. K8s ingress, AWS ALB, Cloudflare — all negotiate HTTP/2 by default with TLS. Understand the binary framing model.
  • Status codes tell the story. 502 Bad Gateway = upstream is down. 504 Gateway Timeout = upstream is slow. 503 = service unavailable. Know what each means instantly.
  • curl timing breakdown saves hours. DNS slow? TCP slow? TLS slow? TTFB slow? curl -w isolates each phase so you know exactly where the bottleneck is.

🔑 Chapter 12 Key Takeaways

  1. HTTP is a stateless, text-based request/response protocol at L7. Request line + headers + body → status line + headers + body. Extensible via headers.
  2. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses connections but has serial HOL blocking. 6-connection limit per origin. Headers repeated on every request.
  3. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over ONE TCP connection with binary framing. HPACK compresses headers. Still has TCP-level HOL blocking.
  4. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC/UDP, eliminating TCP HOL blocking. Per-stream independence, 0-RTT, connection migration. The future of HTTP.
  5. curl -v is your HTTP debugger. curl -w for timing breakdown. curl --resolve to bypass DNS. curl -k for TLS testing (dev only).

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 12

📤HTTP Request
Request line (method + path + version), headers (metadata), empty line, optional body. Methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS.
📥HTTP Response
Status line (version + status code + reason), headers, empty line, body. Status codes grouped: 1xx info, 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
🔀Keep-Alive
HTTP/1.1 feature that reuses TCP connections for multiple requests. Reduces TCP handshake overhead. Limited by 6 connections per origin and serial request ordering.
📦Multiplexing
HTTP/2 feature: multiple concurrent streams over ONE TCP connection using binary frames. Eliminates the 6-connection limit. Still has TCP-level head-of-line blocking.
⚡QUIC
HTTP/3's transport: runs over UDP, built-in TLS 1.3, per-stream flow control, 0-RTT handshake, connection migration. Fixes TCP HOL blocking once and for all.
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 12.1 — HTTP Status Code Diagnosis

For each scenario, identify the HTTP status code and the most likely root cause:

  1. User submits a job posting form. The POST request spins for 30 seconds then shows "504 Gateway Timeout" in DevTools.
  2. After deploying a new version, the health check returns HTTP 503. Pods show Running but Ready: 0/1.
  3. User uploaded a 50MB resume. The server returned 201 Created but the file is only 14MB on disk.
  4. Curl to https://api.anihpj.com returns 502 Bad Gateway. The nginx error log shows "connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream."
  5. A security scan reports /admin/ returns 200 OK without authentication on the public internet. What status code SHOULD it return?
💡 Hint: 5xx = server-side. 502 = proxy can't reach upstream. 504 = upstream timed out. 503 = intentionally unavailable. The client_max_body_size directive is the culprit for truncated uploads.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. 504 Gateway Timeout on POST:
# Backend didn't respond within nginx's proxy_read_timeout.
# Check: gunicorn worker timed out processing the form submission.
# Possible: slow database write, external API call hangs, missing DB index.
# Fix: increase timeout OR optimize the slow operation.

# 2. 503 with Running but not Ready:
# Readiness probe failing. App can't serve traffic yet.
# kubectl describe pod → "Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503"
# Common causes: DB migration pending, Redis unreachable, config not mounted.

# 3. 201 Created but truncated (14MB vs 50MB):
# nginx's client_max_body_size is ~15MB. It truncated the upload.
# Django received partial content, saved it, returned 201 — never knew.
# Fix: client_max_body_size 100M; in nginx config.
# Also check: client_body_timeout (default 60s — 50MB upload may time out).

# 4. 502 + "Connection refused" in nginx error log:
# nginx can reach the IP but gunicorn is NOT listening on port 8000.
# Check: ss -tlnp | grep 8000 on the gunicorn host.
# If gunicorn crashed: dmesg | grep -i oom (OOM killer?).
# If bound to 127.0.0.1:8000: only localhost — fix bind to 0.0.0.0.

# 5. /admin/ returns 200 without auth → should return 401 or 403!
# Authentication middleware not applied to /admin/ path.
# This is a CRITICAL security finding. Fix immediately.
# Expected: 401 Unauthorized (not logged in) or 403 Forbidden (logged in but not admin).
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 12.2 — curl Timing Breakdown

Match each curl timing phase to its most likely root cause:

  1. time_namelookup: 2.5s (everything else < 50ms)
  2. time_connect: 3.0s (everything else < 50ms)
  3. time_appconnect: 2.0s (everything else < 50ms)
  4. time_starttransfer: 3.0s (connect + TLS < 50ms)
  5. All individual times < 50ms but time_total: 3.0s
💡 Hint: DNS = namelookup. TCP handshake = connect. TLS = appconnect. Backend processing = starttransfer. Multiple redirects = total exceeds sum.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. DNS is slow — resolver timeout or unreachable DNS server.
# Fix: dig @1.1.1.1 api.anihpj.com, check /etc/resolv.conf

# 2. TCP handshake slow — SYN being dropped (firewall?), packet loss.
# Fix: tcpdump for SYN retransmissions, check firewall rules.

# 3. TLS handshake slow — OCSP stapling, CRL check, or server CPU overload.
# Fix: openssl s_client -connect to see timing, check server CPU.

# 4. Backend processing slow (TTFB = Time To First Byte).
# Fix: check DB slow queries, app profiling, external API timeouts.

# 5. Multiple redirects inflating total time. Each 302 = full request cycle.
# Fix: curl -v to see redirect chain. Flatten redirects where possible.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 12.3 — HTTP Version Deep Dive

Answer without looking at notes:

  1. Why does HTTP/1.1 open 6 TCP connections per origin? What problem does this solve and what problem does it create?
  2. Does HTTP/2 completely solve HOL blocking? Explain.
  3. Why does HTTP/3 use UDP instead of TCP? What's the ONE thing TCP does that makes it unsuitable for multiplexed streams?
  4. On a lossy mobile network (2% packet loss) loading a page with 50 resources, rank HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 from fastest to slowest. Why?
💡 Hint: TCP guarantees in-order delivery. This is great for a single stream, terrible for multiplexed streams. QUIC (UDP) decouples stream ordering from transport ordering.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. 6 connections = workaround for serial request limitation.
# Solves: parallelism (6 resources load simultaneously).
# Creates: 6× TCP+TLS handshakes, 6× buffers, 6× slow start.

# 2. PARTIALLY. HTTP/2 fixes application-level HOL blocking
# (streams multiplex on one connection).
# BUT: TCP-level HOL blocking remains — one lost segment stalls ALL streams.
# This is why HTTP/3 was created — to fix the TCP-level problem.

# 3. TCP's IN-ORDER DELIVERY GUARANTEE is the problem.
# TCP must deliver segment N before N+1, even if they belong to
# different streams. QUIC delivers per-stream independently.
# Lost data on stream 3 doesn't block streams 1, 2, 4.

# 4. Ranking on 2% loss network with 50 resources:
# FASTEST: HTTP/3 — per-stream independence. Loss isolates to one stream.
# MIDDLE: HTTP/2 — one lost packet blocks ALL 50 resources.
# SLOWEST: HTTP/1.1 — 50 resources competing for 6 connections = queuing.

📝 Chapter 12 — Practice Questions

Q1
What are the three components of an HTTP request? Give an example.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Request line: GET /api/jobs/?location=Lagos HTTP/1.1 (method, path, version). 2. Headers: Host, User-Agent, Accept, Authorization, Content-Type. 3. Optional body: JSON/XML/form data (for POST/PUT/PATCH). Example: POST /api/jobs/ HTTP/1.1\nHost: jobpost.anihpj.com\nContent-Type: application/json\n\n{"title":"DevOps"}

Explanation

The empty line (CRLF) separates headers from body. GET requests typically have no body. The Content-Type header tells the server how to parse the body.

Q2
Explain HTTP status code ranges. What does each range mean?
Show Answer
Answer

1xx Informational (100 Continue), 2xx Success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 3xx Redirection (301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified), 4xx Client Error (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests), 5xx Server Error (500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout).

Explanation

4xx = client's fault (bad request, missing auth). 5xx = server's fault (crash, timeout, upstream down). This distinction is critical for incident response — 5xx means check backend, 4xx means check the request.

Q3
What is HTTP keep-alive and why is it important?
Show Answer
Answer

Keep-alive (Connection: keep-alive) allows multiple HTTP requests to reuse the same TCP connection, avoiding the overhead of a new TCP 3-way handshake for each request. Without it (HTTP/1.0), every request opens a new connection. This dramatically reduces latency and server resource usage.

Explanation

TCP handshake = 1 RTT. TLS handshake = 1-2 RTTs. Without keep-alive, every image, CSS, and JS file on a page would incur this overhead. Keep-alive amortizes the handshake cost across many requests.

Q4
What is Head-of-Line (HOL) blocking in HTTP/1.1? How does HTTP/2 solve it?
Show Answer
Answer

In HTTP/1.1, requests on a single TCP connection are serial — request 2 cannot start until request 1 completes. A slow resource (large image, slow API) blocks everything behind it. HTTP/2 solves this with multiplexing: multiple streams share one connection using binary frames. Stream 2 can deliver frames while stream 1 is still in progress.

Explanation

HTTP/1.1 browsers work around HOL by opening 6 parallel connections. HTTP/2 needs only one. However, HTTP/2 still has TCP-level HOL blocking — if a TCP packet is lost, ALL streams on that connection stall until retransmission.

Q5
What is the key difference between HTTP/2 and HTTP/3? Why was HTTP/3 created?
Show Answer
Answer

HTTP/2 runs over TCP and still suffers from TCP-level HOL blocking — one lost packet stalls ALL streams. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP) with per-stream independence — a lost packet on stream 3 only affects stream 3. HTTP/3 also offers 0-RTT handshakes and connection migration (switch networks without dropping).

Explanation

TCP's in-order delivery guarantee is the root cause. If packet #5 of stream 1 is lost, TCP must retransmit it before delivering packets #6-10 — even if those packets belong to streams 2, 3, and 4. QUIC decouples streams from transport ordering.

Q6
How would you measure DNS lookup time, TCP connect time, TLS handshake time, and TTFB separately using curl?
Show Answer
Answer

curl -w "DNS: %{time_namelookup}s\nTCP: %{time_connect}s\nTLS: %{time_appconnect}s\nTTFB: %{time_starttransfer}s\nTotal: %{time_total}s\n" -o /dev/null -s https://anihpj.com. time_namelookup = DNS resolution time. time_connect = TCP 3-way handshake. time_appconnect = TLS handshake. time_starttransfer = time to first byte (TTFB).

Explanation

This timing breakdown is essential for performance debugging. If DNS is 200ms, fix DNS. If TLS is 500ms, check cipher negotiation. If TTFB is 3 seconds, the backend is slow. Each number points to a different root cause.

Q7
What does a 502 Bad Gateway error mean? What should you check first?
Show Answer
Answer

502 means the proxy/gateway (nginx, ALB, Envoy) received an invalid response from the upstream server. The upstream may be down, returning malformed responses, or the connection was reset. Check: is the upstream process running? Can you curl the upstream directly (bypass the proxy)? Check upstream logs for errors or crashes.

Explanation

502 is the proxy saying "I tried to talk to the backend, but it gave me garbage or nothing." It's almost always a backend issue — the proxy itself is working fine. In K8s: check if the pods behind the Service are Ready and passing health checks.

Q8
How do you force curl to use HTTP/2? How do you verify it worked?
Show Answer
Answer

curl --http2 -v https://anihpj.com. Look for ALPN: h2 in the verbose output — this confirms HTTP/2 was negotiated. You'll also see < HTTP/2 200 in the response. Without --http2, curl may negotiate HTTP/1.1 if the server supports both.

Explanation

ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) happens during the TLS handshake. The client sends a list of supported protocols (h2, http/1.1), and the server picks one. This is how HTTP/2 upgrade happens transparently — no separate port, no redirect.

Q9
Explain the CORS mechanism. Why does curl bypass CORS but browsers don't?
Show Answer
Answer

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is enforced by BROWSERS, not servers. When a web page on domain-a.com tries to call api.domain-b.com, the browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request. The server responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. If the origin doesn't match, the browser blocks the request. curl, Postman, and backend code don't enforce CORS — they're not browsers.

Explanation

CORS is a browser security feature to prevent malicious websites from calling your APIs using the user's cookies. Server-to-server communication doesn't have this risk, so CORS doesn't apply. If curl gets a CORS error, the actual error is something else (usually a 4xx/5xx that the browser misreports as CORS).

Q10
How would you debug a slow API endpoint? List the curl commands and what each reveals.
Show Answer
Answer

1. curl -w timing_breakdown → isolate DNS/TCP/TLS/TTFB phases. 2. curl -v → see full request/response headers, check for unexpected redirects. 3. curl --resolve host:port:IP → bypass DNS and hit a specific backend to isolate DNS/load balancer issues. 4. curl -H "Host: ..." http://pod-ip:8000/ → bypass ingress and hit the pod directly. 5. Compare TTFB across multiple requests — consistent slowness = backend, variable = network/load balancer.

Explanation

Systematic debugging: eliminate variables one at a time. Bypass DNS (--resolve). Bypass load balancer (direct to pod IP). Bypass TLS (use HTTP internally). Whatever's left is the actual problem.

Chapter 13: TLS & SSL — Encryption, Certificates & Trust

TLS is everywhere. Every HTTPS website, every git clone, every kubectl command, every Docker pull — all depend on TLS to encrypt and authenticate. If you run production systems and don't understand TLS, you're debugging blind. This chapter demystifies the handshake, the certificates, the cipher suites, and the trust chain that makes the 🔒 padlock possible. You'll understand exactly what happens between "ClientHello" and "200 OK."

Here's why TLS matters more than ever: certificate expiry is the #1 cause of "it was working yesterday" production outages. Let's Encrypt certificates expire every 90 days. If your auto-renewal fails (and it will, eventually — rate limits, DNS issues, misconfigured cert-manager), your site goes down with NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID. Users see a scary full-page warning. Most click away. Your monitoring might not catch it until customers report it. This chapter teaches you not just how TLS works, but how to operate it reliably in production.

🔴 ADVANCED ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🔒 TLS 📜 Certificates

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:

  • Understand SSL vs TLS history and why SSL is dead but the name stuck
  • Explain symmetric vs asymmetric encryption and how TLS uses BOTH (hybrid encryption)
  • Walk through the TLS 1.3 handshake step by step, knowing exactly what each message does
  • Decode cipher suite strings like TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  • Diagnose every common TLS error (expired cert, hostname mismatch, untrusted CA) in seconds
  • Use openssl s_client to debug TLS connections and check certificate expiry from the command line
  • Understand certificate chains, SANs, and why mTLS is the foundation of zero-trust networking
🔗 Applies To:
DevOps
SRE
Security Eng
Cloud Eng
Backend Dev
Weight: TLS is the foundation of all secure communication. Certificate issues are the #1 cause of "it was working yesterday!" — monitor cert expiry or suffer the consequences.
🎯 SRE Interview Tip

You WILL be asked: "Walk me through the TLS handshake." Key points: ClientHello (supported versions + cipher suites + ECDHE key share) → ServerHello (chosen version + cipher + ECDHE key share + certificate) → both sides compute shared secret via ECDHE → client verifies certificate chain → Finished messages (everything encrypted from here). TLS 1.3 = 1-RTT. TLS 1.2 = 2-RTT. Also know: TLS provides Encryption, Authentication, and Integrity. The padlock 🔒 means the TLS handshake succeeded — it does NOT mean the website is trustworthy.

13.1 SSL vs TLS — What's the Difference?

Everyone says "SSL certificate" but SSL is DEAD. SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are completely broken (POODLE attack, 2014). What people call "SSL" today is actually TLS 1.2 or 1.3. But the term "SSL certificate" stuck — even AWS, GCP, and Azure label their services as "SSL/TLS certificates."

📜 SSL/TLS Version Timeline — What's Safe and What's Dead
VersionYearStatus
SSL 1.01994❌ Never released (too broken)
SSL 2.01995❌ DEPRECATED 2011 — POODLE, DROWN attacks
SSL 3.01996❌ DEPRECATED 2015 — POODLE attack
TLS 1.01999❌ DEPRECATED 2021 — PCI DSS banned
TLS 1.12006❌ DEPRECATED 2021 — same as TLS 1.0
TLS 1.22008✅ SAFE — still widely used, solid security
TLS 1.32018✅ BEST — faster handshake, modern ciphers only

13.2 Why TLS Exists — The Problem of the Open Internet

Without TLS, anyone on the network path can READ your data (passwords, credit cards, API keys), MODIFY your data (inject ads, malware), or IMPERSONATE servers (fake bank websites). TLS provides three guarantees: Encryption (confidentiality), Authentication (you know who you're talking to), and Integrity (data hasn't been tampered with).

⚠️ GOTCHA — TLS Protects the PIPE, Not the Endpoints

TLS provides encryption in transit only. It does NOT protect data at rest (in a database) or data in use (in memory). If an attacker compromises your server, TLS doesn't help — they can read the decrypted data after TLS terminates. TLS protects the communication channel, not the application.

13.3 How Encryption Works — The Two Types You NEED to Understand

There are exactly two types of encryption, and TLS uses both. Understanding the difference is the foundation for understanding everything else about TLS. Symmetric encryption uses ONE key to both encrypt and decrypt — like a physical key that both locks and unlocks a door. It's blazingly fast (gigabytes per second on modern hardware with AES-NI acceleration) but has a chicken-and-egg problem: how do you securely share the key with the other party without someone intercepting it? Asymmetric encryption uses TWO mathematically-linked keys — a public key (share with everyone) and a private key (never share with anyone). It solves the key distribution problem but is 100-1000× slower than symmetric encryption.

The genius of TLS is that it uses both: asymmetric encryption during the handshake to securely negotiate a symmetric key, then symmetric encryption for the rest of the connection. This is called hybrid encryption. The handshake is the slow part (1 round trip, asymmetric crypto); once the symmetric key is agreed upon, data flows at near line speed (hardware-accelerated AES). If you used only asymmetric encryption, your website would be 1,000× slower. If you used only symmetric encryption, you'd have no secure way to share the key. TLS gives you the best of both worlds.

🔑 Symmetric vs Asymmetric — Visual Comparison
SymmetricAsymmetric
Number of keys1 (shared secret)2 (public + private)
SpeedVERY FAST (GB/s)SLOW (KB/s)
Key distributionHard — how to share?Easy — public key is public!
Used forBulk encryption (actual data)Handshake, signing, key exchange
Common algorithmsAES, ChaCha20RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519
TLS roleEncrypts HTTP bodyProves server is real
🔐 TLS Uses BOTH (Hybrid Encryption)

TLS uses asymmetric crypto during the handshake (to authenticate and exchange keys securely), then switches to symmetric crypto for the rest (for speed). This is called hybrid encryption. If you used only asymmetric crypto, your website would be 1000x slower. The handshake is the slow part; once the symmetric key is established, data flies at line speed.

13.4 Public & Private Keys — The Core Concept Made Simple

PUBLIC/PRIVATE KEY — The Mailbox Analogy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Think of it like a special mailbox:                                  │
│                                                                       │
│  PUBLIC KEY = the mailbox slot (anyone can drop a letter in)          │
│  PRIVATE KEY = the physical key to open the mailbox (only you)        │
│                                                                       │
│  Anyone can use the public slot to send you an encrypted message.     │
│  Only you, with the private key, can open the mailbox and read it.    │
│                                                                       │
│  For SIGNING: you put your wax seal (private key) on a letter.        │
│  Anyone can check the seal against your known seal pattern (public    │
│  key) to verify the letter genuinely came from you.                   │
│                                                                       │
│  WHERE KEYS LIVE IN PRODUCTION:                                       │
│  ‣ Server's private key: /etc/nginx/ssl/privkey.pem or K8s Secret    │
│  ‣ Server's public key: inside the TLS certificate (sent to browsers) │
│  ‣ CA's private key: in a Hardware Security Module (HSM), 24/7 guard │
│  ‣ CA's public key: pre-installed in your OS/browser trust store      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ GOTCHA — Lose Your Private Key, Lose Everything

If you lose your private key, you CANNOT recover it. You must generate a NEW key pair and get a NEW certificate. There is NO "forgot password" for private keys. NEVER put private keys in git. NEVER email them. Use K8s Secrets, AWS Secrets Manager, or HashiCorp Vault.

13.5 What Actually IS HTTPS?

HTTPS = HTTP over TLS. The exact same HTTP requests/responses, wrapped in a TLS-encrypted tunnel. The workflow: TCP 3-way handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request/response over encrypted channel. The padlock 🔒 means the TLS handshake succeeded.

⚠️ GOTCHA — HTTPS ≠ Trustworthy Website

HTTPS means "the connection is encrypted." It does NOT mean "the website is trustworthy." A phishing site at "paypaI.com" (capital i instead of l) can have a perfectly valid TLS certificate. TLS proves the identity of the SERVER, not the INTENT of the people running it. Always check the domain name, not just the padlock.

13.6 The TLS Handshake — Step by Step

TLS 1.3 HANDSHAKE — Message Sequence Diagram
┌──────────┐                                    ┌──────────┐
│  CLIENT  │                                    │  SERVER  │
│ (browser)│                                    │ (nginx)  │
└────┬─────┘                                    └────┬─────┘
     │                                               │
     │  ──── ClientHello ─────────────────────────▶  │
     │  (supported versions, cipher suites,           │
     │   key_share: ECDHE public key)                │
     │                                               │
     │  ◀─── ServerHello ─────────────────────────  │
     │  (chosen version, cipher suite,               │
     │   key_share: ECDHE public key)                │
     │                                               │
     │  ◀─── {EncryptedExtensions} ────────────────  │
     │  ◀─── {Certificate} ────────────────────────  │
     │  ◀─── {CertificateVerify} ──────────────────  │
     │  ◀─── {Finished} ───────────────────────────  │
     │                                               │
     │  ──── {Finished} ──────────────────────────▶  │
     │                                               │
     │  🔒 ALL DATA NOW ENCRYPTED 🔒                  │
     │                                               │
     │  ──── GET /api/jobs/ HTTP/1.1 ──────────────▶ │
     │  ◀─── HTTP/1.1 200 OK ──────────────────────  │
     └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 TLS 1.3 Handshake Steps Explained

Step 1 — ClientHello: "I support TLS 1.3, here are my cipher suites, here's my ECDHE key share." Step 2 — ServerHello: "Let's use TLS 1.3 with AES-256-GCM, here's my ECDHE key share + certificate." Step 3 — Key Exchange: Both sides compute the same shared secret using ECDHE. An eavesdropper sees the key shares but CANNOT compute the secret (Diffie-Hellman magic). Step 4 — Certificate Verification: Client checks: signed by trusted CA? Not expired? Hostname matches? Not revoked? Step 5 — Finished: Everything from here is encrypted. Total: 1 round trip (1-RTT). TLS 1.2 = 2-RTT.

⚡ TLS 1.3 vs TLS 1.2 — What Changed and Why It Matters

TLS 1.3 is not just a minor upgrade — it's a fundamental redesign that removes everything known to be weak and streamlines the handshake for speed. The table below captures every meaningful difference:

FeatureTLS 1.2TLS 1.3Impact
Handshake RTT2 round trips (4 flights)1 round trip (2 flights)~100ms faster on first connection
0-RTT ResumptionNot availableYes (PSK mode)Instant reconnect for returning users
Cipher SuitesDozens (many weak)5 AEAD-only ciphersNo more CBC, RC4, 3DES — attack surface minimized
Key ExchangeRSA or (EC)DHE(EC)DHE only (no RSA)Perfect Forward Secrecy MANDATORY
Signature AlgorithmsNegotiated separatelyNegotiated in extensionsCleaner negotiation, fewer round trips
RenegotiationSupported (bug-prone)REMOVED entirelyEliminates renegotiation attacks
CompressionSupported (CRIME attack)REMOVED entirelyNo more CRIME/BREACH compression attacks
Static RSASupportedREMOVED entirelyNo more ROBOT/Bleichenbacher attacks
Downgrade ProtectionWeak (TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV)Built into protocolServerHello.random protects against downgrade
Encrypted Server CertSent in cleartextEncrypted (after ServerHello)Passive eavesdroppers can't see certificate

The bottom line: TLS 1.3 is faster (1-RTT), more secure (weak algorithms removed), and more private (certificate encrypted). If your infrastructure supports it — and almost everything modern does — you should use TLS 1.3 exclusively. The only reason to keep TLS 1.2 is legacy clients that haven't been updated.

🔐 Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) — Why ECDHE Is Critical

Perfect Forward Secrecy means that if an attacker records your encrypted TLS traffic today and later steals your private key, they STILL cannot decrypt the recorded traffic. This is because the session key is derived from ephemeral (temporary) key shares that are discarded after the session — not from the long-term private key. The "E" in ECDHE stands for Ephemeral — each session generates new key shares. Without PFS (plain RSA key exchange), stealing the private key decrypts ALL past recorded traffic. TLS 1.3 mandates PFS by removing static RSA key exchange entirely. Only cipher suites with DHE or ECDHE provide PFS.

🔄 TLS Session Resumption — Skip the Heavy Crypto on Reconnect

Full TLS handshakes are expensive (asymmetric crypto). Session resumption lets a client reconnect using cached parameters, reducing to 0-RTT or 1-RTT with no asymmetric operations:

MethodHow It WorksRTTSecurity
Session IDs (TLS 1.2)Server stores session state. Client sends Session ID on reconnect. Server looks up cached keys.1-RTT (abbreviated)Server must store state (doesn't scale). No PFS for resumed sessions.
Session Tickets (TLS 1.2)Server encrypts session state into a "ticket" sent to client. Client sends ticket back on reconnect. Server decrypts.1-RTT (abbreviated)Server stateless. Ticket key must be rotated. No PFS.
0-RTT (PSK) (TLS 1.3)Client uses Pre-Shared Key from previous session to send encrypted data IMMEDIATELY with the ClientHello.0-RTTReplay attack risk! Data in 0-RTT is NOT replay-protected. Use only for idempotent GETs.

13.7 Cipher Suites — What Those Long Strings Actually Mean

CIPHER SUITE DECODER — How to Read Those Intimidating Strings
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384                                │
│  ─── ───── ─── ──── ─────── ─── ─────                                 │
│   │    │    │    │      │     │     │                                  │
│   │    │    │    │      │     │     └─ Hash/MAC algorithm (SHA384)     │
│   │    │    │    │      │     └─ Block cipher mode (GCM)               │
│   │    │    │    │      └─ Symmetric cipher (AES-256)                  │
│   │    │    │    └─ "WITH" — separator                                 │
│   │    │    └─ Auth algorithm (RSA)                                    │
│   │    └─ Key exchange (ECDHE — Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman)        │
│   └─ Protocol (TLS)                                                    │
│                                                                       │
│  TLS 1.3 SIMPLIFIED: cipher suites only specify symmetric cipher +    │
│  hash. Key exchange and auth are negotiated separately.                │
│  Example: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 (much shorter!)                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔐 Common Cipher Suites — Security Rating & Performance
Cipher SuiteSecurityPerfNotes
TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384✅ Best✅ FastTLS 1.3 default. AES hardware-accelerated on modern CPUs.
TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256✅ Excellent✅ FasterTLS 1.3. AES-128 is unbreakable with current technology.
TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256✅ Best✅ FastTLS 1.3. Best for mobile/ARM (no AES hardware acceleration).
TLS_ECDHE_RSA_AES_256_GCM_SHA384✅ Good⚠️ SlowerTLS 1.2. RSA auth + ECDHE key exchange. Has PFS.
TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_AES_128_GCM_SHA256✅ Good✅ FastTLS 1.2 with ECDSA (smaller keys, faster than RSA).
TLS_RSA_AES_256_CBC_SHA❌ Weak❌ SlowNo PFS (static RSA). CBC mode. Avoid in production.

# CHECK ALL CIPHERS A SERVER SUPPORTS:
$ nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 anihpj.com

Error MessageWhat It Actually MeansFix
CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID
"Your connection is not private"		CA not trusted — self-signed cert, corporate proxy MITM, missing intermediate certAdd CA to trust store, or use Let's Encrypt
CERT_DATE_INVALID
"Your clock is behind"		Certificate expired OR system clock is wrongRenew cert, or date; timedatectl status
COMMON_NAME_INVALID
"Does not match the URL"		Hostname doesn't match CN/SANs in certificateUse correct hostname, add SAN to cert
SSL_ERROR_RX_RECORD_TOO_LONGServer speaking plain HTTP on TLS portEnable TLS on the server
Mixed Content Warning ⚠️HTTPS page loads HTTP resourcesUse protocol-relative URLs or always HTTPS

13.9 TLS in Everyday Tools

Every tool you use daily negotiates TLS: curl (--cacert, -k), git (git config http.sslVerify), kubectl (--certificate-authority in kubeconfig), docker (DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY), pip/npm (package registries over HTTPS). When any of these fail, the error is almost always TLS-related — expired cert, untrusted CA, or hostname mismatch.

⚠️ GOTCHA — Corporate TLS-Intercepting Proxies (Zscaler, Netskope)

When your company uses a TLS-intercepting proxy, it acts as a Man-in-the-Middle — it terminates your TLS connection, inspects the content, then creates a NEW TLS connection to the destination. This is why you need to install your company's CA certificate on your machine. Without it, ALL HTTPS traffic shows CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID errors. To fix: install the corporate CA cert, or configure individual tools: NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS for npm, git config http.sslCAInfo for git, --cacert for curl. The proxy's cert will appear as the issuer in openssl s_client output.

13.10 TLS Termination

TLS termination means decrypting TLS at a proxy/load balancer and forwarding plain HTTP to the backend. This offloads crypto overhead from application servers. Common pattern: Client → ALB (TLS terminates here) → HTTP → K8s pod. The connection between ALB and pod is unencrypted (unless you use mTLS or service mesh). Always consider: is the internal network trusted? If not, re-encrypt (TLS from ALB to pod).

TLS TERMINATION PATTERNS — Where Encryption Ends
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PATTERN 1: TLS OFFLOADING (terminate at LB, plain HTTP inside)           │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌─────────┐    HTTPS (TLS)    ┌──────────┐     HTTP (plain)   ┌───────┐ │
│  │ BROWSER │ ────────────────▶ │   ALB    │ ─────────────────▶ │  Pod  │ │
│  │         │ ◀──────────────── │ (TLS end)│ ◀───────────────── │       │ │
│  └─────────┘                   └──────────┘                    └───────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  ✅ Pros: Offloads crypto from app. LB can inspect HTTP for routing.      │
│  ❌ Cons: Internal traffic is PLAINTEXT. Anyone on the network can read.  │
│  ⚠️  Django request.is_secure() = False unless X-Forwarded-Proto is set.  │
│                                                                           │
│  PATTERN 2: TLS RE-ENCRYPTION (terminate + re-encrypt to backend)        │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌─────────┐   HTTPS (TLS v1)  ┌──────────┐   HTTPS (TLS v2)  ┌───────┐ │
│  │ BROWSER │ ────────────────▶ │   ALB    │ ────────────────▶ │  Pod  │ │
│  │         │ ◀──────────────── │ (TLS end │ ◀──────────────── │       │ │
│  └─────────┘                   │ + re-enc)│                   └───────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  ✅ Pros: End-to-end encryption. Different certs at LB vs backend.        │
│  ❌ Cons: TLS overhead on backend. Two certificates to manage.             │
│                                                                           │
│  PATTERN 3: TLS PASS-THROUGH (LB doesn't decrypt)                        │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌─────────┐    HTTPS (TLS)    ┌──────────┐    HTTPS (same)    ┌───────┐ │
│  │ BROWSER │ ────────────────▶ │   NLB    │ ────────────────▶ │  Pod  │ │
│  │         │ ◀──────────────── │ (L4 only)│ ◀──────────────── │       │ │
│  └─────────┘                   └──────────┘                    └───────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  ✅ Pros: True end-to-end encryption. LB doesn't need cert at all.        │
│  ❌ Cons: No L7 routing (can't route by path/host). Backend does all TLS. │
│  📍 NLB uses this pattern. ALB uses Pattern 1 or 2.                       │
│                                                                           │
│  PATTERN 4: SERVICE MESH mTLS (every hop encrypted and authenticated)    │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌──────┐  mTLS  ┌─────────┐  mTLS  ┌─────────┐  mTLS  ┌────────┐      │
│  │ Pod A│───────▶│ Envoy A │──────▶│ Envoy B │──────▶│ Pod B  │      │
│  │      │◀───────│ (sidecar)│◀──────│(sidecar)│◀──────│        │      │
│  └──────┘        └─────────┘        └─────────┘        └────────┘      │
│                                                                           │
│  ✅ Pros: Zero-trust. Automatic cert rotation. App code unchanged.        │
│  ❌ Cons: Operational complexity. Sidecar resource overhead.              │
│  📍 Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect use this pattern.                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ GOTCHA — X-Forwarded-Proto When Behind TLS-Terminating LB

If your cloud LB terminates TLS and forwards HTTP to your backend, the backend sees HTTP traffic. If your Django app checks request.is_secure(), it will return False! Fix: set the X-Forwarded-Proto header at the LB and configure Django's SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER setting. In nginx: proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

13.11 Certificates — Chain of Trust

Every TLS certificate chains up to a Root CA that your OS/browser trusts implicitly. The chain: Root CA → Intermediate CA → Your Server Certificate. If any link is missing (common: forgetting to include the intermediate cert), the browser can't verify the chain and shows a warning. The Certificate Transparency system publicly logs all issued certificates — you can search for any domain's cert history at crt.sh.

CERTIFICATE CHAIN OF TRUST — How Browsers Verify Your Server
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      CERTIFICATE CHAIN OF TRUST                            │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │                        ROOT CA                                      │ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │ │
│  │  │  Organization: "ISRG Root X1" (Internet Security Research)   │   │ │
│  │  │  Validity:     2015-06-04 → 2035-06-04 (20 years!)          │   │ │
│  │  │  Public Key:   RSA 4096-bit                                  │   │ │
│  │  │  Signed by:    ITSELF (self-signed — the root of all trust)  │   │ │
│  │  │  Location:     Your OS/browser "Trust Store"                 │   │ │
│  │  │  Stored in:    /etc/ssl/certs/ (Linux), Keychain (macOS),    │   │ │
│  │  │                Cert:\CurrentUser\Root (Windows)              │   │ │
│  │  └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘   │ │
│  │                         │ SIGNS (with Root CA's PRIVATE key)        │ │
│  │                         ▼                                           │ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │ │
│  │  │                   INTERMEDIATE CA                            │   │ │
│  │  │  Organization: "R3" (Let's Encrypt Intermediate)             │   │ │
│  │  │  Validity:     2020-09-04 → 2025-09-15 (5 years)            │   │ │
│  │  │  Public Key:   RSA 2048-bit                                  │   │ │
│  │  │  Signed by:    ISRG Root X1 (the Root CA above)              │   │ │
│  │  │  Purpose:       Issues end-entity (server) certificates      │   │ │
│  │  │  Note:          Root CA's private key is OFFLINE (in a vault)│   │ │
│  │  │                 Intermediate does the daily signing work     │   │ │
│  │  └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘   │ │
│  │                         │ SIGNS (with Intermediate CA's PRIVATE key)│ │
│  │                         ▼                                           │ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │ │
│  │  │               LEAF / SERVER CERTIFICATE                      │   │ │
│  │  │  Common Name:  jobpost.anihpj.com                            │   │ │
│  │  │  SANs:         jobpost.anihpj.com, www.jobpost.anihpj.com    │   │ │
│  │  │  Validity:     2026-01-15 → 2026-04-15 (90 days!)            │   │ │
│  │  │  Public Key:   ECDSA P-256 (in the certificate)              │   │ │
│  │  │  Private Key:  /etc/nginx/ssl/privkey.pem (NEVER share!)     │   │ │
│  │  │  Signed by:    R3 (the Intermediate CA above)                │   │ │
│  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  VERIFICATION FLOW (every browser, every TLS connection):                  │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ 1. Browser receives SERVER CERT from nginx during TLS handshake    │ │
│  │ 2. Browser sees: "This cert is signed by R3 (Intermediate CA)"     │ │
│  │ 3. Browser needs R3's certificate to verify the signature          │ │
│  │ 4. nginx MUST send the R3 (Intermediate) cert in the chain         │ │
│  │ 5. Browser verifies: R3's cert is signed by ISRG Root X1           │ │
│  │ 6. ISRG Root X1 is in the browser's Trust Store → TRUSTED!         │ │
│  │ 7. Chain verified: Root → Intermediate → Server. Padlock appears.  │ │
│  │                                                                     │ │
│  │ IF THE INTERMEDIATE CERT IS MISSING:                               │ │
│  │ Browser: "I got the server cert, but who signed it? R3?            │ │
│  │           I don't have R3's certificate. I can't verify."          │ │
│  │ Result:  NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID                           │ │
│  │ Fix:     nginx must send fullchain.pem (server + intermediate)     │ │
│  │          NOT just cert.pem (server cert only)                      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📜 X.509 Certificate Fields — Quick Reference
FieldWhat It Means
Subject (CN)Common Name — the primary hostname
Subject Alternative Names (SANs)List of ALL hostnames/IPs this cert covers. MUST match the URL you're connecting to!
IssuerWho signed this certificate (the CA)
Not Before / AfterValidity window — if expired, TLS fails completely
Public KeyThe public half of the key pair (included in cert)
Signature AlgorithmHow the CA signed (SHA-256 with RSA/ECDSA)
Serial NumberUnique ID for this certificate
Key UsageWhat this cert can be used for (server auth, client auth, code signing)
⚠️ GOTCHA — SAN > CN in Modern TLS

If the SAN field doesn't include the hostname you're connecting to, the browser rejects the cert even if the CN matches. SAN (Subject Alternative Name) takes priority over CN in modern TLS validation. Always include every hostname and IP in the SAN field when generating certificates.

🔍 Certificate Revocation — CRL, OCSP & OCSP Stapling

Certificates can be revoked BEFORE they expire (private key compromised, domain ownership changed). There are three mechanisms to check revocation status:

MethodHow It WorksPrivacy Issue?Performance
CRLCertificate Revocation List: a massive file listing ALL revoked certs from a CA. Client downloads and checks.❌ No (local check)❌ Slow (can be 10s of MB)
OCSPOnline Certificate Status Protocol: client asks the CA "is cert #12345 revoked?" for EVERY connection.❌ YES! CA knows every site you visit.⚠️ Adds latency (OCSP lookup)
OCSP StaplingServer periodically asks CA for OCSP response, then "staples" it to the TLS handshake. Client verifies without contacting CA.✅ CA only sees server's queries, not client's.✅ No extra client latency
 
# CHECK IF A SERVER USES OCSP STAPLING:
$ openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -status -servername anihpj.com 2>&1 | grep -A5 "OCSP"
# OCSP Response Data: ... → OCSP stapling is active!
# Or look for "OCSP response: no response sent" → Not configured

13.12 TLS in Kubernetes — cert-manager & Ingress

In K8s, TLS certificates are stored as Secrets of type kubernetes.io/tls containing tls.crt and tls.key. Ingress controllers reference these Secrets. cert-manager automates certificate issuance and renewal using Let's Encrypt via the ACME protocol.

☸️ cert-manager Workflow — Automatic TLS for K8s
# 1. You create a Certificate resource (or annotate an Ingress):
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: jobpost-anihpj-tls
spec:
  secretName: jobpost-tls-secret
  dnsNames:
  - jobpost.anihpj.com
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-prod
    kind: ClusterIssuer

# 2. cert-manager creates an Order → ACME Challenge (HTTP-01 or DNS-01)
# 3. Let's Encrypt verifies you control the domain
# 4. Certificate issued → stored in Kubernetes Secret
# 5. Ingress references the Secret for TLS
# 6. cert-manager auto-renews 30 days before expiry!

# CHECK CERTIFICATE STATUS:
$ kubectl get certificate -A
NAMESPACE  NAME                 READY  SECRET              AGE
default    jobpost-anihpj-tls   True   jobpost-tls-secret  45d

# The flow: Ingress annotation → Certificate → Order → Challenge → Secret

13.13 Debugging TLS with openssl s_client

🔍 openssl s_client — Your TLS Debugger
# CONNECT TO A TLS SERVER AND SEE EVERYTHING:
$ openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -servername anihpj.com
# Shows: certificate chain, cipher suite, TLS version, SANs, validity dates

# CHECK CERTIFICATE EXPIRY DATE:
$ echo | openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
notBefore=Jan  1 00:00:00 2026 GMT
notAfter=Mar 31 23:59:59 2026 GMT

# CHECK CERTIFICATE SANs (Subject Alternative Names):
$ echo | openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltName

# CHECK THE FULL CERTIFICATE CHAIN:
$ openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -showcerts
⚠️ GOTCHA — openssl s_client Exit Code Is ALWAYS 0

openssl s_client exits with code 0 even when TLS verification FAILS. You MUST check the verify return code in the output: 0 = ok, 18 = self-signed certificate, 19 = self-signed certificate in chain, 20 = unable to get local issuer certificate, 21 = unable to verify the first certificate. Also: openssl s_client does NOT use SNI (Server Name Indication) by default. Always add -servername or you'll get the wrong certificate!

13.14 Mutual TLS (mTLS)

In regular TLS, only the server proves its identity. In mTLS, BOTH sides present certificates. The client must prove its identity too.

Standard TLS vs mTLS — Certificate Flow Comparison
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STANDARD TLS (server-only auth):                                     │
│  ┌────────┐                         ┌────────┐                       │
│  │ CLIENT │ ──── ClientHello ─────▶ │ SERVER │                       │
│  │        │ ◀── ServerHello+Cert ── │        │                       │
│  │        │    (client verifies     │        │                       │
│  │        │     server's cert)      │        │                       │
│  │        │ ──── Encrypted data ──▶ │        │                       │
│  └────────┘                         └────────┘                       │
│                                                                       │
│  mTLS (mutual auth):                                                  │
│  ┌────────┐                         ┌────────┐                       │
│  │ CLIENT │ ──── ClientHello ─────▶ │ SERVER │                       │
│  │        │ ◀── ServerHello+Cert ── │        │                       │
│  │        │ ◀── CertificateRequest─ │ "Show me YOUR certificate!"    │
│  │        │ ──── ClientCert ──────▶ │ (client sends its cert)        │
│  │        │ ──── CertificateVerify▶ │ (client proves it owns the key)│
│  │        │ ◀── ServerFinished ──── │                                │
│  │        │ ──── ClientFinished ──▶ │                                │
│  │        │ ◀════ Encrypted ══════▶ │ BOTH sides authenticated!      │
│  └────────┘                         └────────┘                       │
│                                                                       │
│  WHERE mTLS IS USED:                                                  │
│  ‣ Service Mesh (Istio/Linkerd): every pod-to-pod call is mTLS       │
│  ‣ Zero-Trust Networks: no network is trusted, every connection authd│
│  ‣ API Gateway → Backend: gateway proves its identity to the backend  │
│  ‣ Database connections: app proves identity to PostgreSQL via cert   │
│                                                                       │
│  IN KUBERNETES WITH ISTIO:                                            │
│  ‣ Istio sidecar (Envoy proxy) automatically provisions certs        │
│  ‣ Every pod gets its own certificate from Istio's CA (citadel)      │
│  ‣ mTLS enforced transparently — zero application code changes       │
│  ‣ STRICT mode: all connections MUST use mTLS (reject plain HTTP)    │
│  ‣ PERMISSIVE mode: accept both mTLS and plain text (migration)      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

13.15 LAB: TLS Hands-On

🛠️ TLS Lab — 5 Hands-On Exercises
1
Inspect a Real TLS Certificate
$ echo | openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -servername anihpj.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text | head -30
# Find: Issuer, Subject, Validity, SANs, Public Key Algorithm
2
Check Certificate Expiry
$ echo | openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
# When does the certificate expire? Set a calendar reminder!
3
See the TLS Handshake in Real Time
$ curl -v https://anihpj.com 2>&1 | grep -E "TLS|ALPN|Server certificate|SSL"
# See: TLS version negotiated, ALPN protocol, certificate subject
4
Test TLS 1.3 vs TLS 1.2
$ curl --tlsv1.3 -v https://anihpj.com -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep "TLS"
$ curl --tlsv1.2 -v https://anihpj.com -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep "TLS"
# Which version does the server prefer? Which is faster?
5
Debug a TLS Error (Self-Signed Cert)
$ curl https://self-signed.badssl.com
# Fails with certificate error. Now try with -k:
$ curl -k https://self-signed.badssl.com
# Works! -k disables verification (DEV ONLY!)

🔭 Chapter 13 — Visual Summary

📜SSL is Dead

SSL 2.0/3.0 are broken. TLS 1.2 (safe) and TLS 1.3 (best) are what "SSL" actually means today.

🔑Hybrid Encryption

Asymmetric (slow) for handshake + key exchange. Symmetric (fast) for bulk data. Best of both worlds.

🤝TLS 1.3 Handshake = 1-RTT

ClientHello → ServerHello+Cert+Finished → Client Finished → Encrypted. TLS 1.2 takes 2-RTT.

📜Certificate Chain

Root CA → Intermediate CA → Server Cert. Missing intermediate = browser warning. Trust flows down.

🔍openssl s_client

Your TLS debugger. Check certs, cipher suites, expiry, chain, SANs. No GUI needed.

🔄mTLS

Both sides present certificates. Service mesh (Istio) uses mTLS for all pod-to-pod traffic automatically.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 13

🔑TLS Handshake
The negotiation that establishes a secure connection. ClientHello → ServerHello + Certificate → Key Exchange → Finished. TLS 1.3 = 1-RTT. Agreement on cipher suite + shared symmetric key.
📜Certificate Chain
Root CA → Intermediate CA → Server Certificate. Each link is signed by the one above. Browsers trust Root CAs implicitly. Any missing link = trust failure.
🔐Cipher Suite
Negotiated set of algorithms: key exchange (ECDHE), authentication (RSA/ECDSA), symmetric cipher (AES-256-GCM), hash (SHA384). TLS 1.3 simplified to just symmetric cipher + hash.
🔄TLS Termination
Decrypting TLS at a proxy/load balancer and forwarding plain HTTP to backends. Offloads crypto overhead. Pattern: Client → ALB (TLS) → HTTP → Pod.
🔒mTLS
Mutual TLS: both client and server present certificates. Used in zero-trust networks and service mesh (Istio/Linkerd). Every pod-to-pod call is encrypted and authenticated.
🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work
  • Certificate expiry is the #1 cause of "it was working yesterday." Set up monitoring for certificate expiry dates. Let's Encrypt certs expire every 90 days — automate renewal with cert-manager.
  • openssl s_client is your TLS debugger. Before checking application logs, check the TLS connection. Expired cert? Wrong hostname? Weak cipher? It tells you instantly.
  • TLS termination at the load balancer offloads crypto from your app. AWS ALB, Nginx, and Envoy handle TLS so your Django/gunicorn pods don't have to.
  • Service mesh (Istio) adds mTLS automatically. Every pod-to-pod call encrypted without changing a single line of application code.

🔑 Chapter 13 Key Takeaways

  1. SSL is dead. TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are the standards. "SSL certificate" is a misnomer that stuck. TLS 1.3 is faster (1-RTT) and more secure.
  2. TLS uses hybrid encryption. Asymmetric (RSA/ECDSA) for handshake + key exchange. Symmetric (AES/ChaCha20) for bulk data.
  3. The TLS handshake negotiates a shared secret without anyone eavesdropping being able to discover it. ECDHE key exchange is the magic.
  4. Certificate chains must be complete. Root → Intermediate → Server. Missing intermediate = browser warning.
  5. openssl s_client -connect host:443 is your primary TLS debugging command. Check certs, cipher suites, expiry dates, and chains instantly.
🛡️ SRE Reality Check — Certificate Expiry Is Your #1 Operational Risk

Let's Encrypt certificates expire every 90 days. If cert-manager's auto-renewal fails (DNS challenge timeout, rate limit exceeded, RBAC misconfiguration), your site goes dark. This happens to someone every day. Don't let it be you.

Monitoring you MUST set up:

  • cert-manager metrics: certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds — alert when < 30 days remaining.
  • External TLS monitoring: Probe your endpoints from outside (Blackbox Exporter, UptimeRobot, Datadog Synthetic). Check cert expiry from an external perspective — internal monitoring can miss issues if the renewal process runs on the same infrastructure that's broken.
  • openssl one-liner for scripts: echo | openssl s_client -servername example.com -connect example.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate | cut -d= -f2
  • Dashboard: Grafana panel showing days-until-expiry for every certificate. If the number is under 30 and dropping, something is broken.
# PROMETHEUS ALERT RULE for cert-manager:
- alert: CertificateExpiringSoon
  expr: certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds - time() < 2592000  # 30 days
  for: 1h
  annotations:
    summary: "Certificate {{ $labels.name }} expires in less than 30 days"
    runbook: "https://wiki.anihpj.com/runbooks/tls-cert-renewal"
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 13.1 — Decode TLS Errors

For each error below, identify the root cause and the openssl command to diagnose it:

  1. Browser shows: "Your connection is not private. NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID" when accessing your staging environment.
  2. curl https://api.anihpj.com returns: "SSL certificate problem: certificate has expired"
  3. openssl s_client -connect jobpost.anihpj.com:443 shows: "verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate"
  4. Browser shows padlock but with ⚠️ "Mixed Content" warning. The page loaded over HTTPS but some images are broken.
  5. curl https://10.0.1.50 returns: "SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name '10.0.1.50'"
💡 Hint: Each error maps to a specific TLS verification failure. Authority = CA not trusted. Expired = date check. Local issuer = missing intermediate. Mixed content = HTTP resources on HTTPS page. Name mismatch = SANs don't include the hostname you used.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID on staging:
# Staging likely uses a self-signed or internal CA certificate.
# The CA is not in your OS/browser trust store.
# DIAGNOSE: openssl s_client -connect staging.anihpj.com:443 -showcerts
# Look at the issuer — it's probably "Anihpj Internal CA" not "Let's Encrypt"
# FIX: Add the internal CA cert to your trust store, or use -k for dev only.

# 2. Certificate expired:
# DIAGNOSE: echo | openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
# Shows: notAfter=Jun 15 00:00:00 2026 GMT (it's Jun 21!)
# FIX: Renew the certificate. If using cert-manager, check: kubectl get certificate -A
# Check cert-manager logs for renewal errors.

# 3. "unable to get local issuer certificate" (verify error 20):
# The server didn't send the INTERMEDIATE CA certificate.
# DIAGNOSE: openssl s_client -connect jobpost.anihpj.com:443 -showcerts
# If you see only 1 certificate (depth 0), the intermediate is missing.
# FIX: Configure nginx to send the full chain: ssl_certificate /path/to/fullchain.pem
# NOT just the server cert: ssl_certificate /path/to/cert.pem ← WRONG!

# 4. Mixed Content Warning:
# Some resources on the page are loaded over HTTP, not HTTPS.
# DIAGNOSE: Browser DevTools → Console → filter "Mixed Content"
# Look for: http://cdn.anihpj.com/images/logo.png (http, not https!)
# FIX: Change URLs to https:// or protocol-relative //cdn.anihpj.com/...
# Add Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests header as safety net.

# 5. Hostname mismatch (IP vs cert SANs):
# The cert's SAN field doesn't include the IP address 10.0.1.50.
# DIAGNOSE: openssl s_client -connect 10.0.1.50:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltName
# Shows SANs: DNS:jobpost.anihpj.com — no IP addresses listed!
# FIX: Use the hostname (not IP) to connect, or add the IP to the cert's SAN field.
⏱️ Target: 7 minutes
Drill 13.2 — Inspect a Real TLS Certificate

On your machine, run these commands and answer the questions:

  1. echo | openssl s_client -connect google.com:443 -servername google.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates — When does Google's certificate expire?
  2. echo | openssl s_client -connect google.com:443 -servername google.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -subject — Who issued the certificate? Who is it issued to?
  3. echo | openssl s_client -connect google.com:443 -servername google.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltName — How many SANs does Google's certificate include? Why so many?
  4. Run the same commands for expired.badssl.com. What do you see?
  5. Check the TLS version: echo | openssl s_client -connect google.com:443 -servername google.com 2>/dev/null | grep "Protocol" — Is Google using TLS 1.3 or 1.2?
💡 Hint: Google uses a wildcard certificate (*.google.com) with dozens of SANs covering all their domains. badssl.com is a testing site with intentionally bad/expired certs for learning TLS debugging.
📝 View Solution 
# EXPECTED FINDINGS:
# 1. Google cert typically expires in 60-90 days (they rotate frequently)
# 2. Issuer: "GTS CA 1C3" (Google Trust Services — Google is its own CA!)
#    Subject: CN=*.google.com
# 3. Dozens of SANs: *.google.com, *.android.com, *.cloud.google.com, ...
#    One certificate covers ALL Google properties. Efficient!
# 4. expired.badssl.com → certificate has EXPIRED. You'll see an error.
#    This is a test site specifically for TLS error debugging.
# 5. Protocol: TLSv1.3 (Google was one of the earliest TLS 1.3 adopters)

# KEY INSIGHT: Google operates its own Certificate Authority (GTS).
# This means they can issue certificates instantly, with any validity,
# for any Google domain — no external dependency on Let's Encrypt or DigiCert.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 13.3 — Cipher Suite Security Assessment

Which of these cipher suites provide Perfect Forward Secrecy? Which are safe to use in production?

  1. TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA
  2. TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  3. TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  4. TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256
  5. TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA
💡 Hint: Look for "E" in the key exchange field (ECDHE or DHE). The "E" = Ephemeral = Perfect Forward Secrecy. Without "E" (plain RSA key exchange), the private key can decrypt ALL past traffic if stolen. Also: 3DES is broken, CBC mode is vulnerable to padding oracle attacks.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA
#    PFS: ❌ NO (static RSA key exchange)
#    Safe: ❌ NO (CBC mode — vulnerable to padding oracle attacks like Lucky13)
#    If private key stolen → ALL past sessions decryptable.

# 2. TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
#    PFS: ✅ YES (ECDHE = Ephemeral Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman)
#    Safe: ✅ YES (GCM mode = authenticated encryption, no padding oracle risk)
#    TLS 1.2. Widely used. Good choice.

# 3. TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
#    PFS: ✅ YES (TLS 1.3 mandates ECDHE, so PFS is guaranteed)
#    Safe: ✅ YES (TLS 1.3 cipher, AES-GCM, strongest option)
#    Note: TLS 1.3 cipher suites don't specify key exchange — it's always ECDHE.

# 4. TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256
#    PFS: ✅ YES (ECDHE)
#    Safe: ✅ YES (ChaCha20-Poly1305 is modern, fast on mobile/ARM)
#    ECDSA auth = smaller keys, faster than RSA auth.

# 5. TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA
#    PFS: ❌ NO (static RSA)
#    Safe: ❌ NO (3DES is broken — Sweet32 attack, effective key size ~112 bits)
#    Should be DISABLED on every server. CBC mode + 3DES = worst possible combo.

# RULE OF THUMB:
# ✅ Safe: ECDHE/DHE key exchange + AEAD cipher (GCM or Poly1305) + SHA-256/384
# ❌ Unsafe: Static RSA + CBC mode + SHA-1 or MD5
# 🚫 Dead: 3DES, RC4, EXPORT ciphers, NULL ciphers, anonymous key exchange

📝 Chapter 13 — Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between SSL and TLS? Why does everyone still say "SSL certificate"?
Show Answer
Answer

SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) was the original protocol (1995-1996). TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the standardized successor (1999-present). SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are completely broken and deprecated. TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are the current standards. "SSL certificate" is a misnomer — the certificates are actually X.509 certificates usable by both SSL and TLS. The name stuck because it was the original term, and even cloud providers label their services as "SSL/TLS."

Q2
Explain symmetric vs asymmetric encryption. How does TLS use both?
Show Answer
Answer

Symmetric: one shared key, very fast (GB/s), used for bulk data. Problem: how to securely share the key? Asymmetric: public+private key pair, slow (KB/s), solves key distribution. TLS uses asymmetric (ECDHE/RSA) during the handshake to authenticate and securely exchange a symmetric key, then switches to symmetric (AES/ChaCha20) for the rest of the connection. This is hybrid encryption.

Q3
Walk through the TLS 1.3 handshake step by step.
Show Answer
Answer

1. ClientHello: client sends supported TLS versions, cipher suites, and ECDHE key share. 2. ServerHello: server chooses TLS 1.3 + cipher suite, sends its ECDHE key share + certificate. 3. Both sides compute the same shared secret using ECDHE. 4. Client verifies certificate (trusted CA? not expired? hostname matches?). 5. Finished messages exchanged. All subsequent data encrypted with the symmetric key. Total: 1 round trip.

Q4
Decode this cipher suite: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
Show Answer
Answer

TLS protocol. ECDHE = key exchange (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral). RSA = authentication. AES_256_GCM = symmetric cipher (AES-256 in GCM mode). SHA384 = hash/Pseudo-Random Function. In TLS 1.3, this is simplified to just TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 — key exchange and auth are negotiated separately.

Q5
What does a "NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID" error mean? What are the possible causes?
Show Answer
Answer

The certificate's validity period (notBefore to notAfter) does not include the current time. Most common: certificate EXPIRED (forgot to renew). Also possible: system clock is wrong (check with `date`), or the certificate's notBefore date is in the future (issued with future start date). Fix: renew the certificate, or correct the system clock.

Q6
How do you check a TLS certificate's expiry date using openssl?
Show Answer
Answer

echo | openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -servername anihpj.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates. Shows notBefore and notAfter dates. For monitoring: openssl s_client -connect host:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate returns just the expiry date.

Q7
What is TLS termination? When would you use it and when would you NOT?
Show Answer
Answer

TLS termination: decrypting TLS at a proxy/load balancer and forwarding plain HTTP to backends. Use when: internal network is trusted (VPC), you want to offload crypto overhead, or you need the LB to inspect HTTP headers for routing. Do NOT use when: internal network is untrusted, compliance requires end-to-end encryption, or you're in a zero-trust environment. In those cases, re-encrypt (TLS from LB to backend) or use mTLS.

Q8
What is mTLS? How does it differ from regular TLS?
Show Answer
Answer

Regular TLS: only the server proves its identity (client verifies server's certificate). mTLS: BOTH client and server prove their identities by presenting certificates. The server also verifies the client's certificate. Used in zero-trust networks, service mesh (Istio/Linkerd), and API gateway authentication. In K8s, Istio automatically provisions certificates and enforces mTLS between all pods.

Q9
What happens if an intermediate CA certificate is missing from the chain?
Show Answer
Answer

The browser cannot build a trust chain from the server certificate to a trusted Root CA. It shows CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID ("Your connection is not private"). This is one of the most common TLS configuration errors — the server sends its own certificate but forgets to include the intermediate CA certificate. Fix: configure the server to send the full chain (server cert + intermediate cert).

Q10
How would you debug "curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate"?
Show Answer
Answer

This means curl can't verify the certificate chain — the issuing CA is not in curl's trust store. Common causes: self-signed certificate, corporate proxy doing TLS inspection, or missing CA cert on the system. Diagnosis: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -showcerts to see the chain. Fix: curl --cacert /path/to/ca.pem to trust a specific CA, or add the CA to the system trust store (update-ca-certificates on Linux). NEVER use curl -k in production.

Chapter 14: Load Balancing, Proxies & CDNs — Scaling HTTP

Once you have HTTP and TLS working, the next challenge is scale. A single server can only handle ~10,000 concurrent connections before it saturates — running out of file descriptors, CPU, or network bandwidth. Load balancers are the architectural pattern that turns one server into many, distributing traffic transparently. Reverse proxies add security, caching, and routing intelligence. CDNs push content to the edge, serving users from the nearest location on Earth. Together, these three patterns form the backbone of every production web service. If you run anything that serves HTTP traffic, you need to understand every concept in this chapter.

Here's the critical insight that most engineers learn the hard way: adding a load balancer doesn't magically make your application scalable. You need to understand which algorithm to choose (round-robin for stateless apps, least-connections for WebSockets), where to terminate TLS (at the LB or end-to-end?), how health checks work (active vs passive), and what happens when a backend fails mid-connection (existing TCP connections break — only new connections get routed to healthy backends). This chapter gives you that understanding, grounded in real anihpj architecture patterns.

🟡 INTERMEDIATE ⏱️ ~2 hours ⚖️ Load Balancing 🌍 CDN

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:

  • Design production-ready multi-tier load balancing architectures (L4 + L7 together)
  • Choose the right load balancing algorithm for any workload (sticky, stateless, streaming)
  • Configure health checks that actually detect failures (not just "port is open")
  • Architect high-availability load balancers with VIPs and VRRP/keepalived
  • Understand when DSR is worth the complexity and when it's not
  • Design CDN strategies with cache invalidation that don't break your application
  • Debug proxy header issues (X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto) that silently break auth and logging
🔗 Applies To:
DevOps
SRE
Cloud Eng
Backend Dev
SysAdmin
Weight: Every production service sits behind a load balancer. LB misconfiguration is the #2 cause of production outages (after TLS certificate expiry).
💡 Understanding "Why" Before "How"

Load balancing and reverse proxying are patterns, not products. nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB, and Envoy are implementations of the same core ideas. Key concepts to internalize:

  • The proxy chain is invisible to your application — until it breaks. Your Django app sees a request from 127.0.0.1 (nginx) not the real client IP. X-Forwarded headers carry the truth — but only if you trust the proxy sending them. A misconfigured proxy chain silently breaks authentication, rate limiting, and audit logging.
  • Health checks are the most important 10 lines of configuration you'll write. A health check that returns 200 OK but doesn't verify the database is connected gives you a false sense of safety. Design health checks that exercise the critical path — database connectivity, cache availability, disk space.
  • Load balancing algorithms have profound performance implications. Round-robin on WebSocket connections creates severe imbalance. Least-connections on stateless HTTP wastes CPU comparing connection counts. The right algorithm depends entirely on your workload characteristics.

14.1 Reverse Proxies — The Front Door to Your Application

A forward proxy sits in front of clients (your office proxy that filters web traffic). A reverse proxy sits in front of servers — it receives requests from the internet and forwards them to backend servers. Every modern web application, including anihpj, uses a reverse proxy as its first line of defense.

The genius of the reverse proxy pattern is separation of concerns. Your application code (Django/gunicorn) focuses purely on business logic — handling requests, querying databases, returning JSON. The reverse proxy handles everything else: TLS termination, request buffering, rate limiting, compression, caching, and security headers. This means your app developers don't need to be TLS experts, and your operations team can update TLS configuration without touching application code. When you debug a production issue, the reverse proxy is always your first stop — its access logs show every request before it reaches your app, making it the single best place to understand what's happening to your traffic.

🔄 Forward Proxy vs Reverse Proxy
FeatureForward ProxyReverse Proxy
Sits in front ofClients (your laptop)Servers (your web app)
PurposeHide client identity, filter content, cacheHide server identity, TLS termination, load balance, cache
ExamplesSquid, corporate proxy, VPNnginx, HAProxy, Envoy, AWS ALB
anihpj usageYour office network proxynginx in front of gunicorn/Django

A reverse proxy is the single entry point for all external traffic to your application. Instead of exposing gunicorn directly to the internet (which would require gunicorn to handle TLS, deal with slow clients, and manage security), you place nginx in front. Nginx handles the tedious cross-cutting concerns — TLS certificates, request buffering, rate limiting, compression — while gunicorn focuses purely on running your Django application. This separation of concerns is why virtually every production web deployment uses a reverse proxy.

Why Every Production App Uses a Reverse Proxy

The reverse proxy pattern solves a fundamental design problem: HTTP servers (like gunicorn) are not suitable for direct internet exposure. Gunicorn is designed to run your Python code fast — not to handle TLS negotiation, buffer slow clients, or defend against malicious requests. If you expose gunicorn directly to the internet, a single slow client (sending 1 byte per second) can tie up a worker process indefinitely. A malicious client can send garbage data that crashes your WSGI parser. The reverse proxy absorbs all of this — it buffers complete requests before forwarding them, handles TLS with hardware-accelerated AES, and drops obviously malicious traffic at the edge.

This is the separation of concerns that makes modern web architecture work: your application code handles business logic, your reverse proxy handles everything else. When you need to update TLS ciphers, you change the nginx config — not your Django settings. When you need to add rate limiting, it's a few lines in nginx — no application code changes. This decoupling is why the pattern is universal: every major web framework (Django, Rails, Express, Spring) recommends running behind a reverse proxy in production.

NGINX REVERSE PROXY — The Front Door to Your Django Application
