🛡️ SRE Reality Check — The Reverse Proxy Is Your First Line of Defense

When an incident strikes and your application is returning 500s, the reverse proxy's access log is your single most valuable diagnostic tool. It shows every request — including the ones that never reached your application. Key patterns to recognize in nginx access logs:

  • 499 (Client Closed Request): The client disconnected before nginx finished processing. Usually means your backend is too slow — users are giving up. Check upstream_response_time.
  • 502 (Bad Gateway): nginx received an invalid response from gunicorn. Gunicorn might be crashing mid-response. Check gunicorn logs for tracebacks and OOM kills.
  • 504 (Gateway Timeout): gunicorn didn't respond within proxy_read_timeout (default 60s). Your Django view is too slow — check database query performance.
  • 200 with 0 bytes: Application returned empty body. Often means gunicorn worker died between accepting and processing the request. Check worker timeout settings.

Pro tip: Always configure proxy_set_header X-Request-ID $request_id; in nginx (nginx 1.11.0+). This generates a unique ID for every request that you can trace through nginx → gunicorn → Django → logs. When debugging a specific user's problem, this UUID connects all the dots.

14.2 Load Balancing — Spreading the Load

A single server can only handle so many requests before it saturates — running out of CPU, memory, or network bandwidth. A load balancer distributes incoming requests across multiple backend servers, making your application horizontally scalable. Add more backends, handle more traffic — no code changes needed.

Load balancers operate at two different layers of the network stack, and choosing the right one has profound implications for your architecture. An L4 load balancer works at the TCP/UDP level — it sees IP addresses and ports, nothing more. It's blindingly fast because it operates in the kernel, but it can't route based on URL paths or HTTP headers. An L7 load balancer understands HTTP — it can inspect headers, cookies, and URL paths to make intelligent routing decisions. The tradeoff is performance vs flexibility: L4 is faster but dumber, L7 is smarter but consumes more resources. In modern infrastructure, you often use both: an L4 load balancer (like AWS NLB) in front of L7 load balancers (like nginx or Envoy), getting the best of both worlds.

⚖️ Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing
FeatureL4 (TCP/UDP)L7 (HTTP/HTTPS)
How it routesBy IP:Port (5-tuple hash)By HTTP headers, path, host, cookies
Can route by URL?❌ No✅ Yes (/api/ → backend-a, /static/ → backend-b)
TLS termination?❌ Pass-through only✅ Can terminate and re-encrypt
PerformanceVery high (kernel-level)High (user-space, but optimized)
ExamplesAWS NLB, HAProxy (TCP mode)AWS ALB, nginx, Envoy, Traefik

The Load Balancing Decision — It's All About Your Workload

Choosing a load balancing algorithm isn't about picking the "best" one — it's about matching the algorithm to your workload characteristics. Here's what happens when you get it wrong:

  • Round-robin on WebSocket connections: WebSocket connections are long-lived (minutes to hours). Round-robin distributes them evenly at connection time, but over time, some backends accumulate more long-lived connections than others. You end up with connection imbalance — one backend at 90% memory while others are idle.
  • Least-connections on stateless HTTP: For short-lived HTTP requests (milliseconds), connection counts are meaningless — they change too fast. The overhead of tracking and comparing connection counts actually adds latency with no benefit.
  • IP hash on mobile users: Mobile users switch IPs constantly (Wi-Fi → cellular → different cell towers). IP hash sends the same user to DIFFERENT backends as they move, breaking session affinity exactly when you need it most.

The golden rule: For stateless HTTP APIs (like a REST API serving JSON), round-robin is perfect — simple, fast, and fair. For stateful connections (WebSocket, gRPC streams), use least-connections. For caching layers, use consistent hashing. For heterogeneous server pools, use weighted algorithms.

LOAD BALANCING ALGORITHM DECISION TREE — Choose the Right Algorithm
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  START: What type of workload are you load balancing?                      │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌─ STATELESS HTTP (REST APIs, web pages)?                                │
│  │  └─ Are all backends identical?                                        │
│  │     ├─ YES → ROUND-ROBIN (simple, fair, fast)                         │
│  │     └─ NO (different instance sizes) → WEIGHTED ROUND-ROBIN           │
│  │                                                                        │
│  ├─ STATEFUL / LONG-LIVED (WebSocket, gRPC, SSH tunneling)?              │
│  │  └─ LEAST CONNECTIONS (prevents connection pile-up on one backend)    │
│  │                                                                        │
│  ├─ CACHING LAYER (Redis cluster, Memcached, CDN origin)?               │
│  │  └─ CONSISTENT HASHING (minimizes cache invalidation on scale-up/down)│
│  │                                                                        │
│  ├─ NEED SESSION AFFINITY (sticky sessions)?                              │
│  │  ├─ Can use cookies? → L7 COOKIE-BASED STICKINESS (most reliable)    │
│  │  └─ No cookies? → IP HASH (works but breaks on mobile/NAT changes)   │
│  │                                                                        │
│  └─ CANARY DEPLOYMENTS (10% traffic to new version)?                     │
│     └─ WEIGHTED (set weights: v1=90, v2=10. Adjust gradually.)          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🎯 Load Balancing Algorithms — Complete Reference
AlgorithmHow It WorksBest ForPitfall
Round RobinEach backend gets requests in turn. Simple, fair.Identical backends, stateless appsIgnores connection duration — can create imbalance with long-lived connections
Least ConnectionsSend to the backend with fewest active connectionsLong-lived connections (WebSocket, gRPC)Overhead for short-lived HTTP; connection count is stale by the time you read it
IP HashHash client IP to always send to same backendSticky sessions without cookiesBreaks on mobile (IP changes), NAT (many users share one IP → all go to same backend!)
WeightedBackends have weights; larger instances get more trafficHeterogeneous servers, canary deploysWeights must be tuned; wrong weights cause over/under-utilization
RandomPick a random healthy backendSimple, surprisingly effective at scaleNot deterministic; hard to reason about during debugging
Consistent HashingHash request attribute to a ring. Backend change only remaps ~1/N keys (minimal disruption)Distributed caches (Redis cluster), CDN originsMore complex to implement; requires ring management
🏥 Health Checks — How Load Balancers Know Backends Are Alive

A load balancer is only as good as its health checks. Two types: Active (LB probes /health every N seconds) and Passive (LB observes real traffic failures and marks backend unhealthy).

Check TypeHow It WorksDetection SpeedBest For
TCP ConnectCan the LB establish a TCP connection to backend:port?Fast (~1s)Any TCP service
HTTP GETDoes GET /health return 200 OK?Fast (~1s)Web apps, APIs
HTTP with Body CheckDoes response body contain expected text (e.g., "ok")?Medium (~1-2s)Apps that return 200 even when broken
Custom ScriptRun a script that checks DB connectivity, disk space, etc.Slow (~5-30s)Complex health dependencies
Passive (observing)Track real requests: 3 consecutive TCP errors = unhealthyDepends on trafficReducing probe load at scale
 
# K8s READINESSPROBE (active health check):
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8000
  initialDelaySeconds: 5   # Wait 5s after start before first probe
  periodSeconds: 10         # Probe every 10 seconds
  failureThreshold: 3       # 3 consecutive failures = pod removed from Service
⚠️ GOTCHA — Sticky Sessions Break on Pod Restart

Sticky sessions (session affinity) bind a client to a specific backend. In K8s, when a pod restarts, it gets a NEW IP — breaking the stickiness. Use external session stores (Redis) instead of LB stickiness for stateful apps. AWS ALB supports application-based stickiness via cookies which survives backend IP changes.

14.3 VIPs & High Availability Load Balancing

If your load balancer is a single server, it's a single point of failure. When it goes down, your entire application becomes unreachable — even if all your backend servers are perfectly healthy. This is the "load balancer paradox": the thing that's supposed to make your system more reliable has itself become the biggest reliability risk. The solution is a Virtual IP (VIP): one IP address that floats between multiple load balancer servers. If the active LB fails, the VIP seamlessly moves to a standby LB, and traffic continues flowing without clients even noticing the change.

How VRRP Actually Works — The Heartbeat Protocol

The magic behind VIPs is VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol), implemented on Linux by keepalived. Two servers share a virtual IP. One is the MASTER (owns the VIP), the other is BACKUP (watches and waits). They exchange VRRP advertisement packets (heartbeats) every 1 second by default. If the backup misses 3 consecutive heartbeats (configurable), it assumes the master is dead and promotes itself.

But here's the critical detail most engineers miss: the failover isn't instantaneous. With default settings (1s advertisements, 3s timeout), failover takes 3-4 seconds. During those 3-4 seconds, ALL traffic to the VIP is blackholed — TCP connections timeout, HTTP requests fail, users see errors. This is why you tune VRRP for faster failover in production: advert_int 0.5 (500ms advertisements) with a 3x multiplier = 1.5 second failover. But go too fast and you risk flapping — a brief network hiccup causes the backup to take over, then the master comes back and takes over again, then the backup takes over... each transition causing a few seconds of downtime.

When the backup promotes to MASTER, it takes ownership of the VIP and sends a gratuitous ARP — a special ARP packet that says "the IP 10.0.1.100 is now at MY MAC address." Every switch on the network updates its MAC address table, and within seconds, all traffic flows to the new master. This is the same mechanism that MetalLB and kube-vip use to provide LoadBalancer-type Services in bare-metal Kubernetes clusters — they announce Service IPs via ARP or BGP, and if the announcing node fails, another node takes over.

⚠️ GOTCHA — Both VRRP Nodes Must Be in the Same L2 Domain

VRRP works at Layer 2 — it uses multicast MAC addresses (01:00:5E:00:00:12) and gratuitous ARP, neither of which cross routers. If your two load balancer nodes are in different subnets (different availability zones), VRRP CANNOT work. This is a fundamental limitation: VRRP-based HA requires both nodes on the same broadcast domain. For cross-AZ HA, you need DNS-based failover (Route 53), BGP-based VIP announcements (MetalLB BGP mode), or cloud-native load balancers (AWS NLB/ALB which handle HA internally).

KEEPALIVED — Two Nodes Sharing a VIP, One Is Master
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NODE 1 (MASTER)                         NODE 2 (BACKUP)              │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐                ┌─────────────────────┐       │
│  │ IP: 10.0.1.10       │                │ IP: 10.0.1.11       │       │
│  │ VIP: 10.0.1.100 ✓   │   VRRP         │ VIP: (standby)      │       │
│  │ keepalived: MASTER  │◄──────────────►│ keepalived: BACKUP  │       │
│  │                     │  heartbeats    │                     │       │
│  │ Sends gratuitous ARP│                │ If master fails:     │       │
│  │ "10.0.1.100 is at   │                │ ① Detects failure   │       │
│  │  MAC aa:bb:cc:dd"   │                │ ② Takes MASTER role │       │
│  └─────────────────────┘                │ ③ Sends gratuitous  │       │
│                                          │    ARP for VIP      │       │
│  WHEN MASTER FAILS:                     │ ④ Traffic now flows │       │
│  ‣ Backup detects no heartbeats         │    to Node 2!       │       │
│  ‣ Backup promotes to MASTER            └─────────────────────┘       │
│  ‣ Backup sends gratuitous ARP                                       │
│  ‣ Network switches update MAC table                                 │
│  ‣ Traffic flows to new master (Node 2)                              │
│                                                                       │
│  IN KUBERNETES (bare-metal):                                          │
│  ‣ MetalLB: announces Service LoadBalancer IPs via ARP/BGP           │
│  ‣ kube-vip: provides VIP for control plane HA                       │
│  ‣ Same principle: one IP, multiple possible owners                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

14.4 DSR — Direct Server Return

In normal load balancing, ALL traffic flows through the LB (both directions). This creates a bottleneck — the LB's bandwidth limits total throughput. Direct Server Return solves this: the LB forwards the request to a backend, but the backend responds directly to the client, bypassing the LB on the return path. Used in high-throughput scenarios (video streaming, CDN origins). Tradeoffs: DSR breaks TLS termination (backend must handle TLS), complicates firewalls (asymmetric routing), and requires backend servers to respond with the VIP as source IP.

How DSR Actually Works — Two Implementation Approaches

There are two ways to implement DSR, and they operate at different network layers:

L2 DSR (MAC Address Rewriting): The load balancer receives the packet destined for the VIP. Instead of changing the destination IP (which would require the LB to also handle the return path), the LB rewrites the destination MAC address to the chosen backend's MAC — and forwards the packet unchanged at L3. The backend receives a packet destined for the VIP (its loopback interface is configured with the VIP), processes it, and responds directly to the client. The client sees the response coming from the VIP — it has no idea the response bypassed the LB. This requires the LB and all backends to be in the same L2 broadcast domain (same VLAN, same switch). It's the simplest and fastest form of DSR.

L3 DSR (IP Tunneling / IPIP): The LB encapsulates the original packet inside a new IP packet addressed to the backend. The backend decapsulates (strips the outer IP header), processes the original request, and responds directly to the client with the VIP as source IP. This works across L3 boundaries — backends can be in different subnets, even different data centers. The cost is encapsulation overhead (~20 bytes per packet for the outer IP header) and additional configuration complexity on every backend (tunnel interfaces).

When DSR Makes Sense — and When It Doesn't

DSR shines when response traffic dwarfs request traffic. Video streaming: request is "GET /video.mp4" (~200 bytes), response is the 500MB video file. Without DSR, the LB must handle 500MB of egress for every request. With DSR, the LB handles 200 bytes, and the backend's NIC handles the 500MB directly. At scale (10 Gbps+), this is the difference between needing a $50K load balancer appliance and using commodity servers.

DSR is a poor fit when you need TLS termination, L7 routing, or response inspection. Since the response bypasses the LB entirely, the LB can't add security headers, compress responses, or log response codes. TLS must be handled by the backend (increasing backend CPU load). Firewalls see asymmetric traffic (request goes through LB, response comes from backend directly) and may drop the response as "unsolicited." And debugging is harder because tcpdump on the LB only shows half the conversation.

The rule of thumb: Use DSR only when you've measured that egress bandwidth through the LB is your bottleneck, and you've exhausted simpler optimizations (enabling sendfile, increasing MTU, using HTTP/2 multiplexing). For 95% of applications, a standard reverse proxy with TLS termination is the right architecture. DSR is an advanced optimization pattern, not a default choice.

Normal LB (Symmetric) vs DSR (Asymmetric — Response Bypasses LB)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NORMAL LB (all traffic flows through LB in both directions):         │
│  ┌────────┐     request     ┌────────┐     request     ┌──────────┐  │
│  │ CLIENT │ ──────────────▶ │   LB   │ ──────────────▶ │ BACKEND  │  │
│  │        │ ◀────────────── │        │ ◀────────────── │          │  │
│  └────────┘    response     └────────┘    response     └──────────┘  │
│  LB handles both directions → LB bandwidth = total system capacity!  │
│                                                                       │
│  DSR (response bypasses LB — backend sends directly to client):      │
│  ┌────────┐     request     ┌────────┐     request     ┌──────────┐  │
│  │ CLIENT │ ──────────────▶ │   LB   │ ──────────────▶ │ BACKEND  │  │
│  │        │ ◀────────────── │        │                 │          │  │
│  └────────┘    response     └────────┘                 └──────────┘  │
│       ▲                        │                                      │
│       └────────────────────────┘  (response bypasses LB entirely!)   │
│                                                                       │
│  TRADEOFFS:                                                           │
│  ‣ Breaks TLS termination (backend must handle TLS)                  │
│  ‣ Complicates firewalls (asymmetric routing)                        │

│  ‣ Used for: video streaming, CDN origins, high-throughput scenarios │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

14.6 CDNs — Caching at the Edge

A CDN (Content Delivery Network) caches your content at edge locations worldwide. When a user requests jobpost.anihpj.com, the CDN serves cached content from the nearest edge (5ms latency) instead of the origin server (100ms latency). This isn't just a performance optimization — it's the difference between a usable application and an unusable one for users far from your origin. CDN providers: CloudFront (AWS, 400+ edge locations), Cloudflare (330+ cities), Fastly (high-performance edge compute).

Why CDNs Matter — The Physics of Light

Light travels at ~200,000 km/s through fiber optic cable. That means every 1,000 km of distance adds ~5ms of latency — and that's just the speed of light, ignoring router hops, congestion, and TCP slow start. A user in Lagos, Nigeria accessing a server in us-east-1 (Virginia, USA) is ~8,500 km away — that's ~42ms of unavoidable physics-induced latency. Add DNS (5ms), TCP handshake (10ms), TLS handshake (50ms), and application processing (100ms), and you're at 200ms+ just to load a single page. A CDN edge in Lagos (or nearby) brings that down to ~5ms network latency — a 40× improvement. This is why CDNs aren't optional for global applications — they're a fundamental requirement.

The fundamental tradeoff of a CDN is freshness vs latency. If you cache aggressively, users get lightning-fast responses but may see stale data. If you cache conservatively, data is fresh but every request hits the origin — defeating the purpose. The solution is a cache invalidation strategy: when content changes at the origin, you must tell the CDN to purge the old cached version. Versioned URLs (/static/style.a1b2c3d.css) make this trivial — each deploy generates new filenames, so there's nothing to invalidate. For API responses, use short TTLs or surrogate key-based invalidation.

│  │Sydney Eg.│     │Paris Edge│     │ consolidates │     │             │  │
│  │(miss)────┘     │(miss)────┘     │ requests ────┘     │             │  │
│  └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────────┘     └─────────────┘  │
│  Without shield: 10 edges all miss simultaneously → 10 origin requests!   │
│  WITH shield: Shield makes ONE origin request, serves all 10 edges.       │
│                                                                           │
│  CACHE INVALIDATION STRATEGIES:                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │ 1. VERSIONED URLs:  /static/main.a1b2c3d.js → new hash = new URL│     │
│  │ 2. CACHE-BUSTING:   /api/jobs/?v=123 → query string change       │     │
│  │ 3. PURGE API:       POST /purge { "path": "/api/jobs/" }         │     │
│  │ 4. TTL-BASED:       Cache-Control: max-age=3600 (auto-expire)   │     │
│  │ 5. SURROGATE KEYS:  Tag responses, purge by tag (Fastly/Akamai) │     │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Cache Invalidation — The Hardest CDN Problem, Solved

Cache invalidation is famously one of the "two hard problems in computer science" (along with naming things and off-by-one errors). When content changes at the origin, every CDN edge that cached the old version must be told to discard it. If your TTL is 24 hours and you deploy a critical bug fix, users see the broken version for up to 24 hours — unless you invalidate. Versioned URLs (/static/main.a1b2c3d.js) are the most elegant solution: each deploy produces new filenames, so there's nothing to invalidate — the CDN sees new URLs and fetches them from origin. This is why modern build tools (webpack, Vite) include content hashes in output filenames by default.

For API responses that can't use versioned URLs, surrogate key-based invalidation (Fastly, Akamai) is the most powerful approach: tag each cached response with keys like job-list page-3, then issue a single purge for job-list to invalidate all cached job listings across all pages simultaneously. CloudFront supports invalidation by path prefix (/api/jobs/*) but charges for invalidation requests beyond 1,000/month — plan your strategy accordingly. Cloudflare's "Cache Everything" with "Cache Rules" gives fine-grained control per URL pattern.

Origin shielding is another critical CDN concept most engineers overlook. Without a shield, when content expires from 10 different edge locations simultaneously, all 10 edges hammer the origin server at the same instant — the "thundering herd" problem. An origin shield sits between the edges and the origin, consolidating requests: only the shield asks the origin, and all 10 edges get the cached response from the shield. This prevents origin overload during cache expiry spikes and is essential for any application with a single origin that can't handle edge-level traffic bursts.

upstream backend {

}

🔭 Chapter 14 — Visual Summary

🔄Reverse Proxy

nginx sits in front of gunicorn. Handles TLS, routing, caching, rate limiting. Forward proxy = client-side, reverse = server-side.

⚖️L4 vs L7 LB

L4 routes by IP:Port (kernel-speed). L7 routes by HTTP headers/path/cookies (application-smart). Use both: L4 in front, L7 behind.

🎯LB Algorithms

Round-Robin (stateless), Least-Conn (WebSocket), Consistent Hash (caching), Weighted (canary). Wrong algorithm = imbalanced backends.

📡VIP + VRRP

One IP, multiple servers. keepalived elects MASTER/BACKUP. Gratuitous ARP on failover. Requires same L2 domain.

🔄DSR

Direct Server Return: backend responds directly to client, bypassing LB. Bandwidth scales to backend NIC speed, not LB speed.

🌍CDN Physics

Content at edge = 5ms. Origin = 100ms+. Speed of light is the ultimate limiter. Cache invalidation is the hardest CDN problem.

🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work

Every API you deploy should sit behind a reverse proxy. Directly exposing gunicorn, Express, or Flask to the internet is a recipe for slow-client DoS and TLS complexity. nginx or Envoy should always be the first thing that receives external traffic. In Kubernetes, this means your Ingress controller (nginx-ingress, Traefik, Istio Gateway) is your reverse proxy — configure it properly.

When the site is slow, check the load balancer first — not the app. Are backends healthy? Is one backend overloaded (check connection counts)? Is the health check path correct? A misconfigured health check can mark perfectly healthy backends as unhealthy, routing all traffic to a single surviving backend and causing a cascading overload.

X-Forwarded headers silently break authentication and logging. If your Django app sees all requests coming from 10.0.1.5 (the nginx pod IP), your rate limiting blocks everyone after one user exceeds the limit, your audit logs are useless, and your geo-IP features break. Always verify your proxy header chain end-to-end.

CDN cache invalidation strategy affects your deployment process. If you deploy a new frontend but the CDN still serves the old JavaScript bundle for 24 hours, users see a broken application. Use versioned filenames (main.a1b2c3d.js) tied to your build process — deploy = new filenames = no invalidation needed.

🔑 Chapter 14 Key Takeaways

  1. Reverse proxies are non-negotiable in production. They handle TLS, buffering, rate limiting, and security — concerns your application code should never touch. nginx in front of gunicorn is the universal pattern for a reason.
  2. Choose your load balancing algorithm based on your workload. Round-robin for stateless HTTP APIs. Least-connections for WebSocket/gRPC. Consistent hashing for caching layers. Wrong algorithm = imbalanced backends + wasted capacity.
  3. Health checks must exercise the critical path. A TCP-connect health check tells you the port is open — nothing about whether the app can query the database. Design health checks that fail when the application is degraded, not just when it's crashed.
  4. VRRP/keepalived HA requires same L2 domain. For cross-AZ HA, use cloud-native LBs (ALB/NLB), BGP-based VIPs (MetalLB), or DNS failover (Route 53). VRRP cannot cross subnets.
  5. CDNs solve the physics problem. Speed of light limits long-distance latency. CDN edges bring content physically closer to users. Versioned URLs eliminate cache invalidation — the most elegant solution to the hardest CDN problem.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 14

🔄Reverse Proxy
Sits in front of servers. Receives requests from clients, forwards to backends. Handles TLS termination, routing, caching, compression. Examples: nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, AWS ALB.
⚖️Load Balancer
Distributes traffic across multiple backends for scale and reliability. L4 (TCP, by IP:Port) or L7 (HTTP, by path/headers/cookies). Algorithms: round-robin, least-conn, IP hash, weighted.
🔀DSR
Direct Server Return: request flows through LB, response goes directly from backend to client. Eliminates LB bandwidth bottleneck. Used in high-throughput scenarios.
🌍CDN
Content Delivery Network: caches content at edge locations worldwide. Reduces latency (edge = 5ms vs origin = 100ms). Cache invalidation via versioned URLs or purge APIs.
🔧X-Forwarded-For
HTTP header added by proxies to preserve the original client IP. Essential for logging, rate limiting, and geo-IP when behind a load balancer or CDN.
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 14.1 — Choose the Right Load Balancing Algorithm

For each scenario below, identify the best load balancing algorithm and explain why the alternatives would be wrong:

  1. A stateless REST API serving JSON. 4 identical backend pods in a Kubernetes Deployment. Requests take ~20ms each. No session state.
  2. A WebSocket chat application with 1,000 concurrent users. Connections stay open for 10-60 minutes. Some users are more chatty than others.
  3. A Redis cluster with 6 shards. Each key is hashed to a specific shard. You want to add a 7th shard with minimal cache invalidation.
  4. A canary deployment: 5% of traffic should go to the new version (v2), 95% to the stable version (v1). You'll gradually increase v2's share.
  5. An NGINX reverse proxy forwarding to gunicorn backends of different sizes: two 4-core instances and one 8-core instance.
💡 Hint: The algorithm must match the workload. Stateless + fast = simple. Stateful + long-lived = connection-aware. Caching = minimal disruption. Heterogeneous = weighted.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. REST API: ROUND-ROBIN
# Stateless, fast, identical backends. Round-robin is simple and fair.
# Least-connections adds unnecessary overhead for 20ms requests.
# IP hash adds no value (no sessions).

# 2. WebSocket chat: LEAST CONNECTIONS
# Connections are long-lived and chatty users accumulate.
# Round-robin at connection time is fair, but over hours, some
# backends have more active chatters → connection pile-up.
# Least-connections continuously rebalances based on current load.

# 3. Redis cluster: CONSISTENT HASHING
# Adding a 7th shard with modulo hashing invalidates 6/7 (~86%) of keys!
# Consistent hashing only remaps ~1/7 (~14%) of keys to the new shard.
# This minimizes cache misses during cluster scaling.

# 4. Canary deployment: WEIGHTED
# Set weights: v1=95, v2=5. Gradually shift to v1=0, v2=100.
# Only algorithm that lets you control traffic distribution percentages.

# 5. Different-sized backends: WEIGHTED ROUND-ROBIN
# 8-core instance gets 2× weight of 4-core instances.
# Without weights, the 8-core runs at 50% while 4-cores run at 100%.
# Weighted distributes proportional to capacity.
⏱️ Target: 7 minutes
Drill 14.2 — Debug Proxy Header Issues

Your Django application's rate limiter is blocking ALL users after just one user exceeds the limit. Looking at the Django access logs, you notice every request shows the same IP: 10.244.1.5. The X-Forwarded-For header shows: 203.0.113.42, 10.244.1.5.

  1. Why does Django see 10.244.1.5 as the client IP instead of the real IP?
  2. What is the X-Forwarded-For chain telling you about the request path?
  3. How would you fix this in Django and in nginx?
  4. What's the security risk of blindly trusting X-Forwarded-For?
  5. On your machine, run: curl -v http://localhost:8000/api/health (direct to gunicorn) and curl -v http://localhost/api/health (through nginx). Compare the headers. Which request has X-Forwarded-For?
💡 Hint: Django's REMOTE_ADDR is the IP of the machine that established the TCP connection — which is the proxy, not the client. X-Forwarded-For carries the original IP but Django doesn't use it unless configured to trust proxies.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. Django sees 10.244.1.5 because that's the nginx pod IP —
#    the TCP connection is from nginx → gunicorn, so REMOTE_ADDR = nginx IP.
#    Django doesn't use X-Forwarded-For unless configured.

# 2. The X-Forwarded-For chain: 203.0.113.42 (real client), 10.244.1.5 (nginx).
#    In this case, the chain is short but reveals the traffic path.

# 3. FIX — Django settings:
#    USE_X_FORWARDED_HOST = True
#    SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ('HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO', 'https')
#    # For the IP, use django-ipware or configure trusted proxies:
#    # MIDDLEWARE: 'django.middleware.security.SetRemoteAddrFromForwardedFor'
#    # (Only works if you trust the proxy sending the header!)

#    FIX — nginx:
#    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
#    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
#    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;

# 4. SECURITY RISK: Any client can send X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1!
#    If Django trusts this header from untrusted sources, attackers
#    can spoof IPs — bypass rate limiting, access controls, audit trails.
#    ALWAYS: nginx must STRIP incoming X-Forwarded-For, then SET its own.
#    nginx $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for does this correctly.

# 5. curl direct to gunicorn → NO X-Forwarded-For (no proxy involved)
#    curl through nginx → HAS X-Forwarded-For (nginx adds it)
#    This confirms: the proxy adds the header. Without it, the backend
#    can't know the real client IP.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 14.3 — Design a Multi-Tier Load Balancing Architecture

Design the load balancing architecture for anihpj jobpost that needs to:

  1. Handle 50,000 requests/second globally
  2. Serve static assets (CSS, JS, images) from edge locations
  3. Route API requests based on URL path: /api/auth/* → auth service, /api/jobs/* → jobs service
  4. Support WebSocket connections for real-time job notifications
  5. Survive the failure of an entire AWS availability zone

Draw the architecture (on paper). Identify each component, what type of load balancer it is (L4/L7), and what algorithm it should use.

💡 Hint: Use multiple tiers. CDN at the edge (CloudFront). L7 LB for path-based routing (ALB or nginx). Separate handling for WebSocket connections. Cross-AZ requires cloud-native LB or DNS failover — VRRP can't cross subnets.
📝 View Solution 
# ARCHITECTURE LAYERS (front to back):

# LAYER 1 — CDN (CloudFront):
# - Static assets cached at 400+ edge locations
# - Cache behavior: /static/* → S3 origin, /api/* → ALB origin
# - DDoS protection, TLS termination at edge
# Algorithm: Geographic routing (nearest edge). Cache TTL-based.

# LAYER 2 — L7 Load Balancer (AWS ALB, cross-AZ):
# - Path-based routing rules:
#   /api/auth/* → auth-service target group
#   /api/jobs/* → jobpost-service target group
#   /ws/*        → websocket target group (sticky sessions via cookie)
# - TLS termination at ALB
# - Health checks: HTTP GET /health on each target group
# Algorithm:
#   - auth/jobs: Round-robin (stateless REST)
#   - websocket: Least outstanding requests (long-lived connections)

# LAYER 3 — Kubernetes Ingress (nginx-ingress, per-cluster):
# - Receives from ALB, routes to ClusterIP Services
# - Handles finer-grained routing within K8s
# Algorithm: Round-robin (pods are identical)

# CROSS-AZ RESILIENCE:
# - ALB spans 3 AZs automatically (AWS managed)
# - Target groups have instances in all 3 AZs
# - If AZ-1 fails, ALB health checks detect it
# - Traffic automatically routed to AZ-2 and AZ-3
# - No VRRP needed — ALB handles HA internally

# WHY THIS ARCHITECTURE:
# - CDN handles 90% of traffic (static assets) at edge
# - ALB handles dynamic routing + TLS + cross-AZ HA
# - K8s Ingress handles internal pod routing
# - Multiple tiers = each tier optimized for its job
# - No single point of failure at any tier

📝 Chapter 14 — Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy?
Show Answer
Answer

Forward proxy sits in front of CLIENTS — it makes requests on behalf of clients (hiding client identity, filtering content). Reverse proxy sits in front of SERVERS — it receives requests from clients and forwards them to backends (hiding server identity, TLS termination, load balancing). Forward = client-side, Reverse = server-side.

Q2
What's the difference between L4 and L7 load balancing? When would you use each?
Show Answer
Answer

L4 (TCP/UDP) routes by IP:Port using 5-tuple hash. No visibility into HTTP. Very high performance. Use for: non-HTTP protocols (gRPC, databases), simple TCP load balancing. L7 (HTTP) routes by headers, path, host, cookies. Can terminate TLS, compress, cache. Use for: HTTP APIs, path-based routing (/api/ vs /static/), cookie-based stickiness.

Q3
Explain three load balancing algorithms and when to use each.
Show Answer
Answer

Round-Robin: each backend gets requests in turn. Best for stateless apps with identical backends. Least Connections: send to backend with fewest active connections. Best for long-lived connections (WebSocket, streaming). IP Hash: hash client IP to always send to same backend. Use for sticky sessions without cookies. Weighted: assign weights to backends for heterogeneous server sizes or canary deploys.

Q4
What is Direct Server Return (DSR) and why is it used?
Show Answer
Answer

DSR is a load balancing pattern where the LB forwards requests to backends, but backends respond DIRECTLY to the client — bypassing the LB on the return path. This eliminates the LB as a bandwidth bottleneck. Used for high-throughput scenarios (video streaming, CDN origins). Tradeoffs: breaks TLS termination, complicates firewalls, requires backends to respond with VIP as source IP.

Q5
How does a CDN work? What happens on a cache miss vs cache hit?
Show Answer
Answer

CDN caches content at edge locations worldwide. Cache hit: user request → nearest edge → cached content served (~5ms). Cache miss: user request → edge → origin server → edge caches and serves (~100ms). Subsequent requests get cache hits. Cache invalidation: purge cached content when origin changes. Use versioned URLs (style.v2.css) to avoid stale cache issues.

Q6
What is a reverse proxy and what functions does it typically perform?
Show Answer
Answer

A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers, receiving client requests and forwarding them. Functions: TLS termination (decrypt HTTPS, forward HTTP), load balancing (distribute across backends), caching (store responses), compression (gzip), rate limiting, authentication, request routing (path-based). Examples: nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, AWS ALB. In anihpj: nginx sits in front of gunicorn/Django.

Q7
How does keepalived/VRRP provide high availability? What happens during failover?
Show Answer
Answer

keepalived uses VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol). Two nodes share a Virtual IP (VIP). The MASTER owns the VIP and sends gratuitous ARP. The BACKUP monitors heartbeats. If the master fails (no heartbeats for 3× advert interval), the backup promotes to MASTER, sends its own gratuitous ARP to update switch MAC tables, and takes over the VIP. Failover typically takes 3-10 seconds. Both nodes must be in the same L2 domain.

Q8
What is Consistent Hashing and why is it important for load balancing?
Show Answer
Answer

Consistent Hashing maps requests to backends via a hash ring. When a backend is added or removed, only ~1/N of keys are remapped (vs all keys with modulo hashing). This minimizes cache invalidation and connection disruption. Critical for distributed caches (Redis cluster, Memcached) and CDN origin selection. Without it, adding one server invalidates ALL cached data across the entire cluster.

Q9
What are active vs passive health checks? Give examples of each.
Show Answer
Answer

Active: LB periodically probes backends (TCP connect, HTTP GET /health). Detects failures in ~1-10 seconds. Example: AWS ALB health checks, K8s readinessProbe. Passive: LB observes real traffic — if a backend returns 3 consecutive TCP errors or 5xx responses, it's marked unhealthy. Detects failures based on traffic volume. Example: Envoy outlier detection, HAProxy observe mode. Best practice: use BOTH for fastest detection.

Q10
What are X-Forwarded headers and why are they essential behind a proxy/LB?
Show Answer
Answer

When a request passes through proxies, the backend sees the PROXY's IP, not the client's. X-Forwarded-For preserves the original client IP through a chain of proxies (comma-separated list). X-Forwarded-Proto tells the backend whether the client used HTTP or HTTPS (essential when TLS terminates at LB). X-Forwarded-Host preserves the original Host header. Without these, logging shows wrong IPs, Django request.is_secure() returns False, and rate limiting breaks.

🟡 Part 5: Container Networking — Docker Under the HoodChapters 15-17

Chapter 15: Docker Networking Fundamentals — Under the Hood

Docker networking is Linux networking with a friendly CLI. Every container gets its own network namespace, a virtual Ethernet interface, and an IP from the Docker bridge. Understanding how veth pairs, bridges, iptables, and DNS work inside Docker is essential for debugging "my containers can't talk to each other" — and it's the foundation for understanding Kubernetes networking. This chapter pulls back the curtain on Docker networking.

🟡 INTERMEDIATE ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🐳 Docker 🔧 iptables

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:

  • Understand how Docker creates isolated networks using Linux network namespaces and veth pairs
  • Master all 6 Docker network drivers (bridge, host, none, overlay, macvlan, ipvlan) and when to use each
  • Trace a packet through Docker port mapping (-p 8000:8000) using iptables DNAT rules
  • Explain how Docker's built-in DNS (127.0.0.11) enables container name resolution
🔗 Applies To:
DevOps
SRE
Backend Dev
Cloud Eng
SysAdmin
Weight: Docker networking is Linux networking. Understanding it makes K8s networking intuitive.

15.1 How Docker Creates Isolated Networks

Docker uses Linux network namespaces — each container gets its own isolated network stack (interfaces, routing table, iptables rules). veth pairs act as a virtual Ethernet cable — one end in the container, one end plugged into the docker0 bridge on the host.

The beauty of Docker networking is that it uses standard Linux kernel features — there is no "Docker networking magic." Every container network is built from the same building blocks you'd use if you were manually creating isolated network environments with the ip command. This means that by understanding Docker networking, you're actually learning Linux networking — and that knowledge transfers directly to Kubernetes, systemd-nspawn, LXC, and any other container runtime.

Think about what happens when you run docker run -d --name web nginx. Before Docker existed, if you wanted to run nginx in isolation, you'd have to: create a network namespace, create a veth pair, move one end into the namespace, assign an IP address, set up routing, configure iptables for NAT, and start nginx inside the namespace. That's seven distinct Linux commands. Docker does all seven automatically in under a second. Understanding what's happening under the hood is what separates engineers who can debug container networking from those who just restart Docker and hope for the best.

The foundation of all container networking is the network namespace — a Linux kernel feature that gives a process its own private view of the network. Inside a network namespace, a process can have its own lo interface, its own eth0 with its own IP address, its own routing table, and its own iptables rules — completely invisible to processes in other namespaces. Two containers can both bind to port 8000 without conflict because they're in different namespaces. Two containers can have different default routes. One can have IPv6 enabled while another doesn't. This isolation is the magic that makes containers work — and it's all standard Linux, available since kernel 2.6.24 (2008).

But a network namespace alone is a lonely place — it has no connection to the outside world. To connect a namespace to the host's network, Docker creates a veth pair — think of it as a virtual Ethernet cable with two ends. One end goes inside the container's namespace (where it's renamed to eth0). The other end stays on the host and gets plugged into the docker0 bridge. The bridge acts like a virtual network switch — any frame that arrives on one port gets forwarded to the correct destination port based on MAC address. When container A pings container B by IP, ARP resolves the IP to MAC, and the bridge forwards between the two veth ports. When a container needs to reach the internet, the bridge forwards to the host's real eth0, and iptables MASQUERADE rewrites the source IP from the container's private IP to the host's public IP — the same NAT that your home router uses.

DOCKER DEFAULT BRIDGE NETWORK — Under the Hood
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          HOST (Linux)                                  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │                    iptables (NAT rules)                        │   │
│  │  -A POSTROUTING -s 172.17.0.0/16 ! -o docker0 -j MASQUERADE  │   │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐                       │

│  │  anihpj  │    │ postgres │    │  redis   │                       │

│  │ eth0     │    │ eth0     │    │ eth0     │                       │
│  └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘                       │
│       │veth           │veth            │veth                          │
│       │pair           │pair            │pair                          │
│  ┌────┴─────┐    ┌────┴─────┐    ┌────┴─────┐                       │
│  │ vethXXX  │    │ vethYYY  │    │ vethZZZ  │                       │
│  └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘                       │

$ sudo lsns -t net
        NS TYPE NPROCS   PID USER    COMMAND
4026531840 net     123     1 root    /sbin/init
4026532590 net       3  1234 root    /usr/bin/containerd-shim-runc-v2

🧬 Linux Network Namespaces — The Magic Behind Container Isolation

Every Docker container gets its own network namespace — a completely isolated network stack with its own interfaces, routing table, iptables rules, and socket list. This is a Linux kernel feature, not a Docker invention. Docker just automates the creation and wiring of namespaces.

# LIST ALL NETWORK NAMESPACES on the system:
$ sudo lsns -t net
        NS TYPE NPROCS   PID USER COMMAND
4026531840 net     145     1 root /sbin/init         # Host namespace
4026532590 net       3  5678 root containerd-shim    # Container 1
4026532710 net       2  6234 root containerd-shim    # Container 2

# INSPECT A CONTAINER'S NETNS FROM THE HOST:
$ PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' anihpj)
$ sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ip addr show
1: lo:  mtu 65536
2: eth0@if5:  mtu 1500
    inet 172.17.0.2/16 brd 172.17.255.255 scope global eth0
# We're now "inside" the container's network namespace from the host!

# RUN A COMMAND IN THE CONTAINER'S NETNS:
$ sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ip route show
default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0         # Gateway = docker0 bridge
172.17.0.0/16 dev eth0 proto kernel     # Local bridge subnet
� Docker IPAM — How IP Addresses Are Assigned and Managed

Docker's IP Address Management (IPAM) driver handles subnet allocation, IP assignment, and pool exhaustion. Understanding IPAM helps debug "why did my container get a weird IP?" and "why can't I create more containers?".

DOCKER IPAM — Subnet Allocation Hierarchy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     DOCKER IPAM SUBNET ALLOCATION MAP                       │
│                                                                           │
│  DEFAULT BRIDGE (hardcoded):  docker0: 172.17.0.0/16, Gateway: .1         │
│  Containers get sequential IPs: 172.17.0.2, .3, .4, ... (65,534 max)      │
│                                                                           │
│  USER-DEFINED NETWORKS (auto-allocated /16 blocks in sequence):            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1st net: 172.18.0.0/16     2nd: 172.19.0.0/16                      │ │
│  │  3rd:     172.20.0.0/16     ...up to 172.31.0.0/16 (14 total)       │ │
│  │  THEN wraps: 192.168.0.0/20, 192.168.16.0/20, 192.168.32.0/20...   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  CUSTOM SUBNET (user-specified with --subnet and --ip-range):             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  $ docker network create --subnet=10.10.0.0/16 \                    │ │
│  │      --gateway=10.10.0.254 --ip-range=10.10.1.0/24 mynet           │ │
│  │                                                                      │ │
│  │  10.10.0.0/16 ────────────────────────────────────────┐             │ │
│  │  │  10.10.0.x       10.10.1.x        10.10.2-255.x    │             │ │
│  │  │  (reserved for   (dynamic pool)   (available for    │             │ │
│  │  │   static IPs)     ip-range limit   expansion)       │             │ │
│  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘             │ │
│  │                                                                      │ │
│  │  Static IP:  docker run --network mynet --ip 10.10.1.10 ...        │ │
│  │  Dynamic:    docker run --network mynet ...  (gets next pool IP)   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  POOL EXHAUSTION: /29 = 8 IPs (6 usable). After 6 containers → ERROR.    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# SEE THE DEFAULT IPAM CONFIGURATION:
$ docker network inspect bridge | jq '.[].IPAM'
{
  "Driver": "default",
  "Config": [{
    "Subnet": "172.17.0.0/16",
    "IPRange": "172.17.0.0/16",
    "Gateway": "172.17.0.1"
  }]
}
# Default bridge uses 172.17.0.0/16. Gateway = docker0 at .1
# Containers get sequential IPs: 172.17.0.2, .3, .4, ...

# EACH USER-DEFINED NETWORK GETS ITS OWN /16 SUBNET:
$ docker network create anihpj-net
$ docker network inspect anihpj-net | jq '.[].IPAM.Config'
[{"Subnet": "172.18.0.0/16", "Gateway": "172.18.0.1"}]
# 2nd network: 172.19.0.0/16, 3rd: 172.20.0.0/16, up to 172.31.0.0/16
# Then wraps to 192.168.0.0/20, 192.168.16.0/20, ...

# CREATE A NETWORK WITH CUSTOM SUBNET & IP RANGE:
$ docker network create --subnet=10.10.0.0/16 --gateway=10.10.0.254 mynet
$ docker network create --subnet=10.10.0.0/16 --ip-range=10.10.1.0/24 mynet
# ip-range limits dynamic IPs to 10.10.1.x — reserve rest for static IPs

# ASSIGN A STATIC IP TO A CONTAINER:
$ docker run -d --name web --network mynet --ip 10.10.1.10 anihpj/jobpost
# IP must be within the subnet and not already allocated

# WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE IP POOL EXHAUSTS:
$ docker network create --subnet=10.0.0.0/29 tiny-net  # 8 total, 6 usable
# After 6 containers: "Error: failed to allocate IP address"
# Fix: larger subnet, or connect container to multiple networks

# LIST ALL CONTAINER IPs ON A NETWORK:
$ docker network inspect anihpj-net --format '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}}: {{.IPv4Address}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'
web: 172.18.0.2/16
db: 172.18.0.3/16
redis: 172.18.0.4/16
🔬 Docker Network Creation — What Happens Step-by-Step Internally

When you run docker network create -d bridge anihpj-net, Docker orchestrates a precise sequence of Linux kernel operations. Every step is a standard Linux networking command:

# WHAT "docker network create -d bridge anihpj-net" ACTUALLY DOES UNDER THE HOOD:

# Step 1: Create a new Linux bridge
$ sudo ip link add br-NETID type bridge
# Docker names it br-<first-12-chars-of-network-ID>
# VERIFY: ip link show type bridge | grep br-

# Step 2: Assign gateway IP to the bridge
$ sudo ip addr add 172.18.0.1/16 dev br-NETID
# This is why containers see 172.18.0.1 as their default gateway

# Step 3: Bring the bridge up
$ sudo ip link set br-NETID up

# Step 4: Insert iptables rules for inter-network isolation
$ sudo iptables -t filter -A DOCKER -i br-NETID -j ACCEPT
$ sudo iptables -t filter -I DOCKER-ISOLATION-STAGE-2 \
    -i br-NETID ! -o br-NETID -j DROP
# ↑ THIS is why containers on different Docker networks CANNOT communicate!

# Step 5: Setup MASQUERADE for outbound internet access
$ sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 172.18.0.0/16 ! -o br-NETID -j MASQUERADE
# Traffic from this subnet leaving via any other interface gets SNAT'd

# Step 6: Start embedded DNS resolver (internal sandbox)
# Docker creates an internal process listening on 127.0.0.11:53
# Every container's /etc/resolv.conf gets "nameserver 127.0.0.11"

# ================================================================
# WHEN A CONTAINER JOINS THE NETWORK:
# ================================================================

# 1. Create veth pair (virtual cable)
$ sudo ip link add vethCONTAINER type veth peer name eth0CONTAINER

# 2. Move one end into the container's network namespace
$ sudo ip link set eth0CONTAINER netns /proc/CONTAINER_PID/ns/net

# 3. Rename to eth0 inside the container
$ sudo nsenter -t CONTAINER_PID -n ip link set eth0CONTAINER name eth0

# 4. Attach the host end to the bridge
$ sudo ip link set vethCONTAINER master br-NETID

# 5. Assign IP from the subnet pool to the container
$ sudo nsenter -t CONTAINER_PID -n ip addr add 172.18.0.2/16 dev eth0

# 6. Add default route via bridge gateway
$ sudo nsenter -t CONTAINER_PID -n ip route add default via 172.18.0.1

# 7. Inject /etc/resolv.conf into container
# Docker writes "nameserver 127.0.0.11" into container's resolv.conf

# VERIFY THE BRIDGE AND ITS CONNECTED PORTS:
$ brctl show br-NETID
bridge name     bridge id               STP enabled     interfaces
br-NETID        8000.0242ac120001       no              vetha1b2c3d
                                                        vethd4e5f6g
# Each veth interface = one container connected

# SEE THE INTER-NETWORK ISOLATION RULES:
$ sudo iptables -t filter -L DOCKER-ISOLATION-STAGE-2 -n -v
# Any packet crossing between different Docker bridges is DROPped here
�🔗 iptables Chain Walkthrough — How Docker Routes Container Traffic

Docker creates iptables rules in multiple chains. Understanding the full path helps debug "my container can reach X but not Y" issues:

DOCKER iptables CHAIN FLOW — Outbound & Inbound Packet Path

│  │ │  :8000→      │    │  ACCEPT      │    │  DNAT on reply packets │  │ │
│  │ │  172.17.0.2  │    │  eth0→docker0│    │  automatically!        │  │ │
│  │ └──────────────┘    └──────┬───────┘    └────────────────────────┘  │ │
│  │                            │                                         │ │

│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  INSPECTION COMMANDS:                                                     │
│  iptables -t nat -L PREROUTING -n -v     (DNAT for -p published ports)   │
│  iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -n -v    (MASQUERADE for internet access)│
│  iptables -t filter -L FORWARD -n -v     (Inter-network forwarding)      │
