│  ┌──────────────────┐                                                     │
│  │ docker-compose up │──scale web=3                                       │
│  └──────────────────┘                                                     │
│  Three web containers join. DNS registers ALL their IPs under "web."     │
│  nslookup web → returns ONE IP, cycling through 172.20.0.4, .5, .6      │
│  This is DNS round-robin — NOT true load balancing.                      │
│  Some clients cache the first IP → always hit same container.            │
│  For real load balancing: put nginx/HAProxy in front.                    │
│                                                                           │
│  ALIASES ARE PER-NETWORK (a service can have different aliases per net): │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  web:                                                             │    │
│  │    networks:                                                       │    │
│  │      frontend:                                                     │    │
│  │        aliases: [api-v2, www]    ← External-facing names          │    │
│  │      backend:                                                      │    │
│  │        aliases: [internal-api]   ← Internal-only name             │    │
│  │  api resolves to web on frontend. internal-api resolves on backend.│    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# WHAT HAPPENS WHEN web RESOLVES "db" IN COMPOSE:
# 1. web sends DNS query: "db.anihpj_default" → 127.0.0.11:53
# 2. Docker DNS checks its internal registry:
#    db = {IP: 172.20.0.3, Aliases: [database]}
# 3. Returns A record: db → 172.20.0.3

# THE DNS REGISTRY IS DYNAMIC — updated as containers join/leave:
# Container joins → DNS adds entry
# Container leaves → DNS removes entry
# Container restarts with new IP → DNS updates entry

# SEE THE DNS REGISTRY (from inside a container):
$ docker-compose exec web nslookup db
Server:   127.0.0.11
Address:  127.0.0.11#53
Name:     db
Address:  172.20.0.3

# MULTIPLE ALIASES FOR ONE SERVICE:
services:
  db:
    networks:
      default:
        aliases: [database, postgres, anihpj-db]
# All four names resolve to db's IP: db, database, postgres, anihpj-db

# ALIASES ARE PER-NETWORK:
# A service on network A and network B can have DIFFERENT aliases per network
services:
  api:
    networks:
      frontend:
        aliases: [api-v2]
      backend:
        aliases: [internal-api]

# DNS TTL BEHAVIOR:
# Compose DNS uses a TTL of 600 seconds (10 minutes) for cached entries
# Container IP changes are reflected immediately (DNS registry updates)
# But some apps cache DNS results — restart them after network changes

# CHECK THE ACTUAL CONTAINER HOSTNAME:
$ docker-compose exec web hostname
anihpj-web-1  # Default hostname = project-service-replica
# The SERVICE NAME (not hostname) is what DNS resolves!
🌐 External Networks — Sharing Networks Across Compose Files

When you have multiple compose files that need to share a network, you use external networks. Compose won't create or destroy the network — it references a pre-existing one. This is the standard pattern for microservices split across multiple compose files:

EXTERNAL NETWORKS — Connecting Containers Across Compose Files
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     CROSS-COMPOSE-FILE NETWORKING                           │
│                                                                           │
│  Step 1: Create the shared network ONCE (manually):                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  $ docker network create anihpj-shared                               │ │
│  │  Network "anihpj-shared" created (172.25.0.0/16)                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────────────┐      │
│  │  frontend/docker-compose.yml│    │  backend/docker-compose.yml │      │
│  │                             │    │                             │      │
│  │  services:                  │    │  services:                  │      │
│  │    web:                     │    │    db:                      │      │
│  │      networks:              │    │      networks:              │      │
│  │        - anihpj-shared ─────┼────┼──────── anihpj-shared       │      │
│  │        - frontend-only      │    │        - backend-only       │      │
│  │    nginx:                   │    │    redis:                   │      │
│  │      networks:              │    │      networks:              │      │
│  │        - frontend-only      │    │        - backend-only       │      │
│  │                             │    │                             │      │
│  │  networks:                  │    │  networks:                  │      │
│  │    anihpj-shared:           │    │    anihpj-shared:           │      │
│  │      external: true ────────┼────┼────── external: true        │      │
│  │    frontend-only:           │    │    backend-only:            │      │
│  │      driver: bridge         │    │      driver: bridge         │      │
│  │                             │    │      internal: true         │      │
│  └─────────────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                           │
│  RESULT: web can resolve db by name! (both on anihpj-shared)             │
│  nginx and db CANNOT communicate (different networks, no shared net)     │
│  db has NO internet (backend-only is internal:true)                      │
│                                                                           │
│  LIFECYCLE: docker-compose down does NOT remove external networks.        │
│  Must manually: docker network rm anihpj-shared                          │
│  This is intentional — prevents one compose file from breaking others.   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# 1. Create the shared network once (manually or via a script):
$ docker network create --driver bridge anihpj-shared
$ docker network create --driver overlay --attachable anihpj-cluster

# 2. Reference it in compose file A (frontend services):
# frontend/docker-compose.yml
services:
  web:
    networks: [anihpj-shared, frontend-only]
  nginx:
    networks: [frontend-only]
networks:
  anihpj-shared:
    external: true              # "Don't create this — it already exists"
    name: anihpj-shared         # Optional: override the external name
  frontend-only:
    driver: bridge

# 3. Reference it in compose file B (backend services):
# backend/docker-compose.yml
services:
  db:
    networks: [anihpj-shared, backend-only]
  redis:
    networks: [backend-only]
networks:
  anihpj-shared:
    external: true
  backend-only:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true              # Backend-only has no internet

# 4. Start them (order doesn't matter for the network):
$ docker-compose -f backend/docker-compose.yml up -d
$ docker-compose -f frontend/docker-compose.yml up -d
# web (frontend) can now resolve db (backend) by name!

# 5. Cleanup: the external network survives docker-compose down
$ docker-compose -f frontend/docker-compose.yml down
$ docker-compose -f backend/docker-compose.yml down
$ docker network ls | grep anihpj-shared  # Still exists!
$ docker network rm anihpj-shared         # Manual cleanup needed

# KEY RULE: External networks are NEVER removed by docker-compose down.
# This prevents one compose file from destroying the network others rely on.
🔍 docker-compose exec vs docker exec — Critical Differences

Both let you run commands inside a container, but they behave differently in ways that matter for networking diagnostics:

Featuredocker-compose execdocker exec
Service name resolutionWorks by SERVICE name: docker-compose exec web bash — Compose finds the containerRequires CONTAINER name/ID: docker exec anihpj-web-1 bash
Working directoryRespects working_dir: from compose fileDefaults to / (container root)
TTY allocationAuto-allocates pseudo-TTY (-t implicit)Must specify -it manually for interactive
Environment variablesRespects environment: and env_file: from composeUses container's runtime env (same, but no compose overrides)
Stopped containers❌ Won't exec into stopped containers❌ Same — container must be running
Scaling awarenessdocker-compose exec --index=2 web bash — targets specific replicaMust know exact container name: anihpj-web-2
User flag--user root (respects compose user: setting)-u root
 
# NETWORKING DIAGNOSTICS — which to use:
# Compose exec is better for DNS tests (service names):
$ docker-compose exec web nslookup db        # Uses service name
$ docker exec anihpj-web-1 nslookup db       # Same, but you must know container name

# Docker exec is better for raw network inspection:
$ docker exec anihpj-web-1 ip addr show      # Raw Linux command
$ docker exec anihpj-web-1 ss -tlnp          # Check listening ports
$ docker exec anihpj-web-1 cat /etc/resolv.conf  # DNS config

# Compose exec for scaling scenarios:
$ docker-compose up -d --scale web=3
$ docker-compose exec --index=1 web hostname -I   # web-1 IP
$ docker-compose exec --index=2 web hostname -I   # web-2 IP
$ docker-compose exec --index=3 web hostname -I   # web-3 IP
🖥️ Compose CLI Networking Commands — Quick Reference

All the docker-compose commands you need for networking diagnostics and management:

# ===== NETWORK INSPECTION =====
$ docker-compose ps                         # List all services + ports
$ docker network ls                         # See the compose-created network
$ docker network inspect anihpj_default      # Full JSON: subnets, containers, IPs
$ docker-compose port web 8000              # Show host:port mapping for a service

# ===== DNS TESTING =====
$ docker-compose exec web nslookup db       # Resolve service name → IP
$ docker-compose exec web ping -c 3 db      # Test connectivity by name
$ docker-compose exec web getent hosts db   # Alternative name resolution

# ===== NETWORK MANAGEMENT =====
$ docker-compose up -d                      # Creates network + starts services
$ docker-compose down                       # Stops services + REMOVES network
$ docker-compose stop                       # Stops services, KEEPS network
$ docker-compose restart web                # Restart one service (keeps IP usually)

# ===== MULTIPLE COMPOSE FILES =====
$ docker-compose -f a.yml -f b.yml up       # Merge configs, one default network
$ docker-compose -f a.yml -f b.yml config   # Preview merged YAML (debugging!)
$ docker-compose -p myproject up -d         # Custom project name → myproject_default

# ===== NETWORK TROUBLESHOOTING =====
$ docker-compose logs web                   # See if app logged connection errors
$ docker-compose run --rm web bash          # One-off container on same network
$ docker-compose run --rm web nslookup db   # Test DNS from fresh container
$ docker-compose events                     # Real-time compose events stream
🏷️ Project Name — How Compose Names Networks and Containers

The project name controls how Compose names everything — networks, containers, volumes. Understanding this prevents name collisions and helps organize multi-environment setups:

# DEFAULT PROJECT NAME = directory name of docker-compose.yml
# /home/user/anihpj/docker-compose.yml → project = "anihpj"
# Network: anihpj_default
# Container: anihpj-web-1, anihpj-db-1, anihpj-redis-1

# OVERRIDE PROJECT NAME (4 ways):
# 1. -p flag (highest priority):
$ docker-compose -p production up -d        # → production_default network

# 2. COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME env var:
$ export COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=staging
$ docker-compose up -d                      # → staging_default network

# 3. In .env file (next to docker-compose.yml):
COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=development

# 4. Top-level "name:" in compose file (Compose v2.3+):
name: anihpj-prod
services:
  web: ...

# WHY PROJECT NAMES MATTER:
# You can run the SAME compose file multiple times with different names:
$ docker-compose -p dev up -d      # → dev_default network
$ docker-compose -p staging up -d  # → staging_default network
$ docker-compose -p prod up -d     # → prod_default network
# Three completely isolated instances! No port conflicts if using
# dynamic port mapping (ports: ["8000"] instead of "8000:8000")

# NETWORK NAMING WITH CUSTOM PROJECT:
networks:
  default:
    name: ${COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME}-network   # Variable substitution
# Now docker-compose -p dev up → network named "dev-network"
⚙️ Network Driver Options — Fine-Tuning Bridge Behavior

Docker's bridge driver accepts driver_opts that map directly to Linux bridge configuration. These options control MTU, multicast, and bridge-level settings:

# FULL NETWORK WITH DRIVER OPTIONS:
networks:
  optimized-net:
    driver: bridge
    driver_opts:
      com.docker.network.bridge.name: "anihpj-br0"      # Custom bridge name (not br-<hash>)
      com.docker.network.bridge.enable_ip_masquerade: "true"  # SNAT for internet access
      com.docker.network.bridge.host_binding_ipv4: "0.0.0.0"  # Which IP to bind port mappings to
      com.docker.network.driver.mtu: "9000"                   # Jumbo frames!
      com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc: "true"            # Inter-Container Communication
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 10.50.0.0/16
          gateway: 10.50.0.1

# OVERLAY NETWORK DRIVER OPTIONS:
networks:
  swarm-net:
    driver: overlay
    driver_opts:
      com.docker.network.driver.overlay.vxlanid_list: "4096"  # Custom VNI
    attachable: true           # Allow non-swarm containers to connect

# DISABLE INTER-CONTAINER COMMUNICATION (icc=false):
networks:
  secure-net:
    driver: bridge
    driver_opts:
      com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc: "false"
# Containers can ONLY talk to ports you explicitly publish with -p
# This is like AWS Security Groups — default deny, explicit allow

# MACVLAN DRIVER OPTIONS:
networks:
  macvlan-net:
    driver: macvlan
    driver_opts:
      parent: eth0              # Physical interface to attach to
      macvlan_mode: bridge      # bridge | private | vepa | passthru

# SET A SPECIFIC MAC ADDRESS FOR A CONTAINER:
services:
  legacy-app:
    networks:
      macvlan-net:
        mac_address: "02:42:ac:11:00:ff"  # For DHCP reservations / license servers
🌐 IPv6 in Docker Compose — Dual-Stack Networking

Docker supports IPv6 alongside IPv4. Enabling IPv6 in Compose gives containers both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses — essential for modern cloud environments and IPv6-only deployments:

# ENABLE IPv6 ON A COMPOSE NETWORK:
networks:
  dual-stack:
    enable_ipv6: true
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 10.20.0.0/24          # IPv4
        - subnet: 2001:db8:1::/64       # IPv6 (ULA or GUA)
          gateway: 2001:db8:1::1

# VERIFY IPv6 INSIDE A CONTAINER:
$ docker-compose exec web ip -6 addr show
eth0:  mtu 1500
    inet6 2001:db8:1::2/64 scope global

# PING VIA IPv6:
$ docker-compose exec web ping6 -c 3 db
PING db(2001:db8:1::3) 56 data bytes

# PREREQUISITE: Docker daemon must have IPv6 enabled
# In /etc/docker/daemon.json:
{
  "ipv6": true,
  "fixed-cidr-v6": "2001:db8:1::/64"
}
# Restart dockerd after adding this: systemctl restart docker

# IPv6-ONLY NETWORK (no IPv4):
networks:
  ipv6-only:
    enable_ipv6: true
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 2001:db8:2::/64
    driver_opts:
      com.docker.network.bridge.enable_ip_masquerade: "false"
# No IPv4 subnet → containers only get IPv6 addresses

# LINK-LOCAL ADDRESSES (always present when IPv6 enabled):
$ docker-compose exec web ip -6 addr show
eth0: ... 
    inet6 fe80::42:acff:fe14:2/64 scope link  # Link-local (always)
    inet6 2001:db8:1::2/64 scope global         # Global/ULA from IPAM
📝 docker-compose.override.yml — Network Patterns for Dev/Prod

Compose supports override files that merge with the base docker-compose.yml. This is how you keep one base config but customize networking per environment — dev exposes ports, prod uses internal networks:

# ===== BASE: docker-compose.yml (production defaults) =====
services:
  web:
    build: .
    networks: [backend]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    networks: [backend]
networks:
  backend:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true             # PROD: no internet for DB tier

# ===== OVERRIDE: docker-compose.override.yml (dev overrides) =====
# Compose AUTO-APPLIES this when you run docker-compose up
services:
  web:
    ports: ["8000:8000"]       # DEV: expose ports for local dev
    networks: [backend, debug] # DEV: add debug network
  db:
    ports: ["5432:5432"]       # DEV: expose DB for GUI tools
networks:
  backend:
    internal: false            # DEV: allow internet for apt-get
  debug:
    driver: bridge             # DEV-only network

# ===== OVERRIDE: docker-compose.prod.yml (production-specific) =====
# Use with: docker-compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml up
services:
  web:
    networks: [backend, frontend]
    environment:
      - DJANGO_DEBUG=0
    restart: always
networks:
  frontend:
    driver: bridge
    # Prod adds a frontend network for the reverse proxy

# ===== MERGE BEHAVIOR =====
# Arrays (ports, networks): override REPLACES base array
# Maps (environment, labels): override MERGES with base
# Single values (image, restart): override REPLACES
# Networks section: override EXTENDS base networks

# PREVIEW THE MERGED CONFIG (essential for debugging):
$ docker-compose config                        # Base + override.yml
$ docker-compose -f base.yml -f prod.yml config # Base + prod override
🔧 Advanced Compose Network Options — attachable, labels, internal, and More

Beyond the basics, Compose networks support several advanced options for production environments:

OptionValuesEffectUse Case
attachabletrue / falseAllow containers outside of Compose to join this network via docker network connectDebugging: connect a netshoot container to inspect traffic
internaltrue / falseBlocks internet access. Containers can only reach other containers on this network.Security: DB tier should never reach the internet
enable_ipv6true / falseAdd IPv6 addressing to the network. Requires dockerd with IPv6 enabled.Dual-stack or IPv6-only deployments
labelskey: value mapAdd Docker labels to the network object. Queryable via docker network ls --filterOrganization: label by team, env, compliance tier
namestringOverride the auto-generated {project}_{network} namePredictable names for external scripts and monitoring
driverbridge / overlay / macvlan / ipvlanWhich network driver to useMatch the connectivity model to the workload
 
# FULL PRODUCTION NETWORK CONFIGURATION WITH ALL OPTIONS:
networks:
  frontend:
    driver: bridge
    name: "anihpj-prod-frontend"
    labels:
      com.anihpj.env: "production"
      com.anihpj.tier: "frontend"
      com.anihpj.compliance: "pci-dss"
    driver_opts:
      com.docker.network.bridge.name: "anihpj-front-br"
      com.docker.network.driver.mtu: "1500"

  backend:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true
    name: "anihpj-prod-backend"
    labels:
      com.anihpj.env: "production"
      com.anihpj.tier: "backend"
      com.anihpj.compliance: "pci-dss"
    enable_ipv6: false

  monitoring:
    driver: bridge
    attachable: true        # Allow external monitoring tools to connect
    name: "anihpj-prod-monitoring"
    labels:
      com.anihpj.env: "production"
      com.anihpj.tier: "monitoring"
    internal: true          # Monitoring network also isolated from internet

# QUERY NETWORKS BY LABEL:
$ docker network ls --filter label=com.anihpj.env=production
$ docker network ls --filter label=com.anihpj.compliance=pci-dss
# Shows only production PCI-compliant networks

# ATTACH A DEBUG CONTAINER TO AN ATTACHABLE NETWORK:
$ docker run --rm -it --network anihpj-prod-backend nicolaka/netshoot
$ nslookup db     # Resolves to backend network's db container!
$ tcpdump -i eth0 # Sniff traffic on the backend network

16.2 LAB: Docker Compose Networking Lab

🛠️ Compose Networking Lab
1
Start Stack & Inspect
$ docker-compose up -d
$ docker network inspect anihpj_default
# See all containers and IPs on the compose network
2
Test DNS Resolution
$ docker-compose exec web ping db
$ docker-compose exec web getent hosts db
# "db" resolves to postgres container IP
3
Test DB Connectivity
$ docker-compose exec web bash
$ apt-get install -y postgresql-client
$ psql -h db -U anihpj -d anihpj -c "SELECT 1"
4
Test Custom Network with Static IP
$ docker network create --subnet=10.99.0.0/24 custom-net
$ docker-compose up -d
$ docker-compose exec web ip addr show eth0
# Verify container got IP from custom subnet
5
Test Network Alias Resolution
$ docker-compose exec web nslookup database
$ docker-compose exec web nslookup postgres
# Both aliases resolve to the db container's IP!
6
Debug DNS Search Domain Delay
$ docker-compose exec web cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Note the "search anihpj_default" line
$ docker-compose exec web time nslookup google.com
# Musl (Alpine) may retry with search domain first
🛠️ Compose Networking Debugging Toolkit

When Compose networking breaks, these are the commands that find the root cause. Work through them in order.

# ===== QUICK HEALTH CHECK =====

# 1. Are ALL services actually running?
$ docker-compose ps
# Look for "Up" status. "Exit 1" = crashed.

# 2. Are all services on the SAME network?
$ docker network inspect anihpj_default --format '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{.IPv4Address}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'
# Every service should be listed here. Missing = not connected.

# 3. Does DNS work from inside a container?
$ docker-compose exec web nslookup db
$ docker-compose exec web nslookup db.           # Trailing dot = FQDN, bypasses search
# If "db." works but "db" doesn't → search domain issue (musl vs glibc)

# ===== DEEP DIAGNOSTICS =====

# 4. Check the container's /etc/resolv.conf:
$ docker-compose exec web cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Should have: nameserver 127.0.0.11
# If it has 8.8.8.8 or host DNS → embedded DNS is overridden

# 5. Check the container's /etc/hosts (should NOT have service names):
$ docker-compose exec web cat /etc/hosts
# Compose uses DNS, not /etc/hosts (unlike --link)

# 6. Trace DNS queries with tcpdump inside a container:
$ docker-compose exec web tcpdump -i lo port 53 -n &
$ docker-compose exec web nslookup db
# You'll see the DNS query to 127.0.0.11 and the response

# 7. Check if DNS forwarding to external names works:
$ docker-compose exec web nslookup google.com
# If internal names resolve but external don't → host DNS issue

# 8. Check if the Compose network's bridge exists:
$ ip link show br-$(docker network inspect anihpj_default --format '{{.Id}}' | cut -c1-12)
# Should show UP state. DOWN → network didn't start properly

# 9. Check iptables rules for the Compose network:
$ sudo iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -n -v | grep 172.20
# Should show MASQUERADE rule for the compose subnet

# 10. Restart networking without recreating containers:
$ docker-compose down && docker-compose up -d
# This re-creates the network and DNS registry from scratch

🔭 Chapter 16 — Visual Summary

🌐One Network Per Project

docker-compose creates {project}_default bridge. All services join automatically. DNS resolution by service name.

🔤Service Names = Hostnames

web reaches db:5432 by name. Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) handles resolution.

🔀Multiple Networks

Services can join multiple networks for isolation. Control traffic flow between service groups.

🏥Health Check Deps

depends_on with condition: service_healthy waits for DB readiness. No race conditions.

🧬DNS Internals

127.0.0.11 maintains a dynamic registry. Service names resolve to IPs instantly. Aliases add extra DNS names.

📊IPAM in Compose

Custom subnets, static IPs, and dual-stack IPv4/IPv6. Default address pools configurable in daemon.json.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 16

🌐Compose Network
Dedicated bridge network created per compose project. Named {project}_default. All services join automatically. Docker's DNS enables name-based resolution between services.
🏷️Network Alias
Additional DNS name for a service on a network. Example: aliases: [api, backend]. Useful for migrations and multi-role services.
🔀Network Isolation
Services on different networks cannot communicate. Use multiple networks to enforce traffic boundaries. internal: true blocks internet access entirely.
🧬Embedded DNS (127.0.0.11)
Docker's internal DNS server running inside each container on user-defined networks. Maintains a dynamic registry of service-name→IP mappings. Updated when containers join/leave. NOT on default bridge.
🔄depends_on (condition)
Controls service startup order AND readiness. condition: service_healthy waits for HEALTHCHECK to pass before starting the dependent service. Without it, only container start is guaranteed — not application readiness.
🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work
  • "DB connection refused" after docker-compose up: The DB isn't ready yet. Use condition: service_healthy in depends_on, not bare depends_on. Always add HEALTHCHECK to stateful services.
  • "Can't resolve service name" in Compose: Check if the service is on the same network. Compose creates a network per file by default. Services in different compose files are on different networks unless you use external networks.
  • Multi-compose-file projects: Use docker-compose -f a.yml -f b.yml up to merge configs. Or create an external network shared between compose files: docker network create shared-net and reference it in both files.
  • Production hardening: Use internal: true for backend networks. Place only reverse proxies/API gateways on frontend networks. DBs and caches should never have internet access.

🔑 Chapter 16 Key Takeaways

  1. Compose = automatic network. Every compose file gets a dedicated bridge network. All services join. DNS resolves service names to container IPs via 127.0.0.11.
  2. Network isolation is a security boundary. DB on a backend network with internal: true literally cannot reach the internet. No firewall rules to maintain — it's enforced at the network level.
  3. depends_on WITHOUT healthcheck is broken. "Started" ≠ "ready." PostgreSQL takes seconds to initialize. condition: service_healthy ensures your app doesn't connect until the DB accepts connections.
  4. Aliases enable zero-downtime migrations. network-alias lets you point multiple names at one container, or swap which container backs an alias — the DNS updates when containers restart.
  5. Debug with docker-compose exec. Run nslookup, ping, curl from inside a running service container to test DNS resolution and connectivity without modifying images.

📝 Chapter 16 — Practice Questions

Q1
You have two separate docker-compose.yml files (project-a and project-b). Containers in project-a need to reach containers in project-b by service name. How do you enable cross-compose-file DNS resolution?
Show Answer
Answer

Create an external network and reference it in both compose files. Services in both projects join the same external network and DNS resolves across compose file boundaries:

# 1. Create the network once:
$ docker network create shared-net
# 2. In project-a/docker-compose.yml:
networks:
  shared-net:
    external: true  # References the pre-created network
services:
  web:
    networks: [default, shared-net]
# 3. In project-b/docker-compose.yml — same network reference
# Now project-a's web can ping project-b's services by name
Explanation

Compose's default network is scoped to one compose file. external: true tells Compose "don't create this network, expect it to already exist." Docker's embedded DNS works across the entire network, regardless of which compose file created the container. This is the standard pattern for microservices that span multiple compose files.

Q2
Your compose file has depends_on: [db] without a healthcheck. The web app starts, tries to connect to db:5432, and crashes with "Connection refused." db's logs show it takes 20 seconds to initialize. Why did depends_on not prevent this?
Show Answer
Answer

Bare depends_on: [db] only waits for the container to start (process running), not for PostgreSQL to be ready for connections. PostgreSQL starts its process, the container is "started," but the database is still running crash recovery or initializing data files — rejecting connections for 20 seconds.

# WRONG — only waits for container start:
depends_on: [db]

# CORRECT — waits for PostgreSQL to accept connections:
depends_on:
  db:
    condition: service_healthy
# Requires HEALTHCHECK on db service:
db:
  healthcheck:
    test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U anihpj"]
    interval: 5s
    timeout: 3s
    retries: 5
    start_period: 10s
Explanation

This is one of the most common Compose pitfalls. Docker's "started" state means the process is running — not that it's serving requests. For databases, message queues, and any service with initialization time, always define a HEALTHCHECK and use condition: service_healthy in depends_on.

Q3
You define the anihpj compose file with three services: web, db, redis. What is the DEFAULT network name Compose creates? How can you override it to a custom name?
Show Answer
Answer

If your compose file is in a directory named anihpj, the default network name is anihpj_default. The pattern is {project_name}_default where project_name defaults to the directory name.

# Override with a custom name:
networks:
  default:
    name: anihpj-production  # Explicit name
    driver: bridge

# Or define a custom network (not "default"):
networks:
  anihpj-net:
    driver: bridge
services:
  web:
    networks: [anihpj-net]  # Must specify per-service
Explanation

If you define a custom network, Compose does NOT automatically connect services to it — you must list it in each service's networks: array. The special default network IS auto-connected. Override its name property to control the Docker network name without changing auto-connect behavior.

Q4
A developer adds dns: 8.8.8.8 to a service in docker-compose.yml. Suddenly, service-name resolution between containers breaks. Why?
Show Answer
Answer

The dns: option replaces Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) with the specified nameserver. Container name resolution relies on 127.0.0.11 — removing it breaks all inter-service DNS.

# WRONG — overrides Docker DNS:
dns: 8.8.8.8
# Container can resolve google.com but NOT other services

# CORRECT — add external DNS WITHOUT removing Docker DNS:
dns:
  - 127.0.0.11  # Keep Docker's DNS first!
  - 8.8.8.8     # Fallback for external names
Explanation

Docker's embedded DNS intercepts all DNS queries at 127.0.0.11. If a query matches a container name on the same network, it returns the container's IP. If not, it forwards to the host's DNS servers. By overriding dns:, you bypass this mechanism entirely. Always keep 127.0.0.11 in the list if you need container name resolution.

Q5
You need to host anihpj's database on a network with NO internet access for security compliance. How do you configure this in docker-compose.yml using ONLY network settings?
Show Answer
Answer

Use internal: true on the backend network. Containers on an internal network cannot reach the internet — they can only communicate with other containers on the same network:

services:
  db:
    networks: [backend]
  redis:
    networks: [backend]
  web:
    networks: [backend, frontend]  # Bridge between networks

networks:
  backend:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true    # NO internet access!
  frontend:
    driver: bridge     # CAN reach internet
Explanation

internal: true prevents Docker from adding MASQUERADE rules for traffic from this network to external interfaces. The kernel literally has no route to the internet from containers on this network. This is enforced at the network layer — no iptables rules to accidentally delete, no application-level configuration to forget.

Q6
You run docker-compose down and then docker-compose up. The web app starts before db and crashes. The compose file has depends_on: db. The FIRST time you ran it, it worked. Why does it fail on the second run?
Show Answer
Answer

The first run created the PostgreSQL volume (pgdata) and initialized the database. On subsequent runs, the volume persists, so PostgreSQL skips initialization and starts faster — sometimes faster than the web app's connection attempt. But the first run INITIALIZED the DB from scratch, taking 10-30 seconds, giving the web app time to start and retry connections.

But that's actually the reverse — the FIRST run is usually when it fails. The second run works because the volume is initialized and PostgreSQL starts fast. If it fails on the second run and worked on the first, look for: (1) volume mount issue, (2) PostgreSQL crash recovery (data corruption from unclean shutdown in docker-compose down), or (3) the depends_on was actually satisfied quickly enough on the first run by chance.

# Proper fix: always use condition: service_healthy
depends_on:
  db:
    condition: service_healthy
# And always stop gracefully:
$ docker-compose stop  # NOT docker-compose down (which removes containers abruptly)
Explanation

This is a race condition. Without healthchecks, depends_on only guarantees ORDER, not READINESS. The web app's startup might take 2 seconds or 10 seconds depending on system load. PostgreSQL's startup might take 3 seconds or 30 seconds. The only reliable solution is healthcheck-based dependencies.

Q7
You're migrating from docker run --link old-db:database to Docker Compose. The app code has DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@database:5432/db. What changes are needed in docker-compose.yml to make this URL work?
Show Answer
Answer

Use a network-alias so the service responds to the name database even though the service name is something else:

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    networks:
      anihpj-net:
        aliases: [database]  # Also resolves as "database"
  web:
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://user:pass@database:5432/db
    networks: [anihpj-net]
# "database" resolves to db's IP. No code change needed.
Explanation

--link allowed renaming (old-db:database). In Compose, aliases serve the same purpose. Each alias is an additional DNS A record pointing to the container's IP. Multiple containers can share an alias for round-robin DNS (though Docker doesn't do true round-robin — it returns one IP at a time).

Q8
A Compose service needs to reach both other services (via Compose DNS) AND an external API (api.third-party.com). The container uses Alpine Linux (musl libc). DNS resolution for internal services is instant, but external names take 5+ seconds. Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer

Musl libc (Alpine) tries search domains sequentially with a 5-second timeout per domain. If /etc/resolv.conf has search anihpj_default, every external query tries api.third-party.com.anihpj_default first, waits 5 seconds for timeout, then tries the actual name.

# Check the search domain:
$ docker-compose exec web cat /etc/resolv.conf
search anihpj_default  # ← This causes the delay!

# Fix: Override in compose:
services:
  web:
    dns_search: .  # Single dot = no search domain
# Or use FQDN in app code: api.third-party.com.
Explanation

Docker injects the network name as a search domain into /etc/resolv.conf so short names like "db" resolve. The side effect is that ALL queries get the search domain appended. Glibc (Debian/Ubuntu) has options ndots:1 which helps; musl (Alpine) does not respect this. The trailing dot in a hostname disables search domain expansion.

Q9
You run docker-compose up -d and docker-compose ps shows all services running. But docker network ls shows TWO networks: anihpj_default and anihpj_anihpj-net. Why two networks?
Show Answer
Answer

Your compose file defines a custom network AND also has the implicit default network. If services don't explicitly list networks:, Compose connects them to default automatically. If some services use networks: [anihpj-net] and others don't specify, you get two networks with services split between them.

# PROBLEM: web on custom network, db on default
services:
  web:
    networks: [anihpj-net]  # Only on custom network
  db:
    # No networks: specified → auto-joins DEFAULT only
# Result: web and db CANNOT resolve each other!

# FIX: All services must specify the same network:
services:
  web:
    networks: [anihpj-net]
  db:
    networks: [anihpj-net]  # Explicit
# OR disable the default network:
networks:
  default:
    external: false
    # Actually, just don't define 'default' and put all services on anihpj-net
Explanation

The confusing part: Compose ALWAYS creates a default network. If you define a custom network AND don't explicitly assign all services to it, those unassigned services go to default — creating a split-brain configuration where DNS doesn't work across the two networks.

Q10
You want to scale the web service: docker-compose up -d --scale web=3. All three instances are on the same Compose network. How does DNS resolution work when another service resolves web? Which IP does it get?
Show Answer
Answer

Docker's embedded DNS returns one IP per query, cycling through all healthy containers in round-robin fashion. It is NOT a load balancer — it's DNS round-robin:

# Scale web service:
$ docker-compose up -d --scale web=3
$ docker-compose exec db nslookup web
Name: web
Address: 172.20.0.2
$ docker-compose exec db nslookup web
Name: web
Address: 172.20.0.4  # Different IP!

# BUT: Docker DNS doesn't use traditional round-robin
# It returns a RANDOM IP from the healthy pool each time
Explanation

Docker's DNS-based load distribution works for stateless services. However, many clients cache DNS results (nginx caches for the lifetime of the process). For true load balancing, place a reverse proxy (nginx/HAProxy) in front of the scaled services. Docker Swarm's VIP-based load balancing handles this better than docker-compose's DNS approach.

⏱️ Target: 2 minutes
Drill 16.1 — Debug Broken Compose DNS

Given: docker-compose.yml with web+db+redis. docker-compose up -d succeeds. docker-compose exec web ping db returns "ping: bad address." List the 4 most likely causes in order.

💡 Hint: Check (1) Is db on the same network? (2) Did you override DNS? (3) Is db actually running? (4) Typo in service name?
📝 View Solution
# 1. Verify db is on same network (most common):
$ docker network inspect anihpj_default | jq '.[].Containers | keys'
# 2. Check if dns: overrode 127.0.0.11:
$ docker-compose exec web cat /etc/resolv.conf
# 3. Verify db container is running:
$ docker-compose ps db
# 4. Check service name spelling (case-sensitive):
$ docker-compose config --services
⏱️ Target: 2 minutes
Drill 16.2 — Design a Three-Tier Network

Design the networks for: (a) nginx reverse proxy (internet-facing), (b) Django web app, (c) PostgreSQL, (d) Redis cache, (e) Prometheus monitoring. Requirements: DB and Redis must NOT have internet access. Monitoring must be isolated from production traffic.

💡 Hint: Use 3 networks — frontend (nginx+web), backend (web+db+redis, internal=true), monitoring (isolated). Web bridges frontend↔backend.
📝 View Solution
networks:
  frontend:           # Internet access OK
    driver: bridge
  backend:            # NO internet access
    driver: bridge
    internal: true
  monitoring:         # Isolated
    driver: bridge
services:
  nginx:
    networks: [frontend]          # Internet-facing only
  web:
    networks: [frontend, backend] # Bridge between tiers
  db:
    networks: [backend]           # No internet
  redis:
    networks: [backend]           # No internet
  prometheus:
    networks: [monitoring]        # Isolated
⏱️ Target: 2 minutes
Drill 16.3 — Fix the depends_on Race Condition

Your compose file has depends_on: [db, redis]. Web crashes on startup 3 out of 5 times with "connection refused" to db. Rewrite the depends_on section with proper healthcheck conditions so web always starts AFTER the database is ready.

💡 Hint: Add healthcheck to db, use condition: service_healthy. Add start_period to give PostgreSQL time to initialize.
📝 View Solution
services:
  web:
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started   # Redis starts fast
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U anihpj"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s   # Wait for init
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s

Chapter 17: Building an anihpj Dockerfile — Reference Implementation

This chapter provides the complete, production-ready Dockerfile for the anihpj/jobpost Django application, with every line annotated. Use this as your reference for any Python/Django container.

🟡 INTERMEDIATE ⏱️ ~30 min 🐳 Dockerfile

17.1 Complete anihpj/jobpost Dockerfile — Every Line Annotated

A Dockerfile is not just a script that builds a container image — it's a declaration of your application's entire runtime environment. Every line you write makes a promise about what your application needs to run: which operating system packages, which Python version, which dependencies, which user, which ports. Get it right, and your application runs identically on every machine from your laptop to your production Kubernetes cluster. Get it wrong, and you'll be debugging "it works on my machine" for hours.

The Dockerfile below represents the culmination of everything we've learned about container networking in Chapters 15 and 16. It's not a minimal example — it's a production-grade reference implementation for a real Django application. Every choice has a reason: the multi-stage build eliminates the compiler toolchain from the final image (reducing size by 60-80% and removing hundreds of CVEs). The non-root user limits the blast radius if the container is compromised. The HEALTHCHECK ensures that orchestrators know when the application is actually ready, not just when the process started. The exec-form CMD ensures the application receives SIGTERM for graceful shutdown. The COPY order maximizes Docker's build cache, making code changes rebuild in seconds instead of minutes.

What makes this Dockerfile "production-ready" isn't any single line — it's the combination of security, performance, and observability concerns addressed simultaneously. A beginner's Dockerfile might be 5 lines and work fine on a laptop. A production Dockerfile is 30 lines and works reliably at scale, survives security audits, deploys quickly in CI/CD, and self-heals when things go wrong. The difference between those two Dockerfiles is what separates developers who "use Docker" from engineers who understand containers.

📦 Production Dockerfile — Multi-Stage Build
# ===== STAGE 1: BUILDER =====
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential libpq-dev && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /app

# COPY requirements FIRST (cached layer — changes less often than code)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# ===== STAGE 2: RUNTIME (minimal) =====
FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    libpq-dev curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Non-root user (NEVER run as root in production!)
RUN groupadd -r anihpj && useradd -r -g anihpj -d /app anihpj
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /usr/local
WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=anihpj:anihpj . .
USER anihpj

# EXPOSE = documentation only. Still need -p or K8s Service.
EXPOSE 8000

# HEALTHCHECK — tells Docker/K8s if app is actually healthy
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
    CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health/ || exit 1

# EXEC form (NOT shell!) for correct SIGTERM handling
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "4", "--access-logfile", "-"]
MULTI-STAGE BUILD — How It Reduces Image Size by 60-80%
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     DOCKER MULTI-STAGE BUILD                               │
│                                                                           │
│  STAGE 1: BUILDER (python:3.12-slim + build tools)                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder            ← 150 MB base          │ │
│  │  RUN apt-get install build-essential libpq-dev ← +200 MB gcc, etc   │ │
│  │  COPY requirements.txt .                                           │ │
│  │  RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt   ← +120 MB wheels     │ │
│  │                                                                     │ │
│  │  Total builder stage: ~470 MB                                       │ │
│  │  (includes gcc, headers, dev libraries — NEVER goes to production)  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                              │                                            │
│                              │ COPY --from=builder /root/.local          │
│                              │ (only the compiled .whl files — ~80 MB)   │
│                              ▼                                            │
│  STAGE 2: RUNTIME (python:3.12-slim, NO build tools)                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  FROM python:3.12-slim                        ← 150 MB base         │ │
│  │  RUN apt-get install libpq-dev curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* │ │
│  │                                              ← +15 MB runtime libs  │ │
│  │  COPY --from=builder /root/.local /usr/local  ← +80 MB wheels       │ │
│  │  COPY --chown=anihpj:anihpj . .              ← +15 MB source code  │ │
│  │                                                                     │ │
│  │  FINAL IMAGE: ~260 MB  (45% smaller than single-stage)              │ │
│  │  No gcc. No headers. No pip cache. No build-essential.              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  SINGLE-STAGE ALTERNATIVE (for comparison):                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  FROM python:3.12  (NOT slim)                  ← 920 MB base!       │ │
│  │  RUN apt-get install build-essential libpq-dev ← +200 MB            │ │
│  │  COPY . .                                                           │ │
│  │  RUN pip install -r requirements.txt           ← +120 MB            │ │
│  │                                                                     │ │
│  │  FINAL IMAGE: ~1,240 MB  (4.8× larger!)                            │ │
│  │  Contains: gcc, git, perl, python dev headers, 500+ CVEs            │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔀 ADD vs COPY — When to Use Which

Docker has two instructions for getting files into the image. COPY is preferred 99% of the time. ADD has extra features that create surprising behavior:

FeatureCOPYADD
Copy local files✅ Yes✅ Yes
Auto-extract tar archives❌ No✅ Yes (auto-extracts .tar, .tar.gz, .tgz)
Download from URL❌ No⚠️ Yes, but deprecated. Use RUN curl/wget instead.
--chown flag✅ Yes (COPY --chown=user:group)✅ Yes (ADD --chown=user:group)
Predictable behavior✅ Always does exactly what you expect⚠️ Auto-extraction can be surprising
Docker best practice✅ PREFERRED for 99% of casesOnly for local tar auto-extraction
 
# CORRECT: Use COPY for everything
COPY requirements.txt /app/
COPY --chown=anihpj:anihpj . /app/

# ACCEPTABLE: ADD for auto-extract tar
ADD myapp.tar.gz /app/   # Extracted to /app/ automatically
# Equivalent (but more explicit) with COPY + RUN:
COPY myapp.tar.gz /app/
RUN tar -xzf /app/myapp.tar.gz -C /app/ && rm /app/myapp.tar.gz

# WRONG: ADD for URL downloads (deprecated, unpredictable)
ADD https://example.com/file.tar.gz /app/
# Use RUN curl/wget instead — you control the download:
RUN curl -fsSL https://example.com/file.tar.gz -o /tmp/file.tar.gz && \
    tar -xzf /tmp/file.tar.gz -C /app/ && rm /tmp/file.tar.gz
🧬 ARG vs ENV — Build-Time vs Run-Time Variables

ARG is only available during docker build. ENV persists into the running container. Mixing them up causes secrets to leak into images and configuration to be missing at runtime:

FeatureARGENV
Available duringdocker build onlyBuild AND runtime
Persists in image❌ No (unless used in ENV)✅ Yes
Visible in docker inspect❌ No (only build-time)✅ Yes (docker inspect shows all ENV)
Override at builddocker build --build-arg KEY=valNot directly (set via ARG→ENV pattern)
Override at runtime❌ Cannotdocker run -e KEY=val
Best forBuild-time secrets, versions, platformRuntime configuration, feature flags
 
# ARG FOR BUILD-TIME (not in final image):
ARG PYTHON_VERSION=3.12
FROM python:${PYTHON_VERSION}-slim
ARG BUILD_DATE
RUN echo "Built at ${BUILD_DATE}" > /app/build-info.txt
# BUILD_DATE is gone after build. Not in final image.

# ENV FOR RUNTIME (persists in image):
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings

# ARG→ENV PATTERN (build-time config → runtime env):
ARG APP_VERSION=dev
ENV APP_VERSION=${APP_VERSION}
# Now APP_VERSION is in the image AND overridable at runtime
$ docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=v2.1.0 -t anihpj/jobpost .
$ docker run -e APP_VERSION=v2.1.1 anihpj/jobpost  # Override at runtime

# SECURITY: NEVER use ARG for secrets!
# ARG values are visible in docker history:
$ docker history anihpj/jobpost
# Shows: ARG SECRET_KEY=abc123  ← LEAKED!
# Use BuildKit secrets instead: --secret id=mysecret,src=/path/to/secret
🐚 SHELL Directive — Control How RUN Commands Execute

The SHELL directive changes the default shell for all subsequent RUN, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT instructions. Essential for Windows containers and for enabling pipefail in Linux:

# DEFAULT SHELL (Linux): /bin/sh -c
# DEFAULT SHELL (Windows): cmd /S /C

# ENABLE PIPEFAIL (fail if ANY command in a pipe fails):
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-eux", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]
RUN curl -fsSL https://example.com/script.sh | bash
# Without pipefail: curl fails but bash runs with empty input → SUCCESS (wrong!)
# WITH pipefail: curl fails → entire RUN fails immediately ✓

# SWITCH TO BASH FOR ADVANCED FEATURES:
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
RUN source /app/venv/bin/activate && python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
# /bin/sh doesn't support 'source' — you need bash for this

# WINDOWS CONTAINERS — switch to PowerShell:
SHELL ["powershell", "-Command", "$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop';"]
RUN Write-Host "Building on Windows"; \
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\app

# RESET TO DEFAULT:
SHELL ["/bin/sh", "-c"]

# WHY PIPEFAIL MATTERS IN DOCKERFILES:
# Without pipefail, this is undetectably broken:
RUN wget https://example.com/bigfile.tar.gz | tar -xz
# wget fails (network error) → empty stdout → tar succeeds → RUN succeeds!
# Your image builds "successfully" but is missing all the data.
# With pipefail: wget fails → pipefail kills the pipe → RUN fails → build stops.
🎯 ENTRYPOINT vs CMD — The Two Ways to Start a Container

Both define what runs when a container starts, but they serve different purposes and interact in subtle ways. Understanding the difference is essential for writing flexible, reusable Dockerfiles:

ENTRYPOINT vs CMD — Three Patterns for Container Startup
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     ENTRYPOINT vs CMD — Container Startup Patterns          │
│                                                                           │
│  PATTERN 1: CMD ONLY (most common — easy to override)                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Dockerfile:                        Runtime behavior:                │ │
│  │  CMD ["gunicorn", "..."]            $ docker run image               │ │
│  │                                      → gunicorn starts               │ │
│  │                                     $ docker run image bash          │ │
│  │                                      → bash starts (CMD replaced!)   │ │
│  │                                     $ docker run image python shell  │ │
│  │                                      → Django shell (debugging!)     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  PATTERN 2: ENTRYPOINT ONLY (container IS this binary)                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Dockerfile:                        Runtime behavior:                │ │
│  │  ENTRYPOINT ["nginx"]               $ docker run nginx               │ │
│  │  CMD ["-g", "daemon off;"]           → nginx -g "daemon off;"        │ │
│  │                                      $ docker run nginx -t           │ │
│  │                                       → nginx -t (CMD appended!)     │ │
│  │                                      $ docker run nginx bash         │ │
│  │                                       → ERROR: nginx bash (fails)    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  PATTERN 3: ENTRYPOINT SCRIPT + CMD (most flexible — production standard) │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Dockerfile:                                                        │ │
│  │  COPY docker-entrypoint.sh /usr/local/bin/                          │ │
│  │  ENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"]                                 │ │
│  │  CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000"]             │ │
│  │                                                                      │ │
│  │  docker-entrypoint.sh:                                              │ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │ │
│  │  │ #!/bin/bash                                                 │    │ │
│  │  │ set -e                                                      │    │ │
│  │  │ if [ "$1" = "gunicorn" ]; then                              │    │ │
│  │  │     until pg_isready -h db; do sleep 1; done  # Wait for DB │    │ │
│  │  │ fi                                                          │    │ │
│  │  │ exec "$@"  # ← MAGIC: replaces script with CMD as PID 1     │    │ │
│  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │ │
│  │                                                                      │ │
│  │  $ docker run image                      → waits for DB, gunicorn   │ │
│  │  $ docker run image python manage.py migrate → waits, then migrate  │ │
│  │  $ docker run --entrypoint bash image    → bypass entrypoint!       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  THE exec "$@" RULE: Without exec, script stays as PID 1 (no SIGTERM).   │
│  With exec, script REPLACES itself with CMD → CMD IS PID 1 → gets signal.│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
FeatureCMDENTRYPOINT
PurposeDefault command/args — easily overriddenFixed executable — container IS this process
Override at runtimedocker run image COMMAND replaces entirelydocker run image --flag appends to ENTRYPOINT
When both are setCMD becomes default ARGS to ENTRYPOINTENTRYPOINT is the executable, CMD is default args
Shell formCMD gunicorn ... (via /bin/sh -c)ENTRYPOINT gunicorn ... (via /bin/sh -c)
Exec formCMD ["gunicorn", "..."]ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn", "..."]
Best forDefault app with easy override for debuggingWrapper/init scripts that prep the container
 
# PATTERN 1: CMD only (most common — easy to override for debugging):
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
$ docker run anihpj/jobpost                           # Runs gunicorn
$ docker run anihpj/jobpost python manage.py shell    # Override: Django shell
$ docker run anihpj/jobpost bash                      # Override: debug shell

# PATTERN 2: ENTRYPOINT only (container IS this binary):
ENTRYPOINT ["nginx"]
CMD ["-g", "daemon off;"]
$ docker run nginx                                    # Runs: nginx -g "daemon off;"
$ docker run nginx -t                                 # Runs: nginx -t  (CMD overridden, appended!)
$ docker run nginx bash                               # ERROR: nginx bash (nginx doesn't accept bash arg)

# PATTERN 3: ENTRYPOINT script + CMD (most flexible):
# docker-entrypoint.sh:
#!/bin/bash
set -e
# Wait for database
if [ "$1" = "gunicorn" ]; then
    until pg_isready -h db -U anihpj; do sleep 1; done
fi
exec "$@"  # Run CMD (or runtime override)

# Dockerfile:
COPY docker-entrypoint.sh /usr/local/bin/
ENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"]
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
$ docker run anihpj/jobpost                           # Entrypoint waits for DB, then gunicorn
$ docker run anihpj/jobpost python manage.py migrate  # Entrypoint runs, then migrate
$ docker run --entrypoint bash anihpj/jobpost         # Override entrypoint entirely!

# THE exec "$@" MAGIC: Runs CMD (or docker run override) as PID 1 replacement.
# Without exec, the script stays as PID 1 and CMD becomes a child.
# With exec, the script REPLACES itself with CMD → CMD IS PID 1 → gets SIGTERM.
🔄 ONBUILD — Triggers for Downstream Images

ONBUILD stores instructions that run LATER — when another Dockerfile uses this image as its base with FROM. The ONBUILD triggers fire right after the downstream FROM, before any of the child's own instructions:

# PARENT Dockerfile (anihpj-base:latest):
FROM python:3.12-slim
ONBUILD COPY requirements.txt /app/
ONBUILD RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt
# These instructions are STORED but NOT executed during THIS build.

# CHILD Dockerfile (uses parent as base):
FROM anihpj-base:latest
# ⬆ ONBUILD triggers fire HERE (after FROM, before COPY .):
# 1. COPY requirements.txt /app/  (from ONBUILD)
# 2. RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  (from ONBUILD)
COPY . /app
CMD ["gunicorn", "..."]

# SEE ONBUILD TRIGGERS IN AN IMAGE:
$ docker image inspect anihpj-base | jq '.[].Config.OnBuild'
["COPY requirements.txt /app/", "RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt"]

# WARNING: ONBUILD is surprising behavior!
# If someone uses FROM anihpj-base without knowing about ONBUILD,
# their build may fail (no requirements.txt) or do unexpected things.
# Docker best practice: DOCUMENT prominently that the image has ONBUILD.
# Modern alternative: Provide a base image WITHOUT ONBUILD and a separate
# "onbuild" variant (e.g., python:3.12-onbuild) so users opt in explicitly.
🛑 STOPSIGNAL — Control Which Signal Stops Your Container

Docker sends SIGTERM by default when stopping containers. But not all applications handle SIGTERM correctly. STOPSIGNAL lets you change which signal Docker sends — critical for apps that expect SIGINT, SIGQUIT, or custom signals for graceful shutdown:

# DEFAULT: Docker sends SIGTERM (signal 15) → 10s wait → SIGKILL (signal 9)
# This works for gunicorn, nginx, and most modern apps.

# SOME APPS NEED DIFFERENT SIGNALS:
# - Apache httpd: graceful stop = SIGWINCH (28)
STOPSIGNAL SIGWINCH
# - Node.js: graceful shutdown = SIGINT (2) if not handling SIGTERM
STOPSIGNAL SIGINT
# - Redis: shutdown = SIGTERM (default, works)
# - PostgreSQL: fast shutdown = SIGINT, smart shutdown = SIGTERM
# - Custom apps: may use SIGUSR1 (10) or SIGUSR2 (12)

# CHECK WHAT SIGNAL AN IMAGE USES:
$ docker image inspect nginx | jq '.[].Config.StopSignal'
"SIGQUIT"  # nginx uses SIGQUIT for graceful shutdown!

# OVERRIDE STOPSIGNAL AT RUNTIME:
$ docker run --stop-signal SIGINT anihpj/jobpost
$ docker stop --signal SIGINT anihpj-web

# DEBUG: How does your app handle signals?
$ docker exec anihpj-web kill -TERM 1   # Does PID 1 handle SIGTERM?
$ docker exec anihpj-web kill -INT 1    # How about SIGINT?
# If the container exits gracefully, the signal is handled.
# If it stays running, the app ignores that signal → use STOPSIGNAL.

# SIGNAL QUICK REFERENCE:
# SIGTERM (15) — "Please stop" (default, polite)
# SIGINT  (2)  — Ctrl+C (interrupt from terminal)
# SIGQUIT (3)  — Quit with core dump (nginx, HAProxy)
# SIGHUP  (1)  — Hangup (often used for config reload)
# SIGKILL (9)  — Force kill (uncatchable, last resort)
# SIGUSR1 (10) — User-defined (application-specific)
🏷️ Image Tagging Strategies — Version, Deploy, and Rollback

How you tag Docker images directly impacts deploy safety, rollback speed, and cache efficiency. Poor tagging causes "latest" hell — you never know what's actually running:

StrategyExampleProsCons
latest onlyanihpj/jobpost:latestSimple, always newest❌ Can't rollback. Don't know what's deployed.
Semantic versionanihpj/jobpost:2.1.0Clear meaning, human-readableTag must be generated. CI must bump version.
Git commit SHAanihpj/jobpost:a1b2c3dImmutable, traceable to codeNot human-readable. Which is newer?
Build timestampanihpj/jobpost:2026-06-21Sortable. Know exactly when built.Multiple builds same day conflict.
CI build numberanihpj/jobpost:build-1423Sequential. Easy to find "previous."Tied to CI system. Not portable.
Multi-tagAll of the above on same image✅ Best of all worlds!Slightly more CI complexity.
 
# BEST PRACTICE: Multi-tag strategy:
$ IMAGE=anihpj/jobpost
$ SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
$ VERSION=$(cat VERSION)  # 2.1.0
$ docker build -t $IMAGE:$SHA \
               -t $IMAGE:$VERSION \
               -t $IMAGE:latest .
$ docker push $IMAGE:$SHA
$ docker push $IMAGE:$VERSION
$ docker push $IMAGE:latest
# Now you can: deploy by SHA (precise), reference by version, and
# "latest" always points to the most recent build.

# ROLLBACK IS JUST A TAG CHANGE:
$ docker tag $IMAGE:$PREVIOUS_SHA $IMAGE:latest
$ docker push $IMAGE:latest
# Or in K8s: kubectl set image deploy/web web=$IMAGE:$PREVIOUS_SHA

# BRANCH-BASED TAGS FOR ENVIRONMENTS:
# main → anihpj/jobpost:prod-20260621-a1b2c3d
# staging → anihpj/jobpost:staging-20260621-d4e5f6g
# PR #42 → anihpj/jobpost:pr-42-h7i8j9k

# NEVER USE :latest IN PRODUCTION!
# K8s imagePullPolicy: Always + latest = every pod restart may get
# a different image. Chaos. Always use specific tags in production.
⚠️ GOTCHA — Django runserver Binds to 127.0.0.1

127.0.0.1 is only reachable from INSIDE the container. Always use 0.0.0.0:8000 for containerized Django. Also: CMD must use exec form (["gunicorn", "..."]) not shell form — shell form doesn't receive SIGTERM properly, causing 10-second shutdown delays.

17.2 Container Networking Best Practices

The six practices below are not arbitrary rules — each one solves a real production problem that has caused real outages. Collectively, they represent the difference between a container that "works on my laptop" and one that survives the chaos of production: rolling deployments, security scans, auto-scaling events, and 3 AM incident pages.

The unifying theme is design for the environment, not for development. In development, you can hardcode IPs, run as root, skip health checks, and restart containers manually. In production, IPs change on every deploy, root access is a security liability, orchestrators need health checks to make decisions, and connections must drain gracefully during rolling updates. Every practice below is about making your container a good production citizen — one that Docker, Kubernetes, and your operations team can manage without surprises.

The most important practice — the one that causes the most production incidents — is the first one: bind to 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1. This single mistake is so common because every major web framework defaults to 127.0.0.1 in development mode. Django's runserver, Flask's dev server, Rails' puma in development — they all bind to localhost. In a VM or on bare metal, localhost means "this machine" and external users reach you through the machine's IP. In a container, localhost means only this container — the Docker bridge, the host, and other containers are all external. What works perfectly in development silently breaks in a container. The fix is always the same: explicitly bind to 0.0.0.0, which means "all interfaces" — the loopback, the veth connected to the Docker bridge, and any additional networks the container joins.

📋 Production Checklist
  1. Bind to 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1. 127.0.0.1 = container-only.
  2. Use DNS for inter-container communication. Never hardcode IPs.
  3. Use exec form for CMD. Ensures SIGTERM reaches the app.
  4. Always set HEALTHCHECK. "Process running" ≠ "application healthy."
  5. Run as non-root user. USER 1001. Limits blast radius.
  6. Multi-stage builds. Smaller images, fewer CVEs, faster deploys.
📦 Docker Layer Caching — Why COPY Order Matters

Docker builds images as ordered layers. Each instruction (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a new layer. Docker caches layers and reuses them if nothing changed. This is why COPY order is critical for fast builds:

DOCKER BUILD LAYER LIFECYCLE — How Caching Works
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     DOCKER BUILD — Layer by Layer                           │
│                                                                           │
│  BUILD 1 (first build — NO cache, everything runs):                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  FROM python:3.12-slim    → [CREATED]  150MB  (pulled from registry)│ │
│  │  COPY requirements.txt .  → [CREATED]  2KB    (new file)            │ │
│  │  RUN pip install -r ...   → [CREATED]  120MB  (all deps downloaded) │ │
│  │  COPY . .                 → [CREATED]  15MB   (source code copied)  │ │
│  │  CMD ["gunicorn",...]     → [CREATED]  0B     (metadata only)       │ │
│  │  TOTAL: ~285MB, ~45 seconds                                        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  BUILD 2 (code change only — 3 of 5 layers CACHED):                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  FROM python:3.12-slim    → [CACHED]   ← Same base image            │ │
│  │  COPY requirements.txt .  → [CACHED]   ← requirements.txt unchanged │ │
│  │  RUN pip install -r ...   → [CACHED]   ← No dependency changes      │ │
│  │  COPY . .                 → [CREATED]  ← ONLY this layer rebuilds!  │ │
│  │  CMD ["gunicorn",...]     → [CACHED]   ← Metadata unchanged         │ │
│  │  TOTAL: ~5 seconds (9× faster!)                                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  BUILD 3 (requirements.txt changed — 3 of 5 layers REBUILT):              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  FROM python:3.12-slim    → [CACHED]   ← Same base image            │ │
│  │  COPY requirements.txt .  → [CREATED]  ← File changed! Cache breaks │ │
│  │  RUN pip install -r ...   → [CREATED]  ← Must reinstall ALL deps    │ │
│  │  COPY . .                 → [CREATED]  ← Everything after break     │ │
│  │  CMD ["gunicorn",...]     → [CACHED]   ← Metadata still same        │ │
│  │  TOTAL: ~45 seconds (same as first build)                           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  THE GOLDEN RULE: Order layers from LEAST to MOST frequently changing.    │
│  Base image (rarely) → Dependencies (occasionally) → Config (sometimes)  │
│  → Source code (constantly). Every layer after a change is rebuilt.      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# WRONG ORDER (cache broken on EVERY code change):
COPY . .                           # ← Changes on every commit!
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt # ← Re-runs EVERY time (cache broken above)

# CORRECT ORDER (cache works for requirements):
COPY requirements.txt .            # ← Only changes when deps change (rarely)
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt # ← CACHED 99% of the time!
COPY . .                           # ← Code changes (fast, no pip reinstall)

# BUILD TIME COMPARISON (typical Django app):
# Wrong order:  ~45 seconds every time (pip install always runs)
# Right order:  ~5 seconds for code changes (pip install cached)
# That's 9× faster builds on every code change!
⚠️ GOTCHA — Shell Form CMD Breaks Signal Handling

Docker sends SIGTERM to PID 1 when stopping a container. With exec form (["gunicorn", "..."]), gunicorn IS PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly — graceful shutdown in <1 second. With shell form ("gunicorn ..."), /bin/sh is PID 1 and gunicorn is a child. /bin/sh does NOT forward signals to children. Docker waits 10 seconds, then sends SIGKILL (force kill). Your app never gets a chance to finish in-flight requests or close database connections cleanly.

EXEC FORM vs SHELL FORM — The Signal Handling Difference
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     EXEC FORM (CORRECT) — app IS PID 1                     │
│                                                                           │
│  $ docker stop anihpj-web                                                 │
│       │                                                                    │
│       ▼  Docker sends SIGTERM                                             │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                                │
│  │  PID 1: gunicorn master             │ ← Receives SIGTERM directly     │
│  │  │                                   │                                │
│  │  ├── PID 7: gunicorn worker 1       │ ← Master tells workers: quit    │
│  │  ├── PID 8: gunicorn worker 2       │ ← Workers finish requests       │
│  │  ├── PID 9: gunicorn worker 3       │ ← Workers drain connections     │
│  │  └── PID 10: gunicorn worker 4      │ ← Then exit gracefully          │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                                │
│  RESULT: All in-flight requests complete. DB connections closed.         │
│  Container exits in ~2 seconds. Zero dropped connections.                │
│                                                                           │
│  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│                                                                           │
│                     SHELL FORM (WRONG) — /bin/sh IS PID 1                  │
│                                                                           │
│  $ docker stop anihpj-web                                                 │
│       │                                                                    │
│       ▼  Docker sends SIGTERM to PID 1                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                                │
│  │  PID 1: /bin/sh -c "gunicorn ..."   │ ← RECEIVES SIGTERM             │
│  │  │                                   │ ← BUT DOES NOT FORWARD IT!     │
│  │  └── PID 7: gunicorn master         │ ← NEVER sees SIGTERM           │
│  │       │                              │ ← Continues running happily    │
│  │       ├── PID 8: worker 1           │ ← Still processing requests    │
│  │       ├── PID 9: worker 2           │ ← Unaware of shutdown           │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                                │
│       │                                                                    │
│       │  Docker waits 10 seconds...                                       │
│       │  Still running. Docker gives up.                                  │
│       ▼  Docker sends SIGKILL (uncatchable!)                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                                │
│  │  EVERYTHING FORCE-KILLED            │ ← PID 1, PID 7, all workers     │
│  │  In-flight connections: RST (reset) │ ← Clients get connection errors │
│  │  DB transactions: rolled back       │ ← Data may be inconsistent      │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                                │
│  RESULT: Brute-force kill after 10s wait. Dropped connections.           │
│  Corrupted requests. Users see 502 errors.                                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧟 PID 1 & Zombie Reaping — Why Your Container Needs an Init Process

PID 1 has special responsibilities in Linux — it must reap orphaned child processes (zombies). If your app runs as PID 1 but doesn't handle SIGCHLD, child processes that exit become zombies forever — consuming process table slots until the container is restarted:

# SEE ZOMBIE PROCESSES IN A CONTAINER:
$ docker exec web ps aux
USER  PID  STAT  COMMAND
1001  1    Ss    gunicorn: master
1001  7    S     gunicorn: worker
1001  8    Z     [gunicorn]   # ZOMBIE! Gunicorn master didn't reap it.

# THE PROBLEM: gunicorn master doesn't call waitpid() for dead children.
# Over days, zombie count grows → process table fills → fork() fails.

# SOLUTION 1: Use tini (tiny init) as PID 1:
# Dockerfile: RUN apk add tini; ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini", "--"]
# tini reaps zombies and forwards signals correctly.

# SOLUTION 2: Docker's built-in init (--init flag):
$ docker run --init anihpj/jobpost
# --init runs docker-init (tini-based) as PID 1. Your CMD runs as child.
# This ensures zombies are reaped and SIGTERM reaches your app.

# SOLUTION 3: K8s automatically adds a pause container as PID 1
# in the pod's namespace. But your app containers still need to reap
# their own children or use an init process.
📂 Overlay2 Filesystem — How Docker Stores Image Layers

Docker uses the overlay2 storage driver to combine multiple image layers into a single unified filesystem. Each instruction in your Dockerfile creates a new layer. overlay2 stacks these layers and presents a merged view:

OVERLAY2 FILESYSTEM — How Docker Layers Stack Together
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     OVERLAY2 — Layered Filesystem Architecture              │
│                                                                           │
│  CONTAINER VIEW (what the process sees):                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │                        / (unified root)                              │ │
│  │  /app/              /usr/              /var/              /etc/      │ │
│  │  (source code)      (python + libs)    (logs, data)      (config)   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                              ▲ MERGED VIEW                                 │
│                              │ (overlay2 combines all layers)              │
│                                                                           │
│  ON DISK (/var/lib/docker/overlay2/):                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  LAYER 6: Container R/W layer (copy-on-write)      [CONTAINER]      │ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│ │
│  │  │  LAYER 5: CMD ["gunicorn", "..."]             0B   [METADATA]  ││ │
│  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐││ │
│  │  │  │  LAYER 4: COPY . .                       15MB  [SOURCE CODE]│││ │
│  │  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│││ │
│  │  │  │  │  LAYER 3: RUN pip install -r reqs    120MB  [PIP DEPS] ││││ │
│  │  │  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐││││ │
│  │  │  │  │  │  LAYER 2: COPY requirements.txt     2KB  [DEPS LIST]│││││ │
│  │  │  │  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│││││ │
│  │  │  │  │  │  │  LAYER 1: FROM python:3.12-slim 150MB  [BASE]  ││││││ │
│  │  │  │  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│││││ │
│  │  │  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘││││ │
│  │  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│││ │
│  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘││ │
│  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                           │
│  KEY PRINCIPLES:                                                          │
│  ‣ Each layer only stores files that CHANGED from the layer below        │
│  ‣ Unchanged files are SHARED via hard links — massive space savings     │
│  ‣ Container writes trigger COPY-ON-WRITE: file copied UP to R/W layer   │
│  ‣ Multiple containers from same image share all layers below LAYER 6    │
│  ‣ Deleting a file in a layer = whiteout file (0-byte marker)            │
│                                                                           │
│  SPACE SAVINGS: 10 containers from same image = 10 × R/W layer only      │
│  NOT 10 × (150+2+120+15+0) = 2.87 GB. Just 10 × (small writes).         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# SEE IMAGE LAYERS:
$ docker image history anihpj/jobpost
IMAGE          CREATED BY                                      SIZE
abc123def456   CMD ["gunicorn" ...]                            0B
def456abc789   COPY . .                                        15MB
ghi789def012   RUN pip install -r requirements.txt             120MB
jkl012ghi345   COPY requirements.txt .                         2KB
mno345jkl678   WORKDIR /app                                    0B
pqr678mno901   FROM python:3.12-slim                           150MB

# HOW OVERLAY2 STORES LAYERS ON DISK:
$ ls /var/lib/docker/overlay2/
l/  # Short symbolic links to layer directories
abc123.../diff/  # Each layer's files (only what changed from parent)
abc123.../merged/ # Unified view of this layer + all parents below
abc123.../work/   # Working directory for copy-on-write operations

# KEY: Each layer only stores files that CHANGED from the parent.
# Unchanged files are shared via hard links → massive space savings.
# When a container writes to a file, overlay2 copies it UP to the
# container's own layer (copy-on-write) — original layer unchanged.
0️⃣ Bind 0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1 — The Most Common Container Networking Mistake

Inside a container, 127.0.0.1 means "this container only" — NOT "the Docker host." Understanding this distinction is the difference between a working app and hours of debugging:

127.0.0.1 vs 0.0.0.0 Inside a Container
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BIND 127.0.0.1:8000 (WRONG for containers)                      │
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────┐             │
│  │   Docker Host       │     │   Container          │             │
│  │   eth0: 192.168.1.10│     │   lo: 127.0.0.1      │             │
│  │                     │     │   eth0: 172.17.0.2   │             │
