│  STEP 8: Pod B receives the original TCP SYN                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Pod B kernel: sees TCP SYN src=10.244.1.5:54321 dst=10.244.2.8:8000      │ │
│  │  Matches listening socket on port 8000 (nginx/gunicorn)                    │ │
│  │  Sends TCP SYN-ACK back to 10.244.1.5:54321                               │ │
│  │  SYN-ACK follows same path in reverse (VXLAN encaps from node-2 to node-1)│ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│        │                                                                       │
│        ▼                                                                       │
│  STEP 9: TCP handshake completes, HTTP flows bidirectionally                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  All subsequent packets follow the same VXLAN-encapsulated path.           │ │
│  │  Pod A has NO IDEA the packet was VXLAN-encapsulated.                      │ │
│  │  Pod B has NO IDEA the packet was VXLAN-encapsulated.                      │ │
│  │  From their perspective: direct IP communication between pods.            │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  KEY DIFFERENCE: Same-node = bridge forwarding (0.1ms).                       │
│                 Cross-node = VXLAN encaps/decaps + physical wire (1-5ms).     │
│                 Both are transparent to the application.                       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ GOTCHA — Cross-Node Latency: Same-Node 0.08ms vs Cross-Node 1-5ms

The performance difference between same-node and cross-node pod communication is significant:

MetricSame-NodeCross-Node (VXLAN)Cross-Node (BGP)
Typical RTT0.05–0.15ms0.5–5ms0.3–3ms
OverheadZero50 bytes (VXLAN)Zero
MTUFull (1500)Reduced (1450)Full (1500)
CPU CostMinimalEncapsulation + decapsulationMinimal
Failure ModeBridge/cni0 downUDP 4789 blocked, route missingBGP session down

Why this matters for anihpj: If you deploy the jobpost-web and postgres pods on different nodes, every database query adds 1-5ms of cross-node latency. For a page that makes 20 database queries, that's 20-100ms of extra latency just from pod placement. This is why pod affinity rules matter — pinning the web and database pods to the same node (or same AZ) can dramatically improve response times. But be careful: co-locating them means that node failure takes down both.

Cross-Node Pod-to-Pod Debugging — traceroute + tcpdump bash 
# 1. Verify pods are on DIFFERENT nodes
$ kubectl get pods -o wide -n anihpj
NAME                IP           NODE
jobpost-web-7d4f8   10.244.1.5   node-1
jobpost-api-9k3m2   10.244.2.8   node-2
# Different nodes → cross-node communication (VXLAN/BGP)

# 2. Test connectivity and measure latency
$ kubectl exec jobpost-web-7d4f8 -- ping -c 5 10.244.2.8
64 bytes from 10.244.2.8: icmp_seq=0 ttl=62 time=1.234 ms
64 bytes from 10.244.2.8: icmp_seq=1 ttl=62 time=1.189 ms
# ~1.2ms = cross-node (VXLAN encapsulation overhead + physical wire)
# TTL=62 (decremented by 2: once on source node, once on VXLAN decap)

# 3. Check the VXLAN tunnel — capture encapsulated traffic
$ ssh node-1
$ tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 4789' -nn -c 5
12:34:56.789012 IP 192.168.1.10.54321 > 192.168.1.11.4789: VXLAN
# You should see VXLAN packets for every cross-node pod communication

# 4. Check the VXLAN FDB — which node IP for which pod network?
$ bridge fdb show dev vxlan.calico
00:00:00:00:00:00 dst 192.168.1.11 self permanent
# "dst 192.168.1.11" = VXLAN tunnel endpoint for pod subnet on node-2

# 5. Trace the route from the pod's perspective
$ kubectl exec jobpost-web-7d4f8 -- traceroute -n 10.244.2.8
traceroute to 10.244.2.8, 30 hops max
 1  169.254.1.1  0.045 ms  0.038 ms  0.041 ms     ← Host proxy ARP gateway
 2  10.244.2.8   1.201 ms  1.189 ms  1.234 ms      ← Destination pod
# 2 hops: gateway → destination pod. VXLAN tunnel is transparent!

# 6. On destination node: capture decapsulated traffic
$ ssh node-2
$ tcpdump -i cni0 -nn 'host 10.244.2.8' -c 5
# You'll see the INNER packet (src=10.244.1.5, dst=10.244.2.8)
# The VXLAN headers were stripped before reaching cni0
🔄 How the Routing Table Makes Cross-Node Communication Work

The host's routing table is the "brain" of cross-node pod communication. After the CNI plugin sets up the VXLAN tunnel, it adds routes like:

# On node-1 (192.168.1.10):
$ ip route show
10.244.1.0/24 dev cni0 proto kernel scope link src 10.244.1.1
# △ Local pod subnet — delivered via cni0 bridge (same-node pods)

10.244.2.0/24 via 10.244.2.0 dev vxlan.calico onlink
# △ Remote pod subnet — delivered via VXLAN tunnel to node-2

# On node-2 (192.168.1.11):
$ ip route show
10.244.2.0/24 dev cni0 proto kernel scope link src 10.244.2.1
# △ Local pod subnet

10.244.1.0/24 via 10.244.1.0 dev vxlan.calico onlink
# △ Remote pod subnet — VXLAN tunnel back to node-1

# How VXLAN knows the destination node IP:
$ bridge fdb show dev vxlan.calico
00:00:00:00:00:00 dst 192.168.1.11 self permanent
# "dst 192.168.1.11" is the remote VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint (VTEP)
# All traffic to 10.244.2.0/24 is encapsulated and sent to 192.168.1.11:4789

Key insight: When a new node joins the cluster, the CNI plugin automatically: (1) assigns the node a pod CIDR block, (2) updates the VXLAN FDB with the new node's IP, and (3) adds the route for the new pod subnet via the VXLAN interface. All other nodes learn this new route — no manual configuration needed. This is the magic of CNI.

VXLAN Kernel Internals — How the Linux Kernel Encapsulates Your Pod Packets

VXLAN isn't just a protocol — it's a Linux kernel driver (drivers/net/vxlan.c in the kernel source). When the CNI plugin creates a VXLAN interface (e.g., vxlan.calico), it's creating a virtual network device backed by this driver. Understanding how the driver works is essential for debugging cross-node pod communication issues, MTU problems, and performance bottlenecks.

VXLAN Interface Creation — What Actually Happens

When Calico creates the VXLAN interface with a command equivalent to:

ip link add vxlan.calico type vxlan id 4096 local 192.168.1.10 dev eth0 dstport 4789 nolearning

The kernel does the following:

  • VNI 4096 (Virtual Network Identifier): This is the "VXLAN network ID" — think of it as a VLAN ID for overlay networks. All K8s pod traffic on this cluster uses VNI 4096. If you had multiple K8s clusters on the same physical network, you'd use different VNIs to isolate them. The VNI is a 24-bit field, so you can have up to 16 million isolated overlay networks.
  • local 192.168.1.10: This is the VTEP (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint) IP — the source IP address that appears in the outer IP header of every VXLAN-encapsulated packet leaving this node. It must be a real IP on the node's physical interface, routable by the physical network.
  • dev eth0: The physical device the VXLAN interface is bound to. Encapsulated packets are sent out through this device. The kernel uses this to determine the source MAC for the outer Ethernet header.
  • dstport 4789: The UDP destination port for VXLAN traffic. 4789 is the IANA-assigned port for VXLAN. Some implementations use 8472 (Linux default before standardization), which causes interoperability issues. Always verify your CNI uses 4789.
  • nolearning: Disables automatic FDB learning from incoming VXLAN packets. Calico manages the FDB entries explicitly (via its own control plane) rather than relying on data-plane learning. This is important: in a Kubernetes cluster, pods come and go rapidly, and data-plane FDB learning would create stale entries and cause traffic blackholes.
The VXLAN FDB — How the Kernel Knows Where to Send Encapsulated Packets

The VXLAN driver maintains its own Forwarding Database (FDB), separate from the bridge FDB used for same-node communication. This FDB maps destination MAC addresses (or the "all-zero" wildcard) → remote VTEP IP addresses. When the kernel needs to send a packet via the VXLAN interface:

  1. The IP routing table says: 10.244.2.0/24 dev vxlan.calico. The kernel forwards the packet to the vxlan.calico device.
  2. The VXLAN driver looks at the inner Ethernet frame's destination MAC. It checks the FDB: "What's the remote VTEP for this MAC?"
  3. If the inner destination MAC is unknown, the VXLAN driver checks for the all-zero wildcard entry (00:00:00:00:00:00). This is the "default" VTEP — used when the specific MAC isn't in the FDB. Calico sets this to the remote node's IP: 00:00:00:00:00:00 dst 192.168.1.11. All cross-node pod traffic uses this wildcard entry.
  4. The VXLAN driver constructs the encapsulation: VXLAN header (VNI=4096) → UDP header (src=ephemeral, dst=4789) → outer IP header (src=192.168.1.10, dst=192.168.1.11) → outer Ethernet header. The original pod packet becomes the inner payload.
  5. The encapsulated packet is transmitted out the physical device (eth0).
🔬 VXLAN vs Geneve vs IPIP — Which Encapsulation Does Your CNI Use?
ProtocolHeader SizePort/ProtocolExtensibilityUsed By
VXLAN8 bytes (VXLAN header) + 8 bytes (UDP) + 20 bytes (outer IP) + 14 bytes (outer Eth) = 50 bytes totalUDP port 4789Fixed 24-bit VNI field. Limited.Calico VXLAN mode, Flannel VXLAN backend, Cilium (VXLAN mode)
GeneveVariable — base 8 bytes + TLV options. Typically 8 (Geneve) + 8 (UDP) + 20 (outer IP) + 14 (outer Eth) = 50+ bytesUDP port 6081Highly extensible — TLV (Type-Length-Value) options can carry any metadata (NSH, service chaining info, tenant ID, etc.)Cilium (default mode), OVN-Kubernetes
IPIP (IP-in-IP)20 bytes (outer IP header only, no UDP, no VXLAN) = 20 bytes overheadIP protocol 4 (not UDP!)None. Just IP inside IP.Calico IPIP mode (cross-subnet only, simpler than VXLAN)

Why Calico offers both IPIP and VXLAN: IPIP is simpler and faster (20 bytes overhead vs 50 bytes for VXLAN), but it ONLY carries IPv4 inside IPv4 — no IPv6 support, no Ethernet frame preservation (pod MAC addresses are lost). VXLAN preserves the full inner Ethernet frame, which matters for NetworkPolicy enforcement at L2 and for certain service mesh features. IPIP also uses IP protocol 4, which some cloud firewalls block by default (they expect TCP, UDP, and ICMP — protocol 4 is none of those). VXLAN uses standard UDP port 4789, which is easier to allow through firewalls.

The MTU Problem — Why Your Pod's 1500-byte Packet Becomes 1550 Bytes on the Wire

The MTU mismatch is the most common cross-node performance issue in Kubernetes. Here's the math that every platform engineer should internalize:

Without VXLAN: Pod A sends a 1500-byte IP packet (20 bytes IP header + 1480 bytes TCP payload). The Ethernet frame is 1514 bytes (1500 + 14 byte Eth header). This fits perfectly on a link with MTU 1500 — no fragmentation needed.

With VXLAN: Pod A sends the same 1500-byte IP packet. The VXLAN driver encapsulates it: adds 50 bytes of headers (14 outer Eth + 20 outer IP + 8 UDP + 8 VXLAN). Total = 1550 bytes. This EXCEEDS the physical link MTU of 1500. The kernel must either fragment the outer IP packet (if DF bit is cleared) or drop it and send an ICMP "Fragmentation Needed" message back (if DF bit is set).

Why fragmentation doesn't solve it: IP fragmentation is expensive — the sender must split the packet, the receiver must reassemble it (with timeouts), and if ANY fragment is lost, the entire packet is retransmitted. Fragmentation also bypasses some firewalls and load balancers that don't handle fragments correctly. Most importantly, many cloud providers and network devices block ICMP "Fragmentation Needed" messages, which means the sender never knows the packet was too big (this is called a PMTUD black hole). The sender keeps sending 1500-byte packets, they keep getting dropped, and TCP connections hang — exactly the "database is slow on Tuesdays" scenario from our incident.

The fix — lower pod MTU: The CNI plugin must set the pod's MTU to physical link MTU - VXLAN overhead. For a standard 1500 MTU link: pod MTU = 1450. The CNI plugin does this when creating the veth pair: it sets the MTU on both ends. The pod's eth0 and the host's caliXXXX both get MTU 1450. When the pod generates a 1450-byte IP packet, VXLAN adds 50 bytes = exactly 1500 bytes — a perfect fit. No fragmentation, no drops, no PMTUD issues. This is why ip addr show eth0 inside any pod in a VXLAN cluster shows mtu 1450 — it's not arbitrary, it's mathematically derived from the physical MTU.

Jumbo frames: If your physical network supports jumbo frames (MTU 9000), pod MTU can be 8950, and VXLAN overhead becomes negligible in percentage terms (50/9000 = 0.55% overhead vs 50/1500 = 3.3% overhead). This is why high-performance K8s clusters on bare metal often enable jumbo frames — the encapsulation cost becomes almost zero.

⚠️ CRITICAL — How to Detect an MTU Black Hole in Your Cluster

An MTU black hole is when packets are silently dropped because they exceed the path MTU, but the ICMP "Fragmentation Needed" message never reaches the sender. This is the most insidious networking problem because it's intermittent (small packets work, large ones don't), application-dependent (APIs with small responses work, large file downloads don't), and looks like "the network is slow" rather than "the network is broken." Here's how to detect it:

# 1. Test with increasing payload sizes — find the boundary
kubectl exec pod-a -- ping -M do -s 1422 10.244.2.8    # 1422+8+20 = 1450 — should work
kubectl exec pod-a -- ping -M do -s 1423 10.244.2.8    # 1423+8+20 = 1451 — may fail!
# -M do = "Don't Fragment" (sets DF bit). If this fails at a specific
#   payload size, that's your PMTU boundary.

# 2. Check the actual PMTU to a destination
kubectl exec pod-a -- tracepath -n 10.244.2.8
# This discovers the path MTU by sending probes with DF set.

# 3. Check current pod MTU
kubectl exec pod-a -- ip link show eth0 | grep mtu
# Should show mtu 1450 (for VXLAN). If 1500 → MTU mismatch!

# 4. Quick test: small vs large HTTP request
kubectl exec pod-a -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://10.244.2.8:8000/health
# Should return 200 quickly. Now try a large response:
kubectl exec pod-a -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n%{time_total}s' \
  http://10.244.2.8:8000/api/jobs/  # Large JSON response
# If this hangs or takes >5s while /health is fast → MTU problem.

19.4 LAB: Pod Networking Hands-On

🛠️ Pod Networking Lab — 6 Hands-On Exercises

Complete these exercises on your K8s cluster. Each builds on the last, taking you from basic inspection to full packet tracing.

1

Get Pod IPs and Node Placement

Deploy two test pods and identify their IPs and which nodes they're on.

$ kubectl run pod-a --image=nginx --restart=Never
$ kubectl run pod-b --image=nginx --restart=Never
$ kubectl get pods -o wide
NAME    IP           NODE
pod-a   10.244.1.9   node-1
pod-b   10.244.2.3   node-2
# Same node or different? This determines the communication path.
2

Ping from One Pod to Another

Test L3 connectivity and measure latency. The RTT tells you if pods are same-node or cross-node.

$ kubectl exec pod-a -- ping -c 3 10.244.2.3
PING 10.244.2.3: 64 bytes, icmp_seq=0 ttl=62 time=1.234 ms
# ~1ms = cross-node (VXLAN). ~0.08ms = same-node (bridge).
# TTL=62 means 2 hops (gateway + VXLAN decap). TTL=63 = 1 hop.
3

Inspect the Pod's Network from Inside

See exactly what the pod sees: its IP, routes, DNS config, and ARP table.

$ kubectl exec pod-a -- ip addr show eth0
$ kubectl exec pod-a -- ip route show
$ kubectl exec pod-a -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
$ kubectl exec pod-a -- ip neigh show
# The pod's world: one IP, one default route, one DNS server.
4

Trace the Route with traceroute

See the hop count and per-hop latency from inside the pod.

$ kubectl exec pod-a -- traceroute -n 10.244.2.3
 1  169.254.1.1  0.045 ms  0.038 ms  0.041 ms
 2  10.244.2.3   1.201 ms  1.189 ms  1.234 ms
# 2 hops: host gateway → destination pod. VXLAN is invisible!
5

Capture Traffic on the Node

SSH to the node and capture pod traffic on the cni0 bridge and the VXLAN interface.

$ ssh node-1
# Same-node traffic:
$ sudo tcpdump -i cni0 -nn 'host 10.244.1.9' -c 5
# Cross-node traffic (VXLAN-encapsulated):
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 4789' -nn -c 5
# You'll see: IP 192.168.1.10.xxxxx > 192.168.1.11.4789: VXLAN
6

Inspect Pod Network from the Node with nsenter

Enter the pod's network namespace from the host — useful when the pod has no tools.

$ ssh node-1
$ POD_ID=$(crictl pods --name pod-a -q)
$ POD_PID=$(crictl inspectp $POD_ID | jq '.info.pid')
$ sudo nsenter -t $POD_PID -n ip addr show
$ sudo nsenter -t $POD_PID -n ip route show
$ sudo nsenter -t $POD_PID -n nc -zv 10.244.2.3 80
# You're now running commands INSIDE the pod's network namespace
# from the host, with all host tools available!

19.5 Debugging Pod Networking — The Complete Toolkit

When pod communication breaks, you need a systematic toolkit — not guesswork. This section gives you every command you'll need, organized by where you run them (inside the pod vs on the node) and what layer they test (L3, L4, L7). Bookmark this section — it's your go-to reference during incidents.

Debugging FROM Within a Pod — Essential Commands

📋 Pod-Level Debug Toolkit — Run with kubectl exec
CommandLayerWhat It Tests
ip addr showL2/L3Pod has an IP? Interface is UP? MTU correct?
ip route showL3Default route exists? Routing table complete?
ping <target-ip>L3ICMP reachability. RTT tells you same-node vs cross-node.
nc -zv <ip> <port>L4TCP port open? Connection refused vs timeout?
dig <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.localL7 (DNS)DNS resolution working? Returns Service ClusterIP?
curl -v http://<svc>:<port>/L7HTTP reachable? Response code, headers, timing?
ip neigh showL2ARP cache — gateway MAC resolved?
traceroute -n <target-ip>L3Path visibility. Hop count reveals overlay topology.
cat /etc/resolv.confL7 (DNS)DNS config — nameserver IP, search domains, ndots

Debugging FROM the Node — Essential Commands

📋 Node-Level Debug Toolkit — SSH to the Node
CommandWhat It Shows
nsenter -t <pid> -n ip addrInspect pod's network namespace from the host
crictl podsList all pods on this node with container IDs
crictl inspectp <pod-id>Pod details: PID, network namespace path, labels
ip netns identify <pid>Find which network namespace a process lives in
conntrack -L -s <pod-ip>All tracked connections for this pod
bridge fdb show br cni0MAC → veth mappings on the pod bridge
tcpdump -i cni0 -nn host <pod-ip>Capture this pod's traffic on the bridge
tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 4789'Capture VXLAN-encapsulated cross-node traffic
ip route | grep <pod-subnet>Verify routes to pod subnets on other nodes
🔧 The Ultimate Debug Pod: netshoot

When your pod doesn't have curl, ping, dig, or tcpdump, deploy a netshoot debug container. It's a Swiss Army knife with every networking tool pre-installed:

# Deploy a temporary debug pod with EVERY networking tool:
$ kubectl run netshoot --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- /bin/bash

# Tools inside netshoot:
# curl, dig, nc, tcpdump, iperf3, nmap, mtr, socat,
# netcat-openbsd, iproute2, ethtool, conntrack, and more

# Now test from the debug pod:
netshoot$ curl -v http://jobpost-service.anihpj:8000/api/health
netshoot$ dig jobpost-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
netshoot$ nc -zv 10.244.2.8 8000
netshoot$ tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 8000 -c 10
⚠️ GOTCHA — kubectl exec Defaults to the First Container

In multi-container pods, kubectl exec runs commands in the first container defined in the pod spec. If that container doesn't have the tools you need (no curl, no ping — common in distroless images), your debug commands will fail. Always specify the container explicitly:

# WRONG: Runs in default container (might be distroless, no tools)
$ kubectl exec jobpost-web-7d4f8 -- ping 10.244.2.8
# rpc error: ... executable file not found in $PATH

# RIGHT: Specify the container with tools (or use the sidecar)
$ kubectl exec jobpost-web-7d4f8 -c gunicorn -- curl localhost:8000/health
$ kubectl exec jobpost-web-7d4f8 -c envoy-sidecar -- ping 10.244.2.8

# Check which containers are in the pod:
$ kubectl get pod jobpost-web-7d4f8 -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'
gunicorn envoy-sidecar
📖 Reading a Pod's DNS Configuration — /etc/resolv.conf Deep Dive

Every pod's /etc/resolv.conf is configured by the kubelet based on the pod's DNS policy. Understanding this file is critical for debugging DNS issues:

$ kubectl exec pod-a -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.96.0.10
search anihpj.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5

What each line means:

  • nameserver 10.96.0.10 — The CoreDNS Service ClusterIP. All DNS queries go here. If CoreDNS pods are down, NO DNS resolution works.
  • search anihpj.svc.cluster.local ... — DNS search domains. When you query jobpost-service, the resolver tries: jobpost-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local → jobpost-service.svc.cluster.local → jobpost-service.cluster.local → jobpost-service (absolute).
  • options ndots:5 — Names with fewer than 5 dots are tried as relative names first (using search domains). Names with 5+ dots are tried as absolute first. This is the #1 cause of slow DNS in Kubernetes — a query for api.stripe.com (3 dots) generates 4 DNS queries (each search domain) before the absolute query. Fix with ndots:1 for pods that query external domains frequently.

conntrack — Connection Tracking for Pod Traffic

conntrack (Connection Tracking) is the Linux kernel subsystem that tracks every network connection flowing through the node. It's the "memory" of the network stack — without it, stateful firewalls (iptables), NAT (SNAT/MASQUERADE), and load balancing (kube-proxy) wouldn't work. Every pod-to-pod TCP connection, every NATed external request, every Service ClusterIP DNAT — they all have entries in the conntrack table.

Why should you care? When the conntrack table fills up (default: 262,144 entries on most Linux systems), new connections are DROPPED — not rejected, not timed out, silently dropped. This is a catastrophic failure that looks like random, intermittent connectivity loss. Pods can reach some things but not others. Existing connections work but new ones fail. This is one of the hardest problems to diagnose without knowing about conntrack.

Conntrack Deep Dive — Inspecting Pod Connection State bash 
# 1. See ALL connections tracked for a specific pod
$ conntrack -L -s 10.244.1.5
tcp 6 431999 ESTABLISHED src=10.244.1.5 dst=10.244.2.8 sport=54321 dport=8000 \
    src=10.244.2.8 dst=10.244.1.5 sport=8000 dport=54321 [ASSURED] mark=0 use=1

# Format: [protocol] [ttl] [state] [original direction] [reply direction] [flags]
# [ASSURED] = bidirectional traffic seen (not just SYN). Won't be evicted early.
# [UNREPLIED] = only one direction seen. Will be evicted after timeout if no reply.

# 2. See NAT/SNAT entries for pod traffic going to internet
$ conntrack -L -s 10.244.1.5 -p tcp --dport 443
tcp 6 300 ESTABLISHED src=10.244.1.5 dst=34.120.45.67 sport=65432 dport=443 \
    src=34.120.45.67 dst=192.168.1.10 sport=443 dport=65432 [ASSURED]
# ▲ Notice: reply dst=192.168.1.10 (NODE IP, not pod IP!) = SNAT/MASQUERADE

# 3. See Service ClusterIP connections (kube-proxy DNAT)
$ conntrack -L -d 10.96.100.50 -p tcp --dport 8000
tcp 6 86399 ESTABLISHED src=10.244.1.5 dst=10.96.100.50 sport=54321 dport=8000 \
    src=10.244.2.8 dst=10.244.1.5 sport=8000 dport=54321 [ASSURED]
# ▲ Original: dst=ClusterIP. Reply: src=actual backend pod IP!
# This is kube-proxy DNAT in action — conntrack remembers the translation.

# 4. Check conntrack table capacity and usage
$ cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max
262144                                          # Max entries
$ cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count
198432                                          # Current entries
# Usage: 198432/262144 = 75.7%. Set alert at 80%.

# 5. Increase conntrack max (for high-connection clusters)
$ echo 524288 > /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max
# Or permanently: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=524288
# Rule of thumb: 65,536 per GB of RAM for high-connection nodes.

# 6. Check conntrack timeout values
$ conntrack -L --output xml 2>/dev/null | head -1
# Or check /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_*
# Default TCP established timeout: 432000 sec (5 days!) — very long.
# TIME_WAIT: 120 sec. CLOSE_WAIT: 60 sec.
⚠️ CRITICAL — Conntrack Table Exhaustion = Silent Connection Drops

When nf_conntrack_count reaches nf_conntrack_max, the kernel logs nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet and silently drops all new connections. There's no TCP RST, no ICMP error — the client just hangs. Symptoms:

  • Existing connections (SSH, established TCP sessions) continue working
  • New connections intermittently fail — sometimes work, sometimes hang
  • Kubernetes health checks start failing (kubectl get pods shows increased restarts)
  • DNS lookups fail (each lookup creates a new UDP conntrack entry)

Root causes of conntrack exhaustion in K8s:

  • Too many pods on one node — each pod with open connections. 110 pods × 500 connections = 55,000 entries.
  • DNS-heavy workloads — each DNS query creates a short-lived UDP conntrack entry (default timeout: 30s). At 10,000 DNS queries/sec, that's 300,000 entries.
  • Service mesh sidecars — Envoy/Linkerd proxies create connections to every upstream, multiplying the connection count.
  • Connection pooling gone wrong — apps that open thousands of idle connections without closing them.

Fix: Increase nf_conntrack_max (requires kernel memory — each entry ~300 bytes). Monitor with: watch -n 5 'cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count'. Set Prometheus alert: node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit > 0.8.

ip netns — Managing Network Namespaces on the Node

The ip netns command lets you list, inspect, and even execute commands inside network namespaces from the host. This is different from nsenter — ip netns manages named network namespaces (created via ip netns add), while pod network namespaces are typically anonymous (created by the container runtime). However, you can still use ip netns identify to find which namespace a process is in:

ip netns — Network Namespace Management on the Node bash 
# 1. List all NAMED network namespaces (pod namespaces are anonymous)
$ ip netns list
# Usually empty on K8s nodes — pod netns are not "named".
# But crio/containerd sometimes create named ones depending on config.

# 2. Identify which namespace a PROCESS is in
$ ip netns identify 12345
cni-0a58e7f2-3b4c-4d5e-8f6g-7h8i9j0k1l2m
# Shows the network namespace identifier for PID 12345

# 3. Create a named network namespace (for testing/learning)
$ ip netns add test-ns
$ ip netns exec test-ns ip addr show
1: lo: <LOOPBACK> mtu 65536 ...
# A brand new, isolated network namespace — no interfaces except lo!

# 4. Connect two namespaces with a veth pair (the manual way CNI does it!)
$ ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1
$ ip link set veth0 netns test-ns
$ ip netns exec test-ns ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev veth0
$ ip netns exec test-ns ip link set veth0 up
$ ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev veth1
$ ip link set veth1 up
$ ip netns exec test-ns ping 10.0.0.2
# Success! Two namespaces communicating via veth pair.
# This is EXACTLY what the CNI plugin does for every pod!
🔬 Hands-On Learning — Build Pod Networking from Scratch

The best way to truly understand pod networking is to replicate what CNI does manually. On any Linux machine, create two network namespaces, connect them with a veth pair, assign IPs, set up routes, and create a bridge. It takes 10 minutes and the mental model will stay with you forever:

# Step 1: Create two namespaces (like two pods)
ip netns add pod-a
ip netns add pod-b

# Step 2: Create a bridge (like cni0)
ip link add br0 type bridge
ip addr add 10.244.0.1/24 dev br0
ip link set br0 up

# Step 3: Create veth pairs and connect (like CNI ADD)
# Pod A: veth-a-host (host side) ↔ veth-a-pod (pod side)
ip link add veth-a-host type veth peer name veth-a-pod
ip link set veth-a-pod netns pod-a
ip netns exec pod-a ip addr add 10.244.0.10/24 dev veth-a-pod
ip netns exec pod-a ip link set veth-a-pod up
ip netns exec pod-a ip link set lo up
ip link set veth-a-host master br0
ip link set veth-a-host up

# Pod B: same pattern
ip link add veth-b-host type veth peer name veth-b-pod
ip link set veth-b-pod netns pod-b
ip netns exec pod-b ip addr add 10.244.0.11/24 dev veth-b-pod
ip netns exec pod-b ip link set veth-b-pod up
ip netns exec pod-b ip link set lo up
ip link set veth-b-host master br0
ip link set veth-b-host up

# Step 4: Test! Same-node pod-to-pod communication
ip netns exec pod-a ping 10.244.0.11
# PING 10.244.0.11: 64 bytes ... time=0.042 ms
# ← SAME-NODE POD NETWORKING, BUILT FROM SCRATCH!

# Step 5: Add default route + proxy ARP for external access
ip netns exec pod-a ip route add default via 10.244.0.1
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward                  # Enable routing
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/br0/proxy_arp           # Enable proxy ARP
# Now pod-a can reach the internet via the host!
ip netns exec pod-a ping 8.8.8.8
# This is EXACTLY what Kubernetes does — proxy ARP + NAT.

Run this on any Linux machine. When you see those caliXXXXX interfaces on your K8s nodes, you'll know exactly what they are and how they got there.

Reading tcpdump Output for Pod Networking — A Practical Guide

tcpdump is the ultimate source of truth for pod networking — packets don't lie. But reading tcpdump output for Kubernetes traffic requires understanding what you're looking at. Here's how to recognize the key patterns:

Pattern 1: Same-Node Pod-to-Pod (Common)
tcpdump on cni0 — Same-Node Pod Communication bash 
# tcpdump -i cni0 -nn 'host 10.244.1.5 and host 10.244.1.6'
12:34:56.789012 ARP, Request who-has 10.244.1.6 tell 10.244.1.1, length 28
12:34:56.789234 ARP, Reply 10.244.1.6 is-at 0a:58:0a:f4:01:06, length 28
12:34:56.789345 IP 10.244.1.5.54321 > 10.244.1.6.8000: Flags [S], seq 1000
12:34:56.789456 IP 10.244.1.6.8000 > 10.244.1.5.54321: Flags [S.], seq 5000, ack 1001
12:34:56.789567 IP 10.244.1.5.54321 > 10.244.1.6.8000: Flags [.], ack 1
# KEY OBSERVATIONS:
# 1. ARP happens first (host asks, pod B responds)
# 2. No VXLAN headers, no node IPs — pure pod IPs!
# 3. Port numbers are from pod's ephemeral range (54321) and pod's listening port (8000)
# 4. TCP handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK completes in ~0.2ms
Pattern 2: Cross-Node Pod-to-Pod via VXLAN (On Physical Interface)
tcpdump on eth0 — Cross-Node VXLAN-Encapsulated Traffic bash 
# tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 4789' -nn
12:34:56.789678 IP 192.168.1.10.45678 > 192.168.1.11.4789: VXLAN, flags [I] (0x08), vni 4096
IP 10.244.1.5.54321 > 10.244.2.8.8000: Flags [S], seq 1000
# KEY OBSERVATIONS:
# 1. OUTER packet: src=192.168.1.10 (node-1 IP), dst=192.168.1.11 (node-2 IP), UDP port 4789
# 2. "VXLAN, flags [I], vni 4096" — the VXLAN header with VNI (cluster identifier)
# 3. INNER packet (indented): pod IPs and pod ports — the ACTUAL pod communication
# 4. The physical network sees ONLY node IPs. Pod IPs are hidden inside.
# 5. If you DON'T see this on eth0 when cross-node pods communicate → routing or FDB issue.
Pattern 3: Cross-Node Pod-to-Pod After Decapsulation (On Destination cni0)
tcpdump on cni0 — Destination Node Shows Decapsulated Traffic bash 
# tcpdump -i cni0 -nn 'host 10.244.2.8' (on node-2)
12:34:56.790123 IP 10.244.1.5.54321 > 10.244.2.8.8000: Flags [S], seq 1000
12:34:56.790234 IP 10.244.2.8.8000 > 10.244.1.5.54321: Flags [S.], seq 5000, ack 1001
# KEY OBSERVATIONS:
# 1. VXLAN headers are GONE — the kernel decapsulated before delivering to the bridge.
# 2. Pod B sees the ORIGINAL source IP (10.244.1.5) — no NAT!
# 3. From pod B's perspective, this looks identical to same-node traffic.
# 4. This is the beauty of VXLAN: pods have no idea they're on different nodes.
Pattern 4: SNAT/Masquerade — Pod Reaching the Internet
tcpdump on eth0 — Pod Traffic to the Internet (SNAT) bash 
# tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'host 8.8.8.8' (pod pinging Google DNS)
12:34:56.790345 IP 192.168.1.10 > 8.8.8.8: ICMP echo request, id 1234, seq 1
12:34:56.790456 IP 8.8.8.8 > 192.168.1.10: ICMP echo reply, id 1234, seq 1
# KEY OBSERVATIONS:
# 1. Source IP is 192.168.1.10 (NODE IP), NOT 10.244.1.5 (pod IP)!
# 2. The kernel SNATed (MASQUERADE) the pod's IP to the node's IP.
# 3. Google has NO IDEA this came from a pod — it just sees a normal ICMP from a node.
# 4. On the return path, the kernel de-SNATs: 8.8.8.8 → 192.168.1.10 → 10.244.1.5.
# 5. Verify with: iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING | grep MASQUERADE
🎯 The tcpdump Mental Checklist — What to Look For in Any Capture

When you capture pod traffic, ask these questions in order:

  1. Is there ANY traffic? If you see zero packets, the pod isn't sending or the capture filter is wrong. Check: is the pod's IP correct? Is the interface correct?
  2. Are there ARP requests with no replies? ARP "who-has X tell Y" with no response = the target doesn't exist or a firewall is blocking ARP. On a bridge, every pod should respond to ARP.
  3. Are there TCP SYNs with no SYN-ACKs? The destination pod is reachable at L3 (ARP worked) but not responding at L4. Either the port is closed, a NetworkPolicy is blocking, or the pod is crashed.
  4. Are there TCP retransmissions? The same SYN packet repeated = no response at all (firewall DROP, not REJECT). Repeated data packets with same sequence number = packet loss.
  5. Are there TCP RSTs? RST = port closed or connection refused. This is BETTER than a timeout — it means the destination is reachable but not listening on that port.
  6. Are the IPs what you expect? Pod-to-pod should show pod IPs (10.244.x.x). Internet traffic should show node IPs (SNAT). Service traffic should show ClusterIP → pod IP (DNAT). If you see unexpected IPs, conntrack or iptables is rewriting traffic.

19.6 K8s Pod Network Debug Decision Tree — Systematic Isolation

When "Pod A can't reach Pod B," don't guess — use this decision tree. It systematically isolates the failure by scope: pod status → same-node connectivity → cross-node connectivity → Service connectivity → internet connectivity. Each step eliminates a layer of the stack.

POD NETWORK DEBUG DECISION TREE — 7 Steps to Isolate ANY Failure
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SYMPTOM: "Pod A can't reach Pod B" → SYSTEMATIC ISOLATION                    │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 1: Are BOTH pods Running AND have IPs?                                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  $ kubectl get pods -o wide -A | grep -E 'pod-a|pod-b'                    │ │
│  │  ├─ Both Running, both have IPs → Go to Step 2                           │ │
│  │  ├─ Not Running → Check pod events: kubectl describe pod                 │ │
│  │  │  └─ ContainerCreating with "failed to set up pod network"? → CNI     │ │
│  │  └─ Running but NO IP (column shows ) → CNI failed. Check CNI pod. │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│        │                                                                       │
│        ▼                                                                       │
│  STEP 2: Can Pod A ping Pod B's IP? (L3 test)                                 │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  $ kubectl exec pod-a -- ping -c 3                              │ │
│  │  ├─ PING succeeds → L3 works! Go to Step 4 (check L4/L7).                │ │
│  │  └─ PING fails → L3 broken. Go to Step 3.                                │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│        │                                                                       │
│        ▼                                                                       │
│  STEP 3: Same Node or Different Node?                                          │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  $ kubectl get pods -o wide | grep -E 'pod-a|pod-b'                       │ │
│  │  ├─ SAME NODE → Problem is LOCAL:                                          │ │
│  │  │  • Check cni0 bridge: bridge fdb show br cni0 | grep        │ │
│  │  │  • Check ARP: kubectl exec pod-a -- ip neigh show                      │ │
│  │  │  • Check veth: ip link show | grep cali (on node)                      │ │
│  │  │  • Check NetworkPolicy: kubectl get networkpolicy -A                   │ │
│  │  └─ DIFFERENT NODES → Problem is CROSS-NODE:                               │ │
│  │     • Check VXLAN: tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 4789' (on both nodes)        │ │
│  │     • Check firewall: Is UDP 4789 allowed between nodes?                  │ │
│  │     • Check routes: ip route | grep  (on node-1)            │ │
│  │     • Check CNI pod logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system            │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│        │                                                                       │
│        ▼                                                                       │
│  STEP 4: Are there NetworkPolicies blocking? (L3/L4 firewall)                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  $ kubectl get networkpolicy -A | grep                           │ │
│  │  ├─ Policies exist → Check if they block pod-a → pod-b:                   │ │
│  │  │  kubectl describe networkpolicy  -n                         │ │
│  │  └─ No policies → All traffic allowed. Go to Step 5.                      │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│        │                                                                       │
│        ▼                                                                       │
│  STEP 5: Check CNI plugin logs — what does the CNI see?                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  $ kubectl logs -n kube-system  --tail=100             │ │
│  │  $ kubectl logs -n kube-system  --tail=100             │ │
│  │  Look for:                                                                 │ │
│  │  • "failed to program routes" → IPAM or routing table issue               │ │
│  │  • "failed to apply iptables" → iptables conflict                        │ │
│  │  • "VXLAN tunnel down" → UDP 4789 blocked or node unreachable            │ │
│  │  • "BGP session down" → BGP peer unreachable                             │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│        │                                                                       │
│        ▼                                                                       │
│  STEP 6: Check node-level routing — can the host reach the pod?                │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  $ ssh node-1                                                              │ │
│  │  $ ip route | grep                                           │ │
│  │  ├─ Route exists → Go to Step 7                                           │ │
│  │  └─ Route MISSING → CNI didn't install route. Restart CNI pod.           │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  $ ssh node-2                                                              │ │
│  │  $ ip route | grep                                               │ │
│  │  ├─ Route exists → Host can reach pod. Check pod's interface.             │ │
│  │  └─ Route MISSING → Pod's veth not properly attached to bridge.           │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│        │                                                                       │
│        ▼                                                                       │
│  STEP 7: tcpdump end-to-end — where do packets stop?                           │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  NODE-1:                                                                    │ │
│  │  $ tcpdump -i cni0 -nn 'host  and host ' -c 10        │ │
│  │  ├─ Sees traffic LEAVING pod-a → Pod sends packets. Go to next capture.   │ │
│  │  └─ NO traffic → Pod-A's app or kernel is broken.                          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  NODE-1:                                                                    │ │
│  │  $ tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 4789' -nn -c 5                                │ │
│  │  ├─ Sees VXLAN traffic → Packets are leaving node-1. Go to node-2.        │ │
│  │  └─ NO VXLAN → Routing issue on node-1. Check: ip route get .   │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  NODE-2:                                                                    │ │
│  │  $ tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 4789' -nn -c 5                                │ │
│  │  ├─ Sees VXLAN arriving → Packets reach node-2. Go to next capture.       │ │
│  │  └─ NO VXLAN → Network/firewall between nodes blocking UDP 4789.          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  NODE-2:                                                                    │ │
│  │  $ tcpdump -i cni0 -nn 'host ' -c 10                             │ │
│  │  ├─ Sees decapsulated traffic → Packets reach bridge.                       │ │
│  │  └─ NO traffic → VXLAN decap or route to bridge broken.                    │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  GOLDEN RULE: Isolate by scope. Same-node → cross-node → Service → internet.  │
│  The failure scope tells you EXACTLY which component is broken.                │
│  THE PACKETS DON'T LIE. Trust tcpdump over assumptions.                        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔴 Real Incident — "The Job Board Is Slow, but Only on Tuesdays"

It's Tuesday morning. Users report the jobpost app is taking 3-4 seconds to load, but only on certain pages. Yesterday it was fine. The database team says PostgreSQL is healthy. The app team says the code hasn't changed. What's going on?

Symptoms:

  • 🔴 Pages that query the database are slow (3-4s). Static pages are fast (<100ms).
  • 🔴 Only pods on node-3 are affected. Pods on node-1 and node-2 are fast.
  • 🔴 The postgres pod is on node-1. jobpost-web pods on node-3 are slow.

Debugging with the decision tree:

Step 1-2: Pods are Running, have IPs. Ping succeeds. L3 is fine.

Step 3: Different nodes! jobpost-web on node-3, postgres on node-1. Cross-node communication.

Step 6-7: ping -s 1400 (large payload) between node-3 and node-1: fails. But ping -s 100 succeeds! MTU problem.

Root Cause: A network engineer changed the switch MTU from 1500 to 1400 on Tuesday morning (scheduled maintenance). The VXLAN overhead (50 bytes) + 1400 byte switch MTU = pod MTU must be ≤1350. But pods had MTU 1450 (1500-50). Large database responses (exceeding 1350 bytes) were fragmented or dropped, causing TCP retransmissions and 3-4 second delays.

Fix: Set pod MTU to 1350 in the CNI config (veth_mtu: "1350") and restart pods. Or revert the switch MTU change. The latter was chosen — switch MTU restored to 1500.

Lesson: MTU mismatches are silent performance killers. TCP connections work (SYN packets are small), but large data transfers hang, timeout, or crawl. Always test with large payloads (ping -s 1400) when debugging cross-node slowness. And document your pod MTU dependencies — if the network team changes switch MTU, pods break in ways that look like "the database is slow."

📊 Chapter 19 Visual Summary — What You've Learned

📦 Pod Network Namespace Every pod gets its own isolated network stack. Pause container holds the namespace open. All containers in a pod share the same IP, interfaces, and port space.
🔗 veth Pair — Pod's Doorway Virtual patch cable: eth0 in pod ↔ caliXXXX on host. Every packet enters/leaves the pod through this single interface pair.
🌉 Same-Node: Bridge Forwarding Pod A → veth → cni0 bridge → veth → Pod B. No encapsulation. ~0.08ms latency. Pure kernel forwarding with FDB-based MAC learning.
📦 Cross-Node: VXLAN Tunnel 9-step journey: veth → route → VXLAN encaps (50B overhead) → UDP 4789 → physical wire → decaps → veth. ~1-5ms latency. Transparent to pods.
🔍 nsenter — Debug from Host Enter pod's network namespace from the node: nsenter -t <pid> -n. Inspect pod's IP, routes, ARP — even if pod has no tools installed.
🐞 7-Step Debug Decision Tree Isolate by scope: pod status → L3 ping → same/cross node → NetworkPolicy → CNI logs → node routes → tcpdump end-to-end. Packets don't lie.
🔄 How This Applies to Your Daily Work

When a pod can't reach another pod, your first question is: same node or different node? kubectl get pods -o wide tells you in 2 seconds. Same-node failures are almost always bridge or veth issues. Cross-node failures are almost always VXLAN tunnel, firewall, or route issues. Narrowing the scope immediately eliminates 80% of debugging dead ends.

nsenter is your secret weapon. When a pod has no debugging tools (distroless images, minimal containers), don't rebuild the image — nsenter into the pod's network namespace from the node and use all the host's tools. This saves hours during incidents and requires no pod restarts or image changes.

MTU is the silent killer of cross-node performance. If everything works but is mysteriously slow (especially database queries), test with large payloads: ping -s 1400 <pod-ip>. If it fails while small pings work, you have an MTU mismatch. Pod MTU must be ≤ (physical MTU - VXLAN overhead). For 1500 MTU links: pod MTU = 1450. For 1400 MTU links: pod MTU = 1350.

Pod affinity isn't just about availability — it's about latency. Co-locating pods that chat frequently (web ↔ database) on the same node or same AZ eliminates VXLAN encapsulation overhead and cuts latency from 1-5ms to 0.08ms. The tradeoff is blast radius — a node failure takes both down. Balance latency vs resilience based on your application's requirements.

🔑 Chapter 19 Key Takeaways

  1. Every pod has its own network namespace — isolated IP stack, routing table, and ARP cache. The pause container holds the namespace open. All containers in a pod share the same namespace (same IP, same port space — no port conflicts allowed between containers in the same pod).
  2. The veth pair is the pod's only network connection to the outside world. Pod eth0 ↔ host caliXXXX. Every packet entering or leaving the pod traverses this single veth pair. The host's proxy ARP gateway (169.254.1.1) is the pod's default route — the pod sends everything through the host's routing table.
  3. Same-node pod communication uses the cni0 bridge — zero overhead, ~0.08ms. The bridge learns MAC addresses dynamically (FDB) and forwards frames directly between veth ports. No VXLAN, no physical network traversal.
  4. Cross-node pod communication uses VXLAN encapsulation — 50 bytes overhead, ~1-5ms. Pod packets are wrapped in VXLAN headers and sent over UDP 4789 between node IPs. Pods have no idea encapsulation happened — they just see direct IP communication.
  5. nsenter lets you debug pod networking from the host — no pod tools needed. nsenter -t <pid> -n <command> runs commands inside the pod's network namespace. Essential for debugging distroless or minimal containers.
  6. Use the 7-step decision tree to isolate any pod-to-pod failure. Isolate by scope: pod status → L3 ping → same/cross node → NetworkPolicy → CNI logs → node routes → tcpdump. The failure scope tells you exactly which component is broken.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 19

⏸️Pause Container
The first container created in every pod. Runs /pause — a minimal binary that sleeps forever. Its sole purpose is to hold the pod's network namespace open. If it dies, the pod sandbox is destroyed and all containers lose networking. Also called the infra container or sandbox container.
🔗veth Pair (Virtual Ethernet)
A Linux kernel construct that acts like a virtual patch cable — data written to one end appears at the other. In K8s, one end is in the pod's network namespace (eth0) and the other in the host's root namespace (caliXXXX or lxcXXXX). The pod's only network connection to the outside world.
🌉cni0 Bridge
A Linux bridge interface acting as a virtual switch. All pod veth host-side endpoints on a node attach to this bridge. Handles L2 forwarding between same-node pods using a dynamically learned Forwarding Database (FDB). Gateways the pod subnet (e.g., 10.244.1.1/24).
🔍nsenter
Linux command that enters a process's namespaces. nsenter -t <pid> -n enters the network namespace of a process — effectively giving you a shell inside the pod's network environment from the host. Essential for debugging pods that lack network tools.
📋FDB (Forwarding Database)
The Linux bridge's MAC address table. Maps MAC addresses to bridge ports (veth interfaces). Dynamically learned — when a frame arrives on a port, the source MAC is recorded. Entries expire after 300 seconds of inactivity. View with bridge fdb show br cni0.
🎯Proxy ARP Gateway
The host's 169.254.1.1 link-local address that acts as the pod's default gateway. The host responds to ARP requests for any IP (not just its own), then routes traffic based on its routing table. Enables pods to reach any destination without knowing the cluster topology.
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 19.1 — Pod Network Inspection

On your Kubernetes cluster, complete these tasks using kubectl and node access:

  1. Deploy two nginx pods. Get their IPs and node placement.
  2. From pod-a, ping pod-b. Is the RTT consistent with same-node or cross-node communication?
  3. Inspect pod-a's network: IP, routes, DNS config, ARP table. What's the default gateway?
  4. On the node where pod-a runs, find the host-side veth for pod-a. What's its name?
  5. Use nsenter to inspect pod-a's network namespace from the host. Verify it matches what kubectl exec showed.
💡 Hint: kubectl get pods -o wide, kubectl exec ... -- ip addr, crictl pods, nsenter -t <pid> -n. The default gateway is always 169.254.1.1. veth names follow the pattern caliXXXX for Calico.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. Deploy pods and get info
kubectl run pod-a --image=nginx --restart=Never
kubectl run pod-b --image=nginx --restart=Never
kubectl get pods -o wide
# Note IPs and NODE column

# 2. Test connectivity
kubectl exec pod-a -- ping -c 3 <pod-b-ip>
# RTT <0.1ms → same node. RTT >0.5ms → cross node.

# 3. Inspect pod network
kubectl exec pod-a -- ip addr show eth0
kubectl exec pod-a -- ip route show
# Default gateway: 169.254.1.1
kubectl exec pod-a -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl exec pod-a -- ip neigh show

# 4. Find host-side veth (SSH to node)
ssh node-1
POD_ID=$(crictl pods --name pod-a -q)
POD_PID=$(crictl inspectp $POD_ID | jq '.info.pid')
nsenter -t $POD_PID -n ip -o link show eth0
# Output: eth0@if5 → peer index is 5
ip link show | grep "^5:"
# 5: cali1234abc@if3 → host-side veth name
⏱️ Target: 8 minutes
Drill 19.2 — Cross-Node Packet Tracing

You suspect cross-node pod communication is broken. Run this systematic trace:

  1. Schedule pod-a on node-1 and pod-b on node-2 (use nodeSelector).
  2. From pod-a, test connectivity to pod-b: ping + nc to port 80.
  3. On node-1: check the route to pod-b's subnet. Is it via VXLAN or BGP?
  4. On node-1: tcpdump VXLAN traffic while pod-a pings pod-b. Do you see encapsulated packets?
  5. On node-2: tcpdump VXLAN traffic. Do you see the same packets arriving?
  6. On node-2: tcpdump on cni0 for pod-b's IP. Do you see decapsulated traffic?
💡 Hint: Use nodeSelector: kubernetes.io/hostname: node-X in pod specs. Check routes with ip route | grep <subnet>. VXLAN uses UDP 4789. cni0 shows decapsulated inner packets.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. Schedule pods on specific nodes
# pod-a.yaml: nodeSelector: { kubernetes.io/hostname: node-1 }
# pod-b.yaml: nodeSelector: { kubernetes.io/hostname: node-2 }
kubectl apply -f pod-a.yaml && kubectl apply -f pod-b.yaml

# 2. Test connectivity
kubectl exec pod-a -- ping -c 3 <pod-b-ip>
kubectl exec pod-a -- nc -zv <pod-b-ip> 80

# 3. Check route on node-1
ssh node-1
ip route | grep <pod-b-subnet>
# Should show: 10.244.2.0/24 via ... dev vxlan.calico

# 4. Capture VXLAN on node-1
ssh node-1
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 4789' -nn -c 5
# Run the ping from pod-a NOW
# Should see: IP 192.168.1.10.xxxxx > 192.168.1.11.4789: VXLAN

# 5. Capture VXLAN on node-2
ssh node-2
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 4789' -nn -c 5
# Should see matching packets arriving from node-1

# 6. Capture decapsulated traffic on node-2 cni0
ssh node-2
sudo tcpdump -i cni0 -nn host <pod-b-ip> -c 5
# Should see ICMP echo request from pod-a-ip TO pod-b-ip
# VXLAN headers already stripped!
⏱️ Target: 6 minutes
Drill 19.3 — Pod Networking Incident Response

A developer reports: "My new pod 'worker-processor' in namespace 'anihpj' can't reach the postgres pod. I can ping it, but nc to port 5432 times out." Use the 7-step decision tree to diagnose:

  1. Which step of the tree does this symptom correspond to? (Ping works → L3 OK. TCP fails → L4 issue.)
  2. What are the 3 most likely causes, given that ping (ICMP) works but TCP (port 5432) fails?
  3. What commands would you run to verify each cause?
  4. How would you determine if a NetworkPolicy is blocking the traffic?
💡 Hint: ICMP works but TCP doesn't = L4 filtering. Think NetworkPolicy, pod-level firewall (iptables), or the target pod not listening on that port. Check: kubectl get networkpolicy, ss -tlnp inside postgres pod, kubectl describe networkpolicy.
📝 View Solution 
# 1. Symptom analysis: Ping (L3/ICMP) works, nc (L4/TCP) fails.
#    This is Step 2 → 4 in the decision tree: L3 OK, check L4.

# 2. Most likely causes (in order):
#    (a) NetworkPolicy blocking TCP 5432 from worker-processor pods
#    (b) postgres pod not listening on port 5432 (crashed, wrong port)
#    (c) iptables rule on the node dropping TCP 5432 from that pod

# 3. Verification commands:
# Check NetworkPolicy:
kubectl get networkpolicy -n anihpj
kubectl describe networkpolicy <policy> -n anihpj

# Check if postgres is listening:
kubectl exec postgres-xxx -- ss -tlnp | grep 5432

# Check iptables on the node (SSH in):
sudo iptables -L -n -v | grep -E '5432|DROP.*anihpj'

# 4. NetworkPolicy diagnosis — look for:
# PodSelector: app=postgres (selects the target pod)
# Ingress rules: which pods are allowed?
# If worker-processor's labels don't match any ingress rule → BLOCKED.
# Fix: Add an ingress rule allowing from podSelector: {app: worker-processor}
# on port 5432, OR add the worker-processor labels to an existing rule.

📝 Chapter 19 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is the pause container, and why does every pod have one?
Show Answer
Answer

The pause container (infra/sandbox container) is the first container created in every pod. It runs a minimal binary (/pause) that sleeps forever. Its sole purpose is to hold the pod's network namespace open. All other containers in the pod join the pause container's network namespace, which means they share the same IP address and can communicate via localhost. If the pause container dies, the pod sandbox is destroyed and all containers lose networking.

Q2
Explain the veth pair. How does it connect a pod to the node's network?
Show Answer
Answer

A veth (virtual Ethernet) pair is a Linux kernel construct that acts like a virtual patch cable. One end (eth0) lives inside the pod's network namespace; the other end (caliXXXX, lxcXXXX, or cilium_XXXX) lives in the host's root network namespace, attached to the cni0 bridge. Data written to one end appears at the other. This veth pair is the pod's ONLY network connection to the outside world — every packet entering or leaving the pod traverses this pair.

Q3
Describe the full packet journey for same-node pod-to-pod communication. What's the typical latency?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Pod A sends packet to Pod B's IP. Kernel checks routing table → default route via 169.254.1.1 (proxy ARP gateway). 2. ARP for Pod B's IP: broadcast on cni0 bridge → Pod B responds with its MAC. 3. L2 frame (src=PodA_MAC, dst=PodB_MAC) sent out Pod A's eth0 → veth pair → cni0 bridge. 4. Bridge FDB lookup: knows PodB_MAC is on port cali5678def → forwards frame only to that port. 5. veth pair → Pod B's eth0 → delivered. Typical latency: ~0.05-0.15ms. No encapsulation, no physical wire.

Q4
Walk through the 9 steps of cross-node pod-to-pod communication with VXLAN.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Pod A sends TCP SYN to Pod B's IP. 2. Packet traverses veth to host root namespace. 3. Host routing table: 10.244.2.0/24 → vxlan.calico interface. 4. VXLAN encapsulation: inner pod packet wrapped in VXLAN+UDP+outer IP (src=node-1 IP, dst=node-2 IP, UDP port 4789). Total 50 bytes overhead. 5. Encapsulated packet sent out physical NIC. 6. Node-2 receives UDP:4789 → kernel recognizes VXLAN → decapsulates (strips outer headers). 7. Inner packet revealed: dst=10.244.2.8 → matches local pod subnet → routed to cali5678def. 8. veth delivers to Pod B's eth0. 9. TCP SYN received, SYN-ACK returned via reverse VXLAN path. Latency: 1-5ms.

Q5
How do you use nsenter to debug a pod's network from the host? When would you use it instead of kubectl exec?
Show Answer
Answer

Find the pod's process ID: crictl inspectp <pod-id> | jq '.info.pid'. Then: nsenter -t <pid> -n <command> — this runs the command inside the pod's network namespace. Use nsenter when: (1) the pod has no debugging tools (distroless/minimal image — no curl, ping, nc), (2) you need host-level tools (tcpdump, conntrack) that can't run inside a container, (3) the pod's container is crashing and kubectl exec won't work. nsenter is always available on the node and requires no pod modifications.

Q6
What does the pod's /etc/resolv.conf contain? What does ndots:5 mean and why does it cause slow DNS?
Show Answer
Answer

Pod's /etc/resolv.conf contains: nameserver (CoreDNS Service ClusterIP, e.g., 10.96.0.10), search domains (anihpj.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local), and options ndots:5. ndots:5 means names with fewer than 5 dots are resolved as relative names first (trying each search domain), then as absolute. A query for "api.stripe.com" (3 dots) generates 4 DNS queries (each search domain + absolute). For pods that query external domains frequently, this causes 4x DNS latency. Fix: set ndots:1 in the pod's DNS config for external-heavy workloads.

Q7
Walk through the 7-step pod network debug decision tree for "Pod A can't reach Pod B."
Show Answer
Answer

Step 1: Are both pods Running with IPs? Step 2: Can Pod A ping Pod B? (L3 test). Step 3: Same node or different node? (narrows scope). Step 4: Are there NetworkPolicies blocking? Step 5: Check CNI pod logs for errors. Step 6: Check node-level routing (ip route). Step 7: tcpdump end-to-end — cni0 on src node → eth0 (VXLAN) on src node → eth0 on dst node → cni0 on dst node. Isolate by scope: same-node → cross-node → Service → internet. The failure scope identifies the broken component.

Q8
Why does same-node pod communication have 0.08ms latency while cross-node has 1-5ms?
Show Answer
Answer

Same-node: pure kernel forwarding through the cni0 bridge. No encapsulation, no physical wire, no network hardware. The packet stays entirely within the node's kernel memory. Cross-node: the packet must be VXLAN-encapsulated (kernel CPU time), sent out the physical NIC (DMA to hardware), traverse physical switches (store-and-forward latency), arrive at destination NIC, be DMA'd into kernel memory, and be VXLAN-decapsulated. Each step adds latency: encaps (~0.05ms) + physical wire (~0.1-2ms depending on distance) + switch (~0.01-0.5ms per switch) + decaps (~0.05ms). Same-AZ cross-node: ~1ms. Cross-AZ: ~2-5ms. Cross-region: 20-100ms+.

Q9
A developer says "I can ping the database pod but nc -zv to port 5432 times out." What are the 3 most likely causes?
Show Answer
Answer

1. NetworkPolicy blocking TCP 5432 from the developer's pod to the database pod (ICMP works because NetworkPolicy only filters TCP/UDP, not ICMP by default). 2. The database process is not listening on port 5432 (crashed, misconfigured, listening on a different port). 3. An iptables rule or security group dropping TCP 5432 specifically (ICMP allowed for diagnostics, TCP blocked for security). Debug: kubectl get networkpolicy -A; kubectl exec postgres-pod -- ss -tlnp | grep 5432; iptables -L -n -v on the node.

Q10
How does MTU affect pod networking? What happens when pod MTU is larger than the VXLAN path MTU?
Show Answer
Answer

Pod MTU must be ≤ (physical MTU - VXLAN overhead). For 1500 MTU physical links: pod MTU = 1450 (1500 - 50 bytes VXLAN). When pod MTU exceeds the path MTU: small packets (SYN, ACK, small HTTP requests) work fine. Large packets (database responses, file transfers, large API responses) are either fragmented (if DF bit not set — adds latency and reassembly overhead) or dropped (if DF bit set — TCP connections hang because PMTUD is often blocked in cloud environments). Symptoms: SSH/health checks work, but data transfers timeout or are extremely slow. This looks like "the database is slow" but is actually an MTU mismatch.

Chapter 20: Services — Stable Networking for Ephemeral Pods

Pods are mortal. They die. They get replaced. They get rescheduled to different nodes. Every time a pod restarts, it gets a brand new IP address — and every other pod that was talking to it by IP suddenly can't reach it. This is the fundamental problem that Kubernetes Services solve. A Service gives you a stable, unchanging virtual IP (the ClusterIP) and a DNS name that always resolves to that IP, regardless of which pods are actually running behind it. If you understand Services, you understand how Kubernetes abstracts away pod ephemerality. If you don't, your applications will break every time a pod restarts — and you won't know why.

This chapter bridges the gap between raw pod networking (Chapter 19) and how real applications talk to each other in production. You'll learn exactly how kube-proxy uses iptables (or IPVS, or eBPF) to turn a virtual ClusterIP into real traffic to backend pods. You'll trace a packet through every iptables chain from PREROUTING to POSTROUTING. And you'll learn why iptables -t nat -L -n -v is the most important debugging command you can run on any K8s node. When "the site is down" and the pods are running, the problem is almost always in the Service layer.

🟡 INTERMEDIATE ⏱️ ~2 hours ☸️ Kubernetes 🔀 Services 🔥 kube-proxy

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:

  • Explain why Services exist and how they solve the pod ephemerality problem with stable virtual IPs
  • Distinguish between all 5 Service types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, ExternalName, and Headless
  • Trace a packet through kube-proxy iptables chains: PREROUTING → KUBE-SERVICES → KUBE-SVC-XXXX → KUBE-SEP-XXXX
  • Compare kube-proxy modes (iptables, IPVS, nftables, eBPF) across performance, scalability, and scheduling algorithms
  • Debug a Service that's silently dropping traffic — from selector mismatch to NetworkPolicy to conntrack
  • Read iptables counters to determine which backend pods are receiving traffic (and which aren't)
☸️ Kubernetes Relevance
SRE CRITICAL Platform Engineering CORE DevOps ESSENTIAL
💡 The Service Mental Model — Stable Identity Over Ephemeral Pods

Think of a Service as a phone number that never changes, even though the people (pods) behind it come and go. Your application code always dials the same number. The phone company (kube-proxy) routes the call to whoever is currently on duty. If someone leaves (pod dies) and a new person takes over (new pod), the phone number stays the same and calls keep flowing. Key principles to internalize:

  • A Service is just a configuration object — it doesn't "run" anywhere. kube-proxy (a DaemonSet pod on every node) reads Service and Endpoint objects from the API server and programs the node's network stack (iptables/IPVS/eBPF) to implement the routing.
  • The ClusterIP is a VIRTUAL IP — nothing owns it. No interface has 10.96.100.50 assigned. It exists only as a destination in iptables DNAT rules. When a packet arrives with dst=10.96.100.50, iptables rewrites the destination to a real pod IP. This is why you can't ping a ClusterIP — there's no interface to respond to ICMP.
  • Services use label selectors, not pod names or IPs. A Service with selector: app=jobpost sends traffic to ALL pods with that label, regardless of their name, namespace, or node.

What You Want to KnowCommandWhere
