Cloud LB Comparison — AWS vs GCP vs Azure

Every major cloud provider has both L4 and L7 load balancers. The concepts are the same; the names differ:

FeatureAWSGCPAzure
L4 TCP/UDP LBNetwork Load Balancer (NLB)TCP/UDP Load Balancer (regional, external or internal)Azure Load Balancer (Standard/Basic)
L7 HTTP(S) LBApplication Load Balancer (ALB)HTTP(S) Load Balancer (global external, regional internal)Application Gateway (v2) — also has WAF built in
Global LBALB is regional. Use Global Accelerator for global.HTTP(S) LB is global by default — single anycast IP routes to nearest region.Azure Front Door — global L7, anycast.
TLS TerminationACM certificates on ALB/NLB. Free public certs.Google-managed or custom certs on HTTP(S) LB. Free public certs via Certificate Manager.Azure Key Vault certs on App Gateway. NOT free for public certs (need third-party or paid).
WebSocketALB: Native. NLB: Native (TCP passthrough).HTTP(S) LB: Native.App Gateway: Native.
gRPCALB: Native (HTTP/2). NLB: Native (TCP passthrough).HTTP(S) LB: Native (HTTP/2).App Gateway: Limited (HTTP/2 support, gRPC requires specific config).
Static IPNLB: Yes (per AZ). ALB: No. Global Accelerator: Yes.HTTP(S) LB: Yes (global anycast IP). TCP/UDP LB: Yes (regional).Load Balancer: Yes (regional). App Gateway: Yes (regional, or via Front Door for global).
WAF IntegrationAWS WAF on ALB (and CloudFront)Cloud Armor on HTTP(S) LB (native)Azure WAF on App Gateway (native) and Front Door
🌍 GCP's Global HTTP(S) LB — The Killer Feature

GCP's HTTP(S) Load Balancer is global by default. You get a single anycast IP address that routes users to the nearest healthy region with capacity. There's no separate "Global Accelerator" service — it's built into the LB. This is fundamentally different from AWS where ALB is regional and you need CloudFront or Global Accelerator for global routing. GCP's approach is simpler for global deployments, but AWS gives you more granular control over regional traffic distribution.

Health Checks — How the LB Knows Your Backend Is Alive

A load balancer without health checks is dangerous — it will happily send traffic to a crashed backend, causing failed requests for users. Health checks are the LB's way of asking "Are you alive?" before forwarding traffic:

HEALTH CHECK MECHANICS — How ALB Determines Target Health
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ALB HEALTH CHECK FLOW — Continuous Monitoring of Backend Health                │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  TARGET GROUP HEALTH CHECK CONFIGURATION (anihpj-jobpost-web)            │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  Protocol:         HTTP                                                  │ │
│  │  Path:             /healthz     ← Your app MUST expose this endpoint!     │ │
│  │  Port:             traffic-port (30080, same as NodePort)                 │ │
│  │  Healthy threshold: 2            ← Consecutive successes to mark healthy  │ │
│  │  Unhealthy threshold: 3          ← Consecutive failures to mark unhealthy │ │
│  │  Timeout:           5 seconds   ← Max time to wait for response          │ │
│  │  Interval:          30 seconds   ← How often to check                    │ │
│  │  Success codes:     200          ← HTTP status codes that mean "healthy"  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  TIMELINE — Node Failure and Recovery                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  T=0s:   EKS Node-2 crashes. Health checks fail.                          │ │
│  │  T=30s:  Check 1 fails (unhealthy count = 1)                              │ │
│  │  T=60s:  Check 2 fails (unhealthy count = 2)                              │ │
│  │  T=90s:  Check 3 fails (unhealthy count = 3 → MARKED UNHEALTHY)          │ │
│  │          ALB stops sending traffic to Node-2.                              │ │
│  │  T=120s: Node-2 recovers, /healthz returns 200                            │ │
│  │  T=150s: Check succeeds (healthy count = 1)                                │ │
│  │  T=180s: Check succeeds → MARKED HEALTHY. ALB resumes traffic.            │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  TOTAL DOWNTIME VISIBLE TO ALB: 90 seconds (3 checks × 30s interval)     │ │
│  │  NOTE: Pods on Node-2 already rescheduled to Node-1 before this          │ │
│  │  (Kubernetes handles pod-level failures faster than ALB health checks)  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  HEALTH CHECK BEST PRACTICES:                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1. Dedicated /healthz endpoint — checks DB connectivity, not just HTTP  │ │
│  │  2. Don't use / (homepage) — it's heavy, cached, and lies about health   │ │
│  │  3. Set aggressive thresholds for production: 2 healthy, 2 unhealthy     │ │
│  │  4. Match interval to your recovery SLA: 10s for critical, 30s for batch │ │
│  │  5. Use different health check paths for readiness vs liveness            │ │
│  │     /healthz = liveness (is the process running?)                         │ │
│  │     /ready = readiness (can the process accept traffic?)                  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Target Groups — The Glue Between LB and Backend

Target groups are the abstraction that connects a load balancer to actual backend instances, IPs, or Lambda functions. A single ALB can have multiple target groups, and routing rules determine which target group receives which requests:

Target TypeWhat It Points ToUse Caseanihpj Example
InstanceEC2 instance ID + portTraditional EC2 deployments. ALB sends traffic to the instance's private IP.EKS worker nodes (via instance ID, port 30080 for NodePort)
IPAny private IP address + portEKS pods (with AWS VPC CNI), on-prem servers via VPN/Direct Connect, other VPCs via Peering/TGW.EKS pods directly (via pod IP + container port) — requires AWS Load Balancer Controller
LambdaLambda function ARNServerless backends. ALB invokes Lambda directly — no EC2 needed.anihpj image processing (Lambda resizes uploaded job images)
ALBAnother ALBNLB → ALB pattern. NLB gets static IP, ALB gets L7 features. Best of both worlds.NLB (static IP for whitelisting) → ALB (content routing + WAF)

SSL/TLS Termination — Where Encryption Ends

TLS termination means the LB decrypts HTTPS and forwards plain HTTP to backends. This offloads crypto overhead from application servers. But it also means traffic between the LB and the backend is unencrypted — which may or may not be acceptable:

TLS TERMINATION PATTERNS — Three Approaches
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TLS TERMINATION — Where the Encryption Envelope Ends                           │
│                                                                               │
│  PATTERN 1: TLS TERMINATION AT ALB (Most Common)                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Browser ──TLS──▶ [ALB] ──HTTP──▶ EKS Pod                                │ │
│  │            ▲              ▲                                                │ │
│  │      Encrypted        Plaintext (inside VPC)                               │ │
│  │  • ALB holds ACM certificate (auto-renewed)                                │ │
│  │  • Backend gets plain HTTP — no crypto overhead                            │ │
│  │  • Risk: Anyone who can sniff VPC traffic sees plaintext                   │ │
│  │  • Mitigation: Use service mesh mTLS (Chapter 23) for internal encryption  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  PATTERN 2: TLS RE-ENCRYPTION (ALB → Backend)                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Browser ──TLS──▶ [ALB] ──NEW TLS──▶ EKS Pod                               │ │
│  │            ▲              ▲       ▲                                        │ │
│  │      Encrypted        Decrypts  Re-encrypts (self-signed or internal CA)  │ │
│  │  • End-to-end encryption                                                 │ │
│  │  • Backend needs its own TLS certificate                                  │ │
│  │  • More CPU overhead (double TLS)                                         │ │
│  │  • Common in regulated industries (PCI-DSS, HIPAA)                        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  PATTERN 3: TLS PASSTHROUGH (NLB Only)                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Browser ──TLS──▶ [NLB] ──SAME TLS──▶ Backend                              │ │
│  │            ▲              ▲                                                │ │
│  │      Encrypted        Does NOT decrypt — forwards encrypted bytes         │ │
│  │  • Backend holds the TLS certificate (not the LB)                         │ │
│  │  • NLB doesn't see the HTTP request — no L7 routing                       │ │
│  │  • True end-to-end encryption — LB never sees plaintext                   │ │
│  │  • Use when: regulatory requirement, or backends manage own certs         │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ANIHPJ TLS STRATEGY:                                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Internet → ALB (TLS termination, ACM cert) → HTTP → EKS NodePort        │ │
│  │  PLUS: Istio mTLS inside the cluster (Chapter 23) for pod-to-pod         │ │
│  │  RESULT: External traffic is encrypted. Internal traffic is encrypted.    │ │
│  │  The gap: ALB → EKS Node (inside VPC, plain HTTP). If this is a concern, │ │
│  │  use TLS re-encryption or NLB passthrough instead.                       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Sticky Sessions — When State Matters

By default, ALB distributes requests evenly across targets (round-robin). But some applications store session state locally (in memory, not in Redis). If a user's requests go to different backends, their session is lost. Sticky sessions (session affinity) ensure the same user always hits the same backend:

ALB Sticky Session Configuration — Application-Based Cookie text 
# ALB Target Group — Sticky Session Configuration
stickiness:
  enabled: true
  type: app_cookie           # Application-based cookie (ALB generates: AWSALBAPP-*)
  cookie_name: SESSIONID      # Or use your app's existing cookie name
  cookie_duration: 86400     # 24 hours (in seconds)

# How it works:
# 1. First request from user — no cookie
# 2. ALB routes to backend-A (round-robin)
# 3. ALB injects Set-Cookie: AWSALBAPP-0=xxxxx (encrypted target info)
# 4. Subsequent requests include the cookie
# 5. ALB reads cookie → routes to SAME backend-A every time
#
# For anihpj: Use Redis for sessions (stateless backends).
# Sticky sessions are a crutch — they prevent proper horizontal scaling
# and make rolling deployments harder (users stick to old version).
# Prefer external session store (Redis/ElastiCache) over stickiness.

AWS Load Balancer Controller — Automatic ALB/NLB for Kubernetes

In the LAB section, you manually created an ALB and registered EKS nodes as targets. But in a real Kubernetes environment, you want the AWS Load Balancer Controller to do this automatically. When you create a Kubernetes Ingress or Service of type LoadBalancer, the controller provisions the actual AWS LB, creates target groups, and manages health checks — all driven by Kubernetes manifests:

AWS LOAD BALANCER CONTROLLER — Kubernetes-Native LB Management
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AWS LOAD BALANCER CONTROLLER — How K8s Ingress Creates an ALB                  │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml                                          │ │
│  │       │                                                                  │ │
│  │       ▼                                                                  │ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐    │ │
│  │  │ K8s API Server  │────▶│ LB Controller   │────▶│ AWS API         │    │ │
│  │  │ (stores Ingress) │     │ (watches K8s)   │     │ (creates ALB)   │    │ │
│  │  └─────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘     └────────┬────────┘    │ │
│  │                                                            │             │ │
│  │                                                            ▼             │ │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │ │
│  │  │  ACTIONS TAKEN BY LB CONTROLLER:                                   │   │ │
│  │  │  1. Creates ALB in public subnets                                  │   │ │
│  │  │  2. Creates Target Group (IP target type, pod IPs directly!)       │   │ │
│  │  │  3. Registers EACH pod's IP as a target (not the node IP!)        │   │ │
│  │  │  4. Creates Listener (HTTPS:443 → Target Group)                    │   │ │
│  │  │  5. Manages Security Group rules                                    │   │ │
│  │  │  6. Updates targets as pods scale up/down                          │   │ │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  MANUAL (NodePort) vs LB CONTROLLER (IP Target):                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  MANUAL:  ALB → Node (port 30080) → kube-proxy → random pod             │ │
│  │  • 2 hops of load balancing (ALB's round-robin + kube-proxy's random)    │ │
│  │  • Client IP lost (kube-proxy NATs it)                                   │ │
│  │  • Health check hits NodePort, not pod directly                          │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  LB CONTROLLER: ALB → Pod IP directly (port 8000)                        │ │
│  │  • 1 hop of load balancing (ALB's round-robin) ✓                         │ │
│  │  • Client IP preserved (ALB → pod, no kube-proxy NAT)                    │ │
│  │  • Health check hits pod directly ✓                                      │ │
│  │  • Automatic target registration as pods come and go ✓                   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ANIHPJ INGRESS EXAMPLE (creates ALB automatically):                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1                                       │ │
│  │  kind: Ingress                                                           │ │
│  │  metadata:                                                               │ │
│  │    name: jobpost-web                                                     │ │
│  │    namespace: anihpj                                                     │ │
│  │    annotations:                                                          │ │
│  │      alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing                   │ │
│  │      alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip    ← Direct to pod IPs!  │ │
│  │      alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /healthz               │ │
│  │      alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:...         │ │
│  │  spec:                                                                   │ │
│  │    rules:                                                                │ │
│  │    - host: anihpj.com                                                    │ │
│  │      http:                                                               │ │
│  │        paths:                                                            │ │
│  │        - path: /api/*                                                    │ │
│  │          backend:                                                        │ │
│  │            service: jobpost-api:8080                                     │ │
│  │        - path: /*                                                        │ │
│  │          backend:                                                        │ │
│  │            service: jobpost-web:8000                                     │ │
│  │  # kubectl apply → ALB appears in AWS console in ~30 seconds!           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

LCU Deep Dive — How You Pay for Load Balancers

ALB and NLB pricing is based on LCUs (Load Balancer Capacity Units) — a measure of how much "work" your LB is doing. You pay for the HIGHEST of four dimensions, not the sum. Understanding this prevents billing surprises:

LCU CALCULATION — How ALB Pricing Actually Works
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ALB LCU DIMENSIONS — You're billed for the HIGHEST one per hour               │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1. NEW CONNECTIONS:       25 new connections per second = 1 LCU         │ │
│  │  2. ACTIVE CONNECTIONS:    3,000 active connections = 1 LCU              │ │
│  │  3. PROCESSED BYTES:       1 GB per hour (for EC2 targets)               │ │
│  │      OR 0.4 GB (for Lambda targets) = 1 LCU                             │ │
│  │  4. RULE EVALUATIONS:      1,000 rule evaluations per second = 1 LCU     │ │
│  │     (sum of requests × rules evaluated across all listeners)            │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ANIHPJ LCU ESTIMATE (1M requests/day, 5KB avg response):                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  New Connections:    ~12/sec      → 12/25  = 0.48 LCU                   │ │
│  │  Active Connections: ~500         → 500/3000 = 0.17 LCU                  │ │
│  │  Processed Bytes:    ~5 GB/hr     → 5/1   = 5.0 LCU ← BOTTLENECK       │ │
│  │  Rule Evaluations:   ~12 × 3 rules = 36/sec → 36/1000 = 0.04 LCU        │ │
│  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────                          │ │
│  │  Billed LCU: 5.0 (processed bytes is the highest)                        │ │
│  │  Hourly cost: 5.0 × $0.008 = $0.04/hour                                  │ │
│  │  Monthly cost: ~$28.80/month in LCU charges                               │ │
│  │  PLUS: $0.0225 × 730 hours = $16.43/month ALB base fee                   │ │
│  │  TOTAL: ~$45/month for the ALB                                            │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  COST OPTIMIZATION TIPS:                                                       │
│  • Byte processing is usually the bottleneck for content-heavy apps         │
│  • Enable gzip compression on backends to reduce processed bytes            │
│  • Use CloudFront in front of ALB — CloudFront caches static content,       │
│    reducing ALB LCU consumption for bytes processed                         │
│  • NLB LCU is cheaper ($0.006 vs $0.008) but lacks L7 features             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Cross-Zone Load Balancing — Fair Distribution Across AZs

By default, cross-zone load balancing is ENABLED on ALB and DISABLED on NLB. This is one of the most important (and confusing) settings:

CROSS-ZONE LB — With and Without
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CROSS-ZONE LB DISABLED (NLB default):                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐                         │ │
│  │  │  AZ-a         │              │  AZ-b         │                         │ │
│  │  │  ALB Node     │              │  ALB Node     │                         │ │
│  │  │  ↓  ↓         │              │  ↓  ↓  ↓  ↓   │  ← 4 targets in AZ-b  │ │
│  │  │  [T1] [T2]    │              │  [T3][T4][T5] │                         │ │
│  │  └──────────────┘              │  [T6]          │                         │ │
│  │                                 └──────────────┘                         │ │
│  │  PROBLEM: Each ALB node ONLY sends to targets in its own AZ.              │ │
│  │  T1/T2 get 50% of traffic each (AZ-a). T3-T6 get 12.5% each (AZ-b).      │ │
│  │  If AZ-a has 2 targets and AZ-b has 4, AZ-a nodes are overloaded!         │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  CROSS-ZONE LB ENABLED (ALB default):                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐                         │ │
│  │  │  AZ-a         │              │  AZ-b         │                         │ │
│  │  │  ALB Node     │──cross-zone──│  ALB Node     │                         │ │
│  │  │  ↓  ↓  ↓  ↓   │              │  ↓  ↓          │                         │ │
│  │  │  [T1] [T2]    │              │  [T3][T4][T5] │                         │ │
│  │  └──────────────┘              │  [T6]          │                         │ │
│  │                                 └──────────────┘                         │ │
│  │  SOLUTION: Each ALB node CAN send to targets in ANY AZ.                   │ │
│  │  All 6 targets receive ~16.7% of traffic each. Fair distribution!         │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WHY NLB DEFAULTS TO DISABLED:                                                 │
│  • Cross-zone = cross-AZ data charges ($0.01/GB each direction)               │
│  • NLB is often used for high-throughput internal traffic                     │
│  • You might not want to pay for cross-AZ data transfer                       │
│  • Enable cross-zone on NLB for true HA across AZs                            │
│                                                                               │
│  FOR ANIHPJ: Enable cross-zone on both ALB and NLB. Pro: Fair traffic         │
│  distribution. Con: Cross-AZ charges (~$50/month for high-traffic apps).      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Connection Draining — Graceful Removal of Targets

When a target is deregistered (instance terminated, pod deleted, or health check fails), existing connections should complete gracefully rather than being abruptly killed. Connection draining (called deregistration delay on ALB) gives in-flight requests time to finish:

CONNECTION DRAINING — How ALB Gracefully Removes Targets
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DEREGISTRATION DELAY TIMELINE (default: 300 seconds)                           │
│                                                                               │
│  T=0s:  Target marked for deregistration (instance terminating)               │
│         ALB stops sending NEW requests to this target                          │
│         Existing connections continue to be served                             │
│                                                                               │
│  T=0-300s: DRAINING WINDOW                                                     │
│         ALB waits for in-flight requests to complete                           │
│         Backend can finish processing and send responses                       │
│         No new connections are established                                     │
│                                                                               │
│  T=300s: DEREGISTRATION TIMEOUT                                                │
│         ALB forcefully closes any remaining connections                        │
│         Target is fully deregistered                                           │
│                                                                               │
│  ANIHPJ RECOMMENDATION:                                                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Set deregistration delay to match your max request processing time    │ │
│  │  • For web apps (jobpost-web): 30-60 seconds is enough for most requests │ │
│  │  • For long-lived connections (WebSocket): 300+ seconds or more          │ │
│  │  • In Kubernetes with LB Controller: pod termination → preStop hook      │ │
│  │    → sleep deregistration_delay seconds → then exit gracefully           │ │
│  │  • This ensures zero-downtime deployments                                │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

ALB Access Logs — Debugging Every Request

ALB can log every request to S3. These logs are essential for debugging, security analysis, and understanding traffic patterns. Each log entry tells you exactly what happened to a request:

Log FieldExampleWhat It Tells You
timestamp2026-06-21T14:30:00ZWhen the request was received
client:port1.2.3.4:51234Real client IP and source port
target:port10.0.10.45:8000Which backend received the request
request_processing_time0.001Time ALB spent processing the request (TLS, routing)
target_processing_time0.045Time the backend took to respond (your app's performance!)
response_processing_time0.000Time ALB spent sending the response to client
elb_status_code200 / 502 / 503HTTP status from the LB. 502 = bad gateway, 503 = no healthy targets
target_status_code200HTTP status from the backend
received_bytes / sent_bytes1024 / 5120Request size / response size
requestGET /api/jobs HTTP/1.1The actual HTTP request line
user_agentMozilla/5.0...The client's browser/application
ssl_cipher / ssl_protocolECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256 / TLSv1.2Which TLS cipher was negotiated
target_group_arnarn:aws:elb:...:targetgroup/anihpj-webWhich target group handled the request

Debugging with access logs: If you see elb_status_code: 502 with target_status_code: -, the backend didn't respond — check if the pod is running. If target_processing_time: -1, the LB timed out waiting for the backend. If elb_status_code: 503, there were no healthy targets — check health checks.

ALB Listener Rules Deep Dive — Conditions, Actions, and Priorities

Each ALB listener has a default rule and up to 100 additional rules evaluated in priority order. Understanding the rule engine unlocks sophisticated routing without application code:

ALB LISTENER RULES — Conditions and Actions Reference
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ALB RULE EVALUATION — First Match Wins (by Priority)                          │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  LISTENER: HTTPS:443                                                     │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  RULE 1 (Priority 1):  host=api.anihpj.com AND path=/v2/*               │ │
│  │    → forward to api-v2-target-group (canary testing!)                    │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  RULE 2 (Priority 10): host=api.anihpj.com                              │ │
│  │    → forward to api-target-group                                         │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  RULE 3 (Priority 20): path=/admin/* AND source-ip=10.0.0.0/8           │ │
│  │    → forward to admin-target-group (only from internal network!)         │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  RULE 4 (Priority 30): path=/admin/*                                     │ │
│  │    → fixed-response 403 (block external admin access)                    │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  RULE 5 (Priority 40): http-header=x-canary=true                        │ │
│  │    → forward to canary-target-group (header-based canary)                │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  DEFAULT (last):                                                          │ │
│  │    → forward to web-target-group (everything else)                       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  AVAILABLE CONDITIONS:                  AVAILABLE ACTIONS:                     │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ • host-header (hostname)       │    │ • forward (to target group)       │  │
│  │ • path-pattern (/api/*, /web/*)│    │ • redirect (HTTP→HTTPS, etc.)    │  │
│  │ • http-header (any header)     │    │ • fixed-response (custom body)   │  │
│  │ • http-request-method (GET/POST│    │ • authenticate-oidc (Cognito,etc)│  │
│  │ • query-string (?version=v2)  │    │ • authenticate-cognito            │  │
│  │ • source-ip (CIDR range)       │    │                                   │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                               │
│  PRIORITY IS CRITICAL: Rules evaluated 1→100→default. First match stops.       │
│  Put most specific rules at LOWER priority numbers.                            │
│  You CAN reorder rules — change priority numbers.                              │
│  Maximum 100 rules per listener (not including default).                       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

NLB → ALB Pattern — Static IP + L7 Features Together

A common enterprise pattern: you need static IP addresses (for firewall whitelisting) AND L7 features (content routing, WAF, OIDC auth). Since ALB doesn't have static IPs and NLB doesn't have L7 features, you chain them:

NLB → ALB PATTERN — Best of Both Worlds
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NLB → ALB ARCHITECTURE — Static IP + L7 Features                              │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │                           INTERNET                                       │ │
│  │                              │                                           │ │
│  │                              ▼                                           │ │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │ │
│  │  │  NLB (Internet-facing)                                             │   │ │
│  │  │  • Static IP: 54.1.2.3 (whitelisted by partner firewall)          │   │ │
│  │  │  • Listener: TCP:443 → forward to ALB                             │   │ │
│  │  │  • Target type: ALB (yes, NLB can target another ALB!)             │   │ │
│  │  │  • No TLS termination — passthrough                               │   │ │
│  │  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘   │ │
│  │                             │                                            │ │
│  │                             ▼                                            │ │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │ │
│  │  │  ALB (Internal — no public IP needed!)                             │   │ │
│  │  │  • Terminates TLS (ACM certificate)                                │   │ │
│  │  │  • Content routing: /api/* → API pods, /web/* → Web pods           │   │ │
│  │  │  • AWS WAF for SQL injection / rate limiting                       │   │ │
│  │  │  • OIDC authentication via Cognito                                 │   │ │
│  │  │  • Target type: IP (EKS pod IPs via LB Controller)                 │   │ │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WHY THIS PATTERN:                                                             │
│  • Partner/vendor requires IP whitelisting → NLB static IP                    │
│  • Need WAF, auth, content routing → ALB                                       │
│  • Internal ALB means it has no public IP → more secure                       │
│  • Only NLB is exposed to the internet                                        │
│                                                                               │
│  COST: NLB ($16.43/mo base + LCU) + ALB ($16.43/mo base + LCU) = ~$60-100/mo │
│  Only use this pattern when you NEED both static IPs and L7 features.         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Internal vs Internet-Facing — The Scheme That Changes Everything

Both ALB and NLB can be internet-facing or internal. The difference is where the LB nodes are placed and what IPs they get:

FeatureInternet-FacingInternal
DNS resolves toPublic IPs (NLB) or public IPs (ALB)Private IPs only (from your VPC CIDR)
Accessible fromInternet (anywhere)Only within the VPC, peered VPCs, VPN, Direct Connect
Subnet placementPublic subnets (with IGW route)Private subnets (no IGW route needed)
Use caseUser-facing web apps, public APIsInternal microservices, service-to-service communication
anihpj exampleALB for jobpost-web (user traffic)Internal NLB for service mesh ingress, internal ALB for admin panel

Gotcha: Internal ALBs in private subnets CANNOT have ACM public certificates (they can't validate domain ownership). Use ACM private CA or import your own certificate for internal ALBs with custom domains.

Slow Start Mode — Protect Newly Registered Targets

When a new target is registered (new EC2 instance, new pod), it immediately starts receiving its fair share of traffic — even though it's still warming up (JIT compilation, cache population, connection pool establishment). Slow start mode gradually ramps up traffic to new targets over a configurable duration:

SLOW START MODE — Gradual Traffic Ramp-Up for New Targets
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WITHOUT SLOW START:                     WITH SLOW START (60s ramp-up):         │
│                                                                               │
│  Traffic to new target:                 Traffic to new target:                 │
│  100% ─────────────────────            100% ─────────────────────              │
│    │                                      │                              ▲     │
│    │  ▲ New target gets                    │                        ▄▄▄▄│     │
│    │  │ 100% traffic                       │                   ▄▄▄▄    │     │
│    │  │ immediately!                       │              ▄▄▄▄         │     │
│    │  │                                    │         ▄▄▄▄              │     │
│    │  │                                    │    ▄▄▄▄                   │     │
│    │  │                                    │▄▄▄▄                        │     │
│    0% └────────────────────               0% └────────────────────            │
│       T=0 (registered)                       T=0  T=15  T=30  T=45  T=60      │
│                                                                               │
│  PROBLEM: JVM/Python/Django need             SOLUTION: Traffic increases       │
│  warm-up time. Instant full load             linearly over slow_start_duration │
│  → timeouts, high latency, OOM.             → backend warms up gracefully.    │
│                                                                               │
│  SLOW START CONFIGURATION (Target Group attribute):                            │
│  • slow_start.duration_seconds: 30-900 (default: disabled/0)                  │
│  • ALB uses round-robin WITHIN slow start:                                     │
│    Target gets: elapsed_time/duration × fair_share of traffic                 │
│  • Best for: Java/Spring Boot apps, Python Django (code loading),             │
│    Lambda cold starts behind ALB, any app with significant warm-up time      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

HTTPS Listeners & Security Policies — Controlling TLS Versions

ALB HTTPS listeners support multiple TLS certificates via SNI (Server Name Indication) — up to 25 certificates per listener. You can also choose a security policy that controls which TLS versions and cipher suites are accepted:

ALB HTTPS Listener — Multi-Cert + Security Policy text 
# ALB Listener Configuration — HTTPS with SNI
Listener: HTTPS:443
  Default Certificate: *.anihpj.com (ACM)
  Additional Certificates (SNI):
    - api.anihpj.com (ACM)
    - admin.anihpj.com (ACM)
    - *.anihpj-staging.com (ACM)
  # ALB picks the right cert based on the TLS SNI hostname!

  Security Policy: ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06
  # This policy allows: TLS 1.3, TLS 1.2
  # Blocks: TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 (insecure!)
  #
  # RECOMMENDED POLICIES (most secure → least):
  # • ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06  (TLS 1.3 + 1.2, latest ciphers)
  # • ELBSecurityPolicy-FS-1-2-Res-2020-10  (Forward Secrecy + TLS 1.2)
  # • ELBSecurityPolicy-2016-08 (legacy — allows TLS 1.0! Don't use!)
  #
  # For anihpj PCI-DSS compliance: Use the FS (Forward Secrecy) policy.
🔐 TLS Security Policies — Check Your Compliance Requirements

Many compliance standards (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP) mandate minimum TLS versions and cipher suites. PCI-DSS 4.0 requires TLS 1.2+ — if your ALB security policy allows TLS 1.0/1.1, you FAIL the audit. Always use the latest security policy (TLS13-1-2-2021-06 or newer). Also check: (1) Are you using Forward Secrecy ciphers? (2) Are weak ciphers (RC4, DES, 3DES) disabled? (3) Is your ACM certificate using RSA 2048+ or ECDSA? These are all checked during security audits.

25.2 LAB: VPC & Load Balancer Hands-On

🛠️ VPC & LB Lab — 5 Hands-On Exercises
1

Design the anihpj VPC on Paper

# Using the VPC design principles from Chapter 24, sketch the anihpj VPC:
#
# VPC: 10.0.0.0/16
#
# Public Subnets:
#   AZ-a: 10.0.1.0/24  → Route: 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW
#   AZ-b: 10.0.2.0/24  → Route: 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW
#   Contains: ALB, NAT Gateway, Bastion
#
# Private Subnets (EKS):
#   AZ-a: 10.0.10.0/24 → Route: 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT-GW-a
#   AZ-b: 10.0.11.0/24 → Route: 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT-GW-b
#   Contains: EKS worker nodes
#
# Private Subnets (DB):
#   AZ-a: 10.0.20.0/24 → Route: local only (no internet!)
#   AZ-b: 10.0.21.0/24 → Route: local only
#   Contains: RDS PostgreSQL, ElastiCache Redis
#
# Verify: No route from DB subnets to IGW or NAT. Fully isolated.
2

Create an ALB with Target Group Pointing to EKS NodePort

# Step 1: Create a Target Group (Instance type, port 30080)
aws elbv2 create-target-group \
    --name anihpj-web-tg \
    --protocol HTTP \
    --port 30080 \
    --vpc-id vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 \
    --target-type instance \
    --health-check-protocol HTTP \
    --health-check-path /healthz \
    --health-check-port 30080 \
    --healthy-threshold-count 2 \
    --unhealthy-threshold-count 3

# Step 2: Register EKS worker nodes as targets
aws elbv2 register-targets \
    --target-group-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:targetgroup/anihpj-web-tg/... \
    --targets Id=i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890,Port=30080 \
              Id=i-0b2c3d4e5f67890ab,Port=30080

# Step 3: Create ALB
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer \
    --name anihpj-web-alb \
    --subnets subnet-public-a subnet-public-b \
    --security-groups sg-alb \
    --scheme internet-facing \
    --type application

# Step 4: Create listener (HTTPS on port 443)
aws elbv2 create-listener \
    --load-balancer-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:loadbalancer/app/anihpj-web-alb/... \
    --protocol HTTPS \
    --port 443 \
    --certificates CertificateArn=arn:aws:acm:...:certificate/... \
    --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:targetgroup/anihpj-web-tg/...
3

Test ALB → EKS NodePort Connectivity

# 1. Get the ALB DNS name
aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers \
    --names anihpj-web-alb \
    --query 'LoadBalancers[0].DNSName' \
    --output text
# Output: anihpj-web-alb-123456789.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com

# 2. Test HTTP access (should work)
curl -v http://anihpj-web-alb-123456789.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/api/jobs/

# 3. Test HTTPS access (requires ACM cert)
curl -v https://anihpj.com/api/jobs/
# (After DNS points anihpj.com to ALB)

# 4. Verify health checks are passing
aws elbv2 describe-target-health \
    --target-group-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:targetgroup/anihpj-web-tg/...
# Look for: "State": "healthy" for all targets

# 5. Check ALB access logs (enable first in ALB attributes)
aws s3 ls s3://anihpj-alb-logs/AWSLogs/123456789012/elasticloadbalancing/us-east-1/
# Download and inspect logs for request details, latency, client IP
4

Set Up Content-Based Routing on ALB

# Create two target groups: web (port 8000) and api (port 8080)
# Then create listener rules for path-based routing:

# Rule 1: /api/* → api-target-group
aws elbv2 create-rule \
    --listener-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:listener/app/anihpj-web-alb/... \
    --priority 10 \
    --conditions Field=path-pattern,Values='/api/*' \
    --actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=arn:...:targetgroup/anihpj-api-tg/...

# Rule 2: /admin/* → web-target-group (with different health check)
aws elbv2 create-rule \
    --listener-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:listener/app/anihpj-web-alb/... \
    --priority 20 \
    --conditions Field=path-pattern,Values='/admin/*' \
    --actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=arn:...:targetgroup/anihpj-web-tg/...

# Default rule (everything else) → web-target-group
# (Already set when the listener was created)

# Test routing:
curl https://anihpj.com/api/jobs/    # → api-target-group (port 8080)
curl https://anihpj.com/admin/       # → web-target-group (port 8000)
curl https://anihpj.com/             # → web-target-group (default)
5

Simulate Backend Failure and Observe Health Checks

# 1. Check current healthy targets
aws elbv2 describe-target-health \
    --target-group-arn <tg-arn> \
    --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[*].TargetHealth.State'
# Should show: ["healthy", "healthy"]

# 2. Break one backend (stop the NodePort service on one node)
kubectl cordon <node-name>          # Stop scheduling new pods
kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets  # Evict pods

# 3. Watch health checks fail on that target
watch -n 5 'aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <tg-arn>'
# After ~90 seconds, you'll see: "unhealthy"

# 4. Verify traffic only goes to healthy targets
for i in {1..20}; do
  curl -s https://anihpj.com/healthz | grep "node"
done
# Should only return the HEALTHY node name, never the drained one

# 5. Fix the backend
kubectl uncordon <node-name>
# Wait for health checks to pass → "healthy" again → traffic resumes

📊 Chapter 25 Visual Summary — What You've Learned

🏗️L4 (NLB) — Fast & DumbTCP/UDP forwarding. No HTTP inspection. Preserves client IP. Millions of rps. Static IP. ~1ms latency. Use for non-HTTP or extreme throughput.
🧠L7 (ALB) — Smart & Feature-RichHTTP/HTTPS routing. Content-based (path, host, header, method). WAF, OIDC auth, redirects. TLS termination. ~2-5ms latency.
🩺Health ChecksContinuous monitoring via /healthz. Healthy/unhealthy thresholds. Automatically removes dead backends. Use dedicated endpoint, not /.
🎯Target Groups + LB ControllerInstance, IP, Lambda, or ALB targets. AWS LB Controller provisions ALBs automatically from K8s Ingress. Direct pod IP routing.
💰LCU PricingBilled on the HIGHEST of 4 dimensions: new connections, active connections, bytes processed, rule evaluations. Anihpj ALB ~$45/month.
🔒TLS TerminationTerminate at ALB (ACM cert), re-encrypt to backend, or passthrough via NLB. Choose based on compliance and architecture.
📊Access Logs & DrainingS3 access logs show every request: timing, status, TLS cipher. Connection draining gives in-flight requests time to finish (default 300s).
🌍AWS vs GCP vs AzureSame concepts, different names. GCP HTTP LB is global by default (anycast). AWS ALB is regional. Azure App Gateway has built-in WAF.

🔑 Chapter 25 Key Takeaways

  1. NLB for L4, ALB for L7. NLB = TCP/UDP, extreme performance, client IP preservation, static IPs. ALB = HTTP/HTTPS, content routing, WAF, auth. Know when to use each.
  2. Use the AWS LB Controller for Kubernetes. It provisions ALBs/NLBs automatically from Ingress/Service manifests, registers pod IPs directly (bypassing NodePort and kube-proxy), and updates targets as pods scale.
  3. Cloud LBs are fully managed. No instances to patch, no HA to configure. AWS handles scaling, redundancy, and AZ failures. LCU-based pricing — you pay for capacity used, not provisioned.
  4. Health checks prevent sending traffic to dead backends. A dedicated /healthz endpoint that checks DB connectivity is the standard. Aggressive thresholds (2 healthy, 2 unhealthy) for production.
  5. Connection draining ensures zero-downtime deployments. Set deregistration delay to match your max request time. In Kubernetes, use a preStop hook that sleeps for the draining duration before the pod exits.
  6. Enable ALB access logs for debugging. They show every request with timing breakdown (ALB time vs backend time), TLS details, and client IP. Invaluable for latency troubleshooting and security analysis.
  7. GCP's HTTP(S) LB is global by default. Single anycast IP routes users to the nearest region. AWS requires Global Accelerator or CloudFront for the same effect. Cross-zone LB ensures fair target distribution across AZs.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 25

🏗️NLB
Network Load Balancer — AWS L4 load balancer. Forwards TCP/UDP/TLS traffic without inspecting payloads. Extreme performance (millions rps), static IP per AZ, preserves client IP. ~$0.0225/hour.
🧠ALB
Application Load Balancer — AWS L7 load balancer. Routes HTTP/HTTPS based on content (path, host, headers). TLS termination, WAF, OIDC auth, sticky sessions. ~$0.0225/hour.
🩺Health Check
Periodic probe by the LB to determine if a target is healthy. Configurable: protocol, path, port, interval, timeout, thresholds. Unhealthy targets are removed from rotation automatically.
🎯Target Group
A logical grouping of backend targets (instances, IPs, Lambda functions) that receive traffic from a load balancer. ALB routes requests to target groups based on listener rules.
🔒TLS Termination
The process of decrypting TLS at the load balancer and forwarding plain HTTP to backends. Offloads crypto overhead. The connection between LB and backend is unencrypted unless re-encryption is configured.
🍪Sticky Session
Session affinity — ensures all requests from a user go to the same backend. Implemented via ALB-generated cookie (AWSALB) or application cookie. Prefer external session stores (Redis) over stickiness.
📊LCU
Load Balancer Capacity Unit — the pricing metric for ALB and NLB. Measured across 4 dimensions: new connections, active connections, bytes processed, and rule evaluations. You're billed for the HIGHEST dimension per hour. NLB LCU: $0.006, ALB LCU: $0.008.
🔄Connection Draining
The process of gracefully removing a target from the LB. ALB stops sending NEW connections but allows existing ones to complete within the deregistration delay window (default 300s). Essential for zero-downtime deployments.
☸️AWS LB Controller
A Kubernetes controller that automatically provisions and manages AWS ALBs/NLBs from Ingress and Service manifests. Registers pod IPs directly (IP target type), bypassing NodePort and kube-proxy for lower latency and preserved client IPs.

📝 Chapter 25 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is the fundamental difference between an L4 (NLB) and L7 (ALB) load balancer?
Show Answer
Answer

L4 (NLB) operates at the transport layer — it forwards TCP/UDP packets based on IP + port without inspecting the payload. It preserves the client IP, has ~1ms latency, supports static IPs, and can handle millions of rps. L7 (ALB) operates at the application layer — it terminates TLS, reads HTTP headers/paths/hostnames, and can route requests to different backends based on content. It adds ~2-5ms latency, provides WAF integration, OIDC authentication, and sticky sessions. L4 is protocol-agnostic (any TCP protocol works). L7 only works with HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC/WebSocket.

Q2
When would you choose NLB over ALB? Give at least 3 specific scenarios.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Non-HTTP protocols — raw TCP, UDP, or custom protocols that ALB can't parse. (2) Client IP preservation at the backend — NLB preserves the source IP; ALB replaces it with its own (client IP in X-Forwarded-For header). (3) Static IP requirements — NLB provides one static IP per AZ (or Elastic IP); ALB uses DNS with changing IPs. (4) Extreme throughput — NLB handles millions of rps with no pre-warming; ALB needs time to scale. (5) TLS passthrough — NLB can forward encrypted traffic without decrypting it; ALB must terminate TLS.

Q3
Explain how ALB health checks work and what happens when a target becomes unhealthy.
Show Answer
Answer

ALB sends periodic HTTP/HTTPS requests to the health check path (e.g., /healthz) on each target. Configuration includes interval (e.g., 30s), timeout (5s), healthy threshold (consecutive successes to mark healthy, e.g., 2), unhealthy threshold (consecutive failures to mark unhealthy, e.g., 3), and expected success codes (e.g., 200). When a target fails 3 consecutive checks (90 seconds at 30s intervals), ALB marks it unhealthy and stops sending traffic to it. ALB continues health checking the unhealthy target. When it passes 2 consecutive checks, it's marked healthy and traffic resumes.

Q4
How does the AWS Load Balancer Controller differ from manually creating an ALB + NodePort setup?
Show Answer
Answer

Manual NodePort: ALB → Node IP:30080 → kube-proxy → random pod IP. This has 2 hops of load balancing (ALB + kube-proxy), loses client IP (kube-proxy NAT), and requires manual target registration when nodes scale. AWS LB Controller: ALB → Pod IP:8000 directly. This has 1 hop (no kube-proxy), preserves client IP, health checks hit pods directly, and targets are automatically updated as pods are created/deleted. The LB Controller watches Kubernetes Ingress/Service objects and automatically provisions the corresponding AWS LB, target groups, listeners, and security group rules.

Q5
Explain how ALB LCU pricing works. What are the four dimensions and how are you billed?
Show Answer
Answer

ALB pricing = base hourly fee ($0.0225/hr) + LCU charges ($0.008/LCU-hour). An LCU measures capacity across 4 dimensions: (1) New connections — 25/sec = 1 LCU. (2) Active connections — 3,000 concurrent = 1 LCU. (3) Processed bytes — 1 GB/hour = 1 LCU. (4) Rule evaluations — 1,000/sec = 1 LCU. You're billed for the HIGHEST dimension, not the sum. For a typical web app, processed bytes is usually the bottleneck. Example: 5 GB/hr processed = 5 LCU × $0.008 × 730 hours = $29.20/month in LCU charges + $16.43 base fee = ~$45/month total.

Q6
What is connection draining and why is it important for zero-downtime deployments?
Show Answer
Answer

Connection draining (deregistration delay) is the process of gracefully removing a target from the ALB. When a target is deregistered: (1) ALB immediately stops sending NEW connections to it. (2) Existing in-flight connections continue to be served. (3) ALB waits for the deregistration delay period (default 300s, configurable 1-3600s). (4) After timeout, remaining connections are forcefully closed. For zero-downtime in Kubernetes: pod termination triggers a preStop hook that sleeps for the deregistration delay duration, allowing in-flight requests to complete before the pod exits. Without draining, users would see 502 errors during deployments.

Q7
What is cross-zone load balancing and why is it enabled by default on ALB but disabled on NLB?
Show Answer
Answer

Cross-zone LB allows each ALB node to distribute traffic to targets in ANY AZ, not just its own. Without it, an ALB node in AZ-a only sends to targets in AZ-a — leading to uneven load if AZs have different numbers of targets. ALB enables it by default because it ensures fair distribution. NLB disables it by default because cross-zone = cross-AZ data charges ($0.01/GB each direction), and NLB is often used for high-throughput internal traffic where you might not want those charges. You can enable cross-zone on NLB for true cross-AZ HA, but be aware of the data transfer cost implications.

Q8
What information do ALB access logs provide and how would you use them to debug a 502 error?
Show Answer
Answer

ALB access logs (stored in S3) record every request with fields including: timestamp, client IP, target IP, request/response processing times, ELB status code, target status code, TLS cipher, user agent, and the full request line. To debug a 502 (Bad Gateway): (1) Filter logs for elb_status_code:502. (2) Check target_status_code — if "-" the backend never responded. (3) Check target_processing_time — if "-1" the LB timed out waiting. (4) Check which target IP received the request — SSH to that instance and check if the process is running. (5) If target_status_code is a valid HTTP code, the backend returned a malformed response that ALB couldn't parse. Access logs are essential because ALB metrics only show aggregate counts, not per-request details.

Chapter 26: Hybrid Cloud Networking — Connecting On-Prem to Cloud

Not every workload lives in the cloud. Most enterprises operate in a hybrid model: some services run in AWS/GCP/Azure, while legacy databases, mainframes, or sensitive systems remain on-premises. The question is: how do you connect these two worlds securely, reliably, and with low latency? This chapter covers the two primary patterns: VPNs (IPsec and WireGuard) for encrypted tunnels over the public internet, and Direct Connect / Cloud Interconnect for dedicated physical connections that bypass the internet entirely.

For the anihpj stack, we'll explore a realistic hybrid scenario: compute in the cloud (EKS + ALB), but the primary database remains on-premises behind a corporate firewall. You'll learn how to build a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel from your VPC back to the office, understand the IPsec protocol stack that makes it secure, and evaluate when a dedicated Direct Connect line is worth the investment. By the end, you'll know exactly which connectivity option fits your latency, bandwidth, and budget requirements.

🟡 INTERMEDIATE ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔐 VPN / IPsec 🔗 Direct Connect 🏢 Hybrid Cloud

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:

  • Explain how Site-to-Site VPNs connect on-premises networks to cloud VPCs over encrypted tunnels
  • Understand the IPsec protocol stack — IKE (key exchange), ESP (encryption), and tunnel mode
  • Compare IPsec with WireGuard — architecture, performance, and simplicity
  • Describe Direct Connect / Cloud Interconnect — dedicated physical connections that bypass the internet
  • Choose between VPN and Direct Connect based on bandwidth, latency, reliability, and cost
  • Design a hybrid architecture for anihpj with on-prem database and cloud compute
🏢 Hybrid Cloud Relevance
Network Engineer CRITICAL Cloud Architect CORE Security Engineer ESSENTIAL
💡 The Hybrid Networking Mental Model — Two Paths to the Same Destination

Think of connecting your office to the cloud like connecting two buildings. You have two options: VPN = using the public road (internet) with an armored car (encryption). It's flexible, quick to set up, and works from anywhere — but traffic jams (latency) and road closures (internet outages) are out of your control. Direct Connect = building a private tunnel directly between the buildings. It's expensive and takes weeks to construct, but once built, you have guaranteed bandwidth, low latency, and no traffic jams. Key principles:

  • VPN is the default starting point. Every hybrid architecture begins with a VPN. It's cheap ($36-72/month per tunnel), quick (hours, not weeks), and secure. Start here and only upgrade when the limitations bite.
  • Direct Connect is for when the internet isn't reliable enough. If your application requires consistent sub-5ms latency, guaranteed bandwidth, or you're transferring terabytes daily, the public internet won't cut it.
  • Most enterprises use BOTH. Direct Connect as primary (high bandwidth, low latency) with VPN as backup (if the fiber gets cut). This is the gold standard for hybrid architectures.

26.1 VPNs — IPsec and WireGuard

A Site-to-Site VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between two networks — your office network (192.168.1.0/24) and your cloud VPC (10.0.0.0/16) — over the public internet. Once established, devices on both sides can communicate as if they were on the same local network. The tunnel is transparent: your EKS pods reach the on-prem database at 192.168.1.50 without knowing it's 500 miles away:

SITE-TO-SITE VPN — Connecting Office to Cloud VPC

IPsec Deep Dive — The Protocol Stack That Powers VPNs

IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) is not a single protocol — it's a suite of protocols working together. Understanding each piece is essential for troubleshooting VPN connectivity issues:

IPSEC PROTOCOL STACK — IKE + ESP + Tunnel Mode
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  IPSEC ARCHITECTURE — Two Phases, Two Protocols                                 │
│                                                                               │
│  PHASE 1: IKE (Internet Key Exchange) — "Hello, let's establish a secure channel"│
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────┐                    ┌─────────────────┐             │ │
│  │  │ AWS VGW         │                    │ On-Prem Gateway │             │ │
│  │  │ 54.1.2.3        │                    │ 203.0.113.10    │             │ │
│  │  └────────┬────────┘                    └────────┬────────┘             │ │
│  │           │                                      │                       │ │
│  │           │  1. IKE_SA_INIT (proposal)           │                       │ │
│  │           │─────────────────────────────────────▶│                       │ │
│  │           │  "I support: AES-256, SHA-256, DH14" │                       │ │
│  │           │                                      │                       │ │
│  │           │  2. IKE_SA_INIT (response)           │                       │ │
│  │           │◀─────────────────────────────────────│                       │ │
│  │           │  "Let's use AES-256 + SHA-256 + DH14"│                       │ │
│  │           │                                      │                       │ │
│  │           │  3. IKE_AUTH (mutual authentication) │                       │ │
│  │           │◀────────────────────────────────────▶│                       │ │
│  │           │  Pre-shared key or certificate auth  │                       │ │
│  │           │                                      │                       │ │
│  │           │  ✅ IKE SA ESTABLISHED               │                       │ │
│  │           │  (IKE Security Association —         │                       │ │
│  │           │   encrypted control channel)         │                       │ │
│  └───────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  PHASE 2: IPSEC SA (ESP) — "Now let's agree on how to encrypt actual traffic"  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Negotiated INSIDE the encrypted IKE channel (secure!)                  │ │
│  │  • Agrees on: encryption algorithm (AES-256-GCM), integrity (SHA-256)    │ │
│  │  • Creates CHILD SA — this is what actually encrypts your data           │ │
│  │  • Result: Two unidirectional SAs (one for each direction)                │ │
│  │  • SAs have LIFETIMES (typically 1 hour for data, 8 hours for IKE)        │ │
│  │  • When SAs expire, they're renegotiated — brief pause in traffic possible│ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) — The Workhorse                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ESP encapsulates the ENTIRE original IP packet:                          │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
│  │  │ NEW IP HDR │ ESP HDR │ ENCRYPTED { Original IP HDR │ TCP │ DATA } │ ESP TRAILER │ │
│  │  │ (public IPs)│         │                                            │ │ │
│  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
│  │  ▲ Original packet is COMPLETELY encrypted (tunnel mode).               │ │
│  │  ▲ Outsider sees: "54.1.2.3 is talking to 203.0.113.10 via ESP."       │ │
│  │  ▲ Insider after decryption: "10.0.10.45 is talking to 192.168.1.50."  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  TUNNEL MODE vs TRANSPORT MODE:                                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • TUNNEL MODE (used in Site-to-Site VPN): Entire original IP packet    │ │
│  │    is encrypted and encapsulated in a NEW IP packet. The original        │ │
│  │    source/destination IPs are hidden.                                    │ │
│  │  • TRANSPORT MODE (used in host-to-host): Only the payload is encrypted. │ │
│  │    Original IP header is preserved. Used less commonly today.            │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

IPsec vs WireGuard — Old Guard vs New Contender

IPsec has been the VPN standard for 25+ years. It's battle-tested, universally supported, and... complex (IKEv1, IKEv2, ESP, AH, tunnel/transport mode, NAT-T, DPD — the acronym list alone is intimidating). WireGuard is the modern alternative: a radically simpler VPN protocol with a codebase of ~4,000 lines (vs IPsec's ~400,000+):

DimensionIPsec (IKEv2)WireGuard
Codebase~400,000+ lines (varies by implementation)~4,000 lines — auditable by a single person
Kernel IntegrationKernel module (complex, varies by OS)Linux kernel module (since Linux 5.6, 2020)
CryptographyNegotiable (AES, 3DES, etc.) — misconfiguration = weak securityNo negotiation. Fixed: ChaCha20 + Poly1305 + Curve25519. Always strong.
Key ExchangeIKEv2: complex state machine, multiple round tripsNo handshake. Pre-shared public keys. Almost instant connection.
RoamingMOBIKE extension for IP change, but complexNative — seamless IP change. Works like SSH.
NAT TraversalNAT-T (encapsulates ESP in UDP 4500)Always uses UDP. NAT traversal is built-in by design.
PerformanceGood (hardware offload on many NICs)Excellent — 4-5x faster than IPsec in many benchmarks
Cloud SupportUniversal — every cloud provider, every routerGrowing: AWS (Transit Gateway + EC2), GCP, Azure. Not yet universal on managed VPN services.
PortUDP 500 (IKE), UDP 4500 (NAT-T), IP Protocol 50 (ESP)UDP 51820 (default, configurable). Single port!
ConfigurationComplex — multiple SAs, proposals, lifetimesTrivial — config file is ~10 lines. Peer public key + allowed IPs.
WireGuard Configuration — 10 Lines vs IPsec's 100+ ini 
# Server (AWS EC2 instance acting as WireGuard peer)
[Interface]
Address = 10.99.0.1/24
ListenPort = 51820
PrivateKey = <server-private-key>

[Peer]                          # On-premises gateway
PublicKey = <onprem-public-key>
AllowedIPs = 192.168.1.0/24    # Route office network through this peer
# That's it. 10 lines. Compare to 100+ lines of IPsec config.

# Client (On-premises gateway)
[Interface]
Address = 10.99.0.2/24
ListenPort = 51820
PrivateKey = <onprem-private-key>

[Peer]                          # AWS WireGuard server
PublicKey = <server-public-key>
Endpoint = 54.1.2.3:51820     # AWS server's public IP
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.0/16       # Route VPC CIDR through this peer
🔐 WireGuard vs IPsec — Which One for anihpj?

Use IPsec for managed cloud VPN (AWS Site-to-Site VPN, GCP Cloud VPN). These are fully managed services that handle HA, BGP, and monitoring. They use IPsec under the hood and are the path of least resistance. Use WireGuard for self-managed VPN. If you're running your own VPN endpoints on EC2 instances, WireGuard is dramatically simpler and faster. For the anihpj hybrid scenario: AWS Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec) as primary, with a WireGuard tunnel on a backup EC2 instance as a cost-effective fallback.

BGP in Hybrid Networking — How Routes Are Exchanged

Static routes work for simple setups, but they don't handle failover or topology changes. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) dynamically exchanges routes between your on-prem network and cloud, automatically adapting when links go up or down:

BGP IN HYBRID CLOUD — Dynamic Route Exchange
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BGP ROUTE EXCHANGE — On-Prem ↔ Cloud                                           │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  ON-PREM ROUTER             │    │  AWS VGW / TGW                      │  │
│  │  ASN: 65000                 │    │  ASN: 64512 (Amazon side)           │  │
│  │                             │    │                                     │  │
│  │  Advertises:                │    │  Advertises:                        │  │
│  │    192.168.1.0/24 (office) │    │    10.0.0.0/16 (VPC CIDR)           │  │
│  │    192.168.10.0/24 (DMZ)   │    │    10.1.0.0/16 (secondary CIDR)     │  │
│  │    172.16.0.0/16 (branch)  │    │                                     │  │
│  │                             │    │                                     │  │
│  │  BGP SESSION                │    │                                     │  │
│  │  ┌───────────────────────┐  │    │  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  │  │
│  │  │ UPDATE: 192.168.1.0/24├──┼────┼─▶│ Learned:                      │  │  │
│  │  │ NEXT_HOP: 169.254.x.x │  │    │  │  192.168.1.0/24 → VGW tunnel │  │  │
│  │  │ AS_PATH: 65000        │  │    │  │  192.168.10.0/24 → VGW tunnel│  │  │
│  │  └───────────────────────┘  │    │  │  172.16.0.0/16 → VGW tunnel   │  │  │
│  │                             │    │  └───────────────────────────────┘  │  │
│  │  ◀─────────────────────────┼────┼──│ UPDATE: 10.0.0.0/16              │  │
│  │  Learned:                   │    │  │ 10.1.0.0/16                     │  │
│  │    10.0.0.0/16 → VGW tunnel │    │  │                                 │  │
│  │    10.1.0.0/16 → VGW tunnel │    │  │                                 │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                               │
│  BGP ATTRIBUTES THAT MATTER FOR HYBRID CLOUD:                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  AS_PATH: Shorter path = preferred. AWS prepends ASNs for less-preferred│ │
│  │  LOCAL_PREF: Higher = preferred. Set on your router to prefer DX over   │ │
│  │    VPN for the same routes. "I want 192.168.1.0/24 via DX, not VPN."    │ │
│  │  MED (Multi-Exit Discriminator): Lower = preferred. Used to influence   │ │
│  │    inbound traffic FROM AWS. "AWS, please send traffic to me via link A."│ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  DX + VPN FAILOVER WITH BGP:                                             │ │
│  │  • DX route: AS_PATH = 65000, LOCAL_PREF = 200 (preferred!)             │ │
│  │  • VPN route: AS_PATH = 65000 65000, LOCAL_PREF = 100 (backup)          │ │
│  │  • When DX link fails → BGP withdraws DX route → VPN route takes over   │ │
│  │  • Convergence time: ~3-30 seconds (BGP hold timer + propagation)        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Transit Gateway VPN — More Scalable Than VGW

The traditional Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) is limited: one VGW per VPC, max 10 IPsec tunnels. For complex hybrid setups, Transit Gateway (TGW) with VPN attachments is the modern alternative — a single TGW can terminate VPN connections from dozens of sites and share them across hundreds of VPCs:

FeatureVGW (Virtual Private Gateway)TGW + VPN Attachment
ScopeOne VPC onlyAll VPCs attached to the TGW
Max VPN Tunnels10 IPsec tunnels50 VPN connections (100 tunnels) per TGW
Bandwidth per TunnelUp to 1.25 GbpsUp to 1.25 Gbps (same)
ECMP (Equal Cost Multi-Path)No — single tunnel active at a timeYes — multiple active tunnels, load-balanced
BGPSupported (dynamic routing)Supported + route table segmentation
Use CaseSimple: single VPC ↔ single officeComplex: many VPCs ↔ many offices + DCs
CostFree (VGW) + $0.05/hour per VPN connection$0.05/hour per VPN attachment + TGW hourly

VPN Monitoring — How to Know When a Tunnel Goes Down

VPN tunnels can fail silently — the tunnel endpoint thinks it's up, but no traffic flows. AWS provides CloudWatch metrics to detect this:

MetricWhat It MeansAlert When
TunnelState0 = DOWN, 1 = UP0 for > 1 minute → tunnel is down
TunnelDataIn / TunnelDataOutBytes flowing through the tunnelZero for > 5 minutes → tunnel is up but no traffic (check routing)
DPD (Dead Peer Detection)IPsec keepalive. If peer doesn't respond to DPD, tunnel marked DOWN.Set DPD timeout to 10-30 seconds for fast detection
BGP Session StateEstablished vs Idle vs ActiveNot "Established" → BGP is down (routes may be stale!)

For anihpj: Set up CloudWatch alarms on TunnelState = 0. Send alerts to Slack/PagerDuty. If the VPN tunnel drops, BGP on the backup tunnel should take over — but you want to know immediately so you can investigate the root cause.

26.2 Direct Connect / Cloud Interconnect — Dedicated Physical Connectivity

VPNs run over the public internet — which means your traffic shares the same pipes as Netflix, YouTube, and every DDoS attack. For workloads that demand consistent performance, Direct Connect (AWS) / Cloud Interconnect (GCP) / ExpressRoute (Azure) provides a dedicated, private physical connection from your data center directly to the cloud provider's network — bypassing the public internet entirely:

DIRECT CONNECT — Dedicated Fiber, No Internet

│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────┐              ┌─────────────────────────────┐    │

│  │                         │              │  LOCATION                   │    │

│  │  │                   │  │  Cross-      │  │ Router                │  │    │

│  │  │ (or 10/100 Gbps)  │  │              │  │ → Virtual Interface   │  │    │

│                                                          │                     │
│                                                          ▼                     │

│                                            │  YOUR VPC (10.0.0.0/16)    │    │

│                                            │  → BGP routes exchanged     │    │
│                                            └─────────────────────────────┘    │

│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • DEDICATED bandwidth: 50 Mbps to 100 Gbps (not shared with internet)  │ │
│  │  • CONSISTENT latency: ~5-15ms (vs 20-80ms over internet VPN)           │ │
│  │  • NO data transfer OUT charges (vs $0.09/GB over internet!)            │ │
