VPN vs Direct Connect — When Does Each Make Sense?

The decision isn't always obvious. Here's a framework for choosing:

FactorVPN (IPsec/WireGuard)Direct Connect
Setup TimeHours — configure and goWeeks to months — physical installation
Monthly Cost (1 Gbps)~$36/tunnel (AWS managed VPN) + data transfer~$219/month (port) + ~$200-500/month (cross-connect at colo)
Data Transfer OUT$0.09/GB (AWS → internet)$0.02/GB (AWS Direct Connect data transfer)
BandwidthUp to 1.25 Gbps per tunnel (AWS managed VPN limit)50 Mbps to 100 Gbps
LatencyVariable (internet routing) — 20-80ms typicalConsistent — 5-15ms (dedicated path)
JitterHigh (internet congestion)Very low (dedicated bandwidth)
Reliability SLANone (best-effort internet)AWS Direct Connect SLA: 99.9% (single) to 99.99% (dual)
EncryptionBuilt-in (IPsec ESP / WireGuard)NOT encrypted by default! You must add IPsec/WireGuard on top for encryption.
Hybrid DNSRoute 53 Resolver endpointsSame — Resolver endpoints work over Direct Connect too
⚠️ Direct Connect Is NOT Encrypted by Default

Direct Connect provides a private, dedicated connection — but the traffic is NOT encrypted. AWS doesn't encrypt data over Direct Connect because it's a physical, private line. If you need encryption (and you probably do for compliance), you must run IPsec or WireGuard OVER the Direct Connect link. This is a common misconception: people assume "private line = secure" and forget that fiber cuts, physical taps, and carrier interception are still possible. Always encrypt over Direct Connect for sensitive workloads.

Direct Connect Resilience — Surviving Fiber Cuts

A single Direct Connect link is a single point of failure — construction crews cut fiber cables all the time. For production, you need resilience:

DIRECT CONNECT RESILIENCE — Maximum Uptime Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DIRECT CONNECT RESILIENCE PATTERNS                                             │
│                                                                               │
│  MODEL 1: SINGLE DX LOCATION, DUAL ROUTERS (99.9% SLA)                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Your DC ──▶ Router-A ──Fiber──▶ DX Location-A ──▶ VPC                   │ │
│  │            ──▶ Router-B ──Fiber──▶ (same location)                        │ │
│  │  Protects against: Router failure. Does NOT protect against: fiber cut.  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  MODEL 2: DUAL DX LOCATIONS (99.99% SLA) — Recommended for production         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Your DC ──▶ Router-A ──Fiber──▶ DX Location-A (us-east-1) ──▶ VPC      │ │
│  │            ──▶ Router-B ──Fiber──▶ DX Location-B (us-east-1) ──▶ VPC      │ │
│  │  Protects against: Router failure + fiber cut + DX location failure.     │ │
│  │  BGP handles failover. Each DX advertises same routes.                   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  MODEL 3: DX + VPN BACKUP (Most Common Hybrid Pattern)                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  PRIMARY:   Direct Connect (LOCAL_PREF=200) — all traffic                 │ │
│  │  SECONDARY: Site-to-Site VPN (LOCAL_PREF=100) — standby                  │ │
│  │  If DX goes down → BGP withdraws DX routes → VPN routes take over        │ │
│  │  Convergence: ~10-30 seconds. Some packet loss during failover.           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  LAG (LINK AGGREGATION GROUP):                                                 │
│  • Bundle multiple physical ports into a single logical link                  │
│  • 4 × 10 Gbps ports = 40 Gbps logical connection                             │
│  • If one port fails, traffic redistributes across remaining ports            │
│  • LACP (Link Aggregation Control Protocol) manages the bundle                │
│  • Only available for dedicated connections, not hosted                      │
│                                                                               │
│  HOSTED CONNECTIONS:                                                           │
│  • Don't need your own router in a colocation facility                        │
│  • Partner (Equinix, Megaport, AT&T) provides the physical connection         │
│  • You get a virtual circuit: 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps                              │
│  • Faster setup (days, not months) — partner already has the fiber            │
│  • Slightly higher cost but dramatically simpler logistics                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SD-WAN — Software-Defined Hybrid Networking

Managing individual VPN tunnels and Direct Connect circuits becomes unwieldy at scale. SD-WAN (Software-Defined Wide Area Network) abstracts the physical connections into a single logical network fabric. Think of it as "Kubernetes for your WAN" — you define policy, and the SD-WAN controller figures out which path to use:

FeatureTraditional HybridSD-WAN
Path SelectionManual BGP configuration per linkPolicy-driven — "Voice traffic: low latency path. Backup: cheapest path."
FailoverBGP convergence (10-30 seconds)Sub-second failover — SD-WAN monitors per-packet, not per-route
Transport MixManual — DX + VPN configured separatelyAutomatic — MPLS + Internet + 4G/5G bonded together transparently
VisibilityPer-device monitoring (router CLI)Centralized dashboard — all sites, all paths, all apps
Cloud On-RampManual VGW/TGW configurationAutomatic — SD-WAN appliance in cloud, VPN to SD-WAN fabric
VendorsCisco, Juniper, pfSenseVMware VeloCloud, Cisco Viptela, Silver Peak (HPE), Fortinet
🌐 SD-WAN for anihpj — When Does It Make Sense?

For a single office connecting to a single VPC, SD-WAN is overkill — a Site-to-Site VPN is sufficient. SD-WAN becomes valuable when: (1) You have 10+ branch offices all needing cloud access. (2) You're using multiple transport types (MPLS for critical traffic, internet VPN for bulk, 4G for backup). (3) You need centralized visibility and policy across all locations. (4) You're doing cloud migration and need to gradually shift traffic from on-prem to cloud. For the current anihpj scope, skip SD-WAN. File it away for when the company grows to multiple offices.

Multi-Cloud Hybrid — AWS + GCP + Azure + On-Prem

The ultimate hybrid scenario: workloads spread across multiple clouds AND on-premises. Each cloud has its own connectivity service, but the patterns are the same:

FeatureAWSGCPAzure
Dedicated ConnectionDirect ConnectCloud Interconnect (Dedicated or Partner)ExpressRoute
Managed VPNSite-to-Site VPN (VGW or TGW)Cloud VPN (Classic or HA)VPN Gateway
Bandwidth Range50 Mbps – 100 Gbps50 Mbps – 200 Gbps (Dedicated); 50 Mbps – 10 Gbps (Partner)50 Mbps – 100 Gbps
SLA99.9% (single) – 99.99% (dual)99.9% (single) – 99.99% (dual)99.9% (single) – 99.95% (dual)
EncryptionNOT built-in — add IPsec/MACsecNOT built-in — add IPsec/MACsecNOT built-in — add IPsec/MACsec
Global ReachDX locations worldwide, but no cross-region DX (use TGW peering or DX Gateway)Cloud Interconnect locations worldwide. GCP's global VPC simplifies routing.ExpressRoute locations worldwide + Global Reach for cross-region connectivity
Multi-CloudUse Megaport/Equinix Fabric — single cross-connect to reach AWS + Azure + GCP + on-premSame — Megaport/Equinix Fabric for multi-cloudSame — Megaport/Equinix Fabric for multi-cloud
🔗 Multi-Cloud Connectivity via Colocation Fabric

To connect to AWS, GCP, AND Azure simultaneously, you don't need three separate Direct Connect circuits. Companies like Megaport and Equinix Fabric provide a single physical cross-connect to their colocation facility, and you provision virtual circuits to each cloud provider on-demand. One physical fiber, unlimited cloud connections. Cost: ~$200-500/month for the physical port + ~$50-200/month per virtual circuit. This is the standard multi-cloud connectivity pattern for enterprises.

Hybrid Architecture for anihpj — Database On-Prem, Compute in Cloud

Let's design the anihpj hybrid scenario: the PostgreSQL primary database stays on-premises (compliance, latency to legacy systems), while EKS and the web tier run in AWS for scalability:

NAT Traversal — Why VPNs Break Behind NAT

IPsec ESP (IP Protocol 50) is NOT TCP or UDP — it's its own IP protocol. Many NAT devices and firewalls don't handle it correctly. NAT-Traversal (NAT-T) solves this by encapsulating ESP inside UDP packets on port 4500:

NAT TRAVERSAL — How IPsec Survives Behind NAT
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NAT-TRAVERSAL — IPsec Through NAT and Firewalls                                │
│                                                                               │
│  WITHOUT NAT-T:                                                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  VPN Gateway ──ESP (IP 50)──▶ [NAT/Firewall] ──DROP──▶ (blocked!)        │ │
│  │  Many firewalls don't forward unknown IP protocols. ESP = dropped.       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WITH NAT-T (UDP 4500):                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  VPN Gateway ──UDP:4500──▶ [NAT/Firewall] ──UDP:4500──▶ (allowed!)       │ │
│  │  ESP packet is wrapped in UDP. NAT device sees "UDP 4500" and forwards.  │ │
│  │  TCP/UDP has port numbers → NAT can track connections and translate.     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  NAT-T HANDSHAKE:                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1. IKE starts on UDP 500 (standard)                                      │ │
│  │  2. IKE detects NAT between peers (NAT-D payloads in IKE messages)       │ │
│  │  3. Both peers switch to UDP 4500 for subsequent IKE + ESP                │ │
│  │  4. ESP is now encapsulated in UDP 4500 (ESP-in-UDP)                      │ │
│  │  5. NAT keepalive packets sent every 20 seconds to keep NAT mapping alive│ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WHY THIS MATTERS:                                                             │
│  • AWS Site-to-Site VPN ALWAYS uses NAT-T (UDP 4500) — no configuration      │
│  • If your on-prem firewall blocks UDP 4500, the VPN won't establish         │
│  • WireGuard uses UDP only (51820 default) — no special IP protocol,         │
│    no NAT-T needed. This is one reason WireGuard is simpler.                 │
│  • Symptom of NAT-T failure: IKE SA establishes, but no data flows.          │
│    Check firewall rules for UDP 4500 bidirectional.                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

MTU and MSS — The Hidden Performance Killers

IPsec adds overhead (ESP header + trailer + new IP header = ~60-80 bytes). If your packets are already at the maximum MTU (1500 bytes), the encrypted packet exceeds the path MTU and gets fragmented — destroying VPN performance. The fix is TCP MSS clamping:

MTU/MSS TUNING — Why Your VPN Is Slow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MTU MATH — How IPsec Overhead Causes Fragmentation                             │
│                                                                               │
│  Original packet (1500 bytes):                                                 │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ IP HDR (20) │ TCP HDR (20) │ PAYLOAD (1460)                             │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                               │
│  After IPsec ESP Tunnel Mode encapsulation (exceeds 1500!):                    │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│
│  │ NEW IP(20)│ESP HDR(8)│ENCRYPTED{Orig IP(20)+TCP(20)+PAYLOAD(1460)}│ESP TRL(36)││
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│  Total: 20+8+20+20+1460+36 = 1564 bytes → MUST FRAGMENT (or drop if DF=1)     │
│                                                                               │
│  SYMPTOMS OF MTU PROBLEMS:                                                     │
│  • SSH works (small packets), but HTTP file transfers hang (large packets)    │
│  • TLS handshake completes, but page never loads (certificate too large)      │
│  • Intermittent connectivity — some packets fragment fine, others don't       │
│                                                                               │
│  SOLUTIONS:                                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1. TCP MSS CLAMPING (best): Router reduces MSS in TCP SYN packets       │ │
│  │     iptables -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN \                │ │
│  │                -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu                              │ │
│  │     This tells clients "send max 1380 bytes per segment" before the      │ │
│  │     packet even enters the tunnel.                                       │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  2. PATH MTU DISCOVERY: Let routers discover the actual MTU. Problems:   │ │
│  │     many firewalls block ICMP (which PMTUD needs). Unreliable.           │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  3. JUMBO FRAMES (MTU 9001): If your path supports it (DX, same-region   │ │
│  │     VPC peering), use jumbo frames. More data per packet = less overhead.│ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  AWS VPN MSS: Automatically clamps MSS to 1387 bytes on VPN tunnels.     │ │
│  │  If you see slow VPN performance, check: Is PMTUD working? Are ICMP      │ │
│  │  unreachables being blocked? Try setting a lower MTU on the tunnel (1350).│ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Direct Connect Gateway — One Connection, Many VPCs

A Direct Connect private VIF connects to ONE VPC (via VGW) or MANY VPCs (via Direct Connect Gateway). The DX Gateway is the hub that shares a single Direct Connect connection across up to 20 VPCs (across accounts and regions):

FeaturePrivate VIF → VGWPrivate VIF → DX Gateway → VGWs
VPCs reachable1 VPCUp to 20 VPCs (across accounts and regions)
Cross-RegionNo — VPC must be in same region as DXYes — DX Gateway is global. Connect to VPCs in ANY region.
Cross-AccountNoYes — via AWS RAM (Resource Access Manager)
Transitive RoutingNo — VPCs can't route through DX to each otherNo — DX Gateway is not transitive (use TGW for that)
Use CaseSingle VPC, simple setupMulti-VPC, multi-account, multi-region enterprise

MACsec — Encryption at the Physical Layer for Direct Connect

We established that Direct Connect isn't encrypted. The standard solution is IPsec over DX. But there's another option: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) encrypts at Layer 2 — every single frame on the wire is encrypted at line rate with near-zero latency overhead. It's available on 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps dedicated Direct Connect connections:

FeatureIPsec over DXMACsec on DX
OSI LayerLayer 3 (IP)Layer 2 (Ethernet frames)
PerformanceCPU-intensive, ~5-10% throughput reductionHardware-accelerated (NIC-level), line-rate, negligible overhead
RequiresVPN software on both endsMACsec-capable router/switch on both ends + DX 10/100 Gbps dedicated
ComplianceMeets PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMPMeets same standards — sometimes preferred for defense/aerospace
ComplexityModerate (IPsec is well understood)High (fewer engineers know MACsec; requires compatible hardware)
For anihpj?Yes — this is the standard approachNo — overkill for most enterprises. Use IPsec over DX.

Direct Connect Virtual Interface Types — Private, Public, and Transit

A Direct Connect connection can have three types of virtual interfaces (VIFs). Each serves a fundamentally different purpose, and you can have multiple VIFs on a single DX connection:

Hybrid DNS — Making On-Prem and Cloud Resolve Each Other's Names

Once the network is connected, the next challenge is DNS: how does an EKS pod resolve db.internal.corp.anihpj.com (on-prem DNS), and how does an on-prem server resolve rds-prod.anihpj.internal (AWS Route 53 private hosted zone)? The answer is Route 53 Resolver Endpoints:

HYBRID DNS — Bidirectional Name Resolution

│  │  │                       │  │    │  │                               │  │  │

│  │              │  10.0.10.50  │    │  │ ENI: 10.0.10.50, 10.0.11.50  │  │  │

│  │              │              │    │  │                               │  │  │
│  │              │  QUERIES:    │    │  │ Forwarding rules:              │  │  │
│  │              │  corp.anihpj │    │  │  corp.anihpj.com → 192.168.1.53│  │  │
│  │              │  .com →      │    │  │  (forward to on-prem DNS)      │  │  │
│  │              │  192.168.1.53│    │  └───────────────────────────────┘  │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────────────────────┘  │

│  • Outbound Endpoint: ~$0.125/hour per ENI (same)                             │
│  • Plus per-query charges (minimal — ~$0.40/million queries)                  │
│  • Total hybrid DNS: ~$360/month for full bidirectional resolution with HA   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

IPsec HA and Failover — Active/Passive vs Active/Active

AWS Site-to-Site VPN provides two tunnels per connection for high availability. Understanding how they fail over is critical for production hybrid deployments:

PatternHow It WorksFailover TimeAWS Support
Active/PassiveOne tunnel active (BGP preferred), one idle. When active fails, BGP converges to passive tunnel.~10-30 seconds (BGP hold timer)AWS VPN default — Tunnel #1 is preferred (lower BGP MED)
Active/Active (ECMP)Both tunnels active simultaneously. Traffic load-balanced across both. If one fails, all traffic shifts to remaining tunnel.~3-10 seconds (faster — no BGP convergence, just flow redistribution)TGW VPN only — TGW supports ECMP across multiple VPN attachments
Dual VPN ConnectionsTwo separate VPN connections to the SAME VGW/TGW — each with 2 tunnels = 4 total tunnels. Redundancy at connection level.~10-30 secondsVGW: up to 10 VPN connections. TGW: up to 50 VPN connections
⚠️ VPN Failover Is Minutes, Not Seconds, With Static Routing

If you use STATIC routing (not BGP), the failover time is determined by how fast you detect the tunnel failure AND update the route tables. DPD (Dead Peer Detection) takes ~10-30 seconds to detect a dead peer. Then you need manual or automated route table updates. Always use BGP for production VPN connections. BGP automatically withdraws failed routes and promotes backup routes — no human intervention needed.

VPN Performance — Real-World Throughput Benchmarks

How fast is a VPN tunnel really? Here are real-world numbers comparing different setups:

SetupEncryptionSingle-Stream ThroughputMulti-Stream ThroughputNotes
AWS Managed VPN (IPsec)AES-256-GCM~500 Mbps~1.25 Gbps (max per tunnel)AWS VPN is NOT designed for raw throughput — it's designed for managed HA
Self-Managed EC2 IPsec (strongSwan, c5.xlarge)AES-256-GCM~800 Mbps~2-3 GbpsCPU-bound — larger instance = more throughput
Self-Managed EC2 WireGuard (c5.xlarge)ChaCha20-Poly1305~1.5 Gbps~4-5 GbpsWireGuard is significantly faster per CPU core
Direct Connect (1 Gbps)None (or IPsec overlay)~940 Mbps (TCP overhead)~940 MbpsNo encryption overhead. Add IPsec for security (reduces to ~700-800 Mbps on c5.xlarge).
Direct Connect (10 Gbps)MACsec~9.4 Gbps~9.4 GbpsMACsec is hardware-offloaded — line rate encryption

For anihpj: A single AWS managed VPN tunnel (~500 Mbps single-stream) is more than sufficient for database write traffic (typically < 50 Mbps). The bottleneck is rarely the VPN — it's usually the database itself or application latency sensitivity.

📡IPsec + BGP Deep DiveIKE→ESP→Tunnel mode. BGP AS_PATH + LOCAL_PREF for DX/VPN failover. NAT-T (UDP 4500). MTU/MSS tuning for performance.
🔗Direct ConnectDedicated fiber, 50Mbps-100Gbps. 3 VIF types: Private (VPC), Public (S3/API), Transit (TGW). Dual locations for 99.99% SLA.

🔑 Chapter 26 Key Takeaways

  1. Start with VPN, upgrade to Direct Connect when the internet isn't enough. VPN is cheap, fast to set up, and sufficient for most hybrid workloads. Direct Connect is the premium option for consistent latency, guaranteed bandwidth, and high data volumes.
  2. IPsec is the universal standard; WireGuard is the modern alternative. IPsec works everywhere (every router, every cloud). WireGuard is simpler, faster, and has a tiny attack surface — but cloud-managed VPN services still use IPsec.
  3. Direct Connect is NOT encrypted by default. It's a private line, not an encrypted line. Always layer IPsec or WireGuard over Direct Connect for sensitive data. Compliance frameworks (PCI-DSS, HIPAA) typically require this.
  4. Use BOTH for production. Direct Connect as primary (guaranteed bandwidth, low latency) + VPN as backup (automatic BGP failover). This gives you the best of both worlds: performance AND resilience.
  5. Optimize with read replicas. In hybrid architectures with on-prem databases, deploy read replicas in the cloud. 90% of web app queries are reads — they stay local to the cloud, reducing expensive cross-premises traffic.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 26

🔐IPsec
Internet Protocol Security — a suite of protocols for encrypting and authenticating IP packets. Uses IKE for key exchange, ESP for encryption, and tunnel mode for site-to-site VPNs. Industry standard for 25+ years.
📡IKEv2
Internet Key Exchange version 2 — the protocol that establishes and maintains IPsec Security Associations. Handles mutual authentication, key negotiation, and SA rekeying. Uses UDP ports 500 and 4500.
⚡WireGuard
A modern, minimalist VPN protocol (~4,000 lines). Uses ChaCha20+Poly1305+Curve25519. No negotiation — pre-shared public keys. Native Linux kernel support since 5.6. Single UDP port. Dramatically simpler and faster than IPsec.
🔗Direct Connect
AWS service providing dedicated physical fiber connectivity from your data center to AWS. 50 Mbps to 100 Gbps. Consistent latency, no internet traversal. Not encrypted by default. ~$219/month for 1 Gbps.
🏢Virtual Private Gateway
The AWS-side endpoint for a Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect private VIF. Connects to your VPC and exchanges routes via BGP (dynamic) or static routing. Highly available by design.
🔀BGP
Border Gateway Protocol — the routing protocol used to exchange network routes between autonomous systems. In hybrid cloud, BGP dynamically advertises routes between your on-prem network and cloud VPC over VPN or Direct Connect.

📝 Chapter 26 — Practice Questions

Q1
Explain how a Site-to-Site VPN connects an on-premises network to a cloud VPC. What are the key components?
Show Answer
Answer

A Site-to-Site VPN creates an encrypted IPsec tunnel between an on-premises VPN gateway (physical router or software like pfSense) and a cloud Virtual Private Gateway (AWS VGW) or Cloud VPN gateway (GCP). Key components: (1) Customer Gateway — the on-prem device with a public IP. (2) Virtual Private Gateway — the cloud-side endpoint. (3) VPN Tunnel — encrypted IPsec ESP tunnel over the public internet. (4) BGP or Static Routes — exchange of network routes so each side knows which CIDRs are reachable through the tunnel. The tunnel uses UDP 500 (IKE) and UDP 4500 (NAT-T), plus IP Protocol 50 (ESP). Once established, instances on both sides communicate using private IPs as if on the same network.

Q2
Describe the IPsec protocol stack. What does IKE do? What does ESP do? What is tunnel mode?
Show Answer
Answer

IPsec has two main phases and protocols: (1) IKE (Internet Key Exchange) — establishes a secure control channel between peers. Phase 1 negotiates encryption parameters and authenticates peers (pre-shared key or certificates). Phase 2 negotiates the actual data encryption SAs (Child SAs). Uses UDP 500 and UDP 4500. (2) ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) — encrypts the actual data traffic using the keys negotiated by IKE. ESP is IP Protocol 50. (3) Tunnel Mode — the ENTIRE original IP packet (headers + data) is encrypted and encapsulated in a new IP packet. The new outer header has the VPN endpoints' public IPs. The original private source/destination IPs are hidden. Transport mode (encrypts only payload, preserves original IP header) is also possible but rarely used for site-to-site.

Q3
Compare WireGuard with IPsec. What makes WireGuard simpler and faster?
Show Answer
Answer

Simplicity: WireGuard is ~4,000 lines of code (vs 400,000+ for IPsec). It has no negotiation — peers exchange public keys out-of-band, and the connection is instant. IPsec requires complex IKE handshakes and SA negotiation. Cryptography: WireGuard uses a fixed, modern suite (ChaCha20+Poly1305 for encryption, Curve25519 for key exchange). No weak cipher options. IPsec allows negotiation of ciphers including weak ones (3DES, MD5). Performance: WireGuard runs entirely in the Linux kernel with minimal overhead — 4-5x faster in benchmarks. Roaming: WireGuard handles IP changes seamlessly (like SSH). IPsec needs MOBIKE for roaming. Configuration: WireGuard config is ~10 lines. IPsec config can be 100+ lines with multiple proposals and SAs.

Q4
What is AWS Direct Connect and when would you choose it over a VPN?
Show Answer
Answer

Direct Connect is a dedicated physical fiber connection from your data center to AWS — traffic never touches the public internet. Choose DX when: (1) You need consistent low latency (5-15ms vs 20-80ms over VPN). (2) You transfer large volumes of data (5+ TB/month) — DX data transfer is $0.02/GB vs $0.09/GB over the internet. (3) You need guaranteed bandwidth (50 Mbps to 100 Gbps) without internet congestion. (4) Compliance requires private connectivity (HIPAA, PCI-DSS — though DX still needs encryption overlay). (5) You need an SLA (99.9% single, 99.99% dual). Downside: weeks to months to set up (physical installation), higher base cost (~$219/month for 1 Gbps + cross-connect fees). Best practice: DX primary + VPN backup with BGP failover.

Q5
Why must you encrypt traffic over Direct Connect? Isn't it already secure?
Show Answer
Answer

Direct Connect is a PRIVATE (dedicated) connection, not an ENCRYPTED connection. The data traverses a physical fiber that only you use, but: (1) The fiber passes through multiple carriers and colocation facilities — physical taps are possible. (2) AWS staff and carrier staff have physical access to the infrastructure. (3) Compliance frameworks (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP) require encryption of data in transit regardless of the network medium. (4) Fiber cuts and misconfigurations could theoretically expose traffic. To secure Direct Connect: run IPsec or WireGuard tunnels OVER the Direct Connect link. This gives you the performance benefits of DX with the encryption of a VPN. AWS VPN over Direct Connect is a supported and recommended pattern.

Q6
Design a hybrid architecture where the database stays on-premises and compute runs in the cloud. What connectivity and optimization strategies would you use?
Show Answer
Answer

Architecture: (1) Connectivity: Direct Connect (1 Gbps+) as primary for database write traffic from cloud to on-prem. VPN as backup with BGP failover. (2) Latency optimization: Deploy a read replica of the on-prem database in AWS RDS. Route all read queries to the local read replica. Only writes go over Direct Connect. Since 90% of web app queries are reads, this dramatically reduces cross-premises traffic. (3) Caching: Use ElastiCache Redis in AWS for frequently accessed data — another layer that avoids cross-premises queries. (4) DNS: Route 53 Resolver endpoints for hybrid DNS — cloud instances can resolve on-prem hostnames and vice versa. (5) Monitoring: Track Direct Connect metrics (connection state, light levels, CRC errors) and VPN tunnel status. Alert if DX goes down and BGP fails over to VPN. (6) Security: IPsec encryption over Direct Connect. Security Groups only allow database port (5432) from EKS node SG. NACLs as defense in depth.

Q7
What are the three Direct Connect VIF types and what is each used for?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Private VIF: Connects to a VGW or DX Gateway to access VPC resources using private IPs (10.x, 172.16.x, etc.). Use for database traffic, application communication, anything within your VPCs. (2) Public VIF: Connects to AWS public services (S3, DynamoDB, SQS, EC2 API) using their public IP addresses over the DX link. Does NOT provide internet access. Use for high-volume S3 transfers or API calls without internet data charges. (3) Transit VIF: Connects to a Transit Gateway instead of a VGW. One Transit VIF can reach hundreds of VPCs across accounts and regions. The modern, scalable enterprise pattern. All three VIF types can coexist on a single DX connection using VLAN tagging.

Q8
Explain how hybrid DNS works between on-premises and AWS. What are Route 53 Resolver Endpoints?
Show Answer
Answer

Route 53 Resolver Endpoints enable bidirectional DNS resolution between on-prem and AWS. (1) Inbound Endpoint: ENIs in your VPC that receive DNS queries from on-prem servers. On-prem DNS servers forward queries for your private hosted zones (e.g., anihpj.internal) to these ENI IPs. The Resolver resolves them against Route 53 private hosted zones. (2) Outbound Endpoint: ENIs that forward specific DNS queries FROM your VPC TO on-prem DNS servers. You create forwarding rules like "*.corp.anihpj.com → 192.168.1.53". When an EC2 instance queries db.corp.anihpj.com, the .2 resolver forwards it to the outbound endpoint, which sends it to the on-prem DNS server. Both endpoints should be deployed in at least 2 AZs for HA. Cost: ~$0.125/hour per ENI (~$180/month per endpoint with 2 ENIs).
