Chapter 28: eBPF — The Kernel's Programmable Network Engine

Chapter 27 covered iptables — the Linux firewall that processes every packet. But iptables has a fundamental problem: it's slow at scale. Every packet must traverse potentially thousands of rules, and each rule check consumes CPU. eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) solves this by allowing you to run custom programs INSIDE the Linux kernel — safely, efficiently, and at the exact hook points where packets flow. What started as a simple packet filter (tcpdump uses BPF!) has evolved into the most powerful kernel technology of the last decade.

This chapter introduces eBPF from the ground up: how the verifier makes it safe, how JIT compilation makes it fast, and how Cilium — the eBPF-based CNI — eliminates iptables entirely from Kubernetes networking. eBPF isn't just the future of Linux networking — it's already here, running in production at Google, Meta, and Netflix.

🔴 ADVANCED ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🐧 Linux ⚡ eBPF ☸️ Kubernetes

🎯 By the End of This Chapter, You Will:

  • Explain what eBPF is and how it safely runs custom programs inside the Linux kernel
  • Understand the eBPF lifecycle: compile → verify → JIT → attach to hooks
  • Describe how Cilium replaces iptables and kube-proxy with eBPF for K8s networking
  • Compare iptables vs eBPF performance for Service routing at scale
  • Use Hubble to see every packet, every flow, and every service dependency in your cluster
  • Run bpftool and bpftrace to inspect eBPF programs on your system
⚡ eBPF / Cloud-Native Relevance
Platform Engineering CRITICAL SRE / DevOps CORE Security Engineer ESSENTIAL
💡 The eBPF Mental Model — A Safe Sandbox Inside the Kernel

Think of the Linux kernel as a locked building. Normally, you can only enter through the front door (syscalls) and ask the kernel to do things for you. eBPF gives you a sandbox inside the building — you can write C programs, but the kernel's verifier checks every instruction before allowing it to run. No infinite loops. No out-of-bounds memory access. No crashes. The verifier mathematically proves your program is safe, then the JIT compiler converts it to native machine code that runs at near-native speed. Key principles:

  • eBPF programs run at kernel hook points. You attach them to network events (XDP, TC), syscall entry/exit (tracepoints), or kernel function calls (kprobes). The program runs EVERY TIME that event fires.
  • eBPF maps are the data layer. Programs can't use global variables. They read/write data through eBPF maps — key-value stores in kernel memory shared between programs and userspace.
  • Cilium is the killer app for eBPF networking. It replaces iptables, kube-proxy, and conntrack with eBPF programs that process packets in microseconds instead of milliseconds.

28.1 What Is eBPF? — From Packet Filter to Universal Kernel Engine

eBPF started in 1992 as BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) — a simple virtual machine for filtering network packets. It's what tcpdump -i eth0 port 80 uses: your filter expression is compiled into BPF bytecode and loaded into the kernel. In 2014, the kernel community extended BPF into eBPF — a general-purpose in-kernel virtual machine with 10× more registers, 64-bit support, and the ability to interact with kernel data structures:

eBPF PROGRAM LIFECYCLE — Compile → Verify → JIT → Attach
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  eBPF LIFECYCLE — From C Code to Kernel Execution                               │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 1: WRITE (in C, compiled with Clang/LLVM)                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  int xdp_filter(struct xdp_md *ctx) {                                    │ │
│  │      void *data_end = (void *)(long)ctx->data_end;                       │ │
│  │      void *data = (void *)(long)ctx->data;                               │ │
│  │      struct ethhdr *eth = data;                                          │ │
│  │      if ((void *)(eth + 1) > data_end) return XDP_PASS;                  │ │
│  │      if (eth->h_proto == htons(ETH_P_IP)) return XDP_DROP;  // Block IPv4│ │
│  │      return XDP_PASS;                                                    │ │
│  │  }                                                                        │ │
│  │  ▲ Simple C program that DROPS all IPv4 packets at the NIC driver level   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                          │                                                     │
│                          ▼                                                     │
│  STEP 2: COMPILE (Clang → eBPF bytecode)                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  clang -O2 -target bpf -c xdp_filter.c -o xdp_filter.o                   │ │
│  │  Output: xdp_filter.o (ELF file containing eBPF bytecode)                 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                          │                                                     │
│                          ▼                                                     │
│  STEP 3: LOAD + VERIFY (kernel verifier checks EVERY instruction)              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│ │
│  │  │  KERNEL VERIFIER — Safety Checks:                                    ││ │
│  │  │  ✅ No loops (DAG — directed acyclic graph only)                     ││ │
│  │  │  ✅ All memory accesses within bounds (ctx->data_end check)          ││ │
│  │  │  ✅ No unreachable instructions                                      ││ │
│  │  │  ✅ Return path always exists                                        ││ │
│  │  │  ✅ Maximum 1 million instructions (complexity limit)                ││ │
│  │  │  ✅ All helper function calls are known and allowed                  ││ │
│  │  │                                                                      ││ │
│  │  │  IF VERIFICATION FAILS → Program is REJECTED. Kernel stays safe.      ││ │
│  │  │  IF VERIFICATION PASSES → STEP 4                                     ││ │
│  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                          │                                                     │
│                          ▼                                                     │
│  STEP 4: JIT COMPILE (bytecode → native x86/ARM machine code)                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  eBPF bytecode:  r1 = *(u32 *)(r10 - 4)                                 │ │
│  │  JIT output:      mov eax, [rbp-4]       ← runs at NATIVE CPU speed!     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                          │                                                     │
│                          ▼                                                     │
│  STEP 5: ATTACH (connect program to a kernel hook)                             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Available attachment points:                                             │ │
│  │  • XDP (eXpress Data Path) — NIC driver level, BEFORE sk_buff allocation│ │
│  │  • TC (Traffic Control) — after sk_buff, before netfilter               │ │
│  │  • cgroup/skb — per-cgroup socket filtering                             │ │
│  │  • kprobe/kretprobe — any kernel function entry/exit                    │ │
│  │  • tracepoint — static kernel trace events                              │ │
│  │  • uprobe — userspace function entry                                    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  THE RESULT: Your C program now runs EVERY TIME a packet arrives —             │
│  directly at the NIC driver, before the kernel even allocates an sk_buff.     │
│  This is how Cloudflare handles DDoS attacks at 100+ Gbps per server.         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

eBPF Hooks — Where Programs Can Attach

The power of eBPF comes from WHERE you can attach programs. Each hook operates at a different layer with different trade-offs:

HookLayerWhat It SeesBest ForPerformance
XDPNIC Driver (earliest possible)Raw Ethernet frames. No sk_buff allocated yet.DDoS mitigation, L4 load balancing, wire-speed filteringFastest — ~20M pps per core
TC (Traffic Control)After sk_buff allocationFull packet with all kernel metadataL7 inspection, Cilium policy enforcement, rewriting packetsVery fast — ~5-10M pps per core
cgroup/skbSocket layer (per-cgroup)Socket-level, per-container filteringCilium NetworkPolicy enforcement per podFast — works at socket level
kprobeAny kernel functionFunction arguments, return valuesObservability, tracing, security monitoring (Falco)Moderate overhead
tracepointStatic kernel eventsPre-defined event dataScheduling, syscalls, network eventsLow overhead (stable API)
⚡ XDP — The Fastest Hook in the Kernel

XDP (eXpress Data Path) is the earliest possible point where you can intercept a packet — literally inside the NIC driver, before the kernel allocates an sk_buff (which takes ~200-300ns). An XDP program can DROP a DDoS packet in ~10-20 nanoseconds. At 100 Gbps line rate, you have ~67ns per minimum-size packet — XDP can keep up. Without XDP, the kernel would spend all its time allocating sk_buffs for attack packets and never get to real work. This is why Cloudflare uses XDP for DDoS mitigation — and why Cilium uses it for high-performance load balancing.

eBPF Maps — How Programs Store and Share Data

eBPF programs can't use global variables or malloc — all persistent data goes through eBPF maps, which are key-value stores in kernel memory that persist across program invocations and can be shared between programs and userspace:

Map TypeStructureUse CaseCilium Example
BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASHGeneric key→value hash table. O(1) lookup.Service IP → Backend endpoints. The most common map type.Cilium's Service map: ClusterIP:port → [pod_ip:port, pod_ip:port, ...]
BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASHHash with LRU eviction. Oldest entries auto-removed when full.Connection tracking, flow cache, DNS cacheCilium's conntrack replacement: no fixed-size overflow, LRU evicts old entries
BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAYFixed-size array. Fastest lookup but can't grow.Configuration, counters, per-CPU dataPer-pod NetworkPolicy lookup table (indexed by pod ID)
BPF_MAP_TYPE_LPM_TRIELongest Prefix Match (LPM) trie. CIDR-style matching.IP routing table, CIDR-based policyCilium's IPCache: pod IP → identity mapping with /32 and /0 entries
BPF_MAP_TYPE_SOCKHASHSocket redirect map. Maps flow to socket.Socket-level load balancing (no DNAT!)Cilium's socket LB: directly redirect to backend socket

The key insight: BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH is the secret to Cilium's conntrack replacement. Traditional conntrack has a fixed maximum (65,536) and drops new connections when full. Cilium's LRU hash automatically evicts the oldest idle connections — no more "table full, dropping packet" incidents. The size is bounded by memory, not a hard limit.

CO-RE — Compile Once, Run Everywhere

A major challenge with eBPF: kernel data structures change between versions. A program compiled for kernel 5.10 might crash on 5.15 because struct offsets shifted. CO-RE (Compile Once, Run Everywhere) solves this with BTF (BPF Type Format) — the kernel exports its type information, and the eBPF loader relocates field offsets at load time:

CO-RE — One eBPF Binary, All Kernel Versions
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WITHOUT CO-RE:                           WITH CO-RE:                          │
│                                                                               │
│  Kernel 5.10: sk_buff.ifindex=124        One .o file compiled once            │
│  Kernel 5.15: sk_buff.ifindex=128        │                                     │
│  Kernel 6.1:  sk_buff.ifindex=136        ▼                                     │
│                                          ┌─────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  Must compile SEPARATE .o files          │ LOAD TIME (libbpf + BTF):        │  │
│  for each kernel version!                │                                  │  │
│  ❌ Impossible for distros                │ 1. Read kernel's BTF info        │  │
│                                          │ 2. Find sk_buff type definition  │  │
│                                          │ 3. Calculate offset of ifindex   │  │
│                                          │ 4. Patch eBPF bytecode:          │  │
│                                          │    *(u32 *)(ctx + 124) →         │  │
│                                          │    *(u32 *)(ctx + 136)           │  │
│                                          │                                  │  │
│                                          │ SAME .o file works on ALL        │  │
│                                          │ kernel versions! ✅               │  │
│                                          └─────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                               │
│  WHY CO-RE MATTERS FOR ANIHPJ (and everyone):                                  │
│  • Cilium ships ONE eBPF binary that works on all supported kernels          │
│  • No kernel-specific builds needed                                           │
│  • EKS node upgrades don't break Cilium                                       │
│  • BTF must be enabled: CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF=y                               │
│  • Check: bpftool btf list (shows BTF info for kernel + loaded modules)       │
│  • Modern distros (Ubuntu 20.04+, Amazon Linux 2+) have BTF by default        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

eBPF Tail Calls and Helper Functions — The Runtime Toolkit

eBPF programs have two unique mechanisms that make complex logic possible within the verifier's constraints:

TAIL CALLS + HELPERS — How eBPF Programs Extend Their Reach
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TAIL CALLS — Chain eBPF Programs (Max 33 Deep)                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Program A (XDP)                     Tail calls are NOT function calls:   │ │
│  │    │                                 • Long jump to another eBPF program  │ │
│  │    │ bpf_tail_call(ctx, &prog_map, 0)• No return — it's a GOTO            │ │
│  │    ▼                                 • Preserves registers (like exec)    │ │
│  │  Program B (Policy Check)            • Max depth: 33 programs              │ │
│  │    │                                 • Key must be constant (verifier!)    │ │
│  │    │ bpf_tail_call(ctx, &prog_map, 1)                                     │ │
│  │    ▼                                  Cilium uses tail calls to chain:     │ │
│  │  Program C (Forward to Pod)           • Policy check → L7 filter → redirect│ │
│  │                                       • Each program is verified separately │ │
│  │  WHY NOT FUNCTION CALLS?              • Combines complexity without        │ │
│  │  The verifier limits total complexity.   exceeding instruction limit      │ │
│  │  Tail calls let you split logic across                                    │ │
│  │  multiple verified programs.                                               │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  HELPER FUNCTIONS — The eBPF Standard Library (~200 functions)                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Category         │  Key Helpers                                        │ │
│  ├───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │  Map access       │  bpf_map_lookup_elem(), bpf_map_update_elem()      │ │
│  │  Packet access    │  bpf_skb_load_bytes(), bpf_skb_store_bytes()       │ │
│  │  Redirect         │  bpf_redirect(), bpf_redirect_map()                │ │
│  │  Tunnel           │  bpf_skb_set_tunnel_key() (VXLAN/Geneve encap)    │ │
│  │  Socket           │  bpf_sk_assign() (socket-level redirect!)          │ │
│  │  Tracing          │  bpf_perf_event_output(), bpf_get_current_comm()   │ │
│  │  Random           │  bpf_get_prandom_u32()                             │ │
│  │  Time             │  bpf_ktime_get_ns()                                │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  These helpers are tightly controlled — the verifier knows each one's   │ │
│  │  signature and what it can/can't do. New helpers are added with each    │ │
│  │  kernel release as eBPF's capabilities expand.                          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

eBPF JIT Compiler — How Bytecode Becomes Native Code

The verifier ensures safety; the JIT compiler ensures SPEED. Without JIT, eBPF bytecode is interpreted instruction-by-instruction — functional but ~10-100× slower than native. With JIT, it becomes native x86_64 or ARM64 machine code:

eBPF JIT COMPILER — Bytecode → x86_64 Native
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  JIT COMPILATION — Interpreted vs Native                                        │
│                                                                               │
│  eBPF Bytecode:                          JIT Output (x86_64):                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ r0 = 0                          │     │ xor eax, eax                    │  │
│  │ r1 = *(u32 *)(r10 - 4)          │     │ mov eax, dword ptr [rbp-4]     │  │
│  │ if r1 > 1500 goto +2            │     │ cmp eax, 1500                   │  │
│  │ r0 = 2                           │     │ jbe +2                          │  │
│  │ exit                             │     │ mov eax, 2                      │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────┘     │ ret                             │  │
│                                           └─────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                               │
│  PERFORMANCE COMPARISON:                                                       │
│  • Interpreted: ~100-200ns per eBPF instruction                                │
│  • JIT compiled: ~1-5ns per eBPF instruction (same as native C code!)         │
│  • Most eBPF programs are 50-500 instructions → JIT is essential              │
│                                                                               │
│  JIT SETTINGS (/proc/sys/net/core/):                                           │
│  • bpf_jit_enable:   1 = enabled (default on modern distros)                  │
│  • bpf_jit_harden:   1 = constant blinding (prevents JIT spraying attacks)    │
│  • bpf_jit_kallsyms: 1 = export JITed code addresses for debugging            │
│  • Check: bpftool feature probe | grep jit                                    │
│  • NEVER disable JIT in production — it's a 10-100× performance penalty.      │
│                                                                               │
│  WHY JIT MATTERS: Without JIT, Cilium's eBPF programs would add ~50-100µs      │
│  per packet — completely negating performance benefits. With JIT, it's         │
│  ~0.5-2µs per packet — faster than iptables by 10-100×.                        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

eBPF Program Types — More Than Just XDP and TC

eBPF programs come in many types beyond networking hooks. Each has a specific context struct, allowed helpers, and return codes:

Program TypeHook / Trigger PointContext StructReturnsPrimary Use
BPF_PROG_TYPE_XDPNIC driver RX path (earliest)struct xdp_mdPASS, DROP, TX, REDIRECTDDoS mitigation, L4 LB (Katran)
BPF_PROG_TYPE_SCHED_CLSTC ingress/egress (skb level)struct __sk_buffTC_ACT_OK, SHOT, REDIRECTCilium L3/L4 policy enforcement
BPF_PROG_TYPE_SCHED_ACTTC action (post-classification)struct __sk_buffTC_ACT_OK, SHOT, PIPE, REPEATCilium L7 proxy redirect
BPF_PROG_TYPE_CGROUP_SKBcgroup socket ingress/egressstruct __sk_buff1 (allow) / 0 (deny)Per-pod NetworkPolicy, socket LB
BPF_PROG_TYPE_CGROUP_SOCKcgroup socket create/releasestruct bpf_sock1 (allow) / 0 (deny)Socket-level ACLs
BPF_PROG_TYPE_SOCK_OPSTCP state machine eventsstruct bpf_sock_opsVarious (e.g., reply to callbacks)Custom TCP CC, socket-level LB
BPF_PROG_TYPE_TRACEPOINTStatic kernel tracepointsVaries by tracepoint0 (always)Observability, bpftrace scripts
BPF_PROG_TYPE_KPROBEAny kernel function entry/exitstruct pt_regs *0 (always)Dynamic tracing, security (Falco)
BPF_PROG_TYPE_LSMLinux Security Module hooksVaries by hook0 (allow) or -EPERMKernel-level mandatory access ctrl
BPF_PROG_TYPE_FLOW_DISSECTORKernel flow dissector overridestruct __sk_buffBPF_FLOW_DISSECTOR_CONTINUECustom RSS hash, flow classification

How Cilium uses these: XDP for DDoS mitigation (~ns-level), SCHED_CLS for L3/L4 policy at TC, SCHED_ACT to redirect to L7 proxy (Envoy), CGROUP_SKB for per-pod enforcement, SOCK_OPS for TCP-level load balancing. One eBPF ecosystem, many program types — each solving a specific layer of the networking stack.

28.2 eBPF in Kubernetes Networking — Cilium and Beyond

eBPF's killer application is Cilium — a CNI plugin that replaces iptables, kube-proxy, and conntrack with eBPF programs. Instead of thousands of iptables rules that every packet must traverse linearly, Cilium uses eBPF maps and programs that look up the destination in O(1) time:

CILIUM eBPF — How It Replaces kube-proxy and iptables
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  IPTABLES MODE (kube-proxy):                   CILIUM eBPF MODE:                │
│                                                                               │
│  Packet arrives at NodePort 30080:             Packet arrives at NodePort 30080│
│       │                                              │                         │
│       ▼                                              ▼                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐                    ┌─────────────────────┐          │
│  │ iptables nat table  │                    │ eBPF program at TC  │          │
│  │ PREROUTING          │                    │ hook                │          │
│  │                     │                    │                     │          │
│  │ Check KUBE-SERVICES │                    │ 1. Lookup socket in │          │
│  │ → Jump KUBE-SVC-XXX │                    │    eBPF map         │          │
│  │ → Check probability │                    │    (O(1) hash!)     │          │
│  │ → Jump KUBE-SEP-YYY │                    │                     │          │
│  │ → DNAT to pod IP    │                    │ 2. If socket found: │          │
│  │                     │                    │    redirect directly │          │
│  │ ~1,000-2,000 rules  │                    │    at socket level  │          │
│  │ for 100 services    │                    │    (no DNAT needed!)│          │
│  │                     │                    │                     │          │
│  │ ~2-5ms latency      │                    │ 3. No conntrack     │          │
│  │ (high rule count)   │                    │    entry needed!    │          │
│  └─────────────────────┘                    │                     │          │
│                                              │ ~0.1-0.3ms latency  │          │
│                                              │ ~100 eBPF map       │          │
│                                              │ entries for 100     │          │
│                                              │ services            │          │
│                                              └─────────────────────┘          │
│                                                                               │
│  KUBE-PROXY REPLACEMENT (Cilium's secret sauce):                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Cilium doesn't use DNAT for pod-to-pod traffic. Instead, it uses       │ │
│  │  eBPF socket-level load balancing:                                       │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  1. Pod-A calls ClusterIP 10.96.1.5:80                                   │ │
│  │  2. eBPF program intercepts the connect() syscall (cgroup hook!)         │ │
│  │  3. Looks up Service IP in eBPF map → finds backend pod IPs              │ │
│  │  4. Selects a backend (round-robin, random, or Maglev consistent hash)   │ │
│  │  5. REWRITES the connect() DESTINATION to the pod IP — at socket level!  │ │
│  │  6. The packet never goes through DNAT, never touches iptables,          │ │
│  │     never creates a conntrack entry. It goes DIRECTLY to the pod.        │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  This is called \"service load balancing at the socket layer\" —           │ │
│  │  and it's how Cilium achieves near-zero latency overhead.                │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  CONNTRACK: GONE. iptables: GONE. kube-proxy: GONE.                           │
│  All replaced by ~100 eBPF programs + hash maps in kernel memory.              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Hubble — eBPF-Based Observability for Kubernetes

One of eBPF's superpowers is observability: because eBPF programs see every packet, they can export flow logs, metrics, and even reconstruct a service dependency graph — all without sidecars, without code changes, and with negligible overhead. Hubble is Cilium's observability layer:

iptables vs eBPF — Performance Comparison for K8s Service Routing

Metrickube-proxy iptablesCilium eBPF
Rule evaluationO(n) linear scan. 5,000 services = ~50K rules = 50K checks.O(1) hash lookup. 5,000 services = 5,000 map entries = 1 lookup.
Pod-to-pod latency (p99)~0.5-2ms (rules) + conntrack overhead + DNAT~0.1-0.2ms (direct socket redirect, no DNAT, no conntrack)
Rule update time (new service)~1-5 seconds (iptables-restore for thousands of rules)~1-10ms (single eBPF map update)
CPU overhead at 10K servicesSignificant — kube-proxy uses 1-2 CPU cores just for rule syncNegligible — eBPF programs run in microseconds, maps are O(1)
Connection trackingEvery pod-to-pod flow = 1 conntrack entry (table overflow risk!)No conntrack for pod-to-pod traffic (socket-level redirect)
NetworkPolicy enforcementiptables rules (complex, error-prone, slow at scale)eBPF programs at socket/cgroup level (fast, per-pod, L7-aware)
ObservabilityNone built-in (add sidecars/metrics)Hubble — automatic flow logs + service map + metrics

Cilium Service Mesh — eBPF Without Sidecars

In Chapter 23, we covered service meshes with sidecar proxies (Istio, Linkerd). Cilium offers a fundamentally different approach: eBPF-based service mesh with NO sidecars. The kernel itself handles encryption, routing, and observability:

FeatureIstio (Sidecar Mesh)Cilium (eBPF Mesh)Why It Matters
ArchitectureSidecar proxy (Envoy) per pod — 50-300MB RAM per podeBPF programs in kernel — no per-pod overheadZero additional RAM per pod
mTLSEnvoy terminates TLS per connectionWireGuard or IPsec at kernel level, transparentNo sidecar TLS overhead; kernel-native
ObservabilityEnvoy metrics → PrometheusHubble — eBPF at packet level, ALL protocolsSees everything, not just HTTP/gRPC
Latency (p99)+2-5ms (sidecar proxy hop)+0.1-0.3ms (kernel eBPF program)10-50x lower latency
Sidecar crashPod isolated if sidecar diesNo sidecar — nothing to crashEliminates the #1 mesh failure mode

eBPF for Security — Falco, Tetragon, and Runtime Defense

Beyond networking, eBPF is revolutionizing Linux security. By attaching to syscall entry points, eBPF programs can monitor every process, file access, and network connection in real-time — enabling runtime threat detection without kernel modules:

ToolWhat It MonitorseBPF HookUse Case
FalcoSyscalls — execve, open, connecttracepoint:syscalls, kprobe"Alert when a shell is spawned inside a container" — K8s runtime security standard
Tetragon (Cilium)Process lifecycle + network + file access + kernel functionskprobe, tracepoint, LSM hooks"Which pod executed this binary? What network did it make?" Full forensic chain
Tracee (Aqua)Runtime behavior, behavioral signaturestracepoint:syscalls, kprobeDetect crypto mining, reverse shells, container escapes via patterns

Key insight: eBPF-based security is verified safe (can't crash kernel) and can't be evaded by userspace malware. This is why it's replacing legacy kernel modules and userspace monitoring across the industry.

Katran — Facebook's eBPF-Based L4 Load Balancer

While Cilium uses eBPF for Kubernetes, Katran (Facebook/Meta) uses eBPF for a different problem: Layer 4 load balancing at data-center scale. Katran handles millions of connections per second with consistent hashing (Maglev) — all in eBPF at the XDP hook:

FeatureKatran (Facebook)Cilium (Isovalent/Cisco)
ProblemL4 load balancing for data center traffic (VIP → backend)Kubernetes CNI + Service routing + NetworkPolicy + mesh
eBPF HookXDP (NIC driver level — fastest!)TC + cgroup/skb + XDP (multi-layer)
AlgorithmMaglev consistent hashing (Google's algorithm)Round-robin, random, Maglev (configurable)
ScaleMillions of connections/sec per serverCluster scale (thousands of pods per node)
Open SourceYes — github.com/facebookincubator/katranYes — github.com/cilium/cilium (CNCF Graduated)

Why Katran matters: It proves that eBPF XDP can handle data-center-scale L4 load balancing with consistent hashing — a workload traditionally requiring expensive hardware (F5, A10). Facebook runs Katran on every edge server. For anihpj, Cilium is the right tool (Kubernetes-native), but Katran shows what's possible when you need raw L4 throughput without Kubernetes.

Cilium's eBPF Datapath — What Programs Run Where

When you install Cilium on a K8s node, it loads ~50-100 eBPF programs across multiple hooks. Understanding this layout is critical for debugging:

CILIUM DATAPATH — eBPF Programs on a K8s Node

│  CILIUM eBPF DATAPATH — Programs Loaded on Every K8s Node                      │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  XDP HOOK (optional, for DDoS/L4 LB):                                     │ │
│  │  • cil_xdp_entry — early packet filter, DDoS mitigation                  │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  TC INGRESS (every packet from wire):                                     │ │
│  │  • cil_from_container — policy check for pod-to-pod                      │ │
│  │  • cil_from_host — policy check for host-to-pod                          │ │
│  │  • cil_from_network — policy check for external-to-pod                   │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │

│  │  • cil_to_host — forward to host namespace                               │ │
│  │  • cil_to_network — forward to external network (after SNAT)             │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │

│  │  • cil_sock4_sendmsg — policy check on send                              │ │
│  │  • cil_sock4_recvmsg — policy check on receive                           │ │
│  │  ▲ These run in the POD's cgroup — isolated per-pod!                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  KEY MAPS (shared between all programs):                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  cilium_ipcache:     Pod IP → Identity (security identity number)        │ │

eBPF Limitations — What eBPF CAN'T Do (Yet)

eBPF is powerful but not omnipotent. Understanding its current limitations prevents architectural mistakes:

⚠️ eBPF Limitations Every Engineer Should Know

1. Maximum program size: 1 million verified instructions (BPF_COMPLEXITY_LIMIT). Complex programs approach this quickly — Cilium uses tail calls to work around it. 2. No loops (mostly): Unbounded loops are rejected by the verifier. Bounded loops (since Linux 5.3) are allowed but add complexity. 3. No dynamic memory allocation: malloc/calloc don't exist. All state must be in pre-allocated maps or the stack (max 512 bytes). 4. Limited helper functions: Only ~200 kernel-approved helpers. Can't call arbitrary kernel functions (though fentry/fexit programs can attach to them). 5. Verifier limitations: The verifier is conservative — some perfectly safe programs are rejected because the verifier can't PROVE they're safe. Debugging verifier rejections is an art. 6. Kernel version dependency: New features require new kernels. CO-RE helps but doesn't solve everything — a 5.15-only eBPF feature won't work on 5.10. 7. No floating point: eBPF registers are integers only. No FP math. 8. Spectre mitigations: JIT hardening (constant blinding) adds overhead. Can be disabled for trusted environments.

28.3 LAB: eBPF Exploration

🛠️ eBPF Lab — 6 Hands-On Exercises
1

Check Kernel eBPF Support

# Install bpftool
apt install linux-tools-common linux-tools-$(uname -r)

# Check eBPF features available in your kernel
bpftool feature probe | grep -E "(bpf|xdp|tc|cg)"

# Key features to look for:
# • bpf() syscall — basic eBPF support (all modern kernels)
# • XDP supported — NIC driver level hook
# • JIT compiler — native code compilation (check: sysctl net.core.bpf_jit_enable)
# • BTF (BPF Type Format) — needed for CO-RE
2

Write and Load a Simple XDP Program in C

# Install build deps
apt install clang llvm libbpf-dev make

# Create xdp_counter.c — count packets by protocol:
cat > xdp_counter.c << 'EOF'
#include <linux/bpf.h>
#include <bpf/bpf_helpers.h>

// eBPF map: count packets per protocol (0=IPv4, 1=IPv6, 2=ARP, 3=other)
struct {
    __uint(type, BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY);
    __uint(max_entries, 4);
    __type(key, __u32);
    __type(value, __u64);
} pkt_count SEC(".maps");

SEC("xdp")
int count_packets(struct xdp_md *ctx) {
    void *data_end = (void *)(long)ctx->data_end;
    void *data = (void *)(long)ctx->data;
    struct ethhdr *eth = data;
    __u32 key;

    // Bounds check (mandatory for verifier!)
    if ((void *)(eth + 1) > data_end) return XDP_PASS;

    // Classify by ethertype
    if (eth->h_proto == __constant_htons(ETH_P_IP)) key = 0;
    else if (eth->h_proto == __constant_htons(ETH_P_IPV6)) key = 1;
    else if (eth->h_proto == __constant_htons(ETH_P_ARP)) key = 2;
    else key = 3;

    // Increment counter (bpf_map_lookup_elem is a helper)
    __u64 *counter = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&pkt_count, &key);
    if (counter) __sync_fetch_and_add(counter, 1);

    return XDP_PASS;  // Always pass — we're just counting
}
char _license[] SEC("license") = "GPL";
EOF

# Compile
clang -O2 -target bpf -c xdp_counter.c -o xdp_counter.o

# Load (attach to eth0)
ip link set dev eth0 xdp obj xdp_counter.o sec xdp

# Check it's loaded
bpftool prog list | grep count_packets

# View counters
bpftool map list | grep pkt_count
MAP_ID=$(bpftool map list | grep pkt_count | awk '{print $1}' | tr -d ':')
bpftool map dump id $MAP_ID
# Shows: key: 0  value: 15234 (IPv4), key: 1  value: 423 (IPv6), ...

# Detach when done
ip link set dev eth0 xdp off
3

List Loaded BPF Programs on Your System

# List ALL loaded BPF programs
bpftool prog list

# Example output (on a Cilium-enabled K8s node):
# 123: sched_cls  name cil_from_container  tag abc123def456
#      loaded_at 2026-06-21T14:30:00  uid 0
#      xlated 488B  jited 312B  memlock 4096B
# 124: cgroup_skb  name cil_to_endpoint  tag def789abc012
# 125: xdp  name cil_xdp  tag 456ghi789jkl

# Show detailed info for one program
bpftool prog show id 123 --pretty

# List eBPF maps
bpftool map list
4

Run a Simple bpftrace Network Trace

# Install bpftrace
apt install bpftrace

# Trace ALL network-related kernel tracepoints
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:net:* { printf("%s: %s\n", probe, comm); }'
# This shows every network event in your system in real-time!
# Press Ctrl+C to stop.

# Trace TCP connections: count by destination port
bpftrace -e 'kprobe:tcp_connect { @[comm, args->dport] = count(); }'

# Trace socket-level events (who's connecting to what?)
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_connect { printf("%s -> %s:%d\n", comm,
    str(args->uservaddr->sa_data+2), args->uservaddr->sa_data[1]); }'
# WARNING: This is very verbose on production systems!
5

Deploy Cilium and Explore Hubble

# Install Cilium CLI
curl -L --remote-name-all https://github.com/cilium/cilium-cli/releases/latest/download/cilium-linux-amd64.tar.gz
sudo tar xzvf cilium-linux-amd64.tar.gz -C /usr/local/bin

# Install Cilium on your K8s cluster (replaces current CNI!)
cilium install

# Verify Cilium is running
cilium status

# Enable Hubble
cilium hubble enable

# Observe live flows
cilium hubble observe

# Open Hubble UI
cilium hubble ui
# Navigate to http://localhost:12000 — see your service map!
6

Compare iptables and Cilium Rule Counts

# Before Cilium: count iptables rules
iptables -t nat -L -n | wc -l
iptables -L -n | wc -l
# Typical output: 300-500 rules for a small cluster, 5,000+ for large

# After Cilium: count eBPF programs and maps
bpftool prog list | wc -l
bpftool map list | wc -l
# Typical output: ~50-100 programs + ~50-100 maps regardless of scale!

# iptables should now be nearly empty — Cilium bypasses it entirely
iptables -t nat -L -n
# Only a few Cilium-specific rules remain (for compatibility)

🔑 Chapter 28 Key Takeaways

  1. eBPF runs custom programs safely inside the kernel. The verifier guarantees safety. JIT compilation gives near-native speed. You can run code at NIC driver level (XDP) or socket level (cgroup).
  2. Cilium replaces iptables, kube-proxy, and conntrack with eBPF. Service routing becomes O(1) hash lookups. No more linear rule scanning. No conntrack table overflow. Socket-level redirect means no DNAT needed.
  3. Hubble gives you packet-level observability with zero overhead. Every flow is visible, every NetworkPolicy drop is logged, and the service dependency map is automatic — without sidecars or code changes.
  4. The performance difference is dramatic at scale. At 5,000+ Services: iptables mode = 50K+ rules with O(n) scanning. Cilium eBPF = 5K map entries with O(1) lookup. Latency: ~0.1ms vs ~2ms.
  5. eBPF is already production-hardened. Google, Meta, Netflix, Cloudflare use eBPF in production. Cilium is the most widely deployed eBPF project for Kubernetes. The future of Linux networking is eBPF.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 28

⚡eBPF
Extended Berkeley Packet Filter — a technology that allows sandboxed programs to run inside the Linux kernel. Programs are verified for safety, JIT-compiled to native code, and attached to kernel hooks (XDP, TC, cgroup, kprobes, tracepoints).
🛡️eBPF Verifier
The kernel component that validates every eBPF program before loading. Checks: no loops (DAG only), bounds-checked memory access, no unreachable code, max 1M instructions. Rejects unsafe programs.
🚀XDP
eXpress Data Path — the earliest possible eBPF hook, inside the NIC driver before sk_buff allocation. Used for wire-speed DDoS mitigation and L4 load balancing. Processes ~20M packets/sec per core.
☸️Cilium
An eBPF-based CNI plugin for Kubernetes. Replaces kube-proxy, iptables, and conntrack with eBPF programs. Provides socket-level load balancing, L7 NetworkPolicy enforcement, and Hubble observability.
🔍Hubble
Cilium's eBPF-based observability layer. Shows every network flow, automatically builds service dependency maps, and logs NetworkPolicy drops — all with near-zero overhead and no sidecars.
🔧bpftrace
A high-level tracing language for eBPF. Similar to DTrace/awk. Allows you to write one-liner eBPF programs for ad-hoc tracing: "Count TCP connections by port" or "Trace all network events in real-time."

📝 Chapter 28 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is eBPF and how does it differ from the original Berkeley Packet Filter?
Show Answer
Answer

BPF (1992) was a simple packet filter VM — used by tcpdump to filter packets with bytecode. eBPF (2014+) extends this into a general-purpose in-kernel VM: 10× more registers, 64-bit support, access to kernel data structures (maps), helper functions, and the ability to attach to ANY kernel hook (not just packets). eBPF programs are written in C, compiled with Clang, verified for safety by the kernel verifier, and JIT-compiled to native machine code. Use cases expanded from packet filtering to networking (Cilium), security (Falco), observability (bpftrace), and tracing.

Q2
Explain the eBPF program lifecycle from C code to kernel execution.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Write: Program written in C (restricted subset — no loops, bounded memory). (2) Compile: Clang/LLVM compiles to eBPF bytecode (.o ELF file). (3) Load: Userspace loader (libbpf) sends bytecode to kernel via bpf() syscall. (4) Verify: Kernel verifier checks every instruction — no infinite loops, all memory accesses bounds-checked, max 1M instructions. Rejects unsafe programs. (5) JIT: Bytecode compiled to native x86/ARM machine code. (6) Attach: Program attached to a kernel hook (XDP, TC, cgroup, tracepoint, kprobe). (7) Execute: Program runs every time the hook event fires, at native CPU speed.

Q3
How does Cilium replace kube-proxy and iptables for Kubernetes Service routing?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium uses eBPF socket-level load balancing: when Pod-A calls a ClusterIP, an eBPF program at the cgroup/socket hook intercepts the connect() syscall. It looks up the Service IP in an eBPF map (O(1) hash) to find backend pod IPs, selects one (round-robin/Maglev), and rewrites the connect() DESTINATION to the pod IP — at the socket layer. The packet goes DIRECTLY to the destination pod. No DNAT. No iptables rules. No conntrack entry. No kube-proxy. For external traffic (NodePort), eBPF programs at the TC hook handle the redirect. Result: ~5K eBPF map entries vs ~50K iptables rules for 5,000 services. Latency drops from ~2ms to ~0.1ms.

Q4
What is XDP and why is it the fastest eBPF hook?
Show Answer
Answer

XDP (eXpress Data Path) is an eBPF hook that runs INSIDE the NIC driver — before the kernel allocates an sk_buff (saves ~200-300ns). The program receives a raw pointer to the packet data. It can return: XDP_PASS (let kernel process), XDP_DROP (silently discard), XDP_TX (bounce back out same interface), XDP_REDIRECT (send to different NIC/CPU). XDP processes ~20M packets/sec per core. At 100 Gbps line rate (~148M pps for minimum-size packets), you have ~67ns per packet — XDP can keep up because it's running directly in the driver. Use cases: DDoS mitigation at wire speed (Cloudflare), L4 load balancing (Cilium XDP-acceleration), packet sampling for observability.

Q5
How does the eBPF verifier guarantee kernel safety?
Show Answer
Answer

The verifier performs static analysis on every eBPF program before loading: (1) Control flow: Program must be a DAG (no back-edges, no loops). Bounded loops allowed since Linux 5.3 with explicit loop counting. (2) Memory access: Every memory read/write is proven to be within bounds. Programs must check ctx->data_end before accessing packet data. (3) Register state tracking: The verifier simulates every possible execution path, tracking register types (PTR_TO_CTX, PTR_TO_STACK, SCALAR_VALUE) and valid value ranges. (4) Dead code elimination: No unreachable instructions allowed. (5) Complexity limit: Max 1 million processed instructions (BPF_COMPLEXITY_LIMIT). (6) Helper restrictions: Only allowed helper functions can be called. Programs that fail ANY check are rejected — the kernel never runs unverified eBPF code.

Q6
What observability does Hubble provide and how is it different from Kiali or sidecar-based monitoring?
Show Answer
Answer

Hubble is Cilium's eBPF-based observability layer. Flow logs with source/destination/verdict/L7 info. Automatic service map (green=healthy, red=errors). NetworkPolicy drop visibility. No sidecars. Near-zero overhead. Sees ALL protocols (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka, DNS, raw TCP). Differs from Kiali (needs Istio sidecars, HTTP/gRPC only) and sidecar monitoring (pod injection, latency overhead, resource cost).

Q7
What are eBPF maps and why are they essential? Name 3 map types and their use in Cilium.
Show Answer
Answer

eBPF maps are key-value stores in kernel memory — the only way eBPF programs can persist data (no global variables, no malloc). (1) HASH: Generic O(1) lookup. Cilium uses it for Service IP→backend endpoints mapping. (2) LRU_HASH: Hash with automatic LRU eviction. Cilium replaces conntrack with LRU hash — no fixed-size overflow, old entries auto-evicted. (3) LPM_TRIE: Longest Prefix Match. Cilium's IPCache uses it for pod IP→identity mapping with CIDR prefixes. (4) SOCKHASH: Socket redirect. Cilium's socket-level LB uses it to redirect directly to backend sockets — no DNAT needed. Maps are shared between eBPF programs and userspace (Cilium agent reads/writes them via bpf() syscall).

Q8
How does Cilium's eBPF-based service mesh differ from Istio's sidecar mesh?
Show Answer
Answer

Architecture: Cilium uses kernel eBPF programs (no per-pod containers); Istio injects Envoy sidecar per pod (50-300MB RAM each). mTLS: Cilium uses WireGuard/IPsec at kernel level (transparent, no per-connection TLS handshake overhead); Istio uses Envoy TLS termination. Observability: Cilium uses Hubble (packet-level, ALL protocols); Istio uses Envoy metrics (primarily HTTP/gRPC). Latency: Cilium +0.1-0.3ms; Istio +2-5ms. Failure mode: Cilium has no sidecar to crash; Istio pods are isolated if sidecar dies. Best for: Cilium = performance-critical, simple mTLS+observability. Istio = complex L7 policies, external auth, multi-cluster mesh. Cilium's mesh is still maturing (fewer L7 policy features than Istio) but dramatically better performance.

eBPF Feature Check: On your Linux machine (or a K8s node), run bpftool feature probe. Document which eBPF features are available. Is JIT enabled? Is BTF supported? Are XDP hooks available?

Chapter 29: Network Observability — Metrics, Logs & Traces

You can't fix what you can't see. Network observability is the discipline of instrumenting your infrastructure so you can answer any question about network behavior — without deploying new code. It's the difference between "users report slowness" and "TCP retransmit rate on eth0 exceeded 2% at 14:32 UTC, correlated with a 5xx spike from payment-service." This chapter covers the three pillars (metrics, logs, traces), the specific metrics that predict incidents, the tooling landscape, and a hands-on lab to wire it all up.

29.1 The Observability Stack for Networking

Observability isn't just monitoring. Monitoring tells you that something is wrong. Observability lets you ask why — by exploring high-cardinality data across multiple dimensions. For networking, this means three pillars working together:

NETWORK OBSERVABILITY PYRAMID — The Three Pillars
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NETWORK OBSERVABILITY — Three Pillars, One Goal                               │
│                                                                               │
│                        ┌───────────────┐                                      │
│                        │    TRACES     │  ← Hardest / Most Valuable           │
│                        │  Distributed  │     Per-request journey across        │
│                        │   Tracing     │     services. Answer: "Where did      │
│                        │               │     the 500ms go?"                   │
│                        └───────┬───────┘                                      │
│                                │                                              │
│                        ┌───────┴───────┐                                      │
│                        │     LOGS      │  ← Moderate / Indispensable           │
│                        │  Flow Logs,   │     Who talked to whom? Was it        │
│                        │  Event Logs   │     allowed? VPC Flow Logs, Cilium    │
│                        │               │     Hubble, syslog, journald          │
│                        └───────┬───────┘                                      │
│                                │                                              │
│                        ┌───────┴───────┐                                      │
│                        │    METRICS    │  ← Easiest / Foundation               │
│                        │  Counters,    │     Bandwidth, packets/sec, errors,    │
│                        │  Gauges,      │     drops, TCP retransmits. Low cost, │
│                        │  Histograms   │     always-on. Prometheus standard.    │
│                        └───────────────┘                                      │
│                                                                               │
│  THE OBSERVABILITY FLOW:                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ALERT FIRES → Dashboard shows spike in TCP retransmits (METRICS)        │ │
│  │  → Query VPC Flow Logs to find affected src/dst pairs (LOGS)             │ │
│  │  → Trace one slow request through service mesh to find bottleneck (TRACES)│ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Pillar 1: Metrics — Always-On Numerical Data

Metrics are time-series numbers collected at regular intervals (every 15s or 30s). They're cheap to collect, store, and query. Prometheus is the standard. Network-specific metrics come from node_exporter (host NIC counters), kubelet (pod network stats), and CNI plugins like Cilium (eBPF-derived metrics):

Metric SourceWhat It ExposesExample MetricCost
node_exporterPer-NIC: bytes, packets, errors, drops, overrunsnode_network_receive_bytes_total{iface="eth0"}Negligible
kubelet cAdvisorPer-pod: network rx/tx bytes, packets, errorscontainer_network_receive_bytes_totalLow
Cilium AgentPer-endpoint: policy drops, forwards, eBPF map metricscilium_drop_count_total{reason="Policy denied"}Low (eBPF)
CloudWatch / Azure MonitorCloud LB: healthy host count, request count, latencyAWS/ApplicationELB HealthyHostCountCloud-native
Envoy / Linkerd proxyPer-service: request rate, error rate, latency histogramsenvoy_cluster_upstream_rq_xxMedium

Pillar 2: Logs — Structured and Flow-Level Records

While metrics give you aggregate trends, logs give you individual events. For networking, the most important log type is flow logs — records of every IP flow (or a sampled subset) showing who talked to whom:

Log TypeWhat It CapturesWhere It LivesBest For
AWS VPC Flow Logs5-tuple + action + bytes/packets per flowS3 → Athena / CloudWatch LogsSecurity audit, network ACL debugging, top talkers
GCP VPC Flow Logs5-tuple + action + bytes/packets, enriched with GKE metadataBigQuery / Cloud LoggingGKE network debugging, IAM policy audit
Azure NSG Flow Logs5-tuple + action, stored in Azure StorageBlob Storage → Log AnalyticsNSG rule debugging, traffic analytics
Cilium Hubble Flows5-tuple + K8s identity + L7 info (HTTP path, gRPC method) + verdictHubble Relay → Prometheus/LokiK8s NetworkPolicy debugging, L7 observability
syslog / journaldKernel and daemon events (iptables logs, conntrack events)Local disk → Loki/ElasticsearchHost-level firewall debugging, kernel network events

Flow log sampling: Cloud providers typically sample flow logs (e.g., AWS captures ~1/10 flows at high throughput). This means you may miss very short connections. For forensics requiring every packet, use tcpdump on the host — but flow logs are perfect for pattern analysis at scale.

Pillar 3: Traces — Distributed Request Journeys

Distributed tracing follows a single request as it traverses multiple services, timing each hop. For networking, traces reveal which network hop is the bottleneck — is it the load balancer? The service mesh proxy? The backend database connection? Traces use W3C Trace Context headers propagated via HTTP/gRPC:

DISTRIBUTED TRACING — How a Request Flows Through the Network
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DISTRIBUTED TRACING — Network Hops in a Trace                                  │
│                                                                               │
│  Client ──→ LB ──→ API-GW ──→ auth-svc ──→ payment-svc ──→ DB                │
│  │          │       │          │            │               │                  │
│  │  Span 1  │ Span 2│  Span 3  │  Span 4    │  Span 5       │ Span 6           │
│  │  2ms     │ 1ms   │  5ms     │  15ms      │  80ms         │ 45ms             │
│  │          │       │          │            │               │                  │
│  │          │       │          │  ← PAYMENT-SVC IS THE BOTTLENECK (80ms) →    │
│  │          │       │          │  Network hop inside payment-svc includes:     │
│  │          │       │          │  DNS resolution (5ms) + TCP connect (2ms)     │
│  │          │       │          │  + HTTP request/response (73ms)               │
│  │                                                                             │
│  │  TRACE CONTEXT HEADERS (W3C standard):                                       │
│  │  traceparent: 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01       │
│  │  tracestate:  vendor-specific key=value pairs                                │
│  │                                                                             │
│  │  HOW TO USE TRACES FOR NETWORK DEBUGGING:                                    │
│  │  1. Identify slow traces (p99 > SLO) in Jaeger/Zipkin UI                    │
│  │  2. Find the span with the longest duration                                 │
│  │  3. Check if the span's service has high TCP retransmits (Prometheus)       │
│  │  4. Correlate: slow traces + high retransmits = network congestion          │
│  │  5. If span is slow but NO retransmits → application-level bottleneck       │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

How tracing works at the network level: Each service adds traceparent and tracestate headers to outgoing HTTP/gRPC requests. Load balancers, API gateways, and service mesh proxies can propagate or create spans. Cilium Hubble can correlate flow logs with trace IDs, giving you both the network view (packet flow) and the application view (trace span) for the same request. This is the holy grail of network observability.

Understanding Prometheus Metric Types — Counters, Gauges, Histograms

Prometheus uses four metric types. Understanding which is which is critical for writing correct PromQL queries and alerts:

Metric TypeBehaviorNetwork ExamplePromQL PatternAlert Rule
CounterMonotonic — only increases (or resets to 0 on restart). Always ends with _total.node_network_receive_bytes_total, node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs_totalrate(counter[5m]) — converts to per-second rate"If rate of retransmits > 0.02 × rate of out-segments for 5 minutes"
GaugeGoes up AND down — represents a point-in-time value.node_sockstat_TCP_tw (TIME_WAIT count), node_nf_conntrack_entriesgauge > threshold or just gauge"If TIME_WAIT > 20000 for 5 minutes"
HistogramTracks distribution of values in configurable buckets. Generates _bucket, _sum, _count series.http_request_duration_seconds (latency distribution), coredns_dns_request_duration_secondshistogram_quantile(0.99, rate(histogram_bucket[5m]))"If p99 latency > 500ms for 5 minutes"
SummaryLike histogram but calculates quantiles client-side (less flexible, more expensive). Generally prefer Histograms.go_gc_duration_seconds (Go runtime), rarely used for network metricssummary_quantile — direct quantile accessPrefer histograms for network observability

Why this matters: You can't aggregate client-side quantiles (Summary). If you have two servers each reporting p99=50ms, the combined p99 is NOT 50ms — it could be 200ms. Histograms fix this by storing bucket counts that can be merged. Always prefer Histograms over Summaries for network metrics. Also, never use irate() for alerting — it's too sensitive to spikes. Use rate() with a 5-minute window for stable, actionable alerts.

Network Observability Maturity Model — Crawl, Walk, Run

You don't build all three pillars on day one. Here's a practical progression for infrastructure teams:

OBSERVABILITY MATURITY — Where Are You?

│  LEVEL 2: WALK — "I can investigate without SSHing"                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Add: VPC Flow Logs → Athena/BigQuery, DNS monitoring (CoreDNS metrics) │ │
│  │  • Alert on: TCP retransmit > 2%, DNS latency p99 > 100ms,                │ │
│  │    conntrack > 80%, HTTP 5xx > 1%                                          │ │
│  │  • Time to value: 1 week. Cost: ~$50/month (flow log storage)             │ │
│  │  • You can now answer "who talked to whom" and catch leading indicators    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  LEVEL 3: RUN — "I can trace every request through the network"                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Add: Distributed tracing (Jaeger), Cilium Hubble, custom Grafana       │ │
│  │    dashboards, SLO-based alerting (not just threshold-based)              │ │
│  │  • Alert on: SLO burn rate > 1% per hour, service dependency anomalies    │ │
│  │  • Time to value: 1 month. Cost: ~$200/month (tracing infrastructure)     │ │
│  │  • You have the holy grail: trace + flow log + metric correlation          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  LEVEL 4: FLY — "The network observes itself" (Netflix/Google level)           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Automated root cause analysis (ML on metrics + traces)                  │ │
│  │  • Chaos engineering for network (intentionally break things to test)      │ │
│  │  • Service-level SLOs with auto-rollback on violation                      │ │
│  │  • eBPF-based always-on profiling of every packet                          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Prometheus TSDB Internals — Why It Matters for Network Metrics

Understanding how Prometheus stores data helps you avoid common mistakes that make dashboards slow or cause data loss. Network metrics are high-volume (every NIC, every pod, every connection) — the TSDB design directly impacts what you can monitor at scale:

PROMETHEUS TSDB — How Network Metrics Are Stored
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PROMETHEUS TSDB INTERNALS — Impact on Network Observability                    │
│                                                                               │
│  HOW DATA IS STORED:                                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Each unique {metric_name + labels} combination = ONE TIME SERIES       │ │
│  │  • Example: node_network_receive_bytes_total{instance="web-01",           │ │
│  │    device="eth0"} is ONE series. Same metric with instance="web-02"       │ │
│  │    is ANOTHER series. 100 nodes × 4 NICs = 400 series for ONE metric.     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  STORAGE STRUCTURE:                                                        │ │
│  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐              │ │
│  │  │ 2h Block │ → │ Compressed Chunks │ → │ SSTable on Disk │              │ │
│  │  │ (memory) │    │ (gorilla encoding)│    │ (immutable)     │              │ │
│  │  └──────────┘    └──────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘              │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  • 2-hour blocks: Recent data in memory (WAL-backed). Fast query.          │ │
│  │  • Compaction: Every 2 hours, memory block → compressed disk block.        │ │
│  │  • Retention: Default 15 days. Older blocks deleted.                       │ │
│  │  • Gorilla encoding: XOR delta-of-delta compression. ~1.3 bytes per        │ │
│  │    sample for typical metrics. Network counters (monotonic) compress       │ │
│  │    even better because values only increase.                               │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  CARDINALITY — THE 10M SERIES LIMIT:                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Prometheus can handle ~10 MILLION active time series per instance.        │ │
│  │  Network metrics explode cardinality:                                      │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  node_network_receive_bytes_total:                                         │ │
│  │    instances × devices per instance = 100 nodes × 4 NICs = 400 series     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  container_network_receive_bytes_total (K8s):                              │ │
│  │    pods × interfaces = 5,000 pods × 1 veth = 5,000 series                  │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Cilium endpoint metrics:                                                  │ │
│  │    endpoints × metrics per endpoint = 50,000 eps × 10 = 500,000 series    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  CARDINALITY EXPLOSION TRIGGERS:                                            │ │
│  │  • Label with high unique values (pod_name, container_id, request_path)   │ │
│  │  • Per-path HTTP metrics: NEVER do this — /users/123 creates a new series  │ │
│  │  • Per-connection metrics: NEVER — millions of unique 5-tuples             │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  MITIGATIONS:                                                               │ │
│  │  • Drop high-cardinality labels at scrape time (relabel_configs)           │ │
│  │  • Aggregate in recording rules before dashboards see raw data              │ │
│  │  • Use Thanos/Mimir/Cortex for horizontal scaling beyond 10M series        │ │
│  │  • For per-path/per-user metrics: use logs (Loki) or traces (Jaeger),      │ │
│  │    NOT Prometheus metrics — different tools for different cardinalities     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

High-Throughput Network Sampling — When You Can't Store Everything

At 100 Gbps line rate, you can't capture every packet or every flow. Sampling is essential — but each approach has trade-offs:

Sampling MethodHow It WorksAccuracyCPU CostBest For
1/N Random Sampling (sFlow)HW ASIC picks every Nth packet (e.g., 1:1000)Statistically accurate for volume, misses rare short flowsNear-zero (hardware)100Gbps+ links, DDoS detection, traffic matrix
Flow Sampling (NetFlow)Router samples flows, not packets. Full stats for sampled flows.Good for top talkers. Elephant flows caught; mice flows missed.Low (cache lookup per flow)Billing, capacity planning, peering analysis
Stratified SamplingDifferent rates for different traffic types (e.g., 1:100 for port 443, 1:10 for port 22)Better detection of rare-but-important trafficMedium (classification per packet)Security monitoring, rare protocol detection
Continuous (eBPF/XDP)Custom sampling logic in eBPF — e.g., sample 1:1000 but always capture TCP SYN/RSTBest of both worlds: statistical for volume, deterministic for signalsVery low (eBPF JIT → native)Modern cloud-native (Cilium, Katran)

The trade-off: Sampling rate inversely affects accuracy for rare events. At 1:1000, you catch ~63% of flows that send 1000 packets. A 10-packet DNS query has only ~1% chance of being sampled. This is why VPC Flow Logs can miss short connections — and why Hubble (eBPF, per-packet) is superior for security-relevant observability where you need to see EVERY connection attempt.

29.2 Key Network Metrics Every Infrastructure Engineer Should Monitor

Not all metrics are equal. The following are the leading indicators that predict incidents before users notice. Organize them by layer:
