MetricWhat It DetectsCritical ThresholdAlert Action
Interface Drops (rx)Ring buffer full — kernel too slow to read packetsAny > 0Increase ring buffer (ethtool -G). Check CPU load.
Interface ErrorsPhysical layer issue — bad cable, duplex mismatch, CRC errorsAny > 0Check cable, switch port, negotiate speed/duplex.
TCP Retransmit RatePacket loss somewhere in the path (congestion, bad link, MTU mismatch)> 2% of total segmentsCheck interface drops, run mtr/traceroute, check MTU.
TIME_WAIT SocketsEphemeral port exhaustion imminent> 20,000Enable tcp_tw_reuse, add more source IPs, reduce connections.
Conntrack UtilizationConnection tracking table near limit, new connections will be dropped> 80%Increase nf_conntrack_max, reduce connection churn, switch to Cilium.
DNS Latency p99DNS resolver bottleneck — every first connection waits for DNS> 100msScale CoreDNS, enable NodeLocal DNSCache, reduce TTLs.
HTTP 5xx RateApplication or upstream failures> 1% of requestsCheck downstream dependencies, correlate with TCP retransmits.
SYN Rate SpikeSYN flood DDoS or connection storm> 5× baselineEnable SYN cookies, rate-limit at LB, DDoS scrubbing.
🟡 SRE OBSERVABILITY — Network Metrics That Impact Your SLOs

SLO: 99.9% Availability → Monitor LB healthy host count, 5xx rate. One unhealthy backend = reduced capacity.
SLO: p99 Latency < 500ms → Monitor TCP retransmit rate, DNS latency. Retransmits add ~200ms each.
SLO: Zero Data Loss → Monitor TCP retransmits, interface drops. Drops = lost data.
SRE RULE: Alert on leading indicators (retransmits, drops, queue depth), not just lagging indicators (5xx rate, user complaints). Leading indicators give you 5-15 minutes of warning before users notice.

Understanding TCP Retransmits — Your #1 Network Health Signal

TCP retransmission rate is the single most informative network health metric. Here's why:

TCP RETRANSMIT — Anatomy of a Leading Indicator
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TCP RETRANSMIT RATE — What Different Levels Mean                               │
│                                                                               │
│  < 0.1%  ✅ Healthy                                                             │
│           Normal operation. Occasional loss from congestion. Nothing to fix.    │
│                                                                               │
│  0.1-1%  ⚡ Elevated — Investigate                                              │
│           Could be: congested link, flaky NIC, bad cable. Check interface       │
│           drops first (ethtool -S eth0). If no drops, check switch side.        │
│                                                                               │
│  1-2%    🟡 Degraded — Users May Notice                                         │
│           Every retransmit adds ~200ms (RTO min). At 2%, 1 in 50 segments is    │
│           lost. TCP throughput drops significantly due to congestion window      │
│           reduction. Users experience as "slowness."                            │
│                                                                               │
│  > 3%    🔴 Critical — Incident                                                  │
│           Severe packet loss. Check: NIC errors (ethtool -S), switch CRC errors, │
│           interface drops (netstat -i), MTU mismatch (path MTU discovery),      │
│           firewall dropping fragments. Run mtr to find the lossy hop.           │
│                                                                               │
│  GET THE RATE:                                                                  │
│  ss -ti | grep -oP 'retrans:\d+' | grep -oP '\d+$' | awk '{s+=$1}END{print s}'│
│  # Or with Prometheus: rate(node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs[5m])                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

DNS Health — The Silent Performance Killer

DNS is the first step in nearly every network connection. If DNS is slow, everything is slow — and users notice. Every microservice call, every DB connection, every external API call starts with a DNS query:

DNS MetricPrometheus SourceCritical ThresholdWhy It Matters
Query Raterate(coredns_dns_requests_total[5m])> 10,000 qps per replicaCoreDNS bottleneck. Scale horizontally before it becomes a problem.
Failure Raterate(coredns_dns_responses_total{rcode="SERVFAIL"}[5m]) / rate(coredns_dns_requests_total[5m])> 1%Upstream resolver failing. Check kube-dns → upstream path.
Latency p50histogram_quantile(0.50, coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds_bucket)> 10msNormal resolution should be < 5ms for cached queries.
Latency p99histogram_quantile(0.99, coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds_bucket)> 100msCache misses hitting upstream. Users feel this as slow page loads.
Cache Hit Raterate(coredns_cache_hits_total[5m]) / rate(coredns_cache_misses_total[5m])< 80%Too many cache misses = too many upstream queries = latency.
🟢 DNS Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet

High DNS latency? (1) Check CoreDNS pod count — scale if CPU > 80%. (2) Enable NodeLocal DNSCache (local DNS cache on every node, bypasses iptables). (3) Check upstream resolver health — if CoreDNS forwards to VPC DNS (.2 resolver), that could be the bottleneck. (4) Reduce TTLs in your DNS records — long TTLs hide failures. High SERVFAIL rate? (1) Check if upstream DNS is reachable. (2) Verify CoreDNS config (Corefile) for forward zones. (3) Check for DNSSEC validation failures. Quick test from a pod: time nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local — should return in < 10ms.

HTTP Observability — RED Method Applied

The RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) is the standard for monitoring HTTP services from a network perspective. Every load balancer, API gateway, and service mesh proxy exposes these:

HTTP OBSERVABILITY — RED Method with Network Context
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  RED METHOD APPLIED TO HTTP NETWORKING                                          │
│                                                                               │
│  RATE (requests/sec):                                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  rate(http_requests_total[5m])                                             │ │
│  │  • Sudden drop → network partition or LB health check failure              │ │
│  │  • Sudden spike → possible DDoS, check SYN rate in parallel                │ │
│  │  • Compare: ingress rate vs egress rate. If ingress >> egress → drops     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ERRORS (failed requests):                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m])│
│  │  • 5xx spike → downstream failure. Correlate with TCP retransmits.         │ │
│  │  • 4xx spike → client error (wrong endpoint, auth failure). Not network.   │ │
│  │  • 502/504 → upstream timeout (network or app). Check upstream TCP stats.  │ │
│  │  • 0 (no response) → connection refused or timeout. Check socket state.    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  DURATION (latency distribution):                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))  │ │
│  │  • p50 vs p99 gap > 10x → tail latency problem. Check GC pauses, queueing. │
│  │  • p99 spike with normal p50 → a subset of requests are slow. Trace them.  │ │
│  │  • TTFB (time to first byte) vs total duration. High TTFB = network.      │ │
│  │  • If p99 > SLO and retransmits are normal → application, not network.    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  SLO DEFINITION FROM RED METRICS:                                              │
│  "99.9% of requests succeed (non-5xx) and complete in < 500ms over 30 days"   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Network Monitoring Prioritization — What to Set Up First

With dozens of possible metrics, where do you start? Here's a time-ordered priority list based on how quickly each item catches real incidents:

PriorityWhat to MonitorSetup TimeWhat It CatchesReal-World Example
🥇 P0node_exporter on every host → Grafana Dashboard 18602 hoursHost down, NIC errors, disk full, CPU/memory"Node prod-web-07 NIC errors spiking — replacing cable fixed 2% packet loss"
🥈 P1TCP retransmit rate alert (Prometheus AlertManager)30 minPacket loss, congestion, failing NIC before users complain"Retransmit rate hit 3.5% at 03:00 — network team found failing switch port"
🥉 P2Conntrack utilization + TIME_WAIT count15 minConnection tracking exhaustion before new connections are dropped"Conntrack at 92% — increased nf_conntrack_max from 65K to 262K, incident averted"
P3HTTP 5xx rate + latency p99 (RED method)1 hourService degradation, upstream failures, slow endpoints"5xx rate spiked after deploy — rollback fixed it. Alert fired before users noticed."
P4DNS monitoring (CoreDNS query rate, latency, SERVFAIL)1 hourDNS bottleneck — the silent performance killer"DNS latency p99 went from 5ms to 250ms — upstream resolver was rate-limiting us"
P5VPC Flow Logs → Athena/S3 queries1 daySecurity violations, top talkers, unexpected traffic patterns"Found SSH brute-force from external IP — flow logs showed 10K REJECTS to port 22"
P6Hubble observability (if using Cilium)30 minComplete K8s network visibility — service map, policy drops, L7"Hubble showed payment-svc talking to 15 unknown IPs — compromised pod detected"

The 80/20 rule: P0-P2 (node_exporter + TCP retransmits + conntrack) catches ~80% of network incidents with ~3 hours of setup. Everything else adds precision and coverage. Start with P0-P2, then iterate.

Network Latency Decomposed — Where the Time Actually Goes

When a packet takes 5ms to travel from Server A to Server B, where is that time spent? Understanding latency components is critical for root-causing slow networks:

NETWORK LATENCY — The Four Components
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LATENCY = Serialization + Propagation + Queuing + Processing                   │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ SERIALIZATION DELAY ────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Time to push bits onto the wire. = Packet Size / Link Bandwidth           │ │
│  │  • 1500-byte packet on 1 Gbps:   1500×8 / 1e9     = 0.012 ms (12µs)       │ │
│  │  • 1500-byte packet on 100 Mbps: 1500×8 / 1e8     = 0.12 ms               │ │
│  │  • 1500-byte packet on 10 Mbps:  1500×8 / 1e7     = 1.2 ms                │ │
│  │  • 64-byte packet on 1 Gbps:     64×8 / 1e9       = 0.0005 ms (0.5µs)     │ │
│  │  KEY INSIGHT: At 10 Gbps+, serialization is negligible (<1µs). The         │ │
│  │  bottleneck shifts to propagation and processing.                          │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ PROPAGATION DELAY ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Time for signal to travel through the medium. = Distance / Signal Speed    │ │
│  │  • Fiber: ~5µs per km (speed of light in glass ≈ 200,000 km/s)             │ │
│  │  • Same AZ (AWS):      ~0.1-0.3 ms  (same building or campus)              │ │
│  │  • Cross-AZ (AWS):     ~0.5-2 ms    (typically < 100km apart)              │ │
│  │  • Cross-Region (US):  ~20-50 ms    (coast to coast fiber)                 │ │
│  │  • Cross-Continent:    ~80-150 ms   (transatlantic/transpacific fiber)      │ │
│  │  • NYC → London: ~70ms minimum (physics limit — nothing can beat this)     │ │
│  │  KEY INSIGHT: You can't reduce propagation delay without moving closer.    │ │
│  │  This is why CDNs and edge computing exist.                                │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ QUEUING DELAY ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Time packets wait in buffers. = Queue Depth / Departure Rate               │ │
│  │  • Empty buffer: 0ms                                                       │ │
│  │  • Busy link with 64KB buffer at 1 Gbps: up to 0.5ms                       │ │
│  │  • Congested link with 1MB buffer at 100 Mbps: up to 80ms                  │ │
│  │  • BUFFERBLOAT: Modern NICs have huge buffers (1-4MB). When full, queuing   │ │
│  │    delay EXPLODES — from microseconds to HUNDREDS of milliseconds!          │ │
│  │  KEY INSIGHT: This is the ONLY component you can fix with configuration.    │ │
│  │  Bufferbloat is the #1 cause of "mysterious" latency spikes.                │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ PROCESSING DELAY ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Time for routers/switches to look up forwarding table.                     │ │
│  │  • Hardware switch (cut-through):     ~0.001-0.01 ms  (microseconds)        │ │
│  │  • Hardware router (store-forward):   ~0.01-0.1 ms   (including FIB lookup) │ │
│  │  • Software router (Linux iptables):  ~0.1-1 ms     (per packet overhead)   │ │
│  │  • Cloud SDN (VPC encapsulation):     ~0.05-0.2 ms  (tunnel encap/decap)    │ │
│  │  • NGFW/IDS (deep packet inspection): ~1-10 ms      (L7 analysis)           │ │
│  │  KEY INSIGHT: Software processing dominates at high pps. This is why eBPF   │ │
│  │  (XDP avoids sk_buff allocation) and hardware offloading matter at scale.   │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  REAL-WORLD BREAKDOWN (pod-to-pod in same K8s node, 1 Gbps):                   │
│  Serialization (1500B @ 1Gbps)  = 0.012 ms                                     │
│  Propagation (same host, veth)  = 0.001 ms                                     │
│  Queuing (light load)           = 0.005 ms                                     │
│  Processing (iptables + conntrack) = 0.5 ms   ← DOMINATES!                     │
│  Total: ~0.5ms. Replace iptables with Cilium eBPF → processing drops to 0.05ms.│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Bufferbloat — When Bigger Buffers Make Things Worse

Bufferbloat is the phenomenon where excessively large network buffers cause high latency and jitter under load. It's counterintuitive: larger buffers seem like they should help, but they actually create latency spikes that destroy interactive application performance:

BUFFERBLOAT — The Hidden Latency Killer
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BUFFERBLOAT — Why Your Network Feels Slow Under Load                           │
│                                                                               │
│  THE PROBLEM:                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  SMALL BUFFER (32KB):                                                      │ │
│  │   • Queue fills quickly → packets drop → TCP slows down (congestion ctrl) │ │
│  │   • Latency: consistent < 1ms (queue never gets deep)                      │ │
│  │   • Throughput: slightly lower (TCP backs off sooner)                      │ │
│  │                                                                             │ │
│  │  LARGE BUFFER (4MB — DEFAULT on many NICs!):                                │ │
│  │   • Queue can hold ~2,700 full-size packets                                 │ │
│  │   • At 1 Gbps: queue drains in 32ms, BUT...                                │ │
│  │   • TCP keeps sending (no drops = no congestion signal!)                   │ │
│  │   • Queue builds to 4MB → EVERY packet experiences 32ms queuing delay      │ │
│  │   • Latency: spikes from < 1ms → 32ms → then back to < 1ms (sawtooth!)    │ │
│  │   • Jitter: MASSIVE. VoIP/unusable. Gaming impossible. SSH laggy.           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  THE FIX:                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1. fq_codel (Fair Queuing + Controlled Delay):                             │ │
│  │     tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root fq_codel                                │ │
│  │     # Dynamically manages queue depth — keeps latency low while            │ │
│  │     # maintaining throughput. Standard on most modern Linux distros.        │ │
│  │                                                                             │ │
│  │  2. BBR congestion control (replaces CUBIC/Reno):                           │ │
│  │     echo bbr > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_congestion_control                   │ │
│  │     # BBR measures available bandwidth, not packet loss. Doesn't            │ │
│  │     # blindly fill buffers. Dramatically reduces bufferbloat.               │ │
│  │                                                                             │ │
│  │  3. Reduce NIC ring buffer:                                                 │ │
│  │     ethtool -G eth0 rx 256 tx 256                                           │ │
│  │     # Smaller ring = less bufferbloat. Trade-off: may drop at very          │ │
│  │     # high throughput (>10M pps). Most workloads: 256 is fine.              │ │
│  │                                                                             │ │
│  │  DIAGNOSE: Check interface overruns (ring buffer full):                      │ │
│  │     ethtool -S eth0 | grep rx_fifo                                          │ │
│  │  DIAGNOSE: Check current qdisc (queuing discipline):                         │ │
│  │     tc qdisc show dev eth0                                                  │ │
│  │  # Look for "fq_codel" or "cake" — if you see "pfifo_fast" or "mq",         │ │
│  │  # you're running the default FIFO queue with bufferbloat risk!              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Reading /proc/net/dev and ethtool -S — The Raw Truth

Before Prometheus existed, there was /proc/net/dev. Understanding these raw kernel counters gives you the ground truth — they're what node_exporter reads, and they can't lie:

DECODING /proc/net/dev — Raw Interface Statistics
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  cat /proc/net/dev                                                              │
│                                                                               │
│  Inter-|   Receive                                                |  Transmit  │
│   face |bytes    packets errs drop fifo frame compressed multicast|bytes    ...│
│    eth0:245893015 5230123 0    0    0    0     0          12543   |11928371 ...│
│    eth1:  1234567   12345 0    12   0    0     0              0   | 1234567 ...│
│                                                                               │
│  COLUMN-BY-COLUMN (Receive side):                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  bytes:       Total bytes received (includes all headers). Good for       │ │
│  │               bandwidth calculation. Counter (only increases).             │ │
│  │  packets:     Total packets received.  packets / bytes ≈ avg packet size.  │ │
│  │  errs:        CRC errors, framing errors — PHYSICAL LAYER ISSUE.           │ │
│  │               Should be 0. If not: check cable, switch port, duplex.       │ │
│  │  drop:        Kernel ran out of buffer space. Packets received by NIC      │ │
│  │               but couldn't be copied to kernel. Should be 0.                │ │
│  │  fifo:        FIFO overruns — NIC ring buffer full. Kernel not reading     │ │
│  │               packets fast enough. Increase ring buffer or spread IRQs.    │ │
│  │  frame:       Frame alignment errors. NIC received a partial/damaged       │ │
│  │               frame. Physical layer issue. Should be 0.                    │ │
│  │  compressed:   PPP/SLIP compressed packets. Legacy. Almost always 0.        │ │
│  │  multicast:    Multicast packets received. Useful for IGMP debugging.       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ethtool -S eth0 — DETAILED NIC COUNTERS:                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  rx_crc_errors:      CRC mismatches → bad cable, EMI, switch port issue    │ │
│  │  rx_missed_errors:   NIC ran out of RX descriptors → driver or HW limit    │ │
│  │  rx_fifo_errors:     Ring buffer overrun → same as fifo in /proc/net/dev   │ │
│  │  rx_length_errors:   Packet too long or too short → MTU mismatch           │ │
│  │  tx_heartbeat_errors: TX timeout — driver/NIC hardware failure             │ │
│  │  rx_long_byte_count: Total good bytes (without bad packets) — BEST for     │ │
│  │                       bandwidth calculation (excludes errored frames).      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  QUICK DIAGNOSIS:                                                               │
│  • errs + drop + fifo > 0 → network problem (hardware or kernel scheduling)    │
│  • Only drop > 0 → kernel buffer exhaustion (increase net.core.rmem_max)       │
│  • Only fifo > 0 → ring buffer too small (ethtool -G to increase)              │
│  • Only errs > 0 → physical layer (cable, switch, interference)               │
│  • ALL zero → network is healthy at the interface level (doesn't guarantee     │
│    no application-level issues, but rules out NIC/hardware problems)           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

29.3 Tools for Network Observability

Each tool covers a different scope — from per-packet deep dives to fleet-wide service maps. The key is knowing which tool to reach for at 3 AM:

ToolScopeWhat It ShowsOverheadBest For
tcpdumpPer-packetFull packet capture + headersHigh (CPU per captured pkt)Ad-hoc deep dives. "Is the SYN reaching the server?"
WiresharkPer-packetFull protocol analysis + graphsNone (offline analysis)Protocol debugging. "Why is the TLS handshake failing?"
ss / netstatPer-hostSocket state, TCP stats, timersNegligibleConnection state check. "How many TIME_WAIT?"
node_exporterPer-hostNIC counters, netstat metricsVery lowPrometheus monitoring. Always-on metrics.
VPC Flow LogsPer-flow (sampled)src/dst IP, port, proto, action (ACCEPT/REJECT)Cloud-native (~$0.50/GB)Security audit. "Who talked to the DB from outside the VPC?"
Cilium HubblePer-packet, per-flowService map, policy audit, L7 visibilityVery low (eBPF)K8s network observability. No sidecars needed.
Prometheus + GrafanaFleet-wideDashboards, alerts, trend analysisLowUSE/RED method applied to network. Long-term trends.
Jaeger / ZipkinPer-requestDistributed trace waterfallMedium (~1% sampling overhead)Microservice latency debugging. "Where is the 500ms going?"
nmapNetwork scanOpen ports, service versions, OS detectionHigh (active probing)Service discovery, security audit, inventory.

Prometheus + node_exporter — Always-On Host Metrics

This is the foundation. node_exporter exposes ~1,000+ metrics from /proc and /sys. The network-specific ones are critical:

PROMETHEUS NETWORK METRICS — Key Queries
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PROMETHEUS — Essential Network Queries You Should Have Bookmarked              │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ Bandwidth ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total{iface="eth0"}[5m])                  │ │
│  │  rate(node_network_transmit_bytes_total{iface="eth0"}[5m])                 │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ Errors & Drops ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  rate(node_network_receive_errors_total[5m])    # Should be ZERO          │ │
│  │  rate(node_network_receive_drop_total[5m])       # Should be ZERO          │ │
│  │  rate(node_network_receive_fifo_total[5m])       # Overruns — ring buffer  │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ TCP Health ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  rate(node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs[5m]) / rate(node_netstat_Tcp_OutSegs[5m])│
│  │  # Retransmit ratio — alert if > 0.02 (2%)                                  │
│  │  node_sockstat_TCP_tw                    # TIME_WAIT count                  │
│  │  node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit  # Utilization │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ Saturation — USE Method ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Utilization: rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total[5m]) / bandwidth_cap    │
│  │  Saturation: rate(node_network_receive_drop_total[5m])  # > 0 = saturated   │
│  │  Errors:     rate(node_network_receive_errors_total[5m]) # > 0 = problems   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

VPC Flow Logs — Who Talked to Whom?

VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about every IP flow in your cloud VPC. They're the definitive answer to "who talked to whom, when, and was it allowed?" They're sampled (not every packet) and delivered to CloudWatch/S3/BigQuery:

VPC FLOW LOGS — Anatomy of a Flow Record
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AWS VPC FLOW LOG RECORD (Version 5)                                            │
│                                                                               │
│  version account-id interface-id srcaddr dstaddr srcport dstport protocol      │
│  packets bytes start end action log-status                                      │
│                                                                               │
│  EXAMPLE (ACCEPT flow — SSH allowed by security group):                         │
│  5 123456789012 eni-0a1b2c3d 10.0.1.50 10.0.2.80 54321 22 6                   │
│  15 2340 1623456789 1623456791 ACCEPT OK                                        │
│                                                                               │
│  EXAMPLE (REJECT flow — blocked by NACL):                                       │
│  5 123456789012 eni-0a1b2c3d 203.0.113.5 10.0.2.80 12345 3306 6               │
│  3 180 1623456789 1623456791 REJECT OK                                          │
│                                                                               │
│  QUERY WITH ATHENA (SQL — find rejected connections to DB):                     │
│  SELECT srcaddr, srcport, COUNT(*) as attempts                                  │
│  FROM vpc_flow_logs                                                             │
│  WHERE action = 'REJECT' AND dstport = 3306                                     │
│    AND window_start > now() - interval '24' hour                                │
│  GROUP BY srcaddr, srcport                                                      │
│  ORDER BY attempts DESC                                                         │
│  LIMIT 20                                                                       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ GOTCHA — nmap and Cloud Abuse Detection

Running nmap -sV -p 1-65535 10.0.1.50 against cloud infrastructure without explicit permission will trigger abuse detection and may get your account suspended. AWS, GCP, and Azure all monitor for port scanning patterns. Always: (1) Use nmap only in approved lab environments, (2) Scan your own resources only, (3) Get written approval before scanning production, (4) Consider using cloud-native tools (VPC Reachability Analyzer, Network Intelligence Center) instead.

Grafana Dashboards — Visualizing Network Health

Prometheus collects the data; Grafana makes it visible. For network observability, these dashboards are essential:

Grafana DashboardIDWhat It ShowsKey Panels
Node Exporter Full1860Complete host health: CPU, memory, disk, networkNetwork traffic per interface, errors/drops, TCP stats, conntrack
Node Exporter Network11159Focused network view per nodeBandwidth (rx/tx), packets/sec, errors, drops, TCP retransmit ratio
Kubernetes / Networking14314K8s cluster-level network viewPod network rx/tx, DNS query rate/latency, kube-proxy metrics
Cilium Metrics16611Cilium-specific eBPF metricsPolicy drops, endpoint status, eBPF map utilization, datapath latency
USE Method — NetworkCustomUtilization/Saturation/Errors per interfacePanel per USE metric, red thresholds at configured limits

Grafana provisioning tip: Store dashboards as JSON in Git (Infrastructure as Code). Use Grafana's dashboard provisioning to auto-load them on startup. Never rely on manually created dashboards that can be lost.

iperf3 — Active Network Performance Testing

Passive monitoring tells you what's happening. Active testing with iperf3 tells you what your network is capable of. Use it to establish baselines, validate upgrades, and prove the network isn't the bottleneck:

iperf3 — Network Throughput Testing
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  iperf3 — ACTIVE NETWORK PERFORMANCE TESTING                                    │
│                                                                               │
│  BASIC TCP THROUGHPUT TEST:                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # Server (on target machine):                                             │ │
│  │  iperf3 -s                                                                 │ │
│  │                                                                            │ │
│  │  # Client (from source machine):                                            │ │
│  │  iperf3 -c 10.0.1.50 -t 30 -P 4                                            │ │
│  │  # -t 30: run for 30 seconds. -P 4: 4 parallel streams                     │ │
│  │                                                                            │ │
│  │  OUTPUT:                                                                    │ │
│  │  [ ID] Interval           Transfer     Bandwidth       Retr                │ │
│  │  [  4]   0.00-30.00  sec  3.52 GBytes  1.01 Gbits/sec  42  sender         │ │
│  │  [  4]   0.00-30.00  sec  3.51 GBytes  1.00 Gbits/sec      receiver       │ │
│  │  # Retr: 42 retransmits in 30s — indicates some packet loss                │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  UDP TEST (fixed bandwidth — finds packet loss):                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  iperf3 -c 10.0.1.50 -u -b 1G -t 30                                       │ │
│  │  # -u: UDP mode. -b 1G: target 1 Gbps.                                     │ │
│  │  OUTPUT:                                                                    │ │
│  │  [ ID] Interval           Transfer     Bitrate         Jitter    Lost/Total│ │
│  │  [  5]   0.00-30.00  sec  3.58 GBytes  1.02 Gbits/sec  0.023 ms  0/2540000│ │
│  │  # 0 lost = clean 1Gbps link. Any loss = capacity issue or congestion.     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WHEN TO USE iperf3:                                                            │
│  • After network changes (upgrade, migration) → validate throughput            │
│  • When users report slowness → prove/disprove network is the bottleneck       │
│  • Capacity planning → establish baseline throughput between AZs/regions       │
│  • MTU verification → test with different packet sizes to find MTU issues      │
│  • Cross-AZ latency: iperf3 -c cross_az_ip → check bandwidth vs same-AZ       │
│                                                                               │
│  CLOUD CAUTION: iperf3 generates significant traffic. Don't run it during      │
│  peak hours. Cross-region iperf3 can be expensive (egress charges). Use short   │
│  tests (-t 10) for diagnostics, longer tests (-t 30) for baselines.            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Network Telemetry Standards — sFlow, NetFlow, IPFIX

Before Prometheus and eBPF, there were network telemetry protocols. Understanding these is critical for working with physical network hardware (switches, routers) and hybrid environments:

StandardCreated ByHow It WorksSamplingWhat You GetBest For
sFlowInMon (industry standard, RFC 3176)Hardware ASIC samples 1/N packets, sends header + counters to collectorStatistically sampled (e.g., 1:1000)Packet headers, interface counters, flow samplesData center switches, high-throughput links (10Gbps+)
NetFlow v5/v9Cisco (proprietary)Router maintains flow cache, exports records when flow ends or timer expiresSampled or full (configurable)5-tuple + bytes, packets, start/end time per flowTraffic accounting, billing, capacity planning
IPFIXIETF (RFC 7011, based on NetFlow v9)Template-based flow export. Extensible via IANA-registered Information ElementsConfigurable samplingRich: 5-tuple + 500+ possible fields (L7 info, app ID, latency)Multi-vendor environments, modern observability pipelines

sFlow vs cloud flow logs: sFlow works at the hardware switch/router level — it's what your top-of-rack switch exports. VPC Flow Logs are the cloud's equivalent but captured at the hypervisor. At massive scale (100Gbps+), hardware sampling (sFlow) is the only feasible approach — you can't capture every packet in software. Modern observability platforms (Kentik, ElastiFlow) ingest sFlow/IPFIX and present it alongside Prometheus metrics.

Managed vs Self-Hosted Observability — The Build vs Buy Decision

At some point, you'll face the decision: self-host Prometheus/Grafana/Loki/Jaeger, or pay for a managed service. Here's the honest comparison:

AspectSelf-Hosted (Prometheus/Grafana/Loki)Managed (Grafana Cloud/Datadog/Honeycomb)
Cost (small, < 50 nodes)$0 (open source) + $50-200/mo server$15-45 per host/month → $750-2,250/mo
Cost (large, 500+ nodes)$1,000-3,000/mo (servers + storage + SRE time)$5,000-15,000+/mo (volume discounts)
RetentionYou control it. 13 months? Yes. Downsample old data.Varies by plan. Often 15-30 days default. Pay extra for longer.
High CardinalityPrometheus struggles above ~10M active series. Thanos/Mimir needed.Designed for it. Datadog handles billions of custom metrics.
Multi-ClusterThanos/Cortex/Mimir required for global view. Complex to operate.Built-in. Single pane of glass across regions.
AlertingAlertManager — powerful but configuration is YAML-only. GitOps-friendly.GUI-based. Easier for non-SREs. Harder to version control.
Long-Term CostFixed (server cost). Scales with your infra, not your metric count.Variable. Grows with every new metric and host.
Best ForTeams with SRE bandwidth, cost-sensitive, compliance requirementsTeams that want to focus on product, not observability infra

Loki for network logs: If you're self-hosting, Loki (from Grafana Labs) is the Prometheus-compatible log aggregator. It indexes only labels (metadata), not full-text — which means it's cheap to run. For network logs (flow logs, iptables logs, Cilium Hubble exports), Loki is a natural fit because network logs are structured and label-heavy (src_ip, dst_port, verdict). Query example: {job="vpc_flow_logs"} |~ "REJECT" | json | dstport=3306.

29.4 LAB: Network Observability

🛠️ Network Observability Lab — 10 Hands-On Exercises
1

Set Up Prometheus + node_exporter + Grafana

# Start node_exporter (binary, no config needed)
wget https://github.com/prometheus/node_exporter/releases/download/v1.8.0/node_exporter-1.8.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar xzf node_exporter-*.tar.gz
./node_exporter-*/node_exporter --web.listen-address=":9100" &

# Verify metrics are exposed
curl http://localhost:9100/metrics | grep node_network_receive_bytes

# Configure Prometheus to scrape it (prometheus.yml)
cat <<EOF >> prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'node'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9100']
EOF

# Start Prometheus and Grafana
docker run -d --name prometheus -p 9090:9090 -v $PWD/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml prom/prometheus
docker run -d --name grafana -p 3000:3000 grafana/grafana

# Import Node Exporter Full dashboard (ID: 1860) in Grafana
# Navigate to http://localhost:3000 → Dashboards → Import → 1860
2

Query Network Metrics with PromQL

# Bandwidth per interface (5-minute average)
rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total[5m])

# Find interfaces with receive errors (should be empty!)
rate(node_network_receive_errors_total[5m]) > 0

# TCP retransmit ratio
rate(node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs[5m]) / rate(node_netstat_Tcp_OutSegs[5m])

# Conntrack utilization percentage
(node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit) * 100

# Generate some traffic, then check
curl -s http://example.com > /dev/null
# Now watch the metrics update in Prometheus UI: http://localhost:9090
3

Enable VPC Flow Logs and Query with Athena (AWS)

# 1. In AWS Console → VPC → Your VPC → Flow Logs → Create Flow Log
#    Destination: S3 bucket, Format: Parquet (for Athena), Max aggregation: 1 min
# 2. Create Athena table pointing to your S3 bucket:
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS vpc_flow_logs (
  version int, account string, interface_id string,
  srcaddr string, dstaddr string, srcport int, dstport int,
  protocol int, packets bigint, bytes bigint,
  window_start bigint, window_end bigint,
  action string, log_status string
)
PARTITIONED BY (dt string)
ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY ' '
LOCATION 's3://your-flow-log-bucket/AWSLogs/';

# 3. Load partitions
MSCK REPAIR TABLE vpc_flow_logs;

# 4. Find REJECTED traffic to port 3306 (MySQL)
SELECT srcaddr, srcport, COUNT(*) as reject_count
FROM vpc_flow_logs
WHERE action = 'REJECT' AND dstport = 3306
  AND dt = '2026-06-21'
GROUP BY srcaddr, srcport
ORDER BY reject_count DESC
LIMIT 20;

# 5. Top talkers by bytes transferred
SELECT srcaddr, dstaddr,
  SUM(bytes) as total_bytes,
  COUNT(*) as flow_count
FROM vpc_flow_logs
WHERE dt = '2026-06-21'
GROUP BY srcaddr, dstaddr
ORDER BY total_bytes DESC
LIMIT 10;
4

Deploy Hubble in a Cilium K8s Cluster

# Prerequisite: Cilium installed on K8s (see Ch28 lab)
# Check Cilium status
cilium status --wait

# Enable Hubble (if not already)
cilium hubble enable --ui

# Port-forward Hubble UI
cilium hubble ui &
# Open http://localhost:12000 — you'll see the Service Map!

# Observe live flows (CLI)
cilium hubble observe

# Filter for dropped flows (NetworkPolicy violations)
cilium hubble observe --verdict DROPPED

# Filter for traffic to a specific pod
cilium hubble observe --to-pod default/nginx-7b9f8c-abc12

# See L7 HTTP details
cilium hubble observe --protocol http

# Export flows as JSON for analysis
cilium hubble observe --output json | jq '.'
5

Ad-Hoc Deep Dive with tcpdump + Wireshark

# Capture 100 packets on eth0, write to file
tcpdump -i eth0 -c 100 -w capture.pcap

# Capture only TCP SYN packets (connection attempts)
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'

# Capture traffic to/from a specific host
tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.0.1.50

# Capture traffic on a specific port
tcpdump -i eth0 port 443

# Capture traffic between two hosts on port 80
tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.0.1.50 and host 10.0.2.80 and port 80

# Show retransmitted packets (seq numbers repeat)
tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'tcp[13] & 8 != 0'

# Count retransmits in capture
tcpdump -r capture.pcap 'tcp[13] & 8 != 0' | wc -l

# Open in Wireshark: File → Open → capture.pcap
# Use "Statistics → IO Graph" for traffic spikes
# Use "Statistics → TCP Stream Graphs → Time-Sequence" for retransmits
6

Check Network Health from Inside a Container

# In your anihpj Django container, check what the app sees:
docker exec -it <container_id> bash

# Socket summary — what connections exist?
ss -tulnp

# TCP statistics
ss -ti
# Look for: retrans (retransmits), rto (retrans timeout), cwnd (congestion window)

# Check interface stats inside the container
cat /proc/net/dev
# Columns: bytes, packets, errs, drop, fifo, frame, compressed, multicast

# Test DNS resolution latency
time dig google.com +short
# In Python (Django shell):
# import socket, time
# start = time.time(); socket.getaddrinfo("google.com", 443); print(f"DNS: {time.time()-start:.3f}s")

# Test TCP latency to DB
time nc -zv dbhost 5432
# Or from Python:
# import time, socket; s = socket.socket()
# start = time.time(); s.connect(("dbhost", 5432)); print(f"TCP: {time.time()-start:.3f}s")

# If DNS is slow (>50ms): Check CoreDNS pods, enable NodeLocal DNSCache
# If TCP connect is slow (>10ms): Check network path, TCP retransmits
7

Build a Custom Grafana Network Dashboard

# In Grafana (http://localhost:3000), create a new dashboard:
# + → Dashboard → Add new panel

# PANEL 1 — Bandwidth per Interface (Time Series)
# Query: rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total[5m]) * 8
# Legend: {{"{{"}}instance{{"}}"}} - {{"{{"}}device{{"}}"}} rx
# Unit: bits/sec (SI)
# Add second query for transmit: rate(node_network_transmit_bytes_total[5m]) * 8

# PANEL 2 — TCP Retransmit Rate (Stat with Threshold)
# Query: rate(node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs[5m]) / rate(node_netstat_Tcp_OutSegs[5m]) * 100
# Unit: percent (0.0-1.0)
# Thresholds: Green=0-0.1, Yellow=0.1-1, Orange=1-2, Red=2-100
# This gives you a single number — red means investigate NOW.

# PANEL 3 — Interface Drops & Errors (Stat)
# Query: rate(node_network_receive_drop_total[5m])
# Threshold: Green=0, Red=>0 (any drops = red)
# Repeat for: rx_errors, tx_errors, rx_fifo (overruns)

# PANEL 4 — Conntrack Utilization (Gauge)
# Query: (node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit) * 100
# Thresholds: Green=0-50, Yellow=50-80, Red=80-100

# PANEL 5 — TIME_WAIT Sockets (Time Series)
# Query: node_sockstat_TCP_tw
# Threshold: Show as line with horizontal marker at 20000

# Save dashboard, export to JSON, and commit to Git!
# Dashboard → Settings → JSON Model → Copy → Save in infrastructure repo
8

Set Up AlertManager for Network Alerts

# 1. Create alerting rules for network health (network_alerts.yml):
cat <<'EOF' > network_alerts.yml
groups:
  - name: network_alerts
    rules:
      - alert: NetworkReceiveErrors
        expr: rate(node_network_receive_errors_total[5m]) > 0
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: critical
          category: network
        annotations:
          summary: "NIC receive errors on {{"{{"}} $labels.instance {{"}}"}} ({{"{{"}} $labels.device {{"}}"}})"
          description: "Interface has {{"{{"}} $value {{"}}"}} errors/sec. Check cable, switch port, duplex settings."

      - alert: NetworkReceiveDrops
        expr: rate(node_network_receive_drop_total[5m]) > 0
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: critical
          category: network
        annotations:
          summary: "NIC receive drops on {{"{{"}} $labels.instance {{"}}"}}"
          description: "Ring buffer full. Increase with: ethtool -G {{"{{"}} $labels.device {{"}}"}} rx 4096"

      - alert: TcpRetransmitHigh
        expr: (rate(node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs[5m]) / rate(node_netstat_Tcp_OutSegs[5m])) > 0.02
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
          category: network
        annotations:
          summary: "High TCP retransmit rate on {{"{{"}} $labels.instance {{"}}"}}"
          description: "Retransmit ratio is {{"{{"}} $value | humanizePercentage {{"}}"}}. Check for packet loss."

      - alert: ConntrackHigh
        expr: (node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit) > 0.8
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
          category: network
        annotations:
          summary: "Conntrack table > 80% on {{"{{"}} $labels.instance {{"}}"}}"
          description: "Conntrack at {{"{{"}} $value | humanizePercentage {{"}}"}}. Increase nf_conntrack_max or switch to Cilium."

      - alert: DnsHighLatency
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) > 0.1
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
          category: network
        annotations:
          summary: "DNS p99 latency > 100ms"
          description: "CoreDNS latency is {{"{{"}} $value {{"}}"}}s. Check CoreDNS pod count and upstream resolver."
EOF

# 2. Configure AlertManager to receive alerts (alertmanager.yml):
cat <<'EOF' > alertmanager.yml
route:
  group_by: ['alertname', 'category']
  group_wait: 10s
  group_interval: 10s
  repeat_interval: 1h
  receiver: 'slack-network'
receivers:
  - name: 'slack-network'
    slack_configs:
      - api_url: 'https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/WEBHOOK/URL'
        channel: '#network-alerts'
        title: '{{"{{"}} .CommonLabels.severity | toUpper {{"}}"}}: {{"{{"}} .CommonAnnotations.summary {{"}}"}}'
        text: '{{"{{"}} range .Alerts {{"}}"}}• {{"{{"}} .Annotations.description {{"}}"}}\n{{"{{"}} end {{"}}"}}'
EOF

# 3. Start AlertManager
docker run -d --name alertmanager -p 9093:9093 \
  -v $PWD/alertmanager.yml:/etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml \
  prom/alertmanager

# 4. Update prometheus.yml to include alert rules
cat <<EOF >> prometheus.yml
rule_files:
  - 'network_alerts.yml'
alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:
        - targets: ['localhost:9093']
EOF

# 5. Trigger a test alert and verify delivery
# Open AlertManager UI: http://localhost:9093 → Alerts
# Prometheus UI: http://localhost:9090 → Alerts → Should show all 5 rules

SLO-Based Alerting — Burn Rate Alerts

# SLO: 99.9% of HTTP requests succeed in < 500ms over 30 days
# Error budget: 0.1% = 43 minutes of downtime per 30 days
# Burn rate: how fast you're consuming your error budget

# BURN RATE ALERT RULES (slo_alerts.yml):
cat <<'EOF' > slo_alerts.yml
groups:
  - name: slo_alerts
    rules:
      # Error rate over 5 minutes
      - record: job:http_errors:rate5m
        expr: |
          rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])
          /
          rate(http_requests_total[5m])

      # Burn rate: 14.4x error budget (alerts in 1 hour for severe burn)
      # For 99.9% SLO, 14.4x burn = 1.44% error rate sustained for 1 hour
      - alert: SLOBurnRateHigh
        expr: job:http_errors:rate5m > 0.0144
        for: 1h
        labels:
          severity: critical
          category: slo
        annotations:
          summary: "Error budget burning at 14.4x rate"
          description: "At current rate, 30-day error budget will be exhausted in ~2 hours"

      # Burn rate: 3x error budget (alerts in 1 hour for moderate burn)
      - alert: SLOBurnRateWarning
        expr: job:http_errors:rate5m > 0.003
        for: 1h
        labels:
          severity: warning
          category: slo
        annotations:
          summary: "Error budget burning at 3x rate"
          description: "At current rate, 30-day error budget will be exhausted in ~10 hours"

      # Network-specific SLO: TCP retransmit budget
      # If > 0.2% retransmits sustained (burning through "network health" budget)
      - alert: NetworkSLOBurn
        expr: |
          (rate(node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs[1h])
          /
          rate(node_netstat_Tcp_OutSegs[1h])) > 0.002
        for: 30m
        labels:
          severity: warning
          category: slo
        annotations:
          summary: "Network SLO burning — retransmits above 0.2% for 30 minutes"
          description: "TCP retransmit ratio: {{"{{"}} $value | humanizePercentage {{"}}"}}. Investigate packet loss."
EOF

# Load the SLO alerts into Prometheus
# Add slo_alerts.yml to prometheus.yml rule_files
# Reload Prometheus: kill -HUP $(pidof prometheus) or POST /-/reload

# VERIFY: Generate errors to trigger burn rate
# In a loop, hit a 500-returning endpoint while watching the alert fire
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s http://your-app/error-endpoint > /dev/null
  sleep 0.5
done
# After 1 hour of sustained errors, SLOBurnRateHigh should fire

Network Chaos Testing — Break It on Purpose

# 💀 WARNING: Only run in lab/staging environments!

# CHAOS 1: Introduce packet loss with tc (traffic control)
# Add 5% packet loss to eth0 — simulate a degraded link
tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem loss 5%
# Now check: TCP retransmit rate should spike → alert should fire
# Run your observability stack and watch the dashboards respond
# CLEANUP:
tc qdisc del dev eth0 root

# CHAOS 2: Add network latency
tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 50ms 10ms distribution normal
# Now all packets have 50ms ± 10ms added latency
# Watch: HTTP p99 latency rises, iperf3 throughput drops
tc qdisc del dev eth0 root

# CHAOS 3: Introduce packet corruption (simulate bad cable)
tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem corrupt 1%
# 1% of packets are randomly corrupted → CRC errors on receiver
# Watch: interface errors (rx_errors) increase on receiver
tc qdisc del dev eth0 root

# CHAOS 4: Bandwidth cap (simulate congested link)
tc qdisc add dev eth0 root tbf rate 10mbit burst 32kbit latency 400ms
# Cap bandwidth to 10 Mbps — any app needing more will feel it
# Watch: iperf3 throughput drops to ~10 Mbps, queuing delay spikes
tc qdisc del dev eth0 root

# CHAOS 5: DNS failure (block port 53 with iptables)
iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --dport 53 -j DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 53 -j DROP
# All DNS queries now fail. Watch: SERVFAIL rate spikes in CoreDNS metrics
# Applications that cache DNS (most do) will survive briefly then fail
# CLEANUP:
iptables -D OUTPUT -p udp --dport 53 -j DROP
iptables -D OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 53 -j DROP

# ═══ AFTER EACH CHAOS TEST ═══
# 1. Verify your alerts fired (AlertManager UI or Slack)
# 2. Check Grafana dashboards reflected the chaos
# 3. Time how long from chaos start → alert fire → alert acknowledge
# 4. Document: Did the right alert fire? Was the description actionable?
# 5. IMPROVE your alerts based on what you learned

📡Interface HealthDrops, errors, and overruns should ALWAYS be zero. If they're not, you have hardware, driver, or kernel scheduling problems.
🔄TCP RetransmitsThe #1 leading indicator. < 0.1% = healthy. 1-2% = degraded. > 3% = incident. Each retransmit costs ~200ms.
🟡SRE SLO MappingAvailability → LB health. Latency → TCP retransmits + DNS. Data loss → drops + retransmits. Alert on leading, not lagging.
📊Prometheus + Grafananode_exporter exposes NIC counters. PromQL: rate(), topk(), histogram_quantile(). Dashboard 1860 for full node view.
☁️VPC Flow LogsPer-flow metadata (src/dst/port/action). Query with Athena/BigQuery. Catch security violations, find top talkers.
🔍HubbleK8s-native observability: service map, L7 visibility, policy audit. Zero overhead (eBPF). No sidecars. Instant value.
🧰Debug Toolkittcpdump for packet capture. Wireshark for protocol analysis. ss for socket state. nmap for scanning (with permission!).
🔗Distributed TracingW3C traceparent headers propagate trace IDs across services. Jaeger visualizes spans. Correlate slow traces with TCP retransmits to find network root cause.
🌐DNS HealthDNS latency p99 > 100ms = resolution bottleneck. Monitor CoreDNS query rate, failure rate, cache hits. Enable NodeLocal DNSCache for lower latency.
🔴HTTP RED MethodRate (rps), Errors (5xx%), Duration (p99 latency). Map directly to SLOs. High TTFB = network. High total duration with low TTFB = app.
⚡iperf3 TestingActive throughput testing: TCP mode for bandwidth, UDP mode for packet loss. Validate upgrades, prove network isn't the bottleneck.
⏱️Latency ComponentsSerialization (packet/bandwidth), Propagation (distance/speed of light), Queuing (buffer depth), Processing (iptables/eBPF overhead).
🛁BufferbloatLarge NIC buffers cause latency spikes under load. Fix with fq_codel qdisc + BBR congestion control. Check with tc qdisc show.
📡Telemetry StandardssFlow (hardware sampling, 100Gbps+), NetFlow/IPFIX (router flow export). Cloud equivalent: VPC Flow Logs. Hardware equivalent: sFlow.
🏗️Build vs BuySelf-host: Prometheus + Grafana + Loki ($0 + servers). Managed: Datadog/Grafana Cloud ($15-45/host/mo). Choose based on SRE bandwidth.
🚨AlertManager + SLOs5 critical network alerts. Burn rate alerting: 14.4x burn = 1h to exhaust error budget. Chaos test to verify alerts fire correctly.

🔑 Chapter 29 Key Takeaways

  1. Observability is metrics + logs + traces working together. Metrics tell you something is wrong. Logs tell you what's affected. Traces tell you exactly where the delay or error is. Build all three.
  2. TCP retransmit rate is your #1 leading indicator. If you monitor only one network metric, make it this. It predicts packet loss, congestion, and user-facing slowness before 5xx spikes appear.
  3. Interface drops and errors should ALWAYS be zero. Any non-zero value means packets are being lost at the NIC level. The ring buffer is too small, the kernel is too slow, or the hardware is failing.
  4. Alert on LEADING indicators, not lagging. Retransmits, drops, and queue depth give you 5-15 minutes of warning. 5xx rates and user reports are lagging — the damage is already done.
  5. Choose the right tool for the scope. tcpdump for point-in-time deep dives. Prometheus for always-on trends. VPC Flow Logs for security audit. Hubble for K8s network observability. Each solves a different problem at a different cost.
  6. DNS is the silent performance killer. DNS latency p99 > 100ms makes every microservice call feel slow. Monitor CoreDNS query rate, failure rate, and cache hit rate. Enable NodeLocal DNSCache to keep DNS local to each node.
  7. Distributed traces complete the observability picture. Traces show you which network hop is slow. W3C Trace Context headers propagate trace IDs. Correlate slow Jaeger spans with Prometheus TCP retransmit metrics to determine network vs. application root cause.
  8. Understand latency components to root-cause slowness. Serialization (packet size ÷ bandwidth), Propagation (distance ÷ speed of light), Queuing (buffer depth ÷ drain rate), Processing (iptables/eBPF overhead). Only queuing is configurable — bufferbloat is the #1 cause of mysterious latency.
  9. Cardinality is Prometheus's kryptonite. Each unique label combination creates a new time series. Never put request paths, user IDs, or connection 5-tuples as metric labels. Use Loki for high-cardinality network logs and Jaeger for traces.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 29

📐Observability
The ability to understand a system's internal state from its external outputs. Goes beyond monitoring (which only tracks known unknowns) to enable exploration of unknown unknowns. Three pillars: metrics, logs, traces.
📊Metrics (Pillar 1)
Time-series numerical data collected at intervals. Counters (monotonic, e.g., total bytes), Gauges (instant value, e.g., connections), Histograms (distribution, e.g., latency p50/p95/p99). Cheap, always-on, stored efficiently by TSDBs.
📄Flow Logs (Pillar 2)
Metadata about network flows: source/destination IP and port, protocol, bytes transferred, action (ACCEPT/REJECT). Captured at the hypervisor or network interface level. VPC Flow Logs (AWS/GCP) are the standard cloud implementation.
🔗Distributed Tracing (Pillar 3)
Tracks a single request as it propagates through multiple services. Each service adds a span (start time, duration, tags). Spans are linked by trace ID. Tools: Jaeger, Zipkin, Honeycomb. Overhead: ~1% with sampling.
🔄TCP Retransmit
When TCP sends a segment but doesn't receive an ACK within the retransmission timeout (RTO, minimum 200ms), it resends the segment. Retransmit rate = retransmitted segments / total segments sent. > 2% indicates packet loss.
📡node_exporter
A Prometheus exporter that exposes Linux kernel metrics from /proc and /sys. Provides per-NIC counters (bytes, packets, errors, drops), TCP stats (retransmits, connections by state), and conntrack utilization. Runs on every host.
🟡USE Method
Utilization, Saturation, Errors — a methodology for analyzing system performance. Applied to network: Utilization = bandwidth used/capacity. Saturation = drops/overruns. Errors = CRC, carrier, collision errors.
🟢RED Method
Rate, Errors, Duration — a methodology for monitoring services. Applied to network: Rate = requests/sec. Errors = 5xx rate. Duration = latency distribution (p50/p95/p99). Used for SLO definitions.

📝 Chapter 29 — Practice Questions

Q1
What are the three pillars of observability and what does each provide for networking?
Show Answer
Answer

Metrics: Always-on numerical data — bandwidth, packets/sec, errors, drops, TCP retransmits. Collected by Prometheus from node_exporter. Logs: Flow-level metadata — who talked to whom, when, and was it allowed (ACCEPT/REJECT). VPC Flow Logs, Hubble flow logs. Traces: Per-request journey across services — shows exactly where latency or errors occur. Jaeger/Zipkin instrument HTTP/gRPC calls with trace IDs. The three pillars work together: alert on metrics → investigate with logs → trace outliers.

Q2
Why is TCP retransmit rate the #1 leading indicator for network health? What thresholds define healthy, degraded, and critical?
Show Answer
Answer

TCP retransmits directly measure packet loss. Every retransmit means a segment was lost and took ~200ms (RTO min) to be resent. Healthy: < 0.1% (normal congestion). Elevated: 0.1-1% (investigate NIC drops, switch errors). Degraded: 1-2% (users notice — throughput drops from congestion window reduction). Critical: > 3% (severe loss — incident). Unlike 5xx rates (lagging), retransmit rate rises BEFORE applications fail. Monitor with: rate(node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs[5m]) / rate(node_netstat_Tcp_OutSegs[5m]).

Q3
Compare VPC Flow Logs, Cilium Hubble, and tcpdump for network debugging. When would you use each?
Show Answer
Answer

VPC Flow Logs: Cloud-native, always-on, per-flow metadata (5-tuple + action), sampled. Best for: security audit (who accessed the DB?), top talkers, long-term trends. Limitation: sampled (not every packet), 1-10 min aggregation delay. Hubble: K8s-native, packet-level, automatic service map, L7 visibility (HTTP/gRPC/Kafka), NetworkPolicy drop logging. Best for: K8s troubleshooting, policy debugging, service dependency mapping. tcpdump: Full packet capture, maximum detail. Best for: point-in-time deep dives ("is the SYN reaching the server?"), protocol debugging, capture-and-analyze. High CPU overhead, not for continuous use.

Q4
Explain the USE and RED methodologies and how they apply to network monitoring.
Show Answer
Answer

USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) — for resources (interfaces, links). Utilization: bandwidth used / capacity (e.g., 800Mbps / 1Gbps = 80%). Saturation: queue depth, drops, overruns (> 0 = saturated). Errors: CRC errors, carrier changes. If any of the three is non-zero, the resource is a bottleneck. RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) — for services (HTTP endpoints, DNS). Rate: requests per second. Errors: failed requests (5xx rate). Duration: latency distribution (p50, p95, p99). RED metrics directly map to SLOs: e.g., "99.9% of requests succeed in < 500ms over a 30-day window."

Q5
What does "conntrack table full" mean and how do you monitor for it?
Show Answer
Answer

The conntrack table tracks all active network connections for NAT and stateful firewalling. It has a fixed size (default ~65K entries). When it fills up, new connections are DROPPED with "nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet" in dmesg. Monitor: node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit. Alert when > 80%. Fix: increase nf_conntrack_max via sysctl, reduce TIME_WAIT duration, or switch to Cilium (eBPF LRU hash auto-evicts old entries — no fixed limit). Happens commonly in NAT gateways and Kubernetes nodes with high connection churn.

Q6
Why should interface drops and errors always be zero? What do non-zero values indicate?
Show Answer
Answer

Interface drops (rx_dropped): The NIC ring buffer is full because the kernel isn't reading packets fast enough. Fix: increase ring buffer (ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096), reduce interrupt moderation, or spread IRQs across more CPUs. Interface errors (rx_errors): Physical layer problems — bad cable, duplex mismatch, CRC errors from electromagnetic interference. Fix: replace cable, verify switch port config, check auto-negotiation. Both should be zero in a healthy system. Even a single drop means data loss that TCP must recover from (via retransmit). Monitor: rate(node_network_receive_drop_total[5m]) > 0.

Q7
How does Cilium Hubble's observability differ from traditional monitoring approaches? What makes it powerful?
Show Answer
Answer

Hubble is eBPF-based — it observes every packet at the kernel level with near-zero overhead. No sidecars (unlike Istio monitoring), no code changes, no per-pod DaemonSets. Automatically builds service dependency maps. Shows NetworkPolicy drops (which rule blocked this flow?). Provides L7 visibility (HTTP methods, gRPC calls, Kafka topics, DNS queries) without parsing pcap files. Flow logs include source/destination identity (not just IP), verdict (FORWARDED/DROPPED/ERROR), and L7 info. Traditional monitoring: needs sidecars (CPU/RAM cost), only HTTP/gRPC, no policy drop visibility, requires manual service map construction.

Q8
You're on call and users report "the app is slow." Walk through your observability-based debugging approach.
Show Answer
Answer

Step 1 — Check Prometheus dashboards: Look at HTTP latency (p99), 5xx rate, TCP retransmit rate. If retransmit rate > 1%, network is the likely cause. Step 2 — Narrow scope: Check interface drops and errors on all nodes. Find the node(s) showing drops. Step 3 — Check DNS: DNS latency p99 > 100ms? DNS failure rate > 1%? Slow DNS makes every connection slow. Step 4 — Flow logs: Query VPC Flow Logs or Hubble to see which service pairs are affected. REJECT flows? Security group change. Step 5 — Trace: If metrics point to a specific service, trace one slow request through Jaeger to find the bottleneck (network hop, DB query, external API). Step 6 — Deep dive: If still unclear, tcpdump on the affected nodes, open in Wireshark, look for retransmits, RSTs, or TLS handshake failures.

Q9
How does distributed tracing help with network debugging? Explain W3C Trace Context and how to correlate traces with network metrics.
Show Answer
Answer

Distributed tracing assigns a unique trace ID to each request and propagates it via W3C Trace Context headers (traceparent, tracestate) through HTTP/gRPC. Each service creates a span with timing data. For network debugging: (1) Find slow traces (p99 > SLO) in Jaeger UI. (2) Identify the span with the longest duration — is it at the service mesh hop? The DB connection? The external API? (3) Cross-reference the slow service's host with Prometheus TCP retransmit metrics. If retransmits are elevated on that host, the network is the cause. (4) If the span is slow but retransmits are normal, it's an application-level bottleneck (CPU, GC, DB query). (5) Cilium Hubble can correlate flow logs with trace IDs, showing both the network path (packets) and application path (spans) for the same request — the ultimate observability integration.

Q10
You suspect network performance degradation after a cloud migration. How would you use iperf3 to validate throughput and prove/disprove the network is the root cause?
Show Answer
Answer

Step 1 — Establish baseline: Run iperf3 TCP test between two instances in the same AZ: iperf3 -c -t 30. Record throughput (should be near NIC speed, e.g., 10 Gbps). Step 2 — Cross-AZ test: Run between different AZs: iperf3 -c -t 30. Record throughput — if significantly lower than same-AZ, there's cross-AZ congestion or rate limiting. Step 3 — UDP loss test: iperf3 -c -u -b 1G -t 30. Look at the Lost/Total column. Any packet loss > 0 = problem. Step 4 — Compare before/after: If throughput dropped from 9.5 Gbps to 2 Gbps, the network IS the bottleneck. If throughput is consistently 9+ Gbps but the app is still slow, the problem is NOT the network — investigate application (CPU, memory, DB queries). Step 5 — MTU test: iperf3 -c -M 1500 vs iperf3 -c -M 9000. If jumbo frames don't improve throughput, the path doesn't support them.

D3
TCP Health Check: On a production-like server, run "ss -ti" and parse the output. Find connections with retrans > 0, retrans timeout (rto) > 200ms, or congestion window (cwnd) < 10. Document which services these connections belong to.

tcpdump Investigation: Generate traffic (curl a website), capture it with tcpdump, open in Wireshark. Use "Statistics → TCP Stream Graphs → Time-Sequence (Stevens)" to visualize the TCP sequence numbers. Find any retransmissions.
D5

D10

🔴 Part 9: TroubleshootingChapters 30-32

Chapter 30: The Systematic Network Debugging Methodology

When the pager goes off at 3 AM, you don't have time to guess. Systematic network debugging is the difference between a 5-minute fix and a 5-hour incident. This chapter gives you a repeatable, layer-by-layer approach that starts at the physical link and works up to the application — so you never waste time debugging DNS when the cable is unplugged. You'll learn the decision tree, the first-5-minutes checklist, how to read error messages precisely (Connection Refused ≠ Connection Timeout), and how to definitively separate network problems from application problems.

🛠️ How to Implement This — Your Network Debugging Toolkit

This chapter teaches a repeatable methodology you can apply immediately to the anihpj/jobpost Django application deployed on Kubernetes:

StepWhat to DoReal anihpj ExampleTool/Command
1. PrepDeploy the triage script to every node and containerCOPY network-triage.sh /usr/local/bin/ in Dockerfile; bake into AMIscp, Dockerfile, Packer
2. L1 MonitorAlert on any interface errors or link flapsnode_network_receive_errors_total > 0 → PagerDuty alertPrometheus + node_exporter
3. L4 VerifyHealth endpoint returns 200 + service port is listeningcurl localhost:8000/health from Django containerK8s readiness probe, curl
4. Incident RunbookFirst 5 minutes: follow the layer-by-layer decision treeSSH → netcheck → identify broken layer → fix or escalate~/network-triage.sh
5. Post-MortemDocument which layer broke, how it was detected, time to fix"L4: kube-proxy iptables rules missing. Fixed by restarting kube-proxy. TTD: 4 min."Incident management tool

Key mindset shift: Stop guessing. Start at the bottom. Every incident becomes a structured investigation instead of frantic trial-and-error. The decision tree in 30.1 is your new best friend — print it, bookmark it, memorize it.

30.1 The Layered Approach — Always Start at the Bottom

The OSI model isn't just theory — it's your debugging playbook. Always start at Layer 1 and work UP. Why? Because a Layer 3 problem could actually be a Layer 2 problem masquerading. If the link is down, no amount of routing table checking will help. Here's the systematic approach:

THE NETWORK DEBUGGING FLOWCHART — Start Here Every Time
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SYSTEMATIC NETWORK DEBUGGING — Layer by Layer                                  │
│                                                                               │
│  START → L1 (Physical): Is the link up?                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ip link show eth0                                                        │ │
│  │  eth0:  mtu 1500 ...                    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ✓ UP + LOWER_UP → Link is active. Proceed to L2.                         │ │
│  │  ✗ NO CARRIER or DOWN → Cable unplugged, switch port down, driver issue.  │ │
│  │    Fix: ip link set eth0 up. Check cable. Check switch port (lldpctl).    │ │
│  │    Check dmesg for "link down" events.                                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│       ↓                                                                        │
│  L2 (Data Link): Can ARP resolve?                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ip neigh show                                                            │ │
│  │  10.0.1.1 dev eth0 lladdr 0a:1b:2c:3d:4e:5f REACHABLE                    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ✓ REACHABLE or STALE → L2 works. Proceed to L3.                          │ │
│  │  ✗ FAILED or INCOMPLETE → ARP isn't getting responses.                     │ │
│  │    Check: Are you on the right VLAN? Is the switch forwarding?             │ │
│  │    Try: arping -I eth0 10.0.1.1 (active ARP probe)                        │ │
│  │    For VXLAN/overlay: check if VTEP can reach remote VTEP.                 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│       ↓                                                                        │
│  L3 (Network): Can I route/ping?                                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ip route show                                                            │ │
│  │  default via 10.0.1.1 dev eth0                                            │ │
│  │  10.0.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.1.50              │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ping -c 3 8.8.8.8                                                        │ │
│  │  ✓ Replies → L3 works upstream. Proceed to L4.                            │ │
│  │  ✗ No replies → Routing issue. Check: ip route get 8.8.8.8.               │ │
│  │    traceroute 8.8.8.8 — where do packets stop? That hop is the problem.   │ │
│  │    For cloud: check security group/NACL outbound rules.                    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│       ↓                                                                        │
│  L4 (Transport): Is the port open?                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  nc -zv 10.0.1.50 8000                                                    │ │
│  │  ✓ "Connection to 10.0.1.50 8000 port [tcp] succeeded!" → L4 works.       │ │
│  │  ✗ "Connection refused" → Port closed. Service not listening.              │ │
│  │  ✗ "Connection timed out" → Firewall blocking. Check iptables/SG.          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ss -tlnp | grep 8000  (check what's actually listening)                  │ │
│  │  iptables -L -n -v | grep 8000 (check firewall rules)                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│       ↓                                                                        │
│  L7 (Application): Is the app responding correctly?                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  curl -v http://10.0.1.50:8000/health                                     │ │
│  │  ✓ HTTP 200 OK → Full stack works.                                        │ │
│  │  ✗ HTTP 502 → Upstream failure (DB, downstream service).                   │ │
│  │  ✗ HTTP 503 → Service unavailable (overloaded, starting up).              │ │
│  │  ✗ TLS error → Certificate issue. Check expiry, CN/SAN match.             │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  GOLDEN RULE: A problem at Layer N could be caused by Layer N-1. Always        │
│  verify that the layers BELOW your suspected problem are working first.        │
│  Never skip layers — you'll waste time debugging the wrong thing.              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
REAL INCIDENT DECISION TREE — "Users Can't Reach jobpost"
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  🚨 INCIDENT: "Users can't reach the jobpost app at jobpost.anihpj.com"        │
│                                                                               │
│  Q1: Is the link up?                                                           │
│  ├── ip link show eth0 → state UP?                                             │
│  │   └── NO → Check cable, switch port, NIC driver. dmesg | grep -i link.     │
│  │                                                                             │
│  Q2: Can you ARP the gateway?                                                  │
│  ├── ip neigh show → gateway MAC present?                                      │
│  │   └── NO → L2 issue. Check VLAN config, switch MAC table, physical cable.  │
│  │                                                                             │
│  Q3: Can you ping an external IP?                                              │
│  ├── ping 8.8.8.8 → replies?                                                   │
│  │   └── NO → Check routing: ip route get 8.8.8.8                              │
│  │       └── No default route? → ip route add default via 10.0.1.1             │
│  │       └── Route exists but no replies? → Check SG/NACL outbound rules,      │
│  │           NAT gateway, Internet Gateway route table.                         │
│  │                                                                             │
│  Q4: Is DNS resolving?                                                         │
│  ├── dig jobpost.anihpj.com → returns correct IP?                              │
│  │   └── NO → Check CoreDNS pods, kube-dns service, /etc/resolv.conf           │
│  │       └── dig +trace → find where resolution breaks                         │
│  │       └── Check: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns            │
│  │                                                                             │
│  Q5: Can you reach the K8s Service port?                                       │
│  ├── nc -zv <LB_IP> 443 → connection succeeded?                               │
│  │   └── NO → Service type wrong (ClusterIP vs LoadBalancer)?                  │
│  │       └── kubectl get svc jobpost → check TYPE and PORT(S)                  │
│  │       └── kubectl get endpoints jobpost → are there backend pods?           │
│  │                                                                             │
│  Q6: Are the pods healthy?                                                     │
│  ├── kubectl get pods -l app=jobpost → all Running and READY?                  │
│  │   └── NO → kubectl describe pod → check Events, readiness probe failures   │
│  │       └── kubectl logs → check app startup errors, DB connection errors     │
│  │                                                                             │
│  Q7: Is the app responding correctly?                                          │
│  ├── curl -v http://localhost:8000/health → 200 OK?                            │
│  │   └── 502 → Upstream issue (DB, Redis, downstream service).                 │
│  │   └── 503 → App overloaded or starting up. Check resource limits.           │
│  │   └── 504 → Upstream timeout. Check DB query times, increase proxy timeout.  │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

L1 Deep Dive — ethtool, Link Negotiation, and MTU

ip link tells you if the link is UP. ethtool tells you WHY — and reveals problems invisible to ip:

ethtool — The L1 Diagnostic Swiss Army Knife
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ethtool — DECODE YOUR PHYSICAL LAYER                                          │
│                                                                               │
│  ethtool eth0                                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Settings for eth0:                                                       │ │
│  │    Supported ports: [ TP ]                                                │ │
│  │    Supported link modes: 10baseT/Half 10baseT/Full ... 1000baseT/Full    │ │
│  │    Speed: 1000Mb/s           ← CURRENT SPEED                              │ │
│  │    Duplex: Full              ← Full duplex = can TX and RX simultaneously │ │
│  │    Auto-negotiation: on      ← Auto-negotiates best speed with switch     │ │
│  │    Link detected: yes        ← PHYSICAL link is good (cable plugged in)   │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  WHAT TO LOOK FOR:                                                         │ │
│  │  • Speed: 1000 or 10000? Should match switch port. Mismatch = problem.    │ │
│  │  • Duplex: HALF = ANCIENT. Full duplex is required for modern networks.   │ │
│  │    Half-duplex at 1Gbps = collision domain = massive packet loss.          │ │
│  │  • Auto-negotiation: Should be ON. If OFF, speed/duplex manually set =     │ │
│  │    potential mismatch with switch. Switch must match EXACTLY.             │ │
│  │  • Link detected: NO = cable unplugged, switch port down, or bad cable.   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ethtool -S eth0 — DETAILED NIC STATISTICS:                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  rx_crc_errors: 0        ← CRC mismatches (cable/EMI). Should be 0.       │ │
