│  │  rx_missed_errors: 0     ← NIC hardware can't keep up. Should be 0.       │ │
│  │  rx_fifo_errors: 0       ← Ring buffer overrun. Should be 0.              │ │
│  │  rx_long_length_errors: 0← MTU mismatch — packet too large. Should be 0.  │ │
│  │  tx_aborted_errors: 0    ← TX aborted (driver/hardware). Should be 0.     │ │
│  │  tx_carrier_errors: 0    ← Carrier sense errors (duplex mismatch).         │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  NON-ZERO = HARDWARE PROBLEM:                                              │ │
│  │  • crc_errors > 0 → Bad cable, EMI, loose connector, failing NIC.         │ │
│  │  • fifo_errors > 0 → Ring buffer too small. Fix: ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096. │ │
│  │  • long_length_errors > 0 → MTU mismatch. Fix: ip link set eth0 mtu 9000. │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

MTU Issues — The Silent Packet Killer

MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) mismatch is one of the hardest networking problems to diagnose because it produces intermittent failures — small packets work, large packets don't. Understanding MTU is critical for cloud and overlay networks:

MTU — When Packet Size Breaks the Network
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MTU MISMATCH — The Intermittent Connectivity Killer                            │
│                                                                               │
│  STANDARD MTU VALUES:                                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Ethernet (standard):     1500 bytes                                      │ │
│  │  Jumbo Frames:            9000 bytes (data center, storage networks)       │ │
│  │  VXLAN overlay (AWS):     Typically 9001 (to accommodate 1500 inside)      │ │
│  │  GENEVE overlay (GCP):    Typically 1460 (auto-tuned)                     │ │
│  │  WireGuard:               1420 (80 bytes overhead for crypto)              │ │
│  │  PPPoE:                   1492 (8 bytes for PPP header)                    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  CLOUD TYPICAL:                                                             │ │
│  │  AWS EC2: 9001 (supports jumbo). But if your VPC has VPN/Direct Connect   │ │
│  │  with MTU 1500, fragmentation breaks TCP. Set consistent MTU everywhere.   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  THE PROBLEM:                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Your server sends 1500-byte packets with DF (Don't Fragment) bit set.    │ │
│  │  Path has a hop with MTU 1450. Router SHOULD send "Fragmentation Needed"  │ │
│  │  ICMP message. BUT: many firewalls/clouds BLOCK ICMP.                     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  RESULT: Large packets silently dropped. Small packets work. SSH works.   │ │
│  │  HTTPS pages partially load (HTML loads, CSS doesn't). Database queries   │ │
│  │  with large result sets fail. MADENINGLY INTERMITTENT.                    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  SYMPTOMS:                                                                  │ │
│  │  • "curl works but git clone hangs" (git uses larger packets)              │ │
│  │  • "SSH works but scp times out"                                           │ │
│  │  • "Website loads but images are broken"                                   │ │
│  │  • "MySQL queries work but large result sets time out"                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  THE FIX:                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1. FIND THE PATH MTU:                                                     │ │
│  │     ping -M do -s 1472 8.8.8.8  # DF set, 1472+28=1500 total             │ │
│  │     # If it fails, reduce -s until it works. 1472=MTU 1500, 8972=MTU 9000 │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  2. SET MTU:                                                                │ │
│  │     ip link set dev eth0 mtu 1500                                          │ │
│  │     # Or for jumbo: ip link set dev eth0 mtu 9000                          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  3. FOR K8s/CILIUM (VXLAN/GENEVE overlay):                                  │ │
│  │     # Overlay adds 50 bytes. If physical MTU is 1500, overlay MTU is 1450. │ │
│  │     cilium config set mtu 1450                                             │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  4. ENABLE TCP MSS CLAMPING (band-aid for broken paths):                   │ │
│  │     iptables -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN \                   │ │
│  │       -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu                                        │ │
│  │     # Forces TCP to use smaller segments even if MTU is larger.             │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

L2 Diagnostics — Bridges, VLANs, and MAC Tables

In container and cloud environments, L2 is often abstracted away — until it breaks. Knowing how to inspect bridges and VLANs saves hours when containers on the same host can't reach each other:

L2 DIAGNOSTICS — Bridges, VLANs, and the MAC Table
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  L2 DEBUGGING IN CONTAINER ENVIRONMENTS                                         │
│                                                                               │
│  INSPECT THE BRIDGE (Docker's docker0, K8s cni0):                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  brctl show                                                               │ │
│  │  bridge name     bridge id               STP enabled     interfaces       │ │
│  │  cni0            8000.0a1b2c3d4e5f       no              veth12345         │ │
│  │                                                           veth67890         │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  bridge fdb show br cni0   ← Forwarding Database (MAC table)              │ │
│  │  0a:1b:2c:3d:4e:5f dev veth12345 master cni0                              │ │
│  │  1a:2b:3c:4d:5e:6f dev veth67890 master cni0                              │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Find which veth belongs to which container:                            │ │
│  │  # Inside container: cat /sys/class/net/eth0/iflink → gives peer ifindex  │ │
│  │  # On host: ip link show | grep "^:" → find veth name            │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  VLANS:                                                                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ip link show eth0.100   ← VLAN subinterface                              │ │
│  │  ip -d link show eth0.100 | grep vlan  → VLAN ID: 100                     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Check if VLAN is trunked correctly:                                     │ │
│  │  cat /proc/net/vlan/eth0.100                                              │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Cloud: VPC subnets are L3, not L2. No VLANs visible to you.            │ │
│  │  # But overlay networks (VXLAN/GENEVE) ARE L2-over-L3 tunnels:            │ │
│  │  bridge fdb show dev vxlan0  ← VXLAN FDB (VTEP mapping)                   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

30.2 The First 5 Minutes — What to Check for ANY Network Issue

When an alert fires or a user reports "it's down," you need a muscle-memory checklist — commands you can type without thinking. Here's the 10-command first response that covers 90% of network incidents:

THE 10-COMMAND FIRST RESPONSE — Copy This to Your .bashrc
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  🩺 NETWORK TRIAGE — Muslce-Memory Commands for ANY Incident                   │
│                                                                               │
│  # 1 — Are interfaces UP?                                                      │
│  ip -br link show                                                              │
│  # Look for: UP in the flags. "DOWN" = cable or config issue.                  │
│                                                                               │
│  # 2 — Are IPs assigned correctly?                                              │
│  ip -br addr show                                                              │
│  # Look for: expected IP on expected interface. Missing IP = DHCP or config.   │
│                                                                               │
│  # 3 — Is there a default route?                                                │
│  ip route show default                                                         │
│  # Missing default route = can't reach anything outside local subnet.          │
│  # Add with: ip route add default via 10.0.1.1                                 │
│                                                                               │
│  # 4 — Is ARP resolving?                                                        │
│  ip neigh show                                                                 │
│  # Look for: REACHABLE or STALE. FAILED = L2 problem.                          │
│                                                                               │
│  # 5 — Are services listening on expected ports?                                │
│  ss -tlnp                                                                      │
│  # Shows all TCP listeners. Missing port = service not started or crashed.     │
│  # Add -u for UDP listeners: ss -ulnp                                         │
│                                                                               │
│  # 6 — Can you reach the service locally?                                       │
│  curl -v localhost:8000/health                                                 │
│  # If local works but remote doesn't → firewall, binding to 127.0.0.1 only.    │
│  # Check: ss -tlnp | grep 8000 → does it say 0.0.0.0:8000 or 127.0.0.1:8000? │
│                                                                               │
│  # 7 — Is DNS working?                                                          │
│  dig +short google.com                                                         │
│  dig +short kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local                               │
│  # No response = DNS broken. Check /etc/resolv.conf, CoreDNS pods.             │
│                                                                               │
│  # 8 — Can you reach the outside world?                                         │
│  ping -c 3 8.8.8.8                                                             │
│  # No reply = routing or firewall issue. Try traceroute.                       │
│  curl -v --connect-timeout 5 https://google.com                                │
│                                                                               │
│  # 9 — What does the firewall say?                                              │
│  iptables -L -n -v | head -50                                                  │
│  # Look for DROP rules at the top. Check packet counts on rules.               │
│  # For K8s: iptables -t nat -L -n | grep                              │
│                                                                               │
│  # 10 — What's in the kernel log?                                               │
│  dmesg -T | tail -50                                                           │
│  # Look for: "link down", "nf_conntrack: table full", "Out of memory".         │
│  journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager                                        │
│                                                                               │
│  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════  │
│  SAVE AS ~/network-triage.sh:                                                   │
│  Run this script the moment you SSH into a troubled host. Copy output to       │
│  the incident channel. You'll look like a hero.                                 │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 Pro Tip: Alias These for Speed

Add to your ~/.bashrc: alias netcheck='ip -br link && ip -br addr && ip route show default && ss -tlnp'. One command, four critical checks. When the pager goes off, you type netcheck and have 80% of the information you need in 2 seconds. Works on every Linux host — no dependencies needed.

tcpdump for Triage — When You Need to SEE the Packets

Sometimes the checklists aren't enough — you need to actually watch what's happening on the wire. tcpdump is your eyes:

tcpdump TRIAGE — Answering the Hard Questions
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  tcpdump — TRIAGE PATTERNS FOR COMMON INCIDENTS                                │
│                                                                               │
│  # "Is traffic even reaching this host?"                                        │
│  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn host 10.0.1.50 and port 8000                             │
│  # If you see SYN packets arriving → network works, app isn't responding.     │
│  # If you see NOTHING → packets aren't reaching this host (firewall/route).   │
│                                                                               │
│  # "Is the app sending RST after SYN?" (ECONNREFUSED diagnosis)               │
│  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-rst) != 0'                │
│  # SYN arriving, RST leaving immediately → service not listening.             │
│  # SYN arriving, SYN-ACK leaving → service is accepting. Check L7 response.   │
│                                                                               │
│  # "Are packets being retransmitted?" (packet loss)                            │
│  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst == 0' -w /tmp/cap.pcap          │
│  # Then open in Wireshark: Statistics → IO Graph.                              │
│  # Or quick check: tcpdump -r cap.pcap -nn | wc -l (high count = bad)        │
│                                                                               │
│  # "Is there a TCP connection at all, or is it blocked?"                       │
│  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn src 10.0.1.50 and dst 10.0.2.80 and 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'
│  # Count SYNs. If 6+ SYNs from same src:dst pair → TCP retransmitting SYN.    │
│  # Means: no response (ETIMEDOUT). Firewall or routing issue.                  │
│                                                                               │
│  # "Is DNS working?" (packet-level verification)                               │
│  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 53                                                   │
│  # Query going out, NO response coming back → DNS server unreachable or        │
│  # firewall blocking UDP 53. Query AND response → DNS works.                   │
│  # DNS over TCP (responses > 512 bytes): tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 53          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

iptables TRACE — Follow a Packet Through the Firewall

When packets are being mysteriously dropped, iptables TRACE shows you exactly which rule in which table is responsible. It's the nuclear option for firewall debugging — use it when nothing else works:

iptables TRACE — See Every Rule a Packet Hits
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  iptables TRACE — FOLLOW A PACKET THROUGH THE FIREWALL                          │
│                                                                               │
│  # 1. Add TRACE rules for the traffic you're debugging:                        │
│  iptables -t raw -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 8000 -j TRACE                   │
│  iptables -t raw -A OUTPUT -p tcp --sport 8000 -j TRACE                       │
│                                                                               │
│  # 2. Watch the kernel log in real-time:                                       │
│  tail -f /var/log/kern.log | grep TRACE                                       │
│  # OR: journalctl -k -f | grep TRACE                                          │
│                                                                               │
│  # 3. Generate test traffic:                                                    │
│  curl http://10.0.1.50:8000                                                    │
│                                                                               │
│  # 4. You'll see output like:                                                   │
│  TRACE: raw:PREROUTING:policy:2 IN=eth0 OUT= MAC=... SRC=10.0.1.100 ...      │
│  TRACE: mangle:PREROUTING:policy:1 IN=eth0 OUT= ...                           │
│  TRACE: nat:PREROUTING:policy:1 IN=eth0 OUT= ...                               │
│  TRACE: filter:FORWARD:rule:5 IN=eth0 OUT=eth1 ... ← DROPPED HERE!            │
│                                                                               │
│  # The LAST line before the trace stops = which rule DROPPED the packet.       │
│  # If trace stops after nat:PREROUTING → DNAT rule has no matching target.    │
│  # If trace stops after filter:FORWARD → FORWARD chain is blocking.           │
│                                                                               │
│  # 5. CLEANUP (IMPORTANT — TRACE is verbose!)                                  │
│  iptables -t raw -D PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 8000 -j TRACE                   │
│  iptables -t raw -D OUTPUT -p tcp --sport 8000 -j TRACE                       │
│                                                                               │
│  ⚠️  TRACE generates a kernel log line for EVERY matching packet. In high-     │
│     traffic scenarios, this can overwhelm your system. Always use specific     │
│     filters (by port, IP, or protocol) and DELETE the rule when done!          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

K8s Network Triage — Quick Commands for Container Incidents

When the incident is in Kubernetes, you need a different set of commands — ones that work through kubectl and understand the overlay network:

What to CheckCommandWhat It Reveals
Pod network statuskubectl get pods -o widePod IP, node assignment. Is the pod even running?
Service endpointskubectl get endpoints <svc>Are there healthy backend IPs? Empty = selector mismatch or no ready pods.
NetworkPolicykubectl get networkpolicies -AAny policies that might be blocking traffic?
CNI statuskubectl get pods -n kube-system \| grep calico\|cilium\|weave\|flannelIs the CNI plugin running on every node?
Test pod connectivitykubectl run debug --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bashSpawn a debug pod with net tools. curl/nc/ping/dig from inside the cluster.
Service DNSkubectl exec -it <pod> -- nslookup <svc>Does the service DNS resolve inside the cluster?
iptables rules (kube-proxy)iptables -t nat -L -n \| grep <svc_ip>Are NAT rules correct for the service? Missing = kube-proxy issue.
Node-to-pod pathip route on node, check pod CIDR routesCan the node route to pod IPs? Missing route = CNI problem.

ICMP Deep Dive — Why "Ping Works" Doesn't Mean "Network Works"

ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is the network's diagnostic protocol — but it's often blocked, rate-limited, or deprioritized. Understanding ICMP types and codes is essential because ICMP is how the network tells you what's wrong:

ICMP — The Network's Diagnostic Language
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ICMP TYPES & CODES — What Your Network Is Trying to Tell You                   │
│                                                                               │
│  TYPE 0  — Echo Reply         (ping response)                                  │
│  TYPE 3  — Destination Unreachable ← CRITICAL FOR DEBUGGING                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Code 0: Net Unreachable      → No route to the destination network.      │ │
│  │  Code 1: Host Unreachable     → Network exists but host not found.        │ │
│  │  Code 2: Protocol Unreachable → TCP/UDP port filtered by firewall.        │ │
│  │  Code 3: Port Unreachable     → NOTHING listening (UDP equivalent of RST) │ │
│  │  Code 4: Frag Needed (DF set) → MTU too large! Router says "fragment me!" │ │
│  │                                 BUT: many firewalls BLOCK this → MTU       │ │
│  │                                 black hole. This is why ping -M do exists. │ │
│  │  Code 13: Admin Prohibited    → Firewall explicitly blocked (policy)      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  TYPE 8  — Echo Request        (ping request)                                  │
│  TYPE 11 — Time Exceeded        (traceroute uses this!)                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Code 0: TTL exceeded in transit → traceroute hop! Each router decrements │ │
│  │          TTL by 1. When TTL=0, router sends Type 11 back to source.       │ │
│  │          traceroute exploits this: sends packets with TTL=1,2,3,...       │ │
│  │          Each hop sends back Type 11 → you map the route!                 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WHY "PING WORKS" IS NOT SUFFICIENT:                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • ICMP is often ALLOWED even when TCP is BLOCKED (firewall hole-punch)   │ │
│  │  • Cloud LBs may respond to ping but drop TCP 443 if target group dead    │ │
│  │  • ICMP is LOW PRIORITY — routers drop ICMP under load before TCP         │ │
│  │  • Some firewalls rate-limit ICMP (1/sec). Ping looks fine, but it's not. │ │
│  │  • "Ping" only tests L3. Tells you NOTHING about L4 (ports) or L7 (app).  │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  BETTER L3 TEST (when ICMP is blocked):                                     │ │
│  │  nc -zv  22   ← TCP to SSH port. If it connects, L3 works.          │ │
│  │  curl -v --connect-timeout 3 http://:80 ← HTTP as L3-L7 test.       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WATCH ICMP IN REAL-TIME:                                                       │
│  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp                                                      │
│  # Then ping from another machine. You'll see Type 8 (request) + Type 0 (reply)│
│  # If you only see Type 8 but NO Type 0 → ICMP reply is being dropped.         │
│  # If you see Type 3 Code 4 → MTU problem! Fix with MSS clamping or set MTU.   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Advanced tcpdump — Reading Sequence Numbers, Windows, and Flags

Basic tcpdump shows you packets. Advanced tcpdump shows you why the connection is slow or broken. Understanding TCP header fields in captures is the difference between "I see packets" and "I know what's wrong":

tcpdump ADVANCED — Decode TCP Conversations
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  tcpdump -nn -v — VERBOSE TCP DUMP WITH HEADER DETAILS                          │
│                                                                               │
│  14:32:01.123456 IP 10.0.1.50.54321 > 10.0.2.80.8000: Flags [S],              │
│    seq 3456789012, win 65535, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 123456 ecr 0,   │
│    nop,wscale 7], length 0                                                     │
│                                                                               │
│  FIELD-BY-FIELD DECODING:                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Flags [S]      = SYN (connection start). [S.] = SYN-ACK. [.] = ACK.     │ │
│  │                   [F] = FIN. [R] = RST. [P] = PSH (push data to app).    │ │
│  │  seq 3456789012  = Initial Sequence Number. Used to track data bytes.     │ │
│  │  win 65535       = Receive Window. "How much data I can buffer."          │ │
│  │                   If win drops to 0 → receiver buffer full → flow control.│ │
│  │  mss 1460        = Maximum Segment Size. Largest TCP payload allowed.     │ │
│  │                   mss + 40 (headers) = MTU. mss 1460 → MTU 1500.          │ │
│  │  sackOK          = Selective ACK supported. Better retransmit handling.   │ │
│  │  wscale 7        = Window scaling (multiply win by 2^7=128). Real win:   │ │
│  │                   65535 × 128 = ~8MB. Essential for high-BDP links.       │ │
│  │  length 0        = No data payload (control packet: SYN/FIN/RST/ACK)      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WHAT TO LOOK FOR IN CAPTURES:                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1. RETRANSMISSIONS: Same seq number appears twice → packet was lost.     │ │
│  │     tcpdump -r capture.pcap -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn == 0' |         │ │
│  │       awk '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -d → duplicate seq numbers          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  2. WINDOW ZERO: win 0 → receiver can't keep up. Application bottleneck.  │ │
│  │     tcpdump -r capture.pcap -nn | grep "win 0"                            │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  3. ZERO WINDOW PROBES: After win=0, sender sends 1-byte probes.          │ │
│  │     tcpdump -r capture.pcap -nn | grep "length 1"                         │ │
│  │     → Indicates receiver is severely overloaded.                          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  4. RESETS (RST): Abrupt connection termination.                          │ │
│  │     tcpdump -r capture.pcap -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0'           │ │
│  │     → RST after SYN = port closed. RST during ESTABLISHED = app crash.    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  5. DUPLICATE ACKs: Same ACK number 3+ times → packet loss detected.      │ │
│  │     tcpdump -r capture.pcap -nn | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c |   │ │
│  │       sort -rn | head → find most repeated ACK numbers                   │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  6. MTU/FRAGMENTATION: Look for "frag" in output.                         │ │
│  │     tcpdump -r capture.pcap -nn -v | grep -i frag                         │ │
│  │     → Fragmentation = MTU mismatch or path MTU discovery failure.         │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

30.3 Connection Refused vs Connection Timeout — The Crucial Difference

These two error messages look similar but mean completely different things. Misreading them is the #1 cause of wasted debugging time — engineers chase network problems when the service is simply down, or restart services when the network is blocked:

THREE CONNECTION FAILURES — What They Actually Mean
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THREE WAYS A TCP CONNECTION FAILS — Read the Error Carefully!                  │
│                                                                               │
│  SCENARIO 1: CONNECTION REFUSED (ECONNREFUSED)                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Client                              Server (10.0.1.50:8000)              │ │
│  │  │                                        │                               │ │
│  │  │────── SYN ───────────────────────────→ │  (packet ARRIVES)              │ │
│  │  │←───── RST ─────────────────────────── │  "Nothing listening on :8000"  │ │
│  │  │                                        │                               │ │
│  │  RESULT: Connection refused (curl: (7) Failed to connect ... Connection    │ │
│  │  refused). nc says "Connection refused". ERRNO = ECONNREFUSED.            │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  WHAT THIS MEANS:                                                          │ │
│  │  ✅ THE NETWORK WORKS! The destination host IS reachable.                  │ │
│  │  ✅ The host received your SYN and ACTIVELY REJECTED it (RST).             │ │
│  │  ❌ Nothing is listening on that port.                                     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  FIX: Start the service. Check if it's bound to the right IP (ss -tlnp).  │ │
│  │  Common: Service bound to 127.0.0.1 but you're connecting to the           │ │
│  │  external IP. Fix: bind to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces).                      │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  NEVER debug the network when you see ECONNREFUSED. The network is fine.  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  SCENARIO 2: CONNECTION TIMEOUT (ETIMEDOUT)                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Client                              ??? (10.0.1.50:8000)                 │ │
│  │  │                                        │                               │ │
│  │  │────── SYN ───────────────────────────→ │  (packet SILENTLY DROPPED)     │ │
│  │  │  (wait 1s)                             │                               │ │
│  │  │────── SYN (retransmit) ──────────────→ │  (still nothing)               │ │
│  │  │  (wait 2s)                             │                               │ │
│  │  │────── SYN (retransmit) ──────────────→ │  (still nothing)               │ │
│  │  │  ... eventually after ~130s ...        │                               │ │
│  │  │                                        │                               │ │
│  │  RESULT: Connection timed out (curl: (28) Failed to connect ...           │ │
│  │  Connection timed out). nc says "Connection timed out". ERRNO=ETIMEDOUT.  │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  WHAT THIS MEANS:                                                          │ │
│  │  ❌ Packets are being SILENTLY DROPPED somewhere.                          │ │
│  │  ❌ The destination might be down, unreachable, or firewalled.              │ │
│  │  ❌ YOU NEED TO DEBUG THE NETWORK.                                         │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  POSSIBLE CAUSES:                                                           │ │
│  │  • Security group / NACL blocking the port                                 │ │
│  │  • iptables DROP rule (check: iptables -L -n -v)                          │ │
│  │  • Host is down (check: ping)                                              │ │
│  │  • Wrong IP (DNS returned wrong address)                                   │ │
│  │  • Route doesn't exist (packets go to black hole)                          │ │
│  │  • Cloud NAT gateway not configured for that subnet                        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  SCENARIO 3: NO ROUTE TO HOST (EHOSTUNREACH)                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Kernel can't find ANY route to the destination.                           │ │
│  │  ERRNO = EHOSTUNREACH. Immediate error (no SYN sent at all).               │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  FIX: ip route show. Add a route if missing.                               │ │
│  │  In K8s: pod may be on wrong network, or CNI plugin not configured.        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
SymptomERRNOcurl Outputnc OutputWhat It MeansDebug Path
Connection RefusedECONNREFUSED"Failed to connect... Connection refused""Connection refused"✅ Network OK. Service not listening.ss -tlnp. Check if service is running. Check binding address.
Connection TimeoutETIMEDOUT"Failed to connect... Connection timed out""Connection timed out"❌ Packets dropped silently. Network or firewall.ping → iptables -L → traceroute → check SG/NACL
No Route to HostEHOSTUNREACH"Failed to connect... No route to host""No route to host"❌ Routing table incomplete.ip route show. Add missing route.
Name Resolution FailedEAI_NONAME"Could not resolve host"N/A (nc with IP only)❌ DNS broken.dig. Check /etc/resolv.conf. Check CoreDNS.
⚠️ GOTCHA — The Most Common Misdiagnosis

"Connection refused" actually means the network WORKS. The destination host received your SYN packet and actively rejected it by sending back a RST. This proves: (1) The destination host is reachable, (2) routing works, (3) no firewall is blocking the SYN. Do NOT waste time debugging the network when you see ECONNREFUSED. Check if the service is running, and verify it's listening on the expected IP:port with ss -tlnp | grep <port>. If the service is running but you're getting refused, check that it's bound to 0.0.0.0 (or the specific interface IP), not 127.0.0.1.

TCP State Machine — Reading Connection Health from Socket States

Every TCP connection goes through a lifecycle of states. Understanding what each state means lets you diagnose problems at a glance — without needing tcpdump:

TCP STATE MACHINE — What Socket States Tell You
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TCP STATE MACHINE — Debugging from Socket States                              │
│                                                                               │
│  CLIENT SIDE (active opener)           SERVER SIDE (passive listener)          │
│  ┌────────────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────────┐         │
│  │                            │        │ LISTEN                     │         │
│  │                            │        │   │  ← Normal. Waiting.    │         │
│  │                            │        │   ▼                        │         │
│  │                            │  SYN → │ SYN_RECV                  │         │
│  │ SYN_SENT                   │        │   │  ← Half-open.          │         │
│  │   │  ← Normal (brief).     │← SYN+ACK│   │  Many = SYN flood.    │         │
│  │   │  Stuck here = no route │        │   ▼                        │         │
│  │   │  or firewall drop.     │  ACK → │ ESTABLISHED               │         │
│  │   ▼                        │        │   │  ← Normal operation.   │         │
│  │ ESTABLISHED                │        │   │                         │         │
│  │   │  ← Data flowing.       │        │   │                         │         │
│  │   │                        │        │   │                         │         │
│  │   ▼ (active close)         │  FIN → │ CLOSE_WAIT                │         │
│  │ FIN_WAIT1                  │        │   │  ← App hasn't closed   │         │
│  │   │                        │← ACK   │   │  yet. Many = app bug.  │         │
│  │   ▼                        │        │   ▼                        │         │
│  │ FIN_WAIT2                  │← FIN   │ LAST_ACK                  │         │
│  │   │  ← Waiting for peer    │        │   │  ← Normal (brief).     │         │
│  │   │  to close.             │  ACK → │                           │         │
│  │   ▼                        │        │                           │         │
│  │ TIME_WAIT                  │        │                           │         │
│  │   │  ← 60-120s. Normal.    │        │                           │         │
│  │   │  > 20,000 = port       │        │                           │         │
│  │   │  exhaustion!           │        │                           │         │
│  └────────────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────────┘         │
│                                                                               │
│  QUICK DIAGNOSIS WITH ss:                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ss -tan state listening     ← What services are accepting connections?   │ │
│  │  ss -tan state established   ← Active connections (should match expected) │ │
│  │  ss -tan state time-wait     ← Recently closed. > 20K = port exhaustion   │ │
│  │  ss -tan state syn-sent      ← Connections stuck in SYN_SENT = TIMEOUT    │ │
│  │  ss -tan state syn-recv      ← Half-open from clients. Many = SYN flood   │ │
│  │  ss -tan state close-wait    ← Server waiting for app to close(). Many =  │ │
│  │                                application bug (not calling close/finish)  │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  COUNT ALL STATES:                                                         │ │
│  │  ss -tan | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn                   │ │
│  │  # Shows distribution across all TCP states at a glance                    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  RED FLAGS BY STATE:                                                            │
│  • SYN_SENT > 10 → Outbound connections failing. Check firewall/routing.       │
│  • CLOSE_WAIT > 100 → Application not closing connections. Memory leak.       │
│  • TIME_WAIT > 20,000 → Ephemeral port exhaustion imminent.                   │
│  • SYN_RECV > 1,000 without ESTABLISHED → SYN flood attack.                   │
│  • LAST_ACK > 100 → Stuck connections. Application hanging on shutdown.       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

strace for Network Debugging — See Every Socket Call

When you've eliminated the network and the service is running but still failing, strace shows you exactly what system calls the application is making — including every socket(), connect(), bind(), send(), and recv() call:

strace — Application-Level Network Debugging
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  strace — WATCH THE APPLICATION'S NETWORK SYSTEM CALLS                          │
│                                                                               │
│  # Attach to a running process (Django on port 8000):                           │
│  strace -f -e trace=network -p $(pgrep -f "python manage.py")                  │
│  # -f: follow child processes. -e trace=network: only network syscalls.        │
│                                                                               │
│  # Start a process under strace:                                                │
│  strace -f -e trace=network python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000            │
│                                                                               │
│  # WHAT YOU'LL SEE:                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_TCP) = 3      ← Creates socket     │ │
│  │  bind(3, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(8000), sin_addr=inet_addr    │ │
│  │       ("0.0.0.0")}, 16) = 0           ← Binds to port 8000               │ │
│  │  listen(3, 128) = 0                    ← Starts listening (backlog=128)   │ │
│  │  accept(3, ...) = 4                    ← Blocks waiting for connection    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # WHEN A CONNECTION ARRIVES:                                              │ │
│  │  accept(3, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(54321),                     │ │
│  │       sin_addr=inet_addr("10.0.1.100")}, [16]) = 4  ← Client connected!  │ │
│  │  recvfrom(4, "GET /health HTTP/1.1\r\n...", 8192, 0, ...) = 156         │ │
│  │  sendto(4, "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n...", 89, 0, ...) = 89                   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  DEBUGGING SCENARIOS WITH strace:                                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  SCENARIO 1: "Service won't start — port already in use"                   │ │
│  │  bind(3, ..., 8000) = -1 EADDRINUSE                                       │ │
│  │  → Port 8000 is occupied. Fix: change port or kill the other process.     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  SCENARIO 2: "Service starts but never accepts connections"                │ │
│  │  bind(...) = 0, listen(...) = 0, but NO accept() calls.                    │ │
│  │  → App is stuck in initialization. Check startup code, DB connection.     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  SCENARIO 3: "Outbound DB connection failing"                               │ │
│  │  connect(5, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(5432),                     │ │
│  │       sin_addr=inet_addr("10.0.2.80")}, 16) = -1 ECONNREFUSED             │ │
│  │  → PostgreSQL is rejecting. Check if it's running, bound to right IP.     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  SCENARIO 4: "App hangs after connecting"                                   │ │
│  │  connect(...) = 0, sendto(...) = OK, then recvfrom() blocks FOREVER.       │ │
│  │  → Server received request but never responds. DB query stuck?             │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  SCENARIO 5: "DNS resolution failures"                                      │ │
│  │  connect(5, ..., 0.0.0.0) = -1  ← App is connecting to 0.0.0.0!          │ │
│  │  → DNS returned 0.0.0.0 or resolution failed silently.                    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  FILTER FOR SPECIFIC SYSCALLS:                                              │ │
│  │  strace -f -e trace=connect,sendto,recvfrom -p PID  # Connection I/O only │ │
│  │  strace -f -e trace=bind,listen,accept -p PID    # Server setup only      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

30.4 Separating "Network Problem" from "Application Problem"

The most important question in any incident: Is the network broken, or is the application broken? Answering this incorrectly wastes hours. Here's a definitive test matrix:

NETWORK vs APPLICATION — The Definitive Test Matrix
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  IS IT THE NETWORK OR THE APP? — Definitive Tests                               │
│                                                                               │
│  TEST 1: Local vs Remote                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # From the SAME machine (SSH into the server):                           │ │
│  │  curl -v http://localhost:8000/health                                     │ │
│  │  ✓ WORKS → App is running. Problem is network/firewall.                    │ │
│  │  ✗ FAILS → App is down. Check logs, check port binding.                   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  TEST 2: Same Pod vs Different Pod                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # From a different pod in the SAME namespace:                            │ │
│  │  kubectl exec -it debug-pod -- curl -v http://jobpost:8000/health         │ │
│  │  ✓ WORKS → App is reachable within the cluster. Problem is external.       │ │
│  │  ✗ FAILS → Likely NetworkPolicy blocking, or CNI issue.                   │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # From a pod in a DIFFERENT namespace:                                    │ │
│  │  kubectl exec -it debug-pod -n other-ns -- curl jobpost.default:8000      │ │
│  │  ✓ WORKS → Cross-namespace networking OK.                                  │ │
│  │  ✗ FAILS → NetworkPolicy may be namespace-restricted.                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  TEST 3: Ping vs Port                                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ping -c 3 10.0.1.50           # L3 test                                   │ │
│  │  nc -zv 10.0.1.50 8000         # L4 test                                   │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ✓ Ping OK + nc FAILS → L3 works. Problem is L4+: port blocked/service    │ │
│  │     down. Check firewall rules, check if service is running.               │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ✗ Ping FAILS → L3 problem. Check routes, SG outbound, host status.        │ │
│  │     If ping fails but you KNOW the host is up: ICMP blocked.              │ │
│  │     Use nc -zv to a known-open port (22) as alternative L3 test.          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  TEST 4: DNS vs Direct IP                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  curl -v http://jobpost:8000/health     # Uses DNS                        │ │
│  │  curl -v http://10.0.1.50:8000/health   # Bypasses DNS                    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ✓ DNS works + Direct IP fails → The service IP is wrong or routing broken│ │
│  │  ✗ DNS fails + Direct IP works → DNS problem only. Fix DNS, app is fine.  │ │
│  │  ✓ Both work → Everything is fine. Check L7 response (502/503/504).       │ │
│  │  ✗ Both fail → Service is unreachable regardless of DNS. Network or app.  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  QUICK RULE:                                                                    │
│  If localhost:PORT works → NOT an app problem. Debug network/firewall/DNS.     │
│  If localhost:PORT also fails → App is down. Check ss -tlnp, logs, probes.    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The SRE 5-Minute Network Triage Playbook

As an SRE, you're often the first responder to "the site is down." Before you even fully open your laptop, here's your mental checklist — timed by the minute:

🎯 SRE INCIDENT RESPONSE — 5-Minute Network Triage
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SRE 5-MINUTE NETWORK TRIAGE — Your Mental Playbook                             │
│                                                                               │
│  ⏱️ MINUTE 0-1: SCOPE THE BLAST RADIUS                                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Is it just you? Check from your phone (cellular, not WiFi).
│  │  • Is it one region or all regions? Check cloud status pages.
│  │  • Is it one service or all services? Quick health endpoint check.         │ │
│  │  • kubectl get nodes → any NotReady?                                      │ │
│  │  • RESULT: You know the SCOPE — single pod, single AZ, or global.         │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ⏱️ MINUTE 1-2: LAYER 7 CHECK (fastest to verify — if app says it's healthy,  │
│                the network underneath is probably fine)                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • curl -v https://jobpost.anihpj.com/health → 200 OK?                    │ │
│  │  • If 5xx → check pod logs, DB connection, downstream dependencies.       │ │
│  │  • If timeout → go to L4 check below.                                     │ │
│  │  • kubectl get pods -l app=jobpost → any in CrashLoopBackOff?             │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ⏱️ MINUTE 2-3: LAYER 4 CHECK                                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • nc -zv <LB_IP> 443 → connection succeeded?                              │ │
│  │  • ss -tlnp on the node → is the service listening?                      │ │
│  │  • kubectl get endpoints jobpost → are there healthy backends?            │ │
│  │    If ENDPOINTS is empty → service selector doesn't match any pods.       │ │
│  │    If ENDPOINTS has IPs but not ready → readiness probe failing.         │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ⏱️ MINUTE 3-4: LAYER 3 CHECK                                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • ping 8.8.8.8 → network reachable?                                     │ │
│  │  • traceroute → where do packets stop? That hop = problem.               │ │
│  │  • ip route → is the routing table correct?                              │ │
│  │  • In cloud: check route tables, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway status.   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ⏱️ MINUTE 4-5: DNS CHECK (IT'S ALWAYS DNS — until it's not)                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • dig jobpost.anihpj.com → correct IP?                                  │ │
│  │  • dig +trace → where does resolution break?                             │ │
│  │  • kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50             │ │
│  │  • Check CoreDNS config for forward/upstream issues.                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  SRE GOLDEN RULE: By MINUTE 5, you must know WHICH LAYER is broken.            │
│  Then go DEEP on that layer. Don't flail across layers — focus your effort.    │
│  Announce to the incident channel: "Network triage complete. Problem is at     │
│  Layer 4 — Service endpoints are empty. Investigating why pods are not ready." │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

DNS Debugging Deep Dive — dig +trace and Resolution Chains

When "dig google.com" works but "dig jobpost.anihpj.com" fails, you need to understand the DNS resolution chain — exactly which server is failing and at which step:

DNS RESOLUTION CHAIN — Tracing a Query End-to-End
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DNS RESOLUTION — From Root to Answer                                           │
│                                                                               │
│  dig +trace jobpost.anihpj.com  ← Shows EVERY step of resolution              │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 1: ROOT SERVERS (.)                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Query: "Who handles .com?"                                               │ │
│  │  Response: a.root-servers.net (198.41.0.4) → NS records for .com TLD     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│       ↓                                                                        │
│  STEP 2: TLD SERVERS (.com)                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Query: "Who handles anihpj.com?"                                         │ │
│  │  Response: ns1.digitalocean.com, ns2.digitalocean.com (your registrar's)  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│       ↓                                                                        │
│  STEP 3: AUTHORITATIVE SERVERS (anihpj.com)                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Query: "What's the A record for jobpost.anihpj.com?"                     │ │
│  │  Response: jobpost.anihpj.com. 300 IN A 34.120.45.67                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WHERE RESOLUTION BREAKS (AND HOW TO FIX IT):                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  BREAKS AT STEP 1 → Can't reach root servers. Internet down or firewall.  │ │
│  │  BREAKS AT STEP 2 → TLD responds but your domain's NS not found.          │ │
│  │    → Domain expired? NS records wrong at registrar?                        │ │
│  │  BREAKS AT STEP 3 → Authoritative server unreachable or misconfigured.    │ │
│  │    → Check DNS hosting (Route53, Cloudflare, DigitalOcean).                │ │
│  │  RETURNS WRONG IP → DNS record is stale or incorrect.                      │ │
│  │    → Check TTL. dig jobpost.anihpj.com @8.8.8.8 (bypass local cache).    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  K8S DNS DEBUGGING:                                                             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # Service DNS:                                                            │ │
│  │  dig jobpost.default.svc.cluster.local @10.96.0.10                         │ │
│  │  # 10.96.0.10 = kube-dns ClusterIP. If no response → CoreDNS is down.     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Check CoreDNS config:                                                    │ │
│  │  kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml                      │ │
│  │  # Look for "forward . /etc/resolv.conf" → forwards to node's DNS.        │ │
│  │  # If node's /etc/resolv.conf points to broken DNS → all pods affected.   │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Check CoreDNS logs for errors:                                           │ │
│  │  kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=100 | grep -i err │ │
│  │  # Look for: "SERVFAIL", "i/o timeout", "no such host"                    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Test from inside a pod:                                                  │ │
│  │  kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.28 -- nslookup jobpost   │ │
│  │  # If this works but external DNS fails → check CoreDNS forward config.    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Network Namespace Debugging — Crossing Container Boundaries

In Kubernetes, every pod has its own network namespace. Debugging across namespaces requires understanding how to enter a pod's network context from the host:

NETWORK NAMESPACES — Debugging Across Container Boundaries
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NETWORK NAMESPACE DEBUGGING — Enter Any Pod's Network                          │
│                                                                               │
│  CONCEPT: Each pod has its OWN network stack (interfaces, routes, iptables).   │
│  The HOST has a separate network stack. They're isolated by network namespaces.│
│                                                                               │
│  METHOD 1: nsenter — Enter a container's network namespace from the host:      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # Find the container's PID:                                               │ │
│  │  docker inspect <container_id> | jq '.[0].State.Pid'                     │ │
│  │  # OR for K8s (containerd):                                                │ │
│  │  crictl inspect <container_id> | jq '.info.pid'                          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Enter its network namespace:                                             │ │
│  │  nsenter -t <PID> -n -- ip addr show                                     │ │
│  │  nsenter -t <PID> -n -- ip route show                                    │ │
│  │  nsenter -t <PID> -n -- ss -tlnp                                         │ │
│  │  nsenter -t <PID> -n -- curl -v http://jobpost:8000/health               │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Now you're running commands AS the container, from the host!            │ │
│  │  # Same interfaces, same routes, same firewall — identical perspective.    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  METHOD 2: ip netns — For pods with named namespaces:                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # List network namespaces:                                                │ │
│  │  ip netns list                                                             │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Execute command in a namespace:                                          │ │
│  │  ip netns exec <namespace_name> ip addr show                              │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # For Docker containers (creates named ns):                                │ │
│  │  # Docker creates a symlink: /var/run/docker/netns/                        │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # For K8s (CNI-specific):                                                  │ │
│  │  # Calico: ip netns list (shows named namespaces)                          │ │
│  │  # Cilium: uses BPF, nsenter method preferred                              │ │
│  │  # Flannel: may not create named netns, use nsenter method                 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  DEBUGGING SCENARIO — "Pod A can't reach Pod B":                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # On the HOST (where both pods run):                                      │ │
│  │  # 1. Enter Pod A's network namespace:                                     │ │
│  │  nsenter -t <podA_PID> -n -- ip addr show  → 10.244.1.5                  │ │
│  │  nsenter -t <podA_PID> -n -- ip route show → default via 10.244.1.1      │ │
│  │  nsenter -t <podA_PID> -n -- ping 10.244.2.8  → FAILS                    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # 2. Enter Pod B's network namespace:                                     │ │
│  │  nsenter -t <podB_PID> -n -- ip addr show  → 10.244.2.8                  │ │
│  │  nsenter -t <podB_PID> -n -- ss -tlnp       → :80 LISTEN                 │ │
│  │  # Pod B is listening! So why can't Pod A reach it?                        │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # 3. Check from HOST perspective:                                         │ │
│  │  ping 10.244.2.8  → Works! So L3 routing between pods is fine.             │ │
│  │  nc -zv 10.244.2.8 80 → Works! So L4 is fine from host.                   │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # 4. Check NetworkPolicy (applies to pods, not host):                      │ │
│  │  kubectl get networkpolicies -A                                            │ │
│  │  # Found: deny-all policy in default namespace!                            │ │
│  │  # Host traffic bypasses NetworkPolicy — why host tests worked!            │ │
│  │  # FIX: add egress rule for Pod A → Pod B.                                 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  KEY INSIGHT: The HOST is NOT restricted by NetworkPolicy. If a test works     │
│  from the host but fails from inside a pod → NetworkPolicy or pod network      │
│  config. This is the #1 reason "it works from the node but not the pod."       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

30.5 LAB: Network Debugging Bootcamp

🛠️ Network Debugging Lab — 7 Hands-On Exercises
1

L1 Diagnosis — Simulate Link Failure

# Bring down the loopback substitute (use a dummy interface)
ip link add dummy0 type dummy
ip link set dummy0 up
# Now check it
ip link show dummy0
ethtool dummy0 2>&1 || echo "No ethtool for dummy — use on real NICs"

# Simulate a cable pull (take interface down)
ip link set dummy0 down
# Run the triage script and observe: L1 failure detected first
ip -br link show | grep dummy0   # Should show DOWN
# Fix it
ip link set dummy0 up
# Cleanup
ip link delete dummy0
2

Reproduce ECONNREFUSED vs ETIMEDOUT

# Start a test listener on port 9999
nc -l 9999 &
# Test: should connect successfully
nc -zv localhost 9999
# Output: Connection to localhost 9999 port [tcp/*] succeeded!

# Kill the listener → ECONNREFUSED
kill %1
nc -zv localhost 9999
# Output: nc: connect to localhost port 9999 (tcp) failed: Connection refused
# VERIFY: curl -v http://localhost:9999 shows "Connection refused"

# Now simulate ETIMEDOUT — add a DROP rule
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9999 -j DROP
nc -zv -w 3 localhost 9999
# Output: nc: connect to localhost port 9999 (tcp) timed out
# VERIFY: tcpdump shows SYN sent, NO response (not even RST)
tcpdump -i lo -nn port 9999 &
# In another terminal: nc -zv localhost 9999 → watch SYN sent, nothing back

# CLEANUP
iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 9999 -j DROP
3

ethtool Deep Dive — Find Hardware Issues

# On a real machine with physical NICs:
ethtool eth0
# Document: Speed, Duplex, Link detected, Auto-negotiation

ethtool -S eth0 | grep -E "err|drop|fifo|discard"
# All should be ZERO. Any non-zero = investigate.

# Check ring buffer size
ethtool -g eth0
# Current vs Maximum. If drops present, increase:
# ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096 tx 4096

# Check driver info
ethtool -i eth0
# driver: ena (AWS ENA), vmxnet3 (VMware), virtio_net (KVM), ixgbe (Intel 10G)

# Find MTU along the path
ping -M do -s 1472 8.8.8.8    # 1472+28=1500 — standard MTU test
# If it fails, reduce: ping -M do -s 1400 8.8.8.8 → keep reducing until it works
# Working MTU = (working -s value) + 28
4

tcpdump Triage — Capture and Analyze Connections

# Terminal 1: Start capture
tcpdump -i any -nn port 8888 -w /tmp/triage.pcap &

# Terminal 2: Run test connections
nc -l 8888 &  # Start listener
nc -zv localhost 8888   # Successful connection
kill %1                 # Kill listener
nc -zv localhost 8888   # ECONNREFUSED

# Stop capture (kill tcpdump)
kill %1

# Analyze: count packets by TCP flag
tcpdump -r /tmp/triage.pcap -nn
# Look for: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK (successful handshake)
# Then: SYN → RST (connection refused)
# Count specifically:
tcpdump -r /tmp/triage.pcap -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' | wc -l
# Should see 2 SYNs (one succeeded, one refused)
5

iptables TRACE — Find the Dropping Rule

# Add a DROP rule you'll "forget" about
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 7777 -j DROP

# Enable TRACE for that port
iptables -t raw -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 7777 -j TRACE

# Start watching kernel log
journalctl -k -f | grep -i trace &

# Test connection (will time out)
nc -zv -w 2 localhost 7777

# Find the TRACE output — see which table/chain/rule drops it
# Stop the journalctl watcher: kill %1

# CLEANUP
iptables -t raw -D PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 7777 -j TRACE
iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 7777 -j DROP
6

K8s Network Debugging with netshoot

# Deploy a debug pod with all network tools
kubectl run netshoot --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash

# Inside the debug pod:
# Check interfaces
ip -br link && ip -br addr

# Check DNS resolution for Kubernetes services
nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
dig jobpost.default.svc.cluster.local +short

# Test connectivity to a service
nc -zv jobpost 8000
curl -v http://jobpost:8000/health

# Test external connectivity
ping -c 3 8.8.8.8
curl -v --connect-timeout 5 https://google.com

# Check routing from pod perspective
ip route show
traceroute 8.8.8.8

# Exit: type 'exit' or Ctrl+D (--rm flag cleans up the pod)
7

Timed 5-Minute SRE Drill

# Have a colleague break ONE of these (don't tell you which):
# Option A: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 8000 -j DROP (firewall block)
# Option B: systemctl stop <service> (service down → ECONNREFUSED)
# Option C: echo "nameserver 1.2.3.4" > /etc/resolv.conf (broken DNS)
# Option D: ip route del default (no default route)

# ⏱️ START THE CLOCK
# Minute 0-1: Scope — check if it's just you or everyone
# Minute 1-2: L7 — curl localhost:8000/health
# Minute 2-3: L4 — nc -zv localhost 8000, ss -tlnp
# Minute 3-4: L3 — ping 8.8.8.8, ip route show
# Minute 4-5: DNS — dig google.com

# GOAL: Identify the BROKEN LAYER within 5 minutes.
# BONUS: Announce the root cause before the 5-minute mark.
# RECORD: Your time-to-diagnosis. Repeat until consistently under 3 min.

⏱️SRE 5-Minute PlaybookMinute-by-minute: Scope → L7 → L4 → L3 → DNS. By minute 5, you know which layer is broken. Announce and focus.
