🔑 Chapter 30 Key Takeaways

  1. Always debug bottom-up: Layer 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 7. A problem at any layer could be caused by the layer below it. Never skip layers — you'll waste time debugging the wrong thing.
  2. Connection Refused means the NETWORK WORKS. The destination host received your SYN and sent back RST. The service simply isn't listening. Don't debug the network — start the service.
  3. Connection Timeout means packets are being SILENTLY DROPPED. Somewhere between you and the destination, a firewall, security group, or routing black hole is discarding your packets. Debug the network path.
  4. The 10-command triage covers 90% of incidents. ip/ss/curl/dig/ping/iptables/dmesg — these tools are on every Linux host. Memorize the checklist. Never SSH into a host without running it.
  5. By minute 5 of an incident, know which layer is broken. Scope the blast radius in minute 0-1. Check L7 in minute 1-2. L4 in minute 2-3. L3 in minute 3-4. DNS in minute 4-5. Announce your finding and focus.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 30

🔽Bottom-Up Debugging
The practice of starting troubleshooting at the lowest layer (physical/data-link) and working upward. Based on the principle that higher-layer problems are often symptoms of lower-layer failures. Never assume the layer you suspect is where the problem actually is.
🚫ECONNREFUSED
Error code returned when a TCP SYN reaches the destination host but nothing is listening on that port. The destination sends back a RST packet. This confirms the network path works — the problem is the application/service not running or bound to the wrong IP.
⏳ETIMEDOUT
Error code returned when TCP SYN packets are sent repeatedly (with exponential backoff) but never receive any response — not even a RST. Indicates packets are being silently dropped somewhere in the path (firewall, security group, routing issue, or destination host down).
🛣️EHOSTUNREACH
Error returned immediately by the kernel when it cannot find any route to the destination IP in its routing table. No packets are sent. Indicates missing routes or a NIC configured on the wrong subnet.
🩺Triage Script
A pre-prepared set of diagnostic commands run immediately upon accessing a troubled host. Covers interfaces (ip link), addresses (ip addr), routes (ip route), ARP (ip neigh), listeners (ss), local connectivity (curl), DNS (dig), external connectivity (ping), firewall (iptables), and kernel logs (dmesg).
⏱️Blast Radius
The scope of an incident's impact. Determined in the first minute of triage by checking: from cellular vs WiFi, different regions, and different services. Knowing the blast radius prevents wasting time on unaffected components.

📝 Chapter 30 — Practice Questions

Q1
Why should you always start network debugging at Layer 1 and work up? Give an example where skipping layers leads to wasted time.
Show Answer
Answer

Higher-layer problems are often symptoms of lower-layer failures. Example: You try to debug a "can't reach the service" issue by checking iptables rules (L4) and DNS (L7), spending 30 minutes. The actual problem: the Ethernet cable was unplugged (L1). If you had started with "ip link show" (L1), you would have seen "NO-CARRIER" and fixed it in 30 seconds. The OSI model is your debugging playbook — exploits the dependency chain between layers.

Q2
What is the crucial difference between "Connection Refused" and "Connection Timeout"? How would you debug each?
Show Answer
Answer

Connection Refused (ECONNREFUSED): The destination host received your SYN and sent back a RST. The network works. The service isn't listening on that port. Fix: start the service, check binding address (ss -tlnp). Connection Timeout (ETIMEDOUT): SYN packets are silently dropped — no response at all. The destination may be down, firewalled, or unreachable. Debug: ping → iptables → traceroute → check security groups/NACLs → check if host is up. Also check: is ICMP blocked? If so, nc to port 22 can serve as an alternative L3 test.

Q3
You get "Connection Refused" when trying curl http://10.0.1.50:8000 from another server, but the service IS running on 10.0.1.50. What's the most likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer

The service is likely bound to 127.0.0.1 (localhost only) instead of 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) or the specific network interface IP. Check with ss -tlnp | grep 8000. If you see "127.0.0.1:8000" (not "0.0.0.0:8000" or "10.0.1.50:8000"), the service only accepts connections from the same machine. Fix: configure the service to bind to 0.0.0.0:8000. Common in Django: python manage.py runserver binds to 127.0.0.1 by default. Use python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 for external access.

Q4
How do you definitively prove that a problem is "network" vs "application"?
Show Answer
Answer

Run the test matrix: (1) Local test: curl localhost:PORT from the same machine. If it works, the app is fine — problem is network/firewall/DNS. If it fails, app is down. (2) Same-pod test: From a different pod in the same namespace, curl the service. If it works, external networking is the problem. If it fails, intra-cluster networking (CNI/NetworkPolicy) is the problem. (3) Ping vs Port: If ping works but nc -zv fails, L3 is fine, problem is L4+ (firewall or service). (4) DNS vs Direct IP: If DNS name fails but direct IP works, DNS is the problem only. These four tests isolate the problem to network, DNS, firewall, or application in under 2 minutes.

Q5
Walk through the SRE 5-minute network triage for an incident where "jobpost.anihpj.com is down."
Show Answer
Answer

Minute 0-1: Check from phone on cellular — is it down for everyone? Check cloud status page. kubectl get nodes → any NotReady? Result: it's down for all users in us-east-1. Minute 1-2: curl https://jobpost.anihpj.com/health → timeout. Check kubectl get pods -l app=jobpost → all Running but some restarting. Minute 2-3: nc -zv LB_IP 443 → succeeds (LB is up). kubectl get endpoints jobpost → ENDPOINTS is empty! This is the problem — no healthy backends. Minute 3-4: ping 8.8.8.8 from a node → works. Network connectivity is fine. Minute 4-5: dig jobpost.anihpj.com → correct LB IP returned. DNS is fine. By minute 5, announce: "Network is fine. Root cause: Service endpoints are empty. Readiness probe is likely failing. Investigating pod health now."

Q6
What are the 10 essential commands for network triage and what does each reveal?
Show Answer
Answer

1) ip -br link — interface status (UP/DOWN). 2) ip -br addr — IP assignments. 3) ip route show default — default gateway exists? 4) ip neigh show — ARP resolution working? 5) ss -tlnp — what's listening on TCP? 6) curl -v localhost:PORT — local connectivity test. 7) dig +short google.com — DNS working? 8) ping -c 3 8.8.8.8 — external connectivity. 9) iptables -L -n -v — firewall rules and counters. 10) dmesg -T | tail -50 — kernel-level events. These 10 commands, run in order, diagnose Layers 1 through 7 and cover approximately 90% of network incidents.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  10-COMMAND TRIAGE — Layers Diagnosed                              │
│                                                                   │
│  L1 (Physical)     → ip -br link show                             │
│  L2 (Data Link)    → ip neigh show                                │
│  L3 (Network)      → ip -br addr, ip route, ping                  │
│  L4 (Transport)    → ss -tlnp, nc -zv                             │
│  L7 (Application)  → curl -v, dig, iptables, dmesg                │
│                                                                   │
│  TIMING: All 10 commands run in < 30 seconds.                      │
│  90% of incidents identified by command #5 (ss -tlnp).            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q7
You SSH into a server and "ip link show eth0" displays "NO-CARRIER". Walk through your L1 debugging approach with ethtool. What are the three most likely causes and how do you verify each?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Cable unplugged or damaged — visually inspect the cable, try a known-good cable. ethtool eth0 will show "Link detected: no". (2) Switch port down/disabled — check switch side. If you have access: show interface status on the switch. If cloud: check the instance's network attachment status. (3) NIC driver issue — check dmesg for driver errors. ethtool -i eth0 shows driver name. Try rmmod + modprobe to reload the driver. If none fix it, the NIC hardware may be faulty — check ethtool -S eth0 for hardware errors. PRO TIP: lldpctl (if installed) shows the switch port you're connected to — if LLDP neighbor is visible, the cable works but the switch port may be admin-disabled.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NO-CARRIER DEBUGGING — Decision Tree                              │
│                                                                   │
│  ethtool eth0 → Link detected: no                                  │
│       │                                                            │
│       ├── Cable check: replace cable → Link detected: yes?        │
│       │   └── YES → Bad cable. FIXED.                              │
│       │                                                            │
│       ├── Switch check: lldpctl → neighbor visible?               │
│       │   └── YES → Switch port admin down. Enable it.             │
│       │   └── NO → Switch port or patch panel issue.              │
│       │                                                            │
│       └── Driver check: dmesg | grep -i "eth0\|e1000\|ena"        │
│           └── Errors found → reload driver or reboot.              │
│           └── No errors → NIC hardware failure. Replace.           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q8
A user reports "the website loads but images are broken, and file uploads fail." You suspect an MTU issue. How do you diagnose and fix this using ping and ethtool?
Show Answer
Answer

Symptoms point to MTU mismatch — small packets (HTML) work, large packets (images, uploads) fail. Diagnosis: (1) Check local MTU: ip link show eth0 | grep mtu. (2) Find path MTU: ping -M do -s 1472 (for MTU 1500). If it fails, reduce -s until it works. Working MTU = (working -s) + 28. Example: if ping -M do -s 1400 works but 1472 fails, path MTU is 1428. (3) If on K8s with VXLAN/GENEVE overlay: physical MTU 1500 - 50 bytes overhead = overlay MTU 1450. Set cilium config set mtu 1450. (4) TCP MSS clamping as temporary fix: iptables -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu. This forces TCP to use smaller segments for the affected path.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MTU BLACK HOLE — How It Happens                                   │
│                                                                   │
│  Server (MTU 1500)              Router (MTU 1450)    Internet     │
│  │                                  │                    │         │
│  │── 1500-byte packet, DF=1 ──────→│                    │         │
│  │                                  │← ICMP "Need Frag" ─┤  BLOCKED│
│  │                                  │   (MTU=1450)        │ by FW   │
│  │── 1500-byte packet (retry) ────→│  DROPPED             │         │
│  │── 1500-byte packet (retry) ────→│  DROPPED             │         │
│  │  ... connection hangs ...        │                      │         │
│  │                                                                   │
│  FIX: ip link set eth0 mtu 1450   OR   iptables MSS clamping         │
│  TEST: ping -M do -s 1422 target  # 1422+28=1450 → should work!      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q9
You run "kubectl get endpoints jobpost" and see an empty list. Walk through your debugging approach. What are the four possible root causes?
Show Answer
Answer

Empty endpoints mean no pods are matching the Service selector AND passing readiness checks. Four root causes: (1) Service selector doesn't match any pod labels — kubectl get svc jobpost -o yaml | grep selector, then kubectl get pods --show-labels. Compare the selectors. (2) Pods exist but readiness probe is failing — kubectl get pods -l app=jobpost, check READY column (e.g., 0/1). kubectl describe pod shows readiness probe failures. (3) Pods are in CrashLoopBackOff or Pending — kubectl get pods shows STATUS. Check events/logs. (4) Service is in wrong namespace — kubectl get svc -A | grep jobpost. Debug flow: Check selector match → check pod readiness → check pod status → verify namespace. Fix is usually: (a) correct the selector, (b) fix the readiness probe endpoint/path, or (c) fix the pod crash.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  EMPTY ENDPOINTS — Root Cause Decision Tree                        │
│                                                                   │
│  kubectl get endpoints jobpost →                             │
│       │                                                            │
│       ├── kubectl get svc jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'  │
│       │   └── selector: {app: jobpost}                             │
│       │                                                            │
│       ├── kubectl get pods -l app=jobpost → any pods?             │
│       │   ├── NO → Selector wrong or pods not deployed.            │
│       │   └── YES → Check READY column                             │
│       │       ├── 0/1 → Readiness probe failing. Fix probe.        │
│       │       ├── CrashLoopBackOff → App crashes on startup.      │
│       │       └── 1/1 → Check namespace. Service in different NS? │
│       │                                                            │
│       └── Fix and verify: kubectl get endpoints jobpost            │
│           Should now show pod IPs with port numbers.               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q10
Explain how iptables TRACE works and when you would use it. Walk through enabling TRACE for a specific port, reading the output, and finding which rule drops the packet. What precautions must you take?
Show Answer
Answer

iptables TRACE is a RAW table target that logs every rule a matching packet traverses across ALL tables (raw → mangle → nat → filter). Use it when you've eliminated all other possibilities and packets are being silently dropped — it's the "nuclear option" for firewall debugging. Process: (1) Add TRACE rules with specific filters: iptables -t raw -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 8000 -j TRACE. (2) Watch kernel log: journalctl -k -f | grep TRACE. (3) Generate one test packet: curl http://target:8000. (4) Read the output — each line shows TABLE:CHAIN:rule#. The last line before silence = the rule that DROPPED/REJECTED the packet. (5) CRITICAL: Delete TRACE rules immediately after! iptables -t raw -D PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 8000 -j TRACE. NEVER leave TRACE rules on high-traffic ports — you'll flood the kernel log and potentially crash the system. Always use the most specific filter possible (single IP:port pair).

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  iptables TRACE — Packet Journey Through Tables                    │
│                                                                   │
│  PACKET IN (dst port 8000)                                         │
│       │                                                            │
│       ▼                                                            │
│  raw:PREROUTING ──→ TRACE rule matches → LOGGED                   │
│       │                                                            │
│       ▼                                                            │
│  mangle:PREROUTING ──→ (no match, policy ACCEPT) → LOGGED         │
│       │                                                            │
│       ▼                                                            │
│  nat:PREROUTING ──→ DNAT rule → destination rewritten              │
│       │                                                            │
│       ▼                                                            │
│  filter:FORWARD ──→ rule #5: DROP ← PACKET DROPPED HERE!          │
│       │                                                            │
│       ✗  NO MORE TRACE LINES — the last line = the killer rule     │
│                                                                   │
│  PRECAUTIONS:                                                      │
│  • Always filter by port AND IP to limit trace volume              │
│  • Delete TRACE rules immediately after diagnosis                  │
│  • On production: brief enable, capture one packet, disable        │
│  • Alternative: nft monitor trace (nftables) for newer kernels    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔨 Chapter 30 — Hands-On Drills

D1
Triage Script: Create a ~/network-triage.sh that runs all 10 commands. Test it on your local machine. Time yourself — can you run through all checks in under 30 seconds?
D2
Error Reproduction: Intentionally stop a service (systemctl stop nginx) and observe "Connection Refused" with curl and nc. Then add an iptables DROP rule and observe "Connection Timeout." Document the exact error messages.
D3
Decision Tree Walk-Through: Simulate "users can't reach the app" by breaking DNS (wrong /etc/resolv.conf). Walk the decision tree. At which question does the flow diverge? Document your debugging path.
D4
Network vs App: Set up a scenario where the app is running but bound to 127.0.0.1. Prove it's NOT a network problem using the test matrix (local vs remote, same pod vs different pod).
D5
SRE 5-Minute Drill: Have a colleague break something (DNS, firewall, service stop, route removal). From the moment they tell you "it's down," time yourself through the 5-minute playbook. Did you identify the broken layer within 5 minutes?
D6
ethtool Exploration: On a physical Linux machine, run ethtool eth0, ethtool -S eth0, and ethtool -g eth0. Document every counter. Are any non-zero? If so, investigate and root-cause each one.
D7
iptables TRACE: Set up a deliberate DROP rule, enable TRACE, generate traffic, and identify the dropping rule from kernel logs. Time how long from TRACE enable → finding the dropping rule. Should be under 2 minutes.
D8
MTU Black Hole: Set MTU to 1400 on one interface and 1500 on the peer. Generate large HTTP transfers. Observe the "works sometimes, fails sometimes" pattern. Fix with path MTU discovery or MSS clamping.

Chapter 31: Common Network Failure Scenarios (With Full Walk-Throughs)

Theory is useless without practice. This chapter walks through five real-world network failure scenarios — the exact kinds of incidents that wake you up at 3 AM. Each scenario is a complete debugging walk-through: symptoms you'll see, the exact commands to run, what the output means, and how to fix it. These are patterned after the anihpj/jobpost Django-on-Kubernetes deployment, but the patterns apply to any networked application. By the end, you'll have a mental playbook for the most common production network failures.

🛠️ How to Use This Chapter — Your Incident Response Playbook

These five scenarios represent ~80% of production network incidents. Here's how to operationalize them for anihpj/jobpost:

If You SeeGo ToFirst CommandExpected Fix Time
Django "could not connect to server"Scenario 31.1kubectl exec → nc -zv DB_SVC 54325-15 min
"jobpost.anihpj.com is down"Scenario 31.2dig +short → curl LB_IP/health5-10 min
Random 502/504 errors, self-healingScenario 31.3Check retransmits + conntrack count10-30 min
"NXDOMAIN" or DNS timeoutsScenario 31.4kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns5-15 min
"SSL certificate problem"Scenario 31.5openssl s_client -connect host:44310-30 min

Incident response workflow: Copy the relevant scenario's commands into your terminal. Follow each step. Don't skip steps — the chain is designed so each step confirms the previous layer works before moving deeper. Bookmark this chapter in your team's runbook.

31.1 Scenario 1: "The Pod Can't Reach the Database"

Symptoms: Django returns "could not connect to server: Connection refused". The jobpost application can't reach PostgreSQL. The pods are running, but the health endpoint returns 503 because the DB check fails.

SCENARIO 1 — Full Debug Walk-Through
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SCENARIO 1: "Pod Can't Reach the Database" — Complete Debugging Guide          │
│                                                                               │
│  INITIAL SYMPTOMS:                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • App returning HTTP 503 (Service Unavailable)                           │ │
│  │  • Django logs: "django.db.utils.OperationalError: could not connect     │ │
│  │    to server: Connection refused"                                         │ │
│  │  • kubectl get pods → jobpost pods are Running but READY 0/1              │ │
│  │  • Readiness probe failing because /health returns 503                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 1 — Verify the connection from inside the pod:                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl exec -it jobpost-7b9f8c-abc12 -- bash                            │ │
│  │  nc -zv postgres-service 5432                                              │ │
│  │  # Output: nc: connect to postgres-service port 5432 (tcp) failed:        │ │
│  │  #         Connection refused                                             │ │
│  │  #                                                                         │ │
│  │  # ECONNREFUSED = network WORKS. The PostgreSQL host IS reachable.         │ │
│  │  # Something is rejecting the connection.                                  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 2 — Check if PostgreSQL is listening:                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl exec -it postgres-0 -- ss -tlnp | grep 5432                      │ │
│  │  # Output: LISTEN 0 244 127.0.0.1:5432 0.0.0.0:*                          │ │
│  │  # ← PostgreSQL is only listening on 127.0.0.1!                           │ │
│  │  # Fix: PostgreSQL config needs listen_addresses = '*' or '0.0.0.0'       │ │
│  │  # In postgresql.conf: listen_addresses = '*'                             │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ALTERNATIVE ROOT CAUSES (if PostgreSQL IS listening on 0.0.0.0):               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  CAUSE 2: Wrong service name. Django config has DB_HOST=postgres-svc but  │ │
│  │    the K8s Service is named postgres-service. Fix: align the names.       │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  CAUSE 3: Wrong namespace. postgres-service is in namespace "db" but      │ │
│  │    Django is connecting to "postgres-service" (default namespace).         │ │
│  │    Fix: DB_HOST=postgres-service.db.svc.cluster.local                     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  CAUSE 4: NetworkPolicy blocking. kubectl get networkpolicies -A.         │ │
│  │    If a policy denies ingress to port 5432, fix by adding allow rule:     │ │

│  │    spec:                                                                   │ │
│  │      podSelector:                                                          │ │
│  │        matchLabels:                                                        │ │

│  │        - port: 5432                                                        │ │
│  │    EOF                                                                     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │

│  │    Django logs "password authentication failed." Check pg_hba.conf and    │ │
│  │    K8s Secret for DB credentials.                                          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │

│  STEP 3 — Verify the fix:                                                       │

│  │  #         succeeded!                                                     │ │

Error MessageMost Likely CauseFirst Command to Run
"Connection refused"PostgreSQL not listening on the interface IP (bound to 127.0.0.1)ss -tlnp inside postgres pod

PostgreSQL pg_hba.conf — The Authentication Gatekeeper

When PostgreSQL rejects connections with "password authentication failed" or "no pg_hba.conf entry," the problem is in PostgreSQL's Host-Based Authentication configuration. This is the #1 cause of post-deployment DB connection failures:

pg_hba.conf — PostgreSQL Authentication Debugging
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  pg_hba.conf — DECODE THE AUTHENTICATION RULES                                  │
│                                                                               │
│  RULE FORMAT: TYPE  DATABASE  USER  ADDRESS        METHOD                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # Allow jobpost user from any pod in the cluster:                        │ │
│  │  host    jobpostdb   jobpost   10.0.0.0/8      md5                       │ │
│  │  # TYPE: host (TCP), local (Unix socket), hostssl (TLS only)              │ │
│  │  # ADDRESS: 10.0.0.0/8 = pod CIDR. 0.0.0.0/0 = anywhere.                 │ │
│  │  # METHOD: md5 (password hash), scram-sha-256 (stronger), trust (no pw!)  │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # If your pod IP is 10.244.3.15 but pg_hba.conf only has 127.0.0.1/32:  │ │
│  │  # → "no pg_hba.conf entry for host 10.244.3.15"                          │ │
│  │  # → Connection arrives but NO rule matches the source IP!                │ │
│  │  # Fix: Add host all all 10.244.0.0/16 md5 (match your pod CIDR).         │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  K8s-SPECIFIC GOTCHAS:                                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Pod IPs CHANGE on restart. Don't hardcode pod IPs in pg_hba.conf.      │ │
│  │  • Use the pod CIDR range (10.244.0.0/16) to cover ALL pods dynamically.  │ │
│  │  • For multi-cluster: each cluster has a different pod CIDR.               │ │
│  │  • StatefulSet PostgreSQL: IP is stable across restarts. Same pod name.   │ │
│  │  • To find your pod CIDR: kubectl cluster-info dump | grep cluster-cidr   │ │
│  │    or check your CNI config (Calico default: 192.168.0.0/16).             │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  VERIFY: From the jobpost pod, connect manually to test:                   │ │
│  │  kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- psql -h postgres-service -U jobpost -d   │ │
│  │    jobpostdb -c "SELECT 1"                                                 │ │
│  │  # If this works → app code/config issue. If not → pg_hba.conf or Secret. │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

TCP Handshake Deep Dive — Reading Connection Success/Failure from Packets

Every database connection starts with a TCP 3-way handshake. Understanding the exact packet exchange helps you diagnose connection failures WITHOUT needing application logs:

TCP 3-WAY HANDSHAKE — Diagnosing DB Connection Failures
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TCP HANDSHAKE — What Each Outcome Means for DB Connections                     │
│                                                                               │
│  SCENARIO A: SUCCESSFUL HANDSHAKE (3 packets)                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Client (jobpost pod)                Server (postgres pod)                │ │
│  │  │  SYN (seq=X)       ─────────────→ │  ← "Can we talk?"                  │ │
│  │  │  ←─────────────  SYN-ACK (seq=Y, ack=X+1) │  ← "Yes, I'm listening"    │ │
│  │  │  ACK (ack=Y+1)     ─────────────→ │  ← "Great, connected!"             │ │
│  │  │  [APPLICATION DATA]               │  ← Now Django sends SQL queries     │ │
│  │  RESULT: Connected. Network works. TLS/DB auth happens next.              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  SCENARIO B: CONNECTION REFUSED (2 packets)                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Client                              Server                               │ │
│  │  │  SYN (seq=X)       ─────────────→ │  ← "Can we talk?"                  │ │
│  │  │  ←─────────────  RST (ack=X+1)    │  ← "NO! Nothing listening here"    │ │
│  │  RESULT: ECONNREFUSED. The server IS reachable (SYN arrived).             │ │
│  │  The kernel sent RST because no socket is bound to port 5432.             │ │
│  │  FIX: Check if postgres is running. Check listen_addresses.              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  SCENARIO C: TIMEOUT (1+ packets, no response)                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Client                              ???                                  │ │
│  │  │  SYN (seq=X)       ─────────────→ │  ???  (dropped by iptables/Policy)  │ │
│  │  │  ... 1 second ...                 │                                     │ │
│  │  │  SYN (seq=X)       ─────────────→ │  ???  (retransmit, still dropped)   │ │
│  │  │  ... 2 seconds ...                │                                     │ │
│  │  │  SYN (seq=X)       ─────────────→ │  ???  (retransmit, still dropped)   │ │
│  │  │  ... ~130 seconds → ETIMEDOUT     │                                     │ │
│  │  RESULT: ETIMEDOUT. SYN packets are silently dropped.                      │ │
│  │  FIX: Check NetworkPolicy, iptables DROP rules, security groups.          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WATCH THE HANDSHAKE WITH tcpdump:                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  tcpdump -i any -nn port 5432                                             │ │
│  │  # Then trigger a connection from the jobpost pod.                         │ │
│  │  # You'll see exactly which scenario plays out — A, B, or C.              │ │
│  │  # This is more reliable than application error messages!                 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

K8s Probe Debugging — When Readiness/Liveness Break Connections

Kubernetes uses probes to determine pod health — but misconfigured probes can CAUSE the very failures they're supposed to detect. Understanding probe mechanics at the network level is essential:

K8s PROBES — Network-Level Debugging of Readiness/Liveness
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  K8s PROBES — How They Impact Network Traffic                                   │
│                                                                               │
│  PROBE TYPES:                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  readinessProbe:  Controls whether the pod receives traffic.              │ │
│  │    • Fails → pod removed from Service Endpoints → NO traffic.             │ │
│  │    • Passes → pod added to Endpoints → receives traffic.                  │ │
│  │    • Runs: continuously (every periodSeconds, default 10s).               │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  livenessProbe:    Controls whether the pod is restarted.                 │ │
│  │    • Fails → kubelet kills and restarts the container.                    │ │
│  │    • Passes → container continues running.                                │ │
│  │    • Runs: continuously. CRITICAL: if DB is slow, liveness probe may      │ │
│  │      timeout and kill the pod, making everything worse.                   │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  startupProbe:     Gives slow-starting apps time before liveness kicks in.│ │
│  │    • Fails → kubelet restarts container (same as liveness).               │ │
│  │    • Passes → liveness probe takes over.                                  │ │
│  │    • CRITICAL for DB-dependent apps (Django needs DB ready first).        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  PROBE FAILURE PATTERNS:                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  PATTERN: Service endpoint shows pod IP but 0/1 READY                     │ │
│  │  → Readiness probe failing. Check: /health endpoint, probe timeout.       │ │
│  │  kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A5 "Readiness:"                      │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  PATTERN: Pod keeps restarting (CrashLoopBackOff) every few minutes       │ │
│  │  → Liveness probe too aggressive. DB connection slow → probe times out.   │ │
│  │  Fix: Add startupProbe with 30s initialDelay, then liveness every 30s.    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  PATTERN: All pods cycling in/out of Ready state (flapping)               │ │
│  │  → Probe threshold too tight. Slow DB queries trigger readiness failure.  │ │
│  │  Fix: failureThreshold: 5 (allow 5 failures before marking unhealthy).    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  PROBE CONFIG FOR DJANGO/POSTGRESQL (anihpj/jobpost):                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  readinessProbe:                                                          │ │
│  │    httpGet:                                                               │ │
│  │      path: /health                                                        │ │
│  │      port: 8000                                                           │ │
│  │    initialDelaySeconds: 10  ← Wait for Django to start                    │ │
│  │    periodSeconds: 10         ← Check every 10 seconds                     │ │
│  │    failureThreshold: 3       ← Allow 3 failures (30s) before removal      │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  livenessProbe:                                                           │ │
│  │    httpGet:                                                               │ │
│  │      path: /health                                                        │ │
│  │      port: 8000                                                           │ │
│  │    initialDelaySeconds: 30  ← Give Django time to connect to DB           │ │
│  │    periodSeconds: 30         ← Check less frequently than readiness       │ │
│  │    failureThreshold: 5       ← Allow 5 failures (2.5 min) before restart  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

31.2 Scenario 2: "External Users Can't Reach the App"

Symptoms: "jobpost.anihpj.com is down." Users report the site won't load. The incident channel explodes. This is the most common "the site is down" scenario — and it has a specific debugging chain from outside-in: DNS → Load Balancer → K8s Service → Endpoints → Pods.

SCENARIO 2 — "External Users Can't Reach the App"
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SCENARIO 2: EXTERNAL ACCESS FAILURE — Outside-In Debugging                     │
│                                                                               │
│  THE REQUEST PATH:                                                              │
│  User → DNS (jobpost.anihpj.com) → Cloud LB → K8s NodePort → Service → Pod    │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 1 — DNS: Does the domain resolve?                                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  dig +short jobpost.anihpj.com                                            │ │
│  │  # ✓ 34.120.45.67 → DNS is fine. Proceed.                                 │ │
│  │  # ✗ No answer → DNS broken. Check DNS hosting (Route53/Cloudflare).      │ │
│  │  # ✗ Wrong IP → Someone changed the A record. Check DNS history.          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 2 — LOAD BALANCER: Is the LB healthy?                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  curl -v --connect-timeout 5 https://34.120.45.67/health                  │ │
│  │  # ✓ 200 OK → LB and backend are working. Problem may be DNS caching.     │ │
│  │  # ✗ 503 → LB can't reach healthy backends. Check target group.           │ │
│  │  # ✗ timeout → LB itself is down, or security group blocking 443.         │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # In cloud: check LB target group health:                                 │ │
│  │  aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <arn>                │ │
│  │  # Look for "Unhealthy" targets. If ALL unhealthy → investigate pods.     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 3 — K8s SERVICE: Is the service routing correctly?                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl get svc jobpost-service                                          │ │
│  │  # NAME              TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     PORT(S)                │ │
│  │  # jobpost-service   LoadBalancer   10.96.100.50   80:30080/TCP           │ │
│  │  # ✓ Type=LoadBalancer, External-IP populated. Check endpoints.           │ │
│  │  # ✗ Type=ClusterIP → Not exposed externally! Change to LoadBalancer.    │ │
│  │  # ✗ External-IP = <pending> → Cloud LB provisioning failed.            │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  kubectl get endpoints jobpost-service                                    │ │
│  │  # NAME              ENDPOINTS                                            │ │
│  │  # jobpost-service   10.244.1.5:8000,10.244.2.8:8000                      │ │
│  │  # ✓ Endpoints populated → Pods are healthy.                              │ │
│  │  # ✗ <none> → No healthy pods! Check pod readiness.                      │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Check NodePort connectivity from outside the cluster:                   │ │
│  │  curl http://<ANY_NODE_IP>:30080/health                                  │ │
│  │  # ✓ Works → K8s networking is fine. LB is the problem.                   │ │
│  │  # ✗ Fails → NodePort not working. Check kube-proxy, firewall rules.      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 4 — PODS: Are the application pods healthy?                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl get pods -l app=jobpost                                          │ │
│  │  # NAME                       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE            │ │
│  │  # jobpost-7b9f8c-abc12       1/1     Running   0          2d            │ │
│  │  # jobpost-7b9f8c-def34       0/1     CrashLoop 12         5m            │ │
│  │  # ← One pod is crashing! Check logs:                                     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  kubectl logs jobpost-7b9f8c-def34 --tail=50                              │ │
│  │  # django.db.utils.OperationalError: could not connect to server...       │ │
│  │  # ← The crashing pod can't reach the DB. See Scenario 31.1.              │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  kubectl describe pod jobpost-7b9f8c-def34                                │ │
│  │  # Look at Events section: OOMKilled? CrashLoopBackOff? ImagePullBackOff? │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ROOT CAUSE SUMMARY TABLE:                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  SYMPTOM                    ROOT CAUSE                   FIX              │ │
│  │  ────────────────────────   ──────────────────────────   ──────────────   │ │
│  │  dig returns no answer      DNS record deleted/misconfig Update A record  │ │
│  │  LB returns 503             All backends unhealthy       Check pod health  │ │
│  │  LB returns timeout         Security group blocks 443    Allow 0.0.0.0:443│ │
│  │  Endpoints shows <none>     No ready pods                Fix readiness    │ │
│  │  NodePort curl fails        kube-proxy or CNI issue     Check kube-proxy  │ │
│  │  Pods in CrashLoopBackOff   App can't connect to DB     See Scenario 31.1 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Ingress Controller Debugging — When the LB Works But Routes Fail

Many K8s deployments use an Ingress controller (nginx-ingress, traefik, ambassador) instead of a direct LoadBalancer Service. When users get 404 or 503 from the Ingress but the LB is healthy, the problem is in the Ingress routing:

INGRESS DEBUGGING — LB Healthy, Routes Broken
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  INGRESS CONTROLLER — When the LB Is Fine but Routes Are Wrong                  │
│                                                                               │
│  FLOW: User → DNS → Cloud LB → Ingress Controller Pod → Ingress Rules → Service│
│                                                                               │
│  CHECK 1 — Is the Ingress resource configured correctly?                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl get ingress -A                                                    │ │
│  │  kubectl describe ingress jobpost-ingress -n default                       │ │
│  │  # Look for:                                                               │ │
│  │  #   Host: jobpost.anihpj.com  ← Must match the domain users use.         │ │
│  │  #   Backend: jobpost-service:8000  ← Must match your Service name/port.  │ │
│  │  #   TLS: jobpost-tls  ← Secret must exist with valid cert.               │ │
│  │  #                                                                         │ │
│  │  # Common mistake: Ingress host is "jobpost.anihpj.com" but users access  │ │
│  │  # "www.jobpost.anihpj.com" → 404. Fix: add both hosts or use wildcard.  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  CHECK 2 — Is the Ingress controller running?                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx                                        │ │
│  │  kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller --tail=50  │ │
│  │  # Look for: "could not find Service", "TLS secret not found",            │ │
│  │  # "connection refused" (backend service not responding).                  │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  kubectl exec -n ingress-nginx <pod> -- curl -v http://jobpost-service:8000/health│
│  │  # If this fails → Ingress to Service communication broken.               │ │
│  │  # Check NetworkPolicy allowing ingress-nginx → app namespace traffic.     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  CHECK 3 — TLS certificate in the Ingress:                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl get secret jobpost-tls -n default                                 │ │
│  │  kubectl exec -n ingress-nginx <pod> -- ls /etc/nginx/certs/              │ │
│  │  # If empty → Ingress controller can't read the Secret (RBAC issue).      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Service Mesh Sidecar Debugging — When the Proxy Is the Problem

If your anihpj deployment uses a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium), every pod has a sidecar proxy that intercepts ALL traffic. When the proxy misbehaves, it looks like a network problem — but it's actually the sidecar:

SERVICE MESH SIDECAR — Debugging the Proxy Layer
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SERVICE MESH DEBUGGING — When the Sidecar Proxy Breaks                          │
│                                                                               │
│  HOW THE SIDECAR INTERCEPTS TRAFFIC:                                             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  WITHOUT MESH:                        WITH ISTIO SIDECAR:                  │ │
│  │  App ──→ Service                     App ──→ Envoy ──→ Envoy ──→ Service  │ │
│  │  (direct TCP)                        (iptables redirects all traffic      │ │
│  │                                       through sidecar proxy)              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ISTIO-SPECIFIC DEBUGGING:                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # Check if sidecar is injected:                                           │ │
│  │  kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'          │ │
│  │  # Should show: "jobpost" AND "istio-proxy"                                │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Check sidecar logs for errors:                                          │ │
│  │  kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy --tail=50                              │ │
│  │  # Look for: "connection refused" (upstream not reachable),                │ │
│  │  # "upstream connect error" (backend down),                                │ │
│  │  # "SSL certificate" errors (mTLS issue).                                  │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Dump Envoy config to see routing rules:                                  │ │
│  │  istioctl proxy-config cluster <pod>                                       │ │
│  │  istioctl proxy-config listeners <pod>                                     │ │
│  │  istioctl proxy-config routes <pod>                                        │ │
│  │  # Check if the backend Service appears. Missing = misconfiguration.       │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Check mTLS certificate status:                                           │ │
│  │  istioctl proxy-config secret <pod> -o json | jq '.certificates[].status' │ │
│  │  # "EXPIRED" = cert needs renewal. Reboot pod to get new cert.            │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  SIDECAR FAILURE PATTERNS:                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  SYMPTOM: All outbound connections from one pod fail                      │ │
│  │  → Sidecar proxy crashed. Check: kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy.      │ │
│  │  → Test by bypassing sidecar: nsenter into pod, use direct IP (not svc). │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  SYMPTOM: Inter-pod communication works but TLS errors in logs            │ │
│  │  → mTLS certificate issue. Pod restart refreshes certs from istiod.       │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  SYMPTOM: Connections time out, sidecar CPU near 100%                     │ │
│  │  → Sidecar overloaded. Increase sidecar resources OR bypass mesh for      │ │
│  │    high-throughput connections (add traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludePorts).│ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

31.3 Scenario 3: "Intermittent Timeouts Between Services"

Symptoms: 5xx errors appearing randomly, then disappearing. Users report "sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't." The hardest type of incident to debug because by the time you investigate, it's working again.

SCENARIO 3 — Intermittent Timeouts Debugging
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SCENARIO 3: INTERMITTENT TIMEOUTS — The Hardest Bug to Catch                   │
│                                                                               │
│  INITIAL SYMPTOMS:                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Prometheus: HTTP 5xx rate spikes to 3% for 2 minutes, then drops to 0 │ │
│  │  • Logs: "upstream request timeout" between payment-svc and order-svc    │ │
│  │  • Pattern: Happens every ~30 minutes, lasts 2-3 minutes                  │ │
│  │  • Between services: NOT external. Internal K8s communication.            │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 1 — Check TCP retransmits during the incident:                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ss -ti | grep -E "retrans|rto|cwnd"                                      │ │
│  │  # Look for: retrans:5/2 (5 retransmitted, 2 segments sent = 250%!)      │ │
│  │  # High retrans on connections between the two services → packet loss.    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Historical: check Prometheus                                           │ │
│  │  rate(node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs[5m])                                   │ │
│  │  # If retransmit rate spikes correlate with 5xx spikes → network loss.    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 2 — Check conntrack table at the time of incident:                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count                           │ │
│  │  cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max                             │ │
│  │  # If count is near max during the spike → conntrack table overflow.      │ │
│  │  # New connections get dropped when table is full.                         │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  FIX: Increase limit or switch to Cilium (eBPF LRU hash).                │ │
│  │  sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=262144                          │ │
│  │  # Default is 65536. Increase to 262144 for high-connection environments. │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 3 — Check MTU (VXLAN/GENEVE overhead):                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # If using VXLAN overlay (Flannel, Calico with VXLAN):                    │ │
│  │  ip link show | grep mtu                                                   │ │
│  │  # Physical MTU 1500 → VXLAN MTU should be 1450 (50 bytes overhead).      │ │
│  │  # If overlay MTU is 1500, packets > 1450 bytes get silently dropped.     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  iperf3 -c <target_pod_ip> -t 30 -M 1400                                │ │
│  │  # Test with reduced MTU to see if large packets are the problem.          │ │
│  │  # If -M 1400 works but default doesn't → MTU issue.                      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 4 — tcpdump analysis during the spike:                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  tcpdump -i any -nn -w /tmp/trace.pcap host <pod_ip>                      │ │
│  │  # After incident: open in Wireshark.                                      │ │
│  │  # Look for: TCP Retransmissions, TCP Dup ACK, TCP Window Full            │ │
│  │  # Statistics → IO Graph → look for spikes during the incident window.    │ │
│  │  # Statistics → TCP Stream Graphs → Time-Sequence (Stevens)               │ │
│  │  #   → Flat line = stall. Dips = packet loss and recovery.                │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ROOT CAUSE QUICK-CHECK:                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  CHECK                     FINDING              FIX                       │ │
│  │  ────────────────────────  ───────────────────  ────────────────────────  │ │
│  │  TCP retransmits > 2%      Packet loss          Check MTU, NIC drops      │ │
│  │  Conntrack > 80% full      Connection overflow  Increase conntrack max    │ │
│  │  MTU mismatch (overlay)    Large packets drop   Set Cilium MTU to 1450    │ │
│  │  tcpdump shows Dup ACKs    Packet loss pattern  Find lossy hop with mtr   │ │
│  │  Node CPU > 90%            CPU saturation        Scale nodes or pods      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

NetworkPolicy Implementation — How iptables Actually Enforces Rules

Understanding HOW NetworkPolicy is implemented helps you debug why traffic is (or isn't) being blocked. It's not magic — it's iptables (or eBPF with Cilium):

NETWORKPOLICY — iptables Implementation Under the Hood
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NETWORKPOLICY — How iptables/Cilium Enforce Rules                              │
│                                                                               │
│  DEFAULT-DENY Policy Creates These iptables Rules:                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # Check the actual iptables rules created by NetworkPolicy:              │ │
│  │  iptables -L -n -v | grep -i calico   # For Calico CNI                   │ │
│  │  iptables -L -n -v | grep -i cilium   # For Cilium CNI                   │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Typical Calico policy chains:                                           │ │
│  │  Chain cali-pi-policy (pod ingress):                                       │ │
│  │    DROP all -- anywhere anywhere  ← Default deny                          │ │
│  │    ACCEPT all -- 10.244.1.5 anywhere  ← Allow from jobpost pod            │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Chain cali-po-policy (pod egress):                                        │ │
│  │    DROP all -- anywhere anywhere   ← Default deny                         │ │
│  │    ACCEPT all -- anywhere 10.96.0.10  ← Allow DNS (CoreDNS)               │ │
│  │    ACCEPT all -- anywhere 10.244.2.8  ← Allow to PostgreSQL pod           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  CILIUM eBPF Implementation (vs iptables):                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # Cilium replaces iptables with eBPF maps:                                │ │
│  │  bpftool map list | grep policy                                            │ │
│  │  # Shows: cilium_policy map — stores allowed identity pairs                │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Check which policies are loaded:                                        │ │
│  │  cilium policy get                                                        │ │
│  │  # Or via kubectl:                                                         │ │
│  │  kubectl get ciliumnetworkpolicies -A                                      │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Cilium advantage: O(1) hash lookup vs O(n) iptables rule scanning.     │ │
│  │  # At scale (100+ policies), iptables degrades, Cilium doesn't.            │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  LOAD BALANCER HEALTH CHECK DEEP DIVE:                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Cloud LB health checks are TCP/HTTP probes FROM the LB TO your nodes.    │ │
│  │  If the LB marks targets unhealthy, check:                                 │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  1. Health check path/port: Does the LB check /health:8000 or :80?        │ │
│  │     → If LB checks port 80 but app listens on 8000 → always unhealthy.    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  2. Health check timeout: Default is often 5 seconds. If your app takes   │ │
│  │     6 seconds to respond (DB query in health check) → LB marks unhealthy. │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  3. Security group: The LB's health check IPs must be allowed INBOUND     │ │
│  │     on the health check port. Check your node's security group rules.     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  4. Flapping: Targets alternate healthy/unhealthy → probe threshold too   │ │
│  │     tight. Set healthy threshold to 3+ consecutive successes.             │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  5. Cross-AZ: In multi-AZ deployments, ensure each AZ has healthy targets │ │
│  │     or disable cross-zone load balancing during maintenance.              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

31.4 Scenario 4: "DNS Resolution Fails Inside Kubernetes"

Symptoms: Pods can't resolve service names. nslookup jobpost-service returns "server can't find jobpost-service: NXDOMAIN" or times out. All inter-service communication breaks because everything depends on DNS.

SCENARIO 4 — K8s DNS Failure Walk-Through
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SCENARIO 4: DNS FAILURE IN KUBERNETES — Complete Debugging                     │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 1 — Verify DNS from a pod:                                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.28 -- nslookup jobpost  │ │
│  │  # ✓ Returns service IP → DNS works. Problem is specific to one pod.     │ │
│  │  # ✗ "can't resolve" → DNS is broken cluster-wide. Continue.             │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  kubectl exec -it <broken_pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf                    │ │
│  │  # nameserver 10.96.0.10 → kube-dns ClusterIP. Should be present.         │ │
│  │  # search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local       │ │
│  │  # If nameserver is wrong or missing → pod's DNS config is broken.        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 2 — Check CoreDNS pods:                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns                     │ │
│  │  # NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE             │ │
│  │  # coredns-5d4dd4b8db-2x7q  1/1     Running   0          5d             │ │
│  │  # coredns-5d4dd4b8db-9m3k  0/1     CrashLoop 999        5d             │ │
│  │  # ← One CoreDNS pod is crashing! Only one replica surviving.             │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  kubectl logs -n kube-system coredns-5d4dd4b8db-9m3k --tail=50           │ │
│  │  # Look for errors: "loop detected", "SERVFAIL", "i/o timeout"            │ │
│  │  # "loop detected" → CoreDNS forwarding to itself. Fix Corefile config.   │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Check CoreDNS deployment replicas:                                      │ │
│  │  kubectl get deployment coredns -n kube-system                            │ │
│  │  # DESIRED: 2  AVAILABLE: 1  ← Not enough replicas for HA.               │ │
│  │  kubectl scale deployment coredns -n kube-system --replicas=3             │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 3 — Check CoreDNS ConfigMap:                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml                     │ │
│  │  # Look at Corefile section:                                               │ │
│  │  # .:53 {                                                                  │ │
│  │  #     errors                                                              │ │
│  │  #     health                                                              │ │
│  │  #     kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {                   │ │
│  │  #         pods insecure                                                    │ │
│  │  #         fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa                               │ │
│  │  #     }                                                                   │ │
│  │  #     prometheus :9153                                                    │ │
│  │  #     forward . /etc/resolv.conf  ← Forwards to node's DNS!              │ │
│  │  #     cache 30                                                            │ │
│  │  # }                                                                       │ │
│  │  #                                                                         │ │
│  │  # If forward . /etc/resolv.conf points to broken DNS → all external      │ │
│  │  # resolution fails. Test the node's DNS: dig google.com @<node_dns_ip>    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  STEP 4 — Check NetworkPolicy blocking UDP 53:                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  kubectl get networkpolicies -A | grep -i dns                             │ │
│  │  # If a policy denies UDP 53 → CoreDNS unreachable.                       │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Allow DNS egress from all pods (if missing):                            │ │
│  │  kubectl apply -f - <<EOF                                                  │ │
│  │  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1                                         │ │
│  │  kind: NetworkPolicy                                                       │ │

│  │    name: allow-dns-egress                                                  │ │
