Chapter 32: Network Performance Analysis

Knowing the network works is table stakes. Knowing how fast it works — and why — is what separates SREs from help-desk technicians. This chapter teaches you to measure, analyze, and tune network performance. You'll learn about the physics of latency, the tools to benchmark throughput, and the kernel parameters that can make a 10x difference. For the anihpj/jobpost deployment targeting p99 < 500ms, every millisecond counts.

32.1 Understanding Network Latency

Latency isn't one thing — it's four separate components that add up. Understanding each one tells you which ones you can optimize and which are governed by physics:

LATENCY COMPONENTS — The Four Sources of Delay
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TOTAL NETWORK LATENCY = Propagation + Serialization + Queuing + Processing     │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ PROPAGATION DELAY (Physics — CANNOT be reduced without moving closer) ───┐│
│  │  Time for a signal to travel through the medium at the speed of light.     ││
│  │  Fiber: ~200,000 km/s. Copper: ~230,000 km/s. Vacuum: 300,000 km/s.       ││
│  │                                                                           ││
│  │  Distance → Time:                                                          ││
│  │    1 km         →  5 µs     (same building)                               ││
│  │    100 km       →  0.5 ms   (same metro area, cross-AZ)                   ││
│  │    1,000 km     →  5 ms     (regional)                                    ││
│  │    5,000 km     →  25 ms    (cross-country, NYC→LA)                        ││
│  │    10,000 km    →  50 ms    (transatlantic, NYC→London)                    ││
│  │    20,000 km    →  100 ms   (halfway around the world)                     ││
│  │                                                                           ││
│  │  RTT (Round Trip) = 2× propagation delay. NYC→London = ~100ms minimum.    ││
│  │  YOU CANNOT BEAT PHYSICS. Route users to the nearest region.              ││
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ SERIALIZATION DELAY (Bandwidth-dependent — increases with packet size) ──┐│
│  │  Time to push all bits onto the wire = Packet Size / Link Bandwidth.       ││
│  │  1500 bytes ÷ 1 Gbps   = 12 µs    (negligible)                            ││
│  │  1500 bytes ÷ 100 Mbps = 120 µs   (noticeable on slow links)               ││
│  │  1500 bytes ÷ 10 Mbps  = 1.2 ms   (significant!)                          ││
│  │  9000 bytes ÷ 1 Gbps   = 72 µs    (jumbo frames still tiny at 1G+)        ││
│  │  64 bytes ÷ 10 Gbps    = 0.05 µs  (tiny packet, fast link = irrelevant)   ││
│  │                                                                           ││
│  │  At 10 Gbps+, serialization is negligible (< 1 µs per packet).            ││
│  │  At 100 Mbps, serialization adds up — 1000 packets = 120 ms just to send! ││
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ QUEUING DELAY (Congestion-dependent — the latency killer at load) ──────┐│
│  │  Time packets wait in buffers when the link is busy.                       ││
│  │  Empty buffer: 0 ms                                                       ││
│  │  Full 4MB buffer at 1 Gbps: up to 32 ms (bufferbloat!)                    ││
│  │  Full 1MB buffer at 100 Mbps: up to 80 ms                                  ││
│  │                                                                           ││
│  │  THIS IS THE ONLY COMPONENT YOU CAN DIRECTLY CONTROL WITH TUNING.         ││
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─ PROCESSING DELAY (Hardware/software-dependent) ─────────────────────────┐│
│  │  Hardware switch (cut-through):    ~1 µs    (line-rate forwarding)         ││
│  │  Hardware router (store-forward):  ~10 µs   (FIB lookup)                  ││
│  │  Linux iptables (per rule):        ~1-10 µs  (depends on rule count)      ││
│  │  Cloud SDN (VPC encapsulation):    ~50-200 µs (tunnel encap/decap)        ││
│  │  NGFW / IPS (deep inspection):     ~1-10 ms   (L7 analysis)               ││
│  │  eBPF XDP (NIC driver level):      ~0.1 µs    (fastest possible!)         ││
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│                                                                               │
│  STACKED BAR — Typical pod-to-pod latency in same K8s node (1 Gbps):           │
│  Propagation (same host):  0.001 ms       ▏                                   │
│  Serialization (1500B):    0.012 ms       ▎                                   │
│  Queuing (light load):     0.005 ms       ▏                                   │
│  Processing (iptables):    0.400 ms       ████████████████████  ← DOMINATES!  │
│  TOTAL: ~0.42 ms                                                              │
│  Replace iptables with Cilium eBPF → processing drops to 0.05 ms.             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Bandwidth-Delay Product — How Much Data Is "In Flight"

The Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) is the amount of data that can be in transit at any given moment. It's critical for TCP tuning — if your TCP buffer is smaller than the BDP, you can never fully utilize the link:

BANDWIDTH-DELAY PRODUCT — Why Bigger Pipes Need Bigger Buffers
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BDP = Bandwidth × RTT  (bits/sec × seconds = bits)                             │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  SCENARIO                      BDP        TCP BUFFER NEEDED              │ │
│  │  ────────────────────────────  ─────────  ─────────────────────────────  │ │
│  │  1 Gbps, 0.1ms RTT (same AZ)  100 Kb     12.5 KB  (small)               │ │
│  │  1 Gbps, 5ms RTT (regional)    5 Mb       625 KB   (typical default OK)   │ │
│  │  1 Gbps, 50ms RTT (cross-US)   50 Mb      6.25 MB  (need tuning!)         │ │
│  │  10 Gbps, 50ms RTT             500 Mb     62.5 MB  (MUST tune)            │ │
│  │  10 Gbps, 100ms RTT            1 Gb       125 MB   (severe bottleneck     │ │
│  │                                                 without tuning!)          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WHY THIS MATTERS:                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Default Linux TCP buffer: ~4 MB max (tcp_rmem max).                      │ │
│  │  At 10 Gbps across 50ms (cross-country): you need 62.5 MB buffer.         │ │
│  │  Default buffer is 15× TOO SMALL → TCP never fills the pipe.              │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  You paid for a 10 Gbps connection. Without BDP tuning, you get ~600 Mbps.│ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  CHECK YOUR BDP:                                                            │ │
│  │  ping -c 5 <target>  → get average RTT                                   │ │
│  │  ethtool eth0 | grep Speed → get bandwidth                                 │ │
│  │  BDP = (bandwidth_bps × rtt_seconds) / 8  → in bytes                      │ │
│  │  Compare with: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_rmem  → third value (max buffer)        │ │
│  │  If BDP > tcp_rmem_max → you are not using your full bandwidth.           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

TCP Window Scaling — Why Bigger Pipes Need Bigger Windows

The original TCP specification (RFC 793) had a 16-bit Window field — maximum 65,535 bytes. At 1 Gbps with 50ms RTT, the BDP is 6.25 MB — 100× larger than the maximum window. Without window scaling, TCP would be limited to ~10 Mbps regardless of link speed:

TCP WINDOW SCALING — How TCP Overcomes the 64KB Limit
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TCP WINDOW SCALING — RFC 1323 (1992)                                           │
│                                                                               │
│  THE PROBLEM:                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  TCP Window field: 16 bits → max value 65,535 bytes.                      │ │
│  │  At 10 Gbps, 50ms RTT: BDP = 62.5 MB → 1,000× larger than max window!    │ │
│  │  Without scaling: max throughput = window / RTT = 65535 / 0.05 ≈ 10 Mbps │ │
│  │  Even on a 10 Gbps link, you'd only get 10 Mbps.                          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  THE SOLUTION:                                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Window Scale option (SYN packet): shift count (0-14).                     │ │
│  │  Actual Window = Window_Field × 2^shift_count                              │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  shift=0: 65,535 bytes      (original)                                    │ │
│  │  shift=7: 65,535 × 128   = 8.3 MB    (typical default)                    │ │
│  │  shift=9: 65,535 × 512   = 33.5 MB                                        │ │
│  │  shift=14: 65,535 × 16384 = 1.07 GB  (maximum possible!)                  │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Linux default: shift=7 (shown as "wscale 7" in tcpdump).                  │ │
│  │  Effective window: 65535 × 128 = ~8 MB. Enough for 1 Gbps × 50ms.         │ │
│  │  For 10 Gbps × 50ms: need ~62 MB → increase tcp_rmem max to 128 MB.       │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  CHECK YOUR SCALING:                                                        │ │
│  │  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' -c 1 -v               │ │
│  │  # Look for "wscale N" in the SYN options. If missing → no scaling!       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Jitter and Bufferbloat — The Real-Time Communication Killers

Jitter is the variation in packet delay. While average latency might be 5ms, jitter means some packets take 2ms and others take 50ms. For real-time applications (VoIP, gaming, video conferencing), jitter is MORE important than average latency:

JITTER — Why Average Latency Is Misleading
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  JITTER — The Hidden Performance Metric                                         │
│                                                                               │
│  TWO PATHS — SAME AVERAGE, DIFFERENT EXPERIENCE:                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  PATH A (Low jitter):                                                     │ │
│  │  Packet 1: 5ms, Packet 2: 5ms, Packet 3: 4ms, Packet 4: 6ms, Packet 5: 5ms│ │
│  │  Avg: 5ms. Jitter: 1ms.  → Smooth VoIP. Happy users.                      │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  PATH B (High jitter — bufferbloat):                                       │ │
│  │  Packet 1: 2ms, Packet 2: 2ms, Packet 3: 48ms, Packet 4: 2ms, Packet 5: 46ms│ │
│  │  Avg: 20ms. Jitter: 23ms. → VoIP choppy. Gaming lag spikes. Unusable.     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  MEASURING JITTER:                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  iperf3 -c <target> -u -b 10M -t 30                                       │ │
│  │  # Jitter column shows variation. < 1ms = good. > 10ms = bad.             │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  mtr <target> → StDev column = jitter. High StDev = bufferbloat.          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ping -c 100 <target> | awk '/rtt/ {print $4}' | tr '/' ' '               │ │
│  │  # Shows min/avg/max/mdev. mdev = jitter.                                 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  FIXING BUFFERBLOAT (the #1 cause of jitter):                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1. Enable fq_codel qdisc (fair queuing + controlled delay):               │ │
│  │     tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root fq_codel                                │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  2. Reduce NIC ring buffer (less buffer = less bloat):                     │ │
│  │     ethtool -G eth0 rx 256 tx 256                                          │ │
│  │     # Default is often 512-4096. 256 is fine for most workloads.          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  3. BBR congestion control (paced, doesn't fill buffers):                  │ │
│  │     sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr                          │ │
│  │     sysctl -w net.core.default_qdisc=fq                                    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  VERIFY: mtr shows reduced StDev after applying these fixes.              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

32.2 Measuring Network Performance

You can't improve what you don't measure. These tools give you the raw numbers — bandwidth, latency, packet loss, and jitter:

ToolWhat It MeasuresProtocolOverheadBest For
iperf3Throughput (TCP/UDP), packet loss, jitterTCP, UDP, SCTPHigh during testBaseline bandwidth between two hosts. THE standard tool.
pingRTT latency, packet lossICMPMinimalQuick L3 reachability + latency snapshot.
mtrPer-hop latency + packet loss (continuous)ICMP/UDPMinimalFind the lossy hop. Combines traceroute + ping.
httpingHTTP-level latency (full request-response)HTTP/HTTPSLowMeasure app latency, not just network. L7 test.
netperfTCP/UDP throughput, request/response rateTCP, UDPHigh during testBenchmarking with many configuration options.
qperfBandwidth + latency between two nodesTCP, UDP, RDMAHigh during testNo server setup needed (uses rsh/ssh). Quick test.
⚠️ GOTCHA — iperf3 Defaults Are Misleading

iperf3 by default tests SINGLE-THREADED TCP. Single-stream TCP is often bottlenecked by latency and window size, not actual bandwidth. For realistic multi-connection performance, use iperf3 -P 10 (10 parallel streams). A 10 Gbps link might only show 600 Mbps with one stream but 9.4 Gbps with 10 parallel streams. Always test with both -P 1 (single stream, latency-sensitive) AND -P 10 (multi-stream, realistic for web servers with many concurrent connections).

iperf3 — The Standard Throughput Benchmark

iperf3 — Bandwidth Testing Between Two Hosts
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  iperf3 — BENCHMARK NETWORK THROUGHPUT                                          │
│                                                                               │
│  TCP TEST (measures achievable throughput):                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # SERVER (listen on port 5201):                                          │ │
│  │  iperf3 -s                                                                 │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # CLIENT (connect to server, 30-second test, 4 parallel streams):         │ │
│  │  iperf3 -c 10.0.1.50 -t 30 -P 4                                           │ │
│  │  # OUTPUT:                                                                 │ │
│  │  [SUM]   0.00-30.00  sec  3.52 GBytes  1.01 Gbits/sec  42  sender        │ │
│  │  [SUM]   0.00-30.00  sec  3.51 GBytes  1.00 Gbits/sec      receiver      │ │
│  │  # Retr: 42 retransmits. 42 ÷ 3.5GB = ~0.001% loss. Healthy.              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  UDP TEST (measures packet loss at target bandwidth):                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  iperf3 -c 10.0.1.50 -u -b 1G -t 30                                       │ │
│  │  # -u: UDP mode. -b 1G: target 1 Gbps send rate.                           │ │
│  │  # OUTPUT:                                                                 │ │
│  │  [  5]   0.00-30.00  sec  3.58 GBytes  1.02 Gbits/sec  0.023 ms  0/2540000│
│  │  # Lost/Total: 0/2,540,000 → ZERO packet loss at 1 Gbps. Clean link.      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  REVERSE MODE (test download speed, not upload):                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  iperf3 -c 10.0.1.50 -R                                                   │ │
│  │  # -R: Reverse. Server sends, client receives. Tests download bandwidth.   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  K8s POD-TO-POD iperf3:                                                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # Start server pod:                                                       │ │
│  │  kubectl run iperf-server --image=networkstatic/iperf3 -- --server         │ │
│  │  kubectl expose pod iperf-server --port=5201                               │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # Run client:                                                              │ │
│  │  kubectl run iperf-client --rm -it --image=networkstatic/iperf3 -- \       │ │
│  │    --client iperf-server --time 30 --parallel 4                            │ │
│  │  # This measures the max throughput between two pods on your CNI.          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

mtr — Finding the Lossy Hop

mtr (My TraceRoute) combines ping and traceroute into one continuous tool. It sends packets to each hop and shows per-hop latency and packet loss in real-time — the single best tool for finding WHERE packet loss occurs:

mtr — Find the Bottleneck Hop
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  mtr — COMBINED TRACEROUTE + PING (Run Continuously)                            │
│                                                                               │
│  mtr -r -c 100 8.8.8.8   (100 pings, report mode)                              │
│                                                                               │
│  HOST              Loss%   Snt   Last   Avg  Best  Wrst  StDev                │
│  1. 10.0.1.1        0.0%   100    0.3   0.3   0.2   0.5    0.1  ← Gateway    │
│  2. 100.64.1.1       0.0%   100    1.2   1.3   1.0   2.1    0.3               │
│  3. 52.93.28.1       0.0%   100    2.5   2.6   2.3   3.8    0.4               │
│  4. 72.21.220.1      3.0%   100    8.2  15.3   7.9  32.1   12.5  ← PROBLEM!  │
│  5. 108.170.240.1    3.0%   100   10.1  16.2   9.5  35.2   13.1  ← Loss here │
│  6. 8.8.8.8          3.0%   100   10.5  16.8   9.8  35.8   13.4               │
│                                                                               │
│  INTERPRETING mtr OUTPUT:                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Loss that STARTS at hop N and continues to the end → Hop N is the      │ │
│  │    problem (or the link between N-1 and N).                               │ │
│  │  • Loss at hop N but NOT at hops N+1 → Hop N is just rate-limiting ICMP.  │ │
│  │    Not a real problem (routers deprioritize ICMP responses).              │ │
│  │  • Loss at the LAST hop only → The destination is rate-limiting ICMP      │ │
│  │    (Google does this). Not a network problem.                              │ │
│  │  • High jitter (StDev column) at a hop → Congestion or bufferbloat.       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  REAL-TIME MODE (interactive):                                                  │
│  mtr 8.8.8.8                                                                   │
│  # Continuously updates. Press 'd' for display mode, 'n' for DNS toggle.      │
│  # Watch for 5+ minutes to catch intermittent issues.                         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

httping — Measure Application Latency, Not Just Network

httping measures the full HTTP request-response cycle — DNS + TCP + TLS + HTTP. Unlike ping (ICMP only), httping tells you what USERS actually experience:

httping — L7 Latency Measurement
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  httping — MEASURE WHAT USERS ACTUALLY EXPERIENCE                               │
│                                                                               │
│  BASIC HTTP TEST:                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  httping -c 10 -g https://jobpost.anihpj.com/health                       │ │
│  │  # OUTPUT:                                                                 │ │
│  │  # connected to 34.120.45.67:443, seq=0 time=85.2 ms                      │ │
│  │  # connected to 34.120.45.67:443, seq=1 time=92.1 ms                      │ │
│  │  # --- https://jobpost.anihpj.com/health statistics ---                   │ │
│  │  # 10 connects, 10 ok, 0 failed, avg 88.5 ms, min 82.1, max 95.3         │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  COMPARE WITH ping:                                                         │ │
│  │  ping -c 10 34.120.45.67 → avg 1.2 ms   (L3 only)                         │ │
│  │  httping → avg 88.5 ms                    (DNS+TCP+TLS+HTTP)               │ │
│  │  Difference: 87.3 ms = TLS handshake + HTTP processing overhead           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  TLS LATENCY BREAKDOWN:                                                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  httping -c 5 http://jobpost.anihpj.com   → avg 35 ms (no TLS)            │ │
│  │  httping -c 5 https://jobpost.anihpj.com  → avg 85 ms (with TLS 1.2)      │ │
│  │  TLS overhead: 50 ms. This is why TLS 1.3 (1-RTT vs 2-RTT) matters.      │ │
│  │  Test with different TLS versions to quantify the handshake cost.         │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

netperf & qperf — Advanced Benchmarking

While iperf3 is the standard, netperf and qperf offer different testing modes that are useful for specific scenarios:

ToolKey FeatureCommand ExampleBest For
netperfRequest/response rate (transactions/sec), not just bulk throughputnetperf -H <server> -t TCP_RR — measures transaction rateDatabase-like workloads. Many small requests, not one big stream.
qperfNo server setup needed. Uses SSH/rsh. Tests bandwidth AND latency.qperf <server> tcp_bw tcp_lat — bandwidth + latency in one commandQuick ad-hoc test without installing anything on the server.

netperf vs iperf3: iperf3 measures bulk throughput (MB/sec) — good for streaming, file transfers. netperf measures transaction rate (requests/sec) — good for databases, APIs, microservices. For anihpj's Django-to-PostgreSQL traffic (many small queries), netperf's TCP_RR test is more representative than iperf3's bulk stream test.

32.3 TCP Tuning for Performance

Linux's default TCP settings are conservative — designed for 1990s internet speeds. Modern 10 Gbps+ networks need tuning. These kernel parameters can deliver a 10x throughput improvement:

sysctl ParameterWhat It DoesDefaultRecommended (10Gbps+)
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_controlCongestion control algorithm. BBR maximizes throughput + minimizes bufferbloat.cubicbbr
net.ipv4.tcp_rmemTCP read buffer (min default max). Max limits throughput over high-BDP paths.4096 131072 62914564096 87380 134217728
net.ipv4.tcp_wmemTCP write buffer (min default max). Same as above for sending.4096 16384 41943044096 65536 134217728
net.core.somaxconnMax SYN backlog. How many pending connections before kernel starts dropping.1284096
net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuseReuse TIME_WAIT sockets for new connections. Reduces port exhaustion.0 (disabled)1 (enabled)
net.ipv4.tcp_fastopenTCP Fast Open. Sends data in SYN packet. Saves 1 RTT on repeat connections.1 (client only)3 (client + server)
net.core.netdev_max_backlogMax packets queued when kernel is slower than NIC. Prevents rx_dropped.10005000
net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idleReset congestion window after idle. Kills long-lived idle connection perf.1 (enabled)0 (disabled)

Why More Bandwidth Doesn't Fix Latency Problems

This is one of the most common misconceptions in networking. Bandwidth is capacity. Latency is delay. Adding more lanes to a highway doesn't make cars drive faster — it just fits more cars. Same with networks:

BANDWIDTH vs LATENCY — Why Bigger Pipes Don't Help
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BANDWIDTH vs LATENCY — The Highway Analogy                                     │
│                                                                               │
│  10 Mbps (2-lane road):                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Serialization (1500B): 1.2 ms.  Propagation (same): 50 ms.              │ │
│  │  Total: 51.2 ms per packet.  1 car every 1.2 ms, 50 ms to drive.        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  10 Gbps (2000-lane highway):                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Serialization (1500B): 0.0012 ms.  Propagation (same): 50 ms.           │ │
│  │  Total: 50.0012 ms per packet.  2000 cars at once, still 50 ms to drive. │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  THE MATH:                                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Request: 1 KB. Response: 100 KB. RTT: 50 ms.                             │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  At 10 Mbps:  Time = RTT + (101KB × 8 / 10Mbps)                           │ │
│  │              = 50ms + 80.8ms = 130.8 ms                                    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  At 100 Mbps: Time = 50ms + 8.08ms = 58.08 ms  (72% improvement)          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  At 1 Gbps:   Time = 50ms + 0.81ms = 50.81 ms  (only 12% better)         │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  At 10 Gbps:  Time = 50ms + 0.08ms = 50.08 ms  (essentially RTT-only)    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  DIMINISHING RETURNS: After ~1 Gbps, latency improvement is marginal.     │ │
│  │  A 1000× bandwidth increase from 10 Mbps to 10 Gbps saves only 80 ms.    │ │
│  │  Moving the server 1000 km closer saves 10 ms — costs far less.           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WHEN BANDWIDTH DOES MATTER:                                                    │
│  • Large file transfers (backups, video, data migration)                      │
│  • Many concurrent users (1000 users × 1 Mbps each = need 1 Gbps)             │
│  • Bulk data pipelines (ETL, log shipping)                                    │
│                                                                               │
│  WHEN LATENCY MATTERS MORE:                                                     │
│  • Small requests (API calls, DB queries, web pages)                           │
│  • Interactive applications (SSH, gaming, video calls)                         │
│  • Microservices communicating (many small RPCs)                               │
│                                                                               │
│  For anihpj/jobpost: Your Django DB queries are small (KB). 1 Gbps is plenty. │
│  Invest in reducing RTT (same-AZ deployment), not buying 10 Gbps links.       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

tcp_slow_start_after_idle — The Hidden Performance Killer

When tcp_slow_start_after_idle=1 (default), TCP resets its congestion window after a connection has been idle. This means a perfectly good long-lived connection suddenly behaves like a brand-new connection — starting from a tiny window and slowly ramping up. For connection-pooled databases, this is devastating:

tcp_slow_start_after_idle — Why Pooled Connections Become Slow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  tcp_slow_start_after_idle — THE CONNECTION POOL KILLER                        │
│                                                                               │
│  THE PROBLEM:                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Django CONN_MAX_AGE=600 → keeps DB connections open for 10 minutes.      │ │
│  │  Connection sits idle for 30 seconds between requests (slow traffic).     │ │
│  │  Next request: TCP congestion window was RESET to initial (10 segments).  │ │
│  │  Instead of sending 100 KB of query results at line rate...               │ │
│  │  ...it slowly ramps up: 10→20→40→80 segments over multiple RTTs.         │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Result: Pooled connection performs WORSE than a new connection!          │ │
│  │  (New connection starts fresh regardless. Pooled connection appears to    │ │
│  │   have a full window but it was silently reset.)                          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  THE FIX:                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0                            │ │
│  │  # NOW: idle connections keep their congestion window.                     │ │
│  │  # When traffic resumes, BBR/CUBIC starts from the SAVED window,          │ │
│  │  # not from scratch. Massive improvement for connection pools.            │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  SAFETY: This was originally a safety measure for 1990s internet —         │ │
│  │  congestion could change drastically while idle. On modern networks       │ │
│  │  (stable datacenter links), it's unnecessary and harmful.                 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Congestion Control Algorithms — CUBIC vs BBR vs Reno

TCP congestion control has evolved over decades. Understanding the algorithm families helps you choose the right one for your workload:

AlgorithmEraHow It WorksBest ForWeakness
Reno1990Additive Increase / Multiplicative Decrease. Cuts window by 50% on loss.Low-BDP paths (dial-up, early internet)Terrible on high-BDP or lossy links.
CUBIC2008 (Linux default)Cubic function for window growth. Recovers faster after loss than Reno.General purpose. Decent on most paths.Still reactive to loss. Causes bufferbloat.
BBR2016 (Google)Model-based. Measures max BW + min RTT. Ignores packet loss.High-BDP paths, lossy links, bufferbloat-prone linksSlightly less aggressive on clean low-BDP links.

NIC Tuning — Interrupt Coalescing and RSS

At 10 Gbps line rate (~14.8 million packets/sec), the CPU can't process every packet interrupt. NIC tuning offloads work from the CPU to the NIC hardware:

NIC TUNING — Hardware Offloading for 10Gbps+
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NIC TUNING PARAMETERS — ethtool for High-Performance                            │
│                                                                               │
│  INTERRUPT COALESCING (ethtool -C):                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  PROB: 14.8M pps = 14.8M interrupts/sec → CPU 100% just handling IRQs.   │ │
│  │  FIX: Batch interrupts. "Wait for N packets OR T microseconds."           │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ethtool -C eth0 rx-usecs 50 rx-frames 256                                │ │
│  │  # Wait up to 50 µs or 256 packets before interrupting CPU.              │ │
│  │  # Reduces interrupts from 14.8M/s to ~20K/s. CPU freed for app work.    │ │
│  │  # Trade-off: slightly higher latency (50 µs). For most apps: worth it.  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  RSS — RECEIVE SIDE SCALING (ethtool -X):                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Distributes incoming packets across multiple CPU cores by hash.           │ │
│  │  Without RSS: all packets go to CPU 0 → bottleneck.                       │ │
│  │  With RSS: packets spread across 4-8 cores → 4-8× throughput.             │ │
│  │                                                                           │
│  │  ethtool -X eth0 equal 4    # Spread across 4 cores                       │ │
│  │  ethtool -x eth0             # Show RSS indirection table                  │ │
│  │  ethtool -l eth0             # Show combined channels (should match cores) │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  CHECK IRQ DISTRIBUTION:                                                    │ │
│  │  cat /proc/interrupts | grep eth0                                         │ │
│  │  # If all interrupts on CPU 0 → RSS not working. Fix above.               │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  OFFLOAD FEATURES (ethtool -k):                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ethtool -k eth0 | grep -E "tso|gso|gro|lro"                              │ │
│  │  tso (TCP Segmentation Offload): NIC splits large TCP segments → HW does  │ │
│  │    the work, not kernel. Saves CPU. Should be ON.                          │ │
│  │  gso (Generic Segmentation Offload): SW version of TSO. ON.               │ │
│  │  gro (Generic Receive Offload): NIC merges small packets → less CPU. ON.  │ │
│  │  lro (Large Receive Offload): HW version of GRO. ON for physical NICs.    │ │
│  │  For VMs (AWS, GCP): these are often handled by the hypervisor.           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

TLS 1.3 Performance — Why One Less Round Trip Matters

TLS 1.3 reduced the handshake from 2-RTT to 1-RTT — cutting TLS latency nearly in half. Understanding the handshake explains why this is the single biggest latency win for HTTPS services:

TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3 — Handshake Latency Comparison
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TLS HANDSHAKE — Why Version Matters                                            │
│                                                                               │
│  TLS 1.2 (2-RTT = ~100ms at 50ms RTT):                                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Client                                  Server                           │ │
│  │  ── ClientHello ──────────────────────→  (RTT 1: negotiate cipher)       │ │
│  │  ←─ ServerHello + Certificate ────────                                     │ │
│  │  ── ClientKeyExchange + Finished ────→  (RTT 2: key exchange + verify)   │ │
│  │  ←─ Finished ─────────────────────────                                     │ │
│  │  ── GET /health ─────────────────────→  (RTT 3: first data = 150ms!)     │ │
│  │  TOTAL: 2-RTT (100ms) before data. 3-RTT for first response.             │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  TLS 1.3 (1-RTT = ~50ms at 50ms RTT):                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Client                                  Server                           │ │
│  │  ── ClientHello + KeyShare ──────────→  (RTT 1: cipher + key in one!)    │ │
│  │  ←─ ServerHello + Certificate + Finished                                   │ │
│  │  ── GET /health ─────────────────────→  (RTT 2: first data = 100ms!)     │ │
│  │  TOTAL: 1-RTT (50ms) before data. 2-RTT for first response.              │ │
│  │  → 50ms saved per new connection. 100ms saved for first response.        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  TLS 1.3 0-RTT RESUMPTION (for repeat connections):                             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Client sends data with the FIRST packet (ClientHello + Application Data) │ │
│  │  0-RTT: ~0ms before data. 1-RTT for first response.                       │ │
│  │  Saves 50ms vs 1.3, 100ms vs 1.2.                                         │ │
│  │  CAUTION: 0-RTT data is replayable. Don't use for non-idempotent requests │ │
│  │  (POST, PUT, DELETE). Use for GET requests only.                           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ENABLE TLS 1.3 (nginx-ingress ConfigMap):                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  data:                                                                     │ │
│  │    ssl-protocols: "TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3"                                        │ │
│  │    ssl-ciphers: "ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:..."                        │ │
│  │  VERIFY: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -tls1_3 2>&1 | grep Protocol │ │
│  │  # "Protocol: TLSv1.3" → TLS 1.3 is active!                               │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip) is Google's congestion control algorithm. Unlike CUBIC (which detects congestion via packet loss), BBR models the network path to find the actual bottleneck bandwidth and RTT — resulting in dramatically better performance on lossy or high-latency links:

BBR vs CUBIC — Why Congestion Control Matters
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BBR vs CUBIC — Google's Congestion Control Revolution                          │
│                                                                               │
│  CUBIC (default):                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Detects congestion by packet loss. Keeps increasing speed until loss.  │ │
│  │  • 1% packet loss → CUBIC cuts throughput by ~30%. Even tiny loss kills  │ │
│  │    performance. This is why Wi-Fi (0.5-2% loss) feels slow.              │ │
│  │  • Fills buffers until they overflow → causes bufferbloat → latency spikes│ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  BBR (enable it!):                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Models the path: measures max bandwidth AND min RTT simultaneously.    │ │
│  │  • Does NOT react to packet loss. Reacts to increased RTT (actual         │ │
│  │    congestion, not random loss).                                           │ │
│  │  • Result: ~10-100x better on lossy links. Lower latency under load.       │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ENABLE BBR:                                                                │ │
│  │  echo "net.core.default_qdisc=fq" >> /etc/sysctl.d/10-bbr.conf             │ │
│  │  echo "net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr" >> /etc/sysctl.d/10-bbr.conf   │ │
│  │  sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/10-bbr.conf                                       │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  VERIFY: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control → should show "bbr"        │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  fq ("fair queuing") qdisc is REQUIRED for BBR. BBR paces packets,         │ │
│  │  and fq provides the per-flow scheduling BBR needs.                        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  TCP FAST OPEN (TFO) — Save 1 RTT:                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  NORMAL TCP:                     TCP FAST OPEN:                           │ │
│  │  Client → SYN                     Client → SYN + DATA (TFO cookie)         │ │
│  │  Server → SYN+ACK                 Server → SYN+ACK + DATA                  │ │
│  │  Client → ACK + DATA              Client → ACK                            │ │
│  │  (3 RTT for first data)           (1 RTT saved on repeat connections!)     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ENABLE: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen=3   (1=client, 2=server, 3=both)   │ │
│  │  App support: Python/Django needs socket.TCP_FASTOPEN flag.               │ │
│  │  For anihpj: saves 10ms per repeat connection to PostgreSQL!              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

HTTP/2 Multiplexing — Fixing Head-of-Line Blocking

HTTP/1.1 has a fundamental performance problem: each connection can only handle ONE request at a time. Browsers work around this by opening 6-8 parallel connections, but each connection still suffers head-of-line blocking. HTTP/2 fixes this with multiplexing — multiple streams over a single TCP connection:

HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 — Multiplexing and Performance
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 — Why Multiplexing Matters                                  │
│                                                                               │
│  HTTP/1.1 (6 connections, head-of-line blocking):                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Connection 1: [GET /css] ───────────────────────────────────────────── │ │
│  │  Connection 2: [GET /js ] ───────────────────────────────────────────── │ │
│  │  Connection 3: [GET /img1]── [GET /img2]  ← BLOCKED until img1 done!     │ │
│  │  Each connection = 1 TCP handshake + 1 TLS handshake per connection.     │ │
│  │  6 connections × (TCP + TLS) = 6 handshake pairs → overhead.              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  HTTP/2 (1 connection, multiplexed streams):                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Connection 1:                                                            │ │
│  │    Stream 1: [GET /css ] ────────────────────────────────────────────    │ │
│  │    Stream 2: [GET /js  ] ────────────────────────────────────────────    │ │
│  │    Stream 3: [GET /img1] ────────────────────────────────────────────    │ │
│  │    Stream 4: [GET /img2] ────────────────────────────────────────────    │ │
│  │  1 TCP + 1 TLS handshake TOTAL. All streams share one connection.        │ │
│  │  No head-of-line blocking. Streams interleave freely.                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ENABLE HTTP/2 ON YOUR INGRESS (nginx-ingress):                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ConfigMap data: use-http2: "true"                                        │ │
│  │  Verify: curl -v --http2 https://jobpost.anihpj.com 2>&1 | grep HTTP     │ │
│  │  Should show: < HTTP/2 200                                               │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  CONNECTION POOLING — Eliminate Handshake Overhead:                             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  WITHOUT POOLING: Every DB query = new connection = 65ms overhead         │ │
│  │  WITH POOLING: Pool of 20 persistent connections. Overhead paid ONCE.     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  DJANGO: DATABASES['default']['CONN_MAX_AGE'] = 600  # 10 minutes         │ │
│  │  POSTGRESQL: PgBouncer sidecar maintains persistent connection pool       │ │
│  │  Reduces PostgreSQL connections from 1000s to 20-50                       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🛠️ How to Implement This — Your Performance Optimization Playbook

Here's how to apply these performance techniques to the anihpj/jobpost Django-on-Kubernetes deployment, ordered by impact-to-effort ratio:

StepChangeCommandImpactRisk
1Enable BBR congestion controlsysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr3-10x on lossy linksNone
2Disable tcp_slow_start_after_idlesysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=02-5x for connection poolsNone
3Enable TCP Fast Opensysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen=31-RTT per repeat connectionMinimal
4Tune TCP buffers for BDPsysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem="4096 87380 134217728"Fills 10Gbps+ pipesUses more RAM
5Enable HTTP/2 on IngressConfigMap: use-http2: "true"60ms saved per page loadNone
6Django CONN_MAX_AGEDATABASES['default']['CONN_MAX_AGE']=60065ms saved per DB queryMay need PgBouncer

Quick win sequence: Steps 1-3 take 5 minutes total and deliver immediate improvement. Steps 4-6 require testing/validation but provide compounding savings. Measure baseline iperf3 + httping BEFORE and AFTER each step to quantify the impact. Roll back if any step causes regressions.

🎯 SRE PERFORMANCE ENGINEERING — Network Tuning for Latency-Sensitive Services

As an SRE, you don't just "make it fast" — you meet SLOs at scale. Here's the latency budget for anihpj/jobpost targeting p99 < 500ms:

ComponentLatency% of BudgetOptimization Strategy
DNS resolution5ms1%NodeLocal DNSCache, CoreDNS replicas
TCP handshake10ms2%TCP Fast Open (1-RTT save)
TLS handshake50ms10%TLS 1.3 (1-RTT save vs 1.2's 2-RTT)
Network transit50ms10%CDN, latency-based DNS routing
App processing350ms70%Profile code, optimize DB queries
Serialization + overhead35ms7%Compression, connection pooling

SRE Performance Patterns: (1) Cross-region latency is PHYSICS — route users to the nearest region with latency-based DNS. (2) Connection pooling eliminates TCP+TLS handshake overhead — one pooled connection saves 60ms per request. (3) HTTP/2 multiplexing eliminates the 6-connection browser limit and head-of-line blocking. Enable it on your Ingress. Golden Rule: Measure the latency budget for every critical path. If any component exceeds its allocation, investigate BEFORE it violates the SLO.

🔑 Chapter 32 Key Takeaways

  1. Latency is four components — only queuing is tunable. Propagation is physics (fiber = 5µs/km). Serialization is bandwidth-dependent (negligible at 10Gbps+). Processing varies by software (iptables = slow, eBPF = fast). Queuing (bufferbloat) is what YOU can fix.
  2. Bandwidth-Delay Product determines if you can fill the pipe. BDP = Bandwidth × RTT. If your TCP buffer is smaller than BDP, you'll never achieve full throughput — no matter how fast the link is. Default Linux buffers are too small for 10Gbps+ cross-country.
  3. Always test with both single-stream AND multi-stream iperf3. Single-stream (-P 1) is bottlenecked by latency + window size. Multi-stream (-P 10) measures actual link capacity. They tell different stories.
  4. BBR is the single biggest performance win you can enable today. It replaces CUBIC's loss-based congestion detection with a model-based approach. 10-100x better on lossy links. Lower latency under load. Free — just a sysctl.
  5. Define a latency budget for every critical path. Don't just say "p99 < 500ms." Break it down: DNS 5ms, TCP 10ms, TLS 50ms, Network 50ms, App 350ms. If DNS starts taking 20ms, you know exactly which component to fix before it breaks the SLO.

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 32

📐Propagation Delay
The time for a signal to travel through a medium at the speed of light. Fiber: ~5µs/km. Cannot be reduced — governed by physics. NYC→London minimum RTT is ~70ms. Mitigation: route users to the nearest region (latency-based DNS, CDN).
🔢Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP)
The amount of data "in flight" on a link: BDP = Bandwidth × Round-Trip Time. 1 Gbps × 50 ms = 6.25 MB. TCP buffer must be ≥ BDP to fully utilize the link. Default Linux buffers max at ~4 MB — insufficient for high-BDP paths.
🚀BBR
Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip — Google's congestion control algorithm (Linux 4.9+). Models the network path by measuring max bandwidth and min RTT simultaneously. Does NOT react to packet loss — reacts to increased RTT. Requires fq qdisc. 10-100x better than CUBIC on lossy links.
⚡TCP Fast Open (TFO)
A TCP extension that allows data to be sent in the initial SYN packet (using a cryptographic cookie). Saves 1 RTT on repeat connections to the same server. For anihpj: saves 10ms per repeat PostgreSQL connection. Requires both client and server support.
🔍mtr
My TraceRoute — combines traceroute and ping into one continuous tool. Shows per-hop latency, packet loss, and jitter. The single best tool for finding WHERE packet loss occurs in a network path. Loss starting at hop N and continuing → hop N is the problem.
🎯Latency Budget
An SRE practice of allocating a maximum latency to each component in a request path. If DNS gets 5ms, TCP gets 10ms, TLS gets 50ms, etc. — and any component exceeds its allocation, it's investigated as an incident BEFORE the overall SLO is violated.

📝 Chapter 32 — Practice Questions

Q1
What are the four components of network latency? Which ones can you control and which are governed by physics?
Show Answer
Answer

Propagation: Time for signal to travel through medium (physics — ~5µs/km in fiber). Cannot reduce without moving closer. Serialization: Time to push bits onto wire = packet size / bandwidth. At 10Gbps+, negligible. At 100Mbps, significant. You can reduce by using faster links or smaller packets. Queuing: Time in buffers. YOU control this — reduce bufferbloat with fq_codel or BBR. Processing: Time in routers/switches/software. Reduce by using eBPF/XDP instead of iptables, or hardware offloading. Propagation dominates at distance; processing dominates in the datacenter; queuing dominates under load.

Q2
What is Bandwidth-Delay Product? If you have a 10 Gbps link with 50ms RTT, what TCP buffer size do you need to fully utilize it?
Show Answer
Answer

BDP = Bandwidth × Round-Trip Time. 10 Gbps × 0.050 s = 500 Mb = 62.5 MB. TCP buffer (tcp_rmem max) must be ≥ BDP to fully utilize the link. Default Linux tcp_rmem max is ~6 MB — only 10% of what's needed. With default settings, a 10 Gbps cross-country link will only achieve ~1 Gbps. Fix: sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem='4096 87380 134217728' (128 MB max). Formula: BDP (bytes) = (bandwidth_bps × rtt_seconds) / 8. Compare with: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_rmem → third value.

Q3
Why does a single iperf3 stream often show much lower throughput than the link's rated capacity? How do you get realistic results?
Show Answer
Answer

Single-stream TCP throughput is limited by: (1) Congestion window size (how much data can be in flight without ACK). (2) Latency — higher RTT means slower window growth. (3) Packet loss — even 0.1% loss causes CUBIC to cut window by 30%. With default settings on a 10 Gbps link with 10ms RTT: single stream may only achieve 2-3 Gbps. Solution: use iperf3 -P 10 (10 parallel streams). Each stream gets its own TCP connection and congestion window. Together they saturate the link. For realistic web server benchmarking: use multiple parallel streams (typical browsers open 6-8 connections). For latency-sensitive applications (SSH, DB queries): test single-stream to understand worst-case performance.

Q4
What is BBR congestion control and why is it better than CUBIC? How do you enable it?
Show Answer
Answer

BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip) models the network path instead of reacting to packet loss. CUBIC: increases speed until packet loss, then cuts by 30%. Result: 1% loss = massive throughput reduction. Also causes bufferbloat by filling buffers until overflow. BBR: continuously measures max BW and min RTT. Does NOT react to packet loss — only to RTT increase (genuine congestion). Result: near-line-rate throughput even with 1%+ loss. Lower latency under load. Enable: sysctl -w net.core.default_qdisc=fq; sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr. fq qdisc is REQUIRED. Verify: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control → "bbr". BBR is safe for production — used by Google on all internal B4 backbone links.

Q5
How do you interpret mtr output? A hop shows 20% packet loss but the next hop shows 0%. Is this a real problem?
Show Answer
Answer

NO — this is NOT a real problem. If loss at hop N does NOT continue to hops N+1 and beyond, hop N is simply rate-limiting or deprioritizing ICMP responses. Routers prioritize forwarding packets over responding to ICMP. The fact that hop N+1 has 0% loss PROVES that packets are passing through hop N successfully. If the loss were real, hop N+1 would also show loss (since all traffic passes through hop N). Only investigate when loss STARTS at hop N and CONTINUES to the final destination. Also: loss only at the last hop (e.g., 8.8.8.8) typically means the destination rate-limits ICMP — Google intentionally does this. High jitter (StDev column) at a hop = congestion or bufferbloat — investigate even without loss.

Q6
You're defining an SLO for anihpj/jobpost: p99 < 500ms. Create a latency budget breaking down the expected latency for each component.
Show Answer
Answer

DNS resolution: 5ms (NodeLocal DNSCache). TCP handshake: 10ms (same-AZ, TFO saves 1 RTT). TLS handshake: 50ms (TLS 1.3, 1-RTT). Network transit: 50ms (same-region). App processing: 350ms (Django + DB queries). Serialization/overhead: 35ms (HTTP headers, JSON parsing). Total: 500ms. If DNS starts taking 20ms → investigate CoreDNS before SLO is violated. If TLS is 80ms → check TLS 1.3 negotiation, cert chain size. Connection pooling eliminates TCP+TLS overhead for repeat requests (saves 60ms each). Monitoring: Prometheus histograms for each component → p50/p95/p99 per component → alert if component exceeds allocation.

D2
