32.4 LAB: Network Performance Lab

🛠️ Network Performance Lab — 6 Hands-On Exercises
1

Baseline iperf3 — Single vs Multi-Stream

# Terminal 1 (server):
iperf3 -s

# Terminal 2 (client — single stream):
iperf3 -c <server_ip> -t 30 -P 1
# Record: [SUM] ... Gbits/sec

# Multi-stream test:
iperf3 -c <server_ip> -t 30 -P 10
# Record: [SUM] ... Gbits/sec

# Compare: Multi / Single ratio. If > 2x → single-stream bottlenecked.
# Calculate: (single / link_speed) * 100 = % utilization.
2

BBR Before/After with Packet Loss

# Add 1% packet loss to simulate a poor link:
tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem loss 1%

# Test with CUBIC (default):
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=cubic
iperf3 -c <target> -t 30   # Record throughput

# Switch to BBR:
sysctl -w net.core.default_qdisc=fq
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr
iperf3 -c <target> -t 30   # Record throughput

# Compare: BBR / CUBIC ratio with 1% loss. Should be 3-10x.
tc qdisc del dev eth0 root  # CLEANUP
3

BDP Calculation and TCP Buffer Tuning

# Measure RTT:
ping -c 10 <target> | tail -1 | awk -F '/' '{print $5}'  # avg RTT in ms

# Get bandwidth:
ethtool eth0 | grep Speed

# Calculate BDP (example: 10 Gbps, 5ms RTT):
# BDP = 10e9 * 0.005 / 8 = 6,250,000 bytes (~6 MB)

# Check current buffer:
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_rmem  # Third number = max buffer
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_wmem

# If BDP > tcp_rmem max → tune:
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem="4096 87380 134217728"
# Re-test iperf3. Throughput should improve if BDP was the bottleneck.
4

mtr — Find the Bottleneck

# Run mtr to an external target for 100 cycles:
mtr -r -c 100 8.8.8.8

# Or interactive mode (watch for 5+ minutes):
mtr 8.8.8.8

# Analyze the output:
# • Which hop has the highest avg latency?
# • Is there any packet loss? Does it continue to the end?
# • Which hop has the highest jitter (StDev)?
# • If loss starts at hop N and continues → hop N is the bottleneck.

# Cross-AZ comparison:
mtr -r -c 50 <cross_az_ip>   # Different AZ
mtr -r -c 50 <same_az_ip>    # Same AZ
# Compare average latencies. Cross-AZ should be ~1-2ms higher.
5

Full TCP Tuning Benchmark

# Save current settings:
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control net.ipv4.tcp_rmem net.ipv4.tcp_wmem \
  net.core.somaxconn net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen \
  net.core.netdev_max_backlog > /tmp/tcp_before.txt

# Run iperf3 BEFORE tuning:
iperf3 -c <target> -t 30 -P 10 -J > /tmp/iperf_before.json

# Apply all 8 tunings:
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr
sysctl -w net.core.default_qdisc=fq
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem="4096 87380 134217728"
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_wmem="4096 65536 134217728"
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=4096
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen=3
sysctl -w net.core.netdev_max_backlog=5000

# Run iperf3 AFTER tuning:
iperf3 -c <target> -t 30 -P 10 -J > /tmp/iperf_after.json

# Compare: jq '.end.sum_sent.bits_per_second' iperf_*.json
# Calculate improvement percentage.
# Restore original settings from /tmp/tcp_before.txt.
6

K8s Pod-to-Pod Throughput Analysis

# Deploy iperf3 server on a pod:
kubectl run iperf-server --image=networkstatic/iperf3 -- --server
kubectl expose pod iperf-server --port=5201

# Test from another pod (same node if possible):
kubectl run iperf-client --rm -it --image=networkstatic/iperf3 -- \
  --client iperf-server --time 30 --parallel 4

# Record same-node throughput.

# Force client to a DIFFERENT node and test cross-node:
kubectl run iperf-client-2 --rm -it --image=networkstatic/iperf3 \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeName":"worker-2"}}' -- \
  --client iperf-server --time 30 --parallel 4

# Compare: same-node vs cross-node throughput.
# If cross-node < same-node by > 10% → CNI overlay overhead.
# If cross-node << same-node → MTU mismatch or network congestion.

# Cleanup:
kubectl delete pod iperf-server
kubectl delete svc iperf-server
Q7
Compare HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 from a network performance perspective. Why does HTTP/2 dramatically reduce page load times even on the same network?
Show Answer
Answer

HTTP/1.1: Each connection handles ONE request at a time. Browsers open 6-8 parallel connections to compensate. Each connection requires TCP+TLS handshake (60ms each). Head-of-line blocking: if request 1 on connection 3 is slow, all subsequent requests on that connection are blocked. HTTP/2: Multiplexes multiple streams over a single TCP connection. No head-of-line blocking between streams. One TCP+TLS handshake total. Benefits: 6 connections × 60ms = 360ms saved on handshake overhead. Server push can proactively send CSS/JS. Header compression (HPACK) reduces overhead. For anihpj/jobpost: enable use-http2: "true" in the nginx-ingress ConfigMap. Verify: curl --http2 https://jobpost.anihpj.com shows HTTP/2 200.

Q8
What is connection pooling and why is it critical for database performance? How do you implement it for Django + PostgreSQL?
Show Answer
Answer

Connection pooling keeps TCP connections to the database open and reuses them, instead of opening a new connection for every query. Without pooling: each query = TCP handshake (10ms) + TLS handshake (50ms) + PostgreSQL auth (5ms) = 65ms overhead. With pooling: connections established once, reused for all queries. 1000 queries/sec saves 65,000 ms of overhead. Django: DATABASES['default']['CONN_MAX_AGE'] = 600 (keep connections for 10 minutes). For high-traffic: deploy PgBouncer as a sidecar. Django connects to localhost:6432 (PgBouncer), which maintains a pool of 20-50 persistent connections to PostgreSQL. Reduces PostgreSQL connection count from 1000s to 20-50, preventing PostgreSQL max_connections exhaustion.

Q9
You run iperf3 between two K8s pods on different nodes and get 500 Mbps, but node-to-node iperf3 shows 9.4 Gbps. What could cause the 95% drop in pod-to-pod throughput?
Show Answer
Answer

Three likely causes: (1) CNI overlay MTU mismatch. VXLAN/GENEVE adds 50-100 bytes overhead. If node MTU is 1500 but overlay MTU is also 1500, packets > 1400 bytes get fragmented or dropped. iperf3 uses large packets by default → massive throughput drop. Fix: set CNI MTU to 1400-1450. (2) Single-stream bottleneck. Pod-to-pod may use a different path with higher latency → TCP window limits single-stream throughput. Test with -P 10. (3) CNI performance. Some CNIs (Flannel, Calico with iptables) add significant overhead. iptables rule count grows with services/policies. Cilium eBPF avoids this overhead. Test with iperf3 -M 1400 to force smaller packets — if throughput improves, it's MTU. If -P 10 improves dramatically, it's single-stream bottleneck. If neither helps, it's CNI overhead.

Q10
You're tasked with reducing p99 latency for anihpj/jobpost from 800ms to 500ms. Create a performance optimization plan using the tools and techniques from this chapter.
Show Answer
Answer

Step 1 — Measure baseline: iperf3 node-to-node and pod-to-pod. mtr to database. httping for app latency. Document current latency budget: DNS XXms, TCP XXms, TLS XXms, Transit XXms, App XXms. Step 2 — Quick wins (30 min): Enable BBR congestion control. Set TCP Fast Open=3. Increase tcp_rmem/wmem for BDP. Enable HTTP/2 on Ingress. Step 3 — Medium effort (2-4 hours): Add CONN_MAX_AGE=600 in Django settings for connection pooling. Deploy NodeLocal DNSCache for lower DNS latency. Enable TLS 1.3 on Ingress. Step 4 — Deep optimization: Deploy PgBouncer if DB connections are high. Profile Django queries with django-debug-toolbar. Move critical services closer (same AZ). After each step, re-measure the latency budget. Stop when p99 < 500ms target is met.

🔴 Part 10: Network SecurityChapters 33-35

Chapter 33: Network Security Fundamentals for SREs

Security isn't something you bolt on after deployment — it's something you embed in every layer of your network architecture. As an SRE, you're on the front line: you configure the firewalls, you write the NetworkPolicies, you manage the TLS certificates. This chapter gives you the mindset, the principles, and the practical knowledge to defend your infrastructure — from zero trust architecture to defending against specific attack types. Every concept is mapped to the anihpj/jobpost deployment so you can apply it immediately.

33.1 The Security Mindset — Assume Breach

Traditional security was a perimeter model: build a strong wall (firewall) around your network, and trust everything inside. Modern security is defense in depth: assume the perimeter WILL be breached, and build multiple layers of defense so no single failure is catastrophic:

DEFENSE IN DEPTH — Multiple Layers of Security
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DEFENSE IN DEPTH — No Single Point of Security Failure                         │
│                                                                               │
│  OLD MODEL (Perimeter Security):                                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Internet ──→ [FIREWALL] ──→ Trusted Internal Network (everything open)  │ │
│  │  PROBLEM: Once past the firewall, attacker has FREE ACCESS to everything.│ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  NEW MODEL (Defense in Depth):                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Internet                                                                │ │
│  │  │                                                                        │ │
│  │  ▼  LAYER 1: Cloud WAF/DDoS protection (Cloudflare, AWS Shield)           │ │
│  │  │                                                                        │ │
│  │  ▼  LAYER 2: Network ACLs / Security Groups (IP/port level)               │ │
│  │  │                                                                        │ │
│  │  ▼  LAYER 3: Load Balancer (TLS termination, request validation)          │ │
│  │  │                                                                        │ │
│  │  ▼  LAYER 4: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (pod-level firewall)                │ │
│  │  │                                                                        │ │
│  │  ▼  LAYER 5: mTLS (service-to-service authentication)                     │ │
│  │  │                                                                        │ │
│  │  ▼  LAYER 6: Application auth (JWT, API keys, OAuth)                     │ │
│  │  │                                                                        │ │
│  │  ▼                                                                         │ │
│  │  anihpj pod (jobpost Django app)                                          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Attacker must breach ALL 6 layers. Defense in depth.                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  PRINCIPLE OF LEAST PRIVILEGE:                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Every component gets ONLY the access it needs to function — nothing more.│ │
│  │  • jobpost needs:  PostgreSQL:5432, Redis:6379, outbound HTTPS            │ │
│  │  • jobpost does NOT need: direct internet ingress, other DBs, SSH         │ │
│  │  • PostgreSQL needs: nothing inbound except from jobpost pods              │ │
│  │  • Redis needs: nothing inbound except from jobpost pods                  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  EAST-WEST vs NORTH-SOUTH TRAFFIC:                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  North-South: Traffic entering/leaving the cluster (user ↔ service).      │ │
│  │  East-West: Traffic between services INSIDE the cluster (jobpost→DB).     │ │
│  │  Most breaches start with North-South, then pivot East-West.              │ │
│  │  Defense: Perimeter (N-S) + Micro-segmentation (E-W) = both directions.   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 DevSecOps Principle: Shift Security Left

Security must be embedded in every layer from the start — not bolted on after deployment. For anihpj/jobpost: (1) Dockerfile: run as non-root user, minimal base image, no secrets in layers. (2) K8s manifests: default-deny NetworkPolicy, readOnlyRootFilesystem, non-root SecurityContext. (3) CI/CD: scan images for CVEs, validate TLS config, check NetworkPolicy syntax. (4) Runtime: mTLS with Cilium/Istio, audit logging, anomaly detection. Security that's added after go-live is security that will be bypassed in production.

33.2 Zero Trust Networking — "Never Trust, Always Verify"

Zero Trust flips the traditional security model: no implicit trust based on network location. Just because a request comes from "inside the VPC" doesn't mean it's safe. Every connection must be authenticated and authorized:

ZERO TRUST ARCHITECTURE — Every Connection Authenticated
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ZERO TRUST — The Three Core Principles                                         │
│                                                                               │
│  1. VERIFY EXPLICITLY                                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Authenticate and authorize EVERY request based on ALL available data    │ │
│  │  points — user identity, device health, location, service identity,      │ │
│  │  anomaly detection. Never trust "it came from the internal network."     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  2. LEAST PRIVILEGE ACCESS                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Grant just enough access for just enough time (JIT/JEA).                 │ │
│  │  jobpost → PostgreSQL:5432 only. NOT jobpost → Redis (if not needed).    │ │
│  │  Access is: specific source → specific destination → specific port.      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  3. ASSUME BREACH                                                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Design as if the perimeter is already compromised.                       │ │
│  │  Micro-segment everything. Encrypt all traffic (mTLS).                     │ │
│  │  Minimize blast radius: one compromised pod can't reach everything.       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  GOOGLE BeyondCorp — Zero Trust in Practice:                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Google eliminated their corporate VPN. Instead:                           │ │
│  │  • Every request is authenticated (user + device certificate).            │ │
│  │  • Access proxy enforces policy (no direct network access to apps).       │ │
│  │  • No "internal network" concept — all traffic is untrusted.              │ │
│  │  Result: Google employees work from anywhere with no VPN.                  │ │
│  │  Same model applies to services: no implicit trust between microservices. │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ZERO TRUST IN KUBERNETES:                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  NetworkPolicies: Pod-level firewall rules (default-deny + specific allow)│ │
│  │  mTLS (Istio/Cilium): Encrypt + authenticate every service-to-service call│ │
│  │  SPIFFE/SPIRE: Cryptographic workload identity (every pod gets an ID)     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  anihpj Zero-Trust Journey:                                                │ │
│  │  Phase 1: default-deny NetworkPolicy (all pods isolated)                   │ │
│  │  Phase 2: Add specific allow rules (jobpost→DB, jobpost→Redis)            │ │
│  │  Phase 3: Enable mTLS via Cilium (encrypt all E-W traffic)                │ │
│  │  Phase 4: SPIFFE identities (every pod cryptographically verifiable)      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

33.4 Firewalls — Stateful and Stateless

Firewalls are the most fundamental security control. Understanding the difference between stateful and stateless firewalls determines what you can (and can't) do with each:

FeatureStateless FirewallStateful Firewall
How it worksChecks each packet independently against rules. No memory of past packets.Tracks connection state (SYN→SYN-ACK→ESTABLISHED). Remembers established flows.
Return trafficMust explicitly allow return traffic (separate rule needed).Automatically allows return traffic for established connections.
PerformanceFast (simple lookup). Good for high-throughput.Slower (conntrack table lookup). Conntrack can overflow.
ExampleAWS NACL, Azure NSG (basic), router ACLAWS Security Group, iptables (with conntrack), cloud NGFW
Rule countLimited (AWS NACL: 20 inbound, 20 outbound).Effectively unlimited (thousands of rules).

iptables as a Firewall — Default DROP vs Default ACCEPT

iptables FIREWALL POLICIES — Default DROP vs Default ACCEPT
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  iptables — BUILDING A HOST FIREWALL                                            │
│                                                                               │
│  DEFAULT ACCEPT (permissive — dangerous!):                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  iptables -P INPUT ACCEPT    ← Default policy: allow everything           │ │
│  │  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT                            │ │
│  │  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT                           │ │
│  │  iptables -A INPUT -j DROP    ← Last rule: drop everything else           │ │
│  │  # PROBLEM: If you flush rules, default ACCEPT exposes everything!        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  DEFAULT DROP (secure — recommended!):                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  iptables -P INPUT DROP      ← Default policy: drop everything            │ │
│  │  iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT   │ │
│  │  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT   ← Explicitly allow SSH   │ │
│  │  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT  ← Explicitly allow HTTPS │ │
│  │  # SAFE: Even if rules are flushed, default DROP protects everything.     │ │
│  │  # The ESTABLISHED,RELATED rule allows return traffic for our outbound.   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  CLOUD FIREWALLS:                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  AWS Security Groups: Stateful. Allow return traffic automatically.       │ │
│  │    Default: deny all inbound, allow all outbound.                          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  AWS NACLs: Stateless. Must allow BOTH inbound AND outbound explicitly.   │ │
│  │    Default: allow all. Use for subnet-level broad blocks.                 │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  GCP Firewall Rules: Stateful (implied). Applied at VPC level.            │ │
│  │    Priority-based (0-65535, lower = higher priority).                      │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Azure NSGs: Stateful. Applied at subnet or NIC level.                     │ │
│  │    Default rules allow VNet-internal and Azure Load Balancer traffic.     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Conntrack Internals — How Stateful Firewalls Track Connections

The connection tracking table (conntrack) is the secret behind stateful firewalls. Understanding its internals explains why they work — and why they can fail:

CONNTRACK INTERNALS — The State Table Behind Firewalls
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CONNTRACK — How Linux Tracks Every Connection                                  │
│                                                                               │
│  STATES: NEW (SYN seen) | ESTABLISHED (handshake done) | RELATED (to existing) │
│  INVALID (doesn't match any known connection — usually dropped).               │
│                                                                               │
│  ONE RULE CONTROLS ALL RETURN TRAFFIC:                                           │
│  iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT        │
│  # Recognizes return packets by conntrack 5-tuple (proto+src_ip+src_port+       │
│  # dst_ip+dst_port). Automatically allows responses to outbound connections.    │
│                                                                               │
│  TABLE SIZE: Default 65,536 entries. Each entry ~300 bytes. ~20MB total.       │
│  TIMEOUTS: TCP ESTABLISHED=5d, TIME_WAIT=120s, UDP=30s, ICMP=30s.             │
│  DNS USES UDP → every query = 30s entry. 10K qps × 30s = 300K entries → OVERFLOW│
│                                                                               │
│  WATCH CONNTRACK LIVE: watch 'cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count'  │
│  INCREASE LIMIT: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=262144               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SYN Cookies — Cryptographic Defense Against SYN Floods

SYN cookies encode connection state into the SYN-ACK sequence number using a cryptographic hash — no memory allocated until the handshake completes:

SYN COOKIES — Stateless Defense Against SYN Floods
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SYN COOKIES — How the Kernel Defeats SYN Floods Without Memory (RFC 4987)      │
│                                                                               │
│  WITHOUT COOKIES (vulnerable):                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Attacker SYN (spoofed) → Kernel allocates memory → SYN-ACK → no response │ │
│  │  Memory held 120s. 1000 spoofed SYNs/s × 120s = 120K dead entries → DoS. │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  WITH COOKIES (defended):                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Attacker SYN → Kernel computes: cookie = hash(secret, src_ip, src_port, │ │
│  │    dst_ip, dst_port, timestamp). ZERO memory allocated.                    │ │
│  │  SYN-ACK with cookie as sequence number → spoofed source never responds.  │ │
│  │  Legitimate client → ACK (cookie+1) → kernel verifies cookie → allocates. │ │
│  │  KEY: Cookie is STATELESS. No memory until handshake completes.            │ │
│  │  COST: TCP options lost during cookies (MSS, SACK, wscale) → slight perf  │ │
│  │  penalty for legitimate connections during attacks.                        │ │
│  │  ENABLE: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1  (default on most distros)      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

33.5 Network Segmentation and Micro-Segmentation

Network segmentation divides your network into isolated zones. Micro-segmentation takes this to the workload level — every pod, every container gets its own security boundary:

SEGMENTATION — From VLANs to Pod-Level Policies
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NETWORK SEGMENTATION — Limiting Blast Radius                                   │
│                                                                               │
│  PHYSICAL SEGMENTATION (VLANs):                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  VLAN 10 (Web):    Public-facing apps. Can reach: VLAN 20 only.           │ │
│  │  VLAN 20 (App):    Business logic. Can reach: VLAN 30 only.               │ │
│  │  VLAN 30 (DB):     Databases. Can reach: NOTHING external.                │ │
│  │  VLAN 40 (Mgmt):   SSH/Bastion. Can reach: ALL VLANs for admin.           │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Traffic between VLANs MUST go through a firewall/router.                  │ │
│  │  Physical separation = strongest isolation. Hardest to manage.            │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  KUBERNETES MICRO-SEGMENTATION (NetworkPolicies):                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  namespace: web                                                            │ │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐                 │ │
│  │  │  jobpost pod                                          │                 │ │
│  │  │  • Ingress: LB only (port 8000)                       │                 │ │
│  │  │  • Egress: PostgreSQL (5432), Redis (6379), DNS (53)  │                 │ │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘                 │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  namespace: data                                                           │ │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐                 │ │
│  │  │  postgres pod                                         │                 │ │
│  │  │  • Ingress: jobpost pods only (port 5432)             │                 │ │
│  │  │  • Egress: NONE                                       │                 │ │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘                 │ │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐                 │ │
│  │  │  redis pod                                            │                 │ │
│  │  │  • Ingress: jobpost pods only (port 6379)             │                 │ │
│  │  │  • Egress: NONE                                       │                 │ │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘                 │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  BENEFITS:                                                                 │ │
│  │  • Compromised jobpost pod cannot access other web pods.                  │ │
│  │  • Compromised jobpost pod cannot access DBs in other namespaces.         │ │
│  │  • PostgreSQL pods are completely isolated from internet.                  │ │
│  │  • Blast radius of ANY compromise is limited to specific paths.           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

How NetworkPolicies Are Enforced — iptables vs eBPF Under the Hood

NetworkPolicies aren't magic — they're implemented by your CNI plugin using either iptables or eBPF. Understanding the implementation helps debug "why is my traffic blocked?" questions:

NETWORKPOLICY ENFORCEMENT — iptables (Calico) vs eBPF (Cilium)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NETWORKPOLICY — How CNI Plugins Enforce Rules                                  │
│                                                                               │
│  CALICO (iptables):                                                             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Calico creates iptables chains for each policy:                          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Chain cali-pi-policy (pod ingress):                                       │ │
│  │    target     prot opt source               destination                   │ │
│  │    MARK       all  --  anywhere             anywhere    MARK match ...    │ │
│  │    DROP       all  --  anywhere             anywhere    /* default deny */│ │
│  │    ACCEPT     tcp  --  10.244.1.5           anywhere    /* jobpost pod */ │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Chain cali-po-policy (pod egress):                                        │ │
│  │    DROP       all  --  anywhere             anywhere    /* default deny */│ │
│  │    ACCEPT     udp  --  anywhere             10.96.0.10  /* DNS */         │ │
│  │    ACCEPT     tcp  --  anywhere             10.244.2.8  /* PostgreSQL */  │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  PROBLEM AT SCALE: Each policy adds rules. 100 policies × 50 pods =       │ │
│  │  5,000 rules. Each packet traverses ALL rules (O(n) scan).                │ │
│  │  Latency increases linearly with policy count.                             │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  CILIUM (eBPF):                                                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Cilium stores policies as eBPF map entries:                               │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  bpftool map dump name cilium_policy                                       │ │
│  │  # Shows: identity → allowed_peer_identities mapping                       │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Each pod gets a numeric "security identity" (e.g., jobpost=12345).       │ │
│  │  Policy lookup: hash(src_identity, dst_identity, port) → ALLOW/DENY.      │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  O(1) hash lookup vs O(n) iptables scan.                                  │ │
│  │  5,000 rules take the SAME time as 5 rules.                               │ │
│  │  Policies enforced at kernel level — no iptables traversal needed.        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  DEBUGGING POLICY ENFORCEMENT:                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  # iptables mode (Calico):                                                 │ │
│  │  iptables -L calico-pi-policy -n -v | grep <pod_name>                      │ │
│  │  # Shows packet counts per rule. If DROP count increases → policy active.  │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  # eBPF mode (Cilium):                                                     │ │
│  │  cilium policy get                                                        │ │
│  │  cilium monitor --type drop   # Watch dropped packets in real-time         │ │
│  │  # Shows exactly which policy and identity caused the drop.               │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

33.6 Common Network Attacks and How to Defend

Knowing how attacks work is the first step to defending against them. Here are the most common network attacks, how they work at the packet level, and how to protect your infrastructure:

AttackLayerDetection MethodMitigationanihpj Example
SYN FloodL4High SYN rate, many half-open connections (SYN_RECV)SYN cookies: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1. Rate limiting at LB level. Cloud DDoS scrubbing (AWS Shield).AWS Shield Standard (free) protects ALB from SYN floods automatically.
DNS AmplificationL7Massive DNS responses to your IP from open resolversRate-limit DNS traffic. Close open DNS resolvers. Use DNSSEC.CoreDNS rate-limiting plugin. Don't expose CoreDNS to internet.
ARP SpoofingL2Duplicate MAC for same IP in ARP tableStatic ARP entries for critical IPs. DHCP snooping on switches. Port security (limit MACs per port).Cloud VPC: ARP spoofing not possible (hypervisor-level isolation).
TLS DowngradeL5Weak ciphers accepted in handshakeHarden TLS config: disable TLS 1.0/1.1, weak ciphers. Enable HSTS.nginx-ingress: ssl-protocols: "TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3". ssl-ciphers: only ECDHE forward secrecy.
BGP HijackL3Unexpected AS_PATH changes, traffic reroutedRPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure). IRR filtering. Prefix allowlists.Cloud providers handle BGP security. Not directly relevant for anihpj.
Credential SniffingL7HTTP (not HTTPS) traffic carrying credentialsEnforce TLS everywhere. HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security). Redirect HTTP→HTTPS.Ingress: redirect HTTP:80→HTTPS:443. HSTS header: max-age=31536000.

│  │  Defense: SYN cookies (kernel handles without state). Rate limiting.      │ │
│  │    sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1 (enabled by default on most distros). │ │

│  │  Detection: unexpected IPs in DNS responses. dig +trace shows anomalies.  │ │

│  │  ARP spoofing redirects traffic through attacker. On wireless: passive    │ │

│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records. Chain of trust:            │ │
│  │  Root (.) → .com (DS record) → anihpj.com (DS record) → A record (RRSIG)  │ │
│  │  Each zone's DNSKEY is signed by the parent's DS record.                   │ │
│  │  Validation: resolver follows chain, verifying each RRSIG signature.       │ │

│  │  For anihpj: enable DNSSEC on your domain registrar. Route53 and           │ │

│  │  Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), path traversal, CSRF, bad user agents.       │ │
│  │  AWS WAF: rules on ALB/CloudFront. Managed rule groups (OWASP Top 10).    │ │

│  │    Each session gets unique keys. Even if server's private key is stolen   │ │
│  │    later, past sessions CANNOT be decrypted.                                │ │

│  │    authenticate in one step. Prevents tampering.                            │ │

🔐Zero TrustNever trust, always verify. No implicit trust based on network location. BeyondCorp eliminated VPNs.
🛡️FirewallsStateful (SG, iptables+conntrack) vs Stateless (NACL). Default DROP is safer than default ACCEPT.
🔲Micro-SegmentationPod-level isolation via NetworkPolicies. Blast radius limited to specific paths. East-West protection.
💥DDoS DefenseVolumetric (scrubbing), Protocol (SYN cookies), Application (WAF + rate limiting). Defend all 3 layers.
🎣DNS PoisoningForged DNS responses poison cache. Defense: DNSSEC. CoreDNS can validate. Monitor for unexpected IP changes.

🔏DNSSEC & WAFDNSSEC signs DNS records cryptographically. WAF blocks SQLi/XSS at L7. AWS WAF on ALB with OWASP rules.

🧩Policy EnforcementCalico: iptables chains (O(n) scan). Cilium: eBPF hash maps (O(1) lookup). 5000 policies = same speed as 5.
🔍Attack MatrixSYN flood, DNS amp, ARP spoof, TLS downgrade, BGP hijack, credential sniff — detection + mitigation for each.

☁️Cloud FirewallsAWS SG (stateful, per-ENI) vs NACL (stateless, per-subnet). GCP Firewall Rules. Azure NSGs. Choose the right tool.

🔑 Chapter 33 Key Takeaways

  1. Assume breach. Build defense in depth. No single firewall or policy is enough. Layer WAF, NACLs, SGs, NetworkPolicies, mTLS, and application auth. Each layer slows the attacker and increases detection chance.
  2. Zero trust means authenticate EVERY connection. Being "inside the VPC" is not authentication. Every service-to-service call must be authenticated (mTLS) and authorized (NetworkPolicy). Never trust network location.
  3. Default DROP is always safer than default ACCEPT. Start with deny-all, then add specific allow rules. A flushed ruleset with default ACCEPT exposes everything. With default DROP, nothing gets through.
  4. Micro-segment at the pod level. Don't just segment by VLAN or subnet. Each pod should only have exactly the network access it needs. Compromised web pod can't reach other web pods or databases in other namespaces.
  5. DDoS defense requires all three layers. Volumetric attacks need cloud scrubbing. Protocol attacks need SYN cookies and rate limiting. Application attacks need WAF. You need ALL three.

📝 Chapter 33 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is defense in depth and how does it differ from perimeter security? Give an example with the anihpj deployment.
Show Answer
Answer

Perimeter security puts one strong firewall at the network edge and trusts everything inside — if breached, the attacker has free access. Defense in depth layers multiple independent security controls: WAF/DDoS protection → Security Groups → NetworkPolicies → mTLS → Application auth. For anihpj: Cloudflare WAF blocks malicious requests at the edge. AWS Security Groups restrict inbound ports. Kubernetes NetworkPolicies limit pod-to-pod communication. Cilium mTLS encrypts and authenticates every service call. Django JWT authentication verifies user identity. An attacker must breach ALL 5 layers — compromising one layer doesn't give access to everything.

Q2
Explain the three principles of Zero Trust. How would you implement them for anihpj/jobpost on Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Verify Explicitly: Every request authenticated and authorized. Implement with mTLS (Cilium/Istio) so every service-to-service call presents a certificate. (2) Least Privilege: Grant minimum access needed. NetworkPolicies: jobpost→PostgreSQL:5432 only, not jobpost→Redis (if not needed). (3) Assume Breach: Design as if perimeter is compromised. Micro-segment all pods. Encrypt all East-West traffic. Minimize blast radius. anihpj journey: Phase 1: default-deny NetworkPolicy. Phase 2: specific allow rules. Phase 3: mTLS via Cilium. Phase 4: SPIFFE workload identities.

Q3
What's the difference between a stateful and stateless firewall? Give cloud (AWS) examples of each.
Show Answer
Answer

Stateless: Checks each packet independently — no memory. Must explicitly allow both inbound AND return traffic. Example: AWS NACL (Network ACL). If you allow inbound port 443, you must also allow outbound ephemeral ports (1024-65535) for return traffic. Limited to 20 rules per direction. Stateful: Tracks connection state. Automatically allows return traffic for established connections. Example: AWS Security Groups. Allow inbound 443, return traffic automatically allowed. No rule limit in practice. Uses conntrack table to track state — can overflow under high connection rates.

Q4
You're configuring iptables on a production server. Should you use default ACCEPT or default DROP? Why?
Show Answer
Answer

Always use default DROP (iptables -P INPUT DROP). With default ACCEPT, if someone accidentally flushes the rules (iptables -F), ALL traffic is suddenly allowed — the server is completely exposed. With default DROP, a flushed ruleset blocks everything — safe failure mode. Essential rule: iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT (allows return traffic for connections WE initiated). Then add explicit ACCEPT rules for needed ports (SSH, HTTPS). The ESTABLISHED,RELATED rule uses conntrack to identify legitimate return traffic without opening those ports to unsolicited inbound.

Q5
What is micro-segmentation and how does it differ from traditional network segmentation? How is it implemented in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

Traditional segmentation: Divide network by VLAN/subnet (web tier, app tier, DB tier). Coarse-grained. Traffic within same VLAN is unrestricted. Micro-segmentation: Segment at the individual workload (pod) level. Every pod has its own firewall boundary. Implemented in K8s with NetworkPolicies: podSelector selects target pods, ingress/egress rules specify allowed sources/destinations/ports. Default-deny + specific allows. Benefits: compromised web pod cannot access other web pods. DB pods are isolated from everything except the app pods. East-West protection within the same namespace/subnet.

Q6
Describe a SYN flood attack. How does it work at the packet level, and what kernel parameter mitigates it?
Show Answer
Answer

A SYN flood sends massive numbers of TCP SYN packets (often with spoofed source IPs) to a target. The server allocates resources for each half-open connection (SYN_RECV state), sending SYN-ACK and waiting for the final ACK. The attacker never completes the handshake. The server's SYN queue fills up → legitimate connections are dropped. Mitigation: SYN cookies (sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1). The kernel encodes connection information in the SYN-ACK sequence number instead of allocating memory. When the legitimate client responds with ACK, the kernel reconstructs the connection from the cookie. No state stored until the handshake completes. Effective against spoofed-source SYN floods.

D2

D3

D4

33.7 LAB: Security Hardening Bootcamp

🛠️ Security Hardening Lab — 6 Hands-On Exercises
1

Build a Default-DROP iptables Firewall

# Start with a clean state
iptables -F && iptables -X && iptables -t nat -F

# Set default DROP policies
iptables -P INPUT DROP
iptables -P FORWARD DROP
iptables -P OUTPUT ACCEPT  # Allow outbound from this host

# Allow loopback
iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT

# Allow established/related connections (critical!)
iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# Allow SSH (port 22)
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

# Verify: try SSH from another machine → should work.
# Try curl from this machine to another → should work (our outbound).
# External machine trying to curl this one → should fail (DROP).
# Flush rules: iptables -F → SSH should STILL be blocked (default DROP!).
2

Simulate and Mitigate a SYN Flood

# Check current SYN cookie status
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies

# Watch SYN_RECV count (half-open connections)
watch -n 1 'ss -s | grep synrec'

# From another machine, generate SYN flood:
# hping3 -S --flood -p 80 <target_ip> --rand-source
# Watch SYN_RECV spike → then cookies kick in → count stabilizes.

# If cookies were disabled (sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0):
# SYN_RECV continues climbing → server becomes unresponsive.
# Re-enable: sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1
3

Apply a Default-Deny NetworkPolicy

# Deploy two test pods
kubectl run web --image=nginx
kubectl expose pod web --port=80
kubectl run client --image=busybox:1.28 -- sleep 3600

# Test connectivity (should work — no policies yet):
kubectl exec client -- wget -qO- --timeout=2 http://web
# Output: nginx welcome page → unrestricted access

# Apply default-deny:
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
EOF

# Test again (should FAIL):
kubectl exec client -- wget -qO- --timeout=2 http://web
# Output: wget: download timed out → BLOCKED by default-deny

# Add explicit allow rule and verify.

docker run --rm drwetter/testssl.sh https://jobpost.anihpj.com

# Check for: Supported TLS versions (should be 1.2, 1.3 only)

ab -n 100 -c 10 https://jobpost.anihpj.com/api/

📖 Key Terms from Chapter 33

🏰Defense in Depth
A security strategy that layers multiple independent controls so that if one fails, others still protect the asset. Contrasts with perimeter security where one firewall breach exposes everything. Layers: physical, network, host, application, data.
🔐Zero Trust
A security model that eliminates implicit trust based on network location. Every connection is authenticated and authorized regardless of source. Three principles: verify explicitly, least privilege access, assume breach. Pioneered by Google's BeyondCorp.
🆔SPIFFE/SPIRE
Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone. SPIFFE defines a standard (X.509 SVID) for workload identity. SPIRE is the implementation. Every pod gets a cryptographically verifiable identity (spiffe://cluster.local/ns/default/sa/jobpost). Used by Istio, Cilium, and other service meshes for mTLS authentication.
🛡️Stateful Firewall
A firewall that tracks the state of network connections (TCP handshake state, UDP pseudo-state). Automatically allows return traffic for established connections. Examples: AWS Security Groups, iptables with conntrack. Uses connection tracking table — can overflow under DDoS.
📋Stateless Firewall
A firewall that evaluates each packet independently against rules, with no memory of past packets. Must explicitly allow both inbound and return traffic. Example: AWS NACL. Simpler, faster, but requires more rules. Limited rule capacity (~20 per direction for NACLs).
🔲Micro-Segmentation
Network segmentation at the individual workload (pod/container) level rather than subnet/VLAN. Each workload has its own security boundary. In Kubernetes: implemented via NetworkPolicies. Limits blast radius — one compromised pod cannot reach all others.
Q7
What is SPIFFE/SPIRE and how does it enable zero trust in Kubernetes? How does a pod prove its identity?
Show Answer
Answer

SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone) is a CNCF standard for workload identity. Every workload gets a SPIFFE ID in the format: spiffe://trust-domain/ns/namespace/sa/serviceaccount. SPIRE is the implementation — it runs as an agent on each node, authenticates pods via K8s service account tokens, and issues X.509 SVIDs (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Documents) — short-lived TLS certificates. Pod A connects to Pod B: both present their SVIDs. Mutual TLS handshake verifies both identities. Neither pod trusts the other based on IP — only based on cryptographic identity. This enables zero trust: even if an attacker gets a pod IP in the same namespace, they can't authenticate without a valid SVID.

Q8
How does Google's BeyondCorp implement zero trust? What lessons can you apply to Kubernetes networking?
Show Answer
Answer

Google eliminated their corporate VPN with BeyondCorp: (1) All applications are exposed to the internet — no "internal" network. (2) Every request goes through an access proxy that authenticates the user AND the device (device certificate + user credentials). (3) Access decisions are based on user identity, device health, location, and sensitivity of the resource — not network location. (4) No special "internal" access — working from office gives no extra privileges. Lessons for K8s: expose services via authenticated proxies (not raw IP access), implement mTLS everywhere (Cilium/Istio), use workload identity (SPIFFE) instead of IP-based trust, default-deny all network traffic, and never assume "same namespace = safe."

Q9
Compare AWS Security Groups and NACLs. When would you use each for the anihpj deployment?
Show Answer
Answer

Security Groups: Stateful. Applied at ENI (instance) level. Default: deny inbound, allow all outbound. Automatically allows return traffic. For anihpj: SG on EC2 nodes — allow inbound 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (public), allow 22 from bastion SG only, allow all traffic between nodes in the same SG. NACLs: Stateless. Applied at subnet level. Default: allow all. Must explicitly allow ephemeral ports for return traffic. For anihpj: NACL on public subnets — block known bad IPs. NACL on DB subnets — allow only from app subnet CIDR. Use SGs for fine-grained per-instance rules. Use NACLs for broad subnet-level blocks (blacklisting IPs, blocking entire protocols).

Q10
Design a complete DDoS defense strategy for anihpj/jobpost covering all three attack categories with specific tools and configurations.
Show Answer
Answer

Volumetric (Layer 3/4): AWS Shield Standard (free, always-on) protects ALB/CloudFront from SYN floods, UDP reflection. Upgrade to Shield Advanced ($3K/mo) for 24/7 DRT access and cost protection. Protocol: Enable SYN cookies on all nodes (sysctl). ALB connection draining. Limit connections per IP at nginx-ingress. Application (Layer 7): AWS WAF on ALB with rate-based rules (block IPs exceeding 2000 req/5min). nginx-ingress limit-req-zones for /api/ endpoints (100 req/sec/IP). CloudFront for caching static content (reduces origin load). Health check endpoints excluded from rate limits. Monitor: CloudWatch DDoS metrics, ALB RequestCount, HTTP 429 spike detection. Runbook: identify attack type → enable Shield Advanced mitigation → adjust WAF rules → contact AWS DRT if needed.

Chapter 35: TLS & Certificate Management in Production

TLS is the foundation of secure communication on the internet. Every HTTPS request, every gRPC call, every database connection — all protected by TLS. But certificates expire, get misconfigured, and break in production. This chapter covers the complete TLS certificate lifecycle, from issuance through monitoring and renewal, with a focus on Kubernetes-native automation via cert-manager. You'll learn mTLS for zero-trust service-to-service communication, monitoring to prevent certificate expiry incidents, and zero-downtime rotation strategies.

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ How cert-manager automates TLS in Kubernetes, from ACME challenges to auto-renewal and Secret management
  • ✅ Mutual TLS (mTLS) and SPIFFE — how to build zero-trust service-to-service authentication with cryptographic identity
  • ✅ Multi-layer TLS monitoring with Prometheus, blackbox_exporter, Grafana dashboards, and alerting rules
  • ✅ Six certificate rotation strategies for zero-downtime renewal — from Overwrite In-Place to Blue/Green swaps
  • ✅ The essential openssl toolkit for TLS debugging — 10 commands every network engineer must know by heart
  • ✅ Production TLS hardening best practices — cipher suites, HSTS, key sizes, OCSP stapling, and CT monitoring
🔐 Security Relevance
TLS / PKI CORE Zero-Trust Architecture ESSENTIAL Kubernetes Security CRITICAL Production SRE MANDATORY
💡 Certificate Expiry Is The #1 Cause of Avoidable Outages

Every major tech company has suffered a certificate expiry outage. In 2024 alone: Microsoft Teams (3-hour outage), Spotify (1-hour outage), and countless smaller incidents. The pattern is always the same: cert was issued, nobody monitored it, it expired silently, production went down. The fix is not "be more careful" — it's automation (cert-manager) + monitoring (Prometheus) + alerting (Alertmanager). This chapter gives you the complete blueprint.

35.1 The TLS Certificate Lifecycle

A TLS certificate goes through five distinct stages in its life. Missing any stage leads to production incidents — most commonly, certificates expiring silently:

TLS CERTIFICATE LIFECYCLE — 5 Stages
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TLS CERTIFICATE LIFECYCLE — Issue → Deploy → Monitor → Renew → Revoke         │
│                                                                               │
│  ① ISSUE: Generate private key + CSR → Submit to CA → CA validates domain      │
│     ownership (HTTP-01/DNS-01 challenge) → CA issues certificate.              │
│     Commands: openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key         │
│               -out tls.csr -subj "/CN=jobpost.anihpj.com"                      │
│                                                                               │
│  ② DEPLOY: Store cert + key as Kubernetes Secret → Mount in pod or reference   │
│     in Ingress. Ingress TLS section references the Secret.                     │
│     kubectl create secret tls jobpost-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key         │
│                                                                               │
│  ③ MONITOR: Track expiry date. Alert when < 30 days remain.                   │
│     Prometheus: certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds           │
│     openssl x509 -noout -enddate -in tls.crt                                   │
│                                                                               │
│  ④ RENEW: Generate new cert BEFORE expiry. cert-manager auto-renews 30 days    │
│     before expiry. Manual: new CSR → new cert → update Secret.                 │
│     ⚠️ cert-manager creates a NEW Secret; ensure Ingress references it!        │
│                                                                               │
│  ⑤ REVOKE (if compromised): Add cert to CRL (Certificate Revocation List)     │
│     or OCSP staple. Replace compromised cert immediately.                      │
│     openssl ca -revoke tls.crt -keyfile ca.key -cert ca.crt                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ GOTCHA — cert-manager Creates a NEW Secret

A cert renewed by cert-manager creates a NEW Secret with a different name or overwrites the existing one. If your Ingress references the OLD Secret name, traffic breaks after renewal. Use cert-manager annotations on the Ingress resource instead of static Secret references. When cert-manager is configured with an Issuer on the Ingress, it automatically updates the correct Secret.

35.2 cert-manager in Kubernetes

cert-manager automates the entire TLS certificate lifecycle within Kubernetes. It creates a pipeline: Issuer → CertificateRequest → Order → Challenge → Certificate → Secret:

cert-manager — Complete Setup for jobpost.anihpj.com

35.3 mTLS (Mutual TLS) — Zero-Trust Service-to-Service Authentication

Standard TLS verifies the SERVER's identity to the client. mTLS adds bi-directional authentication: the CLIENT must also present a valid certificate. This is the cornerstone of zero-trust networking — every service proves who it is on every call:

mTLS HANDSHAKE — Client AND Server Certificates
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  mTLS HANDSHAKE (TLS 1.3 with mutual auth):                                    │
│                                                                               │
│     CLIENT                                    SERVER                           │
│     ──────                                    ──────                           │
│  (1) ClientHello ──────────────────────────→                                  │
│      (supported ciphers, SNI "jobpost.anihpj.com")                            │
│                                                                               │
│  (2)                        ←─────────────── ServerHello + ServerCertificate  │
│                             (server cert for jobpost.anihpj.com)               │
│                             + CertificateRequest (ASK for client cert!)        │
│  ════════════════════ DIFFERENCE FROM STANDARD TLS ═════════════════════════  │
│  The CertificateRequest message is unique to mTLS. It says:                    │
│  "I've proven who I am — now YOU prove who YOU are."                           │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════  │
│                                                                               │
│  (3) ClientCertificate + ClientCertVerify ─→                                  │
│      (client cert for "payment-service.anihpj.local")                          │
│                                                                               │
│  (4) Server validates client cert:                                             │
│      ✓ Signed by trusted CA?    ✓ Not expired?                                │
│      ✓ SAN matches expected?    ✓ Not in CRL?                                 │
│                                                                               │
│  (5) Encrypted session established — BOTH identities verified                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
FeatureStandard TLSmTLS
Server Authentication✅ Server must present valid cert✅ Same
Client Authentication❌ Not required (use API key/JWT)✅ Client MUST present valid cert
Certificate Management1 cert per serverN certs (server + every client)
Key DistributionN/A for clientsEvery client needs a cert + key pair
InfrastructureSingle CA (Let's Encrypt)Internal CA + cert-manager + SPIFFE
Revocation ComplexityLowHigh — every client cert must be revocable
Kubernetes Ecosystemcert-manager (ACME)cert-manager (self-signed/CA) + Istio/Linkerd
💡 Service Mesh mTLS — Istio/Linkerd Handle the Heavy Lifting

In Kubernetes, Istio or Linkerd inject sidecar proxies (Envoy/Linkerd-proxy) into every pod. These proxies automatically negotiate mTLS between services. The application code doesn't need to handle TLS at all. cert-manager handles the certificate issuance; the service mesh handles the mTLS negotiation transparently.

SPIFFE — Universal Identity for Workloads (The Foundation of mTLS at Scale)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone)                     │
│                                                                               │
│  PROBLEM: In a microservices world, how does "payment-service" prove it's       │
│  actually payment-service and not an impostor? IP addresses? Network segments?  │
│  Those are network-level, not identity-level.                                   │
│                                                                               │
│  SOLUTION: SPIFFE — a standard for workload identity backed by cryptographic   │
│  proof. Every workload gets a SPIFFE ID (like a passport) that it uses to      │
│  authenticate to other services via mTLS.                                       │
│                                                                               │
│  SPIRE (SPIFFE Runtime Environment) — THE REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION:            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │                         SPIRE ARCHITECTURE                                │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐                       │ │
│  │  │   SPIRE SERVER   │◀───────▶│   SPIRE AGENT    │  (per-node daemon)    │ │
│  │  │   (centralized)  │   gRPC  │   (node-local)   │                       │ │
│  │  │                  │         │                  │                       │ │
│  │  │  - CA signing    │         │  - Workload       │                       │ │
│  │  │  - Identity      │         │    attestation    │                       │ │
│  │  │    registry      │         │  - SVID issuance  │                       │ │
│  │  │  - Node          │         │  - Key rotation   │                       │ │
│  │  │    attestation   │         │  - SVID caching   │                       │ │
│  │  └──────────────────┘         └────────┬─────────┘                       │ │
│  │                                        │ Unix domain socket              │ │
│  │                              ┌─────────▼─────────┐                       │ │
│  │                              │   WORKLOAD POD    │                       │ │
│  │                              │  (payment-service)│                       │ │
│  │                              │                   │                       │ │
│  │                              │  SPIFFE ID:       │                       │ │
│  │                              │  spiffe://anihpj  │                       │ │
│  │                              │  .com/ns/prod/    │                       │ │
│  │                              │  sa/payment-svc   │                       │ │
│  │                              │  ┌─────────────┐  │                       │ │
│  │                              │  │ x.509 SVID  │  │  ← Short-lived cert   │ │
│  │                              │  │ + Private Key│  │    (auto-rotated)     │ │
│  │                              │  └─────────────┘  │                       │ │
│  │                              └───────────────────┘                       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  SPIFFE IDENTITY FLOW — Step by Step:                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ① WORKLOAD ATTESTATION: SPIRE Agent verifies the workload's identity     │ │
│  │     using kernel-level attributes (UID, GID, process name, cgroup).       │ │
│  │     "Is this process REALLY running as the payment-service pod?"          │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ② SPIFFE ID ASSIGNMENT: Based on Kubernetes metadata (namespace,         │ │
│  │     service account, pod labels), SPIRE assigns a unique SPIFFE ID:       │ │
│  │     spiffe://anihpj.com/ns/prod/sa/payment-svc                            │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ③ x.509 SVID ISSUANCE: SPIRE Agent issues a short-lived (default 1h)     │ │
│  │     x.509 certificate (SVID) bound to that SPIFFE ID. The cert + key      │ │
│  │     are written to a shared memory volume accessible by the workload.     │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ④ mTLS HANDSHAKE: When payment-service calls job-service, the Envoy     │ │
│  │     sidecar presents the SVID as the client certificate. Job-service      │ │
│  │     validates: ✓ Signed by trusted SPIRE CA? ✓ SPIFFE ID matches          │ │
│  │     expected identity? ✓ Not expired? ✓ Not revoked?                      │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  ⑤ CONTINUOUS ROTATION: SPIRE Agent automatically rotates SVIDs before    │ │
│  │     expiry. The workload always has a valid certificate. ZERO manual      │ │
│  │     intervention. Compromised key blast radius: max 1 hour.                │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  SPIFFE IN ANIHPJ — Real Benefits:                                             │
│  - Every microservice (payment, job, user, notification) has a cryptographically│
│    verifiable identity — not just an IP address                                │
│  - Database connections: PostgreSQL accepts connections ONLY from pods with    │
│    specific SPIFFE IDs (e.g., spiffe://anihpj.com/ns/prod/sa/job-service)     │
│  - Audit trail: Every mTLS handshake is logged with SPIFFE IDs of both parties │
│  - Compliance: SPIFFE-based identity satisfies PCI-DSS, SOC 2, FedRAMP        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📝 SPIFFE vs cert-manager — Different Roles, Complementary

cert-manager issues certificates for Ingress/public-facing endpoints (via ACME/Let's Encrypt). SPIFFE/SPIRE issues short-lived identity certificates for internal workload-to-workload mTLS. They work together: cert-manager handles North-South traffic (ingress); SPIFFE handles East-West traffic (service mesh). In a complete zero-trust architecture you need BOTH.

35.4 TLS Monitoring & Alerting — Catch Expiry BEFORE It Happens

Certificate expiry is a leading cause of production outages. The fix is simple — monitor expiry and alert early. cert-manager exposes Prometheus metrics; combine them with blackbox-exporter for external probing and PrometheusRules for alerts:

TLS MONITORING STACK — 3 Layers
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TLS MONITORING — LAYERED APPROACH FOR ZERO BLIND SPOTS                        │
│                                                                               │
│  LAYER 1: KUBERNETES (Internal — cert-manager metrics):                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Prometheus scrapes cert-manager controller @ :9402/metrics:              │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds                     │ │
│  │    {name="jobpost-tls", namespace="default"}  1710614400  # Unix epoch    │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  certmanager_certificate_ready_status                                     │ │
│  │    {name="jobpost-tls"}  1  # 1=Ready, 0=Not Ready                        │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  Days until expiry = (expiration_timestamp - time()) / 86400              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  LAYER 2: EXTERNAL (blackbox_exporter probes):                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Prometheus Job:                                                          │ │
│  │  - job_name: 'blackbox-tls'                                               │ │
│  │    metrics_path: /probe                                                   │ │
│  │    params:                                                                │ │
│  │      module: [http_2xx]                                                   │ │
│  │      target: [https://jobpost.anihpj.com]                                 │ │
│  │    static_configs:                                                        │ │
│  │      - targets: ['jobpost.anihpj.com:443']                                │ │
│  │                                                                           │ │
│  │  probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry — expiry from external perspective        │ │
│  │  probe_success — 1 if TLS handshake OK + cert valid                       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  LAYER 3: ALERTING RULES:                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  groups:                                                                  │ │
│  │  - name: tls-alerts                                                       │ │
│  │    rules:                                                                 │ │
│  │    - alert: CertificateExpiringSoon                                       │ │
│  │      expr: certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds           │ │
│  │              - time() < 30 * 86400                                        │ │
│  │      annotations:                                                         │ │
│  │        summary: "Certificate {{ $labels.name }} expires in < 30 days"     │ │
│  │        runbook: "https://wiki.anihpj.com/tls-renewal"                     │ │
│  │    - alert: CertificateExpiringCritical                                   │ │
│  │      expr: certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds           │ │
│  │              - time() < 7 * 86400                                         │ │
│  │      labels:                                                              │ │
│  │        severity: critical                                                 │ │
│  │    - alert: CertificateNotReady                                           │ │
│  │      expr: certmanager_certificate_ready_status == 0                      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

⚠️ GOTCHA — cert-manager Only Manages Certificates IT Created

cert-manager only renews certificates that have the renewBefore annotation (default: 30 days before expiry). If you manually created a Kubernetes Secret with a TLS certificate, cert-manager will NOT manage, monitor, or renew it. You MUST create a Certificate resource and let cert-manager create the Secret. Always let cert-manager CREATE the Secret. If you need to bring your own certificate, use the Certificate resource with a secretTemplate annotation, not a manual kubectl create secret tls.

35.5 Certificate Rotation Strategies — Zero Downtime

Certificates expire. Rotating them without downtime requires careful orchestration. Here are four strategies, from simple to advanced:

StrategyMechanismDowntimeComplexityBest For
1. Overwrite In-Placecert-manager updates the SAME Secret → Ingress controller detects changeNone (sub-second)Lowcert-manager default — 90% of use cases
2. Hot Reloadnginx/Envoy watch Secret via K8s API, call nginx -s reload on change. Envoy xDS-based — truly zero-downtime, no process restartNone for Envoy; sub-second for nginxLownginx-ingress (k8s watch) or Envoy Gateway (xDS)
3. Dual-Cert Transition (SNI-based)Serve BOTH old and new cert during rotation window via SNI matchingNoneMediumHAProxy, custom nginx configs, legacy clients
4. Dual-Secret SwapCreate new Secret (tls-new) → update Ingress ref → delete oldNone (atomic swap)MediumManual rotation, controlled cut-over, audit trails
5. Rolling Pod Restartkubectl rollout restart deployment anihpj-jobpostNone (rolling)LowPost cert Secret update, reload in-memory certs
6. Blue/Green Cert SwapDeploy new Ingress with new cert Secret → test → switch DNSNone (DNS TTL)HighPCI-DSS, critical prod, 100% pre-validation
