Zero-Downtime Certificate Rotation — Complete Sequence
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ZERO-DOWNTIME ROTATION — END-TO-END TIMELINE (cert-manager + nginx-ingress)   │
│                                                                               │
│  T-30 DAYS: cert-manager detects expiry approaching (renewBefore: 720h)       │
│       │                                                                        │
│  T-29 DAYS: cert-manager creates new CertificateRequest → ACME Order →        │
│       │    HTTP-01 Challenge → CA issues new certificate                       │
│       │                                                                        │
│  T-29 DAYS: cert-manager writes new cert+key to SAME Secret (overwrite)       │
│       │    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐                   │
│       │    │ Secret "jobpost-tls" BEFORE:  OLD cert       │                   │
│       │    │ Secret "jobpost-tls" AFTER:   NEW cert       │                   │
│       │    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘                   │
│       │                                                                        │
│  T-29 DAYS: Kubelet syncs Secret to node (within 60s by default)             │
│       │                                                                        │
│  T-29 DAYS: nginx-ingress watches Secret change via K8s API                   │
│       │    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐                   │
│       │    │ nginx -s reload (graceful shutdown):          │                   │
│       │    │  1. New worker processes start → load NEW cert│                   │
│       │    │  2. Old workers finish active connections     │                   │
│       │    │  3. Old workers exit when connections drain   │                   │
│       │    │  DOWNTIME: < 100ms (connection accept gap)    │                   │
│       │    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘                   │
│       │                                                                        │
│  T-29 DAYS: NEW connections → NEW cert. EXISTING connections → OLD cert       │
│       │         until they complete (keep-alive) or max worker shutdown        │
│       │                                                                        │
│  T-29 DAYS: cert-manager updates Certificate.status:                          │
│       │    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐                   │
│       │    │ Status:                                       │                   │
│       │    │   Conditions:                                 │                   │
│       │    │     Type: Ready    Status: True               │                   │
│       │    │     NotAfter: (new expiry date)               │                   │
│       │    │     RenewalTime: (timestamp)                  │                   │
│       │    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘                   │
│                                                                               │
│  MONITORING CONFIRMS:                                                          │
│  ✓ certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds — reset to new date  │
│  ✓ certmanager_certificate_renewal_count — incremented                        │
│  ✓ probe_success — remains 1 (no interruption)                               │
│  ✓ HTTP 5xx rate — zero during rotation window                               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ GOTCHA — Test Your Ingress Controller's Reload Behavior

Some Ingress controllers (older nginx versions, certain HAProxy configs) require a full process reload for certificate changes — this drops active connections. Before going to production: 1) Test cert rotation under load, 2) Verify zero connection drops with hey -n 100000 -c 50, 3) Check controller logs for "reloading" events, 4) If using nginx, ensure worker-shutdown-timeout is set high enough for long-lived connections (default: 240s for graceful shutdown). Envoy Gateway (xDS) and Traefik handle cert changes without reload — prefer them for zero-downtime critical paths.

⚠️ CRITICAL — cert-manager Overwrites Manually Created Secrets

If a Certificate resource's secretName matches a Secret you manually created, cert-manager WILL overwrite it on the next reconciliation loop. Either let cert-manager OWN the Secret (don't create it manually) or use a different secretName for manual certs. Never fight cert-manager for ownership.

35.6 TLS Debugging with OpenSSL — A Practitioner's Toolkit

When TLS breaks, you need fast diagnostics. These openssl commands are the Swiss Army knife of TLS debugging — from verifying chain trust to inspecting cipher suites:

TLS DEBUGGING — 10 ESSENTIAL OpenSSL COMMANDS
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TLS DEBUGGING — openssl COMMANDS EVERY NETWORK ENGINEER MUST KNOW             │
│                                                                               │
│  1. CHECK CERTIFICATE EXPIRY:                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  openssl x509 -in tls.crt -noout -dates -subject -issuer                │ │
│  │  → notBefore=Mar  1 00:00:00 2025 GMT                                    │ │
│  │  → notAfter=May 30 23:59:59 2025 GMT  (90-day Let's Encrypt cert)        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  2. VERIFY CHAIN OF TRUST:                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  openssl verify -CAfile ca-bundle.crt tls.crt                            │ │
│  │  → tls.crt: OK                                                           │ │
│  │  # Bad chain: error 20 at 0 depth lookup: unable to get local issuer cert│ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  3. FETCH REMOTE CERT (no browser):                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  openssl s_client -connect jobpost.anihpj.com:443 -servername \         │ │
│  │    jobpost.anihpj.com 2>&1 | openssl x509 -noout -text                  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  4. CHECK TLS VERSION + CIPHER NEGOTIATED:                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  openssl s_client -connect jobpost.anihpj.com:443 -tls1_2 \             │ │
│  │    2>&1 | grep -E "Protocol|Cipher"                                      │ │
│  │  → Protocol: TLSv1.3                                                      │ │
│  │  → Cipher: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384                                        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  5. CHECK ALL SAN NAMES ON A CERT:                                             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  openssl x509 -in tls.crt -noout -ext subjectAltName                     │ │
│  │  → DNS:jobpost.anihpj.com, DNS:*.anihpj.com                              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  6. DECODE A PEM CERTIFICATE:                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  openssl x509 -in tls.crt -noout -text | less                            │ │
│  │  # Human-readable: Serial, Issuer, Validity, Public Key, Extensions       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  7. CHECK PRIVATE KEY MATCHES CERT (MODULUS COMPARISON):                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  openssl x509 -in tls.crt -noout -modulus | md5sum                       │ │
│  │  openssl rsa -in tls.key -noout -modulus | md5sum                        │ │
│  │  # Same hash = matching pair ✓                                           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  8. TEST mTLS (client cert required):                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  openssl s_client -connect internal-api.anihpj.local:443 \               │ │
│  │    -cert client.crt -key client.key -CAfile ca.crt                       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  9. GENERATE SELF-SIGNED CERT FOR DEV/TESTING:                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -nodes -days 365 \                   │ │
│  │    -keyout dev-key.pem -out dev-cert.pem \                                │ │
│  │    -subj "/CN=localhost" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost"          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  10. DUMP ALL CERTIFICATES IN A PEM BUNDLE:                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile fullchain.pem | \                    │ │
│  │    openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -noout                                     │ │
│  │  # Shows each cert in the chain: leaf → intermediate → root               │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 Browser vs CLI Debugging

Your browser's TLS information (click the padlock → Certificate) is great for quick checks, but it uses the OS trust store, not your server's CA bundle. Always validate with openssl s_client from a machine that uses the same trust store as your production clients.

35.7 TLS Best Practices — Production Hardening

TLS configuration mistakes are among the most common security audit findings. Here are battle-tested production best practices for TLS configuration:

Category✅ DO❌ DON'T
TLS VersionTLS 1.3 only (or TLS 1.2 with strong ciphers if legacy needed)TLS 1.0/1.1 — deprecated, vulnerable to POODLE, BEAST
Cipher SuitesECDHE + AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305. TLS 1.3 has only 5 secure ciphersRC4, 3DES, CBC-mode ciphers, NULL ciphers, EXPORT-grade
Key SizeRSA 2048-bit minimum, ECDSA P-256 or betterRSA 1024-bit, DSA (broken)
HSTSStrict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preloadOmitting HSTS — allows SSL stripping attacks
Certificate Validity90 days (Let's Encrypt standard). Short-lived = less risk if compromised365+ days — harder to revoke, longer exposure if compromised
Renewal BufferAlert at 30 days, critical at 7 days. cert-manager auto-renews at 30dRenewing on the day of expiry — one glitch and you're down
Private Key StorageKubernetes Secret (encrypted at rest). AWS KMS / HashiCorp Vault for sensitive keysHardcoding in code, committing to git, storing in configmaps
mTLS ScopeAll internal service-to-service traffic (zero-trust principle)mTLS only at the edge — internal traffic remains plaintext
Certificate TransparencyMonitor CT logs for mis-issued certs (crt.sh, Cloudflare CT Mon)Blindly trusting CAs — they have been compromised before (DigiNotar, Comodo)
CRL/OCSPEnable OCSP stapling. Check CRL for internal CAsRelying solely on cert expiry — revocation is for compromised keys
🚨 COMMON TLS MISTAKES THAT CAUSE OUTAGES

1. Missing intermediate cert — Full chain not served. Browsers/curl fail. Fix: concatenate cert + intermediate into fullchain.pem.
2. Secret name mismatch — Ingress references a Secret that doesn't exist. kubectl describe ingress shows the TLS error.
3. Namespace mismatch — cert-manager Certificate is in one namespace, Ingress is in another. Secrets are namespace-scoped.
4. ACME rate limit hit — Let's Encrypt has strict per-domain rate limits (5 certs/week), staging has higher (50/week). Always test with staging first.

35.8 LAB: TLS in Production for anihpj/jobpost

Hands-on lab to deploy TLS end-to-end for the jobpost application using cert-manager, configure mTLS, and simulate certificate expiry scenarios:

Lab 1
Install cert-manager & Issue First Certificate
  • kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.15.0/cert-manager.yaml
  • Create a ClusterIssuer for Let's Encrypt staging
  • Create a Certificate resource for jobpost.anihpj.com
  • Configure the Ingress to reference secretName: jobpost-tls
  • Verify: curl -vI https://jobpost.anihpj.com shows TLSv1.3
Lab 2
Enable HSTS and Security Headers on nginx-ingress
  • Add ConfigMap to nginx-ingress: hsts: "true", hsts-max-age: "31536000", hsts-include-subdomains: "true"
  • Add annotation to Ingress: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet for CSP and X-Frame-Options
  • Verify headers: curl -sI https://jobpost.anihpj.com | grep -i strict
Lab 3
Set Up TLS Monitoring with Prometheus
  • Create ServiceMonitor for cert-manager metrics endpoint
  • Write PrometheusRule: CertificateExpiringSoon at 30d, CertificateExpiringCritical at 7d
  • Set up Alertmanager config to route TLS alerts to #sre-tls Slack channel
  • Test: manually create a cert with 25-day expiry and verify alert fires
Lab 4
Simulate Certificate Expiry — Test Your Alerting
  • Create a self-signed cert with 5-day validity: openssl req -x509 -days 5 ...
  • Deploy as expiring-tls Secret. Create a test Ingress using it
  • Wait for Prometheus alert to fire at 7 days. Verify Alertmanager routes to Slack/email
  • Practice the runbook: renew cert → update Secret → verify → close alert
Lab 5
Configure mTLS Between jobpost Services
  • Create an internal CA: openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -days 3650 ... -subj "/CN=anihpj Internal CA"
  • Generate client certs for payment-service, job-service
  • Configure Django to require client certs (modify settings.py/Django TLS config)
  • Test: curl --cert client.crt --key client.key https://internal-api succeeds; curl without cert fails with 403
Lab 6
Zero-Downtime Certificate Rotation Drill
  • Simulate production load: hey -n 100000 -c 50 https://jobpost.anihpj.com
  • Perform dual-secret swap: create new Secret → update Ingress → verify
  • Monitor hey output — confirm ZERO errors during the swap
  • Check nginx-ingress logs: kubectl logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx | grep "reload\|old_secret\|new_secret"
  • Time the operation: target < 5 seconds from edit to all connections using new cert

Key Takeaways — Chapter 35

🔑 Core Principles
  • cert-manager is a non-negotiable Kubernetes component — Manually managing TLS in Kubernetes is a recipe for outages. Let cert-manager own the entire lifecycle.
  • Monitor expiry at MULTIPLE layers — Internal (cert-manager metrics) + External (blackbox_exporter) + Alerting (PrometheusRules). Never rely on a single source of truth for expiry.
  • mTLS is the foundation of zero-trust networking — In a production microservices environment, every service should prove its identity on every call. Use a service mesh to handle the complexity.
  • Short-lived certificates are MORE secure — 90-day certs limit the blast radius of a compromised key. Automation (cert-manager) makes short-lived certs operationally feasible.
  • Practice certificate rotation BEFORE it's an emergency — The worst time to learn certificate rotation is when your production site is down. Run the LAB exercises quarterly.
  • openssl is your TLS stethoscope — Master s_client, x509 -text, verify, and modulus comparison. These commands diagnose 90% of TLS issues in seconds.
📖 Key Terminology — TLS & Certificates
ACMEAutomated Certificate Management Environment — protocol used by Let's Encrypt for automated domain validation and certificate issuance
cert-managerKubernetes-native certificate controller. Automates issuance and renewal of TLS certificates via ACME or internal CAs
CSRCertificate Signing Request — the signed request a client sends to a CA to obtain a certificate. Contains the public key and claimed identity
Intermediate CAA subordinate CA whose certificate is signed by the Root CA. The intermediate signs leaf certificates. Root CA stays offline
Chain of TrustLeaf cert → Intermediate CA cert → Root CA cert. Every link must be valid for the entire chain to be trusted
SANSubject Alternative Name — extension that lists all domains/IPs the certificate is valid for. Replaces the deprecated Common Name (CN) field
OCSP StaplingThe server includes a cached OCSP response in the TLS handshake, proving the certificate hasn't been revoked without the client making a separate OCSP request
SPIFFESecure Production Identity Framework for Everyone — a standard for workload identity and mTLS in cloud-native environments. SPIRE is the reference implementation
HSTSHTTP Strict Transport Security — a response header that tells browsers to only connect via HTTPS, preventing SSL stripping attacks
CT LogsCertificate Transparency Logs — publicly auditable append-only logs of all issued certificates. Prevents mis-issuance by CAs

📋 Exam-Style Questions

Q1
Explain the difference between standard TLS and mTLS. In what scenario would you choose mTLS over standard TLS + API keys?
Show Answer
Answer

Standard TLS: Only the SERVER presents a certificate. Client authenticates via other means (JWT, API keys, OAuth). mTLS: BOTH client AND server present certificates. mTLS is preferred when: 1) Zero-trust architecture — every service must prove identity on every call, 2) No user-level authentication available (machine-to-machine), 3) Certificate-based identity is tied to SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identity, 4) Regulatory compliance requires cryptographic proof of both parties. mTLS has higher operational cost (managing client certs, rotation, revocation) so use a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) to automate it.

Q2
Your jobpost.anihpj.com certificate expires in 4 hours. You use cert-manager with Let's Encrypt. Walk through your immediate actions using a dual-secret swap strategy.
Show Answer
Answer
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ IMMEDIATE (T-4 hours):                                          │
│  1. Check cert-manager status:                                  │
│     kubectl describe certificate jobpost-tls                    │
│     → If "Ready: False" with ACME error, auto-renewal failed    │
│  2. Generate new cert manually:                                 │
│     openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes \                  │
│       -keyout tls-emergency.key -out tls-emergency.csr \        │
│       -subj "/CN=jobpost.anihpj.com"                            │
│     # Get signed by LE manually or use a backup cert             │
│  3. Dual-secret swap:                                           │
│     kubectl create secret tls jobpost-tls-emergency \           │
│       --cert=tls-emergency.crt --key=tls-emergency.key          │
│     kubectl edit ingress jobpost-ingress \                      │
│       # Change secretName → jobpost-tls-emergency              │
│  4. Verify: curl -vI https://jobpost.anihpj.com                 │
│  5. Post-mortem: Why did cert-manager fail?                     │
│     - ACME rate limit? DNS challenge timeout?                    │
│     - Fix root cause before next renewal cycle                  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q3
Describe the 3-layer TLS monitoring architecture. Why is a multi-layer approach necessary?
Show Answer
Answer

Layer 1 — Internal (cert-manager metrics): Scrapes cert-manager's Prometheus endpoint for expiration timestamps and ready status. Catches issues with the issuance process itself. Layer 2 — External (blackbox_exporter): Probes the TLS endpoint from OUTSIDE the cluster. Verifies the cert from the client's perspective, catching issues like missing intermediate certs or wrong cert served. Layer 3 — Alerting (PrometheusRules): Translates metrics into actionable alerts at 30d (warning) and 7d (critical). Multi-layer is necessary because: A single layer can lie. cert-manager metrics show "Ready" but the Ingress might reference the wrong Secret. blackbox_exporter shows the cert works but doesn't track WHEN it will expire from the source. Redundancy eliminates blind spots.

Q4
You've configured cert-manager with a ClusterIssuer for Let's Encrypt. The Certificate resource shows "Ready: False" with the error "ACME order failed: 400 urn:ietf:params:acme:error:rateLimited". What happened and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

Let's Encrypt rate limit triggered. Production LE has strict limits: 5 certificates per domain per week, 5 duplicate certificates per week. Common causes: 1) Repeatedly deleting/recreating the Certificate resource (each creates a new order), 2) ClusterIssuer recreation resets the ACME account, 3) Testing with production endpoint instead of staging. Fix: 1) Wait until the rate limit resets (max 1 week), 2) Switch to staging ClusterIssuer for testing: letsencrypt-staging (50 certs/week), 3) Use kubectl describe certificate to check the order state, 4) Consider DNS-01 challenge if HTTP-01 is flaky (DNS-01 has fewer rate limits). Prevention: Always test with staging first. Use disableAccountKeyGeneration: true on ClusterIssuer to prevent accidental account recreation.

Q5
Compare the four certificate rotation strategies. Which would you use for a PCI-DSS compliant payment processing service and why?
Show Answer
Answer

For PCI-DSS (which requires audit trails and formal change control): Use Strategy 4 (Blue/Green Cert Swap). Rationale: 1) Pre-deployment validation — the new cert can be tested against the PCI compliance scanner BEFORE it serves real traffic, 2) Atomic cut-over — DNS change allows instant rollback if the new cert fails validation, 3) Audit trail — the blue/green process creates clear audit events: new cert deployed → tested → cut-over → old cert decommissioned. Strategy 1 (auto-renew) is too opaque for PCI auditors. Strategy 2 (dual-secret) is faster but lacks pre-deployment validation. Strategy 3 (rolling restart) doesn't address cert validation. For non-PCI services, Strategy 1 (cert-manager auto-renew) + Strategy 3 (rolling restart) is sufficient.

Q6
You deploy a new TLS certificate to a Kubernetes Secret. The application still serves the old certificate. What are the three most likely causes?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Pod hasn't reloaded — Kubernetes Secrets mounted as volumes are auto-updated by the kubelet (within ~60s), but applications must watch for changes. Secrets mounted as ENV vars are NOT updated until pod restart. Fix: kubectl rollout restart deployment. 2) nginx-ingress cached the old cert — nginx-ingress reloads its config when it detects Ingress Secret changes, but large clusters have a reload delay. Check: kubectl logs ingress-nginx-controller | grep "reloading". Fix: force reload with kubectl delete pod on the ingress controller. 3) Wrong Secret referenced — The Ingress still points to the OLD Secret name. kubectl describe ingress shows the TLS section. Fix: update secretName in the Ingress TLS spec.

Q7
Write the openssl command to verify that a certificate's private key matches the public key in the certificate, AND explain what it checks.
Show Answer
Answer
# Compare modulus (the mathematical heart of the key pair)
$ openssl x509 -in tls.crt -noout -modulus | openssl md5
(stdin)= a1b2c3d4e5f6...

$ openssl rsa -in tls.key -noout -modulus | openssl md5
(stdin)= a1b2c3d4e5f6...

# Same hash → key pair matches ✓
# Different hash → key mismatch ✗

# What it checks:
# The RSA modulus 'n' is derived from p×q (two large primes).
# Both the certificate (public key) and the private key share the
# same modulus 'n'. If the moduli match, the keys are a valid pair.
# This is a one-way check: you can verify the public key matches
# the private key WITHOUT exposing the private components (p, q, d)
Q8
Explain HSTS with the includeSubDomains and preload directives. What risk does HSTS preloading mitigate?
Show Answer
Answer

Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload. max-age: Browser remembers this domain is HTTPS-only for 1 year. includeSubDomains: Applies HSTS to *.anihpj.com (critical — attackers can spoof api.anihpj.com). preload: Domain is hardcoded into browser source code (hstspreload.org). This mitigates the "trust-on-first-use" attack: Without preload, a user's FIRST visit to your site could be intercepted via SSL stripping (the attacker prevents the HTTPS redirect). With preload, the browser KNOWS to use HTTPS even before the first connection. Risk: Once preloaded, ALL subdomains MUST have valid HTTPS — revocation from the preload list takes months.

Q9
Design a TLS certificate hierarchy for anihpj with 3 environments (dev/staging/prod), internal services (mTLS), and external endpoints (public TLS).
Show Answer
Answer
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ANIHPJ TLS CERTIFICATE HIERARCHY:                               │
│                                                                 │
│ ROOT CA (Offline, air-gapped, HSM-backed):                      │
│   └── Internal PKI Intermediate CA (online, signs internal certs)│
│        ├── Dev cluster certs (30d, auto-renewed by cert-manager) │
│        ├── Staging cluster certs (90d)                            │
│        ├── Production internal certs for mTLS (90d)              │
│        │    ├── payment-service.anihpj.local                     │
│        │    ├── job-service.anihpj.local                         │
│        │    └── user-service.anihpj.local                        │
│        └── SPIFFE SPIFFE IDs for workload identity               │
│            └── spiffe://anihpj.com/ns/prod/sa/payment-svc       │
│                                                                 │
│ PUBLIC-FACING (Let's Encrypt via cert-manager):                   │
│   ├── jobpost.anihpj.com (LE prod, 90d, auto-renew)             │
│   ├── api.anihpj.com (LE prod, 90d, auto-renew)                 │
│   └── *.anihpj.com wildcard via DNS-01 challenge                │
│                                                                 │
│ RATIONALE:                                                       │
│ - Internal PKI for mTLS: full control, short-lived certs,        │
│   SPIFFE integration. Not dependent on external service.         │
│ - Let's Encrypt for public: free, automated, widely trusted.     │
│ - Separate internal/external CAs: compromise of internal CA      │
│   doesn't affect public trust.                                   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q10
You're debugging a production TLS outage. curl https://jobpost.anihpj.com returns SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate. List the diagnostic steps in order and the openssl commands you'd use at each step.
Show Answer
Answer
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SYSTEMATIC TLS DEBUGGING — "Unable to get local issuer cert"     │
│                                                                 │
│ STEP 1: Fetch remote cert, check chain:                          │
│ $ openssl s_client -connect jobpost.anihpj.com:443 \             │
│     -servername jobpost.anihpj.com -showcerts 2>&1 | \           │
│     grep -E "depth|verify|subject|issuer"                       │
│ → Check if intermediate cert is missing from the chain           │
│                                                                 │
│ STEP 2: Verify against system trust store:                       │
│ $ openssl s_client -connect jobpost.anihpj.com:443 \             │
│     -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt -servername \    │
│     jobpost.anihpj.com                                          │
│ → If this works but Step 1 fails, the SERVER isn't sending the   │
│   full chain (leaf + intermediate). Fix: concatenate.            │
│                                                                 │
│ STEP 3: Check the Secret contents in K8s:                        │
│ $ kubectl get secret jobpost-tls -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' │
│     | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer          │
│ → Verify tls.crt contains the full chain, not just the leaf      │
│                                                                 │
│ STEP 4: Check if cert-manager issued full chain:                 │
│ $ kubectl describe certificate jobpost-tls                      │
│ → Look for "Full Chain" in events or status                      │
│                                                                 │
│ STEP 5: Verify intermediate is in the same Secret:               │
│ $ openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile fullchain.pem | \           │
│     openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -noout                           │
│ → Should show 2+ certs: leaf + intermediate(+ root)              │
│                                                                 │
│ ROOT CAUSE (90% of cases):                                       │
│ The TLS Secret only contains the leaf cert, not the              │
│ intermediate. cert-manager Certificate resource's secretName     │
│ stores tls.crt as FULL CHAIN by default. If manually created,    │
│ you likely only put the leaf cert.                               │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🎯 Practice Drills — TLS Mastery

Drill 1Speed Run: Certificate Issuance

From scratch (no existing cert-manager): install cert-manager, create ClusterIssuer, create Certificate, configure Ingress — all under 10 minutes. Time yourself. The goal is muscle memory for future incidents.

Drill 2Broken TLS Scenarios

Have a partner break TLS in 5 different ways (expired cert, missing intermediate, wrong SAN, expired CA, mismatched key pair). Diagnose and fix each within 3 minutes using ONLY openssl commands. No browser or GUI.

Drill 3mTLS Configuration

Set up mTLS between two services WITHOUT a service mesh. Create internal CA, generate client/server certs, configure both services, verify with curl. Then do it AGAIN with Istio and compare the effort difference.

Drill 4Alerting Validation

Create a cert with 25-day validity. Deploy it. Verify Prometheus scrapes the metric. Verify the CertificateExpiringSoon alert fires within 5 minutes. Fix it. Verify the alert resolves. Repeat for 6-day validity (critical alert).

Drill 5Let's Encrypt Rate Limit Recovery

Simulate hitting LE's rate limit (create/delete Certificate 5+ times). Document the exact error message, the wait period, and the workaround (staging cluster issuer). Write the runbook for other engineers.

Drill 6Zero-Downtime Rotation Under Load

Generate 1000 req/sec load. Perform all 4 rotation strategies. Measure: did ANY request fail? What was the switch-over time? Which strategy was fastest? Document your findings.
